The Mongol conquests begin (ev.mongol-conquests); China's losses to them and to the Yuan collapse carry Asia's share down toward 1400.
China's own losses in the Yuan collapse bring Asia's share down after 1353.
Revised from 60.8 with the Americas' share, which no longer falls before smallpox reaches the mainland, so the five shares still sum to 100.
Rises only because the Americas' share falls, mid-epidemic in central Mexico.
Revised from 61.3 with the Americas' share, so the five shares still sum to 100. Rises only because the Americas' share falls.

Interpolated. Britain's first war in Burma and the Java War (some 200,000 Javanese dead) open the colonial century in South-east Asia. Asia's share eases because Europe's and the Americas' people grow faster, not because Asia's fall.

Interpolated. The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 kill perhaps 5 to 10 million in India and 9 to 13 million in north China on the usual estimates; Asia's share falls fastest in these decades, as Europe's and the Americas' people multiply while Asia's are cut back. The straight line spreads a loss that was concentrated in 1876 to 1879.
Asia's lowest share in two thousand years.

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor and its conquest of South-east Asia (ev.sea.japanese-occupation, ev.oc.pacific-war): Asia's share holds near 55% through the war. China's war dead and the famines of Henan (1942 to 1943), Bengal (1943), Java and northern Vietnam (1944 to 1945) are set against Europe's heavier losses for its size and Southern and Western Asia's growth; the share moves by hundredths, not points.

The fall of Saigon and the Khmer Rouge's victory. Their killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people, 1.5 to 2 million by 1979, takes about a twentieth of a point from Asia's share; Asia's births keep the share rising.
Vietnam takes Phnom Penh and ends the Khmer Rouge's rule, and China's war on Vietnam follows. Asia's share keeps rising: its deaths have fallen faster than its births.
The Indian Ocean tsunami kills about 230,000, a few thousandths of a point of humanity; Asia's share stands near its peak as births fall across East and South-east Asia.
India overtakes China as the most populous country (ev.as.india-most-populous); Asia's share keeps easing as Africa's grows.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley may hold a brief Homo sapiens presence about 54,000 years ago, among Neanderthals; debated, and with no lasting population.
The Aurignacians of the Danube and the Swabian Jura, with the first figurines and flutes, and Chauvet's paintings about 36,000 years ago.
South-west France, the Franco-Cantabrian refuge, holds Western Europe's people at the glacial maximum; the north and the Alps are empty.
The Linear Pottery farmers spread from the Danube across the loess of Germany and northern France, about 5500 to 5000 BCE.
Celtic Gaul before Caesar's conquest, perhaps six to eight million.
Late Roman Gaul and the Rhineland, after the third-century crisis and before the Rhine frontier breaks at the end of 406.
The high-medieval clearing of forests in France and Germany: Western Europe becomes Europe's largest part.
France perhaps 17 to 20 million, the most populous kingdom in Christendom, before the great famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death (ev.black-death).
Interpolated: France's wars of religion (from 1562) and the Dutch revolt (from 1568) kill hundreds of thousands, yet Western Europe's numbers keep pace with the world's.

Interpolated: the Thirty Years' War begins (1618). Most of Germany's losses to war, plague and hunger, perhaps a third of its people, fall in the 1630s; the value is kept on the line between its neighbours so Europe's parts still sum to Europe, and the band holds a later fall.
The Thirty Years War (1618 to 1648) costs Germany perhaps a third of its people, in some regions more than half, to war, plague and hunger.
The French Revolution begins. France's births have begun to fall, and its wars from 1792 to 1815 kill about a million and a half French soldiers on most estimates, so Western Europe's share eases.
France's births begin to fall a century before the rest of Europe's, and Western Europe's share eases from here.

Interpolated: industry spreads from Britain to Belgium, northern France and the Rhineland, and the first factory laws pass; Western Europe's share holds while France's births stay low and Germany's rise.
The Western Front: France and Germany each lose more than a million and a half soldiers.
Some twelve million Germans expelled from the east arrive in the occupied zones, 1945 to 1950.
Immigration, the refugees of 2015 and of Ukraine since 2022 among them, keeps Germany's and France's numbers rising while their births stay low.

Sahul before people on the later arrival, about 50,000 years ago; luminescence dates at Madjedebe of about 65,000 years would put people here already. The two accounts are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Zero here takes the later arrival in Sahul (about 50,000 years); Madjedebe's 65,000 would make it positive.

Interpolated: Sahul's first people reach New Guinea's highlands (the Ivane valley) and Arnhem Land's ground-edge axes by about 49,000 years ago. When they first arrived is debated, about 65,000 years ago on Madjedebe's dates or about 50,000 on others; this series takes the later date, and the band carries both.
Sahul's first people spread across the continent and New Guinea (ev.oc.sahul-arrival, ev.oc.lake-mungo).
Interpolated: people reach Tasmania across the Bass Strait land bridge and the Bismarcks and Solomons by sea, and bury their dead at Lake Mungo; Sahul's share rises as its people fill the continent.
Sahul's people keep growing as they settle its margins and highlands after the megafauna are gone (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction).

Interpolated: Australia's mid-Holocene changes (new tools, Pama-Nyungan's spread, eel traps at Budj Bim) and New Guinea's gardens add people, but farmers elsewhere multiply faster, so Oceania's share keeps falling.

Interpolated: Lapita voyagers reach the Bismarcks and then Remote Oceania, and voyagers from Island South-east Asia settle Palau and the Marianas; new islands add people, but too few to turn the share.

The value stands but is debated: the usual pre-contact estimates (Aboriginal Australians from about 300,000 to over a million, Maori about 100,000, Melanesia one to two million, Polynesia and Micronesia some hundreds of thousands) sum to about 2 to 3.5 million, 0.4 to 0.7% of the world's people in 1500 and 0.25 to 0.35% in 1788, against this series' 0.2%, about 0.9 to 2 million (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The band now carries both; moving the value needs Asia's and Europe's shares rebalanced with it.

The First Fleet lands at Sydney (ev.oc.first-fleet); smallpox and the frontier wars begin to cut Aboriginal numbers while settlers are still few. The usual pre-contact estimates would put Oceania at 0.25 to 0.35% here; the band carries them.
Before gold is found: about 2.5 million people in Oceania, some 0.47 million of them settlers in Australia and New Zealand and about 2 million islanders and first peoples.
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) nearly double Australia's settlers in four years.
Corrected from 0.2, which left the gold rushes out: settlers reach about 1.1 million against roughly 2 million first peoples and islanders.
Corrected from 0.2: Otago's rush (1861) adds New Zealand's settlers to Australia's.
Corrected from 0.2: about 1.6 million settlers.
Corrected from 0.22: about 1.9 million settlers, while the first peoples keep falling (ev.oc.depopulation).

upsert.lens: To follow where that energy is drawn from, which one total hides: the living harvest of recent years that bounded every economy until about 1800 (Sunbound#c94c), the flows of water, wind and sunlight that machines harness, and the stores laid down over geological time whose use carried the rise from about 20 to 80 GJ a person; so that the energy transitions, from wood to coal, from coal to oil and gas, and the first turn toward wind and sun, each have a home. Range: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, read as world amounts per living person a year in the parent's accounting: primary energy with traditional biomass counted (Smil's and the IEA's world series, as recalled), nuclear as the heat its reactors make and hydro, wind and solar electricity at its energy content, plus the food energy people eat. The feed of working animals and the wind in sails are not counted.

Energy per person is followed as one number though it is made of sources whose histories run apart: the wood and dung that every economy burned until the nineteenth century, the coal, oil and gas that carry the whole modern rise, and the flows of water, wind and sun. This carve opens h.warmth by where its energy is drawn from.

changes.value: Opens the three parts of the carve carve.concept.humanity.wants.sustenance.warmth at every date of the parent, so that with food (h.food read in GJ: kcal a day times 0.001527) they sum to energy for warmth, light and work (h.warmth). Recalled, from Smil's and Fernandes and colleagues' world biomass and fossil series, the IEA's and the Energy Institute's statistics and Kander, Malanima and Warde for the mills, all as recalled and unchecked (EvidenceDependence#23ca). The burned harvest is the parent minus food, stores and flows, so it carries the parent's errors; the stores were set from the recalled fuel totals and kept within their band where the parent's sum forced them. The parent is lowered at the end of the Second World War, where the parts show a dip it had smoothed over.

points.note: Zero: no machine harnesses water, wind or sun before the watermill.
The first watermills, in the Greek east about the third century BCE, then Han China's water-powered trip hammers and bellows.
Roman mills spread (Barbegal's sixteen wheels, about 100 CE).
The medieval mill economy: Domesday Book counts about 6,000 mills in England (1086); mills grind, full and saw across Europe and Song China.
The post windmill spreads in Europe from the late twelfth century.
Dutch windmills drain the polders and saw timber for the Golden Age's ships.
Water power's height as a mill power: New England's and Lancashire's mill towns before steam took over.
Mills decline as steam replaces them; hydroelectricity begins in the 1880s and holds the total.
Hydroelectricity's first large plants (Niagara, 1895).

Hydroelectricity about 1,750 TWh.

Copper smelting and the first towns. The parent's note here names draught animals, whose feed this part does not count: the feed of working animals is a frontier part of the carve, outside the parent's accounting.
Iron smelting spreads; charcoal for iron becomes one of the largest fuel uses of the iron ages.
Roman and Han cities, baths, kilns and smelters: about 12 GJ a person, about 0.8 tonnes of wood, near the most a land-bound economy reaches before 1500 (Sunbound#c94c).
The medieval clearing of Europe's and China's forests: fuel per person near its pre-industrial height before the Black Death.
Flat per person: wood shortages in England, the Low Countries and north China push households toward coal and peat.
The burned harvest per person peaks between 1840 and 1870 at about 18 GJ, with North America's wood-burning frontier, Russia's forests and the world's cooking fires.
From here the burned harvest per person falls: coal replaces wood in the industrial world while the world's total of burned biomass stays near 23 EJ and population grows.
The stores pass the burned harvest between 1900 and 1905 by these values (12.4 against 14.1 GJ a person in 1900); the date is usually given as about 1900, within a decade either way.
About 10 GJ a person as kerosene, coal and electricity replace wood in cities; the world's total of burned biomass still grows, about 25 EJ.
About 7 GJ a person: traditional biomass for about two billion people's cooking, with modern bioenergy; its world total, about 60 EJ, is the largest ever.

England's sea coal (about 2 to 3 million tonnes a year) and the Dutch peat that fuelled the Golden Age.

About 15 million tonnes of coal, most of it British.
Steam's coal: Britain, Belgium, the German lands and the United States.

COVID-19's lockdowns cut oil use by about a tenth for the year.
About 64 GJ a person: oil, coal and gas in roughly equal thirds, nuclear heat about a twentieth.

upsert.lens: To follow where the water that sets the sea's level is held, which one level hides: the northern continental ice sheets that grew and vanished with each glacial cycle and made the land bridges of Beringia, Sundaland, Sahul and Doggerland; Antarctica's and Greenland's ice, which shrank further than today's in the Last Interglacial and are shrinking now; the mountain glaciers; the ocean's own warmth; and the water held on land in lakes, aquifers and reservoirs. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, as contributions in metres to global mean sea level against 2000, in the categories of the sea-level budgets (barystatic and thermosteric), summing to h.sea. Local movements of the land (isostasy, tectonics), which change relative sea level at one coast but not the global mean, are outside the range.

upsert.label: kept whole
provenance: why: No carve of the Christian share pays now. Its branches are kinds born at dated schisms, best read as a Cut over Christians by branch once the religious shares are re-filed under affiliation; its regional division is a cross-classification whose home is each region's religious composition; practice is followed for all people elsewhere. Reading the share for this check showed a value question to settle before any opening: 6% of all people at 500 CE and 12% at 1000 look low. If the Roman world was about half Christian by 400 (Stark's growth model, debated), Christians at 500 would be about 15 to 25% of humanity, and at 1000, with Europe, Byzantium, the Copts, Ethiopia, Armenia and the Church of the East, about 18 to 22%. Raising them needs the sibling shares (above all local and folk traditions) lowered together, so it is left for the pass that re-files the religious shares. Reopen then, or when a regional history opens its religious composition.

Opens the four parts of carve.concept.humanity.means.politics.capacity.revenue at every date of the parent, so that they sum to state revenue as a share of world output (h.revenue). Each is the parent times a recalled share of revenue by base: for pre-modern states from the fiscal histories (Monson and Scheidel's Fiscal Regimes, von Glahn and Hartwell for China, Bonney and Yun-Casalilla and O'Brien for Europe, Habib for Mughal India), for the twentieth century from the IMF's and OECD's revenue statistics, all as recalled and unchecked (EvidenceDependence#23ca); the world shares before 1900 are sketches built from those cases, weighted by the states' shares of world output.

points.note: Zero: no states.
Tolls on goods moving through the first states: a twentieth of their revenue.
Han China's salt and iron monopolies, from 117 BCE, and Rome's harbour and frontier duties.
After the An Lushan rebellion the Tang raise about half their cash revenue from the salt monopoly.
Song China's commercial taxes and monopolies of salt, tea and wine pass its land tax: the first state to live mostly on goods.
Below the Song's height after the Mongol conquest of China.

England's excise state after 1688: by 1750 customs and excise are about three quarters of British revenue (Brewer's fiscal-military state). War between the European powers rewarded the states that could raise more (Warsift#b01b).
Customs and excise carry the nineteenth-century states (the United States lived on its tariff until 1913); the Qing add the lijin transit tax from 1853.
The Soviet turnover tax, levied on goods, pays most of a state that takes about a third of its economy's output.
Value-added tax spreads across Europe after 1967 from France's of 1954, and later to most of the world.
About three tenths of revenue, more in poorer countries, which lean on VAT and customs.
Zero until Britain's income tax of 1799: earlier levies on movables and tithes on produce are counted with land and goods.
Pitt's income tax, 1799, to pay for the war with revolutionary France.
Britain repeals its income tax in 1816: back to about zero.
Peel brings Britain's income tax back in 1842.
The Union's income tax of 1862, for the Civil War.
The American wartime income tax lapses (1872).
Prussia's income tax of 1891 and Bismarck's social insurance from 1883; Japan's income tax of 1887.
The United States' federal income tax, 1913.
Wartime income and excess-profits taxes in every belligerent: revenue from incomes rises more than fourfold in four years (Warsift#b01b: the war rewards the states that can raise more).
Falls back with peace but stays three times its 1913 level.
Income tax withheld from wages (the United States from 1943) turns it into a mass tax.
Incomes pay about half of all revenue at the war's height.

Peacetime: payroll contributions to the welfare states keep it rising for half a century, a rise that war competition does not explain (Warsift#b01b fits the wars, not this; its failure mode 'one path for all').
Income, profit and payroll taxes and social contributions: more than half of world revenue, about three fifths in rich states.
Zero: no states.
The first states (Uruk) take grain, cloth and labour from cultivators: about seven tenths of their revenue; the temple and royal estates' own produce is counted with what the state owns.
Land and poll taxes pay about seven tenths of Rome's and Han China's revenue.
Song China raises more from salt, wine, tea and commerce than from land; elsewhere the land tax still pays most.
The Mughal land revenue, the Ming single-whip land tax and the Ottoman tithe: most of the world's revenue is still levied on the harvest.
Fixed land taxes shrink in value with wartime inflation while income taxes rise.
Land and property taxes are about an eighth of revenue, and a twentieth by 1980.
Zero: no states.
Temple and royal estates are about a quarter of the first states' revenue.
Assyrian tribute from conquered kingdoms.
Achaemenid tribute; Athens' silver from Laurion.
Rome's provincial tribute and plunder after its conquests.
Mongol tribute from subject peoples.
The Spanish crown's fifth of American silver, and the Aztec and Inca tribute systems taken over by Spain.
Crown lands are sold off and American silver fades with Spain's empire.
State railways (Prussia) and colonial monopolies (the Dutch Indies' cultivation system) count here.
Soviet state enterprises' profits paid to the budget.
Oil revenues of the OPEC states after the price rise of 1973.
The second oil shock: resource revenues at their height.
Oil prices fall, and collapse in 1986.
The commodity boom raises oil and mineral revenues.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.

points.note: Shell beads and finished tools passed between bands.
Textiles and metalwork from the first cities' workshops.
Chinese silk, Roman glass and fine pottery, Indian cloth.
Song porcelain and silk carried by sea to South-east Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Indian cotton cloth floods European and West African markets (the calico craze).
British machine-made cotton goods replace Indian cloth in world markets.
Lend-lease arms and machines are much of wartime trade.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now, as Europe's and Japan's industries trade with one another.
East Asia's export manufacturing and the trade in parts between factories.
Global value chains: a phone's parts cross many borders before it is sold.
Goods hold up in the pandemic (medical supplies, electronics for home working) while travel stops.
Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Zero: nothing is sold between bands apart from goods.
Shipping and caravan services begin to be paid apart from the goods they carry: a sliver.
Italian merchant banks and the carrying trade of Venice and Genoa sell finance and freight.
Dutch shipping carries much of Europe's trade: the Republic sells freight and insurance.
Steamship freight, marine insurance and London's finance: about a twelfth of trade.
Travel, shipping and finance resume after the war: about an eighth of trade.
Travel stops in the pandemic: services fall about a fifth while goods hold.
About a quarter of trade: travel recovered, business and digital services growing fastest.
Zero among foragers, whom the account counts as holding no one in bondage.
Captives held to work among the first farmers and settled foragers, as bondage begins (h.freedom).
Corvée and temple dependants in the first states.
Egypt's corvée and the Akkadian and Ur III labour gangs.
Rome's slaves (perhaps a third of Roman Italy) and Han China's corvée: about a ninth of the world's working hours.
Serfs' labour dues in Europe, slaves in the Islamic world, corvée across Asia.
After the Black Death labour dues fade in western Europe.
The second serfdom east of the Elbe and the encomienda and mita in Spanish America.
Atlantic slavery near its height beside Russian serfdom.
Britain abolishes slavery in its colonies from 1834.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs, 1861.
American slavery ends, 1865.
Brazil abolishes slavery in 1888, the last in the Americas; colonial forced labour (the Congo Free State) goes on.
War labour: prisoners of war and deported workers.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Gulag.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
The Gulag is emptied after Stalin's death (1953).
About 28 million people in forced labour by the ILO's count, under 1% of the world's working hours.
Zero: no wage work among foragers.
Hired labour in the first cities of Mesopotamia.
Hired workers' wages are fixed in Hammurabi's laws (about 1750 BCE).
Day labourers in Rome's and Han China's cities, hired hands at harvest.
After the Black Death labour is scarce and wage work grows in western Europe as labour dues fade.
The industrial revolution's wage workers in Britain, Europe's rural day labourers and India's and China's hired hands: about an eighth of all hours.
War industry draws workers into factories.
Employees about a third of the world's working hours.
Wage and salaried work passes half of the world's working hours (the ILO counts employees at about half of all workers from about 2010).
All work is for one's own band and household.
The first states begin to take a share of people's hours for others: from here household hours per worker stop rising although total hours still do.
The industrious revolution lengthens the household's own working year too: more days spent spinning, weaving and growing for sale.
Household hours per worker peak about 1850 to 1865, as freed serfs and slaves work their own plots and peasants work longer for the market.
From here household hours per worker fall, as wage work grows and working days shorten.
Collectivization takes the Soviet peasants' household farms; their hours are counted with compelled and contract work from here.
Wage and salaried work passes work for one's own household in the world's working hours about now.
Farmers, traders and the self-employed of Africa and South Asia still work most of these hours.

points.note: Nearly half of foragers' child deaths come after weaning, at about two to four: hunger, infections and accidents.
In agrarian populations the crowd diseases of childhood (later measles and smallpox) kill most at these ages.
The plague's returns in the decades after the Black Death kill children above all.
Smallpox vaccination (Jenner, 1796) begins to cut deaths at these ages where it spreads.
The wartime famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam kill weaned children most.
Measles vaccine (1963) and the smallpox eradication campaign (1967 to 1977) cut deaths at these ages fastest of the three.
Malaria in sub-Saharan Africa keeps deaths at one to four high as other ages fall.
Insecticide-treated nets and new vaccines (pneumococcal, rotavirus) halve these deaths in fifteen years.
About 9 per 1,000 births, a quarter of deaths before five, from about two fifths for most of history.
About a quarter of foragers' child deaths: infections of the breastfed infant.
Farming raises infancy's deaths: cereal gruels as weaning food, crowding and dirty water.
The urban penalty: infants in the industrial cities die of diarrhoea and dirty water faster than in the countryside.
Clean water, sewers and safer milk begin to cut infancy's deaths in Europe and North America.
Oral rehydration salts, adopted widely from the late 1970s, cut infants' deaths from diarrhoea.
About 10 per 1,000 births.
About a quarter of foragers' deaths before five come in the first month: birth, prematurity and the infections of the newborn.
The first month falls least of the three: its deaths yield to skilled birth care, not to clean water or vaccines.
About 37 per 1,000 births, two fifths of all deaths before five (UN Inter-agency Group, as recalled).
About 17 per 1,000 births, nearly half of all deaths before five: prematurity, birth asphyxia and newborn infections.
Almost every woman who lives through her childbearing years has a first child; about 8% have none.
War and the flu postpone marriages and first births.
Postponed marriages and first births make the start of the baby boom.
Childlessness and postponement rise in East Asia and Europe.

First births fall below 0.9 per woman: in South Korea, China and southern Europe many women now have none (DemographicTransition#6e31's failure mode 'end assumed': births need not settle at replacement).
About two thirds of all births are third and later children, held below the biological maximum by long breastfeeding and birth spacing of three to four years.
Farming shortens birth intervals with earlier weaning onto cereal foods: more later births per woman.
The peak of later births per woman, before family limitation begins anywhere but in France.
Family limitation spreads from France across Europe and North America: couples stop after two or three.
War and the flu cut births of every order.
The last peak: later births per woman, high across Asia, Africa and Latin America and in the rich world's baby boom.
The transition: later births fall by a fifth in five years as East Asia and Latin America stop at two or three, a generation after children's deaths began to fall (DemographicTransition#6e31).
Under two thirds of a later birth per woman, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa: about nine tenths of the fall from five children per woman in 1965 to 2.2 now came here.
China's one-child policy (1979 to 1980) begins to cut second births, the first time they fall at world scale.
About 0.7 second births per woman: one-child families common in East Asia and southern and eastern Europe.

points.note: Most foragers reckon descent through both parents and live in flexible bands; some (Aboriginal Australians, many Amazonian and North American peoples) have clans and moieties: about three in ten, guessed from ethnographic foragers.
Farming makes land and herds property worth holding in common by descent: lineages and clans spread with farmers.
About three in five people live under clans or lineages: China's, India's, the Middle East's tribes, Africa's lineages, the Celtic and Germanic kindreds.

Western Christendom's kin groups dissolve under the Church's bans on cousin marriage and its rules on inheritance (Goody), from about 600 to 1500; the debated root of Europe's individualism and of its guilds, communes and universities (Henrich; Greif; critics stress institutions and the state instead).
South China's lineages, with their halls, estates and genealogies, are at their strongest from the Song to the Qing, while western Europe's kin groups are nearly gone.
Europe's and North America's fast-growing populations, with nuclear families, lower the world's share slowly.
Soviet collectivization and settlement break the clans of Central Asia's herders.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) takes the lineages' estates and ends their courts; collectivization and, from 1966, the attacks on ancestral halls finish them as corporate groups for a generation.
Held near a third: south China's lineages revive after 1980 and Africa's growing share of humanity lives mostly in lineage societies, against cities and schooling everywhere.
About a quarter to a third: much of sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East's and Central and South Asia's tribes and castes, and rural south China.
Foragers count, but nobody reckons ages in years without a calendar of years, so this measure reads about zero.
Writing, calendars and temple accounts in Mesopotamia and Egypt: ages begin to be reckoned by scribes and officials.
Qin and Han household registers record each person's age: China's numeracy runs ahead of the rest of the world's and of its own literacy.
Roman tombstones round ages to multiples of five: perhaps a third to a half of commemorated Romans knew their age; Han China's registers count more.
Lower with the end of Roman administration in the west and the Chinese registers' collapse in the age of division.
The numeracy revolution of north-western Europe (Baten): age heaping falls there from about 1500, with trade, Protestant schooling and parish registers; Qing China and Japan are as numerate or more.
Numeracy far ahead of literacy (12%): most people reckon and know their age without reading.
Mass schooling spreads numeracy with literacy in Europe, the Americas and Japan; South Asia and Africa lag.
Almost every adult knows their age: the age-heaping measure saturates, and numeracy's differences now lie in skills it cannot read (PISA's and PIAAC's tests).

Writing begins in Sumer and Egypt; the first scribal schools are too few to read above zero at this resolution.
The scribal schools of Sumer and Egypt: their first years of sign lists and copying are counted here, the advanced years as secondary; the boundary is this account's reading.
Protestant and Catholic reformers both push reading schools: Luther's call for schools, the Jesuit and parish schools, with Ming and Edo village schools.
The growth is almost all elementary: Prussia's and Scotland's parish schools, New England's common schools, Japan's temple schools (terakoya).
Compulsory elementary schooling spreads: Britain's Education Act (1870), France's Ferry laws (1881 to 1882), Meiji Japan's school law (1872).
Primary's share of all years is at its highest, nine in ten.
From here Barro and Lee's attainment by level (as recalled): primary is still about four in five years of school.
Slowing toward six years, where everyone completes primary; most of the growth is now above it.
The advanced years of scribal training (literary texts, mathematics, law) counted as a middle stage: about a tenth of all years.
Greek grammar and rhetoric schools spread with the Hellenistic cities.
Madrasas spread from the eleventh century and Song China's state schools prepare candidates for the examinations.
Humanist grammar schools and Jesuit colleges in Europe; Ming county and prefectural schools.
Its share of all years falls while mass primary schooling grows faster: lycées and gymnasia stay for the few.

Turns up: the American high-school movement (Goldin and Katz), from about one in ten American teenagers in high school in 1910 to most by 1940; Europe's secondary schools stay narrow until after 1945.
After 1945 secondary schooling spreads in Europe, Japan and the Soviet Union, then in the new states: the secondary turn carries most of the world's growth in years from here.
Secondary years pass a third of all years of school.
Still growing fastest in South Asia and Africa, where lower secondary is becoming universal.

Begins: Plato's Academy (about 387 BCE), Aristotle's Lyceum, the Museum of Alexandria, Taxila's teachers; the Han Imperial Academy (Taixue) follows in 124 BCE. Which ancient schools count as higher learning is a matter of definition.
The Later Han's Imperial Academy is said to have held some 30,000 students in the mid second century.
Nalanda in India (from the fifth century) and the Sui and Tang state academies.
The universities of Bologna, Paris and Oxford, the Nizamiyya madrasas of higher law and the Song academies.
The American GI Bill (1944) sends returning soldiers to college: the first step from elite to mass higher education.
Higher education turns from elite to mass (Trow's terms) in North America, Europe, Japan and the Soviet bloc from about 1960.
China expands its universities from 1999, from under a tenth of young people enrolled to over half by 2020; India and Latin America grow fast too.
About a tenth of all years of school; women now outnumber men in higher education in most countries.

Opens the three ways of moving in the carve of settling down at every date of h.habitat.mobile; they sum to it. Mobile foragers are taken as the parent before farming and about nine in ten of all foragers (h.foraging) after it, lower from 1500 as settled foragers' share of the remaining foragers grows; peripatetic trades are sketched from the size of South Asia's carrier and service castes and Europe's Roma and Travellers; herders are the rest. All sketched and unchecked (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b, EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: All people forage and move camp with the seasons.
The Natufians and the Jomon settle: the first foragers counted as settled.
Falls as farming villages grow far denser than foragers; about nine in ten of the remaining foragers still move.
Herders are now about two in five of the mobile, a little more than the parent's note (a third) says, because this split counts some foragers as settled.
Epidemics and conquest in the Americas take the land and lives of many mobile foragers; the share of remaining foragers who move falls below nine in ten.
Settlers take foragers' lands in North America, Australia, Siberia and southern Africa.
Small bands still move camp to forage for part or all of the year: in the Kalahari, the Congo basin, among the Hadza, in Amazonia and the Andaman Islands, and the sea nomads of South-east Asia.
No domestic animals, so no herders.
Begins: goat and sheep herders of the Zagros and Taurus may already move between seasonal pastures; whether any households were fully mobile this early is debated.
Cattle herders range across the green Sahara, the largest mobile herding population of the age.
Rises: the Yamnaya move with ox-wagons and herds across the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and their descendants spread east and west; the Sahara's herders move south as it dries.
The camel is domesticated in Arabia, opening the deserts to herders.
Mounted nomadism on the steppe: herders ride, range far and raid settled states.
The Xiongnu unite the eastern steppe and press Han China.
Huns and Avars in the west, the Rouran and Turks in the east; camel-herding Berbers cross the Sahara.
The Mongols unite the steppe: perhaps one or two million herders build the largest land empire.
Up a little: the Black Death kills more of the settled, crowded peoples than of the herders.
Herders pass mobile foragers as the larger part of the mobile between 1600 and 1650.
The Qing destroy the Dzungars (1755 to 1758) and Russia advances on the Kazakh steppe: states begin to settle and tax the herders.
Russian peasants settle the Kazakh steppe and France conquers the Sahara's herders; rinderpest kills most of East Africa's cattle in the 1890s.
Falls faster: Soviet collectivization forces the Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Turkmen nomads to settle (1928 to 1934); the famine that follows kills perhaps a third of the Kazakhs.
Mongolia's herders are collectivized, Tibet's herds taken into communes, and new states in the Middle East and Africa push herders to settle.
The Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s drive many herders into towns and camps; Africa's fast-growing herding peoples keep the share from falling faster.
Perhaps 10 to 60 million people: estimates differ because many households now move only part of the family with the herds.
No settled markets to serve.
Begins with the first cities and states: smiths, traders and entertainers who move among settled people; how many lived without a fixed home is unknown.
The Roma, who left India centuries before, reach the Balkans by about 1300; Banjara carriers supply the Delhi Sultanate's armies.

Most of this share is South Asia's carrier and service nomads: Banjara caravans of tens of thousands of bullocks, nomadic smiths, traders and entertainers; Europe's Roma and Travellers and the Middle East's Dom are fewer.
Turns down: railways take the Banjara carrying trade, and India's Criminal Tribes Act (1871) brands many nomadic castes as criminal and forces them to settle.
Nazi Germany and its allies murder perhaps 200,000 to 500,000 Roma and Sinti (the Porajmos), many of them travelling families; the estimate is debated.
Most of India's nomadic castes, the Roma and the Travellers are now settled; some still travel for part of the year.

Opens the two parts of the carve of the wild animals at every date of h.earth.wild-animals: the biomass of wild sea mammals and of wild fish of fishable size, beside the parent's land mammals. Sketched from the biomass census literature and the histories of whaling and fishing, as recalled: Bar-On, Phillips and Milo (2018), Greenspoon and colleagues (2023), Christensen and colleagues (2014), Bianchi and colleagues (2021), Pauly and Zeller's catch reconstructions, Hilborn and colleagues' stock assessments. None checked (EvidenceDependence#23ca); the pre-exploitation levels are model readings with wide bands (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

points.note: About half a billion tonnes of carbon by models of the unfished ocean (Bianchi and colleagues 2021, Jennings and Collingridge 2015, as recalled); how glacial seas changed it is unknown, so it is held level until fishing.
Rome's fisheries and fish-sauce works, China's and the Mediterranean's coastal fishing: large locally, too small to move the world's fish.
Europe's herring and cod fisheries grow (the Hanseatic herring of the Baltic); river fish decline with mills and dams.
European fleets fish the cod of the Newfoundland banks.
Turns down: steam trawlers work the North Sea from 1881 and soon find fewer fish per hour of trawling, the first industrial depletion.
The war keeps trawlers in port and North Sea stocks recover a little.
The second war again halts much fishing, and the North Sea's stocks recover.
World catches about 20 million tonnes of wet weight a year; from here sonar, synthetic nets, diesel trawlers and factory freezers carry fishing to every ocean.
Peru's anchoveta fishery, the world's largest, lands some 12 million tonnes and collapses in 1972 with El Niño and overfishing.
The Newfoundland cod collapse follows (1992): a moratorium ends a fishery of five centuries.
World catches peak: about 86 million tonnes as reported, about 130 by Pauly and Zeller's reconstruction with unreported catch; both fall slowly after.

Debated: stock assessments (Hilborn and colleagues, the RAM Legacy database) find assessed stocks in North America, Europe and Oceania stable or rebuilding since about 2000; catch reconstructions and whole-ocean models (Pauly and Zeller; Christensen and colleagues 2014; Bianchi and colleagues 2021) find fish of fishable size about halved since 1900, predatory fish down by about two thirds. The band carries both readings.

Before whaling: perhaps four to five times today's mass, most of it in the great baleen and sperm whales; read back from population models of the whales before exploitation, which disagree widely. How glacial seas changed it is unknown; held level.
Coastal peoples hunt seals and stranded or small whales from the Arctic to Korea (the Bangudae petroglyphs); a local taking, too small to move the world's mass.
Basque whalers hunt right whales in the Bay of Biscay; the Thule Inuit hunt bowheads across the Arctic. Still local.
Basque whalers at Red Bay in Labrador take thousands of bowhead and right whales: the first whaling across an ocean.
Turns down: Dutch and English fleets hunt the bowheads of Spitsbergen from 1611 for oil and baleen.
American sperm whaling grows from Nantucket after 1712.
Sealers kill millions of fur seals on the southern islands, from Juan Fernández to South Georgia, for skins sold in Canton, and elephant seals for oil.
The American whaling fleet at its height, some 700 ships about 1846; bowheads of the Bering Sea hunted from 1848, gray whales in their Baja lagoons in the 1850s.
Petroleum from 1859 begins to replace whale oil for lamps, but whaling does not end.
Svend Foyn's harpoon cannon and steam catchers (1868) open the fast rorquals, the blue and fin whales, to hunting.
Antarctic whaling begins from South Georgia (1904).
Falls fastest: factory ships with stern slipways (from 1925) process whales at sea; the 1930/31 season takes some 37,000 whales, most of them blue whales.
The war halts most whaling from 1940 to 1945, a short respite.
Fin whales now the main catch; the Soviet fleets secretly take some 180,000 whales beyond what they report (1948 to 1973).
Lowest: blue whales a few per cent of their former numbers, fin and sei whales a small fraction.
The International Whaling Commission's moratorium on commercial whaling, adopted in 1982, takes effect in 1986.

Recovering: humpback, gray, southern right whales and fur seals have come back in many seas, blue whales much less. Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) put wild marine mammals near 40 Mt of wet mass, about 6 Mt C; Bar-On and colleagues (2018) about 4 Mt C. As recalled, to be checked.

Opens the two parts of the carve of marriage at every date of h.marriage: plural unions and how marriages end. Both are population-weighted sketches: regional shares (sub-Saharan Africa's polygyny, the low divorce of China, India and Christian Europe against the high divorce of foragers, Java, the Malay world and Tokugawa Japan) times each region's share of humanity, from Murdock's atlas, Marlowe's forager sample, the Demographic and Health Surveys, Pew's household survey and national divorce statistics as recalled. Unchecked (EvidenceDependence#23ca); concubinage counted as plural, which is a choice (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

points.note: Foragers marry and part easily: among the Hadza and the !Kung a third or more of first marriages end in separation (Blurton Jones and colleagues; Howell, as recalled), with little property to divide.
Falls slowly as farmers outnumber foragers: land, herds and bridewealth bind marriages and kin enforce them.
Rome's elite divorce and remarry freely; most Romans, and most Chinese and Indians, do not.
The Church moves toward indissoluble marriage in the west (made a sacrament, divorce barred by the twelfth century); Islamic law lets husbands divorce easily, and many Muslim societies divorce often.
Down with the collapse of the Americas' peoples, many of whom parted easily.
Lowest: China, India and Christian Europe, most of humanity, almost never divorce; Tokugawa Japan's villages, Java and the Malay world, and many African and Muslim societies divorce often.
Western countries begin to allow civil divorce (England 1857, France 1884); Meiji Japan's code of 1898 lowers its high divorce.
Soviet Russia makes divorce a matter of registration (1917 to 1936), the easiest in the world; wartime marriages end after the war.
Jumps: wartime marriages end in a wave of divorces in the United States and Europe in 1946 and 1947.
China's Marriage Law (1950) lets women divorce: a wave of divorces follows to 1953. Java and Malaya divorce at among the world's highest rates, about half of marriages.
Divorce falls in Java and the Malay world, where marriage becomes later and chosen, while it has not yet risen in the West.
The divorce revolution: California's no-fault law (1969) and its followers across the West; women's earnings and the pill make leaving possible.
About two in five first marriages end in divorce in the United States, northern Europe and the Soviet Union; under one in fifty in India.
China's divorce rate climbs after the 2003 rules make divorce a matter of registration.

Turns level: China's divorces fall after the 2021 cooling-off period, and Western divorce has fallen since about 1990 as people marry later and fewer marry. World divorce is measured unevenly, and periods and cohorts give different shares; the band carries both.

Most foraging societies allow a man more than one wife, but few manage it: a few to a fifth of married women, more where older men control marriages, as among many Aboriginal Australians (Marlowe's forager sample, as recalled).
Rises with farming: where wealth is in land, herds and the labour of wives and children, more men take more wives; polygyny is commonest among hoe farmers and herders in the ethnographic record.
Turns down as states grow: in Egypt and Mesopotamia most men have one wife, kings and the rich add secondary wives and concubines.
Greek cities and Rome allow one wife only; whether socially imposed monogamy spread because it eased competition among men (Henrich, Boyd and Richerson) or for other reasons is debated.
Han China: one principal wife, with concubines for the rich (counted here as plural unions, which is debated, since concubines were not wives in law); India permits more wives but few take them.
Islam permits up to four wives; few men can afford more than one, a few in a hundred marriages in most Muslim societies, and conversion does not lower Africa's polygyny.
Most of it now in sub-Saharan Africa, where a third or more of married women share a husband; China's, India's and the Muslim world's elites add a little.
The United States forces the Mormon church to give up plural marriage (1890).
Turkey bans polygamy (1926).
China's Marriage Law (1950) bans concubinage; India's Hindu Marriage Act (1955) makes Hindu marriage monogamous.

Level since 1900: Africa's growing share of humanity balances the fall of polygyny within Africa, where the share of married women in polygynous unions falls from about two in five in West Africa toward a quarter or a third.

Pew (2020) finds about 2% of the world's people living in polygamous households, most in West and Central Africa (over a third of people in Burkina Faso, Mali and Nigeria's north, as recalled); as a share of married women it is a little higher.

changes.value: Check the parts against the whole. These 22 wholes are, by their parts' own definitions, the sum of their parts in the same unit, divided along one criterion into exclusive and exhaustive parts (MECE#ae19): child mortality by age; births per woman by order; carbon dioxide as the carbon cycle's own level plus the human addition; trade by what is traded; farmland as cropland plus pasture; food by source; forest by climate domain; the mobile by how they move; output per person by sector; state revenue by base; schooling by stage; sea level by where the water is held; hours worked by who directs them; war deaths by kind; violent deaths as homicide plus war; and each M49 area's or intermediate region's share of humanity as the sum of its subregions. Each process is restated unchanged except for scale.aggregate = sum, which lets the values report compare the parts with the whole at every date and name where they disagree. Two earlier attempts through life_values_record (r230, r231) re-recorded each whole's 2025 value but did not store the declaration, since that tool sets aggregate only when it opens a process; their values are unchanged. Energy for warmth is left out: it includes the food people eat, which none of its parts holds.

Fill: the values report names 1950 to 1960 as the coarsest stretch of the Earth's measures, which held only their 1950 and 1960 values while other processes carry fifteen dates inside it. The decade is the start of the great acceleration, so each gets a value at 1955, guessed between its neighbours and the Events of the decade, with parts kept equal to their wholes (carbon dioxide = the carbon cycle's own level + the human addition; forest = its four domains). All recalled, sharing one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: No farming, no fuel beyond campfires and landscape burning, whose carbon the cycle takes back: no human addition that lasts.
Begins: Ruddiman dates the start of a human addition to forest clearing about 6000 BCE; most carbon-cycle modellers find too little cleared carbon to matter before 1000 BCE or later.
Dips: forest returns on fields abandoned after the Black Death.

Falls: the Americas' abandoned fields regrow forest after the Great Dying and draw carbon down, Lewis and Maslin's 1610 'Orbis spike'; how much of the dip is human and how much the Little Ice Age's colder ocean is confounded.
On the eve of industry: a few ppm by most accounts, about 35 by Ruddiman's; the midpoint is taken.
Rises: clearing in North America and Russia and Britain's coal.
The 1940s plateau: depression and war slow emissions, and the ocean takes up more.
Accelerates: oil and coal after 1950, the 'great acceleration'.
China's coal boom makes the 2000s the fastest decade of growth.
About 160 ppm of the air's 427 is people's: two thirds of the cumulative emissions from fossil fuel, a third from clearing land, about 45% of them still airborne.
Before farming all of the air's carbon dioxide is the carbon cycle's own: it swings between about 180 ppm at glacial maxima and 280 in interglacials, as the Antarctic ice cores show.
The MIS 8 glacial: cold oceans and an expanded sea ice hold carbon, and the air's carbon dioxide is low.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: the ocean releases carbon and the level rises near interglacial values.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) sets in: the ocean takes carbon back.
Termination II under way: the ocean releases carbon as the ice melts.
Termination II: the warming Southern Ocean releases carbon as the Last Interglacial begins.
The Last Interglacial has ended; the ocean draws carbon down as the ice returns.
The last deglaciation: carbon dioxide rises from about 190 to 265 ppm in two steps, with the Southern Ocean venting deep carbon.

From here the Holocene's rise from about 260 to 280 ppm is read as mostly natural (ocean carbonate compensation, peat and reef growth) with a small human share: a midpoint between most carbon-cycle modellers, who find it natural, and Ruddiman, who reads it as human and has the natural level falling toward 245 ppm. The band holds both.
The Little Ice Age's colder oceans take up carbon too, so part of the 1610 dip may be natural; the attribution is confounded.
Held at its late-Holocene level from here: the natural level is a counterfactual nobody observes, taken as constant while the human addition grows.
The MIS 8 glacial: carbon dioxide low, as Antarctic ice cores are recalled to show.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: carbon dioxide rises near interglacial levels, then falls into the penultimate glacial.
Antarctic ice cores, as recalled.
Termination II (ev.termination-ii): the warming ocean releases carbon as the Last Interglacial begins; it falls again as the glacial returns.
Toba erupts (ev.toba). Carbon dioxide is sliding toward the MIS 4 glacial, as Antarctic ice cores are recalled to show; whether Toba moved the climate for more than a few years is debated.
The Americas' abandoned fields have not yet regrown enough to draw down carbon; the dip to about 272 ppm by 1610 comes later.
Revised from 278 so the descent into the 1610 minimum begins before it.

The Law Dome minimum. Lewis and Maslin (2015) attribute it to forest regrowing on the Americas' abandoned fields; colder oceans in the Little Ice Age also take up CO2, so the attribution is confounded (ConfoundedAttribution#18ab).
The 1600s dip in CO2 in the Law Dome core.
The 1940s plateau in the ice cores, while war and depression slow emissions.
Law Dome ice cores as recalled, three years before Keeling's Mauna Loa record begins in 1958; the rise resumes after the 1940s plateau.
Mauna Loa's record, as recalled.
Mauna Loa's record, as recalled.
Stone for tools and ochre for colour: a few kilograms per person a year.
Natufian and early Neolithic stone houses, mortars and querns.
Villages of mud brick and lime plaster, as at Çatalhöyük and Jericho; lime is burned from stone. Earth for building is the first large draw on the stores.
Cities of mud brick, copper and then bronze smelted from ores.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant.
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the mines of Spain: lead in Greenland's ice reaches a peak in the first century CE not matched again until the Middle Ages (as recalled from the ice-core studies).
Western Roman building and mining collapse; the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China burns coal for iron, and Europe builds in stone.
Potosí's silver and Britain's first coal boom, small against the stone and earth of building.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
Krausmann and colleagues: about 7 Gt of materials taken in 1900, about a quarter of it coal, ores and building minerals; the rest is harvested biomass, not counted here.
Mines and cities wrecked in Europe and Asia: extraction per person dips in the last year of the war.
Reconstruction and the long boom: steel, cement and oil per person grow about 4% a year from 1950.
The great acceleration: oil, cement and steel for reconstruction and for growth, faster than people.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries build less and use energy better.
China's building boom: it poured more cement in 2011 to 2013 than the United States in the whole twentieth century, and coal and iron ore follow.
The UNEP International Resource Panel counts about 100 Gt taken in 2020, three quarters of it non-metallic minerals, fossil fuels and metal ores.

upsert.reason: From 1900 Krausmann and colleagues' material flows (about 7 Gt of materials in 1900, a quarter of it minerals and fuels) and the UNEP International Resource Panel's (about 100 Gt in 2020, three quarters minerals and fuels), as recalled; before 1900 sketched from building, mining and toolmaking.

points.note: About half a billion tonnes of carbon by models of the unfished ocean (Bianchi and colleagues 2021, Jennings and Collingridge 2015, as recalled); how glacial seas changed it is unknown, so it is held level until fishing.
Rome's fisheries and fish-sauce works, China's and the Mediterranean's coastal fishing: large locally, too small to move the world's fish.
Europe's herring and cod fisheries grow (the Hanseatic herring of the Baltic); river fish decline with mills and dams.
European fleets fish the cod of the Newfoundland banks.
Turns down: steam trawlers work the North Sea from 1881 and soon find fewer fish per hour of trawling, the first industrial depletion.
The war keeps trawlers in port and North Sea stocks recover a little.
The second war again halts much fishing, and the North Sea's stocks recover.
World catches about 20 million tonnes of wet weight a year; from here sonar, synthetic nets, diesel trawlers and factory freezers carry fishing to every ocean.
World catch rises from about 20 to 30 million tonnes of wet weight between 1950 and 1955, mostly from stocks not yet fished down.
Peru's anchoveta fishery, the world's largest, lands some 12 million tonnes and collapses in 1972 with El Niño and overfishing.
The Newfoundland cod collapse follows (1992): a moratorium ends a fishery of five centuries.
World catches peak: about 86 million tonnes as reported, about 130 by Pauly and Zeller's reconstruction with unreported catch; both fall slowly after.

Debated: stock assessments (Hilborn and colleagues, the RAM Legacy database) find assessed stocks in North America, Europe and Oceania stable or rebuilding since about 2000; catch reconstructions and whole-ocean models (Pauly and Zeller; Christensen and colleagues 2014; Bianchi and colleagues 2021) find fish of fishable size about halved since 1900, predatory fish down by about two thirds. The band carries both readings.

Before whaling: perhaps four to five times today's mass, most of it in the great baleen and sperm whales; read back from population models of the whales before exploitation, which disagree widely. How glacial seas changed it is unknown; held level.
Coastal peoples hunt seals and stranded or small whales from the Arctic to Korea (the Bangudae petroglyphs); a local taking, too small to move the world's mass.
Basque whalers hunt right whales in the Bay of Biscay; the Thule Inuit hunt bowheads across the Arctic. Still local.
Basque whalers at Red Bay in Labrador take thousands of bowhead and right whales: the first whaling across an ocean.
Turns down: Dutch and English fleets hunt the bowheads of Spitsbergen from 1611 for oil and baleen.
American sperm whaling grows from Nantucket after 1712.
Sealers kill millions of fur seals on the southern islands, from Juan Fernández to South Georgia, for skins sold in Canton, and elephant seals for oil.
The American whaling fleet at its height, some 700 ships about 1846; bowheads of the Bering Sea hunted from 1848, gray whales in their Baja lagoons in the 1850s.
Petroleum from 1859 begins to replace whale oil for lamps, but whaling does not end.
Svend Foyn's harpoon cannon and steam catchers (1868) open the fast rorquals, the blue and fin whales, to hunting.
Antarctic whaling begins from South Georgia (1904).
Falls fastest: factory ships with stern slipways (from 1925) process whales at sea; the 1930/31 season takes some 37,000 whales, most of them blue whales.
The war halts most whaling from 1940 to 1945, a short respite.
The Antarctic quota of 16,000 blue-whale units a season (from 1946) is filled every year with fin and humpback whales as blue whales grow scarce.
Fin whales now the main catch; the Soviet fleets secretly take some 180,000 whales beyond what they report (1948 to 1973).
Lowest: blue whales a few per cent of their former numbers, fin and sei whales a small fraction.
The International Whaling Commission's moratorium on commercial whaling, adopted in 1982, takes effect in 1986.

Recovering: humpback, gray, southern right whales and fur seals have come back in many seas, blue whales much less. Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) put wild marine mammals near 40 Mt of wet mass, about 6 Mt C; Bar-On and colleagues (2018) about 4 Mt C. As recalled, to be checked.
The Pleistocene's large mammals on every continent: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, diprotodons and the herds of the savannas and steppes, perhaps 20 to 25 Mt C.

Sahul's megafauna (diprotodons, giant kangaroos, Genyornis) vanish soon after people arrive, about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago; whether hunting, fire or drying climate decided it is debated (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction). A small part of the world's wild mass.
The glacial maximum: the mammoth steppe from France to the Yukon holds great herds of grazers even as forests shrink.

After the end-Pleistocene extinctions: the Americas lose about three quarters of their large mammal genera between 13,000 and 11,000 years ago, and northern Eurasia its mammoths, woolly rhinos and giant deer, as people spread and the climate swings at the glacial's end. Hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.
From here fields and pastures slowly take land from wild herds; the loss is gradual for six thousand years.
Most of it now in the bison of North America (perhaps 30 to 60 million), the savanna herds of Africa and the wild ungulates of Asia's steppes and forests.
The slaughter of the bison for hides begins with the railways across the plains.
The bison are down to under a thousand (1889), and rinderpest, brought to the Horn of Africa in 1887, kills up to nine in ten of East Africa's buffalo and wildebeest within a decade.
Tropical forest cleared for fields and pasture, and bushmeat hunting, take wild mammals down by about a third in half a century while livestock doubles.

Bar-On and colleagues (2018): wild land mammals about 0.003 Gt C, against 0.06 for humans and 0.1 for livestock; Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) about 20 Mt of wet mass, the same order. As recalled, to be checked.

upsert.reason: Pleistocene level from the reconstructions of megafaunal biomass (Barnosky 2008; Bar-On and colleagues 2018 put it near 0.02 Gt C), the present from Bar-On and colleagues and Greenspoon and colleagues (2023), as recalled; the path between is sketched from the dated extinctions and the nineteenth-century slaughters.

points.note: MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c, a warm substage of the penultimate interglacial complex.
Penultimate glacial (MIS 6).
Deepest MIS 6.
Last Interglacial peak, warmer than pre-industrial.
MIS 5d.
MIS 5b.
Entering MIS 4.
Toba erupts (ev.toba). A volcanic winter of a few years is argued by some and doubted by others; the slide into the MIS 4 cold stage is orbital, not volcanic.
End of the MIS 4 cold stage.
MIS 3, near Heinrich event 4.
Last Glacial Maximum.
Deglaciation under way, before the Bølling warming.
About 14,000 years ago, the Bølling–Allerød warm interval of the deglaciation.
Start of the Younger Dryas: a pause in global warming, a deep cold in the north Atlantic.
Revised from -1.5: about 12,000 years ago, inside the Younger Dryas; global reconstructions of the deglaciation (Shakun and others, as recalled) reach Holocene levels only about 10,000 years ago.
The Holocene begins.
Early Holocene, near the 8.2 ka cold event.
The 4.2 ka event: drought more than global cooling.
Medieval warmth, regional more than global.
Entering the Little Ice Age.
Maunder Minimum, the coldest part of the Little Ice Age.
The Maunder minimum, deep in the Little Ice Age (ev.little-ice-age).
Just before Tambora: the 1810s are already cool after an unidentified eruption of 1809.
Tambora's sulphate (ev.sea.tambora) cools the Earth by about a quarter to half a degree for a year: 1816 is the year without a summer.
The sulphate washes out within two or three years and the temperature recovers toward the cool decade's level.
After Tambora (1815) and the cold 1810s.
Just before Krakatoa, on the line from 1870 to 1890.
Krakatoa's haze (ev.sea.krakatoa) cools the world by about two tenths of a degree in 1884.
Recovering after Krakatoa; the 1880s stay cool.
The cool mid-1950s: a long La Niña from 1954 to 1956 and rising sulphate aerosols hold the mean slightly below 1950s average.
Aerosols and the Agung eruption of 1963 hold temperature flat (ev.aerosols).
Just before Pinatubo, on the line from 1990 to 1996.
Pinatubo's sulphate spreads through the stratosphere from June 1991; the cooling deepens into 1992.

Corrected from 0.42: Pinatubo's sulphate (ev.sea.pinatubo) cools the world by about 0.2 to 0.3 degrees in 1992's annual mean and up to half a degree at the monthly peak, as climate models predicted beforehand; the instrumental record runs about two tenths below the line from 1990 to 1996 in 1992 despite an El Nino. Check: the annual global means of 1990 to 1994.
The aerosol clears and warming resumes.
The boreal forest moves most with the glacial cycles: it shrinks to refugia south of the ice at glacial maxima and reaches beyond today's treeline in the warmest interglacials.
The MIS 8 glacial: ice covers much of the boreal range and the forest shrinks south of it.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: the boreal forest spreads north again.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) begins: the forest retreats before the ice.
The deepest MIS 6: the boreal forest at a glacial low, in refugia south of the ice.
Termination II under way: the ice melts and the forest follows it north.
The Last Interglacial: boreal forest reaches farther north than now.
The Last Interglacial has ended; the cold of MIS 5d pushes the treeline south.
MIS 5c, a warm substage: the forest spreads again.
MIS 5b, a cold substage: the forest retreats.
Glacial maximum: ice sheets cover most of the boreal forest's range in North America and Scandinavia, and steppe-tundra most of Siberia's; conifers survive south of the ice.
Rises most: the boreal forest follows the melting ice north.
The boreal forest follows the melting ice north: nearly all of the rise from the end of the Younger Dryas to the early Holocene's widest reach comes before here (the note at 7900 BCE).
The ice sheets are nearly gone and the early Holocene's summers are warmer than now: the boreal forest reaches its widest, beyond today's northern treeline.
The Neoglacial cooling pushes the northern treeline south from its mid-Holocene reach.
Logging and fire begin to cut into Scandinavia's, Russia's and Canada's boreal forests; most of it still stands.
About 27% of all forest in FAO's 2020 assessment as recalled; larger fires since 2000 in Siberia and Canada.
Termination II under way.
Turns down: farmers and herders clear the Mediterranean hills, the Ganges plain and southern China; goats and ploughs keep much of it open.
Southern China's rice frontier spreads under the Song.
Qing China's hill frontier: maize and sweet potato carry farmers up the forested hills of the south.
About 11% of all forest in FAO's 2020 assessment as recalled.
The MIS 8 glacial: temperate trees retreat to southern refugia.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: temperate forest spreads north.
Termination II under way: temperate trees spread out of their refugia.
The Last Interglacial: temperate forest reaches its widest, with hippos in the Thames.
The Last Interglacial has ended; MIS 5d's cold thins the temperate forest.
MIS 5c, a warm substage: temperate forest spreads again.
Glacial maximum: temperate trees survive in southern refugia, in Iberia, Italy, the Balkans, the Caucasus, southern China and the south-eastern United States.
Turns down for four thousand years: farmers clear Europe's and northern China's temperate forests.
Forest returns on abandoned land in the post-Roman West while clearing goes on in China; the world share holds.
The high-medieval clearances leave Europe's lowlands largely open.
Turns up briefly: forest returns on fields abandoned after the Black Death.
Europe's wood shortage and the colonists' clearing of eastern North America begin.
Falls fastest in the nineteenth century: the clearing of the American Midwest's and Ontario's forests and of Russia's mixed forest.
Regrowth on abandoned farms in New England and planting in Europe begin about now, but clearing in China and the Soviet Union outweighs them for decades.
The world's temperate forest bottoms out about 1950 to 1976: regrowth in Europe and North America is offset by clearing in China and the Soviet Union until China's planting after 1978.
Turns up: the forest transition reaches China, whose planting from 1978 adds tens of millions of hectares, and continues in Europe and North America.
About 16% of all forest in FAO's 2020 assessment as recalled.
Split from the parent's forest share: in glacial times by how far each domain moves with the ice, tropical forest least; from about 4000 BCE by where people cleared.
The MIS 8 glacial: drier tropics shrink the rainforest a little.
MIS 7c, a warm and wet substage: the rainforest spreads.
Termination II under way: the tropics grow wetter.
The Last Interglacial: tropical forest at its widest, wetter than now in Africa's monsoon belt.

Glacial maximum: drier tropics shrink the rainforest, while the exposed Sunda shelf adds lowland forest. Whether Amazonia broke into refugia (Haffer) or stayed mostly forested (Colinvaux) is debated; the band holds both.

Turns up: fields and gardens of the Americas return to forest as most of their people die (the Great Dying); Koch and others put the regrowth at about 56 million hectares by 1600, and whether it drew down enough carbon to help cool the Little Ice Age is debated.
Turns down: plantations, railways and settlers begin clearing tropical forest in India, Java, Brazil's Atlantic forest and West Africa.
Falls fastest from here: roads, chainsaws, cattle, soy, oil palm and settlement programmes open Amazonia, Indonesia, the Congo basin and West Africa.
About 45% of all forest, about 1.8 billion hectares, in FAO's Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 as recalled.
The MIS 8 glacial: forest retreats before MIS 7's warm stages.
MIS 7c, a warm substage of the penultimate interglacial complex: forest spreads, then retreats into the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) begins: forest retreats.
The deepest MIS 6: forest at its glacial low.
Termination II (ev.termination-ii): forest spreads with the Last Interglacial's warmth, then retreats as ice returns.
The Last Interglacial ends about 116,000 years ago (ev.eu.eemian); forest retreats in the cold of MIS 5d.
MIS 5c, a warm substage: forest spreads again before MIS 5b's cold. Band narrowed from 18 to 72, an artefact of an earlier interpolation.
MIS 5b, a cold substage: forest retreats.
Revised from 45: inside the Younger Dryas (ev.younger-dryas) forest is no larger than at the Holocene's start; the 45 sat above both neighbours with no cause.
Holocene optimum; the Sahara green.
Regrowth on abandoned fields after the plague.

value: inferred: each part's meaning states that it sums to its parent in the parent's quantity

changes.value: Check the parts against the whole, second step. The values report compares a whole declared as a sum only with parts whose unit string is the same as its own, and listed 19 parts as not compared although they measure the same quantity in the same unit, worded differently when the deeper-tree pass opened them. Their unit strings are aligned with their parents' wording; meanings, values, bounds and parents are unchanged: trade by kind ('% of world output' to the parent's 'trade as % of world output'), state revenue by base ('% of world output' to 'state revenue as % of output'), the mobile by how they move ('% of people' to '% of people without a fixed dwelling'), sea level by where the water is held ('m of sea level against 2000' to 'm against 2000') and toil by who directs the hours ('hours per worker a year' to 'hours worked per worker a year'). Left uncompared on purpose: child mortality's age bands ('% of live births' against the parent's '% dying before age 5', where the parent's wording would misdescribe a band), cropland and pasture (the parent's '% of ice-free land as crops or pasture'), and safety's homicide and war, both measures this pass keeps as they are; their sums were checked by reading the values.
