scale.label: Colonial rule
scale.semantic_role: Colonial rule: The share of all living people who live in colonies, protectorates, mandates and other dependencies ruled from a metropole overseas, without equal political membership in it: the overseas empires of Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, Britain, France, Denmark, Belgium, Germany, Italy, the United States and Japan, from Ceuta (1415) to the territories still dependent now. Counted: company rule, protectorates and princely states, League mandates, puppet states such as Manchukuo, and settler colonies until they govern themselves. Not counted: contiguous land empires (Russia's Siberia and Central Asia, Qing Xinjiang and Tibet, the Ottomans), wartime occupation (Japan in China, 1937 to 1945), and ancient and medieval rule over provinces across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome before 212, Venice and Genoa); each boundary is debated and kept as an alternative reading. Zero before 1415 by definition. A kind of scale of rule, not a part of it.

support: initial value copied from the value recorded at 1 (inferred), the date nearest time 0

changes.value: Opens colonial rule, the series the politics carve (carve.concept.humanity.means.politics) recorded as worth its own series: the colonial form of rule over other peoples, a kind of scale of rule, so it is filed under the largest polity's process as a kind (semantic_subtype), not as a part. The breadth check's politics group (279 Events), and the regional groups of the Americas, Asia, Africa and Oceania, hold dozens of conquest, colony and independence Events that no process follows. Values are the people in each empire's dependencies, as recalled from the usual population estimates (Maddison's and the colonial censuses), over world population; the definitional boundaries are stated in the meaning and the debates in the notes (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). None checked (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

upsert.boundary: Potatoes, quinoa, llamas and alpacas domesticated in the Andes, about 6000 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Highland farmers domesticate the potato and quinoa and herd llamas and alpacas, the only large domestic animals of the Americas; coastal peoples grow cotton and squash and fish the rich Pacific upwelling.
provenance: sources to check: Pearsall, in Handbook of South American Archaeology (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Aztec Triple Alliance, 1428 to 1521
upsert.description: Mexica migrants found Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco (1325); in 1428 they ally with Texcoco and Tlacopan and build a tribute empire over central Mexico. Tenochtitlan, with perhaps 200,000 people, is larger than any city in Spain when Cortés arrives.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed. 2012); Townsend, Fifth Sun (2019)

upsert.boundary: The fall of Tenochtitlan, 1519 to 1521
upsert.description: Cortés lands with about 500 men, wins Tlaxcala and other enemies of the Mexica as allies with tens of thousands of warriors, and after smallpox kills Cuitláhuac and much of the city, takes Tenochtitlan by siege in August 1521.
provenance: sources to check: Restall, When Montezuma Met Cortés (2018); Townsend, Fifth Sun (2019)

upsert.boundary: Brazil abolishes slavery, May 1888
upsert.description: The Golden Law frees the last enslaved people in the Americas, about 700,000; the empire falls to a republic the next year.
provenance: sources to check: Conrad, The Destruction of Brazilian Slavery 1850–1888 (1972)

upsert.boundary: Brazil's gold rush, 1695 to 1760
upsert.description: Gold and then diamonds in Minas Gerais draw hundreds of thousands of Portuguese and many more enslaved Africans inland; Rio de Janeiro becomes the colony's capital (1763), and Brazilian gold flows through Lisbon to Britain.
provenance: sources to check: Boxer, The Golden Age of Brazil (1962)

upsert.boundary: Sugar and slavery in Brazil, about 1530 to 1650
upsert.description: Portuguese planters in Pernambuco and Bahia grow sugar on mills worked first by enslaved Native people, then by Africans; by 1600 Brazil is the world's largest sugar producer and the main destination of the Atlantic slave trade.
provenance: sources to check: Schwartz, Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society (1985)

upsert.boundary: The sugar revolution in the Caribbean, about 1640 to 1800
upsert.description: Barbados, then Jamaica, Saint-Domingue and the other islands turn to sugar on large plantations worked by enslaved Africans, who die faster than they are born and are replaced by new captives; by the 1780s Saint-Domingue produces about a third of the world's sugar and is the richest colony on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Dunn, Sugar and Slaves (1972); Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985)

upsert.boundary: Civil wars in Central America, 1979 to 1996
upsert.description: The Sandinista revolution in Nicaragua (1979) and the American-backed Contra war, El Salvador's civil war, and Guatemala's war, in which the army's campaigns against Maya villages are judged genocide; about 300,000 die in all.
provenance: sources to check: Commission for Historical Clarification, Guatemala: Memory of Silence (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Nicaragua, El Salvador, Guatemala)

upsert.boundary: The Chimú kingdom, about 900 to 1470
upsert.description: From its adobe capital Chan Chan, the largest city of the pre-Columbian Andes, Chimú rules the north coast of Peru with vast irrigation canals, until the Inca conquer it.
provenance: sources to check: Moseley and Cordy-Collins (eds.), The Northern Dynasties (1990)

upsert.boundary: The civil rights movement, 1954 to 1968
upsert.description: From Brown v. Board of Education (1954) and the Montgomery bus boycott (1955) to the Civil Rights Act (1964) and the Voting Rights Act (1965), Black Americans and their allies end legal segregation and disenfranchisement in the South; Martin Luther King Jr. is murdered in 1968.
provenance: sources to check: Branch, Parting the Waters (1988)

upsert.boundary: The Classic Maya, about 250 to 900
upsert.description: Dozens of city-states, Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque, Copán and Caracol among them, ruled by divine kings who record their wars and dynasties in a full writing system and track time with the Long Count calendar; the lowlands hold perhaps several million people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; lidar surveys since 2018 suggest larger populations
sources to check: Martin and Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2nd ed. 2008); Canuto et al. 2018, Science 361
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Guatemala, Mexico, Belize, Honduras)

upsert.boundary: Clovis hunters, about 13,050 to 12,750 years ago
upsert.description: Fluted stone spear points made in the same way appear across North America within a few centuries, often with mammoth and mastodon kills; the Anzick child's genome links Clovis people to most later Native Americans.
provenance: sources to check: Waters and Stafford 2007, Science 315; Rasmussen et al. 2014, Nature 506
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America, Central America

upsert.boundary: Columbus reaches the Caribbean, October 1492
upsert.description: Sailing west for Castile to reach Asia, Columbus lands in the Bahamas, then Cuba and Hispaniola, and returns with captives and a little gold; his second voyage (1493) brings settlers, horses, pigs and sugarcane. The hemispheres are joined.
provenance: sources to check: Phillips and Phillips, The Worlds of Christopher Columbus (1992)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean; Europe (Southern Europe: Castile)

upsert.boundary: The Latin American debt crisis, 1982 to 1990
upsert.description: Mexico's default (August 1982) sets off a crisis across the region: with American interest rates high, governments cut spending, inflation soars and income per person falls through the 'lost decade'; the crisis ends with the Brady bonds and a turn to open markets.
provenance: sources to check: Bulmer-Thomas, The Economic History of Latin America since Independence (3rd ed. 2014)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America

upsert.boundary: Military dictatorships in Latin America, 1964 to 1990
upsert.description: Coups in Brazil (1964), Chile and Uruguay (1973) and Argentina (1976) bring juntas that torture and disappear tens of thousands, often with American support, under the doctrine of national security; most fall in the 1980s, Chile's last, in 1990.
provenance: sources to check: Grandin, The Last Colonial Massacre (2004)
corrected 2026-10-15: Uruguay's coup was on 27 June 1973, the same year as Chile's, not 1976 with Argentina's; check: any chronology of Uruguay's civic-military dictatorship (1973 to 1985)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America, Central America

upsert.boundary: Cocaine, the drug trade and the war on drugs, from 1971
upsert.description: Nixon declares a war on drugs (1971); as American demand for cocaine grows, coca from Peru, Bolivia and Colombia is refined in Colombia and smuggled through the Caribbean and, from the 1990s, Mexico; the Medellín and Cali cartels and then Mexico's cartels grow rich and armed. Eradication, extradition and Plan Colombia (2000) shift the trade rather than end it, and fentanyl joins it after 2013. The trade fuels the region's wars and its homicide rates.
provenance: sources to check: Gootenberg, Andean Cocaine (2008); UNODC, World Drug Report
upsert.region: The Americas: South America, Central America, the Caribbean and Northern America

upsert.boundary: English colonies on North America's Atlantic coast, 1607 to 1733
upsert.description: From Jamestown (1607), where tobacco and, from 1619, enslaved Africans take root, and Plymouth (1620) and Massachusetts Bay (1630), to Georgia (1733): thirteen colonies of farmers, planters and merchants, with elected assemblies, grow by migration and high fertility to about 2.5 million people by 1775, pushing Native nations west.
provenance: sources to check: Taylor, American Colonies (2001)

upsert.boundary: The California gold rush, 1848 to 1855
upsert.description: About 300,000 people pour into California from across the world; the Native Californian population, already halved under Spanish missions, falls from perhaps 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killing, disease and starvation.
provenance: sources to check: Madley, An American Genocide (2016)

upsert.boundary: The Haitian Revolution, 1791 to 1804
upsert.description: The enslaved of Saint-Domingue rise in August 1791; under Toussaint Louverture and then Dessalines they defeat French, Spanish and British armies, end slavery, and declare Haiti independent on 1 January 1804: the only slave revolt to found a state.
provenance: sources to check: Dubois, Avengers of the New World (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Inca empire, about 1438 to 1533
upsert.description: From Cusco, Pachacuti and his successors conquer the Andes from Ecuador to central Chile in under a century, ruling perhaps ten million people with roads of 40,000 kilometres, storehouses, labour taxes and knotted-cord records; a succession war between Atahualpa and Huascar is ending when Pizarro arrives.
provenance: sources to check: D'Altroy, The Incas (2nd ed. 2014)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina)

upsert.boundary: Pizarro takes the Inca empire, 1532 to 1533
upsert.description: Arriving as Atahualpa wins a war of succession against Huascar, after epidemics have killed the previous emperor, Pizarro's 168 men capture Atahualpa at Cajamarca, take a room of gold as ransom, execute him, and enter Cusco; Inca resistance from Vilcabamba lasts until 1572.
provenance: sources to check: Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas (1970)

upsert.boundary: Latin America's wars of independence, 1808 to 1826
upsert.description: After Napoleon seizes Spain (1808), juntas and armies across Spanish America fight for independence: Hidalgo's rising in Mexico (1810), Bolívar in the north and San Martín in the south, until Ayacucho (1824) and the fall of Callao (1826); Brazil separates from Portugal peacefully as an empire (1822). About eighteen new states emerge.
provenance: sources to check: Lynch, The Spanish American Revolutions 1808–1826 (2nd ed. 1986)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America

upsert.boundary: Maize spreads through the Americas, about 4700 BCE to 1200 CE
upsert.description: From its domestication in south-western Mexico, maize travels as seed from farmer to farmer: it reaches South America, still only partly domesticated, by about 4500 BCE, the American Southwest by about 2100 BCE and the eastern woodlands by about 200 CE, changing as it goes into hundreds of local varieties. It becomes a staple slowly, as cobs grow larger: the Maya, the Andes and the Southwest depend on it within a few thousand years, the eastern woodlands only between about 900 and 1200. The crop spread farther than any people did.
provenance: sources to check: Kistler et al. 2018, Science 362; Staller, Tykot and Benz (eds.), Histories of Maize (2006)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern, Central and South America

upsert.boundary: The Classic Maya collapse, about 800 to 950
upsert.description: The southern lowland cities stop raising monuments and empty, one after another, as wars multiply and a series of droughts strikes; the north, at Chichén Itzá, carries on.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weight of drought among the causes is debated
sources to check: Kennett et al. 2012, Science 338; Douglas et al. 2015, PNAS 112

upsert.boundary: The Mexican Revolution, 1910 to 1920
upsert.description: Madero's revolt against Díaz opens a decade of civil war (Villa, Zapata, Carranza, Obregón); perhaps one to two million die or flee, and the 1917 constitution promises land reform and national control of oil and minerals.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is contested
sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution (1986)

upsert.boundary: The Mexican–American War, 1846 to 1848
upsert.description: The United States invades Mexico and takes about half its territory, from Texas to California, in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
provenance: sources to check: Greenberg, A Wicked War (2012)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (United States), Central America (Mexico)

upsert.boundary: Latin American migration to the United States, from 1965
upsert.description: The 1965 immigration act ends national-origin quotas, and the end of the Bracero programme (1964) pushes Mexican labour migration outside the law; Mexicans, then Cubans, Dominicans, Central Americans, Colombians and Venezuelans move north, and the Hispanic share of the United States rises from about 4% (1960) to about 19% (2020), some 62 million people. Remittances become a mainstay of Mexico's and Central America's economies, while enforcement and the politics of the border harden from the 1990s.
provenance: sources to check: Massey, Durand and Malone, Beyond Smoke and Mirrors (2002); Pew Research Center, Hispanic population estimates
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean to Northern America

upsert.boundary: The Moche, about 100 to 800
upsert.description: On Peru's north coast, lords buried with gold, as at Sipán, rule irrigated valleys, build adobe pyramids and make portrait vessels; floods and droughts linked to El Niño weaken them.
provenance: sources to check: Bawden, The Moche (1996)

upsert.boundary: Monte Albán and the Zapotec state, about 500 BCE to 750 CE
upsert.description: Zapotec rulers found a hilltop capital over the valley of Oaxaca, conquer neighbouring valleys and carve some of the earliest Mesoamerican writing.
provenance: sources to check: Marcus and Flannery, Zapotec Civilization (1996)

upsert.boundary: Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago
upsert.description: A camp of wooden huts by a creek, with mastodon meat, seaweed and medicinal plants, preserved under peat: the site that broke the 'Clovis first' account.
provenance: sources to check: Dillehay et al. 2008, Science 320; Dillehay et al. 2015, PLoS ONE 10

upsert.boundary: NAFTA, 1994 to 2020
upsert.description: Canada, the United States and Mexico remove most tariffs between them; trade within North America roughly triples and supply chains cross the borders, until the agreement is renegotiated as the USMCA (2020).
provenance: sources to check: Hufbauer and Schott, NAFTA Revisited (2005)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America, Central America (Mexico)

upsert.boundary: The New Deal, 1933 to 1939
upsert.description: Roosevelt's government answers the Depression with relief, public works, bank regulation, union rights and the Social Security Act (1935); federal spending and the reach of the state grow for good.
provenance: sources to check: Kennedy, Freedom from Fear (1999)

upsert.boundary: New France and the fur trade, 1608 to 1763
upsert.description: Champlain founds Quebec (1608); a thin French colony along the St Lawrence and down the Mississippi lives by trading furs with Native allies, Huron, Algonquin and later many others, and fights the Haudenosaunee and the English, until Britain takes Canada in 1763.
provenance: sources to check: White, The Middle Ground (1991)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Canada, United States)

upsert.boundary: The Panama Canal, 1904 to 1914
upsert.description: After the United States backs Panama's secession from Colombia (1903), it builds the canal across the isthmus, at the cost of about 5,600 workers' lives, cutting the sea route from New York to San Francisco by more than half.
provenance: sources to check: McCullough, The Path Between the Seas (1977)

upsert.boundary: The War of the Triple Alliance, 1864 to 1870
upsert.description: Paraguay fights Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay and is destroyed: it loses perhaps a quarter to over half of its people, most of its men, the deadliest interstate war in Latin American history.
provenance: sources to check: Whigham and Potthast 1999, Latin American Research Review 34
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Paraguay, Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay)

upsert.boundary: The conquest of the Plains and the West, 1862 to 1890
upsert.description: From the Dakota war (1862) to Wounded Knee (1890), the US Army and settlers defeat the Plains and western nations, confine them to reservations, and the bison, perhaps 30 million in 1800, are shot to fewer than a thousand by 1889.
provenance: sources to check: Hämäläinen, Lakota America (2019); Isenberg, The Destruction of the Bison (2000)

upsert.boundary: The silver of Potosí, 1545 to 1650
upsert.description: A mountain of silver found in the Andes in 1545 makes Potosí one of the largest cities of the world by 1600; after 1573 the mita forces Andean villages to send men to its mines, where mercury refining kills many. Its silver pays Spain's wars and, through Manila, buys China's goods.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Lane, Potosí (2019)

upsert.boundary: The Preclassic Maya cities, about 1000 BCE to 150 CE
upsert.description: In the lowlands of Guatemala the Maya build El Mirador's huge pyramids, causeways and the first Maya writing; the San Bartolo murals show their gods and kings; many centres collapse about 150 CE.
provenance: sources to check: Estrada-Belli, The First Maya Civilization (2011)

upsert.boundary: Railways cross North America, 1863 to 1885
upsert.description: The first transcontinental railroad (1869), built largely by Chinese and Irish workers, and the Canadian Pacific (1885) cut the crossing from months to a week, open the plains to farming and ranching and bind the continent's markets.
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (United States, Canada)

upsert.boundary: Reconstruction and its end, 1865 to 1877
upsert.description: The Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments give freed people citizenship and Black men the vote; Black Southerners hold office for a decade, until white terror and the withdrawal of federal troops (1877) restore white rule and Jim Crow.

upsert.boundary: Squash and maize domesticated in Mexico, about 8000 to 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Squash is grown in Oaxaca by about 8000 BCE; teosinte, a wild grass with a few hard seeds, is turned into maize in the Balsas valley from about 7000 BCE, and over thousands of years its cobs grow large enough to feed cities. Beans, chili and cotton follow.
provenance: sources to check: Smith 1997, Science 276 (squash); Piperno et al. 2009, PNAS 106 (maize)

upsert.boundary: The Taíno of the Greater Antilles destroyed, 1493 to 1520
upsert.description: Forced into gold mining and farm labour under the encomienda, hit by war, famine and, from 1518, smallpox, the Taíno of Hispaniola fall from perhaps several hundred thousand to a few thousand within a generation; the Spanish raid the Bahamas and the mainland for slaves to replace them.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Hispaniola's 1492 population is estimated from about 100,000 to several million
sources to check: Reséndez, The Other Slavery (2016); Livi Bacci 2003, Hispanic American Historical Review 83
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica)

upsert.boundary: Teotihuacan, about 100 BCE to 550 CE
upsert.description: A planned city of perhaps 100,000 people grows around the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon in the valley of Mexico, among the largest cities in the world in its time; its influence reaches the Maya, whose Tikal it may have conquered in 378. It is burned and abandoned about 550.
provenance: sources to check: Cowgill, Ancient Teotihuacan (2015)

upsert.boundary: Tiwanaku and Wari, about 500 to 1000
upsert.description: Tiwanaku, by Lake Titicaca, farms raised fields and spreads its religion; Wari, near Ayacucho, builds the first Andean empire with roads, administrative centres and knotted-cord records. Both fall apart by about 1000, perhaps in drought.
provenance: sources to check: Janusek, Ancient Tiwanaku (2008); Schreiber, Wari Imperialism in Middle Horizon Peru (1992)

upsert.boundary: Tula and Chichén Itzá, about 900 to 1200
upsert.description: The Toltec capital Tula dominates central Mexico and later Aztecs remember it as the source of civilization; Chichén Itzá, sharing its style, rules much of the Yucatán.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed. 2012)

upsert.boundary: The rebellion of Túpac Amaru II, 1780 to 1783
upsert.description: A descendant of the Inca leads the largest Indigenous rising of colonial Spanish America in the Andes against forced sales and labour; it is crushed, and perhaps 100,000 die.
provenance: sources to check: Walker, The Tupac Amaru Rebellion (2014)

upsert.boundary: The United States Constitution and Bill of Rights, 1787 to 1791
upsert.description: A written constitution with separated powers, federalism and an amendment process, and the first ten amendments' guarantees of speech, religion and due process; it counts an enslaved person as three fifths and leaves slavery in place.
provenance: sources to check: Klarman, The Framers' Coup (2016)

upsert.boundary: The American Revolution, 1775 to 1783
upsert.description: Thirteen colonies rebel against British taxation and rule, declare independence (July 1776) and, with French help, win at Saratoga and Yorktown; the Treaty of Paris (1783) recognizes the United States.
provenance: sources to check: Wood, The Radicalism of the American Revolution (1992)

value: inferred: each Event's description says what it changes

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's Americas group, batch 1 of 4: 48 Events of the Americas' history that named no process now name the processes they change. States rising and falling move the share of humanity under a state (h.politics); conquests, colonies and independence move colonial rule (h.colonial); wars move war deaths by kind; slavery and abolition move bondage (h.freedom) and compelled work; democracy and dictatorship move voice; the first farmers move foraging; booms, crises and the New Deal move the Americas' output (h.means.americas) or revenue; canals and railways move freight; epidemics and migrations move the subregions' shares of humanity. Only the process_ids change; every other field is restated unchanged. Events of local reach (Cahokia, Chaco, Caral, Chavín, the Haudenosaunee, Hopewell, the Olmec, Nazca, the Norse, Thule, Watson Brake, the Pueblo revolt, the Louisiana Purchase, the Monroe Doctrine, populism, the war of 1898, Venezuela's exodus, the Cuban revolution, Indian Removal, White Sands, the banana republics) are left unlinked: their change is below the resolution of the world's and the M49 areas' measures, as the breadth answer will record.

upsert.boundary: Cárdenas: land reform and the oil expropriation, 1934 to 1940
upsert.description: President Lázaro Cárdenas gives about 18 million hectares to peasant communities as ejidos, more than all his predecessors together, organizes workers and peasants within the ruling party, and nationalizes the foreign oil companies (March 1938) to found Pemex; the party of the Revolution becomes the corporate state that rules Mexico until 2000.
provenance: sources to check: Knight 1994, Journal of Latin American Studies 26; Meyer, Sherman and Deeds, The Course of Mexican History (11th ed. 2018)

upsert.boundary: The Caste War of Yucatán, 1847 to 1901
upsert.description: Maya peasants of eastern Yucatán, squeezed by sugar estates and taxes, rise against the creole elite and nearly take Mérida (1848); driven back, rebels guided by the Speaking Cross hold an independent territory in the eastern forests for half a century, until Mexican troops take their shrine town in 1901. Perhaps a third to a half of the peninsula's people die or flee.
provenance: sources to check: Reed, The Caste War of Yucatán (rev. ed. 2001); Rugeley, Yucatán's Maya Peasantry (1996)

upsert.boundary: The cocoliztli epidemic of 1545 to 1548
upsert.description: A haemorrhagic fever the Nahua called cocoliztli sweeps New Spain, killing perhaps 5 to 15 million on the highest estimates, or far fewer on critics' lower counts of the population before it: the deadliest epidemic of the conquest, worse than the smallpox of 1520. What it was is debated: an Old World disease, such as the Salmonella Paratyphi C found in victims' teeth at Teposcolula-Yucundaa, or a native fever spread by rodents in a great drought, as Acuña-Soto argues. On either account forced labour, hunger and the herding of people into new towns made it deadlier.
provenance: inferred: the epidemic as recalled; its toll and its disease are debated
sources to check: Acuña-Soto et al. 2002, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8; Vågene et al. 2018, Nature Ecology & Evolution 2; Borah and Cook (1963)

upsert.boundary: The cocoliztli epidemic of 1576 to 1580
upsert.description: A second great cocoliztli kills perhaps 2 million, about half of the Indigenous people left in central Mexico; with the earlier epidemics it leaves central Mexico's Indigenous population at a tenth or less of its size in 1519 by about 1600, on the usual figures. Its disease is debated as that of 1545 is.
provenance: inferred: the epidemic as recalled; its toll and its disease are debated
sources to check: Acuña-Soto et al. 2002, Emerging Infectious Diseases 8; Borah and Cook (1963)

upsert.boundary: Mexico's drug war, from December 2006
upsert.description: President Calderón sends the army against the cartels; they splinter and fight each other and the state, and homicides rise from about 8,900 (2007) to over 27,000 (2011) and about 36,000 a year (2018 to 2020), the highest in Mexico's modern record, with more than 100,000 people disappeared. American demand for drugs and American guns carried south feed the war, and the cartels move into extortion, fuel theft and the smuggling of migrants.
provenance: sources to check: INEGI homicide statistics; Grillo, El Narco (2011)

upsert.boundary: The Archaic: Mesoamerica's first farmers, 8000 to 2000 BCE
upsert.description: Foraging bands in the highland valleys begin to grow squash (Guilá Naquitz, Oaxaca, by about 8000 BCE), turn teosinte into maize in the Balsas valley from about 7000 BCE, and add beans, chili, avocado and cotton; for thousands of years these crops supplement foraging, until maize cobs grow large enough, after about 2500 BCE, to support settled villages.
provenance: sources to check: Piperno et al. 2009, PNAS 106; Smith 1997, Science 276

upsert.boundary: The Classic: Teotihuacan and the Maya kingdoms, 250 to 900
upsert.description: Teotihuacan, with perhaps 100,000 people, dominates central Mexico and reaches deep into the Maya world until it is burned about 550; Monte Albán rules Oaxaca; dozens of Maya kingdoms, led by Tikal and Calakmul in rival alliances, record their kings and wars in a full script and the Long Count. From about 800 the southern lowland kingdoms fail one after another amid war and repeated droughts.
provenance: sources to check: Martin and Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2nd ed. 2008); Evans (2013)

upsert.boundary: Wars, open markets and the drug wars, 1979 to 2025
upsert.description: The Sandinista revolution (1979) opens a decade of civil wars in Nicaragua, El Salvador and Guatemala, ended by peace accords from 1990 to 1996. Mexico defaults (1982), opens its economy and joins NAFTA (1994), the year of the Zapatista rising and the peso crisis; the party of the revolution loses the presidency in 2000. From 2006 the army's war on the cartels and the cartels' wars with each other drive homicides to the highest numbers in Mexico's modern history, and millions from Mexico and the northern isthmus migrate north.
provenance: sources to check: Meyer, Sherman and Deeds (2018); INEGI homicide statistics

upsert.boundary: New Spain, 1521 to 1821
upsert.description: The Viceroyalty of New Spain rules from Mexico City, built on the ruins of Tenochtitlan. Epidemics, the cocoliztli above all, cut central Mexico's Indigenous population from perhaps 15 to 25 million to about a million by 1620 on Borah and Cook's widely cited figures, which others think too high; Indigenous towns keep their lands and councils under Spanish rule and the Church. Silver from Zacatecas and Guanajuato makes New Spain Spain's richest colony, the Manila galleons link Acapulco with Asia, and a mixed population grows. The Maya highlands and the isthmus form the Captaincy General of Guatemala.
provenance: sources to check: Gibson, The Aztecs under Spanish Rule (1964); Borah and Cook, The Aboriginal Population of Central Mexico on the Eve of the Spanish Conquest (1963)

upsert.boundary: Paleo-Indian Mexico and the isthmus, about 16,000 to 10,000 years ago
upsert.description: The people who reached Monte Verde in Chile by 14,500 years ago must have passed through, but the earliest securely dated sites here are later: at El Fin del Mundo in Sonora, Clovis hunters kill gomphotheres about 13,400 years ago. Claims of people at Chiquihuite Cave in Zacatecas 26,000 years ago rest on stone flakes whose human making is disputed.
provenance: sources to check: Sanchez et al. 2014, PNAS 111 (El Fin del Mundo); Ardelean et al. 2020, Nature 584 (Chiquihuite)

upsert.boundary: The Postclassic: Toltecs, Mixtecs, Maya city-states and the Aztecs, 900 to 1521
upsert.description: Tula and Chichén Itzá rise as the southern Maya cities empty; Mixtec kingdoms record their dynasties in painted books; the northern Maya are ruled from Mayapán until about 1441, then by small rival states. In the valley of Mexico the Mexica found Tenochtitlan (1325) and with Texcoco and Tlacopan build the Triple Alliance's tribute empire (1428), checked in the west by the Tarascan state. The era ends with the Spanish conquest of Tenochtitlan (1519 to 1521).
provenance: sources to check: Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed. 2012); Evans (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Preclassic: villages, the Olmec and the first states, 2000 BCE to 250 CE
upsert.description: Villages with pottery spread from the Pacific coast of Chiapas, where the earliest known ball court is built about 1650 BCE; the Olmec of the Gulf coast (San Lorenzo, La Venta) carve colossal heads and spread a shared art and religion; writing and the 260-day calendar appear by about 600 BCE; Zapotec Monte Albán and Maya El Mirador become cities and states, and Teotihuacan begins to grow about 100 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Pool, Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica (2007); Evans, Ancient Mexico and Central America (3rd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: Independent Mexico and the isthmus republics, 1821 to 1910
upsert.description: Mexico and Central America leave Spain in 1821, and the Central American federation breaks into five republics by 1841. Mexico's decades of coups, Texas's secession and the war with the United States (1846 to 1848) cost it half its territory; La Reforma separates church and state, and Juárez defeats the French-backed Maximilian (1867). The Maya of Yucatán rise in the Caste War (1847). Díaz's long rule (1876 to 1911) brings railways, foreign capital and order while haciendas take village lands; coffee and then bananas tie the isthmus to foreign markets and firms.
provenance: sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution vol. 1 (1986); Woodward, Central America: A Nation Divided (3rd ed. 1999)

upsert.boundary: Revolution, banana republics and the one-party state, 1910 to 1979
upsert.description: The Mexican Revolution (1910 to 1920) kills or drives out one to two million people and leaves a constitution of land reform and national resources; its party rules from 1929, distributes land under Cárdenas, nationalizes oil (1938) and presides over the growth of 1940 to 1970. On the isthmus, United Fruit and coffee planters back dictators such as Ubico and Somoza; Costa Rica abolishes its army (1948); a CIA-backed coup ends Guatemala's land reform (1954). Mexico's wheat programme begins the Green Revolution.
provenance: sources to check: Knight (1986); Woodward (1999); Meyer, Sherman and Deeds, The Course of Mexican History (11th ed. 2018)

upsert.boundary: Mexico's wheat programme begins the Green Revolution, 1943 to 1963
upsert.description: Mexico's government and the Rockefeller Foundation set up a programme to breed better crops; Norman Borlaug's team crosses wheats for resistance to rust and, from the 1950s, for short, stiff stems that carry heavy grain with fertilizer and water. Mexico's wheat yields roughly triple, and the semi-dwarf wheats sent to India and Pakistan in the 1960s begin the Green Revolution; the programme becomes CIMMYT (1966).
provenance: sources to check: Perkins, Geopolitics and the Green Revolution (1997)

upsert.boundary: The Manila galleons, 1565 to 1815
upsert.description: Once Urdaneta finds the eastward return across the North Pacific (1565), one or two Spanish galleons a year sail between Acapulco and Manila for 250 years, carrying American silver west and Chinese silk and porcelain east: the first regular trade route across the Pacific, which binds the economies of the Americas, Asia and Europe together.
provenance: sources to check: Schurz, The Manila Galleon (1939); Flynn and Giráldez 1995, Journal of World History 6
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Acapulco); Asia: South-eastern Asia (Manila)

upsert.boundary: Street gangs and violence in the northern isthmus, from 1992
upsert.description: Gangs formed among Salvadoran refugees in Los Angeles, MS-13 and Barrio 18, are carried home by deportations after the peace accords; with the drug trade's transit routes they push homicide rates in El Salvador and Honduras above 80 per 100,000 in the 2010s, the highest of any countries at peace, and drive families north. El Salvador's state of exception from 2022 jails over 80,000 people and cuts its homicide rate to among the region's lowest, at the cost of due process.
provenance: sources to check: UNODC, Global Study on Homicide (2019); International Crisis Group reports on El Salvador (2022 to 2024)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala)

upsert.boundary: Mexico's democratic alternation, 2000
upsert.description: After reforms that made the Federal Electoral Institute independent (1996), the opposition wins the lower house (1997), and Vicente Fox of the National Action Party wins the presidency (July 2000), ending 71 years of rule by the party of the Revolution; power passes peacefully on 1 December.
provenance: sources to check: Magaloni, Voting for Autocracy (2006)

upsert.boundary: The Porfiriato, 1876 to 1911
upsert.description: Porfirio Díaz rules Mexico for most of 35 years; railways grow from about 600 to 19,000 kilometres, foreign capital flows into mines and oil, and exports multiply, while laws on vacant land let haciendas and companies take village lands, so that by 1910 most rural families own none. The Revolution begins against his re-election.
provenance: sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution vol. 1 (1986); Katz (ed.), Riot, Rebellion and Revolution (1988)

upsert.boundary: La Reforma and the French intervention, 1855 to 1867
upsert.description: Mexico's liberals end the Church's and the army's special courts, force the sale of the corporate lands of the Church and of villages (the Lerdo law, 1856) and write the constitution of 1857; conservatives fight the War of the Reform (1857 to 1861) and then back the French-installed emperor Maximilian, until Benito Juárez's republic defeats him and has him shot (1867).

upsert.boundary: Droughts of the Terminal Classic, about 800 to 1000
upsert.description: Lake sediments and cave stalagmites in the Yucatán and Belize record a series of multi-year droughts between about 800 and 1000, among the driest spells of the past two thousand years there, with rainfall cut by perhaps a third to a half at their worst. Their timing matches the failure of the southern lowland kingdoms; how much they caused it, beside war and the strain of dense populations on cleared land, is debated.
provenance: inferred: the droughts from lake and cave records as recalled; their weight in the collapse is debated
sources to check: Hodell, Curtis and Brenner 1995, Nature 375; Kennett et al. 2012, Science 338; Evans et al. 2018, Science 361
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (the Maya lowlands)

upsert.boundary: Tlaxcala and the Indigenous allies of the conquest, 1519 to 1521
upsert.description: After fighting Cortés's company in September 1519, Tlaxcala, long encircled and besieged by the Triple Alliance, allies with the Spanish; with defectors from Texcoco and other subject towns, tens of thousands of Indigenous warriors, porters and boat-builders do most of the fighting and the labour of the siege of Tenochtitlan. Spanish chronicles played the alliance down; Indigenous records such as the Lienzo de Tlaxcala, and the privileges Tlaxcala won from the Crown, set it out.
provenance: sources to check: Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003); Matthew and Oudijk (eds.), Indian Conquistadors (2007)

upsert.boundary: The silver frontier: Zacatecas and the Chichimeca war, 1546 to 1600
upsert.description: Silver strikes at Zacatecas (1546) and Guanajuato draw Spaniards, Indigenous workers and enslaved Africans north into the lands of the nomadic peoples the Spanish called Chichimecas, who fight a forty-year war of raids on the silver roads (1550 to 1590), ended by gifts of food and goods and by settling Tlaxcalan colonists among them. New Spain's silver soon rivals Potosí's.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico (1971); Powell, Soldiers, Indians and Silver (1952)

upsert.boundary: Banwari Trace, Trinidad, about 6000 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: A shell midden of foragers who came from the South American mainland, then all but joined to Trinidad, holds the oldest human burial in the Caribbean; the people fish, gather shellfish and hunt in the forest.
provenance: sources to check: Boomert, Trinidad, Tobago and the Lower Orinoco Interaction Sphere (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Baptist War and emancipation in the British Caribbean, 1831 to 1838
upsert.description: In the Baptist War of Christmas 1831, perhaps 60,000 enslaved people in Jamaica strike and rise under Samuel Sharpe; its brutal suppression helps push Parliament to abolish slavery (1833, in force 1834). About 670,000 people in the British Caribbean are freed after an 'apprenticeship' of unpaid labour that ends in 1838; the owners, not the enslaved, receive £20 million in compensation, about two fifths of the government's yearly spending.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The Problem of Freedom (1992); Draper, The Price of Emancipation (2010)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: The British Caribbean's independence, 1962 to 1983
upsert.description: After the West Indies Federation breaks up (1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago become independent (1962), then Barbados and, on the mainland, Guyana (1966), the Bahamas (1973), Grenada (1974) and the smaller islands, the last St Kitts and Nevis (1983); most remain parliamentary democracies on the Westminster model. Anguilla, the Cayman Islands and others stay British.
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: The Code Noir, March 1685
upsert.description: Louis XIV's edict governs slavery in France's islands: it requires baptism, forbids work on Sundays and the separation of families by sale, and defines the enslaved as movable property whom masters may chain and whip and the state may mutilate or kill for flight or for striking a master. Its protections are rarely enforced; its definition of people as property is.
provenance: sources to check: Sala-Molins, Le Code noir ou le calvaire de Canaan (1987)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the French islands)

upsert.boundary: Slavery ends in Cuba, 1880 to 1886
upsert.description: A law of 1880 turns Cuba's remaining enslaved people into 'apprentices' (the patronato) bound to their masters; many buy or win their freedom early, and the system ends in October 1886, two years before Brazil's abolition. Puerto Rico had abolished slavery in 1873.
provenance: sources to check: Scott, Slave Emancipation in Cuba (1985)

upsert.boundary: The American century in the Caribbean, 1898 to 1962
upsert.description: The United States takes Puerto Rico, oversees Cuba under the Platt Amendment and occupies Haiti (1915 to 1934) and the Dominican Republic (1916 to 1924); Trujillo and Batista rise from the forces it trained or tolerated. Sugar booms and busts; the British islands' labour rebellions of 1934 to 1939 bring unions, parties and universal suffrage; West Indians migrate to Panama, Cuba, the United States and, after 1948, Britain. The Cuban revolution (1959) and the end of the West Indies Federation (1962) close the era.
provenance: sources to check: Higman (2011); Pérez, Cuba: Between Reform and Revolution (5th ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: The first islanders, about 6000 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers from South America reach Trinidad, then all but joined to the mainland, by about 6000 BCE (Banwari Trace); by about 4000 BCE people cross open sea to Cuba and Hispaniola, from Central America or from South America (their stone tools fit both), and later Archaic peoples settle Puerto Rico and the northern Lesser Antilles. They fish, gather shellfish and tend some plants; ancient genomes show them to be a population distinct from the farmers who come after them.
provenance: sources to check: Keegan and Hofman, The Caribbean before Columbus (2017); Fernandes et al. 2021, Nature 590

upsert.boundary: Emancipation and its limits, 1804 to 1898
upsert.description: Independent Haiti pays France an indemnity for recognition (1825) and is shunned by the slaveholding powers. Britain frees about 670,000 enslaved people in its islands (1834 to 1838) after the Baptist War in Jamaica, France and Denmark in 1848 and the Netherlands in 1863, while Cuba's sugar boom draws hundreds of thousands more Africans until the 1860s and slavery lasts there until 1886. Freed people seek land of their own; planters bring indentured labourers from India and China. Cuba fights two wars for independence (1868 to 1878 and 1895 to 1898), the second ended by the United States' intervention.
provenance: sources to check: Higman (2011); Scott, Slave Emancipation in Cuba (1985)

upsert.boundary: Independent and dependent islands, 1962 to 2025
upsert.description: Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago become independent in 1962 and most British islands follow by 1983, while Puerto Rico, the French departments, the Dutch islands and others stay tied to their metropoles. Cuba becomes a Soviet ally whose missiles bring the world to the brink of nuclear war (1962), then endures the Special Period after 1991; Haiti passes from the Duvaliers to coups, an earthquake (2010) and gang rule. Tourism, offshore finance and remittances replace sugar.

upsert.boundary: Saladoid farmers and potters, about 500 BCE to 600 CE
upsert.description: Arawak-speaking farmers from the lower Orinoco sail up the Lesser Antilles to Puerto Rico with manioc, clay griddles for cassava bread and white-on-red painted pottery; ancient DNA shows a new population from South America that largely replaces or absorbs the Archaic islanders of the eastern islands. Villages are built around plazas with burials at their centre.
provenance: sources to check: Keegan and Hofman (2017); Fernandes et al. 2021, Nature 590

upsert.boundary: Conquest and the Spanish Caribbean, 1492 to 1640
upsert.description: Columbus's landfall begins the conquest of the Greater Antilles; within a generation the Taíno are destroyed by forced labour, war, famine and disease, and the first enslaved Africans and sugar mills arrive on Hispaniola. As Spain's interest moves to Mexico and Peru, the islands become ports and forts for the treasure fleets, with Havana their meeting point, raided by French, English and Dutch privateers; from the 1620s England, France and the Netherlands settle the smaller islands Spain had left.
provenance: sources to check: Elliott (2006); Higman, A Concise History of the Caribbean (2011)

upsert.boundary: The sugar islands, 1640 to 1804
upsert.description: Barbados turns to sugar in the 1640s and the model spreads to Jamaica (English from 1655), the French islands and Saint-Domingue: plantations worked by enslaved Africans, who die faster than they are born and are replaced by new captives. Over the whole slave trade the Caribbean receives almost half the Africans landed in the Americas, most of them in this era; on the sugar islands nine people in ten are enslaved, and maroons hold the mountains of Jamaica. The era ends with the Haitian Revolution, which destroys the richest colony on Earth and founds the first state built by the formerly enslaved (1804).
provenance: sources to check: Dunn, Sugar and Slaves (1972); Higman (2011); Eltis and Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)

upsert.boundary: Ostionoid and Taíno chiefdoms, about 600 to 1492
upsert.description: Farming villages spread west into Hispaniola, Jamaica and Cuba and north into the Bahamas, home of the Lucayans; by about 1200 the Taíno of the Greater Antilles live in chiefdoms (cacicazgos) with ball courts, stone-lined plazas, carved zemí figures and cassava grown in mounded fields, while the Kalinago hold the Lesser Antilles. How many people lived on Hispaniola in 1492 is disputed, from about 100,000 to several million.
provenance: sources to check: Rouse, The Tainos (1992); Keegan and Hofman (2017)

upsert.boundary: Africans and sugar on Hispaniola, 1501 to 1530
upsert.description: The first enslaved Africans are taken to Hispaniola from Spain (1501), and as the Taíno die the Crown licenses shipments direct from Africa (1518); the island's first sugar mills grind by about 1516, and by the 1530s some thirty mills worked by enslaved Africans make Santo Domingo the first plantation colony in the Americas. The first slave revolt in the Americas breaks out there in 1521.
provenance: sources to check: Stevens-Arroyo 1993, Comparative Studies in Society and History 35; Higman, A Concise History of the Caribbean (2011)

upsert.boundary: The first people reach Cuba and Hispaniola, about 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers cross open sea to the Greater Antilles, the first settlement in the Americas of islands out of sight of the mainland; their flaked-stone tools resemble those of Belize and Yucatán, which suggests a crossing from Central America, but a route from South America is also argued, and the evidence fits both. Ground sloths and other island animals disappear in the millennia after people arrive.
provenance: inferred: the arrival as recalled; its source is debated
sources to check: Keegan and Hofman, The Caribbean before Columbus (2017); Steadman et al. 2005, PNAS 102
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Cuba and Hispaniola)

upsert.boundary: The Haiti earthquake, January 2010
upsert.description: A magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes near Port-au-Prince; estimates of the dead range from under 100,000 to over 300,000, the figures disputed, and much of the capital, the presidential palace included, collapses. A cholera epidemic brought by UN peacekeepers follows and kills about 10,000.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is disputed
sources to check: USGS event summary; Piarroux et al. 2011, Emerging Infectious Diseases 17

upsert.boundary: Cuba's War of Independence, 1895 to 1898
upsert.description: José Martí, killed in its first weeks, Máximo Gómez and Antonio Maceo lead a war that burns the sugar estates; Spain's general Weyler herds rural Cubans into reconcentration camps, where perhaps 100,000 to 170,000 die of hunger and disease. The United States intervenes in 1898 and takes the war and the peace into its own hands.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the camp deaths are disputed
sources to check: Ferrer (1999); Pérez, The War of 1898 (1998)

upsert.boundary: Saladoid farmers sail from the Orinoco to Puerto Rico, about 500 to 300 BCE
upsert.description: Canoe-borne farmers from the lower Orinoco settle the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico within a few centuries, skipping islands as they go; ancient DNA shows them to be a population from South America that largely replaces or absorbs the Archaic islanders of the east, though in places the two live side by side for centuries.
provenance: sources to check: Fernandes et al. 2021, Nature 590; Keegan and Hofman (2017)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico)

upsert.boundary: Cuba's Ten Years' War, 1868 to 1878
upsert.description: Carlos Manuel de Céspedes frees his slaves and declares Cuba's independence (October 1868); a decade of war in the east, with Antonio Maceo among its generals, ends in the Pact of Zanjón without independence, but with the end of slavery set in motion.
provenance: sources to check: Ferrer, Insurgent Cuba (1999)

upsert.boundary: Spanish America abolishes slavery, 1821 to 1854
upsert.description: The new republics first free the children of the enslaved (free-womb laws) and the slaves who fought for independence, then abolish slavery outright: Chile (1823), Central America (1824), Mexico (1829), Uruguay (1842), Colombia (1851), Argentina (1853), Venezuela and Peru (1854). Owners are usually compensated; the freed are not.
provenance: sources to check: Andrews, Afro-Latin America 1800-2000 (2004)

upsert.boundary: The society of castas, about 1550 to 1800
upsert.description: Spanish America ranks people by descent and status: Spaniards born in Spain or in America, Indians bound to tribute and labour drafts in their own 'republic' of towns, and the growing numbers of mestizos, mulattos and free and enslaved Africans between and below them, named in a vocabulary of castas that painters of the 1700s illustrate in series. The categories are fluid in daily life and can sometimes be bought out of, but they decide taxes, offices and marriage.
provenance: sources to check: Katzew, Casta Painting (2004); Martínez, Genealogical Fictions (2008)
