Values at the Events that the Americas' links now hold these processes to. Points inside a span are placed on the path between its ends unless an Event there turns it; war deaths, averaged to the next date, are split so the old 1820 to 1850 average is kept, and the whole (h.war) is restated as the sum of its three parts.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

Foragers carry their goods when they move camp and carry home what they kill and gather: a few tonne-km a person a year. Obsidian and shells travel hundreds of kilometres by exchange, but in tiny amounts.
Farmers carry harvests, stores and building stuff, but rarely far.
Donkeys are domesticated in north-east Africa and carry loads.
The wheel and the sail: carts on land, sailing boats on the Nile and the Gulf.
Rome's grain fleet carries some hundreds of thousands of tonnes from Egypt and Africa each year; the empire's sea trade lifts its average to several times the world's.
Falls: Mediterranean shipping shrinks with the Western empire, as shipwreck counts show.
Song China's Grand Canal and coastal junks move rice, salt and iron in bulk.
Dutch and English merchant fleets, and coal shipped from Newcastle to London.
Turns up steeply: railways and steamships cut the cost of moving bulk goods by most of its cost on roads.
Railways spread across North America, Mexico (the Porfiriato), Argentina and India and steamships take over bulk freight once the Suez Canal opens (1869): freight per person grows at about 9% a year.
On the eve of the First World War world trade and shipping stand at their prewar peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from submarine sinkings and blockade.
Submarine warfare sinks a fifth of the world's merchant tonnage.
Supertankers and bulk carriers: oil and ore cross oceans in unprecedented tonnages; the container ship spreads from 1956.
Dips: the oil shocks cut long-haul tanker trade in the early 1980s.
China's trade boom carries ore and coal in and containers out.
COVID-19's first year: world trade volume falls about a twentieth in 2020 and recovers in 2021.
About 130 trillion tonne-km a year, three quarters of it by sea (UNCTAD and the International Transport Forum, as recalled).

upsert.reason: Before 1850 sketched from loads and distances (a forager's camp moves, a farmer's surplus carried to market, Roman, Song and Dutch shipping); 1850 to 1950 from railway and shipping statistics as recalled; after 1970 from UNCTAD's seaborne tonne-miles and the International Transport Forum's land freight, as recalled.

points.note: Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Grain, beef, coffee and sugar from the Americas and wool from Australia flow to Europe as freight rates fall; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Foragers' tubers, wild seeds and staple nuts: perhaps two fifths of their energy, less in cold climates.
Wild grains ground at Ohalo II by the Sea of Galilee about 23,000 years ago: seeds were eaten long before they were sown.
Rises as farming spreads: grain, rice, millet and roots become three quarters of farmers' energy.
Maize, potatoes and cassava begin to spread from the Americas through Eurasia and Africa.
Wartime famines take hold: Henan (1942 to 1943), Bengal (1943), occupied Java and the Burma–Siam railway's camps, while Mexico's wheat programme starts.
Flat per person from here: the Green Revolution's higher yields feed more people at the same staple ration, and the gain in calories goes to animal and other foods.
About half of all calories, most of them cereals.
Before cultivation; some sedentary foragers harvesting wild cereals.
Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent (ev.as.fertile-crescent); foragers are still almost everyone.

Cultivation has begun in several centres at once: the Fertile Crescent's pre-pottery Neolithic, squash in Oaxaca, millet in north China, manioc and squash in south-western Amazonia, and soon the New Guinea highlands. Farmers are still a few in a hundred; the fall quickens only as their villages multiply, so the value lies between 98 at 9500 BCE and 92 at 7900 BCE.

Squash and maize in Mexico, millet in north China, manioc in Amazonia and the New Guinea highlands all begin about now, beside the Fertile Crescent's villages; the Holocene's warm, stable climate made cultivation possible in many places at once.
Pre-pottery Neolithic farming in the Fertile Crescent; early cultivation in China.

Farming established in south-west Asia, Anatolia, the Yellow and Yangtze valleys and arriving in Greece; farmers already perhaps a quarter of all people because their densities were far higher. WaveOfAdvance#4cec for the spread into Europe.
Roman Italy perhaps a third enslaved; most of the world far less.
Serfdom loosening in western Europe after the plague and tightening in the east; slavery across the Islamic world, Africa and South-east Asia.
Enslavement in the Caribbean and the first Atlantic shipments of Africans add little at world scale yet.
Brazil's sugar slavery grows and the first enslaved Africans reach Virginia (1619), while serfdom tightens in Russia and Poland; at world scale the share in bondage holds near 9%.

The sugar revolution begins in Barbados; Russia's Ulozhenie (1649) binds its peasants for good. Growth in Atlantic slavery and eastern serfdom is offset by a world population still recovering from the 1600s' crises.
Russian serfdom ends in 1861, American slavery in 1865, Brazilian in 1888.
A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
Mostly the Soviet camps and colonial forced labour.
Steady at world scale: rising rates in the United States and Latin America from the late 1960s are offset by falls elsewhere; the drug trade's violence grows only later.

The world rate stops falling in the early 1990s: Latin America's homicide epidemic (ev.lac.homicide), with Colombia near its peak and Brazil's rates rising, and Russia's killings after the Soviet collapse offset the long decline elsewhere.
No network exists: computers are single machines; ARPANET is twelve years away.
Cheap smartphones and mobile data bring most of Asia and much of Africa online (ev.internet).
No people live in the Americas until about 16,000 years ago (the White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, put a few earlier).
People are south of the ice (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago): the Americas' first output, a few tens of thousands of foragers.
The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya kingdoms, Moche and Tiwanaku raise the Americas' output per person a little toward the world's.

On the eve of contact the Americas make about a twelfth of world output, the Aztec and Inca states and their tributaries most of it; the size depends on the contact population, which is debated (see h.region-americas).
The Aztec and Inca states fall; smallpox has already run through Mexico and the Andes. Output shrinks with the people, at the rate between 1520 and 1550.
Potosí is found (1545) and the cocoliztli strikes New Spain (1545 to 1548): silver rises as people die.

The Columbian collapse (ev.columbian-exchange, VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd): the Americas' output falls by two fifths from 1520 to 1550 and by two thirds to 1600 with its people, though the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas becomes the most valuable thing the Americas send out.
The nadir: the Americas make under 2% of world output.
The United States' output per person is already more than twice the world's; with Latin America's near the world's, the Americas' output per person is about 1.4 times it.
The Americas pass a tenth of world output, the United States most of it.

Between 1870 and 1890 on a constant growth rate: the United States grows fast after the Civil War despite the depression of 1873, Argentina's export boom begins, and the slave economies of Cuba and Brazil end in the 1880s. About 13.6% of world output, up from 11.3% in 1870.
The First World War: the Americas' output rises while Europe's falls.
The Depression's trough: the Americas' output falls about a fifth from 1929 (ev.nam.depression), more than any other area's.
The war economy: the Americas' output passes Europe's for the first time, the United States making about two fifths of the world's manufactures.
Demobilization: American output falls about a tenth from its wartime peak.
Latin America's lost decade (ev.am.debt-crisis): its output per person falls while Northern America's grows, so the Americas' output grows slower than the world's.
Uruk-period polities, if counted as states.
The Han and Roman empires at their height, with the Parthians, Kushans and Satavahanas, hold most of the world's people; the share falls only as the Han breaks up after 184.

The Tang and Abbasid realms fragment but their people stay under states; the southern Maya kingdoms fail; Polynesians settle eastern islands without states. The share under a state barely moves between 770 and 1000.
Stone tools, wooden spears, skins and shelters: about a sixth of foragers' output.
Pottery, weaving, houses and the first copper: farmers make more things than foragers.
Bronze, monumental building and specialist craftsmen in the first states.
The collapse of Roman manufacturing and trade in the West: pottery, coins and buildings become cruder and fewer.
Song China's iron output, perhaps over 100,000 tonnes a year by 1078 as Hartwell reconstructed it, is not matched until the eighteenth century.
Turns up: the industrial revolution's cotton mills, iron and steam spread from Britain.
Steel, chemicals and electricity: the second industrial revolution in Germany and the United States.
Making passes food-getting in world output about now.
Ford's moving assembly line and the Haber–Bosch process begin in 1913, on the eve of the war.
World industrial production falls by about a third from 1929 to 1932, by the League of Nations' index as recalled: the Depression is above all industry's collapse.
Peak of war production: American and Soviet factories make arms on a scale never seen.
Demobilization: war production stops and factories convert.
Industry's share of world output near its peak, about 37%.
Turns flat: deindustrialization in the old industrial countries and the collapse of Soviet-bloc industry after 1989.
Turns up again: China becomes the world's workshop.
About 28% of world output.

upsert.reason: Industry's share of world output: about 15% for foragers' tools, clothing and shelters, 16 to 22% in agrarian economies, a third by 1950 and its peak about 37% in the 1960s, about 28% now (World Bank value added after 1960, as recalled).

points.note: Before wartime taxation and borrowing.
Wartime taxation and borrowing.
Revenue rises as a share of output while output falls in the Depression, and the New Deal, Japan's war spending and Germany's rearmament start to raise taxes.
Wartime taxation at its height in the belligerents.
Demobilization: revenue falls from its wartime height but stays far above the 1930s (ev.postwar-order).

Foragers' material wealth (tools, ornaments) and relational wealth (ties to others) are shared fairly evenly: wealth Ginis about 0.25 to 0.35 in Borgerhoff Mulder and others' comparison, a top-tenth share of about a quarter.
Rich burials such as Sungir's (about 32,000 years ago) show that some foragers could concentrate prestige goods, rarely and briefly.
Rises with farming: stored grain, fields and herds can be held and handed down, and house sizes begin to diverge.
Draft animals, the plough and states: Kohler and others find Old World house-size Ginis near 0.6 by the Bronze Age, above the New World's, where there were no large draft animals.
The Roman senatorial and Han landlord elites: Scheidel's agrarian empires, where the richest tenth hold most land and slaves.
Falls: the collapse of Roman rule in the West destroys the great senatorial fortunes (Scheidel's leveller of state failure).
Falls: the Black Death kills a third or more in Europe and the Near East, land becomes cheap and labour dear, and wealth inequality falls for a century (Alfani's and Scheidel's plague leveller).
Plantations, colonial fortunes and the first industrial capital; from here the gap between countries adds to the gap within them.
The peak: on the eve of 1914 the richest tenth hold about nine tenths of wealth in Britain and France (Piketty's series), while most of the world's people own almost nothing.
On the eve of the war wealth concentration is at its peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from destroyed capital, taxes and inflation.
Falls: the war destroys capital and raises taxes and inflation.
The crash wipes out paper fortunes in the United States, where the top tenth's share falls after 1929, and Mexico's land reform resumes; at world scale the share barely moves.
The great levelling of the world wars: destruction, inflation, high taxes and expropriation in Japan, Europe and Eastern Europe.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) and the Soviet bloc's expropriations take the wealth of the landlords and owners.
Turns up: privatisation, financial deregulation and rising asset prices.
The privatisation of Soviet-bloc property after 1991 creates new fortunes.
The World Inequality Report 2022 puts the richest tenth's share of world wealth at about 76%, as recalled.

upsert.reason: Sketched before 1995 from the comparative wealth Ginis of foragers and farmers, Kohler and others' house-size Ginis, the agrarian estimates in Scheidel's Great Leveler and Piketty's series for Europe and the United States, all as recalled; from 1995 near the World Inequality Database's world top-tenth share.

points.note: Brush huts, windbreaks and caves; foragers live mostly in the open and sleep a family to a small shelter.
Glacial maximum: the mammoth-bone dwellings of the Russian plain, perhaps 20 to 30 m² for a household, show winter houses where there was no wood.
The Natufians' round stone houses, a few metres across, are the first permanent dwellings.
Rectangular mud-brick houses of the first farmers; at Catalhoyuk a main room of about 25 m² with storerooms for a household of five to eight.
Farmers' houses grow: the longhouses of Europe's first farmers, though part of them housed animals and stores.

Greek houses of the eighth century BCE have a median floor of about 45 m²; by the fourth century several times that (Morris's house-size series), a rise that was not general across the agrarian world.
Crowded insulae in Rome and the cities beside large peasant and villa houses; Han Chinese farmhouses of a few rooms.
After Rome's fall houses in the West are smaller and of timber; whether the world average fell is unknown.
Turns up: the Black Death leaves the same houses to fewer people.
After the plagues, peasants in western Europe and the Near East have more room and better houses, as wages are high.
Turns down: the industrial cities pack workers into cellars, courts and back-to-backs at a few square metres each.
Turns down: bombing and fighting destroy a fifth of Germany's dwellings, much of Japan's cities and of the western Soviet Union; tens of millions are homeless.
The bombing of Germany and Japan and the fighting in the Philippines and Europe destroy dwellings faster than any are built; the GI Bill's houses come after the war.
Turns up for good: mass housing in Europe, the Soviet Union and Japan, suburbs in North America.
China's housing reform of 1998 starts the largest building boom in history: urban floor space per person there rises from about 8 m² in 1978 to near 40 m² by 2020.

The world's buildings hold about 240 billion m² of floor, roughly three quarters of it dwellings (UN Environment's Global Status Reports for Buildings and Construction, as recalled): about 22 m² a person, from over 60 in the United States to under 10 in much of Africa and South Asia.

upsert.reason: Sketched from house floors in the archaeological record and household sizes before 1950, and from housing statistics and the global buildings floor-area estimates after; the band is wide because no one has summed dwelling space for the world before the late twentieth century.

points.note: Zero among foragers, whom the account counts as holding no one in bondage.
Captives held to work among the first farmers and settled foragers, as bondage begins (h.freedom).
Corvée and temple dependants in the first states.
Egypt's corvée and the Akkadian and Ur III labour gangs.
Rome's slaves (perhaps a third of Roman Italy) and Han China's corvée: about a ninth of the world's working hours.
Serfs' labour dues in Europe, slaves in the Islamic world, corvée across Asia.
After the Black Death labour dues fade in western Europe.
The second serfdom east of the Elbe and the encomienda and mita in Spanish America.
Atlantic slavery near its height beside Russian serfdom.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery (1794), but the cotton gin (1793) opens the second slavery in the United States: compelled work falls only slowly.
Britain abolishes slavery in its colonies from 1834.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs, 1861.
American slavery ends, 1865.
Brazil abolishes slavery in 1888, the last in the Americas; colonial forced labour (the Congo Free State) goes on.
War labour: prisoners of war and deported workers.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Gulag.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
The Gulag is emptied after Stalin's death (1953).
About 28 million people in forced labour by the ILO's count, under 1% of the world's working hours.

Raids and ambushes between bands, the main form of forager war in Keeley's and Bowles's readings. Fry and Soderberg argue most forager killings are personal, not between groups, which would move part of the parent's deep values to homicide; the band carries that debate.
Wars of conquest between the first states and against their neighbours.
The Three Kingdoms counted as fighting between polities; that they were the fragments of one fallen empire makes this a matter of definition.
The Arab conquests.
The Mongol conquests' battles and sieges; their massacres of cities are counted as one-sided.
The Hundred Years War and Timur's campaigns from 1370.
The Italian wars, the Ottoman conquests and the conquest of Mexico and Peru.
The Manchu conquest of Ming China and the Thirty Years War. The parent's value appears to include these wars' famine and plague deaths, which belong to hunger and infection.
The Qing conquest of the south and the Swedish Deluge in Poland.
The Great Turkish War and the Nine Years War.
The Great Northern War and the War of the Spanish Succession.
The Seven Years War.
The French Revolutionary wars.
Corrected from 8 with the parent: the Napoleonic wars' first campaigns and the Russo-Persian war.
The Napoleonic wars' deadliest years, the Russo-Turkish war and the War of 1812.
Now 1820 to 1826: Burma's first war with Britain begins (1824); the Mfecane wars in southern Africa, whose toll is debated.
1826 to 1840: the Russo-Persian and Russo-Turkish wars (1826 to 1829), France's conquest of Algeria from 1830 and the Egyptian–Ottoman wars.
1840 to 1850: the first Opium War, the first Anglo-Afghan and the Anglo-Sikh wars and the Mexican–American War. With the earlier points the 1820 to 1850 average stays near 3.
The Crimean war.
The Paraguayan, Franco-Prussian and Russo-Turkish wars and colonial conquests.
The Boer, Philippine-American and Russo-Japanese wars.
The Balkan wars.
The First World War.
The Polish-Soviet and Greco-Turkish wars.
Japan's war on China from 1937 and Italy's on Ethiopia.
The Second World War's deadliest years: the Eastern Front, the Pacific war and China.
Turns down for good: the Long Peace between great powers begins, and fighting between polities never again reaches a tenth of the world wars' rate. The Indochina war and the first Arab-Israeli war.
Revised from 10 with the parent: the Korean War, now averaged to 1954.2.
The Indo-Pakistani war of December 1971, with the Vietnam war.
Averaged to the next date; the 1971.96 rate held: the October War of 1973 and the Vietnam war's last two years.
The Ogaden war.
China's war on Vietnam and Tanzania's on Uganda.
The Iran-Iraq war.
The Gulf war.
The Eritrean-Ethiopian war.
The invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq.
Turns up: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine from February 2022, the deadliest war between states since Iran and Iraq.

upsert.reason: The parent's value at each date split by what kind of organized killing filled that stretch, from the wars its notes name; before 1800 the split is a sketch.

points.note: Massacres of whole camps; Nataruk by Lake Turkana, about 8000 BCE, is the earliest well-dated case.
Farmers' villages can be wiped out whole: the Neolithic massacres at Talheim and Schletz about 5000 BCE.
The first states kill and deport conquered peoples, as the Assyrian reliefs later boast.
The Mongols kill the people of cities that resist: Merv and Nishapur in 1221, Baghdad in 1258.
Timur's massacres from the 1370s.
Massacres in the conquest of the Americas; most of the Americas' dead died of disease, counted under infection.
Zhang Xianzhong's killings in Sichuan, the Qing massacres at Yangzhou, the sack of Magdeburg.
The Qing's destruction of the Dzungars, 1755 to 1758, perhaps half a million or more killed, averaged here over 1750 to 1780.
1826 to 1840: the Indian removals in the United States and the reprisals after the Baptist War; small at world scale.
1840 to 1850: killings in the conquest of Algeria and, from 1848, the California gold rush's killings of Native Californians. The 1820 to 1850 average stays near 0.5.
Massacres in the Dungan revolt and its suppression.
The Herero and Nama genocide, 1904 to 1908.
The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1916, with the Assyrian and Greek killings.
Pogroms in Ukraine and the Red and White terrors.
The Nanjing massacre and, if the parent counts it, part of the Soviet Great Terror of 1937 to 1938, about 680,000 shot; whether the parent's 25 includes the Terror is not recorded.
German and Soviet killings in occupied Poland.
Rises most: the Holocaust's deadliest years, the killing of Soviet prisoners and civilians in the occupied east, and Japanese massacres in China and South-east Asia.
The murder of Hungary's Jews at Auschwitz in 1944.
Falls: the camps are liberated between July 1944 and May 1945; killings of prisoners and civilians go on in the war's last months, in the death marches and in Asia.
Partition's communal killings, 1947.

As the parent counts it. China's land reform and campaign against counter-revolutionaries, 1950 to 1953, killed perhaps one to two million or more, which would add 4 to 8 to the decade's average; whether the parent counts such campaigns is open.
The killings in Indonesia.
The Cultural Revolution's killings, perhaps half a million to a million and a half in 1966 to 1971, are not in the parent's value; open, as for China's campaigns of the early 1950s.
The killings in Bangladesh, March to December 1971.

Revised from 0.5, which was below the rate of even the lowest count. Burundi's army and Tutsi militias kill some 100,000 to 300,000 Hutu, above all the educated, from April to about August 1972; at 150,000 that is about 2.1 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over the 1.8 years to October 1973. Amin's killings in Uganda (1971 to 1979, estimates from 100,000 to 500,000, about 0.8 a year at a middle reading) add the rest; earlier passes had left them out at every date.
Amin's killings in Uganda continue; no other mass killing of civilians on this scale until the Khmer Rouge's and East Timor's in 1975.
Revised from 7 to add Amin's killings in Uganda, about 0.8, to the Khmer Rouge's executions and East Timor.
Revised from 7 with Uganda.
Guatemala's highland massacres and Uganda.
Burundi 1993, Bosnia.
Rises most since 1945: the Rwandan genocide.
Srebrenica, 1995.
Darfur from 2003.
The Islamic State's killings of Yazidis and others.

upsert.reason: The parent's value at each date split by what kind of organized killing filled that stretch. It holds the one-sided killings the parent counts; China's campaigns of 1950 to 1953 and the Cultural Revolution's killings are not in the parent and so not here.

points.note: Zero by definition among bands: killings within the band are homicide, and fights between bands of one people are between polities.
Villages and chiefdoms can split and fight within themselves.
Rebellions and succession wars in the first states.
The Roman civil wars.
The Yellow Turban rising and the warlord wars at the Han's end.
Falls: by 200 the warlord wars give way to the Three Kingdoms, whose wars are counted between polities.
The wars of the Sui-Tang transition and, from 755, the An Lushan rebellion.
The Tang's decline and Huang Chao's rising.
The Red Turbans and the Yuan's collapse.
Japan's Sengoku wars and France's wars of religion.
Russia's Time of Troubles and Japan's last wars of unification.
The rebellions of Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong that brought down the Ming, and the English and Fronde civil wars.
Falls: the Ming has fallen and the great rebel armies are destroyed; the Qing conquest of the south is counted between polities.
The Revolt of the Three Feudatories.
The Vendee, the Haitian revolution and the White Lotus rebellion.
Revised from 1.5 with the parent: Saint-Domingue's war against Leclerc and the White Lotus rebellion's last years.
The wars of Latin American independence from 1810.
Split from 2.5 for 1820 to 1850, now 1820 to 1826: the last campaigns of Latin American independence (Ayacucho, 1824) and the Greek war of independence.
1826 to 1840: the caudillo wars, the Java War (1825 to 1830) and the First Carlist War in Spain (1833 to 1840).
1840 to 1850: the Caste War of Yucatán, the revolutions of 1848; the Taiping war begins only in 1850. With the points at 1820 and 1826, the 1820 to 1850 average stays near 2.5.
Rises most: the Taiping war, with the Nian and Panthay risings and the Indian rebellion of 1857.
The Taiping war's deadliest years and the American Civil War. The parent's value appears to include the Taiping war's famine and disease deaths.
The Dungan revolt and the Nian.
The Mexican revolution and China's revolution of 1911.
The Russian Civil War.
China's warlord and civil wars.
The Spanish and Chinese civil wars.
Civil wars inside the world war: Yugoslavia, Greece, and the communists and nationalists in China.
The Chinese civil war. From here fighting within polities carries most war deaths.
Algeria's war of independence and Colombia's Violencia.
The Vietnam war's civil side, the Congo crisis and Biafra.
Averaged to the next date; the 1971.96 rate held.
Angola, Lebanon, Ethiopia.
Afghanistan.
Afghanistan, Central America, Ethiopia, Mozambique.
Bosnia, Somalia, Angola, Algeria, Afghanistan, Tajikistan.
The Congo wars.
Syria, Iraq and Yemen.
Ethiopia's Tigray war, Myanmar and Sudan.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
Before cultivation; some sedentary foragers harvesting wild cereals.
Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent (ev.as.fertile-crescent); foragers are still almost everyone.

Cultivation has begun in several centres at once: the Fertile Crescent's pre-pottery Neolithic, squash in Oaxaca, millet in north China, manioc and squash in south-western Amazonia, and soon the New Guinea highlands. Farmers are still a few in a hundred; the fall quickens only as their villages multiply, so the value lies between 98 at 9500 BCE and 92 at 7900 BCE.

Squash and maize in Mexico, millet in north China, manioc in Amazonia and the New Guinea highlands all begin about now, beside the Fertile Crescent's villages; the Holocene's warm, stable climate made cultivation possible in many places at once.
Pre-pottery Neolithic farming in the Fertile Crescent; early cultivation in China.

Farming established in south-west Asia, Anatolia, the Yellow and Yangtze valleys and arriving in Greece; farmers already perhaps a quarter of all people because their densities were far higher. WaveOfAdvance#4cec for the spread into Europe.

Maize becomes the eastern woodlands' staple and Polynesian farmers settle the eastern Pacific, while herders and farmers keep pressing into the remaining foragers' lands in Africa and northern Eurasia.
Roman Italy perhaps a third enslaved; most of the world far less.
Serfdom loosening in western Europe after the plague and tightening in the east; slavery across the Islamic world, Africa and South-east Asia.
Enslavement in the Caribbean and the first Atlantic shipments of Africans add little at world scale yet.
Brazil's sugar slavery grows and the first enslaved Africans reach Virginia (1619), while serfdom tightens in Russia and Poland; at world scale the share in bondage holds near 9%.

The sugar revolution begins in Barbados; Russia's Ulozhenie (1649) binds its peasants for good. Growth in Atlantic slavery and eastern serfdom is offset by a world population still recovering from the 1600s' crises.

The Atlantic slave trade near its peak, about 80,000 people a year, and serfdom extended to Ukraine (1783), while the American Revolution opens the age of revolutions whose language of liberty will be turned against slavery.
Russian serfdom ends in 1861, American slavery in 1865, Brazilian in 1888.
A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
Mostly the Soviet camps and colonial forced labour.
No network exists: computers are single machines; ARPANET is twelve years away.
The integrated circuit is invented (1958 to 1959); no network yet.
Cheap smartphones and mobile data bring most of Asia and much of Africa online (ev.internet).
No people live in the Americas until about 16,000 years ago (the White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, put a few earlier).
People are south of the ice (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago): the Americas' first output, a few tens of thousands of foragers.
The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya kingdoms, Moche and Tiwanaku raise the Americas' output per person a little toward the world's.

On the eve of contact the Americas make about a twelfth of world output, the Aztec and Inca states and their tributaries most of it; the size depends on the contact population, which is debated (see h.region-americas).
The Aztec and Inca states fall; smallpox has already run through Mexico and the Andes. Output shrinks with the people, at the rate between 1520 and 1550.
Potosí is found (1545) and the cocoliztli strikes New Spain (1545 to 1548): silver rises as people die.

The Columbian collapse (ev.columbian-exchange, VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd): the Americas' output falls by two fifths from 1520 to 1550 and by two thirds to 1600 with its people, though the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas becomes the most valuable thing the Americas send out.
The nadir: the Americas make under 2% of world output.
The United States' output per person is already more than twice the world's; with Latin America's near the world's, the Americas' output per person is about 1.4 times it.
Spanish America's wars of independence end with its economies smaller than in 1810, while the United States grows; on the path from 1820 to 1850.
Latin America stagnates under the caudillos while the United States grows by canals and cotton; the Americas' output doubles from 1820 to 1850, almost all of the gain in the north.
The Americas pass a tenth of world output, the United States most of it.

Between 1870 and 1890 on a constant growth rate: the United States grows fast after the Civil War despite the depression of 1873, Argentina's export boom begins, and the slave economies of Cuba and Brazil end in the 1880s. About 13.6% of world output, up from 11.3% in 1870.
The First World War: the Americas' output rises while Europe's falls.
The Depression's trough: the Americas' output falls about a fifth from 1929 (ev.nam.depression), more than any other area's.
The war economy: the Americas' output passes Europe's for the first time, the United States making about two fifths of the world's manufactures.
Demobilization: American output falls about a tenth from its wartime peak.
Latin America's lost decade (ev.am.debt-crisis): its output per person falls while Northern America's grows, so the Americas' output grows slower than the world's.
Uruk-period polities, if counted as states.
The Han and Roman empires at their height, with the Parthians, Kushans and Satavahanas, hold most of the world's people; the share falls only as the Han breaks up after 184.

The Tang and Abbasid realms fragment but their people stay under states; the southern Maya kingdoms fail; Polynesians settle eastern islands without states. The share under a state barely moves between 770 and 1000.
The Triple Alliance forms in the valley of Mexico; the Ming, Timurid and Ottoman states hold most of Asia's people.
Pachacuti begins the Inca conquests: within a century about ten million Andean people come under one state.

The killings in Indonesia (ev.sea.indonesia-1965): about half a million killed, by estimates from 400,000 to a million or more, in some nine months, about 20 per 100,000 a year of the world's people on top of the Vietnam war's 6. The 1960s decade reading had left them out, so its average rises from 6 to about 7.5.
The killings end by mid-1966; the Vietnam war's rate, held from 1960, continues.
Averaged to the next date; the 1966.5 rate held: the Vietnam war, with the Tet offensive, and Biafra.
Now averages 1970 to March 1971: the Vietnam war and Cambodia's civil war.

Pakistan's army begins its crackdown in East Pakistan on 25 March 1971; to the surrender at Dhaka on 16 December, killings of Bengalis, above all Hindus, students and intellectuals, and the Indo-Pakistani war of December. The dead are debated: about 270,000 violent deaths by a survey-based estimate (Obermeyer and others, 2008), 300,000 to 500,000 in many scholarly accounts, 1.5 million in Rummel's, 3 million in Bangladesh's official figure. Taken here as about 500,000, some 18 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over nine months, with the Vietnam war's 3. The parent's 1970 reading had left it out.

Revised from 5, now averaged to the October War of 1973: the Vietnam war 2.5, civil wars 2, and one-sided killing 3, chiefly Burundi's of 1972, which the earlier value counted at below its lowest estimate, and Amin's in Uganda, which it left out.
The October War of 1973 and the oil shock that follows it (ev.oil-shocks); the Vietnam war's last years, civil wars and Amin's killings carry the rate to the fall of Saigon.

Revised from 11 to add Amin's killings in Uganda, about 0.8. The Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh (ev.as.khmer-rouge): perhaps a million of their 1.5 to 2 million victims are executed or killed outright, about 6.5 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over 3.7 years; deaths from hunger and disease in the labour camps are not counted here. Angola, Lebanon, East Timor and Ethiopia add about 4.5.
Revised from 11 with Uganda: the Khmer Rouge's killings continue until January 1979.
Vietnam ends the Khmer Rouge regime (January 1979); China's war on Vietnam, Afghanistan's and Uganda's carry the rate to 1980.
To 1990: the end of the Iran–Iraq war, Afghanistan.
Now averages 1990 to April 1994: the Gulf war, the Bosnian and Somali wars, Afghanistan, Angola and Algeria.

The Rwandan genocide, 7 April to mid-July 1994. Estimates run from about 500,000 (Human Rights Watch) through 600,000 to 800,000 in most scholarly work to over a million in Rwanda's own count of victims; taken here as about 650,000 in a hundred days, some 43 per 100,000 a year of the world's people, with other wars at about 1.5. The parent's 1990 reading had left it out.
After the genocide: Chechnya, Bosnia to 1995, Angola, Algeria, Afghanistan and Burundi carry the rate to 1996.
To 2000: the Congo wars, Eritrea–Ethiopia.
Averaged to the next date; the 2000 rate held: Afghanistan, Iraq and Congo.
To 2020: Syria, Iraq, Yemen.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
Roman Italy perhaps a third enslaved; most of the world far less.
Serfdom loosening in western Europe after the plague and tightening in the east; slavery across the Islamic world, Africa and South-east Asia.
Enslavement in the Caribbean and the first Atlantic shipments of Africans add little at world scale yet.
Brazil's sugar slavery grows and the first enslaved Africans reach Virginia (1619), while serfdom tightens in Russia and Poland; at world scale the share in bondage holds near 9%.

The sugar revolution begins in Barbados; Russia's Ulozhenie (1649) binds its peasants for good. Growth in Atlantic slavery and eastern serfdom is offset by a world population still recovering from the 1600s' crises.

The Atlantic slave trade near its peak, about 80,000 people a year, and serfdom extended to Ukraine (1783), while the American Revolution opens the age of revolutions whose language of liberty will be turned against slavery.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery in 1794, while the cotton gin (1793) begins the expansion of slavery in the United States and the slave trade still runs near its peak.
Russian serfdom ends in 1861, American slavery in 1865, Brazilian in 1888.
A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
Mostly the Soviet camps and colonial forced labour.
No people live in the Americas until about 16,000 years ago (the White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, put a few earlier).
People are south of the ice (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago): the Americas' first output, a few tens of thousands of foragers.
The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya kingdoms, Moche and Tiwanaku raise the Americas' output per person a little toward the world's.

On the eve of contact the Americas make about a twelfth of world output, the Aztec and Inca states and their tributaries most of it; the size depends on the contact population, which is debated (see h.region-americas).
The Aztec and Inca states fall; smallpox has already run through Mexico and the Andes. Output shrinks with the people, at the rate between 1520 and 1550.
Potosí is found (1545) and the cocoliztli strikes New Spain (1545 to 1548): silver rises as people die.

The Columbian collapse (ev.columbian-exchange, VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd): the Americas' output falls by two fifths from 1520 to 1550 and by two thirds to 1600 with its people, though the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas becomes the most valuable thing the Americas send out.
The nadir: the Americas make under 2% of world output.
The United States' output per person is already more than twice the world's; with Latin America's near the world's, the Americas' output per person is about 1.4 times it.
Spanish America's wars of independence end with its economies smaller than in 1810, while the United States grows; on the path from 1820 to 1850.
Latin America stagnates under the caudillos while the United States grows by canals and cotton; the Americas' output doubles from 1820 to 1850, almost all of the gain in the north.
The Americas pass a tenth of world output, the United States most of it.

Between 1870 and 1890 on a constant growth rate: the United States grows fast after the Civil War despite the depression of 1873, Argentina's export boom begins, and the slave economies of Cuba and Brazil end in the 1880s. About 13.6% of world output, up from 11.3% in 1870.
The First World War: the Americas' output rises while Europe's falls.
The bank panics of 1930 and 1931 and the collapse of commodity prices take the Americas' output down a tenth from 1929; Latin America's export economies turn to making their own goods.
The Depression's trough: the Americas' output falls about a fifth from 1929 (ev.nam.depression), more than any other area's.
The war economy: the Americas' output passes Europe's for the first time, the United States making about two fifths of the world's manufactures.
Demobilization: American output falls about a tenth from its wartime peak.
Latin America's lost decade (ev.am.debt-crisis): its output per person falls while Northern America's grows, so the Americas' output grows slower than the world's.

(1) Below the resolution of world and M49 measures: a single city, chiefdom, massacre, treaty or doctrine (Cahokia, Chaco, Crow Creek, Mayapán, the Tarascan state, the Falklands, Tordesillas, the Monroe Doctrine, the Louisiana Purchase). (2) Carried by a linked Event: the Mississippian period carries the entradas, the Haitian Revolution Leclerc's expedition, the Second World War Pearl Harbor, the dictatorships Chile's coup and the Dirty War. (3) What they change has no process, and opening one does not pay now: change within Christianity (Pentecostal growth, liberation theology, the Great Awakening) moves people between traditions, not into or out of the faith, and would need a carve of the kept-whole h.religion-4; the missile crisis, a near miss, moves no measure. By the routing test (RoutingSanityCheck#71bd) every Event with a world-scale change found a home among existing processes, so no new process earns its keep for this region (MarginalValueRule#6611). Reopen if a regional history of the Americas is opened, where these Events would move the region's own measures.

upsert.boundary: The alphabet: Phoenician letters and the Greek vowels, about 1050 to 750 BCE
upsert.description: Phoenician scribes write with 22 letters for consonants alone; the Greeks borrow them about 800 BCE and add vowels, the first full alphabet, from which Latin, Cyrillic and most of the world's alphabets descend. The Aramaic, Hebrew and Arabic scripts grow from the same Phoenician root.
provenance: sources to check: Powell, Writing: Theory and History of the Technology of Civilization (2009)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Phoenicia); Europe (Southern Europe: Greece)

upsert.boundary: The Soviet war in Afghanistan, 1979 to 1989
upsert.description: Soviet troops invade (December 1979) to save a communist government; Islamist mujahideen armed by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia fight them for nine years; about a million Afghans die and five million flee before the Soviets withdraw (February 1989), and civil war and the Taliban follow.
provenance: sources to check: Braithwaite, Afghantsy (2011); Coll, Ghost Wars (2004)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (Afghanistan, Pakistan); Europe (Eastern Europe: the Soviet Union)

upsert.boundary: Sargon's empire of Akkad, about 2334 to 2154 BCE
upsert.description: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian cities and rules from the Gulf to Syria, the first empire over many city-states, with Akkadian as the language of rule; it falls amid revolts, invasion and perhaps drought.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates on the middle chronology
sources to check: Westenholz, in Mesopotamien: Akkade-Zeit und Ur III-Zeit (1999)

upsert.boundary: The An Lushan rebellion, 755 to 763
upsert.description: A frontier general of Sogdian and Turkic descent rebels and takes both Tang capitals; the war and its famines cut the registered population from about 53 million to 17 million, though much of that fall is people lost to the census rather than dead. The Tang survive but lose Central Asia and control of the provinces.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is much disputed
sources to check: Twitchett (ed.), The Cambridge History of China vol. 3 (1979)

upsert.boundary: The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1917
upsert.description: The Ottoman government deports the Armenians of Anatolia toward the Syrian desert; through massacre, death marches and starvation perhaps a million or more die, and Assyrian and Greek Christians are also killed in great numbers.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; totals range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million
sources to check: Suny, 'They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else' (2015)

upsert.boundary: The Asian financial crisis, 1997 to 1998
upsert.description: Starting with the fall of the Thai baht (July 1997), foreign capital flees Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia; currencies and output collapse, Indonesia's economy shrinks by about 13% in 1998 and Suharto falls, and the IMF imposes austere rescue terms.
provenance: sources to check: Radelet and Sachs 1998, Brookings Papers on Economic Activity
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia), Eastern Asia (South Korea)

upsert.boundary: The Neo-Assyrian empire, 911 to 609 BCE
upsert.description: From Assur and Nineveh, kings with iron-armed professional armies conquer from Iran to Egypt and deport whole peoples to break resistance; Ashurbanipal gathers a great library; Babylon and the Medes destroy Nineveh in 612 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Radner, Ancient Assyria (2015)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Iraq, Syria); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt, briefly)

upsert.boundary: The Mongols sack Baghdad, February 1258
upsert.description: Hulagu's army takes Baghdad, kills the last Abbasid caliph and a great part of the city's people, ending the caliphate that had reigned there for five centuries.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is unknown
sources to check: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

upsert.boundary: Bangladesh's war of independence, 1971
upsert.description: When Pakistan's army cracks down on East Bengal after the Awami League wins the 1970 election, hundreds of thousands to perhaps three million people are killed and ten million flee to India; India intervenes in December and Bangladesh becomes independent.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is fiercely disputed
sources to check: Raghavan, 1971 (2013); Bass, The Blood Telegram (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Bengal famine, 1943 to 1944
upsert.description: After a cyclone, crop disease and the loss of Burmese rice imports to Japan's conquest, wartime inflation, hoarding and the colonial government's refusal to stop exports or call a famine kill about three million people in Bengal.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weight of each cause is debated
sources to check: Sen, Poverty and Famines (1981); Ó Gráda, Eating People Is Wrong (2015)

upsert.boundary: The British Raj, 1858 to 1947
upsert.description: The Crown rules India through a viceroy, a small civil service and princely allies; railways, canals and telegraphs are built, and English education creates a new middle class, while India's income per head barely grows, famines kill tens of millions and India's taxes and trade surplus help pay for Britain's empire.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Raj's economic effect is debated
sources to check: Roy, The Economic History of India 1857–2010 (4th ed. 2020); Tomlinson, The Economy of Modern India (2013)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Burma until 1937); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: Millet farming in north China, about 8000 to 6000 BCE
upsert.description: Along the Yellow River people domesticate foxtail and broomcorn millet and pigs; villages such as Cishan store millet in pits by about 6000 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Lu et al. 2009, PNAS 106

upsert.boundary: China's civil war, 1927 to 1949
upsert.description: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists turn on their Communist allies (1927); the Communists survive the Long March (1934 to 1935) and grow during the war with Japan, then defeat the Nationalists in 1946 to 1949; Mao proclaims the People's Republic in October 1949 and the Nationalists withdraw to Taiwan.
provenance: sources to check: Westad, Decisive Encounters (2003)

upsert.boundary: The East India Company takes Bengal, 1757 to 1765
upsert.description: At Plassey (June 1757) Robert Clive's small army, helped by the treachery of the nawab's commander, defeats Siraj ud-Daulah; after victory at Buxar (1764), the Mughal emperor grants the Company the diwani, the right to collect Bengal's revenue (1765). A trading company becomes a territorial ruler, and the Bengal famine of 1770 follows.
provenance: sources to check: Marshall, Bengal: The British Bridgehead (1987); Dalrymple, The Anarchy (2019)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Bangladesh: Bengal); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: The Cultural Revolution, 1966 to 1976
upsert.description: Mao mobilizes students as Red Guards against party officials, teachers and 'old' culture; schools and universities close, millions are persecuted and sent to the countryside, and perhaps one to two million die, before the arrest of the Gang of Four ends it in October 1976.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths are very uncertain
sources to check: MacFarquhar and Schoenhals, Mao's Last Revolution (2006)

upsert.boundary: The place-value decimal system with zero, about 499 to 628
upsert.description: Indian mathematicians use nine digits and a zero in a place-value system; Aryabhata (499) computes with it and Brahmagupta (628) gives rules for zero and negative numbers. Through Baghdad's al-Khwarizmi it reaches Europe as 'Arabic numerals'.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dated zero is debated (the Bakhshali manuscript)
sources to check: Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)

upsert.boundary: The El Niño famines in India and China, 1876 to 1902
upsert.description: Monsoon failures in strong El Niño years bring famine to India (1876 to 1878, 1896 to 1897, 1899 to 1900) and north China (1876 to 1879), and also to Brazil and Ethiopia; perhaps 30 to 50 million people die. Grain exports, relief that demanded hard labour for meagre rations, and weakened Qing granaries made drought into mass death.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; death tolls are very uncertain
sources to check: Davis, Late Victorian Holocausts (2001); Edgerton-Tarpley, Tears from Iron (2008)

upsert.boundary: Wheat, barley, sheep, goats and cattle domesticated in the Fertile Crescent, about 9500 to 7000 BCE
upsert.description: Over two thousand years, people from the Levant to the Zagros cultivate einkorn, emmer, barley, lentils, peas and flax until they change into domestic forms, and herd sheep, goats, cattle and pigs: the founder crops and animals of south-west Asian farming.
provenance: sources to check: Zeder 2011, Current Anthropology 52; Fuller et al. 2011, Proceedings of the Royal Society B

upsert.boundary: East and South Asia's fall in births, 1970 to 2025
upsert.description: With falling child deaths, schooling, cities, family-planning programmes and, in China, the one-child policy (1980 to 2015), births per woman fall from five or six to below replacement across East Asia, Iran, Thailand and most of India's states; South Korea's reaches 0.72 in 2023, the lowest ever recorded for a country, and Japan's, China's and Korea's populations begin to shrink.
provenance: sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2024; Statistics Korea
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia, Southern Asia, South-eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: The Hamas attack of 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza
upsert.description: Hamas fighters kill about 1,200 people in Israel and take some 250 hostages; Israel's war in Gaza kills tens of thousands of Palestinians, displaces most of Gaza's 2.1 million people and leaves the territory in ruins, and spreads to Lebanon, Yemen and Iran before a ceasefire in October 2025.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; casualty figures are contested and still being counted
sources to check: UN OCHA reports; Gaza Ministry of Health and independent assessments
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Israel and Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Iran)

upsert.boundary: Oil in the Gulf, from 1938
upsert.description: After oil is found in Bahrain (1932), Saudi Arabia (1938) and Kuwait, the Gulf becomes the world's main source of oil; nationalizations and OPEC (1960) shift control to the producing states, and oil revenue turns small desert monarchies into some of the richest states per head on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Yergin, The Prize (1991)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the Gulf states, Iraq), Southern Asia (Iran)

upsert.boundary: Iraq invades Kuwait and the Gulf War, 1990 to 1991
upsert.description: Iraq occupies Kuwait (August 1990); a coalition of 35 states led by the United States expels it in a six-week air and ground war (January to February 1991), and sanctions on Iraq follow for twelve years.
provenance: sources to check: Freedman and Karsh, The Gulf Conflict 1990–1991 (1993)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia)

upsert.boundary: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, 6 and 9 August 1945
upsert.description: American bombers drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing about 110,000 to 210,000 people by the end of 1945; with the Soviet declaration of war, they bring Japan's surrender. They remain the only nuclear weapons used in war.
provenance: sources to check: Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy (2005); Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)

upsert.boundary: Japan's invasions of Korea, 1592 to 1598
upsert.description: Hideyoshi's armies overrun Korea; Admiral Yi Sun-sin's armoured turtle ships cut their supply lines at sea, Ming China sends armies, and the Japanese withdraw after Hideyoshi's death, leaving Korea devastated.
provenance: sources to check: Swope, A Dragon's Head and a Serpent's Tail (2009)

upsert.boundary: India's independence movement, 1885 to 1947
upsert.description: From the founding of the Indian National Congress (1885), nationalists press for self-rule; after 1915 Gandhi turns the movement into mass non-violent campaigns of non-cooperation (1920 to 1922), the Salt March (1930) and Quit India (1942), while the Muslim League comes to demand a separate Pakistan.
provenance: sources to check: Brown, Modern India (2nd ed. 1994); Guha, Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World (2018)

upsert.boundary: The Indian rebellion, 1857 to 1858
upsert.description: Sepoys of the Bengal army mutiny at Meerut (May 1857) and proclaim the old Mughal emperor their ruler; the revolt spreads across north India and is crushed with great brutality. The British exile the last emperor and the Crown takes India from the East India Company.
provenance: sources to check: Wagner, The Great Fear of 1857 (2010); Dalrymple, The Last Mughal (2006)

upsert.boundary: Indonesia's revolution, 1945 to 1949
upsert.description: Sukarno and Hatta proclaim independence two days after Japan's surrender; the Dutch fight four years to retake their colony before American pressure makes them transfer sovereignty (December 1949).
provenance: sources to check: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (4th ed. 2008)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Indonesia); Europe (Western Europe: the Netherlands)

upsert.boundary: The Indus civilization, about 2600 to 1900 BCE
upsert.description: Planned cities of baked brick, Mohenjo-daro and Harappa among them, with drains, granaries and standard weights, spread over a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia together; their script is still undeciphered; the cities decline after 1900 BCE as rivers shift and monsoons weaken.
provenance: sources to check: Wright, The Ancient Indus (2010); Giosan et al. 2012, PNAS 109

upsert.boundary: The Iran–Iraq War, 1980 to 1988
upsert.description: Saddam Hussein invades revolutionary Iran (September 1980); after eight years of trench warfare, human-wave attacks and poison gas, perhaps half a million or more dead, the war ends in a ceasefire with the border unchanged.
provenance: sources to check: Murray and Woods, The Iran–Iraq War (2014)

upsert.boundary: The Iraq war, 2003 to 2011
upsert.description: An American-led invasion overthrows Saddam Hussein (March to April 2003); disbanding the army and the Baath party feeds an insurgency and a sectarian civil war in which a few hundred thousand Iraqis die, before American troops leave at the end of 2011.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; death tolls range widely
sources to check: Iraq Body Count; Gordon and Trainor, The Endgame (2012)

upsert.boundary: Japan's war in China and the Pacific, 1931 to 1945
upsert.description: Japan seizes Manchuria (1931), invades China proper (1937), massacring civilians at Nanjing, and in 1941 attacks Pearl Harbor and conquers South-east Asia; perhaps 15 to 20 million Chinese and millions more across Asia die. Defeat at sea, the firebombing of its cities, the atomic bombs and the Soviet attack end the war in August 1945.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Chinese deaths are very uncertain
sources to check: Mitter, China's War with Japan 1937–1945 (2013); Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Japan, Korea), South-eastern Asia; Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia); Americas (Northern America: Hawaii)

upsert.boundary: Japan rules Korea, 1910 to 1945
upsert.description: Japan annexes Korea (August 1910) and rules it as a colony: land surveys, railways and later factories, the suppression of the March First movement (1919), forced name changes and the Korean language banned from schools, and in the war mass labour conscription and the sexual slavery of 'comfort women'.
provenance: sources to check: Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

upsert.boundary: Japan's economic miracle, 1950 to 1973
upsert.description: Rebuilt from defeat, Japan's economy grows by nearly 10% a year, from steel and ships to cars and electronics, on high saving, guided industrial policy and open American markets; by 1968 it is the second-largest economy outside the communist world.
provenance: sources to check: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982)

upsert.boundary: Japan's unification, 1568 to 1603
upsert.description: After a century of civil war, Oda Nobunaga uses massed musketeers to take Kyoto (1568) and beat the Takeda at Nagashino (1575); Toyotomi Hideyoshi unites the country (1590), disarms the peasants and invades Korea; Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara (1600) and becomes shogun in 1603.

upsert.boundary: Joseon Korea, 1392 to 1897
upsert.description: General Yi Seong-gye founds a dynasty that rules Korea for five centuries as a Neo-Confucian state with examinations and a hereditary yangban elite; King Sejong's scholars create the Hangul alphabet; Japan invades (1592 to 1598) and the Manchus (1627, 1636), and Korea then keeps out most outsiders until the 1870s.
provenance: sources to check: Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

upsert.boundary: Early states in Korea and Japan, about 57 BCE to 668
upsert.description: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla compete on the Korean peninsula until Silla, allied with Tang China, unifies it (668); in Japan, Yayoi rice farmers from Korea are followed by the great keyhole tombs of the Kofun period and the Yamato state, which adopts Chinese writing and Buddhism.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the founding dates of the Korean kingdoms are traditional
sources to check: Seth, A History of Korea (2010); Farris, Sacred Texts and Buried Treasures (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Korean War, 1950 to 1953
upsert.description: North Korea invades the South (June 1950); a US-led UN force pushes north to the Chinese border, China's armies drive it back, and the war ends in an armistice near the 38th parallel (July 1953) after perhaps three million deaths, leaving Korea divided.
provenance: sources to check: Cumings, The Korean War (2010)

upsert.boundary: The Maurya empire, 321 to 185 BCE
upsert.description: Chandragupta Maurya, said to be advised by Kautilya, author of the Arthashastra, builds the first empire over most of the subcontinent from Pataliputra; his grandson Ashoka extends it to all but the far south.
provenance: sources to check: Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (3rd ed. 2012)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh)

upsert.boundary: Mehrgarh, about 7000 to 2600 BCE
upsert.description: At the foot of the Bolan pass in Baluchistan, villagers farm wheat and barley and herd cattle, sheep and goats, drill teeth and make beads: the roots of farming in South Asia and of the Indus cities.
provenance: sources to check: Jarrige 2008, Pragdhara 18; Coppa et al. 2006, Nature 440

upsert.boundary: Meiji Japan, 1868 to 1912
upsert.description: Young samurai overthrow the shogunate in the emperor's name (1868), abolish the domains and the samurai class, send missions to learn from the West, build railways, factories, a conscript army and compulsory schools, and adopt a constitution (1889); within forty years Japan is an industrial and imperial power.
provenance: sources to check: Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Ming dynasty, 1368 to 1644
upsert.description: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant rebel, founds the Ming; his successors move the capital to Beijing, build the Forbidden City and the brick Great Wall, send Zheng He's fleets, then turn inward; by the 1500s a commercial economy runs on silver from Japan and the Americas. Cold, drought, epidemics, fiscal crisis and rebellion bring it down in 1644.
provenance: sources to check: Brook, The Troubled Empire (2010)

upsert.boundary: The Opium Wars, 1839 to 1860
upsert.description: When the Qing destroy British opium at Canton (1839), Britain goes to war and by the Treaty of Nanjing (1842) takes Hong Kong and opens five ports; in the second war (1856 to 1860) Britain and France occupy Beijing and burn the Summer Palace. The unequal treaties open China to foreign trade, missionaries and extraterritorial law.
provenance: sources to check: Lovell, The Opium War (2011)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China); Europe (Northern and Western Europe: Britain, France)

upsert.boundary: The Ottoman empire is partitioned, 1916 to 1923
upsert.description: Britain and France plan the division of the Arab lands (Sykes–Picot, 1916), Britain promises a Jewish national home in Palestine (1917), and after the Ottoman defeat they rule Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Transjordan as League of Nations mandates; in Anatolia, Mustafa Kemal's nationalists defeat the Greek invasion and found the Republic of Turkey (October 1923).
provenance: sources to check: Rogan, The Fall of the Ottomans (2015); Fromkin, A Peace to End All Peace (1989)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Turkey, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Palestine, Jordan); Europe (Western and Northern Europe: France, Britain)
