value: inferred: each Event's description says what it changes

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's Asia group, batch 1 of 4: 43 Events of Asia now name the processes they change. Wars name war deaths by kind (between polities, within them, one-sided killing), famines name hunger deaths, empires the largest polity or the share under a state, the first farmers foraging, colonial conquest and independence colonial rule, booms and crises Asia's output, the Indus and Uruk the urban share and the largest city, Joseon's hereditary slaves bondage and rank, the alphabet and the zero literacy and numeracy. Only process_ids change; every other field is restated unchanged.

upsert.boundary: Independence and the partition of India, 1947
upsert.description: Britain hands power to two states, India and Pakistan (East and West), at midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947; as the borders cut through Punjab and Bengal, about 15 million people flee across them and perhaps 200,000 to two million are killed in communal violence.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is very uncertain
sources to check: Khan, The Great Partition (2007)

upsert.boundary: Spain in the Philippines, 1565 to 1700
upsert.description: Legazpi founds the first Spanish settlement at Cebu (1565) and Manila (1571), the Asian end of the galleon trade; Spanish friars convert most lowland Filipinos from their local religions to Catholicism within a century, while the Muslim sultanates of Mindanao and Sulu resist.
provenance: sources to check: Phelan, The Hispanization of the Philippines (1959)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines); Europe (Southern Europe: Spain)

upsert.boundary: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904 to 1905
upsert.description: Japan attacks Russia's fleet at Port Arthur, wins the siege and the battle of Mukden, and destroys Russia's Baltic fleet at Tsushima; the first defeat of a European great power by an Asian one in modern war, it inspires nationalists from Egypt to India and helps provoke Russia's 1905 revolution.
provenance: sources to check: Paine, The Japanese Empire (2017)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (Manchuria, Korea, Japan); Europe (Eastern Europe: Russia)

upsert.boundary: The Shang dynasty, about 1600 to 1046 BCE
upsert.description: Kings at Anyang cast great bronze ritual vessels, drive chariots and consult their ancestors on cracked bones and shells, whose inscriptions (from about 1250 BCE) are the oldest Chinese writing.
provenance: sources to check: Keightley, The Ancestral Landscape (2000)

upsert.boundary: Guru Nanak and the Sikh Gurus, about 1499 to 1708
upsert.description: In the Punjab, Guru Nanak teaches devotion to one formless God beyond Hindu and Muslim ritual and caste; nine Gurus follow him, compile the Adi Granth (1604) and resist Mughal persecution, and Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa (1699) before naming the scripture itself the last Guru.
provenance: sources to check: Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1990)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan: the Punjab)

upsert.boundary: The First Sino-Japanese War, 1894 to 1895
upsert.description: Japan's modern army and navy defeat China over Korea; by the Treaty of Shimonoseki China gives up Taiwan, recognizes Korea's independence from it and pays a large indemnity, revealing how far the Qing's own reforms lagged behind Japan's.
provenance: sources to check: Paine, The Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895 (2003)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Korea, Japan, Taiwan)

upsert.boundary: The Sui reunify China, 581 to 618
upsert.description: After nearly four centuries of division, the Sui reunite north and south (589), dig the Grand Canal joining the Yangtze to the Yellow River, and bring back the examination of officials, but exhaust the country in wars with Goguryeo and fall to the Tang.
provenance: sources to check: Wright, The Sui Dynasty (1978)

upsert.boundary: The Sumerian city-states, about 2900 to 2350 BCE
upsert.description: Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Kish and a dozen other cities, each under its god and king, fight over water and fields; the royal tombs of Ur hold gold, lyres and sacrificed attendants; the stories of Gilgamesh begin here.
provenance: sources to check: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (3rd ed. 2016)

upsert.boundary: The Syrian civil war, 2011 to 2024
upsert.description: The Assad regime meets peaceful protests (March 2011) with force; civil war, Russian and Iranian intervention, chemical attacks and the Islamic State's rise kill about half a million people and drive 13 million from their homes, many to Turkey and Europe; rebels take Damascus and Assad flees in December 2024.
provenance: sources to check: UNHCR; Syrian Observatory for Human Rights
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Syria, Iraq, Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan); Europe (as refuge)

upsert.boundary: The Asian tigers, 1962 to 1997
upsert.description: South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore grow from poverty to rich-country incomes in a generation, through land reform, schooling, high saving and exports of manufactures; South Korea's income per head rises about tenfold. Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia follow from the 1970s.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, The East Asian Miracle (1993); Studwell, How Asia Works (2013)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong), South-eastern Asia (Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia)

upsert.boundary: Timur's conquests, 1370 to 1405
upsert.description: From Samarkand, Timur conquers from Anatolia to Delhi, sacking Baghdad, Delhi and Damascus with mass killings, defeats the Ottomans at Ankara (1402) and dies marching on China; his successors make Samarkand and Herat centres of Persian art and astronomy.
provenance: sources to check: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)
upsert.region: Asia: Central Asia, Southern Asia (Iran, Afghanistan, India), Western Asia

upsert.boundary: Tokugawa Japan, 1603 to 1868
upsert.description: The Tokugawa shoguns keep two and a half centuries of peace from Edo, make the lords spend alternate years at court, expel missionaries, persecute Christians and close the country to all but Dutch and Chinese traders at Nagasaki (1639); Edo grows to a million people, literacy spreads, and kabuki, ukiyo-e and haiku flourish.
provenance: sources to check: Totman, Early Modern Japan (1993)

upsert.boundary: The Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami, 26 December 2004
upsert.description: A magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra sends waves across the Indian Ocean, killing about 230,000 people in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand and as far as Somalia, the deadliest tsunami recorded.
provenance: sources to check: Lay et al. 2005, Science 308
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Indonesia, Thailand), Southern Asia (Sri Lanka, India); Africa (Eastern Africa)

upsert.boundary: Uruk, the first city, about 3500 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: On the lower Euphrates, Uruk grows to perhaps 40,000 people or more, with monumental temples, mass-produced ration bowls, cylinder seals, colonies up the river, and the first written accounts.
provenance: sources to check: Algaze, Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Vedic age in north India, about 1500 to 600 BCE
upsert.description: Speakers of Indo-Aryan languages, carrying steppe ancestry, settle the Punjab and then the Ganges plain; their priests compose the Rigveda and later Vedas, the varna order of priests, warriors, traders and servants takes shape, and iron opens the Ganges forests to farming.
provenance: sources to check: Thapar, Early India (2002); Narasimhan et al. 2019, Science 365

upsert.boundary: The Indochina wars, 1946 to 1975
upsert.description: The Viet Minh fight France until Dien Bien Phu (1954) and the division of Vietnam; the Communist North then fights to unify the country against the South and, from 1965, half a million American troops; the war spreads to Laos and Cambodia, and ends with the fall of Saigon (April 1975), after two to three million deaths.
provenance: sources to check: Logevall, Embers of War (2012); Herring, America's Longest War (5th ed. 2013)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia); Americas (Northern America: the United States); Europe (Western Europe: France)

upsert.boundary: The Dutch East India Company, 1602 to 1799
upsert.description: The first joint-stock company with permanent shares, chartered with powers of war, takes Batavia (1619), kills or expels most of the Banda islanders to monopolize nutmeg (1621), takes Malacca and Ceylon from Portugal, and trades at Nagasaki as the only Europeans Japan admits; it is dissolved in debt in 1799.
provenance: sources to check: Gaastra, The Dutch East India Company (2003)
upsert.region: Asia (South-eastern Asia: Indonesia; Southern Asia: Sri Lanka; Eastern Asia: Japan); Europe (Western Europe: the Netherlands)

upsert.boundary: The Warring States, 475 to 221 BCE
upsert.description: Seven Chinese states fight with mass infantry, crossbows and iron, and reform to survive: land registers, salaried officials, written law. War eliminates the states that raise and organize less, and Qin, reformed under Shang Yang, absorbs the rest (Warsift#b01b).
provenance: sources to check: Lewis, Sanctioned Violence in Early China (1990); Hui, War and State Formation in Ancient China and Early Modern Europe (2005)

upsert.boundary: The 1911 revolution ends imperial China, 1911 to 1912
upsert.description: A mutiny at Wuchang (October 1911) spreads to most provinces; the last Qing emperor abdicates (February 1912) and a republic is proclaimed, ending more than two thousand years of imperial rule, but power soon passes to Yuan Shikai and then to warlords.
provenance: sources to check: Spence, The Search for Modern China (3rd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: Rice domesticated in the Yangtze valley, about 7000 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: People of the lower Yangtze, at sites such as Shangshan and Hemudu, gather and then cultivate wild rice until it no longer sheds its grain, over two thousand years; rice later feeds the densest farming populations on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Fuller et al. 2009, Science 323

upsert.boundary: The Yuan dynasty, 1271 to 1368
upsert.description: Kublai Khan proclaims a Chinese-style dynasty, rules from Dadu (Beijing), completes the conquest of the Song (1279) and joins China to the Mongol world; merchants and envoys, Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta among them, travel its roads. Plague, floods and the Red Turban rebellions bring it down.
provenance: sources to check: Rossabi, Khubilai Khan (1988); Brook, The Troubled Empire (2010)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Mongolia, Korea as vassal)

upsert.boundary: The Austronesian expansion, about 3000 BCE to 1300 CE
upsert.description: Rice- and millet-farming speakers of Austronesian languages sail from Taiwan into the Philippines and Indonesia, then east into the Pacific and west to Madagascar, in outrigger and double canoes; by 1300 their languages are spoken across more than half the globe's longitude, from Madagascar to Rapa Nui.
provenance: sources to check: Bellwood, First Islanders (2017); Gray, Drummond and Greenhill 2009, Science 323
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern Asia: Taiwan; South-eastern Asia); Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia, New Zealand); Africa (Eastern Africa: Madagascar)

upsert.boundary: The Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933
upsert.description: Forced collectivization and grain requisitions starve some five to seven million people, about four million in Ukraine, where the regime seals off the starving villages, and more than a million Kazakhs, nearly 40% of them.
provenance: sources to check: Davies and Wheatcroft, The Years of Hunger (2004); Applebaum, Red Famine (2017); Cameron, The Hungry Steppe (2018)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Ukraine, Russia); Asia (Central Asia: Kazakhstan)

upsert.boundary: The oil shocks, 1973 to 1980
upsert.description: In the October 1973 war, Arab producers embargo the United States and the Netherlands and the price of oil quadruples; after Iran's revolution (1979) it more than doubles again. Inflation and recession follow in the rich countries, and oil wealth and debt pour into the producing and borrowing countries.
provenance: sources to check: Yergin, The Prize (1991)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: the Gulf); Americas (Northern America); Europe

upsert.boundary: American rule in the Philippines, 1901 to 1946
upsert.description: The United States rules through Filipino elites: American teachers found a public school system taught in English, an elected assembly meets from 1907, and the Tydings-McDuffie Act (1934) sets up a Commonwealth under Manuel Quezon with independence promised for 1946; landlords keep their estates and the economy is tied to the American market.
provenance: sources to check: Abinales and Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2nd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: The American war in Vietnam, 1965 to 1973
upsert.description: After the Gulf of Tonkin resolution (August 1964) the United States begins bombing the North (March 1965) and lands combat troops, about 540,000 by 1969. Search-and-destroy, defoliants such as Agent Orange, free-fire zones and the Viet Cong's and North's war of attrition kill perhaps a million or more Vietnamese soldiers and civilians in these years and about 58,000 Americans, until the Paris Peace Accords (January 1973) take American forces out. The total Vietnamese toll of the wars is debated, from under two to over three million.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Vietnamese deaths are debated
sources to check: Herring, America's Longest War (5th ed. 2013); Hirschman, Preston and Loi, 'Vietnamese casualties during the American war', Population and Development Review 21 (1995)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam); Americas (Northern America: the United States)

upsert.boundary: Britain conquers Burma in three wars, 1824 to 1885
upsert.description: The first war (1824 to 1826), the costliest in British Indian history, takes Arakan and Tenasserim; the second (1852) takes Lower Burma and its delta; the third (1885) takes Mandalay and exiles King Thibaw, and Burma is ruled as a province of British India until 1937.
provenance: sources to check: Thant Myint-U, The Making of Modern Burma (2001)

upsert.boundary: ASEAN's free trade area and enlargement, 1992 to 2025
upsert.description: The ASEAN Free Trade Area (January 1992) begins cutting tariffs among members; after Brunei (1984), Vietnam (1995), Laos and Myanmar (1997) and Cambodia (1999) join, uniting the region's ten states, and Timor-Leste joins as the eleventh in October 2025. The economic community (2015) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership with China, Japan, Korea, Australia and New Zealand (signed 2020) widen the market, while the ASEAN way leaves Myanmar's coup and the South China Sea unresolved.
provenance: sources to check: ASEAN Secretariat, ASEAN Integration Report; Acharya (2014)

upsert.boundary: Austronesian seafarers reach the Philippines and the islands south, about 2200 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: From Taiwan, voyagers bring red-slipped pottery to the Cagayan valley of Luzon (Nagsabaran) and spread into Borneo, Sulawesi, the Moluccas and Java; their languages replace earlier ones almost everywhere in the islands, while genomes show they mixed with the people already there; rice, important in Taiwan, drops out of many island economies.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the 'out of Taiwan' account is widely held but its pace and the role of earlier island networks are debated
sources to check: Bellwood, First Islanders (2017); Hung et al. 2011, Antiquity 85
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi, the Moluccas)

upsert.boundary: British Malaya: tin, rubber and migrant workers, 1874 to 1941
upsert.description: The Pangkor treaty (1874) puts British residents beside the Malay sultans; Chinese miners make Malaya the world's largest producer of tin, and from about 1900 Tamil workers from India tap rubber on estates that make it the largest producer of rubber too; by 1931 Malays are fewer than half of the peninsula's people, the plural society that independent Malaysia inherits.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Drabble, An Economic History of Malaysia (2000)

upsert.boundary: Burma becomes independent, 4 January 1948
upsert.description: Aung San, who turned the Burma National Army from Japan's side to the Allies' in 1945, agrees independence with Attlee (January 1947) and the Panglong agreement with Shan, Kachin and Chin leaders (February 1947), but is assassinated with most of his cabinet in July 1947. Burma leaves the empire as a republic outside the Commonwealth under U Nu.
provenance: sources to check: Thant Myint-U, The River of Lost Footsteps (2006); Charney, A History of Modern Burma (2009)

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's Asia group, batch 2 of 4: 31 Events of Asia (and some shared with Europe and Oceania) now name the processes they change, by the same rules as batch 1: wars name war deaths by kind, empires the largest polity or the share under a state, conquest and independence colonial rule (the Spanish Philippines keeps its religion links and adds it), the first farmers foraging, hunger deaths for the Soviet famine, Sikhism the share in other faiths (h.religion-6 counts Jewish and other), the Vedic varna order hereditary rank, Uruk the largest city, the Tokugawa spread of reading literacy, the 2004 tsunami injury deaths, the oil shocks the stores burned and the trade in primary goods. Only process_ids change; every other field is restated unchanged.

upsert.boundary: The Burma–Siam railway, 1942 to 1943
upsert.description: To supply its army in Burma, Japan builds a 415-kilometre railway from Ban Pong in Thailand to Thanbyuzayat in Burma with about 60,000 Allied prisoners of war and perhaps 200,000 or more Asian labourers, Tamils, Malays, Burmese, Javanese and Chinese. About 12,000 of the prisoners and perhaps 70,000 to 90,000 or more of the Asian labourers die of overwork, cholera, starvation and beatings.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Asian labourers' numbers and deaths are uncertain
sources to check: Kratoska (ed.), The Thailand–Burma Railway 1942–1946 (2006)

upsert.boundary: Cambodia's civil war and the American bombing, 1970 to 1975
upsert.description: Lon Nol deposes Prince Sihanouk (March 1970), and American and South Vietnamese troops strike North Vietnamese bases across the border. Sihanouk allies with the Khmer Rouge, whose army grows from a few thousand to tens of thousands, while American bombers drop hundreds of thousands of tonnes of bombs on the countryside until August 1973, killing perhaps 50,000 to 150,000, a debated range. About 250,000 to 300,000 or more die in the war in all, and refugees swell Phnom Penh to two million before it falls (17 April 1975).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; bombing tonnage and deaths are debated
sources to check: Kiernan, How Pol Pot Came to Power (2nd ed. 2004); Chandler, A History of Cambodia (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: China's war on Vietnam, February to March 1979
upsert.description: To punish Vietnam for invading Cambodia and allying with the Soviet Union, Deng Xiaoping sends some 200,000 troops into northern Vietnam (17 February 1979); after a month of fighting that kills tens of thousands on both sides and razes Lang Son and other border towns, China withdraws, claiming its lesson taught. Border clashes go on through the 1980s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; casualty figures are disputed by both sides
sources to check: Zhang Xiaoming, Deng Xiaoping's Long War (2015)

upsert.boundary: The Cultivation System in Java, 1830 to 1870
upsert.description: Villages must grow coffee, sugar, indigo and other export crops on part of their land or give labour to the government, which pays them little and sells the crops in Amsterdam; the surplus sent home pays for about a third of the Dutch state's revenue in the 1850s, while rice land is squeezed and famines strike Cirebon (1844) and Demak and Grobogan (1849 to 1850).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how much it impoverished Java is debated
sources to check: Elson, Village Java under the Cultivation System (1994); Fasseur, The Politics of Colonial Exploitation (1992)

upsert.boundary: Dien Bien Phu and the Geneva conference, March to July 1954
upsert.description: Viet Minh divisions under Vo Nguyen Giap, with artillery hauled over the hills, besiege and take the French fortress of Dien Bien Phu (13 March to 7 May 1954). At Geneva (21 July) France agrees to leave; Vietnam is divided at the 17th parallel pending elections that are never held, and Laos and Cambodia are confirmed independent.
provenance: sources to check: Logevall, Embers of War (2012)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia); Europe (Western Europe: France, Switzerland)

upsert.boundary: Doi Moi: Vietnam's reform and opening, from 1986
upsert.description: Facing hunger, inflation of several hundred per cent and the loss of Soviet aid, the Communist Party's Sixth Congress (December 1986) adopts 'renovation': farm households get their land and harvests (1988), prices are freed, and private firms and foreign investment are allowed. Vietnam turns from importing rice to being one of the largest exporters (from 1989), joins ASEAN (1995) and the WTO (2007), and by the 2020s assembles a large share of the world's phones and electronics; extreme poverty falls from about half of the people to a few per cent. Laos's New Economic Mechanism (1986) follows the same path.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, Vietnam 2035 (2016); Beresford, 'Doi Moi in review', Journal of Contemporary Asia 38 (2008)

upsert.boundary: Bronze drums, iron and the first trade with India and China, about 500 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: Dong Son chiefs on the Red River cast great bronze drums that travel as far as eastern Indonesia; iron spreads; Sa Huynh jar burials hold ornaments of Taiwanese jade; Indian beads and pottery reach the Thai-Malay peninsula; Han China conquers the Red River delta (111 BCE).
provenance: sources to check: Higham (2014); Bellina 2014, in Asian Perspectives

upsert.boundary: The classical kingdoms: Angkor, Pagan, Dai Viet and Java, 802 to 1350
upsert.description: Jayavarman II founds Angkor (802); the Sailendras build Borobudur; Pagan unites the Irrawaddy (1044) and turns to Theravada Buddhism; Vietnam wins independence from China (938) and builds a Confucian state; Dai Viet and Champa repel the Mongols (1258 to 1288); Tai peoples move south and found Sukhothai (1238); Majapahit rises in Java (1293). These charter states set the frames of the mainland's later nations.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; 'charter era' is Lieberman's term
sources to check: Lieberman, Strange Parallels, vol. 1 (2003)

upsert.boundary: Colonial conquest and export economies, 1824 to 1941
upsert.description: Britain conquers Burma in three wars (1824 to 1885) and the Malay states; the Dutch subdue Java (1830) and Aceh (1904); France takes Indochina (1858 to 1907); the United States takes the Philippines (1898 to 1902); Siam alone stays independent. Rice frontiers open in the great deltas, Malaya produces most of the world's rubber and tin, Java's people quadruple, Chinese and Indian migrants come by the million, and nationalist movements form from 1908.
provenance: sources to check: Tarling (ed.), The Cambridge History of Southeast Asia, vol. 2 (1992); Owen (ed.), The Emergence of Modern Southeast Asia (2005)

upsert.boundary: Ayutthaya, Malacca and the age of commerce, 1350 to 1700
upsert.description: Ayutthaya (1351) and Lan Xang (1353) rise as Angkor declines; Malacca (about 1400) becomes the great entrepot of Asian trade and turns Muslim, and Islam spreads through the islands; Vietnam expels the Ming (1428) and pushes south; the Portuguese take Malacca (1511), Spain Manila (1571) and the Dutch Batavia (1619); Toungoo Burma conquers the western mainland; pepper, cloves and nutmeg sell across the world until the Dutch monopolies and wars of the 1600s close the age of commerce.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; 'the age of commerce' is Reid's term and its end is debated
sources to check: Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce 1450-1680 (1988, 1993)

upsert.boundary: Consolidated kingdoms and the companies, 1700 to 1824
upsert.description: On the mainland three states absorb their neighbours: Konbaung Burma (from 1752), which sacks Ayutthaya (1767); the Chakri kingdom of Siam, with its capital at Bangkok (1782); and the Nguyen Vietnam that the Tay Son wars leave behind (1802). In the islands the Dutch company rules Java's coasts and trade until it is dissolved (1799); Britain takes Penang (1786) and founds Singapore (1819); Tambora's eruption (1815) cools the world.
provenance: sources to check: Lieberman (2003); Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Early states and Indic kingship, about 100 to 802
upsert.description: Port states and river kingdoms grow on the trade between India and China: Funan on the Mekong delta, Champa on the Vietnamese coast, the Pyu cities of the Irrawaddy, the Mon towns of Dvaravati, Chenla in Cambodia and, from 671, Srivijaya on the Strait; their rulers take up Sanskrit, Hindu gods and Buddhism, while northern Vietnam stays under Chinese rule.
provenance: sources to check: Tarling (ed.), The Cambridge History of Southeast Asia, vol. 1 (1992); Coedes, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia (1968)

upsert.boundary: Farmers and seafarers from the north, about 2500 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Rice and millet farmers from southern China, probably speaking Austroasiatic languages, move into the river valleys of the mainland, and Austronesian speakers from Taiwan sail to the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi and beyond; ancient genomes show both mixing with the foragers already there. Bronze-working begins on the mainland about 1100 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Lipson et al. 2018, Science 361; McColl et al. 2018, Science 361; Bellwood (2017)

upsert.boundary: Peace, growth and ASEAN, 1979 to 2025
upsert.description: Once the Cambodian war ends (1989 to 1991) the region becomes one of the world's fastest-growing: Vietnam's reforms (1986), export factories in Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia, and Singapore's rise among the richest countries; extreme poverty falls from about half of the people to a few per cent; the Philippines (1986) and Indonesia (1998) end their dictatorships while Myanmar's army rules, opens and seizes power again (2021); oil palm and logging clear much of Borneo and Sumatra; ASEAN grows to eleven members.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, World Development Indicators; Owen (2005)

upsert.boundary: Holocene foragers and the drowning of Sundaland, about 10,000 to 2500 BCE
upsert.description: The rising sea floods the Sunda shelf, making Borneo, Sumatra and Java islands and opening the Java Sea and the Strait of Malacca; Hoabinhian foragers live in the hills and rock shelters of the mainland, and island peoples on forest, sago and the sea.
provenance: sources to check: Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014); Bellwood, First Islanders (2017)

upsert.boundary: Modern humans on Sunda and Wallacea, about 70,000 to 12,000 years ago
upsert.description: Homo sapiens arrives, perhaps by 70,000 years ago (Lida Ajer, Tam Pa Ling) and certainly by 45,000 (Niah Cave); foragers live in rainforest and on coasts, cross Wallacea's straits to Sahul, paint the oldest known figurative art in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo and fish the deep sea off Timor. At the glacial maximum Sundaland's land area is about twice today's.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dates are debated
sources to check: Westaway et al. 2017, Nature 548; Barker et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution 52

upsert.boundary: Japanese occupation, revolutions and wars, 1941 to 1979
upsert.description: Japan conquers the whole region (1941 to 1942), and famine and forced labour kill millions; after its surrender Vietnam and Indonesia declare independence and fight France and the Netherlands; the Philippines (1946), Burma (1948), Malaya (1957) and the rest become independent; the Indochina wars draw in the United States; Indonesia's army and its allies kill half a million or more in 1965 to 1966; the Khmer Rouge rule Cambodia until Vietnam invades (January 1979).

upsert.boundary: South-eastern Asia escapes mass poverty, 1979 to 2025
upsert.description: Once the wars end, the region's economies grow among the world's fastest: output per person roughly quadruples in Indonesia and Thailand and grows about sixfold in Vietnam from 1990, Singapore becomes one of the richest places on Earth, and the share of the region's people below the World Bank's extreme-poverty line falls from about half in the early 1980s to a few per cent by the 2020s. The Asian crisis of 1997 to 1998 interrupts it, and the Philippines, Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia lag.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; growth multiples and poverty shares are approximate
sources to check: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform; Maddison Project Database 2023; World Bank, The East Asian Miracle (1993)

upsert.boundary: Modern humans reach Sunda, about 70,000 to 45,000 years ago
upsert.description: Teeth from Lida Ajer in Sumatra, dated to 73,000 to 63,000 years ago, and remains from Tam Pa Ling in Laos suggest Homo sapiens arrived before the main dispersal out of Africa, while the Niah Cave skull in Borneo (about 40,000 years ago) is the oldest firm modern skull; living people's genomes, which all share the Neanderthal admixture of about 47,000 years ago, fit a later arrival, so the early dates and the genomes are still being reconciled.
provenance: exploring: an early arrival is debated against the genomic timing
sources to check: Westaway et al. 2017, Nature 548; Demeter et al. 2015, Journal of Human Evolution 84; Barker et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution 52

upsert.boundary: France conquers Indochina, 1858 to 1907
upsert.description: A Franco-Spanish fleet attacks Da Nang (1858); France takes Cochinchina (1862 to 1867), makes Cambodia a protectorate (1863), takes Tonkin and Annam in wars with Vietnam and China (1883 to 1885), forms the Indochinese Union (1887), takes Laos from Siam (1893) and western Cambodia's provinces (1907).
provenance: sources to check: Brocheux and Hémery, Indochina: An Ambiguous Colonization (2009)

upsert.boundary: Miracle rice: the green revolution in South-east Asia, 1966 to 1990
upsert.description: The International Rice Research Institute at Los Baños in the Philippines, founded by the Ford and Rockefeller foundations (1960), releases IR8 (November 1966), a short-stemmed rice that doubles yields with fertilizer and irrigation; with its successors it spreads across Asia, and Indonesia, the world's largest rice importer in the 1970s, becomes self-sufficient by 1984. Farmers without irrigation or credit gain less, and pests and pesticide use grow.
provenance: sources to check: Hazell, The Asian Green Revolution (IFPRI, 2009); IRRI histories
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines, Indonesia, and across rice-growing Asia)

upsert.boundary: Sukarno's Guided Democracy, 1957 to 1966
upsert.description: Regional rebellions (1957 to 1958) and martial law end Indonesia's parliamentary democracy; Sukarno restores the 1945 constitution (1959) and rules by balancing the army against the growing Communist Party (PKI), seizes Dutch firms (1957) and West New Guinea (1962), confronts Malaysia, and lets inflation run past 600% a year by 1965. It ends in the crisis of 1965 and Suharto's order of 11 March 1966.
provenance: sources to check: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia (4th ed. 2008); Feith, The Decline of Constitutional Democracy in Indonesia (1962)

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's Asia group, batch 3 of 4: 22 Events of South-eastern Asia now name the processes they change. Its periods (ev.sea.era.*) name the subregion's share of humanity, which each moves, and the world process their description turns on; the forced cultivation of Java and the Burma–Siam railway name compelled work; Doi Moi and the escape from poverty name the share in extreme poverty; miracle rice names staple calories; Sukarno's Guided Democracy, about 100 million people leaving competitive elections, names contestation. Only process_ids change; every other field is restated unchanged.

upsert.boundary: Japan conquers and occupies South-east Asia, December 1941 to August 1945
upsert.description: Japanese forces land in Thailand and Malaya on 8 December 1941 and within five months take Malaya, Singapore, the Dutch East Indies, Burma and the Philippines; Thailand allies with Japan and French Indochina is occupied under Vichy's administration. The occupiers requisition rice, conscript labour, back nationalist leaders such as Sukarno and Ba Maw and arm and drill young men (PETA in Java, the Burma Independence Army). Famine in northern Vietnam and Java, forced labour and the fighting kill perhaps three to five million people across the region; the totals are poorly documented and debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the regional death toll is uncertain
sources to check: Kratoska, The Japanese Occupation of Malaya 1941–1945 (1998); Owen (ed.), The Emergence of Modern Southeast Asia (2005); Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia (4th ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Forced labour and hunger in occupied Java, 1943 to 1945
upsert.description: The occupation government conscripts millions of Javanese as romusha, labourers for railways, airfields and fortifications in Java and across the region, some 270,000 of them sent beyond Java, of whom few return; it requisitions rice at fixed prices, and hunger spreads through 1944 and 1945. Estimates of the deaths from hunger and forced labour run from several hundred thousand to over two million; the figures are poorly documented and contested.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; numbers mobilized and dead are contested
sources to check: Sato, War, Nationalism and Peasants: Java under the Japanese Occupation (1994); Ricklefs (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Java War, 1825 to 1830
upsert.description: Prince Diponegoro of Yogyakarta, claiming a mission to purify Java under Islam, leads a war against the Dutch and the courts that serve them; some 200,000 Javanese die, mostly of famine and disease, and 15,000 colonial soldiers, until Diponegoro is seized at a parley and exiled. The war's cost leads the Dutch to the Cultivation System.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Javanese toll is an estimate
sources to check: Carey, The Power of Prophecy (2007)

upsert.boundary: The secret war and the bombing of Laos, 1964 to 1973
upsert.description: As North Vietnam runs the Ho Chi Minh Trail through eastern Laos, the United States flies some 580,000 bombing missions and drops about two million tonnes of bombs on the country, more per person than on any other, while the CIA arms a Hmong army under Vang Pao against the Pathet Lao. Unexploded cluster bombs still kill and maim. The Pathet Lao take power in December 1975, and tens of thousands of Hmong flee to Thailand.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; tonnage figures vary by source
sources to check: Kurlantzick, A Great Place to Have a War (2017); Stuart-Fox, A History of Laos (1997)

upsert.boundary: Sundaland at the glacial maximum, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: With the sea about 120 metres lower, Java, Sumatra and Borneo form one land with the mainland, about twice today's area; drier climate may open a corridor of savanna through its centre that separates the rainforests of the west and the east, which is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the savanna corridor is debated
sources to check: Bird, Taylor and Hunt 2005, Quaternary Science Reviews 24; Wurster et al. 2010, PNAS 107

upsert.boundary: Rice and millet farmers settle mainland South-east Asia, about 2500 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: Villages with rice, millet, pigs and pottery appear at Man Bac in Vietnam and Khok Phanom Di and Ban Non Wat in Thailand; ancient genomes show farmers of East Asian ancestry arriving and mixing with Hoabinhian foragers, and Austroasiatic languages, among them Vietnamese and Khmer, probably spread with them. How much the farmers moved and how much the foragers adopted farming is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the balance of migration and adoption is debated
sources to check: McColl et al. 2018, Science 361; Lipson et al. 2018, Science 361; Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014)

upsert.boundary: Marcos's martial law and dictatorship, 1972 to 1986
upsert.description: Ferdinand Marcos, barred from a third term, declares martial law (September 1972), closes Congress and the press and rules by decree; tens of thousands are detained, thousands tortured and some 3,000 killed, and the Marcos family and its cronies take over monopolies and borrow abroad. When Benigno Aquino returns from exile and is shot at Manila's airport (August 1983), the debt crisis and outrage turn business, the Church and young officers against the regime.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; counts of victims follow Amnesty International's estimates as usually cited
sources to check: McCoy, Closer than Brothers (1999); Abinales and Amoroso (2017)

upsert.boundary: The great cities: Jakarta, Manila and Bangkok, 1950 to 2025
upsert.description: As deaths fall and the countryside fills, migrants crowd the capitals: greater Jakarta grows from under two million people to about 30 million or more, greater Manila to over 25 million, and Bangkok's region to some 15 million, many in informal settlements on flood-prone land; the region's urban share rises from about 15% to about half. Jakarta sinks as its groundwater is pumped, and Indonesia begins building a new capital, Nusantara, in Borneo (2022).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; metropolitan totals depend on where the boundary is drawn
sources to check: UN, World Urbanization Prospects (2018); Demographia World Urban Areas
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand)

upsert.boundary: Malaya becomes independent, 31 August 1957
upsert.description: The Federation of Malaya becomes independent under Tunku Abdul Rahman's Alliance of Malay, Chinese and Indian parties, on a bargain that keeps the Malay rulers and a special position for Malays and gives citizenship to most Chinese and Indians; British and Commonwealth troops stay to finish the Emergency.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: Myanmar's coup and the civil war that follows, from 2021
upsert.description: The army arrests Aung San Suu Kyi and seizes power (1 February 2021), calling the 2020 election fraudulent; it shoots down mass protests, and a resistance of people's defence forces allied with the ethnic armies grows into a nationwide war in which, after Operation 1027 (October 2023), the regime loses much of its border territory. About three million or more are displaced, the economy and public services collapse, and the army plans a staged election from December 2025.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; displacement figures change quickly
sources to check: UNHCR operational data on Myanmar; International Crisis Group reports

upsert.boundary: Myanmar's civil wars, from 1948
upsert.description: Within months of independence the Communist Party of Burma (March 1948) and the Karen National Union (January 1949) rise against the government, later joined by Kachin, Shan, Mon and other armies of the borderlands. The army, the Tatmadaw, makes itself the guardian of the union; the fighting waxes and wanes through ceasefires from 1989 and the opium and methamphetamine economies of the borderlands, and is counted the longest-running civil war in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, Burma: Insurgency and the Politics of Ethnicity (1999); Callahan, Making Enemies (2003)

upsert.boundary: Myanmar's opening, 2010 to 2021
upsert.description: Under the army's 2008 constitution, which reserves a quarter of parliament's seats for the military, a nominally civilian government under Thein Sein frees Aung San Suu Kyi (November 2010) and other political prisoners, lifts censorship and opens the economy; mobile phones reach most people within a few years. Her party wins the elections of 2015 and 2020, and she defends the army over the Rohingya at The Hague (2019).
provenance: sources to check: Thant Myint-U, The Hidden History of Burma (2019)

upsert.boundary: Ne Win's military rule and the Burmese Way to Socialism, 1962 to 1988
upsert.description: General Ne Win seizes power (2 March 1962), nationalizes trade and industry, drives out much of the Indian community, closes the country to foreigners and rules through the army's Burma Socialist Programme Party. Once Asia's largest rice exporter, Burma becomes one of the poorest countries, and applies for least-developed status in 1987.
provenance: sources to check: Charney, A History of Modern Burma (2009); Taylor, The State in Myanmar (2009)

upsert.boundary: Suharto's New Order, 1966 to 1998
upsert.description: Taking power from Sukarno by stages (the order of 11 March 1966, president from 1967), Suharto rules through the army and Golkar. Western-trained technocrats tame inflation, and oil money from 1973 pays for schools, clinics, roads and rice self-sufficiency (1984); the share of Indonesians in poverty falls steeply. Dissent is suppressed, East Timor is occupied, and the Suharto family's businesses grow. The Asian crisis brings him down in May 1998.
provenance: sources to check: Elson, Suharto: A Political Biography (2001); Ricklefs (2008)

upsert.boundary: Oil palm and the clearing of Borneo and Sumatra, 1980 to 2025
upsert.description: Logging, pulpwood and oil palm plantations clear much of the lowland rainforest of Borneo and Sumatra: Indonesia and Malaysia come to grow about 85% of the world's palm oil, and Borneo's forest shrinks by about a third between 1973 and 2010. Fires set to clear land, on drained peat in the El Niño years of 1997 and 2015, send haze across the region and large pulses of carbon into the air; orangutans and other forest animals decline steeply.
provenance: sources to check: Gaveau et al., 'Four decades of forest persistence, clearance and logging on Borneo', PLOS ONE 9 (2014); FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment

upsert.boundary: The Philippine-American War, 1899 to 1902
upsert.description: When the United States annexes the islands it bought from Spain, Aguinaldo's republic fights; about 20,000 Filipino soldiers and 4,200 Americans are killed, and perhaps 200,000 or more civilians die of violence, famine and cholera, while fighting in the Muslim south goes on to 1913. The civilian toll is debated, with estimates up to several times higher.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the civilian toll is debated
sources to check: Linn, The Philippine War 1899 to 1902 (2000); Gates 1984, Pacific Historical Review 53

upsert.boundary: The Philippines becomes independent, 4 July 1946
upsert.description: The United States grants independence on the date the Tydings–McDuffie Act set, to a republic under Manuel Roxas. The Bell Trade Act ties its economy to the American market and gives Americans equal rights to its resources, and the agreements of 1947 keep American bases at Clark and Subic.
provenance: sources to check: Abinales and Amoroso, State and Society in the Philippines (2nd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: Rice frontiers of the great deltas, about 1850 to 1930
upsert.description: Settlers clear the swamps of the Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya and Mekong deltas for export rice: Lower Burma's rice land grows from about one million acres to about ten, and the three deltas feed India, China and Europe; peasants borrow from Chettiar and Chinese lenders, and when rice prices collapse in the Depression (1930) many lose their land.
provenance: sources to check: Adas, The Burma Delta (1974); Brocheux, The Mekong Delta (1995)

upsert.boundary: Siam keeps its independence: Mongkut's and Chulalongkorn's reforms, 1851 to 1910
upsert.description: Mongkut opens Siam to trade with the Bowring Treaty (1855); Chulalongkorn abolishes slavery and corvée step by step (1874 to 1905), builds ministries, railways and schools and brings the provinces under Bangkok, while ceding Laos, western Cambodia and the northern Malay states to France and Britain (1893 to 1909), leaving Siam a buffer between their empires and the only state in the region never colonized.
provenance: sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit, A History of Thailand (3rd ed. 2014); Wyatt, Thailand: A Short History (2nd ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: The spice islands and the world: cloves, nutmeg and pepper, about 1400 to 1650
upsert.description: Cloves from Ternate and Tidore, nutmeg and mace from the six small Banda islands, and pepper from Sumatra and west Java sell in China, India, the Middle East and Europe; their ports grow rich, Ternate's sultan Baabullah expels the Portuguese (1575), and the search for them draws the Portuguese, Spanish, English and Dutch into Asia, in what Anthony Reid calls the region's age of commerce.
provenance: sources to check: Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce (1988 and 1993); Andaya, The World of Maluku (1993)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Moluccas, Banda, Sumatra, Java)

upsert.boundary: The sea drowns Sundaland, about 12,000 to 6,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the ice sheets melt, the sea rises by some sixty metres over the Sunda shelf, in surges that flood a hundred kilometres of coast in a lifetime; Borneo, Sumatra and Java become islands, the Java Sea and the Strait of Malacca open, and the land area is halved; around 4000 BCE the sea stands a metre or two above today's.
provenance: sources to check: Hanebuth, Stattegger and Grootes 2000, Science 288; Sathiamurthy and Voris 2006

upsert.boundary: Thailand's coups and colour-coded conflict, 2006 to 2023
upsert.description: The army overthrows Thaksin Shinawatra, whose parties win every election on rural votes (September 2006); his 'red shirt' supporters and the royalist 'yellow shirts' take turns occupying Bangkok, about 90 die when the army clears the red-shirt protest (2010), and a second coup (May 2014) brings General Prayut, who rules under a constitution written to keep the army's power until 2023.
provenance: sources to check: Baker and Phongpaichit (2014)

upsert.boundary: Vietnam occupies Cambodia: the third Indochina war, 1979 to 1991
upsert.description: After Khmer Rouge raids on its border provinces, Vietnam invades (25 December 1978), takes Phnom Penh (7 January 1979) and installs a government of Khmer Rouge defectors under Heng Samrin and later Hun Sen. China, Thailand, ASEAN and the West back a coalition of the Khmer Rouge and two non-communist factions fighting from the Thai border, which keeps Cambodia's seat at the UN. Vietnam withdraws in 1989, and the Paris Peace Agreements (23 October 1991) end the war.
provenance: sources to check: Chandler, A History of Cambodia (4th ed. 2008); Westad and Quinn-Judge (eds), The Third Indochina War (2006)

upsert.boundary: Famine in northern Vietnam, 1944 to 1945
upsert.description: Japanese and French requisitions of rice, the forced planting of jute and other industrial crops, the Allied bombing of the railway and shipping from the south, and a poor harvest bring famine to Tonkin and northern Annam. About a million people die, by commonly cited estimates of 400,000 to two million. The Viet Minh's seizures of granaries win it the villages of the north.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is debated
sources to check: Gunn, Rice Wars in Colonial Vietnam (2014); Marr, Vietnam 1945 (1995)

upsert.boundary: Seafarers cross Wallacea toward Sahul, about 65,000 to 50,000 years ago
upsert.description: From Sunda's edge, groups cross the straits of Wallacea, by a northern route through Sulawesi and the Moluccas to New Guinea or a southern one through Timor to Australia, with gaps of at least 70 kilometres; to found the people of Sahul they must have crossed on purpose, on rafts or canoes, in groups of men, women and children.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the route and the date of the first crossing are debated
sources to check: Kealy, Louys and O'Connor 2018, Journal of Human Evolution 125; Bird et al. 2019, Scientific Reports 9
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Wallacea: Sulawesi, the Moluccas, Timor)

upsert.boundary: The Seven Years' War, 1756 to 1763
upsert.description: A war fought on four continents: Prussia survives Austria, France and Russia in Europe, while Britain takes Canada from France and wins in India and West Africa; the war's debts lead Britain to tax its American colonies and France toward bankruptcy.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Crucible of War (2000); Baugh, The Global Seven Years War (2011)
upsert.region: Europe; Americas (Northern America, the Caribbean); Asia (Southern Asia: India); Africa (Western Africa: Senegal)

upsert.boundary: The Toba super-eruption, about 74,000 years ago
upsert.description: A volcano in Sumatra erupts, the largest eruption of the last two million years, spreading ash across South Asia and cooling the climate for some years; whether it nearly wiped out humanity, as once argued, is doubted, since tool-makers in India and Africa carry on through it.
provenance: exploring: the eruption's effect on people is contested
sources to check: Petraglia et al. 2007, Science 317; Smith et al. 2018, Nature 555

upsert.boundary: The war on terror, 2001 to 2021
upsert.description: The United States and its allies overthrow the Taliban (2001) and Saddam Hussein (2003), fight insurgencies in both countries for years, strike jihadist groups from Pakistan to Somalia and defeat the Islamic State's territorial caliphate (2014 to 2019); the Taliban retake Afghanistan in August 2021 as the last American troops leave.
provenance: sources to check: Coll, Directorate S (2018); Brown University, Costs of War project
upsert.region: Asia (Southern Asia: Afghanistan, Pakistan; Western Asia: Iraq, Syria, Yemen); Africa (Eastern Africa: Somalia; the Sahel); Americas (Northern America); Europe

Widen, the breadth check's Asia group, batch 4 of 4: 28 Events of South-eastern Asia and some shared Events now name the processes they change. The Japanese occupation and northern Vietnam's famine name hunger deaths; the romusha compelled work; the Java, Myanmar and Philippine-American wars war deaths by kind; the Sunda drowning and the glacial maximum sea level; the megacities the urban share; oil palm and the rice frontiers tropical forest and cropland; Siam's abolition of slavery bondage; the spice trade and ASEAN exchange; the Wallacea crossings the share of humanity in Oceania; the Seven Years' War war deaths and colonial rule; Toba the Earth's temperature; the war on terror war deaths. Only process_ids change; every other field is restated unchanged.
Values at the Events the Asia links now hold these processes to.

points.note: Foragers go hungry in bad seasons but move to food; few die of starvation outright.
Held: hunger as a direct cause in foragers is seasonal and local, not famine of stored grain; a glacial maximum may push it up, which the band allows.
Farmers tied to fields and stores die when a harvest fails; famine becomes a recurring cause of death.
The 4.2 kiloyear drought: Egypt's Old Kingdom and Akkad fall amid famine (ev.event-4-2-ka, if dated so in the model).
The Han collapse and the Roman Empire's third-century crisis: wars and failed harvests together.
Lower than in the crises of the third century, before the volcanic winter of 536 and the plague.
The volcanic winter of 536 to 541, the coldest decade in two thousand years, and the plague's disruption of harvests bring dearth.
After Europe's great famine of 1315 to 1317, which killed perhaps a tenth of northern Europe's people.
The plague empties fields and stops trade: dearth follows the dying.

The Ming-Qing wars and the Thirty Years War begin; their famine and plague deaths are counted in war's toll (h.war, 180 a year to 1650), as the usual tallies of those wars count them, so hunger outside them holds at the century's level.

After Tambora's year without a summer (1816), Europe's last great subsistence crisis.
The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852, about a million dead.

The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879: perhaps 6 to 10 million dead in India, 9 to 13 million in north China, half a million in Brazil's north-east, among about 1.35 billion people. The spike is sharp and short; the band carries the debated tolls (ev.as.el-nino-famines).
The famines end with the rains of 1879; hunger deaths fall back to the level of the 1880s' lull.
A lull between the famines of the late 1870s and those of 1896 to 1902.
The Indian famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 and the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, perhaps 30 to 60 million dead in all, under El Niño droughts and colonial and imperial policy.
The Russian famine of 1921 to 1922, about five million dead.
China's north-west famine of 1928 to 1930 is under way and the Soviet famines follow from 1930: hunger deaths rise from the 1920s' level toward the 1930 peak.
The Soviet famines of 1930 to 1933, the Holodomor and the Kazakh famine among them, and China's famine of 1928 to 1930.

Corrected from 130: the siege of Leningrad and the Greek and Henan famines are counted in the Second World War's toll (h.war), as its 70 to 85 million dead usually are; here they were counted a second time. Hunger outside the war barely moves. Check: war plus hunger from 1941 to 1945 against the war's toll with its famines.

Corrected from 150: the famines of Bengal (1943), northern Vietnam and Java (1944 to 1945) and the Dutch hunger winter are counted in the war's toll (h.war). Whether Bengal's famine belongs to the war is debated (Sen's entitlement failure under wartime inflation against the loss of Burma's rice and the denial policy), but most tallies of the war's dead include it.
After the war's famines the toll falls: the Soviet famine of 1946 to 1947, about a million dead, is the largest of the postwar decade.
Between the postwar famines and the Great Leap famine, hunger deaths are at their lowest yet; the rise to 1960 is that famine's alone, so the series does not climb before 1959.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward, 1959 to 1961: 15 to 45 million excess deaths on the debated estimates, the largest famine in history.
The Great Leap famine ends in 1961 and 1962 as procurement is cut and grain imported: deaths fall back toward the level before it.
After China's famine, deaths from hunger fall to their lowest level yet; the green revolution's wheat and rice begin to spread (ev.green-revolution).
Biafra (1967 to 1970) and the Sahel droughts.
Bangladesh 1974 and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985.
North Korea's famine, 1994 to 1998.
Famine now comes almost only with war: Gaza, Sudan and Yemen.

Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The ASEAN free trade area (1992) and NAFTA (1994) begin and the former Soviet bloc opens to trade; the sum of its three parts on their paths.
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).

Before cultivation; some sedentary foragers harvesting wild cereals.
Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent (ev.as.fertile-crescent); foragers are still almost everyone.

Cultivation has begun in several centres at once: the Fertile Crescent's pre-pottery Neolithic, squash in Oaxaca, millet in north China, manioc and squash in south-western Amazonia, and soon the New Guinea highlands. Farmers are still a few in a hundred; the fall quickens only as their villages multiply, so the value lies between 98 at 9500 BCE and 92 at 7900 BCE.

Squash and maize in Mexico, millet in north China, manioc in Amazonia and the New Guinea highlands all begin about now, beside the Fertile Crescent's villages; the Holocene's warm, stable climate made cultivation possible in many places at once.
Pre-pottery Neolithic farming in the Fertile Crescent; early cultivation in China.

Rice in the Yangtze valley, Mehrgarh in Baluchistan and farmers leaving Anatolia for Europe: farming's area grows several-fold, and because farmers live far more densely, their share of people grows faster than their share of land.

Farming established in south-west Asia, Anatolia, the Yellow and Yangtze valleys and arriving in Greece; farmers already perhaps a quarter of all people because their densities were far higher. WaveOfAdvance#4cec for the spread into Europe.

Maize becomes the eastern woodlands' staple and Polynesian farmers settle the eastern Pacific, while herders and farmers keep pressing into the remaining foragers' lands in Africa and northern Eurasia.
Akkad or Old Kingdom Egypt.
New Kingdom Egypt and the Shang each rule a few million as the Bronze Age collapse begins.
Before the Achaemenid empire: Assyria, Egypt and the Zhou each rule a few million.
Cyrus takes the Median kingdom (ev.as.achaemenid); Lydia and Babylon fall to him within twelve years.
Darius rules from the Indus to Egypt and Thrace: the Achaemenid empire holds perhaps a fifth of humanity (ev.as.achaemenid).
The Achaemenid empire.
Alexander takes the Achaemenid empire whole (334 to 330 BCE): the largest polity changes hands, not size.
Ashoka's Maurya empire, over most of the subcontinent, is the largest; its people are estimated from about 15 to 50 million, a wide debate the band carries.
Qin unifies China (ev.as.qin) as the Maurya empire declines after Ashoka: each holds perhaps a sixth to a fifth of humanity.
Han China.
Rome, about 65 million of 245.
Rome, with the Han breaking up.
Rome's western half has fallen (ev.eu.rome-fall) and China is divided between north and south: no polity holds more than about a seventh of humanity.
Sui China, whose census of 609 counts about 46 million.
Tang China.
The Northern Song, perhaps 80 million of 295 million, before the Jin take the north (ev.as.song).
Southern Song after losing the north to the Jin.
The Southern Song, with the Jin close behind.
Yuan China after the fall of the Song.
Revised from 28: Yuan China holds about the same quarter of humanity as at 1279; the 28 was the coarse fill's value and rose with no cause.
Ming China, about 80 million of 350 million; the 1393 census count of 60 million is taken as an undercount.
Qing China at its population peak.
Qing China and the British Empire about equal.
India passes China as the most populous state about April 2023, on the UN's estimate (ev.as.india-most-populous): the largest polity changes, but its share holds near 17.7% across the change.
Uruk-period polities, if counted as states.
The Han and Roman empires at their height, with the Parthians, Kushans and Satavahanas, hold most of the world's people; the share falls only as the Han breaks up after 184.
The southern Maya kingdoms fail while new states form in South-east Asia (Angkor, 802) and the Abbasid and Carolingian realms hold; the share barely moves.

The Tang and Abbasid realms fragment but their people stay under states; the southern Maya kingdoms fail; Polynesians settle eastern islands without states. The share under a state barely moves between 770 and 1000.
The Triple Alliance forms in the valley of Mexico; the Ming, Timurid and Ottoman states hold most of Asia's people.
Pachacuti begins the Inca conquests: within a century about ten million Andean people come under one state.
Israelite religion and Zoroastrianism (ev.as.israel-bible, ev.as.zoroastrianism) separate from the local traditions they grew out of.
Zoroastrianism becomes the Achaemenid court's religion and Judaism takes its lasting shape in the Babylonian exile and return (ev.as.zoroastrianism, ev.as.israel-bible).
Jews of Judah and the diaspora, and Zoroastrians under the Achaemenids. The anchor of 0 at -1000 leaves Israelite religion among local traditions, a choice that could be revisited.
The Jewish diaspora spreads across the Hellenistic and Roman world, and Zoroastrianism holds Parthian Iran (ev.as.parthia).
Christianity absorbs much of the Roman world's Jewish and pagan population (ev.christianity-rise), and Buddhism and Christianity grow faster than Judaism and Zoroastrianism.
Jews expelled from Spain (1492) and Portugal (1496) move within the world, not out of their faith; Guru Nanak's teaching begins about 1499. The share holds.
Before most of the Holocaust's killing (ev.eu.holocaust).

By early 1943 most of the Holocaust's victims are dead: the death camps of Operation Reinhard and the shootings in the east killed most of them in 1942 (ev.eu.holocaust), so the Jewish share is already near its 1944 low.
By 1944 about five of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust are dead (ev.eu.holocaust): the Jewish share of humanity falls from about 0.7% to under 0.5%.

Revised from 1.95: the series did not subtract the Holocaust's six million dead, about a quarter of a point of humanity, which its own note recorded. The other seven shares rise in proportion by less than their rounding.
Revised from 2.0 with 1945, for the Holocaust's dead.
Revised from 2.0 with 1945: the share recovers only slowly after the Holocaust.
