On the eve of the green revolution's new wheats and rice; the war in Vietnam and Indonesia's crisis hold back two of Asia's poorer populations.
On the eve of China's reforms, about four in ten of the world's people, and most of China's, live in extreme poverty (ev.china-reform).
Zero among foragers, whom the account counts as holding no one in bondage.
Captives held to work among the first farmers and settled foragers, as bondage begins (h.freedom).
Corvée and temple dependants in the first states.
Egypt's corvée and the Akkadian and Ur III labour gangs.
Rome's slaves (perhaps a third of Roman Italy) and Han China's corvée: about a ninth of the world's working hours.
Serfs' labour dues in Europe, slaves in the Islamic world, corvée across Asia.
After the Black Death labour dues fade in western Europe.
The second serfdom east of the Elbe and the encomienda and mita in Spanish America.
Atlantic slavery near its height beside Russian serfdom.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery (1794), but the cotton gin (1793) opens the second slavery in the United States: compelled work falls only slowly.
Java's Cultivation System (from 1830) and the growth of slavery in Cuba, Brazil and the American South offset the first abolitions; Britain's emancipation begins only in 1834.
Britain abolishes slavery in its colonies from 1834.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs, 1861.
American slavery ends, 1865.
Brazil abolishes slavery in 1888, the last in the Americas; colonial forced labour (the Congo Free State) goes on.
War labour: prisoners of war and deported workers.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Gulag.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
The Gulag is emptied after Stalin's death (1953).
About 28 million people in forced labour by the ILO's count, under 1% of the world's working hours.
No state, so no elections of rulers.

Rises: Greek democracies and oligarchies, the Roman Republic, Carthage's elected magistrates and the gana-sangha republics of the Ganges plain, whose councils of clan heads chose their leaders; how competitive the last were is uncertain.
Roman Italy, with citizenship for all free Italians; the provinces are ruled, not represented.
Falls: the Republic gives way to the Principate.
Venice elects its doge.
The Italian communes elect their consuls.
Most Italian communes have fallen to lords (signori).
Rises: Poland-Lithuania's nobles elect their kings from 1573, and the Dutch Republic governs itself from 1581.
Britain's Parliament becomes supreme after 1688, its ministries resting on contested elections among a few percent of men.
The new United States.
Falls: Poland-Lithuania is partitioned (1795) and Napoleon takes power (1799).
France's Second Republic, with Belgium, the Netherlands, Piedmont, Denmark, Switzerland and Latin America's competitive oligarchies.
Falls: Louis-Napoleon's coup of December 1851 ends the Second Republic.
Rises: France's Third Republic (1870) and parliamentary government in united Italy.
The Weimar Republic and the new republics of central Europe.
Mussolini's dictatorship and Poland's coup of 1926.
Falls: Hitler's dictatorship from 1933.
Germany occupies most of Europe's democracies.
Liberated western Europe is under provisional governments; its first postwar elections follow from October 1945 into 1946, the rise to 1946.
Liberated western Europe and the Philippines hold elections.
Rises most: India, Japan and West Germany choose their governments in competitive elections.

Ghana and Malaya become independent with elected governments (1957), about 13 million people. Indonesia's parliamentary democracy ends from 1957 under Guided Democracy; if its 1955 election counts it among competitive polities, about three points of humanity leave, which the 1960 value's lower band carries.
India's Emergency (June 1975) has not yet begun: the fall to 1976 comes with it.
Falls: India's Emergency suspends elections (1975 to 1977), with juntas in Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; indices differ on India, hence the band.
India's election of March 1977 ends the Emergency and the Congress party loses power.
Before the revolutions of late 1989 the rise to 1990 has not yet come: most of it is Eastern Europe's free elections of 1990.
Rises: multiparty elections in Eastern Europe and Latin America's return to elected government.
Indonesia's first free election since 1955 (1999).
Falls slowly as elections lose their competitiveness in several large countries; whether some (India, Turkey) still count is debated, which the band carries.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the populations of republics, competitive oligarchies and parliamentary regimes at each date (as recalled), divided by the world's people.

points.note: Raids and ambushes between bands, the main form of forager war in Keeley's and Bowles's readings. Fry and Soderberg argue most forager killings are personal, not between groups, which would move part of the parent's deep values to homicide; the band carries that debate.
Wars of conquest between the first states and against their neighbours.
The Three Kingdoms counted as fighting between polities; that they were the fragments of one fallen empire makes this a matter of definition.
The Arab conquests.
The Mongol conquests' battles and sieges; their massacres of cities are counted as one-sided.
The Hundred Years War and Timur's campaigns from 1370.
The Italian wars, the Ottoman conquests and the conquest of Mexico and Peru.
The Manchu conquest of Ming China and the Thirty Years War. The parent's value appears to include these wars' famine and plague deaths, which belong to hunger and infection.
The Qing conquest of the south and the Swedish Deluge in Poland.
The Great Turkish War and the Nine Years War.
The Great Northern War and the War of the Spanish Succession.
The Seven Years War.
The French Revolutionary wars.
Corrected from 8 with the parent: the Napoleonic wars' first campaigns and the Russo-Persian war.
The Napoleonic wars' deadliest years, the Russo-Turkish war and the War of 1812.
Now 1820 to 1826: Burma's first war with Britain begins (1824); the Mfecane wars in southern Africa, whose toll is debated.
1826 to 1840: the Russo-Persian and Russo-Turkish wars (1826 to 1829), France's conquest of Algeria from 1830 and the Egyptian–Ottoman wars.
1840 to 1850: the first Opium War, the first Anglo-Afghan and the Anglo-Sikh wars and the Mexican–American War. With the earlier points the 1820 to 1850 average stays near 3.
The Crimean war.
Held across 1850 to 1859 (the Crimean war, 1853 to 1856, and the Second Opium War); restated so the parts add up at 1856.
The Paraguayan, Franco-Prussian and Russo-Turkish wars and colonial conquests.
The Boer, Philippine-American and Russo-Japanese wars.
Now averaged to 1912: the Italo-Turkish war (1911 to 1912).
1912 to 1914.6: the two Balkan wars (October 1912 to August 1913). With 1910's point the average stays 4.
The First World War.
The Polish-Soviet and Greco-Turkish wars.
Now averaged to 1933: Japan takes Manchuria (1931 to 1933) and the Chaco War begins (1932).
1933 to 1936: the Chaco War's last years and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1935 to 1936).

Revised from 14, which held the 1930 to 1939.7 average flat: 1936 to 1939.7 holds Japan's full war on China from July 1937 (Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan) and the Soviet–Japanese border battles. With 1930 and 1933 the 1930 to 1939.7 average of 14 is kept.
The Second World War's deadliest years: the Eastern Front, the Pacific war and China.
Turns down for good: the Long Peace between great powers begins, and fighting between polities never again reaches a tenth of the world wars' rate. The Indochina war and the first Arab-Israeli war.
Revised from 10 with the parent: the Korean War, now averaged to 1954.2.
The Indo-Pakistani war of December 1971, with the Vietnam war.
Averaged to the next date; the 1971.96 rate held: the October War of 1973 and the Vietnam war's last two years.
The Ogaden war.
China's war on Vietnam and Tanzania's on Uganda.
Held across 1979 to 1980: China's war on Vietnam, Tanzania's on Uganda and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan at the year's end; restated so the parts add up.
The Iran-Iraq war.
The Gulf war.
The Eritrean-Ethiopian war.
The invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq.
Now averaged to October 2023: Nagorno-Karabakh (2020) and Russia's invasion of Ukraine from February 2022.

October 2023 to 2025: the war in Ukraine at its deadliest and the war in Gaza and Lebanon. Counting the Gaza war between polities follows the usual coding of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict as one over territory; counting it within a polity would move about a quarter of this value to the next series. The 2020 to 2025 average stays 0.6.

upsert.reason: The parent's value at each date split by what kind of organized killing filled that stretch, from the wars its notes name; before 1800 the split is a sketch.

points.note: Massacres of whole camps; Nataruk by Lake Turkana, about 8000 BCE, is the earliest well-dated case.
Farmers' villages can be wiped out whole: the Neolithic massacres at Talheim and Schletz about 5000 BCE.
The first states kill and deport conquered peoples, as the Assyrian reliefs later boast.
The Mongols kill the people of cities that resist: Merv and Nishapur in 1221, Baghdad in 1258.
Timur's massacres from the 1370s.
Massacres in the conquest of the Americas; most of the Americas' dead died of disease, counted under infection.
Zhang Xianzhong's killings in Sichuan, the Qing massacres at Yangzhou, the sack of Magdeburg.
The Qing's destruction of the Dzungars, 1755 to 1758, perhaps half a million or more killed, averaged here over 1750 to 1780.
1826 to 1840: the Indian removals in the United States and the reprisals after the Baptist War; small at world scale.
1840 to 1850: killings in the conquest of Algeria and, from 1848, the California gold rush's killings of Native Californians. The 1820 to 1850 average stays near 0.5.
Held across 1850 to 1859; restated so the parts add up at 1856.
Massacres in the Dungan revolt and its suppression.
The Herero and Nama genocide, 1904 to 1908.
Unchanged across 1910 to 1914.6; restated so the parts add up at 1912.
The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1916, with the Assyrian and Greek killings.
Pogroms in Ukraine and the Red and White terrors.
The Nanjing massacre and, if the parent counts it, part of the Soviet Great Terror of 1937 to 1938, about 680,000 shot; whether the parent's 25 includes the Terror is not recorded.
Held across 1930 to 1939.7, as the parent's note leaves open whether the Great Terror (1937 to 1938) is counted; restated so the parts add up at 1933.
German and Soviet killings in occupied Poland.
Rises most: the Holocaust's deadliest years, the killing of Soviet prisoners and civilians in the occupied east, and Japanese massacres in China and South-east Asia.
The murder of Hungary's Jews at Auschwitz in 1944.
Falls: the camps are liberated between July 1944 and May 1945; killings of prisoners and civilians go on in the war's last months, in the death marches and in Asia.
Partition's communal killings, 1947.

As the parent counts it. China's land reform and campaign against counter-revolutionaries, 1950 to 1953, killed perhaps one to two million or more, which would add 4 to 8 to the decade's average; whether the parent counts such campaigns is open.
The killings in Indonesia.
The Cultural Revolution's killings, perhaps half a million to a million and a half in 1966 to 1971, are not in the parent's value; open, as for China's campaigns of the early 1950s.
The killings in Bangladesh, March to December 1971.

Revised from 0.5, which was below the rate of even the lowest count. Burundi's army and Tutsi militias kill some 100,000 to 300,000 Hutu, above all the educated, from April to about August 1972; at 150,000 that is about 2.1 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over the 1.8 years to October 1973. Amin's killings in Uganda (1971 to 1979, estimates from 100,000 to 500,000, about 0.8 a year at a middle reading) add the rest; earlier passes had left them out at every date.
Amin's killings in Uganda continue; no other mass killing of civilians on this scale until the Khmer Rouge's and East Timor's in 1975.
Revised from 7 to add Amin's killings in Uganda, about 0.8, to the Khmer Rouge's executions and East Timor.
Revised from 7 with Uganda.

Guatemala's highland massacres and Uganda.
Burundi 1993, Bosnia.

Srebrenica, 1995.
Darfur from 2003.
The Islamic State's killings of Yazidis and others.
Held across 2020 to 2025; restated so the parts add up.

Villages and chiefdoms can split and fight within themselves.
Rebellions and succession wars in the first states.
The Roman civil wars.
The Yellow Turban rising and the warlord wars at the Han's end.

The wars of the Sui-Tang transition and, from 755, the An Lushan rebellion.

The Red Turbans and the Yuan's collapse.

Russia's Time of Troubles and Japan's last wars of unification.
The rebellions of Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong that brought down the Ming, and the English and Fronde civil wars.
Falls: the Ming has fallen and the great rebel armies are destroyed; the Qing conquest of the south is counted between polities.
The Revolt of the Three Feudatories.
The Vendee, the Haitian revolution and the White Lotus rebellion.
Revised from 1.5 with the parent: Saint-Domingue's war against Leclerc and the White Lotus rebellion's last years.
The wars of Latin American independence from 1810.

Held across 1850 to 1859: the Taiping war, the Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and Mexico's War of the Reform; restated so the parts add up at 1856.
The Taiping war's deadliest years and the American Civil War. The parent's value appears to include the Taiping war's famine and disease deaths.

Algeria's war of independence and Colombia's Violencia.
The Vietnam war's civil side, the Congo crisis and Biafra.

Angola, Lebanon, Ethiopia.

Syria, Iraq and Yemen.

The killings in Indonesia (ev.sea.indonesia-1965): about half a million killed, by estimates from 400,000 to a million or more, in some nine months, about 20 per 100,000 a year of the world's people on top of the Vietnam war's 6. The 1960s decade reading had left them out, so its average rises from 6 to about 7.5.

Pakistan's army begins its crackdown in East Pakistan on 25 March 1971; to the surrender at Dhaka on 16 December, killings of Bengalis, above all Hindus, students and intellectuals, and the Indo-Pakistani war of December. The dead are debated: about 270,000 violent deaths by a survey-based estimate (Obermeyer and others, 2008), 300,000 to 500,000 in many scholarly accounts, 1.5 million in Rummel's, 3 million in Bangladesh's official figure. Taken here as about 500,000, some 18 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over nine months, with the Vietnam war's 3. The parent's 1970 reading had left it out.

Revised from 5, now averaged to the October War of 1973: the Vietnam war 2.5, civil wars 2, and one-sided killing 3, chiefly Burundi's of 1972, which the earlier value counted at below its lowest estimate, and Amin's in Uganda, which it left out.
The October War of 1973 and the oil shock that follows it (ev.oil-shocks); the Vietnam war's last years, civil wars and Amin's killings carry the rate to the fall of Saigon.

Revised from 11 to add Amin's killings in Uganda, about 0.8. The Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh (ev.as.khmer-rouge): perhaps a million of their 1.5 to 2 million victims are executed or killed outright, about 6.5 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over 3.7 years; deaths from hunger and disease in the labour camps are not counted here. Angola, Lebanon, East Timor and Ethiopia add about 4.5.
Revised from 11 with Uganda: the Khmer Rouge's killings continue until January 1979.
Vietnam ends the Khmer Rouge regime (January 1979); China's war on Vietnam, Afghanistan's and Uganda's carry the rate to 1980.
Held across 1979 to 1980, the sum of its parts.
To 1990: the end of the Iran–Iraq war, Afghanistan.
Now averages 1990 to April 1994: the Gulf war, the Bosnian and Somali wars, Afghanistan, Angola and Algeria.

The Rwandan genocide, 7 April to mid-July 1994. Estimates run from about 500,000 (Human Rights Watch) through 600,000 to 800,000 in most scholarly work to over a million in Rwanda's own count of victims; taken here as about 650,000 in a hundred days, some 43 per 100,000 a year of the world's people, with other wars at about 1.5. The parent's 1990 reading had left it out.
After the genocide: Chechnya, Bosnia to 1995, Angola, Algeria, Afghanistan and Burundi carry the rate to 1996.
To 2000: the Congo wars, Eritrea–Ethiopia.
Averaged to the next date; the 2000 rate held: Afghanistan, Iraq and Congo.
To 2020: Syria, Iraq, Yemen.
Now averaged to October 2023, the sum of its parts: Tigray, Ukraine from 2022, Myanmar, Yemen.
October 2023 to 2025, the sum of its parts: Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon, Sudan, Myanmar. The 2020 to 2025 average stays 2.

changes.value: The last four processes passing over Events after the Asia links.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
On the eve of the green revolution's new wheats and rice; the war in Vietnam and Indonesia's crisis hold back two of Asia's poorer populations.
On the eve of China's reforms, about four in ten of the world's people, and most of China's, live in extreme poverty (ev.china-reform).
China's rural reforms begin (1978 to 1979) and South-east Asia's wars end; the great fall in extreme poverty starts from here.
No state, so no elections of rulers.

Rises: Greek democracies and oligarchies, the Roman Republic, Carthage's elected magistrates and the gana-sangha republics of the Ganges plain, whose councils of clan heads chose their leaders; how competitive the last were is uncertain.
Roman Italy, with citizenship for all free Italians; the provinces are ruled, not represented.
Falls: the Republic gives way to the Principate.
Venice elects its doge.
The Italian communes elect their consuls.
Most Italian communes have fallen to lords (signori).
Rises: Poland-Lithuania's nobles elect their kings from 1573, and the Dutch Republic governs itself from 1581.
Britain's Parliament becomes supreme after 1688, its ministries resting on contested elections among a few percent of men.
The new United States.
Falls: Poland-Lithuania is partitioned (1795) and Napoleon takes power (1799).
France's Second Republic, with Belgium, the Netherlands, Piedmont, Denmark, Switzerland and Latin America's competitive oligarchies.
Falls: Louis-Napoleon's coup of December 1851 ends the Second Republic.
Rises: France's Third Republic (1870) and parliamentary government in united Italy.
The Weimar Republic and the new republics of central Europe.
Mussolini's dictatorship and Poland's coup of 1926.
Falls: Hitler's dictatorship from 1933.
Germany occupies most of Europe's democracies.
Liberated western Europe is under provisional governments; its first postwar elections follow from October 1945 into 1946, the rise to 1946.
Liberated western Europe and the Philippines hold elections.
Rises most: India, Japan and West Germany choose their governments in competitive elections.

Ghana and Malaya become independent with elected governments (1957), about 13 million people. Indonesia's parliamentary democracy ends from 1957 under Guided Democracy; if its 1955 election counts it among competitive polities, about three points of humanity leave, which the 1960 value's lower band carries.

Burma's army takes power (1962) and Brazil's (1964), about 100 million people leaving competitive elections, while new African and Caribbean states hold their first elections; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
India's Emergency (June 1975) has not yet begun: the fall to 1976 comes with it.
Falls: India's Emergency suspends elections (1975 to 1977), with juntas in Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; indices differ on India, hence the band.
India's election of March 1977 ends the Emergency and the Congress party loses power.
Before the revolutions of late 1989 the rise to 1990 has not yet come: most of it is Eastern Europe's free elections of 1990.
Rises: multiparty elections in Eastern Europe and Latin America's return to elected government.
Indonesia's first free election since 1955 (1999).
Falls slowly as elections lose their competitiveness in several large countries; whether some (India, Turkey) still count is debated, which the band carries.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the populations of republics, competitive oligarchies and parliamentary regimes at each date (as recalled), divided by the world's people.

points.note: Raids and ambushes between bands, the main form of forager war in Keeley's and Bowles's readings. Fry and Soderberg argue most forager killings are personal, not between groups, which would move part of the parent's deep values to homicide; the band carries that debate.
Wars of conquest between the first states and against their neighbours.
The Three Kingdoms counted as fighting between polities; that they were the fragments of one fallen empire makes this a matter of definition.
The Arab conquests.
The Mongol conquests' battles and sieges; their massacres of cities are counted as one-sided.
The Hundred Years War and Timur's campaigns from 1370.
The Italian wars, the Ottoman conquests and the conquest of Mexico and Peru.
The Manchu conquest of Ming China and the Thirty Years War. The parent's value appears to include these wars' famine and plague deaths, which belong to hunger and infection.
The Qing conquest of the south and the Swedish Deluge in Poland.
The Great Turkish War and the Nine Years War.
The Great Northern War and the War of the Spanish Succession.
The Seven Years War.
The French Revolutionary wars.
Corrected from 8 with the parent: the Napoleonic wars' first campaigns and the Russo-Persian war.

1826 to 1840: the Russo-Persian and Russo-Turkish wars (1826 to 1829), France's conquest of Algeria from 1830 and the Egyptian–Ottoman wars.
1840 to 1850: the first Opium War, the first Anglo-Afghan and the Anglo-Sikh wars and the Mexican–American War. With the earlier points the 1820 to 1850 average stays near 3.
The Crimean war.
Held across 1850 to 1859 (the Crimean war, 1853 to 1856, and the Second Opium War); restated so the parts add up at 1856.
The Paraguayan, Franco-Prussian and Russo-Turkish wars and colonial conquests.
The Boer, Philippine-American and Russo-Japanese wars.
Now averaged to 1912: the Italo-Turkish war (1911 to 1912).
Held across 1910 to 1912, the Italo-Turkish war; restated so the parts add up at 1911.
1912 to 1914.6: the two Balkan wars (October 1912 to August 1913). With 1910's point the average stays 4.
The First World War.
The Polish-Soviet and Greco-Turkish wars.
Now averaged to 1933: Japan takes Manchuria (1931 to 1933) and the Chaco War begins (1932).
1933 to 1936: the Chaco War's last years and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1935 to 1936).

Revised from 14, which held the 1930 to 1939.7 average flat: 1936 to 1939.7 holds Japan's full war on China from July 1937 (Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan) and the Soviet–Japanese border battles. With 1930 and 1933 the 1930 to 1939.7 average of 14 is kept.
The Second World War's deadliest years: the Eastern Front, the Pacific war and China.
Turns down for good: the Long Peace between great powers begins, and fighting between polities never again reaches a tenth of the world wars' rate. The Indochina war and the first Arab-Israeli war.
Revised from 10 with the parent: the Korean War, now averaged to 1954.2.
The Indo-Pakistani war of December 1971, with the Vietnam war.
Averaged to the next date; the 1971.96 rate held: the October War of 1973 and the Vietnam war's last two years.
The Ogaden war.
China's war on Vietnam and Tanzania's on Uganda.
Held across 1979 to 1980: China's war on Vietnam, Tanzania's on Uganda and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan at the year's end; restated so the parts add up.
The Iran-Iraq war.
The Gulf war.
The Eritrean-Ethiopian war.
The invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq.
Now averaged to October 2023: Nagorno-Karabakh (2020) and Russia's invasion of Ukraine from February 2022.

October 2023 to 2025: the war in Ukraine at its deadliest and the war in Gaza and Lebanon. Counting the Gaza war between polities follows the usual coding of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict as one over territory; counting it within a polity would move about a quarter of this value to the next series. The 2020 to 2025 average stays 0.6.

points.note: Massacres of whole camps; Nataruk by Lake Turkana, about 8000 BCE, is the earliest well-dated case.
Farmers' villages can be wiped out whole: the Neolithic massacres at Talheim and Schletz about 5000 BCE.
The first states kill and deport conquered peoples, as the Assyrian reliefs later boast.
The Mongols kill the people of cities that resist: Merv and Nishapur in 1221, Baghdad in 1258.
Timur's massacres from the 1370s.
Massacres in the conquest of the Americas; most of the Americas' dead died of disease, counted under infection.
Zhang Xianzhong's killings in Sichuan, the Qing massacres at Yangzhou, the sack of Magdeburg.
The Qing's destruction of the Dzungars, 1755 to 1758, perhaps half a million or more killed, averaged here over 1750 to 1780.
1826 to 1840: the Indian removals in the United States and the reprisals after the Baptist War; small at world scale.
1840 to 1850: killings in the conquest of Algeria and, from 1848, the California gold rush's killings of Native Californians. The 1820 to 1850 average stays near 0.5.
Held across 1850 to 1859; restated so the parts add up at 1856.
Massacres in the Dungan revolt and its suppression.
The Herero and Nama genocide, 1904 to 1908.
Held across 1910 to 1912; restated so the parts add up at 1911.
Unchanged across 1910 to 1914.6; restated so the parts add up at 1912.
The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1916, with the Assyrian and Greek killings.
Pogroms in Ukraine and the Red and White terrors.
The Nanjing massacre and, if the parent counts it, part of the Soviet Great Terror of 1937 to 1938, about 680,000 shot; whether the parent's 25 includes the Terror is not recorded.
Held across 1930 to 1939.7, as the parent's note leaves open whether the Great Terror (1937 to 1938) is counted; restated so the parts add up at 1933.
German and Soviet killings in occupied Poland.
Rises most: the Holocaust's deadliest years, the killing of Soviet prisoners and civilians in the occupied east, and Japanese massacres in China and South-east Asia.
The murder of Hungary's Jews at Auschwitz in 1944.
Falls: the camps are liberated between July 1944 and May 1945; killings of prisoners and civilians go on in the war's last months, in the death marches and in Asia.
Partition's communal killings, 1947.

As the parent counts it. China's land reform and campaign against counter-revolutionaries, 1950 to 1953, killed perhaps one to two million or more, which would add 4 to 8 to the decade's average; whether the parent counts such campaigns is open.
The killings in Indonesia.
The Cultural Revolution's killings, perhaps half a million to a million and a half in 1966 to 1971, are not in the parent's value; open, as for China's campaigns of the early 1950s.
The killings in Bangladesh, March to December 1971.

Revised from 0.5, which was below the rate of even the lowest count. Burundi's army and Tutsi militias kill some 100,000 to 300,000 Hutu, above all the educated, from April to about August 1972; at 150,000 that is about 2.1 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over the 1.8 years to October 1973. Amin's killings in Uganda (1971 to 1979, estimates from 100,000 to 500,000, about 0.8 a year at a middle reading) add the rest; earlier passes had left them out at every date.
Amin's killings in Uganda continue; no other mass killing of civilians on this scale until the Khmer Rouge's and East Timor's in 1975.
Revised from 7 to add Amin's killings in Uganda, about 0.8, to the Khmer Rouge's executions and East Timor.
Revised from 7 with Uganda.
Held across 1979 to 1980; restated so the parts add up.
Guatemala's highland massacres and Uganda.
Burundi 1993, Bosnia.
Rises most since 1945: the Rwandan genocide.
Srebrenica, 1995.
Darfur from 2003.
The Islamic State's killings of Yazidis and others.
Held across 2020 to 2025; restated so the parts add up.

upsert.reason: The parent's value at each date split by what kind of organized killing filled that stretch. It holds the one-sided killings the parent counts; China's campaigns of 1950 to 1953 and the Cultural Revolution's killings are not in the parent and so not here.

points.note: Zero by definition among bands: killings within the band are homicide, and fights between bands of one people are between polities.
Villages and chiefdoms can split and fight within themselves.
Rebellions and succession wars in the first states.
The Roman civil wars.
The Yellow Turban rising and the warlord wars at the Han's end.
Falls: by 200 the warlord wars give way to the Three Kingdoms, whose wars are counted between polities.
The wars of the Sui-Tang transition and, from 755, the An Lushan rebellion.
The Tang's decline and Huang Chao's rising.
The Red Turbans and the Yuan's collapse.
Japan's Sengoku wars and France's wars of religion.
Russia's Time of Troubles and Japan's last wars of unification.
The rebellions of Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong that brought down the Ming, and the English and Fronde civil wars.
Falls: the Ming has fallen and the great rebel armies are destroyed; the Qing conquest of the south is counted between polities.
The Revolt of the Three Feudatories.
The Vendee, the Haitian revolution and the White Lotus rebellion.
Revised from 1.5 with the parent: Saint-Domingue's war against Leclerc and the White Lotus rebellion's last years.
The wars of Latin American independence from 1810.
Split from 2.5 for 1820 to 1850, now 1820 to 1826: the last campaigns of Latin American independence (Ayacucho, 1824) and the Greek war of independence.
1826 to 1840: the caudillo wars, the Java War (1825 to 1830) and the First Carlist War in Spain (1833 to 1840).
1840 to 1850: the Caste War of Yucatán, the revolutions of 1848; the Taiping war begins only in 1850. With the points at 1820 and 1826, the 1820 to 1850 average stays near 2.5.
Rises most: the Taiping war, with the Nian and Panthay risings and the Indian rebellion of 1857.
Held across 1850 to 1859: the Taiping war, the Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and Mexico's War of the Reform; restated so the parts add up at 1856.
The Taiping war's deadliest years and the American Civil War. The parent's value appears to include the Taiping war's famine and disease deaths.
The Dungan revolt and the Nian.

The Russian Civil War.
China's warlord and civil wars.
The Spanish and Chinese civil wars.

Civil wars inside the world war: Yugoslavia, Greece, and the communists and nationalists in China.
The Chinese civil war. From here fighting within polities carries most war deaths.
Algeria's war of independence and Colombia's Violencia.
The Vietnam war's civil side, the Congo crisis and Biafra.
Averaged to the next date; the 1971.96 rate held.
Angola, Lebanon, Ethiopia.
Afghanistan.

Afghanistan, Central America, Ethiopia, Mozambique.
Bosnia, Somalia, Angola, Algeria, Afghanistan, Tajikistan.
The Congo wars.
Syria, Iraq and Yemen.

The last three gaps after the Asia links: colonial rule at the Raj's start, contestation at Marcos's martial law, and war at Japan's attack in December 1941 (the war's rates held, restated so the parts add up).

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
No state, so no elections of rulers.

France's Second Republic, with Belgium, the Netherlands, Piedmont, Denmark, Switzerland and Latin America's competitive oligarchies.

Rises: France's Third Republic (1870) and parliamentary government in united Italy.

Liberated western Europe and the Philippines hold elections.
Rises most: India, Japan and West Germany choose their governments in competitive elections.

Ghana and Malaya become independent with elected governments (1957), about 13 million people. Indonesia's parliamentary democracy ends from 1957 under Guided Democracy; if its 1955 election counts it among competitive polities, about three points of humanity leave, which the 1960 value's lower band carries.

Burma's army takes power (1962) and Brazil's (1964), about 100 million people leaving competitive elections, while new African and Caribbean states hold their first elections; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Marcos's martial law (1972) takes the Philippines, about 1% of humanity, out of competitive elections; Chile's and Uruguay's coups follow in 1973.
India's Emergency (June 1975) has not yet begun: the fall to 1976 comes with it.
Falls: India's Emergency suspends elections (1975 to 1977), with juntas in Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; indices differ on India, hence the band.
India's election of March 1977 ends the Emergency and the Congress party loses power.
Before the revolutions of late 1989 the rise to 1990 has not yet come: most of it is Eastern Europe's free elections of 1990.
Rises: multiparty elections in Eastern Europe and Latin America's return to elected government.
Indonesia's first free election since 1955 (1999).
Falls slowly as elections lose their competitiveness in several large countries; whether some (India, Turkey) still count is debated, which the band carries.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

Averaged to the next date: the 1940 rate held, so the 1940–1945.7 average is conserved.
To 1950: the Chinese Civil War and Partition.
Averaged to the next date; the 1945.7 rate held: the Chinese civil war and Partition.
Averaged to the next date; the 1945.7 rate held: the Chinese civil war and the first Arab–Israeli war.
Revised from 14, now averaged to 1954.2: the Korean War, about 2.5 to 3 million dead in three years, falls here. With 1954.2's 5.3 the 1950–1960 average of 14 is conserved.
Averaged to 1960: after Korea's armistice, the end of the French Indochina war, Algeria's war and Colombia's Violencia.
Averaged to the next date: the 1960 rate held, so the 1960–1970 average is conserved; Vietnam and the 1965 Indo-Pakistani war fall here.

The killings in Indonesia (ev.sea.indonesia-1965): about half a million killed, by estimates from 400,000 to a million or more, in some nine months, about 20 per 100,000 a year of the world's people on top of the Vietnam war's 6. The 1960s decade reading had left them out, so its average rises from 6 to about 7.5.
The killings end by mid-1966; the Vietnam war's rate, held from 1960, continues.
Averaged to the next date; the 1966.5 rate held: the Vietnam war, with the Tet offensive, and Biafra.
Now averages 1970 to March 1971: the Vietnam war and Cambodia's civil war.

Pakistan's army begins its crackdown in East Pakistan on 25 March 1971; to the surrender at Dhaka on 16 December, killings of Bengalis, above all Hindus, students and intellectuals, and the Indo-Pakistani war of December. The dead are debated: about 270,000 violent deaths by a survey-based estimate (Obermeyer and others, 2008), 300,000 to 500,000 in many scholarly accounts, 1.5 million in Rummel's, 3 million in Bangladesh's official figure. Taken here as about 500,000, some 18 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over nine months, with the Vietnam war's 3. The parent's 1970 reading had left it out.

Revised from 5, now averaged to the October War of 1973: the Vietnam war 2.5, civil wars 2, and one-sided killing 3, chiefly Burundi's of 1972, which the earlier value counted at below its lowest estimate, and Amin's in Uganda, which it left out.
The October War of 1973 and the oil shock that follows it (ev.oil-shocks); the Vietnam war's last years, civil wars and Amin's killings carry the rate to the fall of Saigon.

Revised from 11 to add Amin's killings in Uganda, about 0.8. The Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh (ev.as.khmer-rouge): perhaps a million of their 1.5 to 2 million victims are executed or killed outright, about 6.5 per 100,000 a year of the world's people over 3.7 years; deaths from hunger and disease in the labour camps are not counted here. Angola, Lebanon, East Timor and Ethiopia add about 4.5.
Revised from 11 with Uganda: the Khmer Rouge's killings continue until January 1979.
Vietnam ends the Khmer Rouge regime (January 1979); China's war on Vietnam, Afghanistan's and Uganda's carry the rate to 1980.
Held across 1979 to 1980, the sum of its parts.
To 1990: the end of the Iran–Iraq war, Afghanistan.
Now averages 1990 to April 1994: the Gulf war, the Bosnian and Somali wars, Afghanistan, Angola and Algeria.

The Rwandan genocide, 7 April to mid-July 1994. Estimates run from about 500,000 (Human Rights Watch) through 600,000 to 800,000 in most scholarly work to over a million in Rwanda's own count of victims; taken here as about 650,000 in a hundred days, some 43 per 100,000 a year of the world's people, with other wars at about 1.5. The parent's 1990 reading had left it out.
After the genocide: Chechnya, Bosnia to 1995, Angola, Algeria, Afghanistan and Burundi carry the rate to 1996.
To 2000: the Congo wars, Eritrea–Ethiopia.
Averaged to the next date; the 2000 rate held: Afghanistan, Iraq and Congo.
To 2020: Syria, Iraq, Yemen.
Now averaged to October 2023, the sum of its parts: Tigray, Ukraine from 2022, Myanmar, Yemen.
Held across 2020 to October 2023, the sum of its parts.
October 2023 to 2025, the sum of its parts: Ukraine, Gaza and Lebanon, Sudan, Myanmar. The 2020 to 2025 average stays 2.

changes.value: The last gap: colonial rule between 1910 and 1914.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

changes.value: 9c972bdd65f750827b0b2dcd2bacb51ac69eadc4426b27626a4d8642b7a019e0
Colonial rule at the exact date of the three Events of 8 December 1941.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

Of the 274 Events placed in Asia, 124 more now name the processes they change (r256 to r259), and values were added where the links found the processes silent (r260 to r269), until the coverage report again found none passing over its Events. Every kind of change the group showed already had a process: war deaths by kind (the Opium, Korean, Iran–Iraq, Indochina and Syrian wars, the Armenian genocide, the Cultural Revolution, Partition), hunger deaths (Bengal, the El Niño famines, northern Vietnam, the Soviet famine), colonial rule (the Company, the Raj, the VOC, French Indochina, Japan's Korea, the independences of 1946 to 1957), the largest polity and the share under a state (Akkad, Assyria, Maurya, Sui, Ming, Yuan), foraging (the Fertile Crescent, millet, rice, Mehrgarh, the Austronesian and mainland farmers), Asia's output (Japan's miracle, the tigers, the Asian crisis), extreme poverty (Doi Moi, the New Order, the region's escape from poverty), compelled work (the Cultivation System, the romusha, the Burma railway), bondage and rank (Joseon's slaves and yangban, the Vedic varnas, Siam's abolition), sea level (Sundaland), tropical forest (oil palm) and South-eastern Asia's share of humanity. About 126 judged for Asia stay unlinked: dynasties and courts whose change is in who rules rather than in any world measure (the Parthians, Sasanians, Seljuks, Kushans, Heian, Kamakura, Joseon's founding is linked but the Zhou conquest is not), single battles, sieges and treaties (Constantinople 1453, Bach Dang, Malacca's fall, the Six-Day War), cities and monuments (Angkor, Borobudur, Çatalhöyük, Göbekli Tepe), inventions whose world-scale effect comes through other Events (paper, printing, the Hangul alphabet, the house of wisdom) and archaic humans before Homo sapiens (the Denisovans, floresiensis, luzonensis, the last erectus), whom humanity's measures do not count.
