Values at the Events the Africa links now hold these processes to; exchange is restated with its three parts so they still add up.

points.note: Foragers go hungry in bad seasons but move to food; few die of starvation outright.
Held: hunger as a direct cause in foragers is seasonal and local, not famine of stored grain; a glacial maximum may push it up, which the band allows.
Farmers tied to fields and stores die when a harvest fails; famine becomes a recurring cause of death.
The 4.2 kiloyear drought: Egypt's Old Kingdom and Akkad fall amid famine (ev.event-4-2-ka, if dated so in the model).
The Han collapse and the Roman Empire's third-century crisis: wars and failed harvests together.
Lower than in the crises of the third century, before the volcanic winter of 536 and the plague.
The volcanic winter of 536 to 541, the coldest decade in two thousand years, and the plague's disruption of harvests bring dearth.
After Europe's great famine of 1315 to 1317, which killed perhaps a tenth of northern Europe's people.
The plague empties fields and stops trade: dearth follows the dying.

The Ming-Qing wars and the Thirty Years War begin; their famine and plague deaths are counted in war's toll (h.war, 180 a year to 1650), as the usual tallies of those wars count them, so hunger outside them holds at the century's level.

Corrected from 220, which counted the famines of the Ming-Qing transition and the Thirty Years War that war's toll (h.war) already counts. What remains is the Little Ice Age's own dearths. Check: at 1618 to 1650 the six causes of death no longer count those wars' famine deaths twice.
After Tambora's year without a summer (1816), Europe's last great subsistence crisis.
The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852, about a million dead.

The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879: perhaps 6 to 10 million dead in India, 9 to 13 million in north China, half a million in Brazil's north-east, among about 1.35 billion people. The spike is sharp and short; the band carries the debated tolls (ev.as.el-nino-famines).
The famines end with the rains of 1879; hunger deaths fall back to the level of the 1880s' lull.

Rinderpest kills most of the cattle of eastern and southern Africa from 1888, and Ethiopia's great famine (1888 to 1892) kills perhaps a third of its people: a bump in the world's rate between the El Niño famines of the 1870s and the 1890s.
A lull between the famines of the late 1870s and those of 1896 to 1902.
The Indian famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 and the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, perhaps 30 to 60 million dead in all, under El Niño droughts and colonial and imperial policy.
The Russian famine of 1921 to 1922, about five million dead.
China's north-west famine of 1928 to 1930 is under way and the Soviet famines follow from 1930: hunger deaths rise from the 1920s' level toward the 1930 peak.
The Soviet famines of 1930 to 1933, the Holodomor and the Kazakh famine among them, and China's famine of 1928 to 1930.
The Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933 at its worst: five to seven million dead in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Russia among about 2.08 billion people (ev.eu.holodomor).
The Soviet famine ends with the harvest of 1933; hunger deaths fall back.

Corrected from 130: the siege of Leningrad and the Greek and Henan famines are counted in the Second World War's toll (h.war), as its 70 to 85 million dead usually are; here they were counted a second time. Hunger outside the war barely moves. Check: war plus hunger from 1941 to 1945 against the war's toll with its famines.

Corrected from 150: the famines of Bengal (1943), northern Vietnam and Java (1944 to 1945) and the Dutch hunger winter are counted in the war's toll (h.war). Whether Bengal's famine belongs to the war is debated (Sen's entitlement failure under wartime inflation against the loss of Burma's rice and the denial policy), but most tallies of the war's dead include it.
After the war's famines the toll falls: the Soviet famine of 1946 to 1947, about a million dead, is the largest of the postwar decade.
Between the postwar famines and the Great Leap famine, hunger deaths are at their lowest yet; the rise to 1960 is that famine's alone, so the series does not climb before 1959.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward, 1959 to 1961: 15 to 45 million excess deaths on the debated estimates, the largest famine in history.
The Great Leap famine ends in 1961 and 1962 as procurement is cut and grain imported: deaths fall back toward the level before it.
After China's famine, deaths from hunger fall to their lowest level yet; the green revolution's wheat and rice begin to spread (ev.green-revolution).
Biafra (1967 to 1970) and the Sahel droughts.
Bangladesh 1974 and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985.
North Korea's famine, 1994 to 1998.
Famine now comes almost only with war: Gaza, Sudan and Yemen.

Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
Shell beads and finished tools passed between bands.
Textiles and metalwork from the first cities' workshops.
Chinese silk, Roman glass and fine pottery, Indian cloth.
Song porcelain and silk carried by sea to South-east Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Indian cotton cloth floods European and West African markets (the calico craze).
British machine-made cotton goods replace Indian cloth in world markets.
Lend-lease arms and machines are much of wartime trade.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now, as Europe's and Japan's industries trade with one another.
East Asia's export manufacturing and the trade in parts between factories.
Global value chains: a phone's parts cross many borders before it is sold.
Goods hold up in the pandemic (medical supplies, electronics for home working) while travel stops.
On the path between the pandemic's goods boom and 2025.
Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Grain, beef, coffee and sugar from the Americas and wool from Australia flow to Europe as freight rates fall; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Oil, gas, grain and fertilizer prices jump in 2022 with the war in Ukraine; primary goods' share of trade's value rises with them.
Zero: nothing is sold between bands apart from goods.
Shipping and caravan services begin to be paid apart from the goods they carry: a sliver.
Italian merchant banks and the carrying trade of Venice and Genoa sell finance and freight.
Dutch shipping carries much of Europe's trade: the Republic sells freight and insurance.
Steamship freight, marine insurance and London's finance: about a twelfth of trade.
Travel, shipping and finance resume after the war: about an eighth of trade.
Travel stops in the pandemic: services fall about a fifth while goods hold.
Travel recovers from the pandemic; digital services keep growing.
About a quarter of trade: travel recovered, business and digital services growing fastest.
Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The ASEAN free trade area (1992) and NAFTA (1994) begin and the former Soviet bloc opens to trade; the sum of its three parts on their paths.
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).
Trade recovers from the pandemic and its value peaks as energy and food prices jump after Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the sum of its three parts.

changes.value: The eight processes the Africa links left passing over Events. Fighting within polities from 1870 to 1890 is split by what happened in each part, keeping the span's average, and the whole is restated; exchange in 2021 is restated with its three parts; mobile herders take a value on the path between their neighbours so the parts of Settling down still add up.

points.note: Foragers go hungry in bad seasons but move to food; few die of starvation outright.
Held: hunger as a direct cause in foragers is seasonal and local, not famine of stored grain; a glacial maximum may push it up, which the band allows.
Farmers tied to fields and stores die when a harvest fails; famine becomes a recurring cause of death.
The 4.2 kiloyear drought: Egypt's Old Kingdom and Akkad fall amid famine (ev.event-4-2-ka, if dated so in the model).
The Han collapse and the Roman Empire's third-century crisis: wars and failed harvests together.
Lower than in the crises of the third century, before the volcanic winter of 536 and the plague.
The volcanic winter of 536 to 541, the coldest decade in two thousand years, and the plague's disruption of harvests bring dearth.
After Europe's great famine of 1315 to 1317, which killed perhaps a tenth of northern Europe's people.
The plague empties fields and stops trade: dearth follows the dying.

The Ming-Qing wars and the Thirty Years War begin; their famine and plague deaths are counted in war's toll (h.war, 180 a year to 1650), as the usual tallies of those wars count them, so hunger outside them holds at the century's level.

Corrected from 220, which counted the famines of the Ming-Qing transition and the Thirty Years War that war's toll (h.war) already counts. What remains is the Little Ice Age's own dearths. Check: at 1618 to 1650 the six causes of death no longer count those wars' famine deaths twice.
After Tambora's year without a summer (1816), Europe's last great subsistence crisis.
The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852, about a million dead.

The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879: perhaps 6 to 10 million dead in India, 9 to 13 million in north China, half a million in Brazil's north-east, among about 1.35 billion people. The spike is sharp and short; the band carries the debated tolls (ev.as.el-nino-famines).
The famines end with the rains of 1879; hunger deaths fall back to the level of the 1880s' lull.
The lull between the El Niño famines and those of 1888 onward in Ethiopia and the 1890s in India.

Rinderpest kills most of the cattle of eastern and southern Africa from 1888, and Ethiopia's great famine (1888 to 1892) kills perhaps a third of its people: a bump in the world's rate between the El Niño famines of the 1870s and the 1890s.
A lull between the famines of the late 1870s and those of 1896 to 1902.
The Indian famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 and the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, perhaps 30 to 60 million dead in all, under El Niño droughts and colonial and imperial policy.
The Russian famine of 1921 to 1922, about five million dead.
China's north-west famine of 1928 to 1930 is under way and the Soviet famines follow from 1930: hunger deaths rise from the 1920s' level toward the 1930 peak.
The Soviet famines of 1930 to 1933, the Holodomor and the Kazakh famine among them, and China's famine of 1928 to 1930.
The Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933 at its worst: five to seven million dead in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Russia among about 2.08 billion people (ev.eu.holodomor).
The Soviet famine ends with the harvest of 1933; hunger deaths fall back.

Corrected from 130: the siege of Leningrad and the Greek and Henan famines are counted in the Second World War's toll (h.war), as its 70 to 85 million dead usually are; here they were counted a second time. Hunger outside the war barely moves. Check: war plus hunger from 1941 to 1945 against the war's toll with its famines.

Corrected from 150: the famines of Bengal (1943), northern Vietnam and Java (1944 to 1945) and the Dutch hunger winter are counted in the war's toll (h.war). Whether Bengal's famine belongs to the war is debated (Sen's entitlement failure under wartime inflation against the loss of Burma's rice and the denial policy), but most tallies of the war's dead include it.
After the war's famines the toll falls: the Soviet famine of 1946 to 1947, about a million dead, is the largest of the postwar decade.
Between the postwar famines and the Great Leap famine, hunger deaths are at their lowest yet; the rise to 1960 is that famine's alone, so the series does not climb before 1959.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward, 1959 to 1961: 15 to 45 million excess deaths on the debated estimates, the largest famine in history.
The Great Leap famine ends in 1961 and 1962 as procurement is cut and grain imported: deaths fall back toward the level before it.
After China's famine, deaths from hunger fall to their lowest level yet; the green revolution's wheat and rice begin to spread (ev.green-revolution).
Biafra (1967 to 1970) and the Sahel droughts.
Bangladesh 1974 and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985.
North Korea's famine, 1994 to 1998.
Famine now comes almost only with war: Gaza, Sudan and Yemen.

Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
Shell beads and finished tools passed between bands.
Textiles and metalwork from the first cities' workshops.
Chinese silk, Roman glass and fine pottery, Indian cloth.
Song porcelain and silk carried by sea to South-east Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Indian cotton cloth floods European and West African markets (the calico craze).
British machine-made cotton goods replace Indian cloth in world markets.
Lend-lease arms and machines are much of wartime trade.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now, as Europe's and Japan's industries trade with one another.
East Asia's export manufacturing and the trade in parts between factories.
Global value chains: a phone's parts cross many borders before it is sold.
Goods hold up in the pandemic (medical supplies, electronics for home working) while travel stops.
The goods boom of the pandemic's second year.
On the path between the pandemic's goods boom and 2025.
Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Grain, beef, coffee and sugar from the Americas and wool from Australia flow to Europe as freight rates fall; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Commodity prices recover from the pandemic's low.
Oil, gas, grain and fertilizer prices jump in 2022 with the war in Ukraine; primary goods' share of trade's value rises with them.
Zero: nothing is sold between bands apart from goods.
Shipping and caravan services begin to be paid apart from the goods they carry: a sliver.
Italian merchant banks and the carrying trade of Venice and Genoa sell finance and freight.
Dutch shipping carries much of Europe's trade: the Republic sells freight and insurance.
Steamship freight, marine insurance and London's finance: about a twelfth of trade.
Travel, shipping and finance resume after the war: about an eighth of trade.
Travel stops in the pandemic: services fall about a fifth while goods hold.
Travel still mostly closed; digital and business services grow.
Travel recovers from the pandemic; digital services keep growing.
About a quarter of trade: travel recovered, business and digital services growing fastest.
Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The ASEAN free trade area (1992) and NAFTA (1994) begin and the former Soviet bloc opens to trade; the sum of its three parts on their paths.
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).
Goods trade rebounds from the pandemic while travel is still closed; the sum of its three parts.
Trade recovers from the pandemic and its value peaks as energy and food prices jump after Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the sum of its three parts.
Before cultivation; some sedentary foragers harvesting wild cereals.
Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent (ev.as.fertile-crescent); foragers are still almost everyone.

Cultivation has begun in several centres at once: the Fertile Crescent's pre-pottery Neolithic, squash in Oaxaca, millet in north China, manioc and squash in south-western Amazonia, and soon the New Guinea highlands. Farmers are still a few in a hundred; the fall quickens only as their villages multiply, so the value lies between 98 at 9500 BCE and 92 at 7900 BCE.

Squash and maize in Mexico, millet in north China, manioc in Amazonia and the New Guinea highlands all begin about now, beside the Fertile Crescent's villages; the Holocene's warm, stable climate made cultivation possible in many places at once.
Pre-pottery Neolithic farming in the Fertile Crescent; early cultivation in China.

Rice in the Yangtze valley, Mehrgarh in Baluchistan and farmers leaving Anatolia for Europe: farming's area grows several-fold, and because farmers live far more densely, their share of people grows faster than their share of land.

Farming established in south-west Asia, Anatolia, the Yellow and Yangtze valleys and arriving in Greece; farmers already perhaps a quarter of all people because their densities were far higher. WaveOfAdvance#4cec for the spread into Europe.

Bantu-speaking farmers begin to move out of West Africa's borderlands, and rice and millet farmers and Austronesian seafarers reach South-east Asia: the last great farming expansions into lands held by foragers.

Maize becomes the eastern woodlands' staple and Polynesian farmers settle the eastern Pacific, while herders and farmers keep pressing into the remaining foragers' lands in Africa and northern Eurasia.
Roman Italy perhaps a third enslaved; most of the world far less.
Serfdom loosening in western Europe after the plague and tightening in the east; slavery across the Islamic world, Africa and South-east Asia.
Enslavement in the Caribbean and the first Atlantic shipments of Africans add little at world scale yet.
Brazil's sugar slavery grows and the first enslaved Africans reach Virginia (1619), while serfdom tightens in Russia and Poland; at world scale the share in bondage holds near 9%.

The sugar revolution begins in Barbados; Russia's Ulozhenie (1649) binds its peasants for good. Growth in Atlantic slavery and eastern serfdom is offset by a world population still recovering from the 1600s' crises.

The Atlantic slave trade near its peak, about 80,000 people a year, and serfdom extended to Ukraine (1783), while the American Revolution opens the age of revolutions whose language of liberty will be turned against slavery.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery in 1794, while the cotton gin (1793) begins the expansion of slavery in the United States and the slave trade still runs near its peak.

Haiti's independence (1804) ends slavery for about half a million people, while Usman dan Fodio's jihad (from 1804) founds the Sokoto caliphate on plantation slavery; at world scale the share drifts down.
Russian serfdom ends in 1861, American slavery in 1865, Brazilian in 1888.
A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
Mostly the Soviet camps and colonial forced labour.
No domestic animals, so no herders.
Begins: goat and sheep herders of the Zagros and Taurus may already move between seasonal pastures; whether any households were fully mobile this early is debated.
On the path between its neighbours: cattle herding begins in the eastern Sahara and sheep and goat herders move with farmers into Europe.
Cattle herders range across the green Sahara, the largest mobile herding population of the age.
Rises: the Yamnaya move with ox-wagons and herds across the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and their descendants spread east and west; the Sahara's herders move south as it dries.
The camel is domesticated in Arabia, opening the deserts to herders.
Mounted nomadism on the steppe: herders ride, range far and raid settled states.
The Xiongnu unite the eastern steppe and press Han China.
Huns and Avars in the west, the Rouran and Turks in the east; camel-herding Berbers cross the Sahara.
The Mongols unite the steppe: perhaps one or two million herders build the largest land empire.
Up a little: the Black Death kills more of the settled, crowded peoples than of the herders.
Herders pass mobile foragers as the larger part of the mobile between 1600 and 1650.
The Qing destroy the Dzungars (1755 to 1758) and Russia advances on the Kazakh steppe: states begin to settle and tax the herders.
Russian peasants settle the Kazakh steppe and France conquers the Sahara's herders; rinderpest kills most of East Africa's cattle in the 1890s.
Falls faster: Soviet collectivization forces the Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Turkmen nomads to settle (1928 to 1934); the famine that follows kills perhaps a third of the Kazakhs.
Mongolia's herders are collectivized, Tibet's herds taken into communes, and new states in the Middle East and Africa push herders to settle.
The Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s drive many herders into towns and camps; Africa's fast-growing herding peoples keep the share from falling faster.
Perhaps 10 to 60 million people: estimates differ because many households now move only part of the family with the herds.
Zero among foragers, whom the account counts as holding no one in bondage.
Captives held to work among the first farmers and settled foragers, as bondage begins (h.freedom).
Corvée and temple dependants in the first states.
Egypt's corvée and the Akkadian and Ur III labour gangs.
Rome's slaves (perhaps a third of Roman Italy) and Han China's corvée: about a ninth of the world's working hours.
Serfs' labour dues in Europe, slaves in the Islamic world, corvée across Asia.
After the Black Death labour dues fade in western Europe.
The second serfdom east of the Elbe and the encomienda and mita in Spanish America.
Atlantic slavery near its height beside Russian serfdom.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery (1794), but the cotton gin (1793) opens the second slavery in the United States: compelled work falls only slowly.
Java's Cultivation System (from 1830) and the growth of slavery in Cuba, Brazil and the American South offset the first abolitions; Britain's emancipation begins only in 1834.
Britain abolishes slavery in its colonies from 1834.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs, 1861.
American slavery ends, 1865.
Cuba's slaves become 'apprentices' (1880) and Brazil's slavery is ending; colonial forced labour is about to grow in Africa.
Leopold's Congo Free State (from 1885) imposes forced rubber collection, while Cuba's last slaves are freed (1886) and Brazil's follow in 1888.
Brazil abolishes slavery in 1888, the last in the Americas; colonial forced labour (the Congo Free State) goes on.
War labour: prisoners of war and deported workers.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Gulag.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
The Gulag is emptied after Stalin's death (1953).
About 28 million people in forced labour by the ILO's count, under 1% of the world's working hours.

Raids and ambushes between bands, the main form of forager war in Keeley's and Bowles's readings. Fry and Soderberg argue most forager killings are personal, not between groups, which would move part of the parent's deep values to homicide; the band carries that debate.
Wars of conquest between the first states and against their neighbours.
The Three Kingdoms counted as fighting between polities; that they were the fragments of one fallen empire makes this a matter of definition.
The Arab conquests.
The Mongol conquests' battles and sieges; their massacres of cities are counted as one-sided.
The Hundred Years War and Timur's campaigns from 1370.
The Italian wars, the Ottoman conquests and the conquest of Mexico and Peru.
The Manchu conquest of Ming China and the Thirty Years War. The parent's value appears to include these wars' famine and plague deaths, which belong to hunger and infection.
The Qing conquest of the south and the Swedish Deluge in Poland.
The Great Turkish War and the Nine Years War.
The Great Northern War and the War of the Spanish Succession.
The Seven Years War.
The French Revolutionary wars.
Corrected from 8 with the parent: the Napoleonic wars' first campaigns and the Russo-Persian war.
The Napoleonic wars' deadliest years, the Russo-Turkish war and the War of 1812.
Now 1820 to 1826: Burma's first war with Britain begins (1824); the Mfecane wars in southern Africa, whose toll is debated.
1826 to 1840: the Russo-Persian and Russo-Turkish wars (1826 to 1829), France's conquest of Algeria from 1830 and the Egyptian–Ottoman wars.
1840 to 1850: the first Opium War, the first Anglo-Afghan and the Anglo-Sikh wars and the Mexican–American War. With the earlier points the 1820 to 1850 average stays near 3.
The Crimean war.
Held across 1850 to 1859 (the Crimean war, 1853 to 1856, and the Second Opium War); restated so the parts add up at 1856.
The Paraguayan, Franco-Prussian and Russo-Turkish wars and colonial conquests.
Held across 1864 to 1890; restated so the parts add up at 1878.
The Boer, Philippine-American and Russo-Japanese wars.
Now averaged to 1912: the Italo-Turkish war (1911 to 1912).
Held across 1910 to 1912, the Italo-Turkish war; restated so the parts add up at 1911.
1912 to 1914.6: the two Balkan wars (October 1912 to August 1913). With 1910's point the average stays 4.
The First World War.
The Polish-Soviet and Greco-Turkish wars.
Now averaged to 1933: Japan takes Manchuria (1931 to 1933) and the Chaco War begins (1932).
1933 to 1936: the Chaco War's last years and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1935 to 1936).

Revised from 14, which held the 1930 to 1939.7 average flat: 1936 to 1939.7 holds Japan's full war on China from July 1937 (Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan) and the Soviet–Japanese border battles. With 1930 and 1933 the 1930 to 1939.7 average of 14 is kept.
The Second World War's deadliest years: the Eastern Front, the Pacific war and China.
Held across 1941.5 to 1944: the war's deadliest years, now in the Pacific as well; restated so the parts add up.
Turns down for good: the Long Peace between great powers begins, and fighting between polities never again reaches a tenth of the world wars' rate. The Indochina war and the first Arab-Israeli war.
Revised from 10 with the parent: the Korean War, now averaged to 1954.2.
The Indo-Pakistani war of December 1971, with the Vietnam war.
Averaged to the next date; the 1971.96 rate held: the October War of 1973 and the Vietnam war's last two years.
The Ogaden war.
China's war on Vietnam and Tanzania's on Uganda.
Held across 1979 to 1980: China's war on Vietnam, Tanzania's on Uganda and the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan at the year's end; restated so the parts add up.
The Iran-Iraq war.
The Gulf war.
The Eritrean-Ethiopian war.
The invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq.
Now averaged to October 2023: Nagorno-Karabakh (2020) and Russia's invasion of Ukraine from February 2022.
Held across 2020 to October 2023; restated so the parts add up.

October 2023 to 2025: the war in Ukraine at its deadliest and the war in Gaza and Lebanon. Counting the Gaza war between polities follows the usual coding of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict as one over territory; counting it within a polity would move about a quarter of this value to the next series. The 2020 to 2025 average stays 0.6.

upsert.reason: The parent's value at each date split by what kind of organized killing filled that stretch, from the wars its notes name; before 1800 the split is a sketch.

points.note: Massacres of whole camps; Nataruk by Lake Turkana, about 8000 BCE, is the earliest well-dated case.
Farmers' villages can be wiped out whole: the Neolithic massacres at Talheim and Schletz about 5000 BCE.
The first states kill and deport conquered peoples, as the Assyrian reliefs later boast.
The Mongols kill the people of cities that resist: Merv and Nishapur in 1221, Baghdad in 1258.
Timur's massacres from the 1370s.
Massacres in the conquest of the Americas; most of the Americas' dead died of disease, counted under infection.
Zhang Xianzhong's killings in Sichuan, the Qing massacres at Yangzhou, the sack of Magdeburg.
The Qing's destruction of the Dzungars, 1755 to 1758, perhaps half a million or more killed, averaged here over 1750 to 1780.
1826 to 1840: the Indian removals in the United States and the reprisals after the Baptist War; small at world scale.
1840 to 1850: killings in the conquest of Algeria and, from 1848, the California gold rush's killings of Native Californians. The 1820 to 1850 average stays near 0.5.
Held across 1850 to 1859; restated so the parts add up at 1856.
Massacres in the Dungan revolt and its suppression.
Held across 1864 to 1890; restated so the parts add up at 1878.
The Herero and Nama genocide, 1904 to 1908.
Held across 1910 to 1912; restated so the parts add up at 1911.
Unchanged across 1910 to 1914.6; restated so the parts add up at 1912.
The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1916, with the Assyrian and Greek killings.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882), about eight million people; the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) follows.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882), about eight million people; the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) follows.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan (January 1956), Morocco and Tunisia (March 1956) become independent, about 23 million people; Ghana and Malaya follow in 1957.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.

Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

points.note: Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882), about eight million people; the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) follows.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan (January 1956), Morocco and Tunisia (March 1956) become independent, about 23 million people; Ghana and Malaya follow in 1957.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.
Portugal's African empire, Rhodesia and small territories, with Hong Kong; their numbers grow while their count of territories does not, until the independences of 1974 and 1975.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
