changes.value: Most of the group is now linked, and the rest is not worth a new process. Of the Events judged for Africa, 63 more now name the processes they change (r271, r272), and values were added where the links found the processes silent (r273 to r278), until the coverage report again found none passing over its Events. Among them the transatlantic slave trade, which had named nothing, now names bondage, compelled work and the shares of Africa and the Americas; HIV/AIDS names infection deaths and life expectancy; Africa's periods name Africa's share of humanity; herding's spread names the share of mobile herders for the first time; rinderpest names the wild animals and hunger. What the group changes was already followed: war deaths by kind, hunger, colonial rule, the share under a state and the largest polity, foraging and herding, bondage and compelled work, rank and the vote (apartheid), Africa's output and extreme poverty, exchange and freight (the Suez Canal). The 73 still unlinked are kingdoms, courts and cities whose change is in who rules or what they built rather than in any world measure (Aksum, Kerma, Kush, Meroe, Great Zimbabwe, Mapungubwe, Ife, Igbo-Ukwu, Benin, Kongo, Asante, Oyo, the Almoravids and Almohads, the Fatimids, the Mamluks, the Solomonic line); single battles (Adwa, Tondibi, Mbwila); finds that date the species' early life but change no measure of humanity (the early fossils, Blombos, Pinnacle Point, the Bizmoune beads, Border Cave, the Ishango bone, the Khoe-San split); and Events carried by linked ones (the Second World War in Africa, the Cape Colony by colonial rule's count). Two kinds of change have no process: Christian and Muslim branches (Ethiopia's church, the Coptic split, Sufi orders), as for the Americas and Asia, and land dispossession within a country (the Natives Land Act's 7%), which a wealth-share measure at world scale cannot see. Neither earns a process at this resolution (MarginalValueRule#6611); every Event with a world-scale change found a home by the routing test (RoutingSanityCheck#71bd). Reopen if a regional history of Africa is opened.

upsert.boundary: Convict transportation to Australia, 1788 to 1868
upsert.description: Britain transports about 162,000 convicts, one in six of them women, to New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land and, last, Western Australia (to 1868); assigned to settlers and public works, most stay when freed, and their labour builds the colonies' roads, farms and towns.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987); Nicholas (ed.), Convict Workers (1988)

upsert.boundary: Convict and settler colonies, 1788 to 1901
upsert.description: Britain founds convict colonies at Sydney (1788) and Hobart (1803) and annexes New Zealand (1840); pastoralists take Aboriginal land across the south-east, and frontier wars and epidemics follow; Maori fight the New Zealand Wars. Gold (from 1851) brings mass migration; the colonies win self-government, the secret ballot and manhood suffrage in the 1850s, and New Zealand gives women the vote in 1893.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (4th ed. 2016); Belich, Making Peoples (1996)

upsert.boundary: Federation, dominions and the world wars, 1901 to 1945
upsert.description: Australia federates (1901) behind the White Australia policy and New Zealand becomes a dominion (1907); both build arbitration courts, pensions and Labour governments; they lose about 60,000 and 18,000 dead in the First World War and are shaken by the Depression, and Japan's advance in 1942 turns them from Britain toward the United States.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre (2016); King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

upsert.boundary: The first Australians, about 65,000 or 50,000 to 30,000 years ago
upsert.description: People cross from Wallacea to Sahul's northern shores and spread across the continent: the coasts, the rivers of the south-east, the arid interior and, by about 40,000 years ago, Tasmania, joined to the mainland while the sea was low. They grind the edges of stone axes, bury their dead with ochre at Lake Mungo, and within some thousands of years of their arrival the giant marsupials, birds and reptiles are gone. When the first people came is debated: luminescence dates at Madjedbebe put them there by 65,000 years ago, while most secure sites are about 50,000 years old.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the start of the era is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature 547 (Madjedbebe); O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS 115; Hiscock, Archaeology of Ancient Australia (2008)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Australia, with Tasmania)

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum's deserts and refuges, about 30,000 to 12,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the last glacial deepens, Australia's interior dries, dunes spread and lakes such as Mungo empty; people withdraw from much of the arid interior to refuges in the ranges, along rivers and on the coastal plains then exposed, and their numbers may fall. Tasmania's hunters live on wallaby at the southern edge of the inhabited world. From about 18,000 years ago the climate eases and the seas rise.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how far people left the deserts is debated
sources to check: Smith, The Archaeology of Australia's Deserts (2013); Williams et al. 2013, Quaternary Science Reviews 61

upsert.boundary: Holocene Australia, about 12,000 years ago to 1280
upsert.description: The rising sea cuts off Tasmania and then New Guinea and drowns the coastal plains. In a warmer and, from about 5,000 years ago, more variable climate, Aboriginal societies change: small backed tools spread, seed-grinding and eel-trapping grow, the Pama-Nyungan languages spread across most of the continent, and about 3,500 years ago the dingo arrives from island South-east Asia. Aotearoa New Zealand, the subregion's other land, has no people yet.
provenance: sources to check: Mulvaney and Kamminga, Prehistory of Australia (1999); Hiscock (2008)

upsert.boundary: Migration, Asia and the first peoples' rights, 1945 to 2025
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish' millions of migrants arrive, first from Britain and Europe and, after White Australia ends (1973), from Asia; trade turns from Britain to Japan and China; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people win citizenship rights, land rights and native title, and Maori a tribunal for Treaty claims and a revival of their language; both countries grow rich on minerals, farm exports and services.

upsert.boundary: Aboriginal Australia and Maori Aotearoa, about 1280 to 1788
upsert.description: East Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa, the last large land on Earth to be peopled; within two centuries the moa are gone, and Maori live from gardens of kumara, fern root and the sea, building fortified pa and forming iwi and hapu. Across the Tasman, hundreds of Aboriginal nations keep their country by law, ceremony and fire; Makassan fishermen visit the north coast from about 1720, and Dutch and English ships chart the west and south from 1606.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Binney and Harris, Tangata Whenua (2014); Mulvaney and Kamminga (1999)

upsert.boundary: Smallpox at Sydney, 1789
upsert.description: Fifteen months after the First Fleet, smallpox breaks out among the Eora and their neighbours around Port Jackson (April 1789), killing perhaps half of them or more, while almost no colonists fall ill; it spreads inland along the rivers. Whether it came from variolous matter carried by the fleet's surgeons or with Makassan visitors in the north is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the source of the virus is debated
sources to check: Campbell, Invisible Invaders (2002); Warren 2014, Journal of Australian Colonial History 16
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Sydney and New South Wales)

upsert.boundary: The squatters' wool frontier, about 1820 to 1860
upsert.description: Merino sheep and the men who 'squat' on Crown land spread across the grasslands of New South Wales, Port Phillip and the Western District; wool becomes the colonies' chief export and by the 1840s Australia is the largest supplier of Britain's mills, while the frontier of dispossession and massacre moves with the flocks.
provenance: sources to check: Roberts, The Squatting Age in Australia (1935); Butlin, Investment in Australian Economic Development (1964)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (south-eastern Australia)

upsert.boundary: Traders, labour recruiters, missions and colonies, 1840 to 1942
upsert.description: Sandalwood and beche-de-mer traders, missionaries and labour recruiters come; France takes New Caledonia (1853) for convicts and nickel, Britain takes Fiji (1874) and brings Indian indentured labourers, and New Guinea is divided among the Dutch, Germans and British (1884); measles kills a quarter or more of Fijians in 1875. Gold draws prospectors inland, and in the 1930s patrols find about a million people in the New Guinea highlands unknown to the outside world.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon et al., The Cambridge History of the Pacific Islanders (1997)

upsert.boundary: Big men, chiefs and exchange, about 500 BCE to 1840
upsert.description: After Lapita, people with Papuan ancestry reshape the population of Vanuatu and other islands while their languages stay Austronesian; Melanesian societies form around big men who win followings by giving, and around hereditary chiefs in Fiji and New Caledonia; rings of exchange such as the kula of the Massim and the hiri of the Papuan coast carry shell valuables, pots and sago; and some three centuries ago the sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands, where people and pig herds multiply.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the highland changes after the sweet potato are debated
sources to check: Spriggs (1997); Posth et al. 2018, Nature Ecology and Evolution 2; Kirch (2017)

upsert.boundary: Pleistocene New Guinea and the Bismarcks, about 65,000 or 50,000 to 12,000 years ago
upsert.description: The first people of Sahul reach New Guinea, then joined to Australia, and by about 49,000 years ago are in its highlands, harvesting pandanus nuts and yams and thinning forest with waisted axes; voyagers cross to New Ireland and New Britain by about 40,000 years ago and to Buka in the northern Solomons by about 30,000, and later carry obsidian and animals between the islands. Beyond the main Solomons no one yet lives.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the first arrival's date is debated as for Sahul
sources to check: Summerhayes et al. 2010, Science 330; Spriggs, The Island Melanesians (1997)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (New Guinea, the Bismarck Archipelago, the northern Solomons)

upsert.boundary: The first gardens, about 10,000 to 1350 BCE
upsert.description: As the climate warms, New Guineans at Kuk and elsewhere in the highlands tend taro, bananas, yams and sugarcane, then dig drains and build mounded gardens, one of the world's few independent beginnings of farming; the rising sea separates New Guinea from Australia.
provenance: sources to check: Denham et al. 2003, Science 301; Golson et al., Ten Thousand Years of Cultivation at Kuk Swamp (2017)

upsert.boundary: Independent Melanesia, 1980 to 2025
upsert.description: Papua New Guinea's people grow from about three million to ten million or more, speaking over 800 languages; the war over the Panguna mine on Bougainville (1988 to 1998) ends in autonomy and a vote for independence (2019); Fiji passes through four coups (1987 to 2006), Solomon Islands through ethnic conflict and an Australian-led intervention (2003 to 2017), and New Caledonia through three referendums on independence (2018 to 2021) and the riots of 2024.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Papua New Guinea's population is uncertain
sources to check: Denoon, A Trial Separation (2005); UN World Population Prospects

upsert.boundary: Lapita voyagers in island Melanesia, about 1350 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Austronesian-speaking potters with pigs, chickens, dogs and outrigger canoes appear in the Bismarck Archipelago about 1350 BCE and within three centuries settle the empty islands beyond the Solomons: Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji; their earliest cemetery, at Teouma on Efate, holds people of East Asian ancestry. The dentate-stamped pottery fades after about 500 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017); Bedford et al. 2006, Antiquity 80
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (the Bismarcks, Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji)

upsert.boundary: War, new movements and independence, 1942 to 1980
upsert.description: Japan's invasion turns the north coast of New Guinea, the Kokoda track and Guadalcanal into battlefields (1942 to 1945), with tens of thousands of Melanesians as carriers and scouts; afterwards movements such as John Frum's on Tanna and Paliau's on Manus seek the wealth and dignity the war revealed; Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), Solomon Islands (1978) and Vanuatu (1980) become independent, while New Caledonia stays French.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon et al. (1997)

upsert.boundary: Measles kills a quarter of Fijians, 1875
upsert.description: Cakobau's party, back from Sydney with the disease, lands without quarantine; within months measles kills about 40,000 Fijians, between a quarter and a third of them, adults as well as children, and the sick go untended as whole villages fall ill at once.
provenance: sources to check: Cliff and Haggett, The Spread of Measles in Fiji and the Pacific (1985)

upsert.boundary: Papua New Guinea becomes independent, 16 September 1975
upsert.description: Australia's territories of Papua and New Guinea become one independent state under Michael Somare, with more than 800 languages; it has kept elected parliamentary government ever since, through frequent changes of government.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon, A Trial Separation (2005)

upsert.boundary: The sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands, about 1600 to 1750
upsert.description: A South American crop, carried by Spanish and Portuguese ships to the Moluccas in the 1500s, spreads by exchange into the highlands, where it grows higher up and on poorer soils than taro and feeds pigs; people, pig herds and the great exchange ceremonies such as the Melpa moka and the Enga tee grow. Whether this was a sudden 'Ipomoean revolution' or the speeding-up of a long intensification already under way is debated.
provenance: exploring: the size and speed of the change are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Watson 1965, Ethnology 4; Golson, in May and Nelson (eds.) (1982); Bayliss-Smith, Golson and Hughes, in Golson et al. (2017)

upsert.boundary: Free association and rising seas, 1986 to 2025
upsert.description: Under Compacts of Free Association (1986, Palau 1994, renewed 2023) the United States funds and defends the Marshall Islands, the Federated States and Palau, whose citizens may live and work in the United States, where a large share of them now live; Kiribati and the Marshall Islands face rising seas, and Nauru's phosphate runs out.
provenance: sources to check: Hezel, Making Sense of Micronesia (2013)

upsert.boundary: German, Japanese and British rule, 1899 to 1945
upsert.description: Germany mines phosphate and plants copra; Japan takes Germany's islands in 1914 and governs them as the League of Nations' South Seas Mandate, bringing Japanese, Okinawan and Korean settlers who outnumber the islanders by 1940; Britain rules the Gilberts and mines Banaba, and Australia administers Nauru; from 1941 the islands are battlefields of the Pacific war, from Tarawa to Saipan and Tinian.
provenance: sources to check: Peattie, Nan'yo (1988); Hezel, Strangers in Their Own Land (1995)

upsert.boundary: Latte houses, Nan Madol and island chiefdoms, about 1000 to 1668
upsert.description: In the Marianas, Chamorro houses stand on stone pillars, the latte, and rice is grown, the only rice in Oceania before contact; on Pohnpei the Saudeleur build Nan Madol and on Kosrae chiefs build Leluh; Yap's chiefs bind the outer islands in the sawei exchange and quarry stone money on Palau; Carolinian navigators keep the star compass. Magellan reaches Guam in 1521 and the Manila galleons call there from 1565.
provenance: sources to check: Rainbird, The Archaeology of Micronesia (2004)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers settle the Marianas and the Carolines, about 1500 BCE to 1000 CE
upsert.description: Seafarers from the Philippines make the longest open-sea crossing of their time to settle the Marianas about 3,500 years ago; about 2,000 years ago, as the falling sea leaves coral atolls habitable, voyagers from island Melanesia settle the Carolines, the Marshalls and Kiribati, speaking the Nuclear Micronesian languages.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the first settlement's date and origin are debated
sources to check: Carson et al. 2013, Journal of Island and Coastal Archaeology 8; Pugach et al. 2021, PNAS 118; Kirch (2017)

upsert.boundary: Spanish Guam, whalers and missions, 1668 to 1899
upsert.description: Jesuits found a mission on Guam (1668); the Spanish-Chamorro wars and epidemics reduce the Chamorro by nine-tenths and Spain resettles the survivors; in the 1800s whalers, traders and Protestant missionaries from Hawai'i and New England reach the Carolines and Marshalls, and smallpox strikes Pohnpei (1854); Germany claims the Marshalls (1885), and after the war of 1898 Spain cedes Guam to the United States and sells the rest to Germany (1899).
provenance: sources to check: Hezel, The First Taint of Civilization (1983); Rogers, Destiny's Landfall (1995)

upsert.boundary: The Trust Territory and the nuclear tests, 1945 to 1986
upsert.description: The United States governs most of Micronesia as a UN strategic trust (from 1947) and tests 67 nuclear weapons at Bikini and Enewetak (1946 to 1958); Nauru (1968) and Kiribati (1979) become independent, and the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands and Palau negotiate free association, while Guam and the Northern Marianas stay American.

upsert.boundary: Seafarers from the Philippines settle the Marianas, about 1500 to 1300 BCE
upsert.description: Bringing red-slipped pottery like that of the northern Philippines, voyagers cross more than 2,000 kilometres of open ocean to Saipan, Tinian and Guam, the longest sea crossing of its time; ancient genomes link the first Chamorro ancestors to the Philippines. The date (1500 or about 1100 BCE) and the exact origin are debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; date and origin debated
sources to check: Carson et al. 2013; Hung et al. 2011, Antiquity 85; Pugach et al. 2021, PNAS 118

upsert.boundary: Smallpox on Pohnpei, 1854
upsert.description: Brought by a whaling ship, smallpox kills perhaps half of Pohnpei's people within months; the missionaries from Hawai'i who arrived in 1852 gain converts among the survivors.

upsert.boundary: The Spanish-Chamorro wars, 1668 to 1698
upsert.description: Jesuit missionaries under Sanvitores arrive on Guam (1668); resistance after his killing (1672) turns into decades of war, and soldiers resettle the Chamorro into mission villages; war, smallpox and influenza cut them from perhaps 40,000 or more to about 5,000 by 1710. Their number before contact is debated (from about 20,000 to 100,000).
provenance: sources to check: Rogers (1995); Hezel 1982, Journal of Pacific History 17

upsert.boundary: Women win the vote, 1893 to 1971
upsert.description: New Zealand (1893), South Australia, Finland (1906) and Norway lead; after the First World War Britain, Germany, Russia and the United States follow; France and Italy after the Second, and Switzerland only in 1971.
provenance: sources to check: Paxton and Hughes, Women, Politics, and Power (3rd ed. 2016)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand); Europe; Americas

value: inferred: each Event's description says what it changes

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's Oceania group, batch 1 of 2: 30 Events now name the processes they change. Oceania's people are under one percent of humanity, so most of its Events move its own subregions' shares rather than world measures: the periods of Australia and New Zealand, Melanesia and Micronesia (ev.anz.era.*, ev.mel.era.*, ev.mic.era.*) name their subregion's share, and so do the epidemics (smallpox at Sydney and on Pohnpei, measles in Fiji, the Spanish–Chamorro wars), convict transport and the sweet potato's spread in the highlands; colonial periods and Papua New Guinea's independence name colonial rule; New Guinea's first gardens name foraging; the wool frontier names pasture. Women winning the vote (1893 to 1971), which had named nothing, now names the share of adults with the vote, its first Event. Only process_ids change; every other field is restated unchanged.

upsert.boundary: Oceania becomes Christian, 1797 to about 1900
upsert.description: London Missionary Society missionaries land on Tahiti from the Duff (1797); after Pomare II's victory at Fei Pi (1815) Tahiti turns Christian, followed by Hawai'i (from 1820), Tonga and Samoa (1820s and 1830s), Fiji (1850s) and, largely through Pacific Islander teachers, much of Melanesia; Marsden preaches in New Zealand from 1814. Missions bring writing in the islanders' own languages; today about nine in ten Pacific Islanders are Christian.
provenance: sources to check: Garrett, To Live Among the Stars (1982)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia, Melanesia, Micronesia, Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: Rising seas threaten the atoll nations, from about 1990
upsert.description: With sea level rising and storm surges and salt intrusion worsening, Kiribati, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands, whose land stands a few metres above the sea, plan for relocation; Tuvalu and Australia sign a treaty of climate mobility in 2023.
provenance: sources to check: IPCC AR6 WGII chapter 15 (Small Islands)

upsert.boundary: Oceania's indigenous peoples decimated, 1788 to 1920
upsert.description: Smallpox, measles, influenza, venereal disease, violence and the loss of land cut Aboriginal Australians from perhaps 800,000 to under 100,000, Māori to about 42,000 (1896) and Hawaiians from some 300,000 to about 40,000 (1890), and many smaller island peoples by more; populations recover only in the 1900s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; pre-contact numbers are uncertain
sources to check: Butlin, Our Original Aggression (1983); Pool, Te Iwi Maori (1991)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand; Polynesia; Melanesia)

upsert.boundary: Ancient Sahul and Near Oceania, about 65,000 to 3,500 years ago
upsert.description: People cross from Wallacea to Sahul at least 50,000 and perhaps 65,000 years ago, spread across the continent, reach Tasmania, the New Guinea highlands and the Bismarck and Solomon islands; most of the megafauna vanish by about 40,000 years ago; the Lake Mungo burials, about 42,000 years old, are among the oldest ritual burials known. Rising seas cut off Tasmania and then New Guinea; New Guineans drain the Kuk swamp to grow taro and bananas from about 10,000 to 7,000 years ago.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the first arrival is contested
sources to check: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature 547 (Madjedebe); O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS 115 (a later arrival); Denham et al. 2003, Science 301 (Kuk)

upsert.boundary: Contact and colonization in Oceania, 1768 to 1901
upsert.description: Cook's voyages (1768 to 1779); the First Fleet at Sydney (1788), smallpox (1789) and the frontier wars; the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and the New Zealand Wars (1845 to 1872); gold rushes (from 1851); Kamehameha unites Hawai'i (1810) and the United States annexes it (1898); missionaries; islanders recruited or kidnapped for plantation labour; epidemics halve many island populations.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (5th ed. 2020); Belich, Making Peoples (1996)

upsert.boundary: Island kingdoms and the continent before contact, 1300 to 1768
upsert.description: Māori iwi spread through Aotearoa; the Tu'i Tonga's maritime state; Rapa Nui's moai; Hawai'i's chiefdoms; Aboriginal Australia's hundreds of nations with their trade routes, songlines and burning of the land. Magellan crosses the Pacific (1521), Spain takes Guam (1668), Dutch ships chart western Australia and Tasman sights Tasmania and New Zealand (1642), and Makassan fishermen visit Arnhem Land.
provenance: sources to check: Denoon (ed.), The Cambridge History of the Pacific Islanders (1997)

upsert.boundary: Federation, war and the island nations, 1901 to 2025
upsert.description: Australia federates (1901) under the White Australia policy; Gallipoli (1915); the Pacific war (1941 to 1945); nuclear tests in the Marshall Islands, Australia and French Polynesia (1946 to 1996); the Stolen Generations; Samoa (1962), Nauru (1968), Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975) and others become independent; Australia's 1967 referendum and the Mabo judgment (1992); rising seas threaten the atolls.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (5th ed. 2020); Fischer, A History of the Pacific Islands (2nd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: Lapita and the settling of Remote Oceania, about 1500 BCE to 1300 CE
upsert.description: Austronesian-speaking voyagers with pottery, pigs, chickens and outrigger canoes, the Lapita culture, reach the Bismarcks about 1350 BCE, then Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE; Micronesia is settled from the Philippines and from Melanesia; the dingo arrives in Australia. After a long pause East Polynesia is settled in a burst from about 1000 CE: the Society Islands, Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa last, about 1280. The sweet potato, a South American plant, is growing in East Polynesia before Europeans arrive, and Native American ancestry dated to about 1200 is found in East Polynesians: contact with South America is likely, but whether Polynesians sailed there and back or South Americans reached Polynesia is debated.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017); Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108 (East Polynesian chronology); Ioannidis et al. 2020, Nature 583 (contact with the Americas)

exploring: corrected 2026-10-13 after a blind reading of the events pass: contact with South America is likely from the sweet potato and the genetic evidence (Ioannidis et al. 2020); who made the voyage is debated

upsert.boundary: The First Fleet founds a convict colony at Sydney, January 1788
upsert.description: Eleven British ships land some 1,400 convicts, marines and officials at Sydney Cove (26 January 1788) on the land of the Gadigal people; Britain will send about 160,000 convicts to Australia by 1868.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: Australia); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: The gold rushes of Australia and New Zealand, 1851 to 1900
upsert.description: Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria (1851), Otago (1861) and Western Australia (1890s) draws hundreds of thousands of migrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese; Victoria's population grows sevenfold in a decade and Melbourne becomes one of the richest cities in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Blainey, The Rush That Never Ended (5th ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Lapita voyagers settle Remote Oceania, about 1300 to 800 BCE
upsert.description: Potters who decorate their wares with dentate stamps spread from the Bismarck Archipelago to Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries, crossing gaps of hundreds of kilometres to islands no one had reached before; they are the ancestors of the Polynesians.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: Sahul's giant animals die out, about 46,000 to 40,000 years ago
upsert.description: Diprotodon, the rhino-sized marsupial, giant kangaroos, the flightless bird Genyornis and giant lizards disappear within some thousands of years of people's arrival; hunting, burning and a drying climate are all blamed.
provenance: exploring: timing and causes are debated
sources to check: Roberts et al. 2001, Science 292; Saltré et al. 2016, Nature Communications 7
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: Australia; Melanesia: New Guinea)

upsert.boundary: The moa hunted to extinction, about 1300 to 1450
upsert.description: Within about 150 years of people's arrival, all nine species of moa, giant flightless birds up to 3.6 metres tall, and the Haast's eagle that preyed on them are gone: one of the fastest human-caused extinctions known.
provenance: sources to check: Perry et al. 2014, Quaternary Science Reviews 105; Holdaway et al. 2014, Nature Communications 5
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Farming begins in the New Guinea highlands, about 8000 to 4500 BCE
upsert.description: At Kuk Swamp highland people dig drains and mound gardens and cultivate taro, bananas and yams, one of the world's independent inventions of farming; sugarcane and some bananas spread from here across the tropics.
provenance: sources to check: Denham et al. 2003, Science 301

upsert.boundary: The island states claim the ocean: exclusive economic zones and tuna, 1977 to 2025
upsert.description: As states declare 200-nautical-mile zones (from 1977) and the Law of the Sea Convention (1982, in force 1994) confirms them, small island states gain rights over seas many thousand times their land; Kiribati's zone is about 3.4 million square kilometres. Through the Forum Fisheries Agency (1979) and the Parties to the Nauru Agreement (1982), whose vessel day scheme (from 2007) makes distant-water fleets bid for fishing days, licence revenue from the world's largest tuna fishery rises several-fold, to over half a billion dollars a year.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; revenue figures approximate
sources to check: Aqorau, Fishing for Success (2019); Forum Fisheries Agency economic and development indicators

upsert.boundary: The Pacific divided among empires, 1842 to 1900
upsert.description: France takes Tahiti (1842) and New Caledonia (1853), Britain Fiji (1874) and part of New Guinea, Germany north-east New Guinea, the Marshalls and Samoa, and the United States annexes Hawaii (1898) after American planters overthrow its queen (1893); by 1900 hardly an island is independent.
provenance: sources to check: Fischer, A History of the Pacific Islands (2nd ed. 2013)
upsert.region: Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia); Europe; Americas (Northern America: the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Pacific island nations become independent, 1962 to 1980
upsert.description: Samoa (1962) is first, then Nauru (1968), Tonga's full sovereignty and Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), Solomon Islands and Tuvalu (1978), Kiribati (1979) and Vanuatu (1980); others remain territories or freely associated states.
provenance: sources to check: Fischer, A History of the Pacific Islands (2nd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: Polynesians settle the eastern Pacific, about 900 to 1300
upsert.description: After a pause of nearly two thousand years in Samoa and Tonga, voyagers navigating by stars, swells and birds settle the Society Islands and the Marquesas, then within a few centuries Hawaii, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa New Zealand (about 1280), the last large land on Earth to be peopled.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates follow the 'short chronology'
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108

upsert.boundary: Postwar migration remakes Australia and New Zealand, from 1945
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish', Australia takes millions of migrants from Britain, then southern and eastern Europe; the White Australia policy ends (1973) and migrants from Asia follow, until nearly a third of Australians are born overseas; Oceania grows from about 13 to 46 million people.
provenance: sources to check: Jupp, From White Australia to Woomera (2nd ed. 2007); Australian Bureau of Statistics

upsert.boundary: Settlers multiply Oceania's people, 1788 to 1950
upsert.description: Convicts, assisted migrants, gold-seekers and their children grow Australia's and New Zealand's settler populations from nothing to about 10 million by 1950, while the indigenous peoples shrink: Oceania's share of humanity rises from about 0.2% to 0.5%.
provenance: inferred: from the model's own regional shares
sources to check: Australian Bureau of Statistics historical population; UN historical estimates

upsert.boundary: Whalers, sealers and traders across the Pacific, about 1790 to 1860
upsert.description: Sealers and whalers from Britain, the United States and France work the southern and central Pacific, using the Bay of Islands, Honolulu and Lahaina as their ports; beachcombers, muskets, alcohol and venereal disease spread with them, and traders buy sandalwood, beche-de-mer and pork for the China and colonial markets.
provenance: sources to check: Campbell (1989); Shineberg, They Came for Sandalwood (1967)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia, Micronesia, Melanesia, Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: The first Polynesians: Tonga and Samoa, about 900 BCE to 900 CE
upsert.description: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga about 880 BCE and Samoa soon after; there, and on Futuna and 'Uvea, their descendants become the first Polynesians, with the Proto-Polynesian language, chiefs, tapu and mana, and stop making pottery. For nearly two thousand years, the 'long pause', no one settles the islands to the east; its length and its reasons are debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the pause and its reasons are debated
sources to check: Kirch and Green, Hawaiki, Ancestral Polynesia (2001); Burley et al. 2012, PLOS ONE 7

upsert.boundary: Chiefdoms and island states, about 1200 to 1767
upsert.description: On every high island chiefs build marae and ahu; the Tu'i Tonga's maritime chiefdom reaches Samoa, 'Uvea and Fiji; Hawai'i's paramount chiefs rule irrigated taro lands and fishponds through land divisions and kapu; Rapa Nui's clans raise the moai; voyaging between distant archipelagos grows rarer. Europeans pass by: Mendana in the Marquesas (1595), Le Maire and Schouten (1616), Roggeveen at Rapa Nui (1722).
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, How Chiefs Became Kings (2010)

upsert.boundary: Colonial rule and resistance, 1900 to 1962
upsert.description: Samoa is divided between Germany and the United States (1899) and New Zealand takes the German part (1914); influenza kills a fifth of Western Samoans in 1918, and the Mau movement demands self-rule; Tonga remains a protected kingdom; Pearl Harbor (1941) brings the Pacific war; Hawai'i becomes an American state (1959).
provenance: sources to check: Meleisea, Lagaga (1987); Campbell (1989)

upsert.boundary: Contact, missions, island kingdoms and annexation, 1767 to 1900
upsert.description: Wallis (1767), Bougainville and Cook bring Tahiti into Europe's imagination; diseases cut island peoples by half or more; Protestant missions convert Tahiti, Tonga, Samoa and Hawai'i; chiefs with muskets build kingdoms (Kamehameha's Hawai'i, Pomare's Tahiti, Tupou's Tonga); France annexes Tahiti, Peruvian slavers take a third of Rapa Nui's people (1862), and Hawai'i's monarchy is overthrown (1893) and annexed by the United States (1898).
provenance: sources to check: Denoon et al. (1997); Campbell, A History of the Pacific Islands (1989)

upsert.boundary: Island nations, territories and the diaspora, 1962 to 2025
upsert.description: Samoa (1962), Tonga (1970) and Tuvalu (1978) become independent, and the Cook Islands and Niue self-governing in free association with New Zealand; France tests nuclear weapons at Moruroa until 1996; more Cook Islanders and Niueans, and very many Samoans and Tongans, come to live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States; the voyaging canoe Hokule'a revives navigation without instruments; the atolls face rising seas.
provenance: sources to check: Campbell (1989); Denoon et al. (1997)

upsert.boundary: The great voyages east, about 900 to 1200
upsert.description: Voyagers in double-hulled canoes, navigating by stars, swells and birds, settle the Society and Cook Islands, then the Marquesas, Hawai'i and Rapa Nui, carrying taro, breadfruit, pigs, dogs, chickens and the Pacific rat. The dating is debated: a short chronology puts the Society Islands about 1025 and the remotest islands about 1200, a longer one centuries earlier.
provenance: exploring: the chronology of East Polynesian settlement is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108; Kirch (2017)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (East Polynesia, with Hawai'i and Rapa Nui)

upsert.boundary: The Marquesas lose nine-tenths of their people, 1790s to 1920
upsert.description: With whalers, traders and the French (1842) come venereal disease, tuberculosis, smallpox (1863), opium, alcohol and wars fought with muskets; the islanders fall from perhaps 50,000 or more at contact to about 2,000 by the 1920s, the steepest fall of any Polynesian people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the population at contact is debated, from about 35,000 to over 100,000
sources to check: Dening, Islands and Beaches (1980); Rallu, Les populations océaniennes aux XIXe et XXe siècles (1990)

upsert.boundary: Influenza in Samoa, November 1918
upsert.description: New Zealand's administration lets the steamer Talune land passengers with influenza at Apia; about 8,500 die, a fifth of Western Samoa's people, while American Samoa, under strict quarantine, has no deaths: one of the clearest tests of quarantine in the pandemic.
provenance: sources to check: Tomkins 1992, Social History of Medicine 5; Shanks et al. 2012

upsert.boundary: Voyagers settle the Society Islands, about 1025 to 1120
upsert.description: After the long pause, canoes from Samoa reach the Society Islands; radiocarbon dates on short-lived plant remains put the first settlement about 1025 to 1120, and Ra'iatea, with the marae of Taputapuatea, becomes a centre from which voyagers go on to the remoter islands. Other scholars date the settlement centuries earlier.
provenance: exploring: the short chronology is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108; Kirch (2017)

upsert.boundary: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga and Samoa, about 880 to 800 BCE
upsert.description: Potters from Fiji settle Nukuleka in Tonga about 880 BCE, a date fixed by uranium in their coral tools, and soon Samoa, where the Mulifanua site now lies under the lagoon: the first people of what becomes Polynesia.
provenance: sources to check: Burley et al. 2012, PLOS ONE 7; Kirch (2017)

Widen, the breadth check's Oceania group, batch 2 of 2: 31 Events now name the processes they change. Polynesia's periods (ev.pol.era.*) and Oceania's (ev.oc.era.*) name their share of humanity; the Marquesas' collapse, Samoa's influenza, the Lapita and East Polynesian voyages, the first fleet, the gold rushes, settler growth and postwar migration name the subregion's share they moved (the last three keep their link to Oceania's share); the extinctions of Sahul's megafauna and of the moa name the wild animals; the whalers and sealers name wild sea mammals and the island states' tuna zones wild fish, the first Events to name either; rising seas over the atolls name sea level; Christianization names the Christian and local-tradition shares; the Pacific's partition and independence name colonial rule; New Guinea's farming names foraging. Only process_ids change; every other field is restated unchanged.

Kept so the eight shares sum to one hundred with Buddhism still small at Ashoka's accession (h.religion-2).
Raised by the 1.4 points the line would have given Islam, which in 610 is a few followers in Mecca (h.religion-5).
Local traditions lose most in the Americas, where their people die and the survivors are baptized.
The first Protestant missions land on Tahiti (1797); the conversions of the Pacific that follow move well under a tenth of a point of humanity, so the share keeps its slow drift.
Bohemia, Poland, the Rus' and Scandinavia are baptized from the 960s (ev.eu.christianization-north).
The Reformation (1517) divides Western Christianity without changing its share.
Revolutionary France's dechristianization (1793 to 1794) is reversed within a decade and the Pacific missions begin (1797); the Christian share holds near 22%.

Because Oceania's people are under one percent of humanity, most of them move Oceania's own subregions' shares (Australia and New Zealand, Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia), which every period, epidemic, voyage of settlement and wave of migration now names; others move world measures whose change happens here: the wild animals (Sahul's megafauna, the moa), wild sea mammals (the whalers and sealers) and wild fish (the island states' tuna zones), the first Events to name these last two; sea level (the atolls); colonial rule (the Pacific's partition and independence); foraging (New Guinea's gardens); pasture (the wool frontier); the Christian share; and the share of adults with the vote, through women's suffrage from New Zealand's 1893 on, which had named nothing. upsert.boundary: The movement to abolish the slave trade and slavery, 1787 to 1888.
upsert.description: From the London committee of 1787 and the Haitian revolution of 1791 to Brazil's Golden Law of 1888: Britain abolishes the trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1834, and its navy suppresses the Atlantic trade.

upsert.boundary: Aerosol pollution, from about 1850 to now.
upsert.description: Sulphate and other particles from burning coal and oil reflect sunlight and brighten clouds, masking part of the warming; cleaner air since the 1980s in Europe and North America, and since about 2010 in China and in shipping, removes part of the mask.
provenance: inferred: IPCC AR6 attribution, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The African Humid Period, about 12,500 to 6,000 years ago
upsert.description: As northern summer sunlight peaks, the monsoon moves north: the Sahara and Arabia become grassland and savanna with lakes as large as Mega-Chad, and hippos, crocodiles, fishers and later herders live where there is now desert. It ends as the monsoon retreats again (ev.aridification).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its end was abrupt in some places and gradual in others
sources to check: deMenocal et al. 2000, Quaternary Science Reviews 19; Kuper and Kröpelin 2006, Science 313
upsert.region: Northern, Western and Eastern Africa; Western Asia (Arabia)

upsert.boundary: Alexander's conquests, 334 to 323 BCE
upsert.description: Alexander of Macedon conquers the Persian empire from Egypt to the Indus in eleven years; after his death his generals divide it, and Greek kingdoms rule Egypt, Syria, Mesopotamia and Bactria for centuries, spreading Greek cities, language and art as far as Gandhara.
provenance: sources to check: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (1988)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Greece, Macedonia); Asia (Western, Southern and Central Asia); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt)

upsert.boundary: Antibiotics, from sulfa drugs (1935) to now.
upsert.description: Sulfonamides, then penicillin from 1942 and streptomycin from 1944, cure pneumonia, sepsis, puerperal fever and tuberculosis, which had been the commonest killers of adults.

upsert.boundary: The end of the African Humid Period, about 4000 to 3000 BCE.
upsert.description: The Sahara and Arabia dry out again over a millennium; herders and farmers move toward the Nile, the Tigris and the Euphrates, crowding the valleys where the first states form.
provenance: exploring: the link between drying and state formation is argued, notably for Egypt, and contested

upsert.boundary: The Atlantic economy enriches north-west Europe, about 1600 to 1760.
upsert.description: Colonies, sugar, tobacco and the slave trade, with the trade of the Indies, make London and Amsterdam the richest cities of their time; in Britain wages are high and coal is cheap, so machines that save labour by using energy pay there first.
provenance: exploring: the high-wage, cheap-energy account (Allen's) is one of several rival accounts of why industry began in Britain

upsert.boundary: The Atlantic revolutions, 1775 to 1826
upsert.description: Revolutions in British North America, France, Saint-Domingue and Spanish America overthrow monarchies and colonial rule in the name of popular sovereignty and rights, found the United States, Haiti and the Latin American republics, and spread the idea that rulers answer to the governed.
provenance: sources to check: Palmer, The Age of the Democratic Revolution (1959–64, new ed. 2014); Polasky, Revolutions without Borders (2015)

upsert.boundary: Britain turns to coal, about 1560 to 1760.
upsert.description: As wood grows dear, London and the British towns heat, brew, bake and smelt with coal from seams near water: output rises from perhaps a quarter of a million to about five million tonnes a year, more than the rest of Europe together. Mines need pumping, which is where the steam engine is first used.

upsert.boundary: The Bronze Age collapse, about 1200 to 1150 BCE
upsert.description: Within a few decades the palaces of Mycenaean Greece, the Hittite empire and cities of the Levant such as Ugarit are destroyed and abandoned; Egypt fights off the 'Sea Peoples' but declines; writing disappears in Greece for four centuries. Drought, earthquakes, raiders and the breakdown of the trade that brought tin are all blamed.
provenance: sources to check: Cline, 1177 B.C. (2014); Kaniewski et al. 2013, PLoS ONE 8
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia); Europe (Southern Europe: Greece); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt)

upsert.boundary: Modern contraception and family planning, from 1960 to now.
upsert.description: The pill (1960), the IUD and sterilization, with national family-planning programmes from India (1952) to Bangladesh and Iran: by 2025 most women of reproductive age who are married use a modern method.

upsert.boundary: COVID-19 vaccines, December 2020 to May 2023.
upsert.description: Vaccines developed within a year are given as over 13 billion doses by 2023.

upsert.boundary: The Crimean War, 1853 to 1856.
upsert.description: Russia is defeated by Britain, France and the Ottoman empire; its rulers conclude that a state of serfs cannot field a modern army or economy.

upsert.boundary: The 4.2-kiloyear drought, about 2200 to 1900 BCE
upsert.description: A centuries-long dry spell in the Mediterranean, south-west Asia and South Asia, seen in lake, cave and sea records. Whether it brought down Akkad, Egypt's Old Kingdom and the Indus cities, or only strained them, is debated.
provenance: exploring: its extent and its effects on states are contested
sources to check: Weiss et al. 1993, Science 261; Staubwasser and Weiss 2006, Quaternary Research 66; Middleton 2018, Journal of Archaeological Research 26
upsert.region: Northern Africa; Western and Southern Asia; Southern Europe

upsert.boundary: Clearing for farms before 1700, from about 7900 BCE.
upsert.description: Farmers clear forest for fields and pasture as farming spreads and populations grow, in Europe, China, India and the Middle East above all; much of it by 1700, before industry.
provenance: exploring: how much forest pre-industrial farming cleared is disputed; KK10-type reconstructions give far more than HYDE

upsert.boundary: Adults stop dying of infection, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Tuberculosis, typhoid, cholera, smallpox, malaria and pneumonia, the commonest killers of young and middle-aged adults in 1900, become rare causes of death outside the poorest countries.

upsert.boundary: Children stop dying of infection, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Deaths before age five, mostly from diarrhoea, pneumonia, measles, malaria and neonatal infection, fall from about 38% of children born to 3.6%.

upsert.boundary: Deaths from heart disease and stroke are postponed, 1965 to 2025.
upsert.description: Less smoking, blood-pressure and cholesterol drugs, and emergency and surgical care cut age-specific deaths from cardiovascular disease by half or more in rich countries, and less elsewhere.

upsert.boundary: Famine nearly ends, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Famines killed tens of millions until the 1960s; since then their tolls are a small fraction, and undernourishment, which raises deaths from infection, falls from about half of people to under a tenth.

upsert.boundary: Mothers stop dying in childbirth, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Maternal deaths fall from perhaps 1 in 100 births to about 1 in 4,000, and with fewer births each woman faces the risk fewer times.

upsert.boundary: The global financial crisis, 2007 to 2009
upsert.description: Losses on American mortgage securities freeze credit; Lehman Brothers fails (September 2008), banks are rescued across the rich world, world output falls in 2009 for the first time since 1945, and Europe's debt crisis follows.

upsert.boundary: Burning fossil fuels, from about 1760 to now.
upsert.description: Coal, then oil and gas, from Britain's engines to about 37 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year in 2025; with cement, about 1,800 billion tonnes since 1750.
provenance: inferred: the Global Carbon Project's totals, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The germ theory of disease, 1857 to 1890.
upsert.description: Pasteur, Lister and Koch show that microbes cause infection and identify the bacteria of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera; boiling, antisepsis and hygiene follow from it, and later vaccines and antibiotics.

upsert.boundary: The Great Famine of northern Europe, 1315 to 1322.
upsert.description: Years of rain ruin harvests, and a cattle plague follows: perhaps a tenth of northern Europe's people die, and the children of these years grow up undernourished, a generation before the plague.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the claim that famine-born cohorts died more readily of plague is argued from skeletons and is exploring

upsert.boundary: The Great Leap Forward, 1958 to 1960.
upsert.description: Mao's campaign collectivizes farming into communes, diverts labour to steel, and procures grain on inflated harvest reports; after the Lushan conference of 1959 the reports cannot be questioned.

upsert.boundary: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer, from 1913 to now.
upsert.description: The Haber–Bosch process fixes nitrogen from the air: from the first plant at Oppau in 1913 to over 100 million tonnes of fixed nitrogen a year, on which perhaps two fifths to a half of the food people eat depends.

upsert.boundary: The Holocene, from 11,700 years ago to now.
upsert.description: An interglacial whose climate stays within about a degree of its mean for ten thousand years, with carbon dioxide between 260 and 280 ppm, unlike the swings of the glacial before it. Every independent origin of farming falls inside it.
provenance: inferred: ice-core and stacked temperature reconstructions, as recalled

upsert.boundary: Horses tamed for riding and the war chariot, about 2200 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: The modern domestic horse is bred on the steppe north of the Caucasus about 2200 BCE and spreads across Eurasia within a few centuries; the light spoked-wheel chariot, first found in Sintashta graves east of the Urals, becomes the weapon of elites from Egypt to China.
provenance: sources to check: Librado et al. 2021, Nature 598; Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: the Pontic–Volga steppe and the Urals); Asia (Central, Western, Southern and Eastern Asia)

upsert.boundary: India's democracy, from its constitution of 1950 to now.
upsert.description: Universal adult suffrage from the first election of 1951–52: the largest electorate on Earth, suspended only in the Emergency of 1975–77. India alone is about a sixth of humanity.

upsert.boundary: The failed Indian monsoon, 1918 to 1919.
upsert.description: The 1918 monsoon fails across much of India; grain prices rise and hunger weakens people in the months the deadliest wave of influenza arrives.

upsert.boundary: India's liberalization, from 1991 to now.
upsert.description: After a balance-of-payments crisis India ends industrial licensing and opens to trade; growth roughly doubles to 6 or 7% a year.

upsert.boundary: The interwar crisis, October 1929 to September 1939.
upsert.description: The Wall Street crash of 1929 opens a depression that cuts world trade by two thirds and puts a quarter of German and American workers out of work. In Germany it brings the Nazis to power in 1933; in Japan it strengthens the army, which seizes Manchuria in 1931 and invades China in 1937. Italy takes Ethiopia; the League of Nations fails to stop any of them, and Germany rearms, remilitarizes the Rhineland, annexes Austria and dismembers Czechoslovakia.

upsert.boundary: Irrigation farming on the Mesopotamian alluvium, about 6000 to 3500 BCE.
upsert.description: In the Ubaid and Uruk periods farmers canal the Euphrates onto the plain, so yields far exceed rain-fed fields but depend on works and land that cannot be left: people are tied to the valley, the condition ExitCage#eef7 describes.

upsert.boundary: The late Ming crisis, about 1550 to 1650.
upsert.description: After a century of growth China holds perhaps 150 to 200 million people; degree-holders multiply faster than offices, the Wanli court's finances fail, the defence of Liaodong against the Jurchen needs new land taxes, and the silver on which taxes are paid stops arriving in the 1630s. The structural-demographic cycle's state crisis, in the decades before the collapse.
provenance: exploring: the reading as StructuralDemographicCycle#8433 and the silver-shortage argument are both contested

upsert.boundary: Copper smelted, then bronze, about 5000 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Smelting copper from ore begins in the Balkans and Iran by about 5000 BCE; arsenical and then tin bronze follows in south-west Asia, giving harder tools and weapons and a trade in metal and tin across thousands of kilometres.
provenance: sources to check: Radivojević et al. 2010, Journal of Archaeological Science 37; Roberts, Thornton and Pigott 2009, Antiquity 83
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Eastern Europe: the Balkans); Asia (Western and Southern Asia)

upsert.boundary: The Natufian, about 15,000 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: In the Levant foragers settle in stone houses, bury their dead in villages and harvest wild cereals with sickles: the first dense, sedentary populations, which the cold, dry Younger Dryas then strains.

upsert.boundary: Northern summer sunlight rises with the Earth's orbit, about 23,000 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: As the Earth's tilt and the timing of its closest approach to the Sun shift, summer sunlight at 65° north rises by roughly a tenth to a peak near 11,000 years ago. The ice sheets begin to melt; carbon dioxide released from the Southern Ocean and the loss of reflecting ice amplify the warming. The same cycle ended earlier glacials, Termination II among them.
provenance: inferred: Milankovitch theory and the deglacial chronology, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The postwar order, from 1944 to now.
upsert.description: Bretton Woods (1944), the United Nations (1945), the GATT (1947) and the American alliances: open trade among most market economies, and institutions in which great powers settle disputes short of war.

upsert.boundary: Printing with movable type spreads across Europe, 1450 to 1500.
upsert.description: From Mainz, presses reach some 250 European towns by 1500 and print perhaps twenty million volumes: books fall in price by an order of magnitude.

upsert.boundary: The Reformation, 1517 to 1648.
upsert.description: Protestant churches ask every believer to read scripture; Protestant lands, and Catholic ones competing with them, open schools.

upsert.boundary: Russia emancipates its serfs, March 1861.
upsert.description: About 23 million privately held serfs become free in law, with land they must buy back over 49 years; the state peasants follow in 1866.

upsert.boundary: Clean water and sewers, from about 1850 to now.
upsert.description: After the cholera epidemics, London, then the cities of Europe and North America, filter and pipe water and carry sewage away (the London sewers 1859 to 1875, chlorination from 1908); after 1950 piped water spreads through the world's towns. By 2025 about three quarters of people have safely managed drinking water.

upsert.boundary: The Silk Roads, about 130 BCE to 1450
upsert.description: After Zhang Qian's missions to Central Asia, chains of caravan routes and oasis cities join China, Central Asia, Iran, India and the Mediterranean; silk, horses, glass, paper, spices and silver travel along them, and so do Buddhism, Christianity, Manichaeism and Islam, and the plague.
provenance: sources to check: Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012); Frankopan, The Silk Roads (2015)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern, Central, Southern and Western Asia); Europe; Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: The Spanish conquest of the Aztec and Inca states and the forced labour after it, 1519 to 1572.
upsert.description: From Cortés's landing in 1519 to the fall of Vilcabamba in 1572: war, enslavement, the encomienda's tribute and labour, and the silver mines' draft remove the care, food and refuge that recovery from epidemics needed.

upsert.boundary: The steam engine, from Newcomen's (1712) to Watt's rotary engine (1784).
upsert.description: Newcomen's atmospheric engine pumps coal mines; Watt's separate condenser cuts its coal use by three quarters, and the rotary engine drives mills. Energy from a stock of fossil carbon can now do work anywhere.

upsert.boundary: Clearing the temperate frontiers for farms, 1700 to 1950.
upsert.description: Forest and grassland are ploughed and grazed across North America, Russia and Siberia, Australia, Argentina, and the farmlands of India and China: farmland roughly triples.
provenance: inferred: HYDE-type land-use reconstructions, as recalled

upsert.boundary: Clearing tropical forest, 1950 to now.
upsert.description: Cattle, soy, oil palm, smallholders and logging clear forest in Amazonia, south-east Asia and central Africa.

upsert.boundary: The American Civil War and emancipation, April 1861 to December 1865.
upsert.description: The war, the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 and the Thirteenth Amendment of December 1865 free about four million enslaved people.

upsert.boundary: Mass vaccination, from about 1920 to now.
upsert.description: Diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccines, then polio and measles; smallpox is eradicated in 1980, and the Expanded Programme on Immunization (1974) takes the basic vaccines to most of the world's children.

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check: 49 world Events that named no process now name the processes they move, each by what its own description says it changed (the processes already hold values across their spans). Health: antibiotics, germ theory, vaccines, sanitation, COVID-19 vaccines and the five falls in deaths by cause (infection in adults and children, chronic disease, famine, childbirth) name the cause-of-death rates, adult survival and child mortality by age, which no Event named before. Food and energy: Haber-Bosch, Britain's coal, the steam engine and fossil fuels name food, staples, the stores burned and the human addition of carbon dioxide. Land: clearing before 1700, the temperate frontiers and the tropics name forest, its domains, farmland and cropland; irrigation names cropland. The Earth: the Holocene, the orbital rise of sunlight and aerosols name temperature, sea level, the northern ice sheets and the carbon cycle's own level; the African Humid Period and its end name Northern Africa's share and the herders. Politics and war: Alexander, the drought of 4.2 ka (Akkad), the Bronze Age collapse, the chariot, the Crimean War, the Crusades, the Atlantic revolutions, the Spanish conquest, the US Civil War, the late Ming crisis, India's democracy, the interwar crisis and the postwar order name war by kind, the largest polity, colonial rule, voice and its parts. Work and rank: abolitionism and Russia's emancipation name bondage, compelled work and rank. Exchange and output: the Atlantic economy, the Silk Roads, the 2008 crisis and India's reform name trade, output by area and poverty. Knowledge: printing and the Reformation name literacy, mass media and primary schooling. Contraception names births per woman and third and later births; the Natufian names the mobile foragers. Left unlinked, with reasons for the breadth record: the Americas' isolation (a condition, not a change), the wild cereals (a condition of farming), the Middle Stone Age innovations and the scientific revolution (no process follows discovery), gunpowder and nuclear weapons (no process follows the means of war yet), the Glorious Revolution (constraint on rulers has no measure), Constantinople 1453 (a change of rulers).

upsert.boundary: Athenian democracy and the classical age, 508 to 322 BCE
upsert.description: Cleisthenes' reforms give power to the assembly of citizens; Athens leads the Greeks against Persia, builds the Parthenon and stages the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, until Macedon ends its democracy in 322 BCE. Women, slaves and foreigners have no vote.
provenance: sources to check: Ober, The Rise and Fall of Classical Greece (2015)

upsert.boundary: The Berlin Wall falls, 9 November 1989
upsert.description: After months of protest and flight to the west, East Germany opens its border; crowds cross and break down the Wall, and within a year Germany is reunited.
provenance: sources to check: Sarotte, The Collapse (2014)

upsert.boundary: Europe's commercial revolution, about 1200 to 1500
upsert.description: Italian merchant cities develop banks, bills of exchange, partnerships, insurance and double-entry bookkeeping; the fairs of Champagne and the Hanseatic League of northern towns join the Mediterranean and the Baltic in one trading world.
provenance: sources to check: Lopez, The Commercial Revolution of the Middle Ages (1971); Spufford, Power and Profit (2002)

upsert.boundary: The Roman crisis of the third century, 235 to 284
upsert.description: Some twenty emperors in fifty years, most murdered; Persians, Goths and Alamanni break the frontiers, the Plague of Cyprian strikes, the silver coinage collapses, and the empire splits for a time into three, until Diocletian restores it with a larger army and heavier taxes.
provenance: sources to check: Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Western Europe); Asia (Western Asia); Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: The Cucuteni–Trypillia mega-sites, about 4800 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Farmers between the Carpathians and the Dnieper build the largest settlements of their time, such as Talianki, with perhaps 10,000 people or more around 4000 BCE, and every few generations burn their own houses.
provenance: sources to check: Müller, Rassmann and Videiko (eds.), Trypillia Mega-Sites and European Prehistory (2016)

upsert.boundary: Doggerland drowns and Britain becomes an island, about 8000 to 6000 BCE
upsert.description: Rising seas flood the plain between Britain and the continent; around 6150 BCE the Storegga submarine slide off Norway sends a tsunami across the North Sea, and by about 6000 BCE Britain is cut off.
provenance: sources to check: Gaffney, Fitch and Smith, Europe's Lost World (2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Northern and Western Europe: the North Sea)

upsert.boundary: The Dutch Republic's golden age, 1581 to 1672
upsert.description: The northern Netherlands renounce Spanish rule (1581) and become the richest society in Europe: Amsterdam's exchange bank (1609) and stock exchange, the East India Company, the largest merchant fleet, religious toleration, and the painting of Rembrandt and Vermeer, until the French invasion of 1672.
provenance: sources to check: de Vries and van der Woude, The First Modern Economy (1997); Israel, The Dutch Republic (1995)

upsert.boundary: The war in the east, June 1941 to May 1945
upsert.description: Germany invades the Soviet Union in the largest war ever fought; after Moscow, Stalingrad and Kursk the Red Army drives to Berlin; some 27 million Soviet citizens die.
provenance: sources to check: Glantz and House, When Titans Clashed (2nd ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: The Last Interglacial in Europe, about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago
upsert.description: For some fifteen thousand years Europe is warmer than today: hippopotamuses and straight-tusked elephants live along the Thames and the Rhine, forests reach Scandinavia and the sea stands several metres higher. Neanderthals live through it, mostly in the south.
provenance: sources to check: Turner, The Eemian interglacial (2000); Stringer, Homo Britannicus (2006)

upsert.boundary: The great European emigration, 1815 to 1914
upsert.description: Some 50 to 55 million Europeans, Irish, British, Germans, Scandinavians, Italians, Poles, Jews and others, leave for the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, driven by land hunger, famine and persecution and drawn by wages, cheap land and steamships.
provenance: sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)
upsert.region: Europe; Americas; Oceania (Australia and New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Europe's postwar expulsions, 1944 to 1950
upsert.description: As borders move west, some 12 to 14 million Germans flee or are expelled from Poland, Czechoslovakia and the east, and millions of Poles, Ukrainians and others are moved; perhaps half a million or more die.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths are disputed
sources to check: Douglas, Orderly and Humane (2012)

upsert.boundary: Farmers from Anatolia spread across Europe, about 6700 to 4000 BCE
upsert.description: PLACEHOLDER
provenance: sources to check: Ammerman and Cavalli-Sforza, The Neolithic Transition and the Genetics of Populations in Europe (1984); Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522
