Widen, the breadth check's Europe group: 50 Events of Europe's history that named no process now name the processes they move. Wars name war between polities (the Persian, Peloponnesian and Punic wars, the migration period, Justinian's wars, the Vikings, the Hundred Years' War, the Thirty Years' War, Napoleon's wars, the eastern front, Russia's war on Ukraine) or within them (the third-century crisis, the wars of religion, the Yugoslav wars); massacres and terror name one-sided killing (the Great Terror, the postwar expulsions, Srebrenica). Voice: Athens, the Roman Republic and the Greek poleis name contestation, which rises with them about 500 BCE and falls with the Principate; fascism, the Iron Curtain, the Berlin Wall and the Soviet breakup name contestation again; the French Revolution and 1848 name the vote and rank, and 1848 the end of serfdom in Austria. Work and rank: manorialism names compelled work and rank, Varna's gold names rank. The state: the fiscal-military state names revenue, its goods taxes and force; the welfare states name revenue and its income taxes. Output and trade: the commercial revolution, the Dutch Republic, industrialization and integration name trade, manufactures, Europe's output, making and the urban share; railways name passenger speed and freight. Health and knowledge: Jenner names infection, the Irish famine hunger, the first universities higher learning. Europe's share and its parts: the arrival of Homo sapiens, the Gravettian, the glacial refuges, the Magdalenians, the Mesolithic, the farmers and the steppe herders name Europe's share; the emigration names Europe's, Northern and Southern Europe's and Northern America's shares, the expulsions Eastern and Western Europe's, the Mongol conquest of Rus' Eastern Europe's, the Irish famine and the Vikings Northern Europe's, the poleis and the migration period Southern Europe's, the Thirty Years' War Western Europe's: the first Events to name Europe's subregion shares. The Earth: Doggerland names sea level and the northern ice sheets; the Last Interglacial names temperature, sea level and the Greenland and Antarctic ice whose melt raised it several metres. Cucuteni's mega-sites name the largest city and the urban share. Left unlinked: Europe's eras (carried by the Events inside them), al-Andalus, Byzantium, the Franks, the Ottoman Balkans and Russia's expansion (changes of who rules), the Congress of Vienna, Westphalia, Versailles, the partitions of Poland and the unifications (the number of polities, which no process follows yet), the Renaissance, the Enlightenment and Greek philosophy (no process follows discovery), art and monuments (Aurignacian art, the megaliths, Minoan and Mycenaean palaces), Neanderthals (not counted by humanity's measures), Thera, the Campanian eruption, Magna Carta and the witch hunts (below the resolution of world measures), and the Great Schism (a change between branches of one faith).

upsert.boundary: Farmers from Anatolia spread across Europe, about 6700 to 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Farming families descended from Anatolia's first farmers reach Greece about 6700 BCE, the Danube and central Europe with the Linear Pottery culture about 5500 BCE, and Britain and Scandinavia about 4000 BCE, mostly replacing the hunter-gatherers and mixing with some of them: a wave of advance of about a kilometre a year (WaveOfAdvance#4cec).
provenance: sources to check: Ammerman and Cavalli-Sforza, The Neolithic Transition and the Genetics of Populations in Europe (1984); Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522

upsert.boundary: Fascism in Europe, 1922 to 1945
upsert.description: Mussolini takes power in Italy (1922) and Hitler in Germany (1933), building one-party states of mass rallies, secret police and racial or national myth; Franco wins Spain's civil war (1939); fascist and allied regimes rule much of Europe until 1945.
provenance: sources to check: Paxton, The Anatomy of Fascism (2004); Evans, The Third Reich trilogy (2003 to 2008)

upsert.boundary: The fiscal-military state, about 1550 to 1815
upsert.description: Gunpowder fortresses, standing armies and navies multiply the cost of war; Europe's states that tax, borrow and administer most survive and absorb the rest (Warsift#b01b), so that the five hundred or so polities of 1500 shrink to about thirty by 1900, and Britain, France, Prussia, Austria and Russia emerge as great powers.
provenance: sources to check: Tilly, Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990); Brewer, The Sinews of Power (1989); Parker, The Military Revolution (1988)

upsert.boundary: The French Revolution, 1789 to 1799
upsert.description: Bankrupt after its wars, the monarchy calls the Estates-General; the Third Estate makes itself a National Assembly, Parisians storm the Bastille, the assembly abolishes feudal privileges and declares the Rights of Man; the king is executed (1793), the Terror follows, and war with Europe's monarchies brings Napoleon to power (1799).
provenance: sources to check: Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (2nd ed. 2002)

upsert.boundary: Gravettian Europe, about 33,000 to 26,000 years ago
upsert.description: Mammoth hunters from France to Russia carve Venus figurines such as Willendorf's, fire clay figures at Dolní Věstonice, and bury some of their dead with thousands of ivory beads, as at Sunghir.
provenance: sources to check: Svoboda et al., in Gravettian studies; Trinkaus et al., The People of Sunghir (2014)

upsert.boundary: Archaic Greece: the city-states and their colonies, about 800 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Greek-speaking communities organize as self-governing poleis, found colonies from Marseille to the Black Sea, hold the first Olympic games (776 BCE by tradition) and set down the Iliad and the Odyssey.
provenance: sources to check: Osborne, Greece in the Making (2nd ed. 2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe); Asia (Western Asia: Ionia); Africa (Northern Africa: Cyrene)

upsert.boundary: The Hundred Years' War, 1337 to 1453
upsert.description: The kings of England claim the throne of France and fight a long series of wars; English longbowmen win at Crécy and Agincourt, Joan of Arc revives the French cause, and France ends the English holdings by 1453 with cannon, a standing army and a permanent tax.
provenance: sources to check: Sumption, The Hundred Years War (1990 to 2015)
upsert.region: Europe (Western and Northern Europe: France, England)

upsert.boundary: Industrialization spreads across Europe, 1830 to 1914
upsert.description: Belgium, France, Germany, Switzerland and northern Italy follow Britain into coal, iron, textiles and machines, then Germany leads in steel, chemicals and electricity, and Russia industrializes from the 1890s; Europe's towns fill with factory workers.
provenance: sources to check: Pollard, Peaceful Conquest (1981)
upsert.region: Europe (Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe)

upsert.boundary: European integration, from 1951
upsert.description: Six states pool coal and steel (1951) and found the European Economic Community (1957); it grows into a European Union of up to 28 members with a single market (1993), the euro (1999) and enlargement to the former communist east (2004); the euro crisis and Britain's exit (2020) test it.
provenance: sources to check: Dinan, Ever Closer Union (4th ed. 2010)
upsert.region: Europe (Western, Southern, Northern and Eastern Europe)

upsert.boundary: The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852
upsert.description: Potato blight destroys the crop of a people who live on it; about a million die of hunger and disease and over a million emigrate, while food is exported and relief is grudging; Ireland's population falls by a quarter and keeps falling for a century.
provenance: sources to check: Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond (1999)

upsert.boundary: Europe divided by the Iron Curtain, 1946 to 1989
upsert.description: Soviet-backed communists take power across eastern Europe; Germany is split, NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955) face each other, risings in Berlin (1953), Hungary (1956) and Prague (1968) are crushed, and the Berlin Wall (1961) closes the last gap.
provenance: sources to check: Judt, Postwar (2005); Applebaum, Iron Curtain (2012)

upsert.boundary: Jenner's smallpox vaccine, 1796 to 1802
upsert.description: Edward Jenner shows that cowpox protects against smallpox (May 1796); within a few years vaccination spreads across Europe and to the Americas and Asia, the start of the end of a disease that killed perhaps a tenth of Europeans.
provenance: sources to check: Riedel 2005, Baylor University Medical Center Proceedings 18

upsert.boundary: Justinian's reconquest and law, 527 to 565
upsert.description: Justinian's generals retake North Africa from the Vandals and Italy from the Goths in long, ruinous wars; he codifies Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis, the root of most of Europe's later civil law, and builds Hagia Sophia; plague strikes in 541.
provenance: sources to check: Maas (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe); Asia (Western Asia); Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: Europe at the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: Ice sheets cover Scandinavia, Britain and the Alps, and tundra and steppe the north; people withdraw to refuges in Iberia, southern France, Italy, the Balkans and Ukraine, where Solutrean flint-workers make thin laurel-leaf points.
provenance: sources to check: Posth et al. 2023, Nature 615

upsert.boundary: The Magdalenians: Lascaux and Altamira, about 20,000 to 14,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the ice retreats, Magdalenian hunters of reindeer and horse spread back over western and central Europe, paint the caves of Lascaux and Altamira, and carve spear-throwers and harpoons of antler.
provenance: sources to check: Bahn, Cave Art (2007)

upsert.boundary: Lords, serfs and the manor, about 800 to 1350
upsert.description: Across western Europe most peasants hold land from a lord in return for labour, rents and dues, tied to the manor as serfs, while a warrior aristocracy holds land for military service; serfdom fades in the west after the Black Death but deepens in the east.
provenance: sources to check: Bloch, Feudal Society (1939); Wickham, Medieval Europe (2016)

upsert.boundary: Mesolithic foragers of Europe, about 9700 to 5500 BCE
upsert.description: In the forests of the Holocene, hunter-gatherers with dark skin and often blue eyes, as their genomes show, fish, gather hazelnuts and hunt deer and boar; some live in settled villages, such as Lepenski Vir on the Danube, until farmers arrive.
provenance: sources to check: Olalde et al. 2014, Nature 507 (La Braña); Brace et al. 2019, Nature Ecology & Evolution 3 (Cheddar Man)

upsert.boundary: The migration period, 376 to 568
upsert.description: Goths cross the Danube fleeing the Huns (376) and destroy a Roman army at Adrianople (378); Visigoths sack Rome (410), Vandals take Roman Africa (439), Attila's Huns raid Gaul and Italy, Franks, Angles and Saxons settle the west, and the Lombards enter Italy (568).
provenance: sources to check: Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007); Heather, Empires and Barbarians (2009)

upsert.boundary: Mongol rule over Rus', 1237 to 1480
upsert.description: Batu's armies sack Ryazan, Vladimir and Kyiv (1237 to 1240); for more than two centuries the princes of Rus' pay tribute to the Golden Horde and receive their titles from it, while Moscow rises as its tax collector and ends the tribute after the stand on the Ugra (1480).
provenance: sources to check: Halperin, Russia and the Golden Horde (1985)

upsert.boundary: Napoleon's wars, 1799 to 1815
upsert.description: Napoleon seizes power, crowns himself emperor and conquers most of continental Europe, spreading his Civil Code and abolishing the Holy Roman Empire, until the retreat from Moscow (1812) and defeat at Leipzig and Waterloo (1815); some three to six million die.
provenance: sources to check: Bell, The First Total War (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Peloponnesian War, 431 to 404 BCE
upsert.description: Athens and its empire fight Sparta and its allies for 27 years; plague kills perhaps a quarter of the Athenians (430 to 426), the expedition to Sicily is destroyed, and Sparta, with Persian money, wins; Thucydides writes its history.
provenance: sources to check: Thucydides; Kagan, The Peloponnesian War (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Greco-Persian Wars, 499 to 479 BCE
upsert.description: After the Ionian revolt, the Persian empire invades Greece twice; Athens wins at Marathon (490), Sparta's rearguard falls at Thermopylae, the Greek fleet wins at Salamis (480), and Plataea ends the invasion (479).
provenance: sources to check: Herodotus; Holland, Persian Fire (2005)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Greece); Asia (Western Asia: Ionia)

upsert.boundary: The Punic Wars, 264 to 146 BCE
upsert.description: Rome and Carthage fight three wars for the western Mediterranean; Hannibal crosses the Alps and destroys a Roman army at Cannae (216), but Rome wins at Zama (202) and razes Carthage in 146.
provenance: sources to check: Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (2000)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Italy, Sicily, Iberia); Africa (Northern Africa: Tunisia)

upsert.boundary: Railways across Europe, 1825 to 1870
upsert.description: From the Stockton and Darlington (1825) and the Liverpool and Manchester (1830), railways spread across Europe; by 1870 there are over 100,000 kilometres of track, journeys that took days take hours, and markets, armies and newspapers move with them.
provenance: sources to check: Wolmar, Blood, Iron and Gold (2009)

upsert.boundary: The revolutions of 1848
upsert.description: From Paris to Vienna, Berlin, Milan and Budapest, revolts demand constitutions, national unity and the end of serfdom; most are crushed within a year, but serfdom ends in Austria and the idea of the nation-state spreads.
provenance: sources to check: Sperber, The European Revolutions 1848–1851 (2nd ed. 2005)

upsert.boundary: The Roman Republic, 509 to 27 BCE
upsert.description: Rome expels its kings and governs through consuls, a senate and assemblies; it conquers Italy and then the Mediterranean, destroying Carthage and Corinth in 146 BCE; the wealth and armies of conquest breed civil wars that end with Julius Caesar's dictatorship and Augustus' victory.

upsert.boundary: The Western Roman Empire falls, 406 to 476
upsert.description: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine (406); Rome is sacked (410, 455) and its provinces and taxes are lost one by one, until Odoacer deposes the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in 476. Trade, cities, coinage and literacy shrink across the west for centuries.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how far living standards fell is debated
sources to check: Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005); Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
upsert.region: Europe (Western and Southern Europe); Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: Homo sapiens reaches Europe, about 47,000 to 43,000 years ago
upsert.description: Modern humans leave tools and bones at Bacho Kiro in Bulgaria and Ranis in Germany by about 45,000 years ago; early groups mix with Neanderthals (the Oase man had a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back) but most leave no descendants, and later arrivals become Europe's hunter-gatherers.
provenance: sources to check: Hublin et al. 2020, Nature 581; Mylopotamitaki et al. 2024, Nature 626; Fu et al. 2015, Nature 524

upsert.boundary: The Soviet Union breaks up, 1991
upsert.description: After a failed hard-line coup (August 1991) the republics declare independence one by one, and the Soviet Union is dissolved on 26 December 1991 into fifteen states.
provenance: sources to check: Plokhy, The Last Empire (2014)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern and Northern Europe); Asia (Central and Western Asia)

upsert.boundary: Stalin's Great Terror, 1936 to 1938
upsert.description: The NKVD arrests over 1.5 million people and shoots about 680,000, party leaders, officers, kulaks, national minorities and ordinary people alike, while the Gulag camps hold millions.
provenance: sources to check: Khlevniuk, The History of the Gulag (2004); Conquest, The Great Terror (1968)

upsert.boundary: Herders from the steppe move into Europe, about 3000 to 2300 BCE
upsert.description: Yamnaya-descended herders with wagons, and perhaps plague, move west from the Pontic steppe; their descendants of the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker cultures replace most of the ancestry of central and northern Europe, in Britain some 90% within a few centuries, and probably carry the Indo-European languages.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the role of plague is debated
sources to check: Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522; Olalde et al. 2018, Nature 555; Rasmussen et al. 2015, Cell 163
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern, Central, Northern and Western Europe)

upsert.boundary: The Thirty Years' War, 1618 to 1648
upsert.description: A Bohemian revolt grows into a war of most of Europe's powers fought mainly in Germany; armies living off the land, famine and plague kill perhaps a fifth of the German lands' people, more in some regions.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; losses vary greatly by region
sources to check: Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Western Europe: Germany; Eastern Europe: Bohemia)

upsert.boundary: Russia's war on Ukraine, from 2014
upsert.description: Russia annexes Crimea and backs a war in the Donbas (2014), then launches a full-scale invasion (February 2022); Ukraine holds Kyiv and retakes much ground, and the war becomes Europe's largest since 1945, with hundreds of thousands killed or wounded and millions of refugees.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; casualty figures are uncertain
sources to check: Plokhy, The Russo-Ukrainian War (2023)

upsert.boundary: The first universities, about 1088 to 1300
upsert.description: Guilds of masters and students at Bologna, Paris and Oxford teach law, theology, medicine and the arts; scholars such as Thomas Aquinas reconcile Aristotle, newly translated from Arabic and Greek, with Christian teaching.
provenance: sources to check: Rashdall, The Universities of Europe in the Middle Ages; Grant, The Foundations of Modern Science in the Middle Ages (1996)

upsert.boundary: The gold of Varna, about 4600 to 4200 BCE
upsert.description: In a cemetery on the Black Sea coast, a few graves hold more gold than all others of their age combined: the oldest worked gold known, and among the first signs of a ranked elite.
provenance: sources to check: Higham et al. 2007, Antiquity 81

upsert.boundary: The Viking age, 793 to 1066
upsert.description: Scandinavian seafarers raid Lindisfarne (793) and then the coasts and rivers of Europe; they settle in Britain, Ireland and Normandy, found the Rus' state at Novgorod and Kyiv, trade as far as Baghdad, settle Iceland and Greenland, and reach North America at L'Anse aux Meadows about 1021.
provenance: sources to check: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020); Kuitems et al. 2022, Nature 601
upsert.region: Europe (Northern, Western and Eastern Europe); Americas (Northern America: Greenland, Newfoundland)

upsert.boundary: Europe's wars of religion, 1562 to 1648
upsert.description: Catholics and Protestants fight across Europe: the French Wars of Religion (1562 to 1598), the Dutch Revolt against Spain (from 1568) and finally the Thirty Years' War, entangled with the rivalries of dynasties.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The French Wars of Religion (2nd ed. 2005); Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009)

upsert.boundary: The welfare states, 1945 to 1980
upsert.description: Britain's National Health Service (1948), and pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances and free education across western and northern Europe, give most people security from cradle to grave, paid for by taxes of 30 to 50% of national income.
provenance: sources to check: Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism (1990); Lindert, Growing Public (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Yugoslav wars, 1991 to 2001
upsert.description: Yugoslavia breaks apart in wars in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Kosovo and North Macedonia; some 130,000 to 140,000 die, millions are displaced by 'ethnic cleansing', and Bosnian Serb forces murder about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica (1995), a genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Glenny, The Fall of Yugoslavia (3rd ed. 1996); ICTY judgments

changes.value: Correction and completion of r285. r285 was sent cut short: it carried only the first 12 of the 50 Europe Events its reason lists, and it replaced the description of the farmers' arrival in Europe (ev.eu.farmers-arrive) with a placeholder by mistake. This revision restores that description word for word from r283 and links the remaining 38 Events as r285's reason describes: fascism, the fiscal-military state, the French Revolution, the Gravettian, the poleis, the Hundred Years' War, industrialization, integration, the Irish famine, the Iron Curtain, Jenner, Justinian, the glacial refuges, the Magdalenians, manorialism, the Mesolithic, the migration period, the Mongols in Rus', Napoleon's wars, the Peloponnesian, Persian and Punic wars, railways, 1848, the Roman Republic, Rome's fall, the arrival of Homo sapiens, the Soviet breakup, the Great Terror, the steppe herders, the Thirty Years' War, Russia's war on Ukraine, the universities, Varna, the Vikings, the wars of religion, the welfare states and the Yugoslav wars, each naming the processes r285's reason gives. Rome's fall also names the urban share, which fell in the west.

Values at the Events the new links hold these processes to, where the coverage report found them passing over: war between polities across Alexander's conquests, contestation across the poleis and Cleisthenes, hunger across the Irish famine. War is a rate averaged to the next date, so the block from 490 to 200 BCE is split at 334 BCE and its total kept (between 38 over 290 years becomes 32 to 334 BCE and 45 after; war and safety follow as the sums of their parts).

points.note: Foragers go hungry in bad seasons but move to food; few die of starvation outright.
Held: hunger as a direct cause in foragers is seasonal and local, not famine of stored grain; a glacial maximum may push it up, which the band allows.
Farmers tied to fields and stores die when a harvest fails; famine becomes a recurring cause of death.
The 4.2 kiloyear drought: Egypt's Old Kingdom and Akkad fall amid famine (ev.event-4-2-ka, if dated so in the model).
The Han collapse and the Roman Empire's third-century crisis: wars and failed harvests together.
Lower than in the crises of the third century, before the volcanic winter of 536 and the plague.
The volcanic winter of 536 to 541, the coldest decade in two thousand years, and the plague's disruption of harvests bring dearth.
After Europe's great famine of 1315 to 1317, which killed perhaps a tenth of northern Europe's people.
The plague empties fields and stops trade: dearth follows the dying.

The Ming-Qing wars and the Thirty Years War begin; their famine and plague deaths are counted in war's toll (h.war, 180 a year to 1650), as the usual tallies of those wars count them, so hunger outside them holds at the century's level.

Corrected from 220, which counted the famines of the Ming-Qing transition and the Thirty Years War that war's toll (h.war) already counts. What remains is the Little Ice Age's own dearths. Check: at 1618 to 1650 the six causes of death no longer count those wars' famine deaths twice.
After Tambora's year without a summer (1816), Europe's last great subsistence crisis.

Above the line: the Irish famine at its worst (1846 to 1849), about a million dead in six years among some 1.2 billion people, about 14 per 100,000 a year, with the crop failures across Europe in 1846 and 1847.
The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852, about a million dead.

The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879: perhaps 6 to 10 million dead in India, 9 to 13 million in north China, half a million in Brazil's north-east, among about 1.35 billion people. The spike is sharp and short; the band carries the debated tolls (ev.as.el-nino-famines).
The famines end with the rains of 1879; hunger deaths fall back to the level of the 1880s' lull.
The lull between the El Niño famines and those of 1888 onward in Ethiopia and the 1890s in India.

Rinderpest kills most of the cattle of eastern and southern Africa from 1888, and Ethiopia's great famine (1888 to 1892) kills perhaps a third of its people: a bump in the world's rate between the El Niño famines of the 1870s and the 1890s.
A lull between the famines of the late 1870s and those of 1896 to 1902.
The Indian famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 and the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, perhaps 30 to 60 million dead in all, under El Niño droughts and colonial and imperial policy.
The Russian famine of 1921 to 1922, about five million dead.
China's north-west famine of 1928 to 1930 is under way and the Soviet famines follow from 1930: hunger deaths rise from the 1920s' level toward the 1930 peak.
The Soviet famines of 1930 to 1933, the Holodomor and the Kazakh famine among them, and China's famine of 1928 to 1930.
The Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933 at its worst: five to seven million dead in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Russia among about 2.08 billion people (ev.eu.holodomor).
The Soviet famine ends with the harvest of 1933; hunger deaths fall back.

Corrected from 130: the siege of Leningrad and the Greek and Henan famines are counted in the Second World War's toll (h.war), as its 70 to 85 million dead usually are; here they were counted a second time. Hunger outside the war barely moves. Check: war plus hunger from 1941 to 1945 against the war's toll with its famines.

Corrected from 150: the famines of Bengal (1943), northern Vietnam and Java (1944 to 1945) and the Dutch hunger winter are counted in the war's toll (h.war). Whether Bengal's famine belongs to the war is debated (Sen's entitlement failure under wartime inflation against the loss of Burma's rice and the denial policy), but most tallies of the war's dead include it.
After the war's famines the toll falls: the Soviet famine of 1946 to 1947, about a million dead, is the largest of the postwar decade.
Between the postwar famines and the Great Leap famine, hunger deaths are at their lowest yet; the rise to 1960 is that famine's alone, so the series does not climb before 1959.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward, 1959 to 1961: 15 to 45 million excess deaths on the debated estimates, the largest famine in history.
The Great Leap famine ends in 1961 and 1962 as procurement is cut and grain imported: deaths fall back toward the level before it.
After China's famine, deaths from hunger fall to their lowest level yet; the green revolution's wheat and rice begin to spread (ev.green-revolution).
Biafra (1967 to 1970) and the Sahel droughts.
Bangladesh 1974 and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985.
North Korea's famine, 1994 to 1998.
Famine now comes almost only with war: Gaza, Sudan and Yemen.
Steady at world scale: rising rates in the United States and Latin America from the late 1960s are offset by falls elsewhere; the drug trade's violence grows only later.

The world rate stops falling in the early 1990s: Latin America's homicide epidemic (ev.lac.homicide), with Colombia near its peak and Brazil's rates rising, and Russia's killings after the Soviet collapse offset the long decline elsewhere.

No state, so no elections of rulers.

Rises: the Greek poleis choose their magistrates in assemblies or councils, Carthage elects its suffetes, and the gana-sangha republics of the Ganges plain choose their leaders in councils of clan heads; together perhaps half a percent of humanity, the Ganges republics the largest and least certain part.

Rome expels its kings and elects consuls (509), and Cleisthenes gives Athens' assembly its power (508): with the poleis and the Ganges republics about one person in a hundred lives where rulers are chosen by contested votes, however narrow the electorate.

Rises: Greek democracies and oligarchies, the Roman Republic, Carthage's elected magistrates and the gana-sangha republics of the Ganges plain, whose councils of clan heads chose their leaders; how competitive the last were is uncertain.
Roman Italy, with citizenship for all free Italians; the provinces are ruled, not represented.
Falls: the Republic gives way to the Principate.
Venice elects its doge.
The Italian communes elect their consuls.
Most Italian communes have fallen to lords (signori).
Rises: Poland-Lithuania's nobles elect their kings from 1573, and the Dutch Republic governs itself from 1581.
Britain's Parliament becomes supreme after 1688, its ministries resting on contested elections among a few percent of men.
The new United States.
Falls: Poland-Lithuania is partitioned (1795) and Napoleon takes power (1799).
France's Second Republic, with Belgium, the Netherlands, Piedmont, Denmark, Switzerland and Latin America's competitive oligarchies.
Falls: Louis-Napoleon's coup of December 1851 ends the Second Republic.
Rises: France's Third Republic (1870) and parliamentary government in united Italy.
The Weimar Republic and the new republics of central Europe.
Mussolini's dictatorship and Poland's coup of 1926.
Falls: Hitler's dictatorship from 1933.
Germany occupies most of Europe's democracies.
Liberated western Europe is under provisional governments; its first postwar elections follow from October 1945 into 1946, the rise to 1946.
Liberated western Europe and the Philippines hold elections.
Rises most: India, Japan and West Germany choose their governments in competitive elections.

The Russian famine of 1921 to 1922, about five million dead.
China's north-west famine of 1928 to 1930 is under way and the Soviet famines follow from 1930: hunger deaths rise from the 1920s' level toward the 1930 peak.
The Soviet famines of 1930 to 1933, the Holodomor and the Kazakh famine among them, and China's famine of 1928 to 1930.
The Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933 at its worst: five to seven million dead in Ukraine, Kazakhstan and Russia among about 2.08 billion people (ev.eu.holodomor).
The Soviet famine ends with the harvest of 1933; hunger deaths fall back.

Corrected from 130: the siege of Leningrad and the Greek and Henan famines are counted in the Second World War's toll (h.war), as its 70 to 85 million dead usually are; here they were counted a second time. Hunger outside the war barely moves. Check: war plus hunger from 1941 to 1945 against the war's toll with its famines.

Corrected from 150: the famines of Bengal (1943), northern Vietnam and Java (1944 to 1945) and the Dutch hunger winter are counted in the war's toll (h.war). Whether Bengal's famine belongs to the war is debated (Sen's entitlement failure under wartime inflation against the loss of Burma's rice and the denial policy), but most tallies of the war's dead include it.
After the war's famines the toll falls: the Soviet famine of 1946 to 1947, about a million dead, is the largest of the postwar decade.
Between the postwar famines and the Great Leap famine, hunger deaths are at their lowest yet; the rise to 1960 is that famine's alone, so the series does not climb before 1959.
Still at the postwar low as the Great Leap begins; its famine starts with the procurements of 1959.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward, 1959 to 1961: 15 to 45 million excess deaths on the debated estimates, the largest famine in history.
The Great Leap famine ends in 1961 and 1962 as procurement is cut and grain imported: deaths fall back toward the level before it.
After China's famine, deaths from hunger fall to their lowest level yet; the green revolution's wheat and rice begin to spread (ev.green-revolution).
Biafra (1967 to 1970) and the Sahel droughts.
Bangladesh 1974 and Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985.
North Korea's famine, 1994 to 1998.
Famine now comes almost only with war: Gaza, Sudan and Yemen.
About two thirds of foragers' deaths are from illness, mostly respiratory and gut infections and parasites (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled).

Held: infection in small mobile bands without crowd diseases, mostly gut, respiratory and wound infections and parasites in children; the largest share of forager deaths, as in recent forager mortality studies.
Villages, stored grain, livestock and standing water bring crowd diseases and parasites: infections rise with farming, the first epidemiological transition (Armelagos).
Malaria in Italy's lowlands, gut infections in Rome's crowded city: about seven in ten deaths are infections.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), probably smallpox, which killed perhaps a tenth of the Roman Empire's people.
The Justinianic plague (ev.justinian-plague), the first pandemic of Yersinia pestis.
The plague recurs until about 750 and then vanishes from the Mediterranean for six centuries; infection deaths fall back to their agrarian level.
The Black Death at its height (ev.black-death): the infection death rate more than doubles for the years it passes.
Plague returns every decade or two after 1348.
Smallpox reaches the Caribbean in 1518 and Mexico in 1520; the Americas' epidemics raise the world's infection deaths toward the 1550 value, though the Americas hold about a tenth of humanity.
Smallpox, measles and cocoliztli in the Americas (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd) add deaths, though the Americas are a tenth of humanity.
Jenner's vaccine (1796) begins the retreat of smallpox; plague has left Europe.
Cholera pandemics in the new industrial cities; sanitation's retreat of infection begins in Britain after the 1848 Public Health Act.
Germ theory, clean water and sewers cut infection deaths in Europe and North America; most of the world has not yet begun.
Before the influenza: the 1918 value is the pandemic's spike, not a trend, so the fall since 1900 continues to here; wartime typhus in Serbia and the east adds little at the world's scale.
The 1918 influenza kills perhaps 25 to 50 million in little more than a year, most in India and China (ev.flu-1918).
The influenza has passed by 1920 and the long fall of infection deaths resumes.
Sulfa drugs, from 1935, the first antibacterial medicines.
Penicillin, streptomycin and DDT spread after the war: infection deaths fall faster than at any time before.
About 1967 chronic disease passes infection as the world's leading cause of death.
Smallpox is declared eradicated (1980); the Expanded Programme on Immunization reaches most children by 1990.
HIV/AIDS climbs toward its peak of about two million deaths a year (2004).
COVID-19's first year: about four to five million excess deaths in 2020 on the WHO's estimate, under a third of the pandemic's toll, which peaks in 2021.
COVID-19: about 15 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 on the WHO's estimate, most of them in 2021 (ev.covid).

Foragers carry their goods when they move camp and carry home what they kill and gather: a few tonne-km a person a year. Obsidian and shells travel hundreds of kilometres by exchange, but in tiny amounts.
Farmers carry harvests, stores and building stuff, but rarely far.
Donkeys are domesticated in north-east Africa and carry loads.
The wheel and the sail: carts on land, sailing boats on the Nile and the Gulf.
Rome's grain fleet carries some hundreds of thousands of tonnes from Egypt and Africa each year; the empire's sea trade lifts its average to several times the world's.
Falls: Mediterranean shipping shrinks with the Western empire, as shipwreck counts show.
Song China's Grand Canal and coastal junks move rice, salt and iron in bulk.
Dutch and English merchant fleets, and coal shipped from Newcastle to London.
Turns up steeply: railways and steamships cut the cost of moving bulk goods by most of its cost on roads.
Railways spread across North America, Mexico (the Porfiriato), Argentina and India and steamships take over bulk freight once the Suez Canal opens (1869): freight per person grows at about 9% a year.
On the eve of the First World War world trade and shipping stand at their prewar peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from submarine sinkings and blockade.
Submarine warfare sinks a fifth of the world's merchant tonnage.
Supertankers and bulk carriers: oil and ore cross oceans in unprecedented tonnages; the container ship spreads from 1956.
Dips: the oil shocks cut long-haul tanker trade in the early 1980s.
China's trade boom carries ore and coal in and containers out.
COVID-19's first year: world trade volume falls about a twentieth in 2020 and recovers in 2021.
About 130 trillion tonne-km a year, three quarters of it by sea (UNCTAD and the International Transport Forum, as recalled).

upsert.reason: Before 1850 sketched from loads and distances (a forager's camp moves, a farmer's surplus carried to market, Roman, Song and Dutch shipping); 1850 to 1950 from railway and shipping statistics as recalled; after 1970 from UNCTAD's seaborne tonne-miles and the International Transport Forum's land freight, as recalled.

points.note: Dugout canoes, no riding animals yet.
Sail on the Nile; the horse being domesticated on the steppe.
Stagecoaches on turnpikes.
Jumps: the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830) carries passengers on a timetable at about 30 km/h, nearly twice the fastest mail coach.
Railways.
The DC-3 enters service.
Four-engined airliners such as the Constellation begin scheduled transatlantic service.

The de Havilland Comet 1, the first jet airliner, flies scheduled services from May 1952 at about 725 km/h, until its grounding on 8 April 1954 after two crashes; this is the finer reading the note at 1958.75 left open.
After the Comet's grounding the fastest regular speed falls back to the propeller airliners' (DC-7, Super Constellation, about 550 km/h): the first jet age is interrupted.
The Tupolev Tu-104 begins scheduled jet service in the Soviet Union in September 1956, at about 750 to 800 km/h.

Just before the Boeing 707: the fastest scheduled airliners are the Soviet Tu-104 (from 1956) and the British Comet 4 (from 4 October 1958), at about 750 to 800 km/h. The Comet 1's service of 1952 to 1954, at about 725 km/h, and its grounding after crashes lie between 1950 and here, left for a finer reading.

The Boeing 707 begins scheduled service from New York (26 October 1958, ev.nam.jet-age), cruising at about 900 km/h, near the speed jet airliners still fly; with the DC-8 it makes jet travel the norm.
Concorde's first scheduled flights.
Revised from 900: Concorde's scheduled service (1976–2003) at about Mach 2 is the fastest regular passenger speed.
Revised from 900: Concorde.
Revised from 900: Concorde, grounded July 2000 to November 2001 after the Paris crash, retired in October 2003.

Concorde is grounded from the Paris crash (25 July 2000) until 7 November 2001: for these sixteen months the fastest regular passenger speed is the subsonic jets' again, and it returns to Mach 2 until October 2003.
Concorde flies again after the 2000 crash, until October 2003 (ev.concorde).
Concorde's last scheduled flight.
After Concorde: subsonic jets only. The fastest regular speed fell, a rare reversal.
Shell beads and finished tools passed between bands.
Textiles and metalwork from the first cities' workshops.
Chinese silk, Roman glass and fine pottery, Indian cloth.
Song porcelain and silk carried by sea to South-east Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Indian cotton cloth floods European and West African markets (the calico craze).
British machine-made cotton goods replace Indian cloth in world markets.
Lend-lease arms and machines are much of wartime trade.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now, as Europe's and Japan's industries trade with one another.
East Asia's export manufacturing and the trade in parts between factories.
Global value chains: a phone's parts cross many borders before it is sold.
Goods hold up in the pandemic (medical supplies, electronics for home working) while travel stops.
The goods boom of the pandemic's second year.
On the path between the pandemic's goods boom and 2025.
Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Grain, beef, coffee and sugar from the Americas and wool from Australia flow to Europe as freight rates fall; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Commodity prices recover from the pandemic's low.
Oil, gas, grain and fertilizer prices jump in 2022 with the war in Ukraine; primary goods' share of trade's value rises with them.
Zero: nothing is sold between bands apart from goods.
Shipping and caravan services begin to be paid apart from the goods they carry: a sliver.
Italian merchant banks and the carrying trade of Venice and Genoa sell finance and freight.
Dutch shipping carries much of Europe's trade: the Republic sells freight and insurance.
Steamship freight, marine insurance and London's finance: about a twelfth of trade.
Travel, shipping and finance resume after the war: about an eighth of trade.
Travel stops in the pandemic: services fall about a fifth while goods hold.
Travel still mostly closed; digital and business services grow.
Travel recovers from the pandemic; digital services keep growing.
About a quarter of trade: travel recovered, business and digital services growing fastest.
Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The ASEAN free trade area (1992) and NAFTA (1994) begin and the former Soviet bloc opens to trade; the sum of its three parts on their paths.
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).
Goods trade rebounds from the pandemic while travel is still closed; the sum of its three parts.
Trade recovers from the pandemic and its value peaks as energy and food prices jump after Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the sum of its three parts.
Roman Italy perhaps a third enslaved; most of the world far less.
Serfdom loosening in western Europe after the plague and tightening in the east; slavery across the Islamic world, Africa and South-east Asia.
Enslavement in the Caribbean and the first Atlantic shipments of Africans add little at world scale yet.
Brazil's sugar slavery grows and the first enslaved Africans reach Virginia (1619), while serfdom tightens in Russia and Poland; at world scale the share in bondage holds near 9%.

The sugar revolution begins in Barbados; Russia's Ulozhenie (1649) binds its peasants for good. Growth in Atlantic slavery and eastern serfdom is offset by a world population still recovering from the 1600s' crises.

The Atlantic slave trade near its peak, about 80,000 people a year, and serfdom extended to Ukraine (1783), while the American Revolution opens the age of revolutions whose language of liberty will be turned against slavery.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery in 1794, while the cotton gin (1793) begins the expansion of slavery in the United States and the slave trade still runs near its peak.

Haiti's independence (1804) ends slavery for about half a million people, while Usman dan Fodio's jihad (from 1804) founds the Sokoto caliphate on plantation slavery; at world scale the share drifts down.

Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees about 800,000 people in the Caribbean, the Cape and Mauritius, and Spanish America's republics free theirs slowly by law; the world share keeps drifting down.
Russian serfdom ends in 1861, American slavery in 1865, Brazilian in 1888.
A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
Mostly the Soviet camps and colonial forced labour.
Jericho, if a walled village counts as a town.
Çatalhöyük and a few large villages, if counted as towns.
Uruk growing; the Tripolye megasites.
Plague hit towns hardest.
Steady at world scale: rising rates in the United States and Latin America from the late 1960s are offset by falls elsewhere; the drug trade's violence grows only later.

The world rate stops falling in the early 1990s: Latin America's homicide epidemic (ev.lac.homicide), with Colombia near its peak and Brazil's rates rising, and Russia's killings after the Soviet collapse offset the long decline elsewhere.
Neanderthals hold Europe and are not counted; Homo sapiens arrives about 45,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum drives Europe's foragers into southern refuges; its output falls with its people.
The Roman peace: the Mediterranean's output per person about a sixth above the world's, Europe's north below it.

Rome's fall in the west (ev.eu.rome-fall): cities shrink, trade and coin fail and people fall, so Europe's output falls by about two fifths from 200 to 610 and its output per person drops below the world's.
The high-medieval peak: Europe's output more than doubles from 1000 with its people and its towns.
After the Black Death: Europe's output about an eighth below 1300's though output per person is higher, fewer people working the same land (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
Atlantic trade and the Dutch and English economies: Europe's output per person is about two fifths above the world's.
Coal and steam (Sunbound#c94c): Europe's output per person reaches about 1.75 times the world's.
Europe's output passes Asia's for the first time since antiquity, between 1870 and 1890.
Europe's output falls about a tenth from 1913 with the war.
The war's last year: occupied, bombed and fought-over Europe makes about a seventh less than in 1940; Germany's output collapses in 1945.
The postwar boom: Western Europe's recovery and the Soviet Union's growth carry Europe's output back above the Americas'.
The Soviet bloc's collapse: Eastern Europe's output falls about two fifths between 1989 and 1998, so Europe's output grows slowly through the 1990s (ev.eu.soviet-collapse).
Stone tools, wooden spears, skins and shelters: about a sixth of foragers' output.
Pottery, weaving, houses and the first copper: farmers make more things than foragers.
Bronze, monumental building and specialist craftsmen in the first states.
The collapse of Roman manufacturing and trade in the West: pottery, coins and buildings become cruder and fewer.
Song China's iron output, perhaps over 100,000 tonnes a year by 1078 as Hartwell reconstructed it, is not matched until the eighteenth century.
Turns up: the industrial revolution's cotton mills, iron and steam spread from Britain.
Steel, chemicals and electricity: the second industrial revolution in Germany and the United States.
Making passes food-getting in world output about now.
Ford's moving assembly line and the Haber–Bosch process begin in 1913, on the eve of the war.
World industrial production falls by about a third from 1929 to 1932, by the League of Nations' index as recalled: the Depression is above all industry's collapse.
Peak of war production: American and Soviet factories make arms on a scale never seen.
Demobilization: war production stops and factories convert.
Industry's share of world output near its peak, about 37%.
Turns flat: deindustrialization in the old industrial countries and the collapse of Soviet-bloc industry after 1989.
Turns up again: China becomes the world's workshop.
About 28% of world output.

upsert.reason: Industry's share of world output: about 15% for foragers' tools, clothing and shelters, 16 to 22% in agrarian economies, a third by 1950 and its peak about 37% in the 1960s, about 28% now (World Bank value added after 1960, as recalled).

points.note: Rich child burials such as Sungir hint at inherited status in a few groups.
A few sedentary complex foragers, such as the early Natufians, may have had inherited status.
Zero on the usual account; the White Sands footprints in New Mexico, dated 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, would make it a small positive share. Their dating is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
People south of the ice in the far north-west and the Pacific coast (Paisley Caves, Cooper's Ferry) and in the east (Page-Ladson), soon after the ice-free corridor and the coast open.
The Clovis hunters spread across the continent within a few centuries.
Archaic foragers; from here the farming centres of Mesoamerica and the Andes grow faster, and Northern America's part of the hemisphere falls for six thousand years.
Maize farming spreads through the eastern woodlands and the Mississippian towns begin.
Cahokia empties and the Great Drought (1276 to 1299) drives the Ancestral Puebloans from the Four Corners.

Perhaps 4 to 5 million north of Mexico on middle estimates; the range runs from about 2 million (Ubelaker) to 18 million (Dobyns), with Thornton's 7 million between, a debate this value does not settle.
The Native nations' losses begin in earnest after de Soto's entrada (1539 to 1543) and the first coastal epidemics; the settlers are not yet a thousand.
The epidemics among the north-eastern nations of 1616 to 1640 and the Huron losses of the 1630s (ev.nam.northeast-epidemics) (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The low point: about a million Native people and a quarter of a million colonists and enslaved Africans.
The British colonies double every 25 years or so, the fastest growth then known, as Franklin and Malthus both noted.
Immigration is cut by the quota acts of 1921 and 1924, and the share rises more slowly.
Northern America's peak share, with the baby boom; from here births fall below the world's and the share declines.
Immigration keeps the decline slow: about one in seven of its people was born abroad.
Zero until Britain's income tax of 1799: earlier levies on movables and tithes on produce are counted with land and goods.
Pitt's income tax, 1799, to pay for the war with revolutionary France.
Britain repeals its income tax in 1816: back to about zero.
Peel brings Britain's income tax back in 1842.
The Union's income tax of 1862, for the Civil War.
The American wartime income tax lapses (1872).
Prussia's income tax of 1891 and Bismarck's social insurance from 1883; Japan's income tax of 1887.
The United States' federal income tax, 1913.
Wartime income and excess-profits taxes in every belligerent: revenue from incomes rises more than fourfold in four years (Warsift#b01b: the war rewards the states that can raise more).
Falls back with peace but stays three times its 1913 level.
Income tax withheld from wages (the United States from 1943) turns it into a mass tax.
Incomes pay about half of all revenue at the war's height.

Peacetime: payroll contributions to the welfare states keep it rising for half a century, a rise that war competition does not explain (Warsift#b01b fits the wars, not this; its failure mode 'one path for all').
Income, profit and payroll taxes and social contributions: more than half of world revenue, about three fifths in rich states.
Before wartime taxation and borrowing.
Wartime taxation and borrowing.
Revenue rises as a share of output while output falls in the Depression, and the New Deal, Japan's war spending and Germany's rearmament start to raise taxes.
Wartime taxation at its height in the belligerents.
Demobilization: revenue falls from its wartime height but stays far above the 1930s (ev.postwar-order).
Sum of homicide and war.
Homicide 29 plus war 30.
Revised with war: homicide 29 plus war 39.
Homicide 28.8 plus war 52: Alexander's conquests and the Warring States' last century.
Homicide 28.6 plus war 27.4.
The Yellow Turban rising and the warlord wars of 184 to 200 give way to the Three Kingdoms (ev.han-collapse): homicide 28 plus war 45.
Homicide 28 plus war 20.
The Mongol conquests (ev.mongol-conquests): homicide 28 plus war 100.
Homicide 26 plus war 22.
Homicide 25.2 plus war 22.
Homicide 24.3 plus war 20.
Homicide 24.2 plus war 20.
Homicide 15.3 plus war 12.
Homicide 12.7 plus war 15.
Revised from 24 with War at 1780: homicide 12 plus war 7.
Homicide 11.6 plus war 16: the French Revolutionary wars.
Revised from 21 with War: homicide 11 plus war 18.
Homicide 10.8 plus war 40: the Napoleonic wars' deadliest years.
Homicide 9.7 plus war 200: the Taiping war's last years and the American Civil War.
The Taiping war ends in 1864 and the American Civil War in 1865 (ev.taiping, ev.us-civil-war): homicide 9.6 plus war 30.
Homicide 9.6 plus war 30, the 1864 rate held.
Homicide 9.5 plus war 30.
Homicide 9 plus war 190.
Homicide 8.4 plus war 25.
Revised from 508 with War at 1940: homicide 8 plus war 150.
Homicide 8 plus war 650: the war's deadliest years begin with the invasion of the Soviet Union.
Homicide 8 plus war 650.
Homicide 8 plus war 500, the 1940 rate held.
The Second World War ends in August 1945 (ev.ww2, ev.long-peace): homicide 8 plus war 50, now the Chinese civil war and Partition.
Homicide 8 plus war 50.
Revised from 22 with War: homicide 8 plus war 26, the Korean War.
Homicide 8 plus war 5.3, after Korea.
Homicide 8 plus war 6, the 1960 rate held.
Homicide 8 plus war 26: the killings in Indonesia.
Homicide 8 plus war 6, once the killings end.
Homicide 8 plus war 21: the killings in Bangladesh.
Revised from 13 with War: homicide 8 plus war 7.5, with Burundi's killings of 1972 and Amin's in Uganda.
Homicide 8 plus war 5.4.
Revised from 19 with War: homicide 8 plus war 11.8, the Khmer Rouge.
Revised from 19 with War: homicide 8 plus war 11.8.
Homicide 8 plus war 4.5, after the Khmer Rouge.
Homicide 7.6 plus war 44: the Rwandan genocide.
Homicide 7.6 plus war 1.5.
Homicide 6.9 plus war 1.
No schools before writing: learning passed by imitation, stories, initiation and work.
Writing begins in Sumer and Egypt; the first scribal schools are too few to read above zero at this resolution.
The scribal schools of Sumer and Egypt: their first years of sign lists and copying are counted here, the advanced years as secondary; the boundary is this account's reading.
Protestant and Catholic reformers both push reading schools: Luther's call for schools, the Jesuit and parish schools, with Ming and Edo village schools.
The growth is almost all elementary: Prussia's and Scotland's parish schools, New England's common schools, Japan's temple schools (terakoya).
Compulsory elementary schooling spreads: Britain's Education Act (1870), France's Ferry laws (1881 to 1882), Meiji Japan's school law (1872).
Primary's share of all years is at its highest, nine in ten.
From here Barro and Lee's attainment by level (as recalled): primary is still about four in five years of school.
Slowing toward six years, where everyone completes primary; most of the growth is now above it.

Begins: Plato's Academy (about 387 BCE), Aristotle's Lyceum, the Museum of Alexandria, Taxila's teachers; the Han Imperial Academy (Taixue) follows in 124 BCE. Which ancient schools count as higher learning is a matter of definition.
The Later Han's Imperial Academy is said to have held some 30,000 students in the mid second century.
Nalanda in India (from the fifth century) and the Sui and Tang state academies.
The universities of Bologna, Paris and Oxford, the Nizamiyya madrasas of higher law and the Song academies.
The American GI Bill (1944) sends returning soldiers to college: the first step from elite to mass higher education.
Higher education turns from elite to mass (Trow's terms) in North America, Europe, Japan and the Soviet bloc from about 1960.
China expands its universities from 1999, from under a tenth of young people enrolled to over half by 2020; India and Latin America grow fast too.
About a tenth of all years of school; women now outnumber men in higher education in most countries.
Zero among foragers, whom the account counts as holding no one in bondage.
Captives held to work among the first farmers and settled foragers, as bondage begins (h.freedom).
Corvée and temple dependants in the first states.
Egypt's corvée and the Akkadian and Ur III labour gangs.
Rome's slaves (perhaps a third of Roman Italy) and Han China's corvée: about a ninth of the world's working hours.
Serfs' labour dues in Europe, slaves in the Islamic world, corvée across Asia.
After the Black Death labour dues fade in western Europe.
The second serfdom east of the Elbe and the encomienda and mita in Spanish America.
Atlantic slavery near its height beside Russian serfdom.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery (1794), but the cotton gin (1793) opens the second slavery in the United States: compelled work falls only slowly.
Java's Cultivation System (from 1830) and the growth of slavery in Cuba, Brazil and the American South offset the first abolitions; Britain's emancipation begins only in 1834.
Britain abolishes slavery in its colonies from 1834.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs, 1861.
American slavery ends, 1865.
Cuba's slaves become 'apprentices' (1880) and Brazil's slavery is ending; colonial forced labour is about to grow in Africa.
Leopold's Congo Free State (from 1885) imposes forced rubber collection, while Cuba's last slaves are freed (1886) and Brazil's follow in 1888.
Brazil abolishes slavery in 1888, the last in the Americas; colonial forced labour (the Congo Free State) goes on.
War labour: prisoners of war and deported workers.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Gulag.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
The Gulag is emptied after Stalin's death (1953).
About 28 million people in forced labour by the ILO's count, under 1% of the world's working hours.
No writing until about 3300 BCE.
Writing appears about 3300 BCE.
Gutenberg's press begins; its effect on literacy comes over the next centuries (ev.printing).
Printed books are cheap in Europe by now; literacy creeps up there.
Literacy is high in north-west Europe and North America, low almost everywhere else (ev.mass-schooling).
Literacy campaigns in China, the Soviet Union's completed, and the first schooled generations of the new states.
No state, so no national elections: bands decide by consensus, which the parent's measure does not count.
The first states have assemblies of elders and citizens (Mesopotamian city assemblies, as Jacobsen argued), but no elections of rulers by a franchise that can be counted.
Citizens of Athens after 508 BCE and of other Greek democracies and the Roman Republic: a few hundred thousand men in a world of some sixty million adults.
Rome extends citizenship to Italy after the Social War (89 BCE): about a million adult men may vote, if they come to Rome.
Falls: under Augustus the Roman assemblies lose their elections to the Senate and the emperor (by 14 CE).
Iceland's Althing and Venice's popular assembly.
The Italian communes' councils, the Swiss cantons and the county electors of England's Commons.
England's forty-shilling freeholders (1430).
The nobles of Poland-Lithuania, perhaps a tenth of its people, vote in their dietines and elect the king.
Rises: some five to six million Frenchmen vote for the Estates-General, and the new American states widen their franchises.
Napoleon's plebiscites are open to all Frenchmen: votes without a choice of rulers, counted here because the measure is the formal right.
Under Napoleon's empire the plebiscite franchise holds until the Restoration of 1814 cuts the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers; the fall to 1820 comes then.
Falls: the restored French monarchy limits the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers.

Opens fragmentation, the part the re-recorded politics carve promoted, and independent states, its kind. Autonomous polities before 1900 are derived from the model's own series: the people outside states (humanity times one minus the share under a state) divided by the average size of an autonomous unit without a state (35 for forager bands, rising to about 100 by 1000 BCE as villages and chiefdoms replace bands, 200 by 1000 CE and 400 by 1900), plus the states. After 1900 the count is set directly from the remaining unadministered peoples, because the share under a state leaves more people outside states than the record of unpacified groups supports (a tension recorded in the note). Independent states are counted de facto, recognized or not. All values recalled and sketched (EvidenceDependence#23ca); Carneiro's estimate of about 600,000 autonomous units in 1000 BCE and 157 states in 1976, and Tilly's of about 500 European polities in 1490 and some 30 by 1900, are where the order of magnitude is to be checked.

points.note: No states: every autonomous unit is a band.
The first: Uruk and its neighbours on the lower Euphrates, if counted as states.
Some thirty Sumerian city-states, Egypt unified under one king, Elam and the cities of upper Mesopotamia and Syria.
Falls: Akkad unites Mesopotamia's city-states under one king (about 2334 to 2154 BCE).
Rises: the Zhou's vassals become the independent states of the Spring and Autumn period (about 150), the Greek poleis multiply, and the Ganges plain's janapadas and the Phoenician cities form.
The Greek world alone holds about a thousand poleis, of which several hundred answer to no one; how many of the smallest to count as states is the largest uncertainty, carried by the band.
Falls by two thirds: Qin unites the Warring States (221), the Hellenistic kingdoms and Rome absorb the poleis, and the Maurya empire most of the subcontinent (Warsift#b01b).
Rises: the western Roman provinces become kingdoms, China is divided, and the Maya city-states multiply.
Falls: the Mongol conquests absorb the states of China, Central Asia, Iran and Rus'.

Europe's roughly five hundred more or less autonomous units (Tilly's count, the Holy Roman Empire's principalities among them), Japan's warring daimyo, the sultanates of India and the Malay world, Africa's kingdoms and the Americas' states: several hundred in all.

Falls by two fifths: the Holy Roman Empire's some 250 principalities, free cities and church lands are mediatized (1803) and the Empire dissolved (1806), leaving about forty German states; Napoleon annexes much of Italy and the Low Countries.
Falls: Italy (1861 to 1870) and Germany (1871) unify, some thirty states becoming two.
Falls to its low: the Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1914) ends almost every African kingdom but Ethiopia and Liberia, and Burma, Vietnam and the last Indian and Malay states come under colonial rule.
Rises: from the fallen Russian, Austro-Hungarian, German and Ottoman empires come Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, the Baltic states, Austria and Hungary (Versailles, 1919).
Falls: Germany, the Soviet Union, Italy and Japan absorb Austria, Czechoslovakia, Albania, Poland and the Baltic states.
The occupied states are restored as the war ends.
Jumps: the year of Africa, seventeen new states in 1960.
Germany reunites and the two Yemens join; Namibia becomes independent.
Jumps: fifteen states from the Soviet Union and four from Yugoslavia.
The 193 members of the United Nations, the Holy See and the states that govern themselves without general recognition (Taiwan, Kosovo and a few others).
Starts: some 300,000 people in forager bands of about 35, each answering to no one; the band size and the population are both uncertain by a factor of several.
Falls a little with people in the deepest part of the penultimate glacial.
Flat through the Last Glacial Maximum: no more people, so no more bands.
At the Holocene's start, about 130,000 bands: the number of autonomous units grows with people for as long as everyone lives in bands.
Farming multiplies people faster than it enlarges their units: autonomous villages of a hundred or two join the bands, and the count passes a third of a million.

Peaks in the late Bronze Age at about three quarters of a million: states hold a quarter of humanity, but the people outside them, in bands, villages and chiefdoms, are still most and still growing. Carneiro's order of magnitude, about 600,000 in 1000 BCE, lies inside the band.
Falls: the Han, Roman, Parthian and Kushan empires hold six in ten people, and the units left outside them are larger chiefdoms and tribes.
Falls by a quarter: the Black Death and the Mongol and Timurid wars cut people while states (Ming, Ottoman, Vijayanagara, Mali, the Aztec and Inca beginnings) hold three in four of those left.
Falls: the Americas' chiefdoms and villages die with their people after 1492 or come under Spain and Portugal, and Russia's conquest of Siberia reaches the Pacific (1639).

Falls fast: the Scramble for Africa, the conquests of the American West, Patagonia and Siberia's last peoples, and the Dutch, British and French advance in South-east Asia bring hundreds of thousands of stateless villages and bands under states between 1870 and 1900.

Set directly from here on: what remains outside states is the New Guinea highlands' clans (perhaps a million people), the Amazon's villages, interior Borneo, the Sahara's and Arabia's tribes and the Afghan frontier; the model's share under a state (98%) would leave twice as many people outside states, a tension to resolve in a later pass.
Patrols and gold prospectors reach the New Guinea highlands' valleys (the Wahgi, 1933), whose clans had been the largest population on Earth outside any state.
Postwar patrols and missions in New Guinea, the Amazon and Borneo bring most remaining groups under some administration; the count of all autonomous units falls toward that of states.
States now make up half or more of all autonomous units; the rest are uncontacted groups in Amazonia, western New Guinea and the Andamans, perhaps a hundred or two.
Rises: the Soviet Union's breakup makes fifteen states of one, and Yugoslavia's four more.

About 197 states, recognized or not, and perhaps a hundred uncontacted peoples who answer to no state in practice; whether those count as autonomous polities is a matter of definition the band carries.

upsert.boundary: The Berlin conference, November 1884 to February 1885
upsert.description: Fourteen states, no African among them, agree how claims to African coasts will be recognized and give the Congo basin to King Leopold's association.
provenance: sources to check: Förster, Mommsen and Robinson (eds.), Bismarck, Europe and Africa (1988)

upsert.boundary: Liberia founded and independent, 1822 to 1847
upsert.description: The American Colonization Society settles freed Black Americans at Monrovia (1822); Liberia declares independence in 1847, ruled by the settlers' descendants over the indigenous majority.
provenance: sources to check: Clegg, The Price of Liberty (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Scramble for Africa, 1881 to 1914
upsert.description: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain Egypt (1882); the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) sets rules for claiming the rest; with machine guns, quinine and African soldiers, Britain, France, Germany, Belgium's king, Portugal, Italy and Spain partition almost the whole continent by 1914. Peoples who had lived without states, perhaps a third or more of Africans, come under colonial governments.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the share of Africans living without states before conquest is a rough guess
sources to check: Pakenham, The Scramble for Africa (1991); Vansina, Being Colonized (2010)

upsert.boundary: The year of Africa, 1960
upsert.description: Seventeen countries become independent in one year, fourteen of them French colonies, with Nigeria and the Congo; by 1965 most of the continent is independent.
provenance: sources to check: Cooper, Africa since 1940 (2nd ed. 2019)

upsert.boundary: Latin America's wars of independence, 1808 to 1826
upsert.description: After Napoleon seizes Spain (1808), juntas and armies across Spanish America fight for independence: Hidalgo's rising in Mexico (1810), Bolívar in the north and San Martín in the south, until Ayacucho (1824) and the fall of Callao (1826); Brazil separates from Portugal peacefully as an empire (1822). About eighteen new states emerge.
provenance: sources to check: Lynch, The Spanish American Revolutions 1808–1826 (2nd ed. 1986)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America

upsert.boundary: The American Revolution, 1775 to 1783
upsert.description: Thirteen colonies rebel against British taxation and rule, declare independence (July 1776) and, with French help, win at Saratoga and Yorktown; the Treaty of Paris (1783) recognizes the United States.
provenance: sources to check: Wood, The Radicalism of the American Revolution (1992)

upsert.boundary: Israel's founding and the war of 1948
upsert.description: After the UN votes to partition Palestine (November 1947), civil war breaks out; Israel declares independence (May 1948) and defeats the armies of its Arab neighbours; about 700,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled, the Nakba, and hundreds of thousands of Jews later leave or are driven from Arab countries.

upsert.boundary: Qin unifies China, 221 to 206 BCE
upsert.description: The First Emperor conquers the last of the warring states and imposes one script, one coinage, standard weights, axle widths and laws, ruled through appointed officials in commanderies rather than nobles; the dynasty falls soon after his death, but the unified empire endures.
provenance: sources to check: Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires: Qin and Han (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Zhou overthrow the Shang, 1046 BCE
upsert.description: At Muye the Zhou defeat the last Shang king and justify it by the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that heaven grants rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from the wicked, which every later Chinese dynasty invokes.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the date follows the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project
sources to check: Shaughnessy, in The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)

upsert.boundary: The British Caribbean's independence, 1962 to 1983
upsert.description: After the West Indies Federation breaks up (1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago become independent (1962), then Barbados and, on the mainland, Guyana (1966), the Bahamas (1973), Grenada (1974) and the smaller islands, the last St Kitts and Nevis (1983); most remain parliamentary democracies on the Westminster model. Anguilla, the Cayman Islands and others stay British.
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: The Ottomans take Constantinople, 6 April to 29 May 1453
upsert.description: After a siege of seven weeks in which great bronze cannon batter the land walls, Mehmed II takes the city and ends the Byzantine empire, the last remnant of Rome; as Istanbul it becomes the Ottoman capital.
provenance: sources to check: Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453 (1965); Crowley, Constantinople: The Last Great Siege (2005)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Turkey); Europe (Southern Europe: the Byzantine state)

upsert.boundary: Decolonization, 1945 to 1975.
upsert.description: From Indonesia and India to Angola and Mozambique, about eighty colonies become independent states; some keep elected government, many do not.

upsert.boundary: The Congress of Vienna, 1814 to 1815
upsert.description: The victorious powers redraw Europe's map and set up a concert of great powers that keeps a general peace for almost a century, broken by limited wars.
provenance: sources to check: Schroeder, The Transformation of European Politics 1763–1848 (1994)

upsert.boundary: The fiscal-military state, about 1550 to 1815
upsert.description: Gunpowder fortresses, standing armies and navies multiply the cost of war; Europe's states that tax, borrow and administer most survive and absorb the rest (Warsift#b01b), so that the five hundred or so polities of 1500 shrink to about thirty by 1900, and Britain, France, Prussia, Austria and Russia emerge as great powers.
provenance: sources to check: Tilly, Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990); Brewer, The Sinews of Power (1989); Parker, The Military Revolution (1988)

upsert.boundary: Archaic Greece: the city-states and their colonies, about 800 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Greek-speaking communities organize as self-governing poleis, found colonies from Marseille to the Black Sea, hold the first Olympic games (776 BCE by tradition) and set down the Iliad and the Odyssey.
provenance: sources to check: Osborne, Greece in the Making (2nd ed. 2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe); Asia (Western Asia: Ionia); Africa (Northern Africa: Cyrene)

upsert.boundary: The partitions of Poland, 1772 to 1795
upsert.description: Russia, Prussia and Austria divide the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in three steps, the last after a failed national rising, and Poland disappears from the map until 1918.
provenance: sources to check: Lukowski, The Partitions of Poland (1999)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Poland, Lithuania, Belarus, Ukraine)

upsert.boundary: Muscovy becomes Russia and crosses Siberia, 1552 to 1689
upsert.description: Ivan IV takes Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan, Cossacks and fur traders cross Siberia to the Pacific by 1639, and the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) fixes a border with Qing China: the largest country on Earth takes shape.
provenance: sources to check: Forsyth, A History of the Peoples of Siberia (1992)

upsert.boundary: The Soviet Union breaks up, 1991
upsert.description: After a failed hard-line coup (August 1991) the republics declare independence one by one, and the Soviet Union is dissolved on 26 December 1991 into fifteen states.
provenance: sources to check: Plokhy, The Last Empire (2014)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern and Northern Europe); Asia (Central and Western Asia)

upsert.boundary: Italy and Germany unified, 1859 to 1871
upsert.description: Piedmont, with French help and Garibaldi's volunteers, unites Italy (1861, Rome 1870); Bismarck's Prussia defeats Denmark, Austria and France and proclaims the German Empire at Versailles (January 1871).
provenance: sources to check: Breuilly, The Formation of the First German Nation-State (1996); Riall, Risorgimento (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Paris peace settlement, 1919 to 1920
upsert.description: The victors impose the Treaty of Versailles on Germany, with reparations and a war-guilt clause, break up Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman empire, create Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia, and found the League of Nations.

upsert.boundary: The Peace of Westphalia, October 1648
upsert.description: The treaties of Münster and Osnabrück end the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War, recognize Dutch and Swiss independence and let German princes choose their territories' religion, in a settlement later read as the start of the system of sovereign states.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the 'Westphalian system' is partly a later myth
sources to check: Osiander 2001, International Organization 55

upsert.boundary: The Yugoslav wars, 1991 to 2001
upsert.description: Yugoslavia breaks apart in wars in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Kosovo and North Macedonia; some 130,000 to 140,000 die, millions are displaced by 'ethnic cleansing', and Bosnian Serb forces murder about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica (1995), a genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Glenny, The Fall of Yugoslavia (3rd ed. 1996); ICTY judgments

upsert.boundary: The Mongol conquests, 1206 to 1279.
upsert.description: From Chinggis Khan's election in 1206 to the fall of the Southern Song in 1279, the largest contiguous land empire is built through wars that kill millions in northern China, Central Asia and Iran. The empire joins the steppe routes from China to the Black Sea.

upsert.boundary: The Pacific island nations become independent, 1962 to 1980
upsert.description: Samoa (1962) is first, then Nauru (1968), Tonga's full sovereignty and Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), Solomon Islands and Tuvalu (1978), Kiribati (1979) and Vanuatu (1980); others remain territories or freely associated states.
provenance: sources to check: Fischer, A History of the Pacific Islands (2nd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: East Timor votes for independence and becomes Timor-Leste, 1999 to 2002
upsert.description: In the UN-run referendum of 30 August 1999, 78.5% vote for independence; militias organized by the Indonesian army kill some 1,400 people and burn most of the territory's buildings, until an Australian-led force lands in September. After a UN administration, Timor-Leste becomes independent on 20 May 2002.
provenance: sources to check: CAVR, Chega! (2005); Martin, Self-Determination in East Timor (2001)
