points.note: No states: every autonomous unit is a band.
The first: Uruk and its neighbours on the lower Euphrates, if counted as states.
Some thirty Sumerian city-states, Egypt unified under one king, Elam and the cities of upper Mesopotamia and Syria.
Falls: Akkad unites Mesopotamia's city-states under one king (about 2334 to 2154 BCE).

The Zhou conquer the Shang (1046 BCE) and enfeoff kinsmen and allies in vassal states that will become the independent states of the Spring and Autumn period; after the Bronze Age collapse the Levant and Anatolia hold Aramaean, Neo-Hittite and Phoenician city-states.
Rises: the Zhou's vassals become the independent states of the Spring and Autumn period (about 150), the Greek poleis multiply, and the Ganges plain's janapadas and the Phoenician cities form.
The Greek world alone holds about a thousand poleis, of which several hundred answer to no one; how many of the smallest to count as states is the largest uncertainty, carried by the band.
Falls by two thirds: Qin unites the Warring States (221), the Hellenistic kingdoms and Rome absorb the poleis, and the Maurya empire most of the subcontinent (Warsift#b01b).
Rises: the western Roman provinces become kingdoms, China is divided, and the Maya city-states multiply.
Falls: the Mongol conquests absorb the states of China, Central Asia, Iran and Rus'.

Europe's roughly five hundred more or less autonomous units (Tilly's count, the Holy Roman Empire's principalities among them), Japan's warring daimyo, the sultanates of India and the Malay world, Africa's kingdoms and the Americas' states: several hundred in all.

Falls by two fifths: the Holy Roman Empire's some 250 principalities, free cities and church lands are mediatized (1803) and the Empire dissolved (1806), leaving about forty German states; Napoleon annexes much of Italy and the Low Countries.
Falls: Italy (1861 to 1870) and Germany (1871) unify, some thirty states becoming two.
Falls to its low: the Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1914) ends almost every African kingdom but Ethiopia and Liberia, and Burma, Vietnam and the last Indian and Malay states come under colonial rule.
Rises: from the fallen Russian, Austro-Hungarian, German and Ottoman empires come Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, the Baltic states, Austria and Hungary (Versailles, 1919).

changes.value: Opens the two parts of the carve of force (carve.concept.humanity.means.force) and its kind. Arms: the energy of the most destructive single weapon in regular service, in joules on a log scale, from a thrusting spear to the hydrogen bomb: a frontier reading like the fastest passenger speed. Spending: military expenditure as a share of world output, built before 1820 as about 55 to 65% of state revenue (h.revenue) plus about 1% of the output of people outside states, and from 1949 as SIPRI's world military burden as recalled; wartime peaks run beyond revenue on borrowing. Nuclear warheads: the world's stockpiles as recalled from the Federation of American Scientists' estimates. All recalled and sketched or inferred, sharing one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: None before 1945.
Starts: three bombs built by August 1945, the test at Alamogordo and the two dropped on Japan; one or two more cores by the year's end (ev.nuclear-weapons).
The Soviet Union tests its first bomb (1949) and begins its stockpile.
The arms race at its fastest: the American stockpile grows by several thousand a year (SecurityDilemma#a61b).
The peak: about 70,000 warheads, two thirds of them Soviet.
Falls: the INF treaty (1987) and then START cut the arsenals; tactical weapons are withdrawn as the Cold War ends.
About 12,200 warheads in nine states, about nine in ten Russian or American; China's arsenal is the one growing fast.
Starts: a heavy thrusting or thrown spear delivers a few hundred joules, the most any weapon can.
Bows and arrows, by about 64,000 years ago in southern Africa, reach farther but strike with less energy than a spear; the frontier does not move.
The spear-thrower, from about 20,000 years ago, throws a dart harder and farther than an arm alone.
The first states' sieges: rams swung or pushed by many men against city gates.
Assyria's wheeled siege engines with heavy rams.
Jumps: torsion catapults, from Syracuse about 400 BCE, and the Hellenistic stone-throwers that hurl stones of a talent (about 26 kg) or more at city walls.
Falls a little: the great torsion engines go out of use with Rome's armies, and the traction trebuchet, coming west from China, throws lighter stones.
The counterweight trebuchet, in the Mediterranean world from the twelfth century, throws stones of a hundred kilograms and more.
Jumps a hundredfold: the Jin's iron-cased thunder-crash bombs, packed with gunpowder, at Kaifeng (1232) against the Mongols (ev.gunpowder).
Jumps: gunpowder mines of a ton or so under fortress walls, as Pedro Navarro's at Naples (1503), release a thousand times the energy of the great bombards' balls.
Still the black-powder mine: the Union's mine at Petersburg (1864) holds about four tonnes.
High explosives (dynamite, guncotton, lyddite) replace black powder in mines and shells.
Jumps: the largest of the mines under Messines ridge (June 1917) holds about 40 tonnes of ammonal.
Jumps about five hundredfold: the atomic bombs on Hiroshima (about 15 kilotons) and Nagasaki (about 21) (ev.as.hiroshima).
Jumps thirtyfold: the hydrogen bomb in service, the Mark 17 of 10 to 15 megatons, the yield Castle Bravo tested (ev.mic.castle-bravo).
Its peak: the American B41 of 25 megatons enters service; the Soviet Tsar Bomba's 50 megatons (1961) is tested, not deployed.
Falls: the B41 is retired as accurate missiles make yield less needed; the largest left are Soviet warheads of about 20 megatons on the heaviest missiles.

Falls: the single-warhead heavy missiles are replaced by multiple smaller warheads; the American B53 of 9 megatons is about the largest left. When the last 20-megaton Soviet warheads left service is uncertain, and the band holds it.
The B53 retired (1997): the largest warheads in service are China's of about 4 to 5 megatons on the DF-5.
Starts: bands give perhaps a hundredth of their effort to raids, feuds and the weapons kept for them, an order of magnitude the band carries.
Chiefs keep retinues and villages build palisades: a little more of output goes to force.
Rises: the Warring States' conscript armies, the Punic wars and the Maurya army take more of output than any earlier states.
The Roman and Han armies each take about half their states' revenue: perhaps 2 to 3% of their output.
The military revolution: bastion forts, gunpowder armies and navies take a growing share of states' revenue, three quarters or more in Europe's wars.
The Seven Years' War, fought in Europe, the Americas and India.
The Napoleonic wars' peak: Britain spends a fifth or more of its output on war, France and its satellites as much, mostly on credit.
Falls with the peace after 1815: armies are cut and the concert of Europe keeps the great powers from war.
The American Civil War and the Taiping war.
The naval race and the European armies' growth before 1914.
Jumps sixfold: the war economies of 1915 to 1918 give a third to a half of the belligerents' output to war, financed mostly by borrowing and money creation.
Falls with demobilization.
Rearmament: Germany, the Soviet Union and Japan arm first, Britain and France after 1936.
The peak: the belligerents, three quarters of world output, give two fifths to three quarters of theirs to the war (the United States about two fifths, the Soviet Union and Germany more than half).
Falls fast with demobilization after August 1945.
The Korean War and the Cold War's rearmament: the United States spends about 14% of its output, the Soviet Union more.
The American war in Vietnam.
The last Cold War build-up, American and Soviet.
Turns down: the Cold War ends and the Soviet Union's spending collapses with it.
The peace dividend: a third less of output goes to force than in 1990.
The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and output's fall in 2009.
Rising again with Russia's war on Ukraine and rearmament in Europe and Asia: SIPRI puts the world's military burden at about 2.5% of output in 2024.

upsert.boundary: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, 6 and 9 August 1945
upsert.description: American bombers drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing about 110,000 to 210,000 people by the end of 1945; with the Soviet declaration of war, they bring Japan's surrender. They remain the only nuclear weapons used in war.
provenance: sources to check: Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy (2005); Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)

upsert.boundary: The end of the Cold War, 1989 to 1991.
upsert.description: The Soviet bloc's regimes fall in 1989 and the Soviet Union dissolves in December 1991; most of central and eastern Europe holds free elections.

upsert.boundary: The Crusades in the Levant, 1096 to 1291
upsert.description: Answering a Byzantine appeal and the Pope's call, armies from Western Europe take Jerusalem (1099) and found Crusader states on the Levant coast; Saladin retakes Jerusalem (1187), the Fourth Crusade sacks Christian Constantinople (1204), and the Mamluks take Acre, the last Crusader city, in 1291.
provenance: sources to check: Riley-Smith, The Crusades: A History (3rd ed. 2014); Tyerman, God's War (2006)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: the Levant, Anatolia); Europe (Western and Southern Europe); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt, in later crusades)

upsert.boundary: The fiscal-military state, about 1550 to 1815
upsert.description: Gunpowder fortresses, standing armies and navies multiply the cost of war; Europe's states that tax, borrow and administer most survive and absorb the rest (Warsift#b01b), so that the five hundred or so polities of 1500 shrink to about thirty by 1900, and Britain, France, Prussia, Austria and Russia emerge as great powers.
provenance: sources to check: Tilly, Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990); Brewer, The Sinews of Power (1989); Parker, The Military Revolution (1988)

upsert.boundary: Gunpowder, from China to the world, about 850 to 1350
upsert.description: Chinese alchemists searching for elixirs mix saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal by the 800s; the Song arm soldiers with fire lances and bombs; the first guns, metal barrels firing projectiles, appear in China by the late 1200s. The Mongol wars carry the knowledge west, and cannon are used in Europe and the Islamic world by the 1320s and 1340s.
provenance: sources to check: Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 7 (1986); Andrade, The Gunpowder Age (2016)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern Asia: China; Western Asia); Europe

upsert.boundary: No war between great powers, from September 1945 to 2025.
upsert.description: Eighty years without war between great powers, the longest such stretch since the states system began; war deaths fall from about 500 per 100,000 a year in the world war to 1 to 2 in most later decades, though Korea, Vietnam, the Iran–Iraq war, Congo and Ukraine kill millions.
provenance: inferred: the model's own war series

upsert.boundary: Castle Bravo, 1 March 1954
upsert.description: The largest American nuclear test, 15 megatons at Bikini, two and a half times what was expected, rains fallout on Rongelap and Utirik and on the Japanese fishing boat Lucky Dragon No. 5; the islanders' sickness and the crew's set off the worldwide campaign that leads to the partial test-ban treaty (1963).
provenance: sources to check: Hewlett and Holl, Atoms for Peace and War (1989)

upsert.boundary: Nuclear weapons, from 1945 to now.
upsert.description: From Hiroshima, then the Soviet bomb of 1949, to some 12,000 warheads in nine states: a war between great powers could now destroy both.

upsert.boundary: Nuclear tests in the Pacific and Australia, 1946 to 1996
upsert.description: The United States explodes 67 weapons at Bikini and Enewetak (1946 to 1958), displacing islanders and contaminating Rongelap; Britain tests at Maralinga and Christmas Island, and France at Moruroa and Fangataufa until 1996.
provenance: sources to check: Firth, Nuclear Playground (1987)
upsert.region: Oceania (Micronesia: Marshall Islands, Kiribati; Polynesia: French Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand: Australia)

upsert.boundary: The First World War, 1914 to November 1918.
upsert.description: About 9 to 10 million soldiers and some 7 million civilians die.

upsert.boundary: The Second World War, September 1939 to September 1945.
upsert.description: With the Sino-Japanese war already under way, it kills about 70 to 85 million, most of them civilians, the largest share in the Soviet Union and China. Governments take over a third or more of national output.

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's security group: Events that change the means of war now name the parts of force opened at r301. Gunpowder names arms (the thunder-crash bombs raise the most destructive blow a hundredfold); nuclear weapons, Hiroshima and Castle Bravo name arms and nuclear warheads; the Pacific tests name the warheads they proved; the two world wars and the fiscal-military state name spending on force; the end of the Cold War names spending and the warheads, both of which it cut; the Long Peace names war between polities, which it holds down; the Crusades, which named nothing, name war between polities. upsert.lens: To follow what fighting within polities is fought over, which one rate hides: wars for the centre (the Yellow Turbans, the Ming's fall, the Taiping, the Russian and Chinese civil wars), wars over whether a polity holds together (the American Civil War, the Dungan revolt, Biafra, Bangladesh, Eritrea, Sri Lanka), and fighting between armed groups none of which is the state (feuding lords, warlord militias, Somalia after 1991, the cartel wars), so that the shift from wars for the throne to wars of secession and militias after 1945 has a home. Range: Every polity at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, measured for all of humanity; zero among bands, where killing within the group is homicide.

changes.value: Opens the three parts of the carve of fighting within a polity at every date of the parent, each the parent's rate times a share that the wars of each block set: wars for the centre (the Han's, Tang's, Yuan's and Ming's ends, the Taiping, the Russian and Chinese civil wars), wars over territory (Spanish America's separation, the American and Dungan wars, the postcolonial secessions) and fighting between non-state groups (private wars, communal and militia fighting, cartels). The three sum to the parent at every date. Shares are this account's sketched reading of which wars fill each block; the parent's values carry their own uncertainty, including the Taiping war's famine deaths.

points.note: Zero among bands, like its parent.
Villages and chiefdoms fight over who leads them, about a third of their internal fighting.
Rises with the first states: succession wars and rebellions for the throne carry most of their internal fighting.
The Roman civil wars, from Marius and Sulla to Actium, are wars for the centre.
The Yellow Turbans and the warlords' wars for the Han's throne: nearly all of the parent's peak.
The wars of the Sui-Tang transition and An Lushan's rebellion for the throne.
The Red Turbans' war against the Yuan, a war for the throne.
The rebellions of Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong that bring down the Ming, the English Civil War and the Fronde: wars for the centre.
The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom fights to replace the Qing: the largest war for a throne since the Ming's fall.
Falls: the Taiping is crushed (1864) and the Nian follow (1868).
China's revolution of 1911 and the Mexican Revolution, both wars for the centre.
The Russian Civil War between Reds and Whites; the independence wars of Finland, the Baltic states, Poland and Ukraine go to territory.
The civil wars inside the world war, in China, Yugoslavia and Greece, are fought for who will rule after it.
The Chinese civil war's last campaigns (1946 to 1949) and Greece's civil war.
Falls below territory's share for the first time: Colombia's Violencia and Malaya's communist insurgency, against Algeria's war of independence.
Afghanistan's war against the Soviet-backed government.
Syria's, Iraq's and Yemen's wars are fought for the state.
Zero among bands, like its parent.
Feuds between lineages inside villages and chiefdoms: the largest of the three while there are no states.
Lords' private wars and clan feuds in feudal Europe and the fragmented Islamic world: a quarter of internal fighting while central rule is weak.
Falls with the private war: the gunpowder states disarm their nobles.
The Punti-Hakka clan wars in Guangdong (1855 to 1867), fought between communities while the Qing fought the Taiping.
Rises: in occupied Yugoslavia, Ukraine and China armed groups fight each other as well as the occupiers: Partisans against Chetniks, Ukrainian against Polish insurgents.
Lebanon's militias fight each other as much as the state.
Somalia's clans fight each other after Siad Barre's fall (1991).
Rises to a third: Congo's militias fight each other across the east, beside the armies of six states.
Mexico's cartel wars, from 2006, tens of thousands dead a year, and Iraq's sectarian militias.
Zero among bands, like its parent.
Villages split and fight as the splinters leave: fission over who holds which land.
Provinces and subject cities revolt for self-rule against the first kingdoms and empires.
The Pannonian revolt (6 to 9 CE) and, later, the Jewish wars against Rome.
The Dutch Revolt against Spain begins (1568), a war over whether the Habsburg Netherlands hold together.
The Catalan and Portuguese revolts against Spain (1640) and Ireland's rising (1641).
Saint-Domingue's war becomes a war for independence from France.
Rises above wars for the centre: Spanish America's wars of separation, counted within the Spanish empire as the parent counts them.
The Panthay rebellion's sultanate in Yunnan and the Indian rebellion of 1857.
The American Civil War, a war over secession, about 620,000 dead in four years.
Peaks: the Dungan revolt's last and deadliest years in north-west China and Yaqub Beg's state in Kashgaria, with Cuba's Ten Years' War.
Algeria's war of independence, which the parent counts within France, makes territory half of internal fighting's toll.
Biafra's war of secession (1967 to 1970) and southern Sudan's.
Bangladesh's war of separation from Pakistan (1971); its massacres are counted as one-sided killing.
Sri Lanka's Tamil war, Iraq's against the Kurds, Sudan's south and Eritrea.

upsert.boundary: The Nigerian civil war, 1967 to 1970
upsert.description: The Eastern Region secedes as Biafra after massacres of Igbo in the north; the federal blockade starves the enclave, and about one to three million die, most of hunger, before Biafra surrenders.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Heerten, The Biafran War and Postcolonial Humanitarianism (2017)

upsert.boundary: The Congo wars, 1996 to 2003
upsert.description: Rwanda and Uganda invade to pursue the génocidaires and overthrow Mobutu (1997); in the second war, from 1998, nine African states and many militias fight over the Congo and its minerals. Excess deaths are counted in millions, mostly from disease and hunger, though the highest estimates are disputed.
provenance: exploring: the International Rescue Committee's 5.4 million excess deaths to 2007 is contested by the Human Security Report
sources to check: Prunier, Africa's World War (2009); Stearns, Dancing in the Glory of Monsters (2011)
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Democratic Republic of the Congo), Eastern Africa (Rwanda, Uganda)

changes.value: The internal wars name the part of fighting within a polity they fill, opened at r307. Wars for the centre: the fall of the Han, An Lushan, the late Ming crisis, Europe's wars of religion, the Taiping, the Mexican Revolution, the Russian civil war and China's civil war. Wars over territory: Spanish America's separation, the American Civil War, Biafra, the Russian civil war's independence wars and the Yugoslav wars. Fighting between non-state groups: the Congo wars' militias and the drug trade's cartel wars. Existing process_ids are kept; the Russian revolutions also name fighting within a polity, which their civil war filled and which they had not named.

upsert.boundary: Cocaine, the drug trade and the war on drugs, from 1971
upsert.description: Nixon declares a war on drugs (1971); as American demand for cocaine grows, coca from Peru, Bolivia and Colombia is refined in Colombia and smuggled through the Caribbean and, from the 1990s, Mexico; the Medellín and Cali cartels and then Mexico's cartels grow rich and armed. Eradication, extradition and Plan Colombia (2000) shift the trade rather than end it, and fentanyl joins it after 2013. The trade fuels the region's wars and its homicide rates.
provenance: sources to check: Gootenberg, Andean Cocaine (2008); UNODC, World Drug Report
upsert.region: The Americas: South America, Central America, the Caribbean and Northern America

upsert.boundary: Latin America's wars of independence, 1808 to 1826
upsert.description: After Napoleon seizes Spain (1808), juntas and armies across Spanish America fight for independence: Hidalgo's rising in Mexico (1810), Bolívar in the north and San Martín in the south, until Ayacucho (1824) and the fall of Callao (1826); Brazil separates from Portugal peacefully as an empire (1822). About eighteen new states emerge.
provenance: sources to check: Lynch, The Spanish American Revolutions 1808–1826 (2nd ed. 1986)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America

upsert.boundary: The Mexican Revolution, 1910 to 1920
upsert.description: Madero's revolt against Díaz opens a decade of civil war (Villa, Zapata, Carranza, Obregón); perhaps one to two million die or flee, and the 1917 constitution promises land reform and national control of oil and minerals.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is contested
sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution (1986)

upsert.boundary: The An Lushan rebellion, 755 to 763
upsert.description: A frontier general of Sogdian and Turkic descent rebels and takes both Tang capitals; the war and its famines cut the registered population from about 53 million to 17 million, though much of that fall is people lost to the census rather than dead. The Tang survive but lose Central Asia and control of the provinces.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is much disputed
sources to check: Twitchett (ed.), The Cambridge History of China vol. 3 (1979)

upsert.boundary: China's civil war, 1927 to 1949
upsert.description: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists turn on their Communist allies (1927); the Communists survive the Long March (1934 to 1935) and grow during the war with Japan, then defeat the Nationalists in 1946 to 1949; Mao proclaims the People's Republic in October 1949 and the Nationalists withdraw to Taiwan.
provenance: sources to check: Westad, Decisive Encounters (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Russian revolutions and civil war, 1917 to 1922
upsert.description: Wartime collapse brings down the tsar (February 1917); Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power (October), take Russia out of the war and win a civil war of terror, famine and epidemics that kills perhaps eight to ten million, founding the Soviet Union (December 1922), a one-party state that persecutes religion.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, Russia in Revolution (2017)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus); Asia (Central Asia)

upsert.boundary: Europe's wars of religion, 1562 to 1648
upsert.description: Catholics and Protestants fight across Europe: the French Wars of Religion (1562 to 1598), the Dutch Revolt against Spain (from 1568) and finally the Thirty Years' War, entangled with the rivalries of dynasties.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The French Wars of Religion (2nd ed. 2005); Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Yugoslav wars, 1991 to 2001
upsert.description: Yugoslavia breaks apart in wars in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Kosovo and North Macedonia; some 130,000 to 140,000 die, millions are displaced by 'ethnic cleansing', and Bosnian Serb forces murder about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica (1995), a genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Glenny, The Fall of Yugoslavia (3rd ed. 1996); ICTY judgments

upsert.boundary: The fall of the Han and the Three Kingdoms, 184 to 280.
upsert.description: The Yellow Turban rising, warlord wars and the Three Kingdoms: China's registered population falls from about 56 million to about 16 million, partly a collapse of registration, partly real loss. Jin reunifies China in 280.
provenance: inferred: census figures as recalled; the real loss is uncertain

upsert.boundary: The late Ming crisis, about 1550 to 1650.
upsert.description: After a century of growth China holds perhaps 150 to 200 million people; degree-holders multiply faster than offices, the Wanli court's finances fail, the defence of Liaodong against the Jurchen needs new land taxes, and the silver on which taxes are paid stops arriving in the 1630s. The structural-demographic cycle's state crisis, in the decades before the collapse.
provenance: exploring: the reading as StructuralDemographicCycle#8433 and the silver-shortage argument are both contested

upsert.boundary: The Taiping war, 1850 to 1864.
upsert.description: A millenarian rebellion and the Qing response devastate the Yangtze valley; with the famine and disease that followed it killed perhaps 20 to 30 million, the deadliest war of the nineteenth century.

upsert.boundary: The American Civil War and emancipation, April 1861 to December 1865.
upsert.description: The war, the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 and the Thirteenth Amendment of December 1865 free about four million enslaved people.

scale.semantic_role: Colonial rule: The share of all living people who live in colonies, protectorates, mandates and other dependencies ruled from a metropole overseas, without equal political membership in it: the overseas empires of Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, Britain, France, Denmark, Belgium, Germany, Italy, the United States and Japan, from Ceuta (1415) to the territories still dependent now. Not counted: contiguous land empires (Russia's Siberia and Central Asia, Qing Xinjiang and Tibet, the Ottomans), wartime occupation (Japan in China, 1937 to 1945), and ancient and medieval rule over provinces across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome before 212, Venice and Genoa); each boundary is debated and kept as an alternative reading. Zero before 1415 by definition. A kind of scale of rule, not a part of it. Its five parts, by the M49 area where the colonized live, sum to it.

Corrects the Christian share from 1 to 1300, which rose in a smooth line from 6% in 500 to 16% in 1300 and so missed both its fast growth in the Roman Empire and its long plateau after. By 500 most of the Roman world (about 40 million people) and Armenia, Georgia, Aksum and the Church of the East were Christian: about a fifth of humanity, as the World Christian Database's line (about 22%) and Stark's growth model (about 34 million Christians already by 350) both imply. At 200 the old value (1.5%) was above every growth reconstruction: Hopkins and Stark give about 200,000 Christians, near 0.1%. At 1 there were none: the movement begins about 30. The difference is taken from local and folk traditions, where the model counts the Greco-Roman cults the converts left, so the eight shares still sum to 100 at every date. Also adds the missing note on why mobile herders dip at 2200 BCE. Sketched; checked against the published lines named, not against their tables (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

points.note: All people are foragers in Africa. With countries by 2026 borders as cells about 750 km across, a forager whose home lies a few tens of kilometres from where they were born crosses one of today's lines perhaps one time in twenty, adults far more often than children: about one person in fifty. Reasoned from forager residence and marriage distances, not counted.
The green Sahara and the Levant open longer ranges across many of today's borders; the reading barely moves.

Eases: a growing share of humanity lives in Asia and Sahul, in what are now large countries (Australia, India, China, Indonesia's islands, Russia), where a forager's moves cross fewer of today's lines. The dispersal itself adds little: its fronts advance by births where people already live (WaveOfAdvance#4cec), not by people living far from their birthplace.

Falls with farming: villagers marry within a day's walk and stay, so as farmers become most of humanity fewer people live far from where they were born. A hypothesis of this account (exploring): sedentism lowered how far people lived from their birthplaces; a test is the distance between birthplace and burial in strontium isotopes of early farmers against foragers.

The agrarian floor: most people die within a few kilometres of where they were born; nomads crossing today's lines with their herds, deportees (the Assyrians move whole peoples), soldiers, slaves and traders make up the rest.

Rome's wars carry captives from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria to Italy: perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, nearly half a percent of humanity alone; Han settlers and soldiers in Korea and northern Vietnam add a little.

The migration period moves Goths, Vandals, Franks and Saxons from beyond the Rhine and Danube into the Roman west, a few hundred thousand people born in one of today's countries and living in another; as Rome's slave imports end, the share holds.
The Mongol conquests move artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand, and the empire's posts carry merchants from Venice to Khanbaliq: a small rise.

About two million people born in Africa are enslaved in the Americas, a fifth of a percent of humanity, as the Atlantic trade passes its peak; Europeans born in Europe in the Americas, Asians in other Asian countries and Europe's own movers make up the rest.

Turns up: the Irish famine's emigrants, the gold rushes of California and Australia, and the first indentured Indians and Chinese begin the age of mass migration. The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born in 1850.

The peak of the age of mass migration: the United States counts 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina 2.4 million (three in ten of its people), Canada 1.6 million; Indians and Chinese in South-east Asia, Russians in Central Asia and Europe's own movers between today's countries add as many again: some 40 to 45 million people, about 2.5% of humanity.

War and its aftermath move people across today's lines: refugees of the Russian civil war, the Armenians, the exchange of Greeks and Turks (about 1.6 million), Poles and Germans after the new borders.
Falls back: the United States' quota acts (1921 to 1924) cut its immigration by four fifths, and the Depression stops and reverses movement; emigrants of 1900 to 1914 die or return.

Jumps with the war's end: some 11 million displaced persons in Germany alone, millions of Germans fleeing west, and about 6.5 million Japanese to be brought home from Manchuria, Korea, China and the islands.

Partition moves about 14 million people across the new lines of India, Pakistan and East Pakistan (now Bangladesh), and 12 to 14 million Germans have been expelled from the east: the share living outside their country of birth stands near its highest until the 2010s.
The UN's estimate of about 76 million international migrants (2.5%) counts the countries of 1960; by 2026 borders the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants (about 15 million) are added.
The low after the postwar displacement: the displaced of the 1940s die or are counted among the natives' children, and humanity grows faster than the migrants' numbers.

The UN's count for the countries of 2020: about 153 million. The Soviet Union's breakup makes some 25 million people international migrants overnight in the UN's own series; by 2026 borders they were counted all along, so this series has no jump here.

About 304 million people (2024), a fifth of them in the United States; the Gulf states, where most residents were born abroad, Europe, and Syria's, Ukraine's and Venezuela's refugees carry most of the rise since 2000.

upsert.reason: Sketched before 1850 from forager residence and marriage distances (Hill and colleagues 2011; Marlowe 2004), farmers' village exogamy, and the numbers carried by slave trades, conquests and settlement; 1850 to 1960 from the receiving countries' censuses as recalled (the United States, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Australia) and McKeown's global migration (2004); from 1960 the UN's international migrant stock (UN DESA), adjusted to 2026 borders before 1990 by adding the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants. Sources to check: UN DESA International Migrant Stock 2024; McKeown 2004, Journal of World History 15; Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998).

points.note: Homo sapiens shares the Earth with about seven other kinds of human: the early Neanderthals in Europe, the Denisovans in Asia, Homo erectus in Java, the small hominins of Flores and Luzon, Homo naledi in southern Africa and the archaic people of Kabwe. Lineages known only from genomes (the 'ghost' archaics in West Africans' ancestry) are in the upper band.
Homo naledi's last known date is about 236,000 years ago.
The last Homo erectus, at Ngandong on the Solo River, dies out about 108,000 years ago as Java's open woodland turns to rainforest, before Homo sapiens arrives.
Homo floresiensis's last dates at Liang Bua and Homo luzonensis's at Callao Cave are about 50,000 years ago, close to Homo sapiens' arrival in Wallacea; whether the arrival ended them is debated.

The Neanderthals are gone by about 40,000 years ago, within a few thousand years of Homo sapiens' spread through Europe. Competition, small scattered numbers, climate swings and absorption by interbreeding are all argued; the evidence in hand fits more than one (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The Denisovans may live on in South-east Asia or New Guinea.

Homo sapiens is the only human on Earth, on the latest reading of Denisovan admixture into Papuans (about 30,000 years ago); the Red Deer Cave people of southern China (about 14,000 years ago), once proposed as archaic, are now read as Homo sapiens, and stay in the upper band.
Homo sapiens alone; about 2% of the genome of every population outside Africa is Neanderthal, and up to about 5% of Papuans' and Aboriginal Australians' is Denisovan.

upsert.reason: Counted from the hominin fossil and genomic record as recalled: Homo naledi (335,000 to 236,000 years ago), Kabwe (about 300,000), Homo erectus at Ngandong (117,000 to 108,000, the last), Homo floresiensis (to about 50,000), Homo luzonensis (known 67,000 to 50,000; hominins on Luzon since 700,000), Neanderthals (to about 40,000) and Denisovans (admixture into Papuans as late as about 30,000 years ago on one reading). Sources to check: Berger and colleagues 2017 (eLife); Rizal and colleagues 2020 (Nature 577); Sutikna and colleagues 2016 (Nature 532); Détroit and colleagues 2019 (Nature 568); Higham and colleagues 2014 (Nature 512); Jacobs and colleagues 2019 (Cell 177).

points.note: Homo sapiens across Africa (Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Florisbad in the south, Omo in Ethiopia), but in patches between deserts and other hominins' lands: about a tenth of today's ice-free land, Africa being under a quarter of it.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and people hold the wetter east and south of Africa and its coasts.

The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes and opens the Levant and Arabia: the first time Homo sapiens holds land outside Africa for long (Skhul and Qafzeh). Range doubles in a few thousand years.
The glacial returns: the Sahara dries and the Levant goes back to the Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia.
The dispersal: people spread along southern Asia from Arabia to Sunda in a few thousand years, adding about seven million km2.

The largest gain in range in the account: in about ten thousand years people take in Sahul, Europe, eastern and northern Asia; WaveOfAdvance#4cec's fronts on land and long sea crossings to Sahul (the card's long-distance jumps) together.
People live as far north as the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and in Japan, Tibet's margins and Tasmania.

The glacial maximum shrinks range by a quarter: ice and polar desert drive people from northern Europe and much of Siberia, the Australian interior is left for refuges in its ranges and coasts, and the Sahara is at its driest. If White Sands' footprints are 21,000 to 23,000 years old, a few people are already south of the American ice; the upper band carries them.
The Americas are entered (Monte Verde in Chile by 14,500 years ago, the Paisley Caves by 14,300) and Europe's north is resettled in the Bølling warmth: range rises by half in three thousand years.
The Holocene begins: the Americas are filled to Tierra del Fuego, the African Humid Period greens the Sahara, and the north is ice-free except the last of the Laurentide sheet.
Near its prehistoric peak: the Sahara and Arabia are grassland with lakes, hunters and then herders live across them, and the Laurentide ice is almost gone.

Falls a little: the end of the African Humid Period empties the Sahara's core and Arabia's interior, and their herders move to the Nile, the Sahel and the oases: the one large loss of range since the glacial maximum.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic to Greenland's ice-free coasts, adding about three million km2 of tundra no one had lived on.
Lapita voyagers and the Marianas' settlers reach Remote Oceania: the islands are a few hundredths of a percent of the land.
Voyagers from Borneo have settled Madagascar (about 0.4% of the land), the last large uninhabited land of the Old World tropics.
East Polynesians reach Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land to be peopled; Iceland (about 870) and the eastern Pacific islands came just before.
Dips a little: epidemics after 1492 leave parts of the Americas, the Mississippi and Amazon floodplains among them, all but empty for a time; the survivors' ranges still cover most of the land.

Weather stations, mines and bases on the high Arctic islands and the ice-free coasts of Antarctica add the last fractions; the empty cores of the Sahara, the Rub' al Khali and the Taklamakan remain outside regular use.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the archaeology and genomics of each region's first peopling and abandonments, as recalled (Africa's Middle Stone Age sites, the green Sahara corridors, the dispersal through Arabia and southern Asia, Sahul by about 50,000 years ago, Europe by 45,000, Arctic Siberia by 32,000, the Americas by about 16,000 at the latest, the glacial maximum's refuges, the Holocene Sahara and its desiccation, the Paleo-Inuit, Remote Oceania and Aotearoa), with the areas of regions and deserts. The boundary of 'regular use' is soft; the band carries it.

points.note: No forager makes inquiry their main work: zero by the measure's definition, not a judgment that foragers learned nothing new. Most of what people discovered for 300,000 years was found by people whose main work was something else.
The first temple scribes of Uruk keep accounts and calendars; whether any had inquiry as their main work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.

Babylon's astronomers keep their diaries of the sky, Ionia's philosophers argue about nature, the Hundred Schools teach in China and India's grammarians and physicians write: a few hundred people in a world of 160 million.
The Museum of Alexandria (from about 280 BCE) pays perhaps a hundred scholars at a time, the first institution kept for inquiry; with Babylon, Han China and India, about one person in a million.
Falls: the western schools close with Rome's fall in the west, while India's astronomers (Aryabhata, 499) and China's carry on with fewer patrons.
Rises with the patrons: Baghdad's House of Wisdom and its astronomers, Cordoba, Cairo and Song China's bureaus keep several hundred scholars between them.

The Royal Society (1660) and the Académie des sciences (1666) give natural philosophy members and journals; perhaps two thousand people in Europe, the Ottoman world, India, China and Japan make inquiry their main work.

The research university (Berlin's model, from 1810) and the industrial laboratory (Edison's, 1876; the German chemical firms') make research a paid profession: some fifty thousand people, doubling about every fifteen years, as Price measured the growth of science.
War research (radar, the bomb, penicillin) leaves states paying for science: the United States, the Soviet Union and Europe hold about half a million researchers between them.
Rises little in the 1990s: the former Soviet Union's research staff falls by about half while Asia's grows.
China now has the most researchers of any country, about a fifth of the world's; Korea and Israel have the most per person.

upsert.reason: Before 1900 reasoned from the institutions that kept people for inquiry (Babylon's astronomers, the Museum of Alexandria, the Han and Tang bureaus, the House of Wisdom, Maragha and Samarkand, the seventeenth century's academies and their membership), with wide bands; 1900 to 1990 from the growth of the scientific workforce (Price 1963) and national research statistics as recalled (the United States' National Science Foundation, the Soviet Union's scientific workers); from 1990 UNESCO's researchers per million, as recalled, to be checked (UNESCO Science Report 2021).
