points.note: All people are foragers in Africa. With countries by 2026 borders as cells about 750 km across, a forager whose home lies a few tens of kilometres from where they were born crosses one of today's lines perhaps one time in twenty, adults far more often than children: about one person in fifty. Reasoned from forager residence and marriage distances, not counted.
The green Sahara and the Levant open longer ranges across many of today's borders; the reading barely moves.

Eases: a growing share of humanity lives in Asia and Sahul, in what are now large countries (Australia, India, China, Indonesia's islands, Russia), where a forager's moves cross fewer of today's lines. The dispersal itself adds little: its fronts advance by births where people already live (WaveOfAdvance#4cec), not by people living far from their birthplace.

The agrarian floor: most people die within a few kilometres of where they were born; nomads crossing today's lines with their herds, deportees (the Assyrians move whole peoples), soldiers, slaves and traders make up the rest.

Rome's wars carry captives from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria to Italy: perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, nearly half a percent of humanity alone; Han settlers and soldiers in Korea and northern Vietnam add a little.

The migration period moves Goths, Vandals, Franks and Saxons from beyond the Rhine and Danube into the Roman west, a few hundred thousand people born in one of today's countries and living in another; as Rome's slave imports end, the share holds.
The Mongol conquests move artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand, and the empire's posts carry merchants from Venice to Khanbaliq: a small rise.

About two million people born in Africa are enslaved in the Americas, a fifth of a percent of humanity, as the Atlantic trade passes its peak; Europeans born in Europe in the Americas, Asians in other Asian countries and Europe's own movers make up the rest.
Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees about 800,000 people, many born in Africa, but frees them where they live: it changes their status, not the share living outside their country of birth.
The first indentured Indians reach British Guiana (1838) and Mauritius, beginning the indenture that replaces enslaved labour on the sugar colonies.

The Irish famine (from 1845) sends about a million and a half people to Britain and North America by 1852, and the California gold rush (from 1848) draws Chinese, Chileans, Mexicans and Europeans: the turn into the age of mass migration.

Turns up: the Irish famine's emigrants, the gold rushes of California and Australia, and the first indentured Indians and Chinese begin the age of mass migration. The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born in 1850.

Indentured Indians begin arriving in Fiji (1879) as they had in Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana; the European emigration to the Americas, slowed by the depression of the 1870s, picks up again at the decade's end.

Cuba's gradual abolition (1880 to 1886) and Brazil's (1888) end the Atlantic world's slave societies; their places on the plantations are taken by immigrants from Spain, Italy, Portugal, China and India.
The United States' Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) is the first law to bar a people by origin; the European flow it does not touch reaches about 800,000 arrivals that year.

The great immigration to the United States, Argentina and Brazil from southern and eastern Europe begins about 1880; Brazil's abolition (May 1888) and its subsidized Italian immigration that follows add to it.

The peak of the age of mass migration: the United States counts 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina 2.4 million (three in ten of its people), Canada 1.6 million; Indians and Chinese in South-east Asia, Russians in Central Asia and Europe's own movers between today's countries add as many again: some 40 to 45 million people, about 2.5% of humanity.
Falls back: the United States' quota acts (1921 to 1924) cut its immigration by four fifths, and the Depression stops and reverses movement; emigrants of 1900 to 1914 die or return.

Rises with the war: Germany puts millions of foreign workers and prisoners to work in the Reich, the Soviet Union deports Poles, Balts, Volga Germans, Chechens and others across today's lines, and Japan moves Koreans to its mines.

At its wartime height Germany holds about 7.5 million foreign civilian workers and 2 million prisoners of war at work, and about 2 million Koreans live in Japan: forced labour lifts the share living outside their country of birth to near its postwar level.
Most of the forced labourers and displaced persons go home, while the Germans expelled from the east and the Japanese repatriated replace them in the count: the share holds.
Partition: about 14 million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan in 1947 and 1948, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee Israel's war of independence.

Partition moves about 14 million people across the new lines of India, Pakistan and East Pakistan (now Bangladesh), and 12 to 14 million Germans have been expelled from the east: the share living outside their country of birth stands near its highest until the 2010s.
The UN's estimate of about 76 million international migrants (2.5%) counts the countries of 1960; by 2026 borders the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants (about 15 million) are added.
The low after the postwar displacement: the displaced of the 1940s die or are counted among the natives' children, and humanity grows faster than the migrants' numbers.
Afghanistan's war sends some five million refugees into Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia and the Arab world.

The UN's count for the countries of 2020: about 153 million. The Soviet Union's breakup makes some 25 million people international migrants overnight in the UN's own series; by 2026 borders they were counted all along, so this series has no jump here.

About 304 million people (2024), a fifth of them in the United States; the Gulf states, where most residents were born abroad, Europe, and Syria's, Ukraine's and Venezuela's refugees carry most of the rise since 2000.

People live at the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and across the Russian plain: under M49 all of Russia is Europe, so Siberia's peopling is this part's.

Herders and hunters push into the drier steppe and the northern taiga: a quarter of a point over a millennium.

About 86% of Europe's land with Russia in range; the high Arctic islands' interiors and the emptiest tundra are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Europe's land with all of Russia (about 23.4 million km2), the dates of Homo sapiens' arrival, the ice sheets and polar deserts of the glacial maximum and the Arctic's late settlement.

Rises with the war: Germany puts millions of foreign workers and prisoners to work in the Reich, the Soviet Union deports Poles, Balts, Volga Germans, Chechens and others across today's lines, and Japan moves Koreans to its mines.

The war's last year moves people both ways: the Germans of the east begin to flee and be expelled, and forced labourers in the Reich and Koreans in Japan are at their peak, so the share holds near its wartime high.

Partition: about 14 million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan in 1947 and 1948, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee Israel's war of independence.

The UN's estimate of about 76 million international migrants (2.5%) counts the countries of 1960; by 2026 borders the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants (about 15 million) are added.
The low after the postwar displacement: the displaced of the 1940s die or are counted among the natives' children, and humanity grows faster than the migrants' numbers.
Afghanistan's war sends some five million refugees into Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia and the Arab world.

The UN's count for the countries of 2020: about 153 million. The Soviet Union's breakup makes some 25 million people international migrants overnight in the UN's own series; by 2026 borders they were counted all along, so this series has no jump here.

About 304 million people (2024), a fifth of them in the United States; the Gulf states, where most residents were born abroad, Europe, and Syria's, Ukraine's and Venezuela's refugees carry most of the rise since 2000.

The first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola, about 0.1 points of the world's land.

Nearly all the Americas' ice-free land: the Atacama's core and the emptiest Arctic islands are the rest.

upsert.boundary: Early Homo sapiens across Africa, about 300,000 to 230,000 years ago
upsert.description: Jebel Irhoud in Morocco (about 315,000 years old, just before this account's span), Florisbad in South Africa (about 260,000) and Omo Kibish in Ethiopia (about 233,000) show modern faces with longer, lower braincases, at three corners of the continent. The species formed across Africa as a web of populations that split and rejoined, not in one valley.
provenance: inferred: fossil ages as recalled, each uncertain by tens of thousands of years
sources to check: Hublin et al. 2017, Nature 546; Grun et al. 1996, Nature 382 (Florisbad); Vidal et al. 2022, Nature 601 (Omo Kibish)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Morocco), Southern Africa, Eastern Africa (Ethiopia)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers from Borneo settle Madagascar, about 500 to 900
upsert.description: Austronesian-speaking seafarers from south-east Borneo reach the uninhabited island and later mix with Bantu-speaking Africans: Malagasy is an Austronesian language, and Malagasy genomes are about half Asian and half African.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; earlier human traces on the island are debated
sources to check: Pierron et al. 2017, PNAS 114; Adelaar, in The Austronesian Languages of Asia and Madagascar (2005)
upsert.region: Africa: Eastern Africa (Madagascar); from South-eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: The African Humid Period, about 12,500 to 6,000 years ago
upsert.description: As northern summer sunlight peaks, the monsoon moves north: the Sahara and Arabia become grassland and savanna with lakes as large as Mega-Chad, and hippos, crocodiles, fishers and later herders live where there is now desert. It ends as the monsoon retreats again (ev.aridification).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its end was abrupt in some places and gradual in others
sources to check: deMenocal et al. 2000, Quaternary Science Reviews 19; Kuper and Kröpelin 2006, Science 313
upsert.region: Northern, Western and Eastern Africa; Western Asia (Arabia)

upsert.boundary: Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago
upsert.description: A camp of wooden huts by a creek, with mastodon meat, seaweed and medicinal plants, preserved under peat: the site that broke the 'Clovis first' account.
provenance: sources to check: Dillehay et al. 2008, Science 320; Dillehay et al. 2015, PLoS ONE 10

upsert.boundary: People spread through the Americas, about 16,000 to 13,000 years ago
upsert.description: Descendants of a population that lived isolated in Beringia move south, probably along the Pacific coast first, then through an ice-free corridor; within a few thousand years they reach Tierra del Fuego. Genomes show one main founding population, splitting early into northern and southern branches.
provenance: sources to check: Moreno-Mayar et al. 2018, Science 362; Braje et al. 2017, Science 357

upsert.boundary: Footprints at White Sands, about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago
upsert.description: Human footprints in the dried lake beds of New Mexico, beside those of mammoths and giant sloths, dated by seeds, pollen and quartz to the height of the last glacial: if the dates hold, people lived south of the ice sheets thousands of years before Clovis.
provenance: exploring: the dates are contested but have held up to repeated testing
sources to check: Bennett et al. 2021, Science 373; Pigati et al. 2023, Science 382

upsert.boundary: Discovery and exploration of Antarctica, 1820 to 1959
upsert.description: The continent is first sighted in 1820 (Bellingshausen, Bransfield, Palmer); sealers nearly exterminate the fur seals; Ross charts the ice shelf (1841); the heroic age of exploration (1897 to 1922); Amundsen reaches the South Pole in December 1911 and Scott a month later; whaling peaks in the 1930s; seven states claim territory; the International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958).
provenance: sources to check: Fogg, A History of Antarctic Science (1992)

upsert.boundary: The Antarctic Treaty, 1959 to 2025
upsert.description: The Antarctic Treaty (signed 1959, in force 1961) sets the continent aside for peace and science and freezes territorial claims; the ozone hole is found above it (1985); the Madrid Protocol bans mining (1991); ice shelves collapse (Larsen B, 2002) and the ice sheets' losses add to rising seas.
provenance: sources to check: Antarctic Treaty Secretariat (ats.aq); Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin 1985, Nature 315 (ozone)

upsert.boundary: The heroic age of Antarctic exploration, 1897 to 1922
upsert.description: The Belgica's crew are the first to winter in the Antarctic (1898); Scott, Shackleton, Amundsen, Mawson and others sledge inland, reach the magnetic pole and the geographic pole, and Shackleton's Endurance is crushed in the ice (1915), its crew all saved.
provenance: sources to check: Fiennes, Race to the Pole (2004); Huntford, Scott and Amundsen (1979)

upsert.boundary: Antarctica loses ice, from 1992
upsert.description: Satellites show Antarctica losing ice at an accelerating rate, about 150 billion tonnes a year by the 2010s, mostly from West Antarctic glaciers such as Thwaites and Pine Island; the Larsen B ice shelf breaks up in weeks (2002), and sea ice reaches record lows in 2023.
provenance: sources to check: IMBIE team 2018, Nature 558; Otosaka et al. 2023, Earth System Science Data 15

upsert.boundary: Antarctica's ice through the glacial cycles, before 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: The ice sheets, up to four kilometres thick, grow and shrink with the glacial cycles; the air trapped in their layers records 800,000 years of temperature and carbon dioxide, read in cores drilled from the 1960s on.
provenance: sources to check: EPICA community members 2004, Nature 429; Lüthi et al. 2008, Nature 453

upsert.boundary: The International Geophysical Year in Antarctica, 1957 to 1958
upsert.description: Twelve nations build some fifty research stations, among them the American station at the South Pole and the Soviet Vostok, and the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition makes the first overland crossing; cooperation in science sets the pattern for the Treaty.
provenance: sources to check: Belanger, Deep Freeze (2006)

upsert.boundary: Sealing and whaling in the Southern Ocean, 1820 to 1986
upsert.description: Sealers nearly exterminate the fur seals of the sub-Antarctic islands by the 1830s; from South Georgia (1904) and then factory ships, whalers kill more than two million whales in the Southern Ocean in the twentieth century, until the International Whaling Commission's moratorium (1986).
provenance: sources to check: Rocha, Clapham and Ivashchenko 2014, Marine Fisheries Review 76
upsert.region: Antarctica (the Southern Ocean and sub-Antarctic islands)

upsert.boundary: Antarctica first sighted, January 1820
upsert.description: Within days of each other, Fabian von Bellingshausen's Russian expedition (27 January 1820) and Edward Bransfield's British one (30 January) sight the ice shelves and mountains of the continent; the first landing comes in 1821 or 1895.
provenance: sources to check: Headland, A Chronology of Antarctic Exploration (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Antarctic Treaty, 1959 to 1961
upsert.description: Twelve nations sign in Washington (1 December 1959) a treaty, in force from June 1961, that freezes territorial claims, bans military activity, nuclear tests and waste, and reserves the continent for peace and science: the first arms-control treaty of the Cold War.
provenance: sources to check: Berkman et al. (eds.), Science Diplomacy (2011)

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum: Aboriginal people withdraw to refuges, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the continent cools and dries, dunes advance and inland lakes fail; people leave much of the arid interior for refuges in the ranges, along rivers and on the broad coastal plains then exposed, and their numbers may fall by half or more before they reoccupy the deserts as the climate eases. How far the deserts were abandoned and how far numbers fell are debated: radiocarbon dates used as a proxy for population are read both ways.
provenance: exploring: the size of the fall is debated
sources to check: Williams et al. 2013, Quaternary Science Reviews 61; Smith, The Archaeology of Australia's Deserts (2013)

upsert.boundary: People reach Tasmania, about 41,000 to 39,000 years ago
upsert.description: Walking across the land bridge the low sea has exposed in Bass Strait, people reach Tasmania by about 40,000 years ago (Parmerpar Meethaner, Warreen Cave), the southernmost humans on Earth; through the glacial maximum they hunt red-necked wallaby in the cold grasslands of the south-west valleys.
provenance: sources to check: Cosgrove 1999, Journal of World Prehistory 13; Allen and O'Connell 2014, Australian Archaeology 79

upsert.boundary: The end of the African Humid Period, about 4000 to 3000 BCE.
upsert.description: The Sahara and Arabia dry out again over a millennium; herders and farmers move toward the Nile, the Tigris and the Euphrates, crowding the valleys where the first states form.
provenance: exploring: the link between drying and state formation is argued, notably for Egypt, and contested

upsert.boundary: Homo sapiens in the Levant: Misliya, Skhul and Qafzeh, about 180,000 to 90,000 years ago
upsert.description: A jaw at Misliya Cave (about 180,000 years old) and burials at Skhul and Qafzeh (about 120,000 to 90,000) show Homo sapiens in south-west Asia long before the main dispersal; these groups, living beside Neanderthals, leave few or no descendants among people alive today.
provenance: sources to check: Hershkovitz et al. 2018, Science 359; Grun et al. 2005, Journal of Human Evolution 49

upsert.boundary: The first people reach Cuba and Hispaniola, about 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers cross open sea to the Greater Antilles, the first settlement in the Americas of islands out of sight of the mainland; their flaked-stone tools resemble those of Belize and Yucatán, which suggests a crossing from Central America, but a route from South America is also argued, and the evidence fits both. Ground sloths and other island animals disappear in the millennia after people arrive.
provenance: inferred: the arrival as recalled; its source is debated
sources to check: Keegan and Hofman, The Caribbean before Columbus (2017); Steadman et al. 2005, PNAS 102
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Cuba and Hispaniola)

upsert.boundary: The main dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa, about 60,000 to 45,000 years ago.
upsert.description: Small groups leave Africa, meet and interbreed with Neanderthals about 47,000 years ago, and reach South Asia, Sahul and Europe. Earlier ventures, such as those at Misliya and Skhul, left few or no living descendants. When Sahul was reached is contested: 65,000 years at Madjedebe, or about 50,000, which would fit the shared Neanderthal admixture.
provenance: inferred: genomic and archaeological chronology as recalled; the start date is contested

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum and the peopling of the Americas, about 26,000 to 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: Ice sheets at their greatest drive people from the far north into refugia. Dogs are domesticated, pottery appears in East Asia, and people enter the Americas. As the world warms after about 19,000 years ago, the Natufians of the Levant settle in villages and harvest wild cereals; the Younger Dryas cold closes the age.
provenance: sources to check: Clark et al. 2009, Science 325 (the Last Glacial Maximum); Wu et al. 2012, Science 336 (Xianrendong pottery)

upsert.boundary: The Last Interglacial and its aftermath, about 132,000 to 62,000 years ago
upsert.description: The interglacial proper, warmer than today, ends about 116,000 years ago; the era runs on through the milder stretches of the early last glacial that followed. A green Sahara and Arabia open corridors: Homo sapiens reaches the Levant (Skhul and Qafzeh) and perhaps Arabia and beyond, but those groups leave few descendants. In southern Africa coastal groups make engraved ochre and shell beads (Blombos, about 75,000 years ago) and the Still Bay and Howiesons Poort toolkits. As the glacial returns after about 71,000 years ago, populations shrink and fragment.
provenance: sources to check: Henshilwood et al. 2002, Science 295 (Blombos engravings); Groucutt et al. 2015, Evolutionary Anthropology 24 (routes out of Africa)

inferred: corrected 2026-10-13 after a blind reading of the events pass: the interglacial proper (marine isotope stage 5e) ends about 116,000 years ago; the era is named for it and its aftermath, as its boundary says

upsert.boundary: Europe at the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: Ice sheets cover Scandinavia, Britain and the Alps, and tundra and steppe the north; people withdraw to refuges in Iberia, southern France, Italy, the Balkans and Ukraine, where Solutrean flint-workers make thin laurel-leaf points.
provenance: sources to check: Posth et al. 2023, Nature 615

upsert.boundary: Homo sapiens reaches Europe, about 47,000 to 43,000 years ago
upsert.description: Modern humans leave tools and bones at Bacho Kiro in Bulgaria and Ranis in Germany by about 45,000 years ago; early groups mix with Neanderthals (the Oase man had a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back) but most leave no descendants, and later arrivals become Europe's hunter-gatherers.
provenance: sources to check: Hublin et al. 2020, Nature 581; Mylopotamitaki et al. 2024, Nature 626; Fu et al. 2015, Nature 524

upsert.boundary: Voyagers settle the Bismarcks and the Solomons, about 40,000 to 29,000 years ago
upsert.description: Crossing straits mostly within sight of land, people reach New Ireland and New Britain by about 40,000 years ago (Buang Merabak, Matenkupkum) and Buka in the northern Solomons by about 29,000 (Kilu), the eastern edge of the inhabited world for the next 25,000 years.
provenance: sources to check: Leavesley et al. 2002, Australian Archaeology 54; Spriggs (1997)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (the Bismarck Archipelago and northern Solomons)

upsert.boundary: People at the Paisley Caves, about 14,300 years ago
upsert.description: In caves above a vanished lake in Oregon, dried human faeces dated about 14,300 years ago carry Native American mitochondrial DNA, and stemmed points lie in layers as old as Clovis: people lived in the Great Basin before the Clovis hunters spread. Questions about contamination of the samples have been raised and answered; most now accept the dates.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; contamination of the samples has been argued and answered
sources to check: Gilbert et al. 2008, Science 320; Jenkins et al. 2012, Science 337

upsert.boundary: The first Arctic peoples cross to Greenland, about 2500 BCE
upsert.description: Hunters of the Arctic Small Tool tradition, with tiny chipped blades, bows and skin tents, move from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland within a few centuries (Saqqaq, Independence I). A 4,000-year-old Saqqaq genome shows they came from Siberia in a migration separate from that of other Native Americans; their Dorset successors hold the high Arctic until the Thule arrive.
provenance: sources to check: Rasmussen et al. 2010, Nature 463; Raghavan et al. 2014, Science 345
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Arctic and Greenland)

upsert.boundary: Polynesians settle the eastern Pacific, about 900 to 1300
upsert.description: After a pause of nearly two thousand years in Samoa and Tonga, voyagers navigating by stars, swells and birds settle the Society Islands and the Marquesas, then within a few centuries Hawaii, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa New Zealand (about 1280), the last large land on Earth to be peopled.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates follow the 'short chronology'
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108

upsert.boundary: People reach Sahul, about 50,000 years ago
upsert.description: Crossing at least 70 kilometres of open sea through the islands of Wallacea, the first people reach Sahul, the continent that joined Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania at low sea level; the earliest secure sites date to about 50,000 years ago, and Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land may be 65,000 years old. Their descendants are the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and Papuan peoples.
provenance: exploring: the earliest date is contested, from about 65,000 to 47,000 years ago
sources to check: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature 547; O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS 115
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: Australia; Melanesia: New Guinea)

upsert.boundary: Modern humans reach Sunda, about 70,000 to 45,000 years ago
upsert.description: Teeth from Lida Ajer in Sumatra, dated to 73,000 to 63,000 years ago, and remains from Tam Pa Ling in Laos suggest Homo sapiens arrived before the main dispersal out of Africa, while the Niah Cave skull in Borneo (about 40,000 years ago) is the oldest firm modern skull; living people's genomes, which all share the Neanderthal admixture of about 47,000 years ago, fit a later arrival, so the early dates and the genomes are still being reconciled.
provenance: exploring: an early arrival is debated against the genomic timing
sources to check: Westaway et al. 2017, Nature 548; Demeter et al. 2015, Journal of Human Evolution 84; Barker et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution 52

upsert.lens: To say where the people living away from their birthplace live, so that each migration the account records (the slave trade, Rome's captives, the mass migrations, the wars' forced labour and expulsions, Partition, the Gulf's workers, today's refugees) has a home in the area that received it, and so that regional counts (censuses from about 1850, the UN's series from 1960) test the world curve. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living Homo sapiens, over the five inhabited areas of the UN M49 standard by 2026 borders (Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe with all of Russia, Oceania).

changes.value: Opens the five parts of the carve of migration (carve.concept.humanity.means.connection.migration) at every date of migration, each the share of all living people who live in one area and were born in another country, so the five sum to migration at every date; migration is declared their sum (MECE#ae19), its 2025 value re-recorded unchanged to carry the declaration. From 1990 the parts follow the UN DESA migrant stock by region of destination as recalled (inferred, to be checked), adjusted so they sum to the whole; from 1850 to 1960 they are reasoned from censuses as recalled (the United States, Argentina, Canada, Australia) and the flows the account's Events record; before 1850 from where people lived and the flows of each era (sketch). All share one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca). Station residents in Antarctica are left out as negligible, as the carve records.

points.note: All of humanity's movers live in Africa, the only area Homo sapiens holds.
Falls as a share of humanity, not in Africa: the dispersal puts a growing part of humanity, and so of its movers, in Asia, Sahul and Europe.
The Arab conquest of North Africa (from 640) and the Berber and Arab movements that follow add settlers born in Arabia and across today's lines.
About two million: Europeans in Algeria, South Africa and Egypt, Indians in Natal and East Africa, and the first labour migrants to the Rand's mines from Mozambique and beyond.

Rises with the postwar labour migrations of the colonial economies (Burkinabé and Malians to the Gold Coast's and Côte d'Ivoire's cocoa, Mozambicans and Malawians to the mines and farms of the south) and with Europeans settling in the Rhodesias and Kenya.
About nine million by the UN's count for Africa in 1960: labour migrants between the new states and the last of the settlers.
Algeria's independence sends about 900,000 pieds-noirs to France in a year.
About 16 million, the UN's count for Africa in 1990, swollen by refugees from Mozambique's, Ethiopia's and Sudan's wars.
About 29 million, most of them from neighbouring countries: South Sudan's and Sudan's refugees in Uganda, Chad and Egypt, and workers in South Africa and Côte d'Ivoire.

upsert.reason: Before 1850 the part follows Africa's share of humanity and its many small cells on today's map; then colonial settlers and labour migrants; from 1990 the UN's count for Africa.

points.note: If the White Sands footprints' dates hold, a few people live south of the ice; how many, and how far they moved, is unknown.
The Americas are peopled to Tierra del Fuego: a tenth of humanity's movers now live there, at forager rates.
The Aztec and Inca states move conquered peoples (the Inca mitmaq resettled whole communities across today's lines from Ecuador to Chile).
The first Spanish settlers and the first enslaved Africans reach the Caribbean.
Iberian settlers and enslaved Africans arrive as the Americas' own peoples die of epidemics: the foreign-born become a growing share of a shrinking population.
The Atlantic slave trade at its height brings about 60,000 to 80,000 Africans a year to Brazil and the Caribbean, where deaths are so high that the African-born stay most of the enslaved.

Britain and the United States end their slave trades (1807 and 1808): the African-born begin to age out of the count in North America and the British Caribbean, though Brazil and Cuba import for decades more.
The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born (1850), with Irish and Germans arriving by the hundred thousand a year.
About twenty million: the United States' 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina's 2.4 million, Canada's 1.6 million, Brazil's and the rest; nearly half of the world's migrants live in the Americas.
The United States' quota acts (1921 and 1924) cut arrivals by four fifths; the foreign-born age and die faster than new ones come.
Near its low: about nineteen million by the UN's count for Northern and Latin America, the old European-born dying out faster than new arrivals replace them.
The United States' Hart-Celler Act (1965) ends the national-origins quotas; arrivals from Latin America and Asia begin the climb of the next sixty years.
About 35 million by the UN's count: 28 million in Northern America and 7 million in Latin America and the Caribbean.
About 78 million: some 61 million in Northern America (the United States alone about a fifth of the world's migrants) and 17 million in Latin America, swollen by Venezuela's exodus.

upsert.reason: Zero before the Americas are peopled; then foragers' movers; from 1500 the Spanish and Portuguese settlers and the enslaved; from 1850 the censuses of the United States, Canada, Argentina and Brazil as recalled; from 1990 the UN's counts for Northern America and Latin America together.

points.note: The few Homo sapiens of the Levant (Misliya) carry the first movers outside Africa.
The dispersal along southern Asia: a growing share of humanity, and of its movers, lives in Asia.
Assyria deports whole peoples across its empire (Israelites, Arameans, Babylonians), perhaps several million over three centuries.
The Mongol empire moves artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand: Persian craftsmen to Karakorum, Central Asians to Yuan China.
About nine million: the Chinese and Indians of Malaya, Burma, Siam and the Indies, Russians settled in today's Kazakhstan and Central Asia, Japanese in Korea and Taiwan.

Japan's empire at its height: about two million Koreans in Japan, Japanese settlers in Korea, Manchuria and Taiwan, and the Soviet deportees (Volga Germans, Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Koreans) in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.
Japan's surrender begins the repatriation of some six million Japanese and the return of most Koreans from Japan.

Partition (1947 to 1948): about fourteen million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee: Asia's part rises by two fifths in two years.
About 35 million by the UN's count for Asia in 1960 with the Soviet republics' movers added: Partition's refugees still the largest group.
Falls as Partition's generation dies and Asia's population grows faster than its migrants.
Afghanistan's war puts some five million refugees in Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia, Egypt and the Philippines.
About 48 million, the UN's count for Asia in 1990.
Asia's low share: most Afghan refugees have gone home and Asia's population has grown by half since 1970.
About 92 million: the Gulf states (where most residents were born abroad), Syria's refugees in Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan, and Afghans and Rohingya in their neighbours.

upsert.reason: From the first excursions into the Levant on; deportations, nomads and captives in the agrarian millennia; the Nanyang Chinese and Indians, Koreans in Japan and Russians in Central Asia; Partition; the Gulf; from 1990 the UN's count for Asia.

points.note: Homo sapiens has reached Europe and western Siberia, a land of many small cells on today's map.
The steppe herders' descendants spread across Europe (the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker peoples), crossing today's lines by the hundred thousand.
Rome's wars begin to fill Italy with captives from Carthage, Spain and Greece.
Perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria: Europe holds about two fifths of the world's migrants.
The migration period: Goths, Vandals, Franks, Saxons and Lombards settle inside the old Roman frontier, while Rome's slave imports end.
The Irish famine sends hundreds of thousands to Britain's cities, which by 2026 borders are another country.

About twelve million, most of them moves inside empires that today's borders divide: Czechs and Galicians in Vienna, Poles of Posen in the Ruhr, Ukrainians, Poles and Balts in Russia's cities; besides them Italians in France and the Irish in Britain.
The war adds about eight million prisoners of war held abroad and millions of refugees (Belgians in Britain and France, Serbs, Poles and Balts driven into Russia).
Germany brings in millions of foreign workers and prisoners, and the Soviet Union deports Poles and Balts into Russia.
At the war's height Germany holds about 7.5 million foreign civilian workers and 2 million prisoners at work: Europe holds two fifths of the world's migrants.
The expulsions: some twelve million Germans born in today's Poland, Czechia and Russia's Kaliningrad are driven west into today's Germany and Austria while most forced labourers go home.

About 23 million by the UN's count for Europe in 1960 with the Soviet republics' movers added; guest workers from Italy, Spain, Turkey and Yugoslavia begin to replace the war's displaced in the count.
About 49 million by the UN's count for Europe in 1990, a third of them people born in one Soviet republic living in another.
About 94 million: movers inside the European Union, Ukraine's refugees since 2022, Syrians, Turks and Africans in the west, and Central Asians in Russia.

upsert.reason: Zero before Homo sapiens reaches Europe; Rome's captives and the migration period; the moves across today's lines inside the Habsburg, German and Russian empires; the wars' forced labour and expulsions; the guest workers and the European Union; from 1990 the UN's count for Europe.

points.note: Sahul is reached; its peoples live in what are now three countries (Australia, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia's Papua), so few moves cross today's lines.
The rising sea cuts New Guinea from Australia (about 6500 BCE) and farming begins in New Guinea's highlands: Oceania's share of humanity falls as the farming lands of Asia grow.
The First Fleet (1788) lands about 1,400 people at Sydney Cove, the first of some 160,000 convicts sent to Australia by 1868.
Free settlers and transported convicts make the British-born a growing share of the Australian colonies and, from 1840, of New Zealand.

upsert.boundary: Cash crops, mines and migrant labour: the colonial economy, about 1900 to 1950

upsert.boundary: The California gold rush, 1848 to 1855

upsert.boundary: Latin American migration to the United States, from 1965
upsert.description: The 1965 immigration act ends national-origin quotas, and the end of the Bracero programme (1964) pushes Mexican labour migration outside the law; Mexicans, then Cubans, Dominicans, Central Americans, Colombians and Venezuelans move north, and the Hispanic share of the United States rises from about 4% (1960) to about 19% (2020), some 62 million people. Remittances become a mainstay of Mexico's and Central America's economies, while enforcement and the politics of the border harden from the 1990s.
provenance: sources to check: Massey, Durand and Malone, Beyond Smoke and Mirrors (2002); Pew Research Center, Hispanic population estimates
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean to Northern America

upsert.boundary: Venezuela's collapse and exodus, from 2013

upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Venezuela, Colombia, Peru)

provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987); Nicholas (ed.), Convict Workers (1988)

upsert.boundary: The White Australia policy, 1901 to 1973

The policy is relaxed from 1966 and ended by the Whitlam government in 1973.
provenance: sources to check: Tavan, The Long, Slow Death of White Australia (2005)

upsert.boundary: Israel's founding and the war of 1948

upsert.boundary: Independence and the partition of India, 1947

sources to check: Douglas, Orderly and Humane (2012)

upsert.boundary: The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852
upsert.description: Potato blight destroys the crop of a people who live on it; about a million die of hunger and disease and over a million emigrate, while food is exported and relief is grudging; Ireland's population falls by a quarter and keeps falling for a century.
provenance: sources to check: Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond (1999)

upsert.boundary: The migration period, 376 to 568
upsert.description: Goths cross the Danube fleeing the Huns (376) and destroy a Roman army at Adrianople (378); Visigoths sack Rome (410), Vandals take Roman Africa (439), Attila's Huns raid Gaul and Italy, Franks, Angles and Saxons settle the west, and the Lombards enter Italy (568).
provenance: sources to check: Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007); Heather, Empires and Barbarians (2009)

upsert.boundary: Russia's war on Ukraine, from 2014
upsert.description: Russia annexes Crimea and backs a war in the Donbas (2014), then launches a full-scale invasion (February 2022); Ukraine holds Kyiv and retakes much ground, and the war becomes Europe's largest since 1945, with hundreds of thousands killed or wounded and millions of refugees.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; casualty figures are uncertain
sources to check: Plokhy, The Russo-Ukrainian War (2023)

upsert.boundary: Indentured labour from India and China, 1838 to 1917
upsert.description: After emancipation, planters bring workers bound by contracts of five years or more: about 240,000 Indians to British Guiana, about 145,000 to Trinidad, others to Suriname, Jamaica and the French islands; about 125,000 Chinese to Cuba (1847 to 1874) and about 100,000 to Peru's guano islands and plantations. Their descendants are the largest group in Guyana and Trinidad today.
provenance: sources to check: Northrup, Indentured Labor in the Age of Imperialism (1995); Hu-DeHart 1993, Slavery and Abolition 14
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean and South America; Asia: Southern and Eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: Indian indentured labour in Fiji, 1879 to 1916
upsert.description: To work the sugar plantations without disturbing Fijian villages, the colonial government brings 60,965 Indians under five-year contracts (girmit); most stay, and by 1946 Indo-Fijians outnumber indigenous Fijians, while most land stays in Fijian hands: the root of the political conflicts after independence.

upsert.boundary: The great immigration, 1880 to 1924
upsert.description: About 25 million immigrants arrive in the United States, most from southern and eastern Europe (Italians, Poles, Jews from the Russian empire), others from Scandinavia, Germany, Ireland, Mexico and, until the exclusion act of 1882, China; by 1910 about one American in seven was born abroad. Canada takes another three million, many of them to the prairies. They work the mines, mills and building sites of the industrial cities.
provenance: sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)

upsert.boundary: The United States restricts immigration, 1921 to 1924
upsert.description: Quota acts limit arrivals by national origin to a small share of each group's numbers in the census of 1890, cutting immigration from southern and eastern Europe by about nine tenths and barring Asians altogether; Mexicans and Canadians stay outside the quotas. Mass immigration to the United States ends for forty years.
provenance: sources to check: Ngai, Impossible Subjects (2004)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The gold rushes of Australia and New Zealand, 1851 to 1900
upsert.description: Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria (1851), Otago (1861) and Western Australia (1890s) draws hundreds of thousands of migrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese; Victoria's population grows sevenfold in a decade and Melbourne becomes one of the richest cities in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Blainey, The Rush That Never Ended (5th ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Postwar migration remakes Australia and New Zealand, from 1945
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish', Australia takes millions of migrants from Britain, then southern and eastern Europe; the White Australia policy ends (1973) and migrants from Asia follow, until nearly a third of Australians are born overseas; Oceania grows from about 13 to 46 million people.
provenance: sources to check: Jupp, From White Australia to Woomera (2nd ed. 2007); Australian Bureau of Statistics

upsert.boundary: The Polynesian diaspora, from 1962
upsert.description: Samoans, Tongans, Cook Islanders and Niueans migrate to New Zealand, Australia and the United States for work; by the 2000s more Cook Islanders and Niueans live in New Zealand than at home, and remittances are among the largest shares of national income in the world for Tonga and Samoa.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, remittance data; Lee and Francis (eds.), Migration and Transnationalism (2009)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: Hawai'i's sugar plantations and their workers, 1850 to 1946
upsert.description: Planters bring some 400,000 contract workers from China, Japan, Portugal, Korea and the Philippines; by 1900 Japanese are the largest group in the islands and Native Hawaiians, about 40,000, a minority; the reciprocity treaty with the United States (1875), renewed in 1887 in return for Pearl Harbor, gives Hawaiian sugar free entry.
provenance: sources to check: Takaki, Pau Hana (1983)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: Argentina's export boom and mass immigration, 1880 to 1914
upsert.description: Railways built with British capital open the pampas, taken from their Indigenous peoples in the Conquest of the Desert (1878 to 1885), to wheat and to cattle shipped as chilled beef; about four million immigrants arrive, mostly Italians and Spaniards, and by 1914 a third of the people of Argentina are foreign-born. Growth puts Argentina among the ten or so richest countries per person by 1913 on Maddison's figures, a ranking some economists think overstated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the ranking is debated
sources to check: Della Paolera and Taylor (eds.), A New Economic History of Argentina (2003); Maddison Project Database

upsert.boundary: Coffee makes São Paulo, 1850 to 1930
upsert.description: Coffee spreads from the Paraíba valley onto the red soils of São Paulo, and Brazil grows most of the world's coffee, at first with enslaved labour and, after the slave trade's end (1850) and abolition (1888), with about two million subsidized immigrants from Italy, Portugal, Spain and Japan. Coffee money builds São Paulo's railways and first factories, and the collapse of its price in 1929 helps bring Vargas to power.
provenance: sources to check: Holloway, Immigrants on the Land (1980); Dean, The Industrialization of São Paulo (1969)

upsert.boundary: Re-education camps and the boat people, 1975 to 1996
upsert.description: After the fall of Saigon the victors send hundreds of thousands of former officials and officers to re-education camps, and from 1978, as Vietnam turns on its ethnic Chinese and on private trade, people flee by sea. About 800,000 reach Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Hong Kong and the Philippines, and many die at sea of storms and pirates, estimates running from tens of thousands to 200,000 or more. Most are resettled in the United States, Canada, Australia and France under the Geneva agreements of 1979 and the Comprehensive Plan of Action (1989), which ends in 1996.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths at sea are unknown and debated
sources to check: Robinson, Terms of Refuge (1998); UNHCR, The State of the World's Refugees 2000
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam and the countries of first asylum), Eastern Asia (Hong Kong)

upsert.boundary: British Malaya: tin, rubber and migrant workers, 1874 to 1941
upsert.description: The Pangkor treaty (1874) puts British residents beside the Malay sultans; Chinese miners make Malaya the world's largest producer of tin, and from about 1900 Tamil workers from India tap rubber on estates that make it the largest producer of rubber too; by 1931 Malays are fewer than half of the peninsula's people, the plural society that independent Malaysia inherits.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Drabble, An Economic History of Malaysia (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Chinese diaspora in South-east Asia, the Nanyang, from about 1400
upsert.description: Chinese traders settle in Malacca, Ayutthaya, Manila and Batavia; Spanish Manila's Chinese are massacred in 1603 and 1639 and Batavia's in 1740; in the 1800s and early 1900s millions come to work in tin mines and on plantations, and Chinese merchants come to dominate the region's commerce; violence against them recurs, in Indonesia in 1965 and 1998 among other times, and about 30 million people of Chinese descent live in the region today.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the present number depends on how descent is counted
sources to check: Wang Gungwu, The Chinese Overseas (2000); Kuhn, Chinese among Others (2008)

upsert.boundary: Filipino workers overseas, from 1974
upsert.description: The Labor Code of 1974 makes labour export a national policy, at first to the Gulf's construction boom. By the 2010s about two million Filipinos work abroad under contract at any time, as domestic workers in Hong Kong and the Gulf, as nurses and as about a quarter of the world's merchant seafarers, and their remittances, about a tenth of national income, sustain households across the islands.
provenance: sources to check: Rodriguez, Migrants for Export (2010); Philippine Statistics Authority, Survey on Overseas Filipinos
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines), Western Asia (the Gulf), Eastern Asia (Hong Kong)

upsert.boundary: The expulsion of the Rohingya, 2016 to 2017
upsert.description: After attacks by a small Rohingya armed group on border posts (October 2016 and August 2017), Myanmar's army and local mobs burn hundreds of Rohingya villages in northern Rakhine, killing thousands, at least 6,700 in the first month by one survey, and raping women. About 740,000 Rohingya, whom Myanmar had denied citizenship since 1982, flee to Bangladesh, where some 900,000 or more live in camps around Cox's Bazar; the Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar is before the International Court of Justice.
provenance: sources to check: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar, report (2018); Médecins Sans Frontières mortality surveys (2017)

upsert.boundary: The transatlantic slave trade, 1501 to 1867.
upsert.description: About 12.5 million Africans are embarked for the Americas, of whom about 10.7 million survive the crossing; the plantations they are forced to work grow the sugar and the cotton of the Atlantic economy.
provenance: inferred: the voyages database's totals, as recalled

points.note: Egypt's first temple and palace scribes keep calendars and records beside Uruk's: about a third of the world's few specialists.
The Rhind papyrus's mathematics and the Edwin Smith papyrus's surgery come from New Kingdom Egypt's temple and palace scholars.
The Museum and Library of Alexandria (from about 280 BCE) keep Euclid, Eratosthenes and their successors on royal salaries: Africa's part nearly quadruples.
Alexandria's schools dwindle after the Serapeum's destruction (391) and Hypatia's murder (415).
Fatimid Cairo's House of Knowledge (1005) and Ibn al-Haytham's optics.
About 300,000 people, a fortieth of the world's researchers for a fifth of its people; Egypt, South Africa, Nigeria and the Maghreb hold most of them.

upsert.reason: Egypt's temples, Alexandria's Museum, Fatimid Cairo, Fez and Timbuktu, then the colonial and national universities and institutes.

points.note: Mesoamerica's first writing and Long Count calendars (from about 650 to 36 BCE) imply a few calendar specialists.
Classic Maya astronomers and scribes at Tikal, Palenque and Copan, with their eclipse and Venus tables.
The conquest ends the Aztec and Maya priests' learning; the first colonial colleges (Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, 1536; the University of Mexico, 1551) begin to replace a little of it.

The war sends the United States' chemists and physicists into war research and leaves it a National Research Council; American industry's laboratories (General Electric, Bell, DuPont) grow fastest of any.

Europe's and Japan's science lies in ruins while the American wartime laboratories stand: the Americas' share of the world's researchers jumps to about two fifths, and German and other European scientists come west.
Flat as a share of humanity's researchers falls: the United States' research staff grows slowly after 2000 while China's triples.
About 2.6 million, most of them in the United States, with Canada, Brazil and Mexico next: a fifth of the world's researchers.

upsert.reason: The Maya calendar specialists, then the colonial colleges, the American Philosophical Society, the land-grant and research universities, the industrial laboratories and the twentieth century's federal science.

points.note: The Parramatta observatory (1821) is the first institution of inquiry in Oceania.
Australia's Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (1926), later CSIRO, begins state-funded research.
About 180,000, nearly all in Australia and New Zealand.

upsert.reason: Zero before the colonial observatories and museums; then Australia's and New Zealand's universities and CSIRO.

Reasoned from recalled histories of science before 1990 (sketch) and UNESCO's regional tables as recalled after (inferred), sharing one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca). Also values at Events the report found passed over: migration and its five parts at the Hart-Celler Act (late 1965) and in mid-1975, the parts of migration at mid-1945, and Antarctica's range at the treaty's signing.

points.note: All of humanity's movers live in Africa, the only area Homo sapiens holds.
Falls as a share of humanity, not in Africa: the dispersal puts a growing part of humanity, and so of its movers, in Asia, Sahul and Europe.
The Arab conquest of North Africa (from 640) and the Berber and Arab movements that follow add settlers born in Arabia and across today's lines.
About two million: Europeans in Algeria, South Africa and Egypt, Indians in Natal and East Africa, and the first labour migrants to the Rand's mines from Mozambique and beyond.

Rises with the postwar labour migrations of the colonial economies (Burkinabé and Malians to the Gold Coast's and Côte d'Ivoire's cocoa, Mozambicans and Malawians to the mines and farms of the south) and with Europeans settling in the Rhodesias and Kenya.
About nine million by the UN's count for Africa in 1960: labour migrants between the new states and the last of the settlers.
Algeria's independence sends about 900,000 pieds-noirs to France in a year.
About 16 million, the UN's count for Africa in 1990, swollen by refugees from Mozambique's, Ethiopia's and Sudan's wars.
About 29 million, most of them from neighbouring countries: South Sudan's and Sudan's refugees in Uganda, Chad and Egypt, and workers in South Africa and Côte d'Ivoire.

upsert.reason: Before 1850 the part follows Africa's share of humanity and its many small cells on today's map; then colonial settlers and labour migrants; from 1990 the UN's count for Africa.

points.note: If the White Sands footprints' dates hold, a few people live south of the ice; how many, and how far they moved, is unknown.
The Americas are peopled to Tierra del Fuego: a tenth of humanity's movers now live there, at forager rates.
The Aztec and Inca states move conquered peoples (the Inca mitmaq resettled whole communities across today's lines from Ecuador to Chile).
The first Spanish settlers and the first enslaved Africans reach the Caribbean.
Iberian settlers and enslaved Africans arrive as the Americas' own peoples die of epidemics: the foreign-born become a growing share of a shrinking population.
The Atlantic slave trade at its height brings about 60,000 to 80,000 Africans a year to Brazil and the Caribbean, where deaths are so high that the African-born stay most of the enslaved.

Britain and the United States end their slave trades (1807 and 1808): the African-born begin to age out of the count in North America and the British Caribbean, though Brazil and Cuba import for decades more.
The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born (1850), with Irish and Germans arriving by the hundred thousand a year.
About twenty million: the United States' 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina's 2.4 million, Canada's 1.6 million, Brazil's and the rest; nearly half of the world's migrants live in the Americas.
The United States' quota acts (1921 and 1924) cut arrivals by four fifths; the foreign-born age and die faster than new ones come.
Near its low: about nineteen million by the UN's count for Northern and Latin America, the old European-born dying out faster than new arrivals replace them.
The United States' Hart-Celler Act (1965) ends the national-origins quotas; arrivals from Latin America and Asia begin the climb of the next sixty years.
Vietnam's first refugees reach the United States (about 130,000 in 1975).
About 35 million by the UN's count: 28 million in Northern America and 7 million in Latin America and the Caribbean.
About 78 million: some 61 million in Northern America (the United States alone about a fifth of the world's migrants) and 17 million in Latin America, swollen by Venezuela's exodus.

upsert.reason: Zero before the Americas are peopled; then foragers' movers; from 1500 the Spanish and Portuguese settlers and the enslaved; from 1850 the censuses of the United States, Canada, Argentina and Brazil as recalled; from 1990 the UN's counts for Northern America and Latin America together.

points.note: The few Homo sapiens of the Levant (Misliya) carry the first movers outside Africa.
The dispersal along southern Asia: a growing share of humanity, and of its movers, lives in Asia.
Assyria deports whole peoples across its empire (Israelites, Arameans, Babylonians), perhaps several million over three centuries.
The Mongol empire moves artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand: Persian craftsmen to Karakorum, Central Asians to Yuan China.
About nine million: the Chinese and Indians of Malaya, Burma, Siam and the Indies, Russians settled in today's Kazakhstan and Central Asia, Japanese in Korea and Taiwan.

Japan's empire at its height: about two million Koreans in Japan, Japanese settlers in Korea, Manchuria and Taiwan, and the Soviet deportees (Volga Germans, Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Koreans) in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.
Japan's surrender begins the repatriation of some six million Japanese and the return of most Koreans from Japan.
Partition's refugees in India and Pakistan, about ten million by December 1947.

Partition (1947 to 1948): about fourteen million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee: Asia's part rises by two fifths in two years.
About 35 million by the UN's count for Asia in 1960 with the Soviet republics' movers added: Partition's refugees still the largest group.
Falls as Partition's generation dies and Asia's population grows faster than its migrants.
Afghanistan's war puts some five million refugees in Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia, Egypt and the Philippines.
About 48 million, the UN's count for Asia in 1990.
Asia's low share: most Afghan refugees have gone home and Asia's population has grown by half since 1970.
About 92 million: the Gulf states (where most residents were born abroad), Syria's refugees in Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan, and Afghans and Rohingya in their neighbours.

upsert.reason: From the first excursions into the Levant on; deportations, nomads and captives in the agrarian millennia; the Nanyang Chinese and Indians, Koreans in Japan and Russians in Central Asia; Partition; the Gulf; from 1990 the UN's count for Asia.

points.note: Homo sapiens has reached Europe and western Siberia, a land of many small cells on today's map.
The steppe herders' descendants spread across Europe (the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker peoples), crossing today's lines by the hundred thousand.
Rome's wars begin to fill Italy with captives from Carthage, Spain and Greece.
Perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria: Europe holds about two fifths of the world's migrants.
The migration period: Goths, Vandals, Franks, Saxons and Lombards settle inside the old Roman frontier, while Rome's slave imports end.
The Irish famine sends hundreds of thousands to Britain's cities, which by 2026 borders are another country.

About twelve million, most of them moves inside empires that today's borders divide: Czechs and Galicians in Vienna, Poles of Posen in the Ruhr, Ukrainians, Poles and Balts in Russia's cities; besides them Italians in France and the Irish in Britain.
The war adds about eight million prisoners of war held abroad and millions of refugees (Belgians in Britain and France, Serbs, Poles and Balts driven into Russia).
Germany brings in millions of foreign workers and prisoners, and the Soviet Union deports Poles and Balts into Russia.
At the war's height Germany holds about 7.5 million foreign civilian workers and 2 million prisoners at work: Europe holds two fifths of the world's migrants.
The expulsions: some twelve million Germans born in today's Poland, Czechia and Russia's Kaliningrad are driven west into today's Germany and Austria while most forced labourers go home.

About 23 million by the UN's count for Europe in 1960 with the Soviet republics' movers added; guest workers from Italy, Spain, Turkey and Yugoslavia begin to replace the war's displaced in the count.
About 49 million by the UN's count for Europe in 1990, a third of them people born in one Soviet republic living in another.
About 94 million: movers inside the European Union, Ukraine's refugees since 2022, Syrians, Turks and Africans in the west, and Central Asians in Russia.

upsert.reason: Zero before Homo sapiens reaches Europe; Rome's captives and the migration period; the moves across today's lines inside the Habsburg, German and Russian empires; the wars' forced labour and expulsions; the guest workers and the European Union; from 1990 the UN's count for Europe.

points.note: Sahul is reached; its peoples live in what are now three countries (Australia, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia's Papua), so few moves cross today's lines.
The rising sea cuts New Guinea from Australia (about 6500 BCE) and farming begins in New Guinea's highlands: Oceania's share of humanity falls as the farming lands of Asia grow.
The First Fleet (1788) lands about 1,400 people at Sydney Cove, the first of some 160,000 convicts sent to Australia by 1868.
Free settlers and transported convicts make the British-born a growing share of the Australian colonies and, from 1840, of New Zealand.
The Victorian gold rush (from 1851) more than doubles Australia's people in a decade, most of the newcomers born in Britain, Ireland, China and the Americas.
About 1.4 million: the British- and Irish-born of Australia and New Zealand and the Indians of Fiji; the White Australia policy (1901) keeps out most others.
The Depression stops immigration and the British-born of the gold rushes and the 1910s die out: Australia's foreign-born fall to about a tenth of its people by 1947, their lowest.
Australia's Department of Immigration is founded (July 1945) and the postwar scheme planned; arrivals begin in 1947.
Australia's postwar scheme (from 1947) brings displaced persons, Britons, Italians and Greeks: about two million arrivals by 1970.
About 4.7 million by the UN's count for Oceania in 1990.
About ten million, nearly all in Australia (three in ten Australians were born abroad) and New Zealand.

upsert.reason: Zero before Sahul is reached; Sahul's foragers; from 1788 the convicts, gold rushes, indentured and labour-trade workers and the postwar schemes; from 1990 the UN's count for Oceania.

points.note: All people are foragers in Africa. With countries by 2026 borders as cells about 750 km across, a forager whose home lies a few tens of kilometres from where they were born crosses one of today's lines perhaps one time in twenty, adults far more often than children: about one person in fifty. Reasoned from forager residence and marriage distances, not counted.
The green Sahara and the Levant open longer ranges across many of today's borders; the reading barely moves.

Eases: a growing share of humanity lives in Asia and Sahul, in what are now large countries (Australia, India, China, Indonesia's islands, Russia), where a forager's moves cross fewer of today's lines. The dispersal itself adds little: its fronts advance by births where people already live (WaveOfAdvance#4cec), not by people living far from their birthplace.

The agrarian floor: most people die within a few kilometres of where they were born; nomads crossing today's lines with their herds, deportees (the Assyrians move whole peoples), soldiers, slaves and traders make up the rest.

Rome's wars carry captives from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria to Italy: perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, nearly half a percent of humanity alone; Han settlers and soldiers in Korea and northern Vietnam add a little.

The migration period moves Goths, Vandals, Franks and Saxons from beyond the Rhine and Danube into the Roman west, a few hundred thousand people born in one of today's countries and living in another; as Rome's slave imports end, the share holds.
The Mongol conquests move artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand, and the empire's posts carry merchants from Venice to Khanbaliq: a small rise.

About two million people born in Africa are enslaved in the Americas, a fifth of a percent of humanity, as the Atlantic trade passes its peak; Europeans born in Europe in the Americas, Asians in other Asian countries and Europe's own movers make up the rest.
Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees about 800,000 people, many born in Africa, but frees them where they live: it changes their status, not the share living outside their country of birth.
The first indentured Indians reach British Guiana (1838) and Mauritius, beginning the indenture that replaces enslaved labour on the sugar colonies.

The Irish famine (from 1845) sends about a million and a half people to Britain and North America by 1852, and the California gold rush (from 1848) draws Chinese, Chileans, Mexicans and Europeans: the turn into the age of mass migration.

Turns up: the Irish famine's emigrants, the gold rushes of California and Australia, and the first indentured Indians and Chinese begin the age of mass migration. The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born in 1850.

Indentured Indians begin arriving in Fiji (1879) as they had in Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana; the European emigration to the Americas, slowed by the depression of the 1870s, picks up again at the decade's end.

Cuba's gradual abolition (1880 to 1886) and Brazil's (1888) end the Atlantic world's slave societies; their places on the plantations are taken by immigrants from Spain, Italy, Portugal, China and India.
The United States' Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) is the first law to bar a people by origin; the European flow it does not touch reaches about 800,000 arrivals that year.

The great immigration to the United States, Argentina and Brazil from southern and eastern Europe begins about 1880; Brazil's abolition (May 1888) and its subsidized Italian immigration that follows add to it.

The peak of the age of mass migration: the United States counts 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina 2.4 million (three in ten of its people), Canada 1.6 million; Indians and Chinese in South-east Asia, Russians in Central Asia and Europe's own movers between today's countries add as many again: some 40 to 45 million people, about 2.5% of humanity.
Falls back: the United States' quota acts (1921 to 1924) cut its immigration by four fifths, and the Depression stops and reverses movement; emigrants of 1900 to 1914 die or return.

Rises with the war: Germany puts millions of foreign workers and prisoners to work in the Reich, the Soviet Union deports Poles, Balts, Volga Germans, Chechens and others across today's lines, and Japan moves Koreans to its mines.

At its wartime height Germany holds about 7.5 million foreign civilian workers and 2 million prisoners of war at work, and about 2 million Koreans live in Japan: forced labour lifts the share living outside their country of birth to near its postwar level.

The war's last year moves people both ways: the Germans of the east begin to flee and be expelled, and forced labourers in the Reich and Koreans in Japan are at their peak, so the share holds near its wartime high.

The war's end starts the largest movement home in history: some ten million forced labourers and prisoners leave the Reich, while expellees from the east and Japanese repatriated from the empire take their place in the count.
Most of the forced labourers and displaced persons go home, while the Germans expelled from the east and the Japanese repatriated replace them in the count: the share holds.
Most of Partition's crossings come between August and December 1947: about ten million people are already living on the other side of the new lines by the year's end.
Partition: about 14 million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan in 1947 and 1948, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee Israel's war of independence.

Partition moves about 14 million people across the new lines of India, Pakistan and East Pakistan (now Bangladesh), and 12 to 14 million Germans have been expelled from the east: the share living outside their country of birth stands near its highest until the 2010s.
The UN's estimate of about 76 million international migrants (2.5%) counts the countries of 1960; by 2026 borders the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants (about 15 million) are added.
The United States' Hart-Celler Act (October 1965) ends the national-origin quotas; its effect on the count comes over the next decades.
The low after the postwar displacement: the displaced of the 1940s die or are counted among the natives' children, and humanity grows faster than the migrants' numbers.
Afghanistan's war sends some five million refugees into Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia and the Arab world.

The UN's count for the countries of 2020: about 153 million. The Soviet Union's breakup makes some 25 million people international migrants overnight in the UN's own series; by 2026 borders they were counted all along, so this series has no jump here.

points.note: No one reaches Antarctica for almost all of human history.
Cook crosses the Antarctic Circle (1773) and circles the continent without seeing it.
Antarctica is first sighted (January 1820); sealers land on the South Shetlands the next summer.
Sealers work the South Shetlands and the Peninsula's islands each summer until the fur seals are nearly gone (by the 1830s).
Sealers' seasonal camps on the South Shetland beaches.
Argentina's station on Laurie Island (1904), the first held year round, and the whalers' station at Deception Island (from 1906).
Britain's Operation Tabarin (1944) sets up the first permanent bases on the Antarctic Peninsula.
The IGY's fifty stations, from McMurdo to Vostok, bring most of the coastal oases and the dry valleys within regular reach.
The treaty (December 1959) keeps the IGY's stations open for science under shared rules.
The International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958) and the treaty that followed put some forty stations on the continent and field parties into the dry valleys.
About seventy stations and the field science of the treaty's members reach most of the ice-free ground at least in summer.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Antarctica's ice-free area (about 45,000 km2 as recalled) and the dates of sealing, the first stations and the treaty's science.

points.note: Uruk's temple scribes, the first people who may have kept records and calendars as their main work.
Babylon's astronomical diaries, Ionia's natural philosophers (Miletus is in Türkiye, so Asia's), the Hundred Schools and India's grammarians: Asia holds about two thirds of the world's inquiry.
Holds while the west's schools close: Aryabhata (499), China's astronomical bureau and Constantinople's scholars carry on, so Asia's share rises to three quarters.
Baghdad's House of Wisdom and its successors, Bukhara (Ibn Sina), al-Biruni, and Song China's bureaus and academies.
The Mongol conquest destroys Baghdad (1258) but its khans found the Maragha observatory (1259): Asia's part falls, Europe's grows.
Meiji Japan's Imperial University (1877) and its institutes make Japan Asia's first modern research system.
Japan's defeat ends its war research and the occupation dismantles its weapons laboratories.
Asia passes Europe and becomes the area with the most researchers, as China's research staff triples between 1996 and 2010.
About 5.7 million, nearly half the world's researchers: China most of all, then Japan, Korea and India.

upsert.reason: Mesopotamia's and the Indus's first specialists; Babylon's astronomers; the Hundred Schools and Indian learning; Constantinople, Baghdad, Bukhara, Song China, Maragha and Samarkand; Meiji Japan; China, Korea and India today.

points.note: Pythagoras's school in southern Italy and the first philosophers of mainland Greece.
The western schools close with Rome's fall in the west; Boethius (died 524) is among the last of them.
Caliphal Córdoba's astronomers and physicians (Spain, so Europe's) and the first cathedral schools.
Toledo's translators carry Arabic and Greek science into Latin.
Europe passes Asia in people kept for inquiry, as printing and the universities multiply and the scientific revolution begins (Copernicus, Vesalius, 1543).
Germany's universities and chemical firms, France's grandes écoles and Britain's laboratories hold about seven in ten of the world's researchers.
The Soviet Union builds the world's largest system of research institutes in the 1930s, while Nazi Germany drives out a quarter of its physicists.
Near its height: the Soviet Union counts about 1.5 million scientific workers, more than any other country.
The Soviet Union's breakup halves Russia's and Ukraine's research staff within a decade, as salaries collapse and scientists leave.
About three million, a quarter of the world's: the European Union's two million, Britain's, Russia's and the rest.

upsert.reason: Athens's schools and Rome's scholars; Córdoba and Toledo; the universities; the scientific revolution, the academies and the research university; Soviet science; the European Research Area.

points.note: No forager makes inquiry their main work: zero by the measure's definition, not a judgment that foragers learned nothing new. Most of what people discovered for 300,000 years was found by people whose main work was something else.
The first temple scribes of Uruk keep accounts and calendars; whether any had inquiry as their main work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.

Babylon's astronomers keep their diaries of the sky, Ionia's philosophers argue about nature, the Hundred Schools teach in China and India's grammarians and physicians write: a few hundred people in a world of 160 million.
The Museum of Alexandria (from about 280 BCE) pays perhaps a hundred scholars at a time, the first institution kept for inquiry; with Babylon, Han China and India, about one person in a million.
Falls: the western schools close with Rome's fall in the west, while India's astronomers (Aryabhata, 499) and China's carry on with fewer patrons.
Rises with the patrons: Baghdad's House of Wisdom and its astronomers, Cordoba, Cairo and Song China's bureaus keep several hundred scholars between them.
Bologna's law school (from 1088), then Paris and Oxford, begin the universities; for a century they teach far more than they discover, so the measure barely moves.

The Royal Society (1660) and the Académie des sciences (1666) give natural philosophy members and journals; perhaps two thousand people in Europe, the Ottoman world, India, China and Japan make inquiry their main work.

The research university (Berlin's model, from 1810) and the industrial laboratory (Edison's, 1876; the German chemical firms') make research a paid profession: some fifty thousand people, doubling about every fifteen years, as Price measured the growth of science.

The First World War brings chemists, physicists and engineers into war research (gas, sound-ranging, aircraft) and leaves states with research councils (Britain's in 1916, the United States' National Research Council in 1916).

War research at its height: the Manhattan Project employs some 130,000 people (most of them builders and operators, not researchers), radar laboratories such as MIT's Radiation Laboratory several thousand scientists, and Germany, Britain, the Soviet Union and Japan their own programmes.
War research (radar, the bomb, penicillin) leaves states paying for science: the United States, the Soviet Union and Europe hold about half a million researchers between them.

The International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958) puts some 60,000 scientists from 67 countries into one programme; Sputnik (October 1957) sets off the United States' National Defense Education Act and NASA, and research staff grow fastest of any time.
Rises little in the 1990s: the former Soviet Union's research staff falls by about half while Asia's grows.

upsert.reason: Before 1900 reasoned from the institutions that kept people for inquiry (Babylon's astronomers, the Museum of Alexandria, the Han and Tang bureaus, the House of Wisdom, Maragha and Samarkand, the seventeenth century's academies and their membership), with wide bands; 1900 to 1990 from the growth of the scientific workforce (Price 1963) and national research statistics as recalled (the United States' National Science Foundation, the Soviet Union's scientific workers); from 1990 UNESCO's researchers per million, as recalled, to be checked (UNESCO Science Report 2021).
