Each question states its contrast first, since a different contrast picks out different causes, and a cause present in both the outcome and its contrast is not offered as the reason (ContrastClass#7398). The readings are sketched judgments of the difference each cause made, from recalled histories, with bands wide enough for the debates named; differences do not sum, since causes act together.

upsert.boundary: Ezana of Aksum becomes Christian, about 330
upsert.description: King Ezana's coins change from the crescent and disc to the cross; Ethiopia's church, linked to Alexandria, becomes one of the oldest continuous Christian churches.
provenance: sources to check: Phillipson, Foundations of an African Civilisation (2012)

upsert.boundary: The rise of Pentecostal and evangelical churches, from about 1970
upsert.description: Pentecostal and evangelical churches, small before 1960, grow among the urban poor and in the countryside to about a fifth of Latin Americans by the 2010s, near half in Guatemala and Honduras and about a third in Brazil: the largest religious change in the region since the conversions of the 1500s, as the Catholic share falls from about nine tenths to about three fifths. Their pastors become a force in politics.
provenance: sources to check: Pew Research Center, Religion in Latin America (2014)

upsert.boundary: The Great Awakening, about 1730 to 1755
upsert.description: Revivals led by Jonathan Edwards, George Whitefield and itinerant preachers sweep the colonies, splitting churches between 'new lights' and 'old lights', bringing enslaved Africans into evangelical Christianity and spreading a religion that is personal, emotional and wary of established authority.
provenance: sources to check: Kidd, The Great Awakening (2007)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the British colonies)

upsert.boundary: The Jesuit missions of Paraguay, 1609 to 1768
upsert.description: Jesuits gather Guaraní into some thirty mission towns along the Paraná and Uruguay rivers, with up to about 140,000 people at their height, where Guaraní is written and spoken, fields and workshops are run in common, and armed militias defend them against slave raiders. Spain and Portugal's exchange of territory brings the Guaraní war (1754 to 1756), and the Jesuits' expulsion (1767 to 1768) ends the missions.
provenance: sources to check: Ganson, The Guaraní under Spanish Rule in the Río de la Plata (2003)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil)

upsert.boundary: Dvaravati, the Mon Buddhist towns of central Thailand, about 550 to 1050
upsert.description: Moated towns of the Chao Phraya valley, Nakhon Pathom and U Thong among them, worship at Buddhist stupas and write in Mon and Pali; their Theravada carries on into the Tai kingdoms that later rule the valley.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; whether Dvaravati was one kingdom is debated
sources to check: Higham, The Civilization of Angkor (2001); Murphy 2016, Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 47

upsert.boundary: Indic kingship, Sanskrit and Brahmi scripts take hold, about 300 to 700
upsert.description: Rulers from Borneo to the Mekong take Sanskrit names, worship Shiva and Vishnu or patronize Buddhism, and leave the region's oldest inscriptions, on the sacrificial pillars of Kutai in Borneo (about 400) and the rock edicts of Tarumanagara in Java (about 450). Older accounts saw Indian colonists founding 'Indianized states'; most historians now see local rulers choosing what served them from Indian ideas, which they reshaped.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the nature of 'Indianization' is debated
sources to check: Coedès, The Indianized States of Southeast Asia (1968); Wolters, History, Culture and Region in Southeast Asian Perspectives (1999)

upsert.boundary: Theravada Buddhism becomes the mainland's religion, about 1050 to 1450
upsert.description: Monks ordained in Sri Lanka's reformed Theravada lineage spread from Pagan to Sukhothai, Lan Na, Cambodia and Laos; village monasteries teach boys to read and write, and by the 1400s Theravada has displaced the Mahayana and Hindu cults of the courts, even at Angkor.
provenance: sources to check: Swearer, The Buddhist World of Southeast Asia (2nd ed. 2010)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia)

upsert.boundary: The Americas' large animals die out, about 13,000 to 10,000 years ago
upsert.description: Mammoths, mastodons, horses, camels, giant ground sloths, glyptodonts and sabre-toothed cats disappear, about three quarters of the large mammal genera; new hunters and the rapid climate swings of the deglaciation are both blamed, and the loss leaves the Americas with few animals to domesticate.
provenance: exploring: the weight of hunting against climate is debated
sources to check: Koch and Barnosky 2006, Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics 37; Faith and Surovell 2009, PNAS 106

upsert.boundary: The Black Summer fires, 2019 to 2020
upsert.description: After Australia's hottest and driest year on record, bushfires burn some 24 million hectares in the south-east, kill 33 people directly, destroy over 3,000 homes and kill or displace perhaps three billion animals; a royal commission links their scale to a warming climate.
provenance: sources to check: Royal Commission into National Natural Disaster Arrangements (2020); Van Oldenborgh et al. 2021, Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences 21
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (south-eastern Australia)

upsert.boundary: The Tōhoku earthquake, tsunami and Fukushima disaster, March 2011
upsert.description: A magnitude 9.0 earthquake off north-east Japan raises a tsunami that kills about 18,000 people and causes meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, forcing more than 150,000 people from their homes and turning several countries away from nuclear power.
provenance: sources to check: Japan National Police Agency figures; IAEA, The Fukushima Daiichi Accident (2015)

upsert.boundary: The ice-free corridor opens, about 13,800 to 12,600 years ago
upsert.description: As the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets pull apart east of the Rockies, a corridor of meltwater lakes and bare ground opens from Alaska to the plains; on one reading of its plant and animal DNA it could support people along its whole length only from about 12,600 years ago, on another bison used it by 13,000. Either way it opened after people were at Monte Verde and the Paisley Caves, which is why most now think the first people came south along the Pacific coast, though the coastal sites lie drowned under the risen sea.
provenance: exploring: when the corridor could support people, and so which route came first, is debated
sources to check: Pedersen et al. 2016, Nature 537; Heintzman et al. 2016, PNAS 113

upsert.boundary: Ibn Khaldun writes the Muqaddimah, 1377
upsert.description: In Algeria the Tunisian scholar writes an introduction to history that explains the rise and fall of dynasties by group solidarity, taxation and the life of cities, an early theory of how societies change.
provenance: sources to check: Irwin, Ibn Khaldun: An Intellectual Biography (2018)

upsert.boundary: Mesoamerican writing and the calendars, about 650 to 36 BCE
upsert.description: Glyphs appear on Olmec and Zapotec monuments by about 600 BCE (the dating of the earliest is disputed), with the 260-day ritual calendar; by the first century BCE the Long Count, a count of days from a fixed date in 3114 BCE written by place value, is carved at Chiapa de Corzo (36 BCE). Writing was invented here independently of the Old World, one of perhaps four inventions anywhere; the Maya script that grows from it is a full system of word signs and syllables, and the Maya later write a sign for zero.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dates are disputed
sources to check: Houston (ed.), The First Writing (2004); Saturno, Stuart and Beltrán 2006, Science 311
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Oaxaca, the Gulf coast and Chiapas)

upsert.boundary: The West African Ebola epidemic, 2013 to 2016
upsert.description: The largest Ebola outbreak known infects about 28,600 people in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone and kills about 11,300, overwhelming health systems already weakened by war.
provenance: sources to check: WHO, Ebola Situation Report, 10 June 2016
upsert.region: Africa: Western Africa (Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone)

upsert.boundary: Leclerc's expedition and yellow fever in Saint-Domingue, 1802 to 1803
upsert.description: Napoleon sends about 30,000 soldiers under his brother-in-law Leclerc to retake Saint-Domingue and, as in Guadeloupe, restore slavery; Toussaint Louverture is seized and shipped to France, where he dies (1803). Yellow fever, carried by mosquitoes among troops who had never met it, kills most of the expedition, Leclerc among them, while Dessalines's army fights on and wins at Vertières (November 1803).
provenance: sources to check: McNeill, Mosquito Empires (2010); Dubois, Avengers of the New World (2004)

upsert.boundary: De Soto and Coronado: the Spanish expeditions of 1539 to 1543
upsert.description: Hernando de Soto's army of about 600 marches from Florida through the Mississippian chiefdoms to the Mississippi, seizing food and porters and fighting at Mabila (1540); Francisco Vázquez de Coronado leads another from Mexico through the Pueblos to the plains of Kansas. When the French come down the Mississippi 140 years later, most of the towns de Soto saw are gone. Whether epidemics spreading ahead of colonists caused most of that loss, or the slave raids and wars of the later 1600s did, is debated.
provenance: inferred: the expeditions as recalled; how far epidemics ran ahead of colonists is debated
sources to check: Hudson, Knights of Spain, Warriors of the Sun (1997); Kelton, Epidemics and Enslavement (2007)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the South-east and the Southwest)

upsert.boundary: The opioid epidemic in the United States, from 1996
upsert.description: After OxyContin's launch (1996) and aggressive marketing, prescribed opioids, then heroin (from about 2010) and fentanyl (from about 2013) kill over 800,000 Americans by 2023, more than 100,000 a year at the peak (2021 and 2022); with suicides and alcohol, these deaths of despair among working-age adults hold US life expectancy down from 2014 to 2017 while it rises in other rich countries. Deaths begin to fall in 2024.
provenance: sources to check: Case and Deaton, Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism (2020); CDC WONDER mortality data
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

points.note: The Pleistocene's large mammals on every continent: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, diprotodons and the herds of the savannas and steppes, perhaps 20 to 25 Mt C.

Sahul's megafauna (diprotodons, giant kangaroos, Genyornis) vanish soon after people arrive, about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago; whether hunting, fire or drying climate decided it is debated (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction). A small part of the world's wild mass.
The glacial maximum: the mammoth steppe from France to the Yukon holds great herds of grazers even as forests shrink.

The Americas lose most of their large mammal genera between about 11,000 and 9,000 BCE, as Clovis hunters spread and the Younger Dryas cold returns; hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.

After the end-Pleistocene extinctions: the Americas lose about three quarters of their large mammal genera between 13,000 and 11,000 years ago, and northern Eurasia its mammoths, woolly rhinos and giant deer, as people spread and the climate swings at the glacial's end. Hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.
From here fields and pastures slowly take land from wild herds; the loss is gradual for six thousand years.
Most of it now in the bison of North America (perhaps 30 to 60 million), the savanna herds of Africa and the wild ungulates of Asia's steppes and forests.
The slaughter of the bison for hides begins with the railways across the plains.
The bison are down to under a thousand (1889), and rinderpest, brought to the Horn of Africa in 1887, kills up to nine in ten of East Africa's buffalo and wildebeest within a decade.
Tropical forest cleared for fields and pasture, and bushmeat hunting, take wild mammals down by about a third in half a century while livestock doubles.

Bar-On and colleagues (2018): wild land mammals about 0.003 Gt C, against 0.06 for humans and 0.1 for livestock; Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) about 20 Mt of wet mass, the same order. As recalled, to be checked.

Values at 650 BCE for discovery and its five parts, between the Events of Greek philosophy, the Hundred Schools and Mesoamerica's first writing that the coverage report found discovery passing over; the five parts sum to the whole there as at every other date.

points.note: Egypt's first temple and palace scribes keep calendars and records beside Uruk's: about a third of the world's few specialists.
The Rhind papyrus's mathematics and the Edwin Smith papyrus's surgery come from New Kingdom Egypt's temple and palace scholars.
The Museum and Library of Alexandria (from about 280 BCE) keep Euclid, Eratosthenes and their successors on royal salaries: Africa's part nearly quadruples.
Alexandria's schools dwindle after the Serapeum's destruction (391) and Hypatia's murder (415).
Fatimid Cairo's House of Knowledge (1005) and Ibn al-Haytham's optics.
About 300,000 people, a fortieth of the world's researchers for a fifth of its people; Egypt, South Africa, Nigeria and the Maghreb hold most of them.

upsert.reason: Egypt's temples, Alexandria's Museum, Fatimid Cairo, Fez and Timbuktu, then the colonial and national universities and institutes.

points.note: The first Olmec and Zapotec glyphs and the 260-day calendar imply a handful of calendar specialists.
Mesoamerica's first writing and Long Count calendars (from about 650 to 36 BCE) imply a few calendar specialists.
Classic Maya astronomers and scribes at Tikal, Palenque and Copan, with their eclipse and Venus tables.
The conquest ends the Aztec and Maya priests' learning; the first colonial colleges (Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco, 1536; the University of Mexico, 1551) begin to replace a little of it.

The war sends the United States' chemists and physicists into war research and leaves it a National Research Council; American industry's laboratories (General Electric, Bell, DuPont) grow fastest of any.

Europe's and Japan's science lies in ruins while the American wartime laboratories stand: the Americas' share of the world's researchers jumps to about two fifths, and German and other European scientists come west.
Flat as a share of humanity's researchers falls: the United States' research staff grows slowly after 2000 while China's triples.
About 2.6 million, most of them in the United States, with Canada, Brazil and Mexico next: a fifth of the world's researchers.

upsert.reason: The Maya calendar specialists, then the colonial colleges, the American Philosophical Society, the land-grant and research universities, the industrial laboratories and the twentieth century's federal science.

points.note: Uruk's temple scribes, the first people who may have kept records and calendars as their main work.
Babylon's astronomical diaries, Ionia's natural philosophers (Miletus is in Türkiye, so Asia's), the Hundred Schools and India's grammarians: Asia holds about two thirds of the world's inquiry.
Holds while the west's schools close: Aryabhata (499), China's astronomical bureau and Constantinople's scholars carry on, so Asia's share rises to three quarters.
Baghdad's House of Wisdom and its successors, Bukhara (Ibn Sina), al-Biruni, and Song China's bureaus and academies.
The Mongol conquest destroys Baghdad (1258) but its khans found the Maragha observatory (1259): Asia's part falls, Europe's grows.
Meiji Japan's Imperial University (1877) and its institutes make Japan Asia's first modern research system.
Japan's defeat ends its war research and the occupation dismantles its weapons laboratories.
Asia passes Europe and becomes the area with the most researchers, as China's research staff triples between 1996 and 2010.
About 5.7 million, nearly half the world's researchers: China most of all, then Japan, Korea and India.

upsert.reason: Mesopotamia's and the Indus's first specialists; Babylon's astronomers; the Hundred Schools and Indian learning; Constantinople, Baghdad, Bukhara, Song China, Maragha and Samarkand; Meiji Japan; China, Korea and India today.

points.note: Pythagoras's school in southern Italy and the first philosophers of mainland Greece.
The western schools close with Rome's fall in the west; Boethius (died 524) is among the last of them.
Caliphal Córdoba's astronomers and physicians (Spain, so Europe's) and the first cathedral schools.
Toledo's translators carry Arabic and Greek science into Latin.
Europe passes Asia in people kept for inquiry, as printing and the universities multiply and the scientific revolution begins (Copernicus, Vesalius, 1543).
Germany's universities and chemical firms, France's grandes écoles and Britain's laboratories hold about seven in ten of the world's researchers.
The Soviet Union builds the world's largest system of research institutes in the 1930s, while Nazi Germany drives out a quarter of its physicists.
Near its height: the Soviet Union counts about 1.5 million scientific workers, more than any other country.
The Soviet Union's breakup halves Russia's and Ukraine's research staff within a decade, as salaries collapse and scientists leave.
About three million, a quarter of the world's: the European Union's two million, Britain's, Russia's and the rest.

upsert.reason: Athens's schools and Rome's scholars; Córdoba and Toledo; the universities; the scientific revolution, the academies and the research university; Soviet science; the European Research Area.

points.note: The Parramatta observatory (1821) is the first institution of inquiry in Oceania.
Australia's Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (1926), later CSIRO, begins state-funded research.
About 180,000, nearly all in Australia and New Zealand.

upsert.reason: Zero before the colonial observatories and museums; then Australia's and New Zealand's universities and CSIRO.

points.note: No forager makes inquiry their main work: zero by the measure's definition, not a judgment that foragers learned nothing new. Most of what people discovered for 300,000 years was found by people whose main work was something else.
The first temple scribes of Uruk keep accounts and calendars; whether any had inquiry as their main work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Rising toward the Axial age: Assyria's and Babylon's scholars, Egypt's temple priests, and the first Greek and Indian thinkers who make inquiry their work.

Babylon's astronomers keep their diaries of the sky, Ionia's philosophers argue about nature, the Hundred Schools teach in China and India's grammarians and physicians write: a few hundred people in a world of 160 million.
The Museum of Alexandria (from about 280 BCE) pays perhaps a hundred scholars at a time, the first institution kept for inquiry; with Babylon, Han China and India, about one person in a million.
Falls: the western schools close with Rome's fall in the west, while India's astronomers (Aryabhata, 499) and China's carry on with fewer patrons.
Rises with the patrons: Baghdad's House of Wisdom and its astronomers, Cordoba, Cairo and Song China's bureaus keep several hundred scholars between them.
Bologna's law school (from 1088), then Paris and Oxford, begin the universities; for a century they teach far more than they discover, so the measure barely moves.

The Royal Society (1660) and the Académie des sciences (1666) give natural philosophy members and journals; perhaps two thousand people in Europe, the Ottoman world, India, China and Japan make inquiry their main work.

The research university (Berlin's model, from 1810) and the industrial laboratory (Edison's, 1876; the German chemical firms') make research a paid profession: some fifty thousand people, doubling about every fifteen years, as Price measured the growth of science.

The First World War brings chemists, physicists and engineers into war research (gas, sound-ranging, aircraft) and leaves states with research councils (Britain's in 1916, the United States' National Research Council in 1916).

War research at its height: the Manhattan Project employs some 130,000 people (most of them builders and operators, not researchers), radar laboratories such as MIT's Radiation Laboratory several thousand scientists, and Germany, Britain, the Soviet Union and Japan their own programmes.
War research (radar, the bomb, penicillin) leaves states paying for science: the United States, the Soviet Union and Europe hold about half a million researchers between them.

The International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958) puts some 60,000 scientists from 67 countries into one programme; Sputnik (October 1957) sets off the United States' National Defense Education Act and NASA, and research staff grow fastest of any time.
Rises little in the 1990s: the former Soviet Union's research staff falls by about half while Asia's grows.

upsert.reason: Before 1900 reasoned from the institutions that kept people for inquiry (Babylon's astronomers, the Museum of Alexandria, the Han and Tang bureaus, the House of Wisdom, Maragha and Samarkand, the seventeenth century's academies and their membership), with wide bands; 1900 to 1990 from the growth of the scientific workforce (Price 1963) and national research statistics as recalled (the United States' National Science Foundation, the Soviet Union's scientific workers); from 1990 UNESCO's researchers per million, as recalled, to be checked (UNESCO Science Report 2021).

The breadth check names the Events judged for those who follow the arts and play: 25 of 27 move no process. Read whole, they change two things the model does not follow: whether populations make lasting art at all (Bizmoune, Blombos, the Aurignacian, Sulawesi, the rock art of Africa and Australia, the Gravettian and the Magdalenians) and how many people are kept to make the arts for courts, temples and markets (the Olmec, Nok, Igbo-Ukwu, Ife, Lalibela, Borobudur, the Gupta, Heian, Minoan Crete, Dong Son, Rapa Nui's moai, the Renaissance). The first record of this carve (r215) kept the arts as a frontier because no world measure seemed readable across the range; discovery (r326, r346) has since been opened on the same kind of measure, people kept for one kind of work per million, so the arts' makers can be too. Re-recorded under the same cut id, with the earlier candidates and verdicts kept.

changes.value: Opens the two parts of the re-recorded carve of beauty and play (carve.concept.humanity.wants.play, r363) at every date of the time schedule: the arts' makers (h.play.makers, people kept for the arts per million) and image and ornament (h.play.images, the share of people in populations that make lasting art). Every value is recalled or reasoned, tagged and banded; the figures share one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Pigments ground at Olorgesailie and Kapthurin, about 300,000 years ago, may have coloured bodies or objects, but no lasting ornament or image of this age is known; how many populations made what has not survived is unknown.
Pierced shells at Bizmoune in Morocco (about 142,000 to 150,000 years ago), the oldest known ornaments; one site is a lower bound, not a census.
Blombos's ochre-mixing kit (about 100,000 years ago) and shell beads at Skhul, Qafzeh and in North Africa: lasting art is made in several regions, though the record holds only a handful of sites.
Blombos's beads and engraved ochre (about 75,000 years ago) and the Still Bay: in southern Africa ornament and image are made widely for a few thousand years.
The record flickers: the Still Bay's and Howiesons Poort's engraving come and go in southern Africa, as models of cultural loss in small, scattered populations predict (CumulativeCulture#4f93).

Ostrich-eggshell beads spread across eastern and southern Africa and the first known figurative painting is made in Sulawesi (at least 51,200 years ago): the share nears half as the dispersal carries the practice.
The Aurignacian ivories, flutes and Chauvet in Europe, hand stencils and animals in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo: most of humanity now lives in populations that make lasting art.
Every living population makes lasting images and ornament, printed and plastic among them.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned from the dated sites, which are a lower bound on the practice, not a census of it (AbsenceEvidence#10a3). Three readings are argued and the bands hold all of them (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): a gradual emergence across Africa from about 300,000 years ago, thinly recorded (McBrearty and Brooks 2000), which would put the early values far too low; a late change in minds or society about 50,000 years ago (Klein), which would put them too high; and a demographic reading in which the practice is kept or lost with population density and connection (Powell, Shennan and Thomas 2009; CumulativeCulture#4f93), which predicts the flickering record of southern Africa. A distinguishing test: if density decides, the oldest ornaments should cluster where and when genomes and site counts show the densest Middle Stone Age populations.

points.note: Zero by the measure's definition: no forager band keeps anyone to make art. The beads, engravings and paintings of the Stone Age were made by people whose main work was getting food.
Sunghir's burials, with thousands of ivory beads that took thousands of hours to make, show great effort spent on ornament, but nothing shows anyone kept for the work.

Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars (from about 9500 BCE) are raised by foragers' communal labour, perhaps with a few carvers who did little else; whether anyone was kept for the work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Chiefdoms begin to keep craftsmen: the goldsmiths behind Varna's graves (about 4500 BCE), the builders and painters of Ubaid Mesopotamia's temples.
The temple and palace workshops of Sumer and Egypt keep the first full-time sculptors, painters, musicians and goldsmiths; perhaps a fifth of humanity now lives under such courts.
The tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, the Shang bronze-casters, the palace painters of Crete and the Olmec sculptors: courts on three continents now keep makers of art.
Greek cities' festivals keep poets, actors and sculptors, and the Persian, Indian and Chinese courts their musicians and craftsmen.

Rome's theatres, games and workshops and the Han court's Music Bureau, about 800 musicians before 7 BCE: a few makers in every thousand people of the great cities, about one in two thousand people worldwide.
Falls with Rome in the west: theatres, games and the patrons who paid for them close; Gupta India, Sasanian Iran and the southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds, beside the courts of the Abbasids, the Fatimids and Heian Japan.
The Black Death and the Mongol wars kill makers and patrons alike.
The workshops of Italy and the Netherlands, the Mughal and Safavid ateliers, Ming porcelain and printed images: art is made for markets as well as for patrons.
Theatres, music halls, the illustrated press and the publishers' authors grow with the cities of the industrial world.
Cinema: the picture houses' actors and pit musicians, and the first professional footballers and boxers.
Hollywood's studios, radio's orchestras and singers, and sport as a profession.
War takes performers into the forces and closes theatres in occupied Europe and Asia.
The pandemic closes theatres, concert halls and stadiums; live performers lose most of a year's work.
About twenty million people of some 3.6 billion workers: artists, musicians, actors, writers, dancers, players of sport and makers of art wares.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned: zero among foragers by definition; a few hundred per million under the agrarian states' courts and temples, bounded by the surplus that keeps them (SurplusBound#7fe3); a few thousand per million now. The 2025 value rests on the recalled count of about 30 million jobs in the cultural and creative industries in 2013 (UNESCO and EY), of which the makers themselves are perhaps two thirds; to be checked. Where the line falls between a maker of art wares and a maker of ordinary goods moves every value before 1900 by a factor of two either way.

upsert.boundary: Aboriginal rock art and the Dreaming, from about 28,000 years ago
upsert.description: From the charcoal drawings of Nawarla Gabarnmang (about 28,000 years old) to the Gwion figures of the Kimberley and the X-ray paintings of Arnhem Land, Aboriginal peoples record on rock the ancestral beings, laws and country of the Dreaming, the oldest continuous artistic tradition on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: David et al. 2013, Journal of Archaeological Science 40; Taçon and Chippindale (eds.), The Archaeology of Rock-Art (1998)

upsert.boundary: Rugby across Oceania, from the 1870s
upsert.description: Brought by British settlers, soldiers and schools, rugby becomes New Zealand's national game, whose All Blacks tour Britain in 1905 and win three World Cups, rugby league becomes the game of eastern Australia's working towns, and rugby the national game of Fiji, Samoa and Tonga; island-born players fill professional teams in New Zealand, Australia, Europe and Japan, and Fiji's sevens team wins the islands' first Olympic gold (2016).
provenance: sources to check: Ryan (ed.), Tackling Rugby Myths (2005); Besnier, Brownell and Carter, The Anthropology of Sport (2018)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand, Melanesia, Polynesia)

upsert.boundary: Borobudur and Prambanan, about 780 to 856
upsert.description: On the Kedu plain of central Java, the Sailendra kings build Borobudur, a stepped mountain of stone with 2,672 carved relief panels and 504 Buddhas, the largest Buddhist monument on Earth; a rival line builds the Shaiva temples of Prambanan (856). Volcanic ash and the court's move to east Java leave both to the forest.
provenance: sources to check: Miksic, Borobudur: Golden Tales of the Buddhas (1990)

upsert.boundary: Dong Son and its bronze drums, about 500 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: Chiefs of the Red River delta, remembered in later Vietnamese tradition as the kings of Van Lang and Au Lac, cast great bronze drums decorated with boats, feathered warriors and houses on stilts; the drums travel as gifts of prestige to Thailand, Malaysia and eastern Indonesia.
provenance: sources to check: Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014); Kim 2015, The Origins of Ancient Vietnam

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's arts and play group (events:importance.dim.arts): 22 of its Events now name the part of beauty and play they change, opened at r364. The first ornaments and images (Bizmoune, Blombos, the Aurignacian, Sulawesi, Aboriginal rock art, the Gravettian's spread across Eurasia) name image and ornament (h.play.images); the arts made by people kept for them (the Olmec, Nok, Igbo-Ukwu, Ife, Lalibela, Borobudur, the Gupta, Heian, Minoan Crete, Dong Son, Paracas and Nazca, Rapa Nui's carvers, the Renaissance, the Festival of Pacific Arts and rugby's professional players) name the arts' makers (h.play.makers). Britain's sack of Benin (1897) ends royal patronage of the bronze-casters' guild and brings the kingdom under colonial rule, so it also names colonial rule and its African part. The Sahara's rock art observes image and ornament: it shows the practice, it does not change its share. Every Event is restated whole from the current model, with only process_ids or observation_process_ids extended.

Fill: the arts' makers and image and ornament at the remaining dates of the time schedule and at the Events linked at r365, guessed on the line between their neighbours except where an Event moves them; and colonial rule with its five parts at the sack of Benin (1897), on the line between 1895 and 1900, so the parts still sum to the whole.

points.note: Zero before 1415, as the parent is by definition.
Portugal's forts on Africa's Atlantic coast, Elmina among them (1482).
Doubles with France's conquest of Algeria (from 1830).
Jumps: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882).
The Scramble's conquests: most of West, East and southern Africa comes under European rule.
Britain's sack of Benin (1897) ends one of the last independent kingdoms of the forest coast, after Dahomey (1894), Asante and Madagascar (1896).
Almost all of Africa but Ethiopia and Liberia is partitioned: Africa now holds about a fifth of the colonized.
Egypt's nominal independence (1922) takes it out of the count.
Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1935 to 1936).
Africa becomes most of colonial rule as South Asia leaves it (1947 to 1948).
Falls by two thirds: the year of Africa (1960) and the independences of 1961.
Falls by two thirds: Portugal's African colonies become independent (1974 to 1975).
Zimbabwe (1980) is independent; Namibia is what remains.
Namibia's independence (1990) leaves only small islands.
Zero before Castile rules Hispaniola (1493 to 1496).
Castile begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over their numbers.
Hispaniola's Taínos have mostly died; Cuba, Puerto Rico and Darién add few.
Central Mexico under Spanish rule after Tenochtitlan falls: almost all of colonial rule is now in the Americas.
The Andes join after Pizarro takes the Inca empire.
Halves without a colony lost: epidemics, war and forced labour kill the colonized (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
Spanish America near its demographic low.
Recovery: Spanish America's people grow again, and the sugar islands, Brazil and the English mainland colonies fill with settlers and enslaved Africans.
The Americas are now the smaller part: Bengal makes Asia the larger.
The thirteen colonies leave the count when they rebel (1776), about 2.8 million people.
Haiti's independence (1804) takes Saint-Domingue out.
Argentina, Chile and Gran Colombia's core are independent; Mexico, Peru, Central America, Brazil and the Caribbean remain.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822): the part falls by almost two thirds.
Peru and Upper Peru leave (1824 to 1825); Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Caribbean colonies, the Guianas and British North America remain.
British North America leaves the count as responsible government comes (1848 to 1855).
Spain takes back the Dominican Republic (1861 to 1865). Maximilian's Mexico (1864 to 1867) is a client empire on the spot, not counted.
Cuba and Puerto Rico pass from Spain to the United States (1898); Hawaii is annexed. Cuba under American occupation until 1902 is still counted.
Cuba's independence (1902) takes it out.
Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana become French départements with deputies in Paris (1946) and leave the count.
Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago leave (August 1962).
Guyana (May 1966) leaves; Barbados follows at the month's end.
Suriname (1975) leaves; the Bahamas and Grenada already have (1973, 1974).
Belize, Antigua and St Kitts leave (1981 to 1983): Puerto Rico is most of what remains.

With Hong Kong and Macau returned, the Americas are almost all of colonial rule: Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands and the British and Dutch Caribbean. The lower band carries the UN's list, which has left Puerto Rico out since 1953.
About 3.7 million people, 3.2 million of them in Puerto Rico.
Zero before the Portuguese in India (1498 to 1510).
Cabral's first factory at Cochin; no territory yet.
Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515) under Portugal.
Spain's Philippines (from 1565) bring the part to about a seventh of colonial rule.
The Dutch company's Batavia (1619), Amboina and Formosa's coast (1624).
The Dutch company rules Java's north coast and the Priangan; Madras, Bombay, Calcutta and Pondicherry are company towns.
Bengal, Bihar and Orissa under the East India Company after Plassey: Asia becomes most of colonial rule, as it stays until 1948.
Mysore falls (1799) and Britain takes the Dutch Ceylon coast (1796). The parent's remainder here implies some 70 million people, above a count of about 55 million: the parent may be high at 1800.
Doubles after the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818): the Company is paramount over most of India, its princely states counted with it.
India, the Dutch Indies, Indochina, the Philippines (American from 1898), Ceylon, Malaya and Taiwan: about 365 million people.
Korea, a Japanese protectorate from 1905, is already counted before its annexation (1910).
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces.
Manchukuo (1932), a puppet state whose counting is debated, adds about 1.4 points.
South-east Asia passes from European and American to Japanese rule without changing the count.
Japan's empire ends: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave, and Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence.
The Philippines become independent (July 1946).
India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon leave (1947 to 1948): the part falls by six sevenths in two years, and Africa becomes the larger part.
Indonesia's independence (December 1949).

After Geneva (1954) Indochina is out. This is the parent's remainder; a count of what is left (Malaya, Singapore, Hong Kong, Aden, Cyprus, the Borneo territories, Goa, Macau, Timor and the Gulf protectorates) gives about 0.6%, so either the parent or Africa's part is about half a point high here; the band reaches down to the count.
Malaya (1957) and Cyprus (1960) are out.
Singapore and the Borneo states join Malaysia (1963) and West New Guinea passes to Indonesia (1963).
Aden leaves (November 1967).
Hong Kong and Macau are almost all that remains, growing faster than the world.
Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China: no colonial rule from overseas is left in Asia.
Zero before Portugal takes Ceuta (1415).
All of colonial rule in 1450: Ceuta, Madeira, the Azores and the first Canaries, which belong to Europe by today's borders.
Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496).
Britain takes Malta (1800).
The Ionian Islands become a British protectorate (1815).
The Atlantic islands send deputies to the Cortes of Madrid and Lisbon (1820 to 1822) and leave the count; Malta and the Ionian Islands remain.
Britain cedes the Ionian Islands to Greece (1864).
Italy takes the Dodecanese (1912).
Italy's Albania (1939 to 1943) is military occupation and not counted.
The Dodecanese pass to Greece (1947).
Malta's independence (September 1964) leaves Gibraltar.
Gibraltar's 34,000 people.
Zero before Spain rules the Marianas (1668).
Spain's mission to Guam (1668) brings the Chamorros of the Marianas under its rule.
The Spanish–Chamorro wars and epidemics cut the Chamorros from tens of thousands to a few thousand by about 1710.
New South Wales (1788) adds about a thousand convicts and soldiers.
The Australian colonies' settlers grow, and Britain claims New Zealand (1840).

The peak before self-government: the Victorian gold rush has not yet begun, but the Australian colonies hold about 400,000 settlers and convicts, and New Zealand about 25,000 settlers beside the Māori counted under the Crown's rule; all still governed from London.

Responsible government in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia (1855 to 1857) and New Zealand (1856) takes them out by the parent's definition; Aboriginal Australians and most Māori, with no vote, are a debated exception the band does not carry. Western Australia, the Marianas and Tahiti remain.
Fiji is ceded to Britain (1874).
Britain and Germany divide eastern New Guinea (1884) and Germany takes the Marshall Islands (1885); their rule reaches the coasts.
Samoa divided (1899), the Carolines and Marianas sold to Germany (1899), Guam to the United States (1898), the Solomons and the Gilberts British (1892 to 1893).
Patrols reach New Guinea's highlands (from 1933), about a million people never contacted before; how fast they count as ruled is a matter of judgment.

New Guinea's highland valleys, reached by patrols from 1933, are counted as administered by about 1940, which with Fiji, the Solomons, New Caledonia and Japan's mandated islands brings the part to about two million people. How much of the highlands counted as ruled by 1940 is a judgment; the band carries it.
Western Samoa becomes independent (1962).
Fiji and Tonga's protectorate end (1970).
Papua New Guinea becomes independent (September 1975): the part falls by three quarters.
The Solomons, Tuvalu (1978) and Kiribati (1979) are independent; Vanuatu follows in 1980.

New Caledonia and French Polynesia, Guam, the Northern Marianas, American Samoa, Wallis and Futuna and Tokelau. The French territories elect deputies to Paris but are on the UN's list of territories to decolonize (New Caledonia from 1986, French Polynesia from 2013); the lower band leaves them out.

Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882), about eight million people; the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) follows.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
Between Madagascar and Asante (1896) and Benin (1897), the conquest of Africa's coasts and their hinterlands is nearly complete; on the line between 1895 and 1900.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan (January 1956), Morocco and Tunisia (March 1956) become independent, about 23 million people; Ghana and Malaya follow in 1957.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.
Portugal's African empire, Rhodesia and small territories, with Hong Kong; their numbers grow while their count of territories does not, until the independences of 1974 and 1975.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

Pigments ground at Olorgesailie and Kapthurin, about 300,000 years ago, may have coloured bodies or objects, but no lasting ornament or image of this age is known; how many populations made what has not survived is unknown.
Pierced shells at Bizmoune in Morocco (about 142,000 to 150,000 years ago), the oldest known ornaments; one site is a lower bound, not a census.
Blombos's ochre-mixing kit (about 100,000 years ago) and shell beads at Skhul, Qafzeh and in North Africa: lasting art is made in several regions, though the record holds only a handful of sites.
Blombos's beads and engraved ochre (about 75,000 years ago) and the Still Bay: in southern Africa ornament and image are made widely for a few thousand years.
The record flickers: the Still Bay's and Howiesons Poort's engraving come and go in southern Africa, as models of cultural loss in small, scattered populations predict (CumulativeCulture#4f93).

Ostrich-eggshell beads spread across eastern and southern Africa and the first known figurative painting is made in Sulawesi (at least 51,200 years ago): the share nears half as the dispersal carries the practice.
The Aurignacian ivories, flutes and Chauvet in Europe, hand stencils and animals in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo: most of humanity now lives in populations that make lasting art.
Sahul's people are drawing on rock by now (Nawarla Gabarnmang, about 28,000 years ago): one more continent's populations in the count.
Every living population makes lasting images and ornament, printed and plastic among them.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned from the dated sites, which are a lower bound on the practice, not a census of it (AbsenceEvidence#10a3). Three readings are argued and the bands hold all of them (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): a gradual emergence across Africa from about 300,000 years ago, thinly recorded (McBrearty and Brooks 2000), which would put the early values far too low; a late change in minds or society about 50,000 years ago (Klein), which would put them too high; and a demographic reading in which the practice is kept or lost with population density and connection (Powell, Shennan and Thomas 2009; CumulativeCulture#4f93), which predicts the flickering record of southern Africa. A distinguishing test: if density decides, the oldest ornaments should cluster where and when genomes and site counts show the densest Middle Stone Age populations.

points.note: Zero by the measure's definition: no forager band keeps anyone to make art. The beads, engravings and paintings of the Stone Age were made by people whose main work was getting food.
Sunghir's burials, with thousands of ivory beads that took thousands of hours to make, show great effort spent on ornament, but nothing shows anyone kept for the work.

Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars (from about 9500 BCE) are raised by foragers' communal labour, perhaps with a few carvers who did little else; whether anyone was kept for the work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Chiefdoms begin to keep craftsmen: the goldsmiths behind Varna's graves (about 4500 BCE), the builders and painters of Ubaid Mesopotamia's temples.
The temple and palace workshops of Sumer and Egypt keep the first full-time sculptors, painters, musicians and goldsmiths; perhaps a fifth of humanity now lives under such courts.
Minoan Crete's palaces keep fresco painters, seal-cutters and goldsmiths beside Egypt's and Mesopotamia's workshops.
Olmec rulers at San Lorenzo keep the sculptors of the colossal heads: makers of art are now kept in the Americas too.
The tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, the Shang bronze-casters, the palace painters of Crete and the Olmec sculptors: courts on three continents now keep makers of art.
Greek cities' festivals keep poets, actors and sculptors, and the Persian, Indian and Chinese courts their musicians and craftsmen.

Rome's theatres, games and workshops and the Han court's Music Bureau, about 800 musicians before 7 BCE: a few makers in every thousand people of the great cities, about one in two thousand people worldwide.
Gupta India's court poets, dramatists and temple sculptors (Kalidasa wrote about 400) rise as Rome's western patrons fail.
Falls with Rome in the west: theatres, games and the patrons who paid for them close; Gupta India, Sasanian Iran and the southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds, beside the courts of the Abbasids, the Fatimids and Heian Japan.
The Black Death and the Mongol wars kill makers and patrons alike.
The workshops of Italy and the Netherlands, the Mughal and Safavid ateliers, Ming porcelain and printed images: art is made for markets as well as for patrons.
Theatres, music halls, the illustrated press and the publishers' authors grow with the cities of the industrial world.
Cinema: the picture houses' actors and pit musicians, and the first professional footballers and boxers.
Hollywood's studios, radio's orchestras and singers, and sport as a profession.
War takes performers into the forces and closes theatres in occupied Europe and Asia.
The pandemic closes theatres, concert halls and stadiums; live performers lose most of a year's work.
About twenty million people of some 3.6 billion workers: artists, musicians, actors, writers, dancers, players of sport and makers of art wares.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned: zero among foragers by definition; a few hundred per million under the agrarian states' courts and temples, bounded by the surplus that keeps them (SurplusBound#7fe3); a few thousand per million now. The 2025 value rests on the recalled count of about 30 million jobs in the cultural and creative industries in 2013 (UNESCO and EY), of which the makers themselves are perhaps two thirds; to be checked. Where the line falls between a maker of art wares and a maker of ordinary goods moves every value before 1900 by a factor of two either way.

changes.value: Read whole, the 25 Events of the arts and play that named no process change two things the model did not follow. (1) Whether populations make lasting art at all: Bizmoune's shells, Blombos, the Aurignacian, Sulawesi, Aboriginal rock art and the Gravettian's spread now name image and ornament (h.play.images), and the Sahara's rock art observes it. (2) How many people are kept to make the arts for courts, temples and markets: the Olmec, Nok, Igbo-Ukwu, Ife, Lalibela, Borobudur, the Gupta, Heian, Minoan Crete, Dong Son, Paracas and Nazca, Rapa Nui's carvers, the Renaissance, the Festival of Pacific Arts, rugby's professional players and the sack of Benin now name the arts' makers (h.play.makers), and Benin colonial rule too. Both were opened from the re-recorded carve of beauty and play (r363) with values at every date of the schedule (r364, r366). Left unlinked, each for its reason: the signs of Neanderthal minds (Neanderthals are not counted among the living people these shares divide), the Amazon's early pottery (no measure follows pottery), the Mokaya ball court (games and sport are a frontier part of the carve, without a world measure), and the Magdalenians, who already name Europe's people.

upsert.lens: To follow the three classes of what is dug from the Earth, which change apart and which one tonnage hides: the stone, sand, gravel and clay that build houses, monuments, cities and roads; the metal ores smelted for tools, weapons, coins and machines; and the coal, oil and gas burned since about 1000 and above all since 1800. So that metalworking (Old Copper, the Balkans' smelters, the Andes, West African iron, mainland bronze), mining booms (Potosí, Zacatecas, Minas Gerais, the gold rushes, the Rand, Panguna, Nauru) and the great acceleration each have a home, and so that the tonnage can be checked against the material flow accounts class by class. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living people; a class may stand at or near zero before it is used, as metal ores do before about 5000 BCE and fossil fuels before about 1000.

Opens the three parts of the carve of the Earth's stores (carve.concept.dim.earth.resources, r368) at every date of the whole, so that building and industrial minerals, metal ores and fossil fuels sum to h.earth.resources at each one; and raises the whole at 1890, 1900 and 1910 to the level its own 1900 note gives. Fossil fuels and metal ores after 1800 rest on recalled production series (coal, oil, gas, pig iron, copper) converted to mass and ore; minerals are the remainder of the whole; before 1800 all three are reasoned guesses with wide bands. The figures share one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Bitumen from seeps in Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea, for mortar, caulking and inlay: fossil carbon taken in tiny amounts.
Song China begins to burn coal: Kaifeng heats with it and the north's iron furnaces run on it as the forests near the cities give out.
Falls back after the Jurchen and Mongol conquests of north China.
England's coal grows several times over in half a century as wood grows dear around London.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
Drake's well (1859) begins oil's century; coal is already over 100 Mt a year.
About 760 Mt of coal and 20 Mt of oil: fuel is nearly half of all that is dug.
Mines wrecked and flooded in Europe and Asia in the last year of the war.
Oil and gas join coal: fossil fuels per person grow by about 70% to 1973.
After the oil shocks fossil fuels per person fall back and stay flat for twenty years.
China's coal grows about two and a half times between 2000 and 2013.
The pandemic year's dip, below the 2014 level per person.
About 9 Gt of coal, 4.4 Gt of oil and 3 Gt of gas: some 16 Gt a year.

upsert.reason: From recalled world output of coal and lignite, crude oil and natural gas (gas at about 0.72 tonnes per thousand cubic metres) divided by the world's people; before 1800 from the scale of English and Chinese coal mining. It must turn with the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores), which counts the same fuels in GJ.

points.note: Native copper is hammered into beads and awls at Çayönü in Anatolia, too little to count.
Copper is smelted from ore in the Balkans (Belovode, Pločnik) and Iran: the first ore taken for metal.
Arsenical and then tin bronze; copper from Oman, Feinan and Cyprus is traded across thousands of kilometres.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant; ores need no long trade, so more is dug.
Rome's mines (Rio Tinto, the lead and silver of Spain, the gold of Las Médulas) and the Han's iron: lead in Greenland's ice peaks in the first century, a level not seen again until the Middle Ages.
Rome's western mines close and the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China's iron industry, perhaps 100,000 tonnes of iron a year about 1080 on Hartwell's much-argued estimate, and Europe's silver mines (Goslar, Kutná Hora later).
The silver century: Potosí's and Zacatecas's ore, refined with mercury from 1573, and Japan's silver, with Sweden's iron and copper.
Iron for rails, ships and machines: about 4.5 Mt of pig iron in 1850, and the gold rushes of California and Victoria.
The steel century begins: about 40 Mt of pig iron, copper for electricity, and the Witwatersrand's gold reef, crushed by the million tonnes.
War production holds up iron and copper while building stops.
Ores per person grow two and a half times from 1950 to 1970, and grades fall: copper ore near 1% means a hundred tonnes dug for each tonne of metal.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries' steel use stops growing.
China's steel and the commodity boom of 2003 to 2014: iron ore mined doubles within a decade.
About 10 Gt of ore a year, iron ore about a quarter of it by mass and copper ore much of the rest.

upsert.reason: From recalled metal output (pig iron and steel, copper, lead, zinc, gold, silver, bauxite) divided by typical ore grades for each period; before 1800 a reasoned guess with a band of three times either way. The ore counted is what is mined and processed, not the overburden moved to reach it.

points.note: Flint, chert and ochre: the first draw on the Earth's stores is stone for tools and colour, a few kilograms per person a year.
Mud brick and lime plaster for the first villages (Çatalhöyük, Jericho): earth for building becomes the largest draw on the stores and stays so.
Cities of mud brick and the first monuments of stone (the pyramids from about 2600 BCE).
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the Han's walls, roads and tombs.
Building in stone and brick collapses in the western Roman lands.
Europe's cathedrals and castles and Song China's cities build in stone and brick.

Nearly flat at about half a tonne a head for sixty years while fossil fuels and ores per person grow tenfold: the first industrial century digs fuel and ore; building in stone and brick grows with Europe's and America's cities, but not faster than the world's people.
War halts building: the dip in the whole falls on building materials, while coal and ores are held up by war production.
Cement and aggregate for reconstruction and growth: building minerals per person grow about 5% a year for twenty years.
Keeps rising after the oil shocks, while fuels and ores per person stall: Asia's and the Gulf's building.
China's building boom: its cement, and the sand and gravel poured with it, drive two thirds of the rise.
About 55 Gt a year, two thirds of all that is dug: sand, gravel and crushed stone for concrete and roads above all.

upsert.reason: The remainder of the whole once fossil fuels and metal ores are counted; all of it before smelting. After 1950 it rests on recalled cement output and the usual ratios of aggregate to cement; before, on reasoning about building.

points.note: Stone for tools and ochre for colour: a few kilograms per person a year.
Natufian and early Neolithic stone houses, mortars and querns.
Villages of mud brick and lime plaster, as at Çatalhöyük and Jericho; lime is burned from stone. Earth for building is the first large draw on the stores.
Cities of mud brick, copper and then bronze smelted from ores.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant.
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the mines of Spain: lead in Greenland's ice reaches a peak in the first century CE not matched again until the Middle Ages (as recalled from the ice-core studies).
Western Roman building and mining collapse; the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China burns coal for iron, and Europe builds in stone.
Potosí's silver and Britain's first coal boom, small against the stone and earth of building.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
Raised from 0.85 so that building minerals, opened as a part at r369, do not fall per person while railways, ports and cities grow.

Krausmann and colleagues: about 7 Gt of materials taken in 1900, about a quarter of it coal, ores and building minerals (about 1.75 Gt, or 1.06 tonnes a head); the rest is harvested biomass, not counted here. Raised from 1.0 to the figure this note gives, so the three parts opened at r369 sum to it.
Raised from 1.2 with 1900.
Mines and cities wrecked in Europe and Asia: extraction per person dips in the last year of the war.
Reconstruction and the long boom: steel, cement and oil per person grow about 4% a year from 1950.
The great acceleration: oil, cement and steel for reconstruction and for growth, faster than people.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries build less and use energy better.
China's building boom: it poured more cement in 2011 to 2013 than the United States in the whole twentieth century, and coal and iron ore follow.
The UNEP International Resource Panel counts about 100 Gt taken in 2020, three quarters of it non-metallic minerals, fossil fuels and metal ores.
