upsert.boundary: Cash crops, mines and migrant labour: the colonial economy, about 1900 to 1950
upsert.description: Railways from ports to mines and plantations; head and hut taxes payable in coin push men into wage work far from home; the Gold Coast becomes the world's largest cocoa grower by 1911, Nigeria and Senegal export groundnuts, the Copperbelt opens in the 1920s; forced labour persists in many colonies into the 1940s.
provenance: sources to check: Austin, African Economic History (1987, 2nd ed.); Frankema and van Waijenburg 2012, Journal of Economic History 72
upsert.region: Africa: Western, Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa

upsert.boundary: Diamonds at Kimberley and gold on the Witwatersrand, 1867 to 1899
upsert.description: Diamonds found in 1867 and the world's richest gold reef in 1886 turn southern Africa into a mining economy: Johannesburg grows from nothing to 100,000 people in a decade, migrant workers from across the region live in compounds under pass laws, and by the late 1890s the Rand produces about a quarter of the world's gold.
provenance: sources to check: Feinstein, An Economic History of South Africa (2005)

upsert.boundary: Egypt's Old Kingdom and the pyramids, about 2686 to 2181 BCE
upsert.description: Kings of a strong central state build the step pyramid of Djoser and the pyramids of Giza (about 2560 BCE), organizing tens of thousands of workers with rations, scribes and boats; Egypt has perhaps one to two million people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; regnal dates conventional
sources to check: Shaw (ed.), The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000)

upsert.boundary: Iron smelting begins in West and Central Africa, about 800 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: Furnaces at Taruga and Nok in Nigeria, in Cameroon, and at Urewe sites around Lake Victoria smelt iron, perhaps invented in Africa, perhaps learned from the north; iron hoes and axes later open the forests and savannas to farming.
provenance: exploring: whether African iron-working was invented independently is debated
sources to check: Alpern 2005, History in Africa 32; Holl 2009, Journal of World Prehistory 22
upsert.region: Africa: Western, Middle and Eastern Africa

upsert.boundary: Brazil's gold rush, 1695 to 1760
upsert.description: Gold and then diamonds in Minas Gerais draw hundreds of thousands of Portuguese and many more enslaved Africans inland; Rio de Janeiro becomes the colony's capital (1763), and Brazilian gold flows through Lisbon to Britain.
provenance: sources to check: Boxer, The Golden Age of Brazil (1962)

upsert.boundary: The California gold rush, 1848 to 1855
upsert.description: About 300,000 people pour into California from across the world; the Native Californian population, already halved under Spanish missions, falls from perhaps 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killing, disease and starvation.
provenance: sources to check: Madley, An American Genocide (2016)

upsert.boundary: The silver of Potosí, 1545 to 1650
upsert.description: A mountain of silver found in the Andes in 1545 makes Potosí one of the largest cities of the world by 1600; after 1573 the mita forces Andean villages to send men to its mines, where mercury refining kills many. Its silver pays Spain's wars and, through Manila, buys China's goods.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Lane, Potosí (2019)

upsert.boundary: Trade turns from Britain to Asia, from 1957
upsert.description: The Australia-Japan commerce agreement (1957) and Britain's entry into the European Community (1973), which ends New Zealand's assured market, turn both economies toward Asia; Japan, then China, become the chief buyers of Australian iron ore, coal and gas, and the China boom of 2003 to 2013 lifts Australia's terms of trade to their highest in over a century.
provenance: sources to check: Reserve Bank of Australia, terms of trade series

upsert.boundary: Floating currencies and open markets, 1983 to 1996
upsert.description: Australia floats its dollar (1983) and cuts tariffs; New Zealand's Labour government (1984) removes farm subsidies, sells state firms and makes its central bank the first with a formal inflation target (1989); both economies are remade, and Australia then goes 29 years without a recession (1991 to 2020).
provenance: sources to check: Kelly, The End of Certainty (1992); Easton, The Commercialisation of New Zealand (1997)

upsert.boundary: The Dunedin carries frozen meat to London, 1882
upsert.description: The first successful shipment of refrigerated mutton from New Zealand reaches London after 98 days at sea; frozen meat, then butter and cheese, make New Zealand Britain's farm across the world, the basis of its prosperity until Britain joins the European Community.
provenance: sources to check: Belich, Paradise Reforged (2001)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Oil in the Gulf, from 1938
upsert.description: After oil is found in Bahrain (1932), Saudi Arabia (1938) and Kuwait, the Gulf becomes the world's main source of oil; nationalizations and OPEC (1960) shift control to the producing states, and oil revenue turns small desert monarchies into some of the richest states per head on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Yergin, The Prize (1991)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the Gulf states, Iraq), Southern Asia (Iran)

upsert.boundary: Song China and its commercial revolution, 960 to 1279
upsert.description: The Song govern through officials chosen by examination, print books in great numbers, issue the first government paper money and grow early-ripening Champa rice; China's population passes 100 million, and Kaifeng and later Hangzhou hold a million people or more, the largest cities in the world. Iron and coal, the compass at sea and gunpowder weapons grow with them, and Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism becomes the orthodoxy of later dynasties. The north falls to the Jurchen in 1127 and the south to the Mongols in 1279.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; city populations are estimates
sources to check: Elvin, The Pattern of the Chinese Past (1973); Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule (2009)

upsert.boundary: Britain turns to coal, about 1560 to 1760.
upsert.description: As wood grows dear, London and the British towns heat, brew, bake and smelt with coal from seams near water: output rises from perhaps a quarter of a million to about five million tonnes a year, more than the rest of Europe together. Mines need pumping, which is where the steam engine is first used.

upsert.boundary: Cárdenas: land reform and the oil expropriation, 1934 to 1940
upsert.description: President Lázaro Cárdenas gives about 18 million hectares to peasant communities as ejidos, more than all his predecessors together, organizes workers and peasants within the ruling party, and nationalizes the foreign oil companies (March 1938) to found Pemex; the party of the Revolution becomes the corporate state that rules Mexico until 2000.
provenance: sources to check: Knight 1994, Journal of Latin American Studies 26; Meyer, Sherman and Deeds, The Course of Mexican History (11th ed. 2018)

upsert.boundary: The Tarascan state, about 1350 to 1530
upsert.description: From Tzintzuntzan by Lake Pátzcuaro, the Purépecha kings build a state in western Mexico that works copper and bronze and defeats an Aztec invasion (1478), the one neighbour the Triple Alliance never conquered; its last king submits to the Spanish in 1522 and is executed in 1530.
provenance: sources to check: Pollard, Taríacuri's Legacy (1993)

upsert.boundary: The silver frontier: Zacatecas and the Chichimeca war, 1546 to 1600
upsert.description: Silver strikes at Zacatecas (1546) and Guanajuato draw Spaniards, Indigenous workers and enslaved Africans north into the lands of the nomadic peoples the Spanish called Chichimecas, who fight a forty-year war of raids on the silver roads (1550 to 1590), ended by gifts of food and goods and by settling Tlaxcalan colonists among them. New Spain's silver soon rivals Potosí's.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico (1971); Powell, Soldiers, Indians and Silver (1952)

upsert.boundary: Burning fossil fuels, from about 1760 to now.
upsert.description: Coal, then oil and gas, from Britain's engines to about 37 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year in 2025; with cement, about 1,800 billion tonnes since 1750.
provenance: inferred: the Global Carbon Project's totals, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The industrial revolution in Britain, about 1760 to 1840.
upsert.description: Coal-fired steam, mechanized textiles and iron, then railways: the first economy to draw its energy from a stock rather than from land. Output per person begins to grow faster than population for generations.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; why it began in Britain is contested

upsert.boundary: The Panguna mine on Bougainville, 1972 to 1989
upsert.description: One of the world's largest open-pit copper and gold mines provides nearly half of Papua New Guinea's exports while its tailings poison the Jaba river; landowners' anger over the damage and the sharing of its wealth closes it in 1989.
provenance: sources to check: Regan, Light Intervention (2010)

upsert.boundary: Copper smelted, then bronze, about 5000 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Smelting copper from ore begins in the Balkans and Iran by about 5000 BCE; arsenical and then tin bronze follows in south-west Asia, giving harder tools and weapons and a trade in metal and tin across thousands of kilometres.
provenance: sources to check: Radivojević et al. 2010, Journal of Archaeological Science 37; Roberts, Thornton and Pigott 2009, Antiquity 83
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Eastern Europe: the Balkans); Asia (Western and Southern Asia)

upsert.boundary: Phosphate mining on Nauru and Banaba, 1900 to the 2000s
upsert.description: British, German and later British, Australian and New Zealand companies strip-mine phosphate for the farms of Australia and New Zealand; the Banabans are moved to Rabi in Fiji (1945); independent Nauru (1968) briefly has one of the world's highest incomes, but by the 2000s four-fifths of the island is mined out and its trust funds are lost.
provenance: sources to check: Williams and Macdonald, The Phosphateers (1985); McDaniel and Gowdy, Paradise for Sale (2000)

upsert.boundary: Old Copper: native copper worked around Lake Superior, about 4000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers of the upper Great Lakes dig pure native copper from veins and glacial drift and cold-hammer and anneal it into spear points, knives, awls and fishhooks, among the earliest metalworking anywhere; recent dates would push its start back to about 7500 BCE, which is disputed. They never smelt ore, and copper later becomes a material of ornament and exchange, reaching the Hopewell across half a continent.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dates are disputed
sources to check: Pompeani et al. 2021, Quaternary International; Martin, Wonderful Power (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the upper Great Lakes)

upsert.boundary: The United States becomes the largest industrial economy, 1870 to 1913
upsert.description: Steel from Carnegie's mills, oil from Rockefeller's refineries, electricity from Edison's and Westinghouse's systems, the corporation, the research laboratory and mass distribution make the United States the world's largest manufacturer by about 1890 and the maker of about a third of the world's manufactures by 1913, with the highest output per worker. A continental market, cheap land, abundant coal, iron and oil, immigrant labour and secure property all played a part; how much each mattered is argued.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weights of its causes are debated
sources to check: Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth (2016); Wright 1990, American Economic Review 80; Bairoch 1982, Journal of European Economic History 11
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The gold rushes of Australia and New Zealand, 1851 to 1900
upsert.description: Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria (1851), Otago (1861) and Western Australia (1890s) draws hundreds of thousands of migrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese; Victoria's population grows sevenfold in a decade and Melbourne becomes one of the richest cities in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Blainey, The Rush That Never Ended (5th ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: The oil shocks, 1973 to 1980
upsert.description: In the October 1973 war, Arab producers embargo the United States and the Netherlands and the price of oil quadruples; after Iran's revolution (1979) it more than doubles again. Inflation and recession follow in the rich countries, and oil wealth and debt pour into the producing and borrowing countries.
provenance: sources to check: Yergin, The Prize (1991)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: the Gulf); Americas (Northern America); Europe

upsert.boundary: The Bolivian revolution, 1952 to 1953
upsert.description: Miners and townspeople of the National Revolutionary Movement defeat the army in April 1952; the new government gives the vote to all adults, most of them Indigenous and unable to read, nationalizes the great tin mines and, as peasants seize the haciendas, decrees a land reform (1953).
provenance: sources to check: Klein, A Concise History of Bolivia (2nd ed. 2011)

upsert.boundary: Peru's guano age, 1840 to 1880
upsert.description: Bird droppings piled on the Chincha islands become the richest fertilizer of Europe and North America; Peru's state earns most of its revenue from them for forty years, dug by about 100,000 Chinese indentured labourers in brutal conditions, and borrows against them until the deposits run out and the state defaults (1876). The Atacama's nitrates follow, and with them war.
provenance: sources to check: Gootenberg, Between Silver and Guano (1989); Cushman, Guano and the Opening of the Pacific World (2013)

upsert.boundary: Andean metalworking begins, about 1500 BCE
upsert.description: Smiths of the southern Peruvian highlands hammer gold into thin foil (Waywaka, about 1500 BCE); later Andean smiths smelt copper, alloy it with arsenic and then tin into bronze, and gild and silver copper by chemical means. In the Andes metal serves rank and ritual far more than work.
provenance: sources to check: Aldenderfer et al. 2008, PNAS 105; Lechtman 1984, Technology and Culture 25

upsert.boundary: The War of the Pacific, 1879 to 1884
upsert.description: Chile, allied with British-owned nitrate companies, fights Bolivia and Peru over the nitrate deserts of the Atacama; it wins at sea, occupies Lima (1881) and takes Bolivia's coast and Peru's southern provinces, leaving Bolivia landlocked and Chile rich on nitrate exports for forty years, until synthetic nitrogen ends the boom.
provenance: sources to check: Sater, Andean Tragedy (2007)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Chile, Bolivia and Peru)

upsert.boundary: British Malaya: tin, rubber and migrant workers, 1874 to 1941
upsert.description: The Pangkor treaty (1874) puts British residents beside the Malay sultans; Chinese miners make Malaya the world's largest producer of tin, and from about 1900 Tamil workers from India tap rubber on estates that make it the largest producer of rubber too; by 1931 Malays are fewer than half of the peninsula's people, the plural society that independent Malaysia inherits.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Drabble, An Economic History of Malaysia (2000)

upsert.boundary: Bronze working spreads on the mainland, from about 1100 BCE
upsert.description: Copper is mined at Phu Lon and Khao Wong Prachan and cast with tin into axes, bangles and bells at Ban Chiang, Ban Non Wat and Non Nok Tha; richer burials show rank growing. Ban Chiang's bronze was once dated to 3600 BCE; the dates are now much later, and a gap remains between the shorter and longer chronologies.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the chronology is debated
sources to check: Higham et al. 2015, Journal of World Prehistory 28; White and Hamilton 2014, in Roberts and Thornton (eds.), Archaeometallurgy in Global Perspective

upsert.boundary: The steam engine, from Newcomen's (1712) to Watt's rotary engine (1784).
upsert.description: Newcomen's atmospheric engine pumps coal mines; Watt's separate condenser cuts its coal use by three quarters, and the rotary engine drives mills. Energy from a stock of fossil carbon can now do work anywhere.

Widen and observe: 32 Events now name the part of the Earth's stores they change (opened at r369) and, where they plainly move them, three processes no Event named before. Metal ores: the first smelting (ev.metallurgy), Old Copper, Andean metalworking, mainland bronze, West African iron, the Tarascans, Song China's iron, Potosí, Zacatecas, Minas Gerais, the California and Australasian gold rushes, the Rand, British Malaya's tin, the United States' steel and Panguna. Building and industrial minerals: the pyramids of the Old Kingdom, the Rand's diamonds, Peru's guano, the nitrates of the War of the Pacific and Nauru's phosphate. Fossil fuels: Song China's coal, Britain's turn to coal, the steam engine, the industrial revolution, the burning of fossil fuels since 1760, Gulf oil and the oil shocks. Output made in Oceania (h.means.oceania): the gold rushes, refrigerated shipping (1882), phosphate, Panguna, the turn of trade to Asia and the market reforms of 1983 to 1996. What the state owns or seizes (h.revenue.property): Peru's state guano, the Mexican oil expropriation (Pemex), Bolivia's nationalized tin mines, Gulf oil and the oil shocks' OPEC revenues. Work for an employer under contract (h.toil.contract): the industrial revolution's factories, the Rand's wage miners and the colonial economy's migrant labour. Bolivia's revolution also names the vote it gave all adults and the land it redistributed. Every Event is restated whole from the current model, with only process_ids extended.

Values at the Events the r371 links hold these processes to, where the coverage report found them passing over: trade and its three parts at 1840 (Peru's guano age), moving goods at 1882 and 1886, and world output with its five areas at 1882 and 1886 (refrigerated shipping, the end of slavery in Cuba and Brazil), each on a constant growth rate between its neighbours so the parts still sum to their wholes.

points.note: Foragers carry their goods when they move camp and carry home what they kill and gather: a few tonne-km a person a year. Obsidian and shells travel hundreds of kilometres by exchange, but in tiny amounts.
Farmers carry harvests, stores and building stuff, but rarely far.
Donkeys are domesticated in north-east Africa and carry loads.
The wheel and the sail: carts on land, sailing boats on the Nile and the Gulf.
Rome's grain fleet carries some hundreds of thousands of tonnes from Egypt and Africa each year; the empire's sea trade lifts its average to several times the world's.
Falls: Mediterranean shipping shrinks with the Western empire, as shipwreck counts show.
Song China's Grand Canal and coastal junks move rice, salt and iron in bulk.
Dutch and English merchant fleets, and coal shipped from Newcastle to London.
Turns up steeply: railways and steamships cut the cost of moving bulk goods by most of its cost on roads.
Railways spread across North America, Mexico (the Porfiriato), Argentina and India and steamships take over bulk freight once the Suez Canal opens (1869): freight per person grows at about 9% a year.
Refrigerated ships (the Dunedin, 1882) begin carrying meat and butter halfway round the world, beside grain, coal and cotton.
On the eve of the First World War world trade and shipping stand at their prewar peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from submarine sinkings and blockade.
Submarine warfare sinks a fifth of the world's merchant tonnage.
Supertankers and bulk carriers: oil and ore cross oceans in unprecedented tonnages; the container ship spreads from 1956.
Dips: the oil shocks cut long-haul tanker trade in the early 1980s.
China's trade boom carries ore and coal in and containers out.
COVID-19's first year: world trade volume falls about a twentieth in 2020 and recovers in 2021.
About 130 trillion tonne-km a year, three quarters of it by sea (UNCTAD and the International Transport Forum, as recalled).

upsert.reason: Before 1850 sketched from loads and distances (a forager's camp moves, a farmer's surplus carried to market, Roman, Song and Dutch shipping); 1850 to 1950 from railway and shipping statistics as recalled; after 1970 from UNCTAD's seaborne tonne-miles and the International Transport Forum's land freight, as recalled.

The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.

All of humanity's output is made in Africa until Homo sapiens settles western Asia in the Last Interglacial; output per person is the forager level (h.provisioning).

Egypt unified (ev.af.egypt-unification): the Nile valley's output per person near the world's, the rest of Africa below it.
Africa's output stalls between 1800 and 1820 while its people's share falls: the Atlantic slave trade's last peak and the wars of the Sokoto jihad and the Mfecane.
Conquest and colonial rule: Africa's share of world output falls toward its low of under 4%, though mines and cash crops raise its output in absolute terms.
Africa's lost decades begin: debt, falling commodity prices and wars hold its output per person flat or falling from about 1980 to 1995 while its people grow fastest.

No people live in the Americas until about 16,000 years ago (the White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, put a few earlier).
People are south of the ice (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago): the Americas' first output, a few tens of thousands of foragers.
The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya kingdoms, Moche and Tiwanaku raise the Americas' output per person a little toward the world's.

On the eve of contact the Americas make about a twelfth of world output, the Aztec and Inca states and their tributaries most of it; the size depends on the contact population, which is debated (see h.region-americas).
The Aztec and Inca states fall; smallpox has already run through Mexico and the Andes. Output shrinks with the people, at the rate between 1520 and 1550.
Potosí is found (1545) and the cocoliztli strikes New Spain (1545 to 1548): silver rises as people die.

The Columbian collapse (ev.columbian-exchange, VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd): the Americas' output falls by two fifths from 1520 to 1550 and by two thirds to 1600 with its people, though the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas becomes the most valuable thing the Americas send out.
The nadir: the Americas make under 2% of world output.
The United States' output per person is already more than twice the world's; with Latin America's near the world's, the Americas' output per person is about 1.4 times it.
Spanish America's wars of independence end with its economies smaller than in 1810, while the United States grows; on the path from 1820 to 1850.
Latin America stagnates under the caudillos while the United States grows by canals and cotton; the Americas' output doubles from 1820 to 1850, almost all of the gain in the north.
The Americas pass a tenth of world output, the United States most of it.

Japan's war in China from 1937: Asia's output falls from 1936 to 1940.

Neanderthals hold Europe and are not counted; Homo sapiens arrives about 45,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum drives Europe's foragers into southern refuges; its output falls with its people.

points.note: Zero: no states.
Tolls on goods moving through the first states: a twentieth of their revenue.
Han China's salt and iron monopolies, from 117 BCE, and Rome's harbour and frontier duties.
After the An Lushan rebellion the Tang raise about half their cash revenue from the salt monopoly.
Song China's commercial taxes and monopolies of salt, tea and wine pass its land tax: the first state to live mostly on goods.
Below the Song's height after the Mongol conquest of China.

England's excise state after 1688: by 1750 customs and excise are about three quarters of British revenue (Brewer's fiscal-military state). War between the European powers rewarded the states that could raise more (Warsift#b01b).
Customs and excise carry the nineteenth-century states (the United States lived on its tariff until 1913); the Qing add the lijin transit tax from 1853.
The Soviet turnover tax, levied on goods, pays most of a state that takes about a third of its economy's output.
Value-added tax spreads across Europe after 1967 from France's of 1954, and later to most of the world.
About three tenths of revenue, more in poorer countries, which lean on VAT and customs.
Zero until Britain's income tax of 1799: earlier levies on movables and tithes on produce are counted with land and goods.
Pitt's income tax, 1799, to pay for the war with revolutionary France.
Britain repeals its income tax in 1816: back to about zero.
Peel brings Britain's income tax back in 1842.
The Union's income tax of 1862, for the Civil War.
The American wartime income tax lapses (1872).

Before wartime taxation and borrowing.
Wartime taxation and borrowing.
Revenue rises as a share of output while output falls in the Depression, and the New Deal, Japan's war spending and Germany's rearmament start to raise taxes.
Wartime taxation at its height in the belligerents.

Foragers' material wealth (tools, ornaments) and relational wealth (ties to others) are shared fairly evenly: wealth Ginis about 0.25 to 0.35 in Borgerhoff Mulder and others' comparison, a top-tenth share of about a quarter.
Rich burials such as Sungir's (about 32,000 years ago) show that some foragers could concentrate prestige goods, rarely and briefly.
Rises with farming: stored grain, fields and herds can be held and handed down, and house sizes begin to diverge.
Draft animals, the plough and states: Kohler and others find Old World house-size Ginis near 0.6 by the Bronze Age, above the New World's, where there were no large draft animals.
The Roman senatorial and Han landlord elites: Scheidel's agrarian empires, where the richest tenth hold most land and slaves.
Falls: the collapse of Roman rule in the West destroys the great senatorial fortunes (Scheidel's leveller of state failure).
Falls: the Black Death kills a third or more in Europe and the Near East, land becomes cheap and labour dear, and wealth inequality falls for a century (Alfani's and Scheidel's plague leveller).
Plantations, colonial fortunes and the first industrial capital; from here the gap between countries adds to the gap within them.
The peak: on the eve of 1914 the richest tenth hold about nine tenths of wealth in Britain and France (Piketty's series), while most of the world's people own almost nothing.
On the eve of the war wealth concentration is at its peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from destroyed capital, taxes and inflation.
Falls: the war destroys capital and raises taxes and inflation.
The crash wipes out paper fortunes in the United States, where the top tenth's share falls after 1929, and Mexico's land reform resumes; at world scale the share barely moves.
The great levelling of the world wars: destruction, inflation, high taxes and expropriation in Japan, Europe and Eastern Europe.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) and the Soviet bloc's expropriations take the wealth of the landlords and owners.
Bolivia's revolution (1952 to 1953) takes the great tin mines and the haciendas, as China's land reform has done on a far larger scale.
Turns up: privatisation, financial deregulation and rising asset prices.
The privatisation of Soviet-bloc property after 1991 creates new fortunes.
The World Inequality Report 2022 puts the richest tenth's share of world wealth at about 76%, as recalled.

upsert.reason: Sketched before 1995 from the comparative wealth Ginis of foragers and farmers, Kohler and others' house-size Ginis, the agrarian estimates in Scheidel's Great Leveler and Piketty's series for Europe and the United States, all as recalled; from 1995 near the World Inequality Database's world top-tenth share.

points.note: No state, so no national elections: bands decide by consensus, which the parent's measure does not count.
The first states have assemblies of elders and citizens (Mesopotamian city assemblies, as Jacobsen argued), but no elections of rulers by a franchise that can be counted.
Citizens of Athens after 508 BCE and of other Greek democracies and the Roman Republic: a few hundred thousand men in a world of some sixty million adults.
Rome extends citizenship to Italy after the Social War (89 BCE): about a million adult men may vote, if they come to Rome.
Falls: under Augustus the Roman assemblies lose their elections to the Senate and the emperor (by 14 CE).
Iceland's Althing and Venice's popular assembly.
The Italian communes' councils, the Swiss cantons and the county electors of England's Commons.
England's forty-shilling freeholders (1430).
The nobles of Poland-Lithuania, perhaps a tenth of its people, vote in their dietines and elect the king.
Rises: some five to six million Frenchmen vote for the Estates-General, and the new American states widen their franchises.
Napoleon's plebiscites are open to all Frenchmen: votes without a choice of rulers, counted here because the measure is the formal right.
Under Napoleon's empire the plebiscite franchise holds until the Restoration of 1814 cuts the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers; the fall to 1820 comes then.
Falls: the restored French monarchy limits the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers.
Rises again: the American states drop property qualifications for white men in the 1820s, and Britain's Reform Act (1832) adds about 300,000 voters.
Jumps: the Second Republic gives every French man the vote (March 1848), about nine million voters, one in seventy of the world's adults.
France adopts manhood suffrage in 1848; most white American men vote.
Britain's Second Reform Act (1867) and the German Reich's manhood suffrage (1871).
New Zealand (1893) and South Australia (1894) give women the vote.
Before the war about a tenth of adults may vote; the great widening comes from 1917 to 1920, in Soviet Russia, Britain, Germany and the United States.
Rises most: women vote in Britain (1918), Germany (1919), the United States (1920) and Soviet Russia, where the franchise excludes only the 'former people'.
The Soviet constitution of 1936 grants universal suffrage in single-candidate elections.
Women vote in France (1944), Italy and Japan (1946).
India's constitution of 1950 gives all adults the vote.
Bolivia's revolution gives the vote to all adults (1952), most of them Indigenous and unable to read; China's elections of 1953 and 1954 are still to come.

China's first elections under its 1953 electoral law, held through 1953 and 1954 with universal suffrage for the lowest people's congresses, add about a quarter of the world's adults to the formal franchise: most of the rise to 1955.
China's first national elections under the constitution of 1954, with universal suffrage for the lowest people's congresses; formal right, not a choice of rulers.
Switzerland gives women the federal vote in 1971, nearly the last democracy to do so.
Myanmar's coup and the Taliban's return end national elections for some ninety million people.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the dates of franchise laws and the adult populations they covered (as recalled from the suffrage histories and V-Dem's suffrage indicator), divided by the world's adults.

The last three stretches the coverage report found passing over the new links: trade and its parts at 1957.5, world output and its five areas at 1973, and state revenue's four bases at 1933, where the whole already held a value its parts lacked. Constant growth between neighbours, so every whole is still the sum of its parts.

points.note: Shell beads and finished tools passed between bands.
Textiles and metalwork from the first cities' workshops.
Chinese silk, Roman glass and fine pottery, Indian cloth.
Song porcelain and silk carried by sea to South-east Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Indian cotton cloth floods European and West African markets (the calico craze).
British machine-made cotton goods replace Indian cloth in world markets.
Lend-lease arms and machines are much of wartime trade.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now, as Europe's and Japan's industries trade with one another.
East Asia's export manufacturing and the trade in parts between factories.
Global value chains: a phone's parts cross many borders before it is sold.
Goods hold up in the pandemic (medical supplies, electronics for home working) while travel stops.
The goods boom of the pandemic's second year.
On the path between the pandemic's goods boom and 2025.
Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
Peru's guano (from 1840) joins cotton, grain and timber as the industrial cities draw on the world's farms, forests and mines; on the path between 1820 and 1850.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Grain, beef, coffee and sugar from the Americas and wool from Australia flow to Europe as freight rates fall; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Refrigerated meat and butter join grain, wool, coffee and sugar; on the path between 1880 and 1890.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Japan's purchases of Australian wool, coal and iron ore under the commerce agreement of 1957 begin to turn Oceania's primary exports toward Asia; on the path between 1954 and 1960.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Commodity prices recover from the pandemic's low.
Oil, gas, grain and fertilizer prices jump in 2022 with the war in Ukraine; primary goods' share of trade's value rises with them.
Zero: nothing is sold between bands apart from goods.
Shipping and caravan services begin to be paid apart from the goods they carry: a sliver.
Italian merchant banks and the carrying trade of Venice and Genoa sell finance and freight.
Dutch shipping carries much of Europe's trade: the Republic sells freight and insurance.
Steamship freight, marine insurance and London's finance: about a twelfth of trade.
Travel, shipping and finance resume after the war: about an eighth of trade.
Travel stops in the pandemic: services fall about a fifth while goods hold.
Travel still mostly closed; digital and business services grow.
Travel recovers from the pandemic; digital services keep growing.
About a quarter of trade: travel recovered, business and digital services growing fastest.
Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The ASEAN free trade area (1992) and NAFTA (1994) begin and the former Soviet bloc opens to trade; the sum of its three parts on their paths.
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).
Goods trade rebounds from the pandemic while travel is still closed; the sum of its three parts.
Trade recovers from the pandemic and its value peaks as energy and food prices jump after Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the sum of its three parts.
All of humanity's output is made in Africa until Homo sapiens settles western Asia in the Last Interglacial; output per person is the forager level (h.provisioning).
Asia's first farmers now make more than Africa's foragers and herders: Africa's output passes below Asia's between 9500 and 7900 BCE.
Egypt unified (ev.af.egypt-unification): the Nile valley's output per person near the world's, the rest of Africa below it.
Africa's output stalls between 1800 and 1820 while its people's share falls: the Atlantic slave trade's last peak and the wars of the Sokoto jihad and the Mfecane.
Conquest and colonial rule: Africa's share of world output falls toward its low of under 4%, though mines and cash crops raise its output in absolute terms.
Africa's lost decades begin: debt, falling commodity prices and wars hold its output per person flat or falling from about 1980 to 1995 while its people grow fastest.
Africa's output has grown faster than the world's since 2000, but at about 5% of world output it is a quarter of its share of people.
No people live in the Americas until about 16,000 years ago (the White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, put a few earlier).
People are south of the ice (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago): the Americas' first output, a few tens of thousands of foragers.
The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya kingdoms, Moche and Tiwanaku raise the Americas' output per person a little toward the world's.

On the eve of contact the Americas make about a twelfth of world output, the Aztec and Inca states and their tributaries most of it; the size depends on the contact population, which is debated (see h.region-americas).
The Aztec and Inca states fall; smallpox has already run through Mexico and the Andes. Output shrinks with the people, at the rate between 1520 and 1550.
Potosí is found (1545) and the cocoliztli strikes New Spain (1545 to 1548): silver rises as people die.

The Columbian collapse (ev.columbian-exchange, VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd): the Americas' output falls by two fifths from 1520 to 1550 and by two thirds to 1600 with its people, though the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas becomes the most valuable thing the Americas send out.
The nadir: the Americas make under 2% of world output.
The United States' output per person is already more than twice the world's; with Latin America's near the world's, the Americas' output per person is about 1.4 times it.
Spanish America's wars of independence end with its economies smaller than in 1810, while the United States grows; on the path from 1820 to 1850.
Latin America stagnates under the caudillos while the United States grows by canals and cotton; the Americas' output doubles from 1820 to 1850, almost all of the gain in the north.
The Americas pass a tenth of world output, the United States most of it.

Between 1870 and 1890 on a constant growth rate: the United States grows fast after the Civil War despite the depression of 1873, Argentina's export boom begins, and the slave economies of Cuba and Brazil end in the 1880s. About 13.6% of world output, up from 11.3% in 1870.
The First World War: the Americas' output rises while Europe's falls.
The bank panics of 1930 and 1931 and the collapse of commodity prices take the Americas' output down a tenth from 1929; Latin America's export economies turn to making their own goods.
The Depression's trough: the Americas' output falls about a fifth from 1929 (ev.nam.depression), more than any other area's.
The war economy: the Americas' output passes Europe's for the first time, the United States making about two fifths of the world's manufactures.
Demobilization: American output falls about a tenth from its wartime peak.
Latin America's lost decade (ev.am.debt-crisis): its output per person falls while Northern America's grows, so the Americas' output grows slower than the world's.
No Homo sapiens lives in Asia before the Last Interglacial; the Denisovans and other archaic humans are not counted.
The dispersal out of Africa (ev.era.dispersal): Asia's output grows with its people, at the forager level per person.
Farming in the Fertile Crescent and then China: Asia's output passes Africa's and keeps about three fifths of the world's or more for the next nine thousand years.
Han China and the Indian kingdoms: Asia makes about seven tenths of world output, close to its share of people (Maddison about 74% as recalled).
Song China's commercial economy at its height: Asia's output per person a little above the world's.
The Mongol wars, the Yuan collapse and the Black Death in western Asia: Asia's output falls from 1300 to 1400 with its people.
Ming China and the Indian kingdoms: Asia makes about 62% of world output, near Maddison's figure as recalled.
The seventeenth-century crisis: the Ming–Qing wars and famines hold Asia's output near flat from 1600 to 1650.
Asia makes about 57% of world output with 65% of its people: the Great Divergence has begun but is still small (MalthusianTrap#0f6b binds Asia as it bound everyone).
Europe's output has passed Asia's for the first time since antiquity, between 1870 and 1890: Asia grows slowly while the El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 cut India's and north China's people.
Japan's war in China from 1937: Asia's output falls from 1936 to 1940.
China's famine of the Great Leap Forward: Asia makes under a quarter of world output, near its lowest share.
China's reform (from 1978), Japan's boom and the Asian tigers: Asia's output about equals Europe's and the Americas'.
Asia's output has passed Europe's and the Americas' in the 1990s, for the first time since about 1880.
Asia makes about half of world output, near its share before 1820, though its output per person is still under the world's.
Neanderthals hold Europe and are not counted; Homo sapiens arrives about 45,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum drives Europe's foragers into southern refuges; its output falls with its people.
The Roman peace: the Mediterranean's output per person about a sixth above the world's, Europe's north below it.

Rome's fall in the west (ev.eu.rome-fall): cities shrink, trade and coin fail and people fall, so Europe's output falls by about two fifths from 200 to 610 and its output per person drops below the world's.
The high-medieval peak: Europe's output more than doubles from 1000 with its people and its towns.
After the Black Death: Europe's output about an eighth below 1300's though output per person is higher, fewer people working the same land (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
Atlantic trade and the Dutch and English economies: Europe's output per person is about two fifths above the world's.
Coal and steam (Sunbound#c94c): Europe's output per person reaches about 1.75 times the world's.
Europe's output passes Asia's for the first time since antiquity, between 1870 and 1890.
Europe's output falls about a tenth from 1913 with the war.
The war's last year: occupied, bombed and fought-over Europe makes about a seventh less than in 1940; Germany's output collapses in 1945.
The postwar boom: Western Europe's recovery and the Soviet Union's growth carry Europe's output back above the Americas'.
The Soviet bloc's collapse: Eastern Europe's output falls about two fifths between 1989 and 1998, so Europe's output grows slowly through the 1990s (ev.eu.soviet-collapse).
No people in Sahul until about 50,000 years ago on the later dates (65,000 on Madjedebe's, debated).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) and wool: Oceania's output more than doubles in a decade.
Australia's settlers are among the richest people on Earth; Oceania's output per person about twice the world's, though its first peoples are falling (ev.oc.depopulation).
Frozen meat and butter (the Dunedin, 1882) join wool and gold as Oceania's exports; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Wool and wheat prices collapse in the Depression: Australia's and New Zealand's output falls about a sixth.
The Australia-Japan commerce agreement (1957) begins the turn of Oceania's trade from Britain to Asia; on the path between 1954 and 1960.
Britain joins the European Community (1973), ending New Zealand's assured market, while Panguna's copper (from 1972) lifts Papua New Guinea's exports; on the path between 1970 and 1975.
