State railways (Prussia) and colonial monopolies (the Dutch Indies' cultivation system) count here.
Rising toward the Soviet budget's enterprise profits and Mexico's oil expropriation (1938): the state's own enterprises pay a growing share of revenue.
Soviet state enterprises' profits paid to the budget.
Bolivia nationalizes the great tin mines (1952) and Iran's oil is nationalized (1951 to 1953) until the coup restores the consortium; on the path between 1950 and 1954.
Oil revenues of the OPEC states after the price rise of 1973.
The second oil shock: resource revenues at their height.
Oil prices fall, and collapse in 1986.
The commodity boom raises oil and mineral revenues.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Before wartime taxation and borrowing.
Wartime taxation and borrowing.
Revenue rises as a share of output while output falls in the Depression, and the New Deal, Japan's war spending and Germany's rearmament start to raise taxes.
Wartime taxation at its height in the belligerents.
Demobilization: revenue falls from its wartime height but stays far above the 1930s (ev.postwar-order).

changes.value: Correction from the seam the carve of the Earth's stores names: fossil tonnage (h.earth.resources.fossil) and the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores) count the same fuels, so their ratio must stay near the fuels' energy per tonne (about 26 to 28 GJ in the coal age, 31 to 34 once oil and gas join, nuclear heat aside). It holds within about a tenth at every date but three: at 1918 fossil tonnage rose while energy dipped, and at 1945 and 1965 the energy needs more tonnage than was given. The three fossil values are corrected and building minerals take the difference, so the parts still sum to the whole.

points.note: Bitumen from seeps in Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea, for mortar, caulking and inlay: fossil carbon taken in tiny amounts.
Song China begins to burn coal: Kaifeng heats with it and the north's iron furnaces run on it as the forests near the cities give out.
Falls back after the Jurchen and Mongol conquests of north China.
England's coal grows several times over in half a century as wood grows dear around London.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
Drake's well (1859) begins oil's century; coal is already over 100 Mt a year.
About 760 Mt of coal and 20 Mt of oil: fuel is nearly half of all that is dug.

Dips in the war's last year with the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores): the mines of northern France and Belgium occupied, Russia's output collapsed. Corrected at r376 from 0.74, which the seam with that energy showed too high (17.4 GJ a head at about 26 GJ a tonne is about 0.67 t).

Mines wrecked and flooded in Europe and Asia in the last year of the war. Corrected at r376 from 0.72: the energy drawn from stores (about 22 GJ a head) at about 28.5 GJ a tonne, with oil's share rising, needs about 0.77 t.
Oil and gas join coal: fossil fuels per person grow by about 70% to 1973.
Corrected at r376 from 1.30: the energy drawn from stores (about 44 GJ a head) at about 32 GJ a tonne needs about 1.38 t; coal about 2.7 Gt, oil 1.55 Gt, gas 0.5 Gt.
After the oil shocks fossil fuels per person fall back and stay flat for twenty years.
China's coal grows about two and a half times between 2000 and 2013.
The pandemic year's dip, below the 2014 level per person.
About 9 Gt of coal, 4.4 Gt of oil and 3 Gt of gas: some 16 Gt a year.

upsert.reason: From recalled world output of coal and lignite, crude oil and natural gas (gas at about 0.72 tonnes per thousand cubic metres) divided by the world's people; before 1800 from the scale of English and Chinese coal mining. It must turn with the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores), which counts the same fuels in GJ.

points.note: Flint, chert and ochre: the first draw on the Earth's stores is stone for tools and colour, a few kilograms per person a year.
Mud brick and lime plaster for the first villages (Çatalhöyük, Jericho): earth for building becomes the largest draw on the stores and stays so.
Cities of mud brick and the first monuments of stone (the pyramids from about 2600 BCE).
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the Han's walls, roads and tombs.
Building in stone and brick collapses in the western Roman lands.
Europe's cathedrals and castles and Song China's cities build in stone and brick.

Nearly flat at about half a tonne a head for sixty years while fossil fuels and ores per person grow tenfold: the first industrial century digs fuel and ore; building in stone and brick grows with Europe's and America's cities, but not faster than the world's people.
War halts building: the dip in the whole falls mostly on building materials. Was 0.285 before the fossil correction of r376.
Cement and aggregate for reconstruction and growth: building minerals per person grow about 5% a year for twenty years.
Keeps rising after the oil shocks, while fuels and ores per person stall: Asia's and the Gulf's building.
China's building boom: its cement, and the sand and gravel poured with it, drive two thirds of the rise.
About 55 Gt a year, two thirds of all that is dug: sand, gravel and crushed stone for concrete and roads above all.

upsert.reason: The remainder of the whole once fossil fuels and metal ores are counted; all of it before smelting. After 1950 it rests on recalled cement output and the usual ratios of aggregate to cement; before, on reasoning about building.

upsert.boundary: The kingdom of Aksum, about 100 to 940
upsert.description: From the highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea, Aksum trades ivory and gold through the Red Sea with Rome, Arabia and India, mints its own coins from about 270 and raises great stelae; under Ezana, about 350, it turns to Christianity and campaigns on the Nile near Meroë, which was already declining; whether Aksum ended the kingdom of Meroë is debated. A Persian writer of the third century counts it among the four great kingdoms of the world.
provenance: sources to check: Phillipson, Foundations of an African Civilisation (2012)

exploring: corrected 2026-10-13 after a blind reading of the events pass: the end of Meroë: Ezana's inscription records a campaign on the Nile about 350; whether Aksum brought Meroë down or found it already broken is debated

upsert.boundary: Carthage, from its founding about 814 BCE to its destruction in 146 BCE
upsert.description: A Phoenician colony becomes the naval and trading power of the western Mediterranean, ruling Sicily, Sardinia and southern Spain; in three wars with Rome (264 to 146 BCE), Hannibal's among them, it loses everything, and Rome razes the city.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the founding date is traditional
sources to check: Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Tunisia); Southern Europe (Sicily, Sardinia, Spain)

upsert.boundary: Dahomey takes the slave ports of Allada and Ouidah, 1724 to 1727
upsert.description: King Agaja conquers the coast so that Dahomey, not its neighbours, sells captives to European ships; the kingdom, with its army of women soldiers, remains a major supplier until the trade's end and falls to France in 1894.

upsert.boundary: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca, 1324 to 1325
upsert.description: Mali's king crosses the Sahara with thousands of followers and so much gold that its value falls in Cairo for years; Mali appears on European maps, the Catalan Atlas (1375) showing him holding a gold nugget, and scholars and architects return with him.
provenance: inferred: as recalled from al-Umari's account
sources to check: Levtzion and Hopkins (eds.), Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
upsert.region: Africa: Western Africa (Mali), Northern Africa (Egypt); Western Asia (Mecca)

upsert.boundary: Ostrich-eggshell beads exchanged across eastern and southern Africa, about 50,000 to 33,000 years ago
upsert.description: Bead styles shared over about 3,000 kilometres show that groups in eastern and southern Africa were linked by exchange, as San hxaro gift-giving later linked camps; the link breaks after about 33,000 years ago as climate shifts the rains.
provenance: sources to check: Miller and Wang 2022, Nature 601

upsert.boundary: The Swahili coast's towns, about 800 to 1500
upsert.description: Bantu-speaking traders build towns of coral stone along the coast from Mogadishu to Sofala, Kilwa, Mombasa, Lamu and Zanzibar among them; Muslim since the 9th to 12th centuries, they trade the interior's gold, ivory and captives across the Indian Ocean for Indian cloth and Chinese porcelain, and speak Kiswahili.
provenance: sources to check: Horton and Middleton, The Swahili (2000); Brielle et al. 2023, Nature 615 (Swahili genomes)
upsert.region: Africa: Eastern Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique, Somalia)

upsert.boundary: The Union of South Africa and the Natives Land Act, 1910 to 1913
upsert.description: The four colonies unite as a self-governing dominion ruled by white men; the Land Act of 1913 confines African ownership to reserves of about 7% of the land.
provenance: sources to check: Ross, A Concise History of South Africa (2nd ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Adena and Hopewell, about 500 BCE to 500 CE
upsert.description: Peoples of the Ohio valley build burial mounds and great geometric earthworks and trade obsidian from the Rockies, copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf across half a continent.
provenance: sources to check: Milner, The Moundbuilders (2004)

upsert.boundary: Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears, 1830 to 1850
upsert.description: Under the Indian Removal Act, the United States forces about 60,000 Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people west of the Mississippi; thousands die on the way.
provenance: sources to check: Saunt, Unworthy Republic (2020)

upsert.boundary: Continental exchange routes, about 2000 BCE to the 1850s
upsert.description: Goods pass hand to hand along routes linked to the songlines: pearl and baler shell from the Kimberley and Cape York to the south coast, greenstone axes from the Mount William quarry, red ochre from Wilgie Mia and Pukardu, and pituri, a stimulant, from the Mulligan River; most routes are known from the last few thousand years, and some quarries are far older.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the routes' ages are mostly unknown
sources to check: McBryde 1984, World Archaeology 16; Mulvaney 1976, 'The chain of connection'

upsert.boundary: The Native Land Court turns Maori land into saleable titles, 1865 to 1900
upsert.description: Created to convert customary title into individual titles that can be sold, the court, with the confiscations after the wars, leaves Maori by the 1890s with perhaps a sixth of New Zealand's land, while Maori numbers fall to about 42,000 by 1896.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the land share is approximate
sources to check: Ward, An Unsettled History (1999); Belich (1996)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: The Portuguese in Asian waters, 1498 to 1641
upsert.description: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut in May 1498 by sailing around Africa; the Portuguese then take Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515), reach Japan (1543) and settle at Macau (1557), using armed ships to tax the Indian Ocean trade through passes rather than conquering inland; the Dutch take Malacca from them in 1641.
provenance: sources to check: Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia 1500–1700 (2nd ed. 2012)
upsert.region: Asia (Southern, South-eastern, Eastern and Western Asia); Europe (Southern Europe: Portugal)

upsert.boundary: Srivijaya, about 671 to 1377
upsert.description: From Palembang in Sumatra, a Malay maritime power controls the Straits of Malacca and Sunda and the trade between China and India; Chinese pilgrims stop there to learn Sanskrit and Buddhist texts. In Java, the Sailendra kings build Borobudur (about 800).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its power had faded long before 1377
sources to check: Wolters, Early Indonesian Commerce (1967); Miksic, Singapore and the Silk Road of the Sea (2013)

upsert.boundary: United Fruit and the banana republics, 1899 to 1954
upsert.description: The United Fruit Company (1899) and its rivals take vast concessions of land, railways and ports in Guatemala, Honduras, Costa Rica and elsewhere, grow bananas for the American market and work closely with governments and dictators such as Ubico; US Marines occupy Nicaragua (1912 to 1933) and fight Sandino. When Guatemala's elected government expropriates the company's unused land, a CIA-backed coup overthrows it (1954).
provenance: sources to check: Bucheli, Bananas and Business (2005); Gleijeses, Shattered Hope (1991)

upsert.boundary: Haiti's independence debt, 1825 to 1947
upsert.description: With warships off Port-au-Prince, France demands 150 million francs, later cut to 90 million, as compensation for former slaveholders and the price of recognizing Haiti; Haiti borrows from French banks to pay, and services the debt and its refinancing for over a century, the last payments made in 1947. How much it held back Haiti's development is argued; one estimate puts the growth lost at 21 to 115 billion dollars today.
provenance: inferred: the debt as recalled; the estimate of its cost is exploring
sources to check: Gaffield (ed.), The Haitian Declaration of Independence (2016); The New York Times, 'The Ransom' (May 2022)

upsert.boundary: Havana and the treasure fleets, 1561 to 1640
upsert.description: From 1561 Spain's silver ships sail in convoys that gather at Havana each year before crossing to Seville; the harbour is ringed with forts and the city grows on provisioning, shipbuilding and repairs. French, English and Dutch privateers raid the coasts, Drake sacks Santo Domingo (1586), and Piet Heyn captures a whole silver fleet off Cuba (1628).
provenance: sources to check: de la Fuente, Havana and the Atlantic in the Sixteenth Century (2008)

upsert.boundary: The hiri voyages of the Papuan coast, about 1500 to the 1960s
upsert.description: Each year Motu potters near today's Port Moresby sail great multi-hulled lakatoi west to the Gulf of Papua with thousands of clay pots, returning with tons of sago; the voyages, perhaps five centuries old, end in the mid-twentieth century and are now remembered in a festival.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its start is uncertain
sources to check: Dutton (ed.), The Hiri in History (1982)

upsert.boundary: The kula ring of the Massim, from about 1000
upsert.description: Across the islands off New Guinea's eastern tip, partners carry shell necklaces clockwise and armshells anticlockwise around a ring of islands, a ceremonial exchange that builds renown and alliances alongside ordinary trade; Malinowski's account (1922) made it a founding case for the study of gift and exchange. Archaeology suggests the ring took its classic form within the last thousand years or so; when exactly is uncertain.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its age is uncertain
sources to check: Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922); Irwin, in Leach and Leach (eds.), The Kula (1983)
upsert.region: Oceania: Melanesia (the Massim, Papua New Guinea)

upsert.boundary: Obsidian and animals carried across the Bismarck Sea, from about 20,000 years ago
upsert.description: Obsidian from Talasea on New Britain is carried to New Ireland, and people release cuscus, and later bandicoots and wallabies, on islands that had none, stocking them with game: among the oldest known long-distance transfers of stone and the earliest deliberate introductions of animals.
provenance: sources to check: Summerhayes and Allen 1993; White 2004, in Smith and Hesse (eds.)

upsert.boundary: Yap's stone money and island empire, from about 1400
upsert.description: Yapese voyagers quarry great limestone discs, rai, on Palau, 400 kilometres away, and ship them home, where ownership passes by agreement without the stones moving, a case economists cite for money as a shared ledger of credit; Yap's chiefs also receive tribute from the outer Caroline atolls in the sawei exchange. Most large stones were quarried in the 1800s with an Irish-American trader's ships; when quarrying began is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its beginning is debated
sources to check: Furness, The Island of Stone Money (1910); Friedman 1991, Hoover Institution Working Paper; Fitzpatrick 2003
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (Yap, Palau and the Carolines)

upsert.boundary: The Beaver Wars and the Great Peace of Montreal, 1640 to 1701
upsert.description: Armed with Dutch guns and seeking beaver pelts and captives to replace their epidemic dead, the Haudenosaunee destroy or scatter the Wendat (1649), the Neutral, the Erie and others and fight New France for half a century, until the Great Peace of Montreal (1701) binds them, the French and some forty nations to peace.
provenance: sources to check: Richter, The Ordeal of the Longhouse (1992)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Lakes and the St Lawrence)

upsert.boundary: Poverty Point, about 1700 to 1100 BCE
upsert.description: On a bluff in north-eastern Louisiana, people who fish, hunt and gather raise six concentric earthen ridges over a kilometre across and mounds up to 22 metres high, one of them heaped up in a few months, and bring copper, galena, soapstone and flint from as far as 1,500 kilometres away: monumental building and long-distance exchange without farming or, as far as is known, a state.
provenance: sources to check: Ortmann and Kidder 2013, Geoarchaeology 28; Gibson, The Ancient Mounds of Poverty Point (2001)

upsert.boundary: Macassan trepangers in northern Australia, about 1720 to 1906
upsert.description: Fleets of praus from Makassar in Sulawesi sail each monsoon to Arnhem Land and the Kimberley to gather and cure sea cucumbers for the Chinese market, trading cloth, metal and tobacco with Yolngu and other peoples, until Australia bans them in 1906.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the start may be earlier
sources to check: Macknight, The Voyage to Marege' (1976)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: northern Australia); Asia (South-eastern Asia: Sulawesi)

upsert.boundary: The Great Mahele, 1848 to 1850
upsert.description: Hawai'i's King Kamehameha III divides the kingdom's land among the crown, the government and the chiefs; the Kuleana Act lets commoners claim the plots they farm, which come to under 1% of the land, and foreigners may buy land (1850); American planters buy large estates for sugar.
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: Chávez's Bolivarian revolution, 1999 to 2013
upsert.description: Hugo Chávez, a former officer who had led a failed coup (1992), wins the presidency (1998), rewrites the constitution, survives a coup (2002) and an oil strike, and spends the oil boom on social programmes, price controls and expropriations while concentrating power; poverty falls while oil prices are high, and the state oil company's output declines.
provenance: sources to check: Corrales and Penfold, Dragon in the Tropics (2nd ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: Dutch Brazil, 1630 to 1654
upsert.description: The Dutch West India Company takes Recife and Pernambuco, the world's richest sugar coast, and seizes Portuguese slaving posts in Angola to supply it; under Johan Maurits it brings painters and naturalists. Luso-Brazilian planters drive the Dutch out by 1654, and Dutch and Sephardic Jewish planters and merchants carry the sugar mill, its credit and its slaving methods to Barbados and the Caribbean.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how much the Dutch carried sugar to the Caribbean is debated
sources to check: Boxer, The Dutch in Brazil (1957); Schwartz (1985)

upsert.boundary: The Amazon rubber boom, 1879 to 1912
upsert.description: Demand for tyres and insulation makes wild Amazonian rubber one of the world's most valuable commodities; Manaus builds an opera house, Brazil takes Acre from Bolivia, and tappers, many of them indebted migrants from the drought-stricken north-east, spread up every river. In the Putumayo the Peruvian Amazon Company's agents enslave and kill tens of thousands of Indigenous people. Plantations in Malaya and Ceylon, grown from seeds taken from Brazil in 1876, undercut it after 1910.
provenance: sources to check: Weinstein, The Amazon Rubber Boom (1983); Goodman, The Devil and Mr Casement (2009)

upsert.boundary: Funan, the port kingdom of the Mekong delta, about 100 to 550
upsert.description: Known from Chinese envoys of the 200s and from the excavated port of Oc Eo, where Roman coins, Indian seals and Chinese mirrors lie together, Funan's kings dig canals across the delta, trade between India and China, and take Indian titles; its trade fades as ships begin to sail straight through the Strait of Malacca.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how far Funan was one state is debated
sources to check: Manguin 2009, in Hauser-Schäublin and Ingvar (eds.); Stark 2006; Vickery 2003, Bulletin de l'EFEO 90

upsert.boundary: Port towns of the Thai-Malay isthmus trade with India and China, about 400 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: At Khao Sam Kaeo and Ban Don Ta Phet, Indian craftsmen make glass and stone beads, carnelian lions travel with Buddhist symbols, and Han bronze mirrors arrive from the north: the first ports of the trade between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.
provenance: sources to check: Bérardé et al. 2017, in Bellina (ed.), Khao Sam Kaeo; Glover 1989

upsert.boundary: Makassar's open port and its fall, about 1600 to 1669
upsert.description: Gowa and Tallo, Muslim from 1605, keep an open port for Portuguese, English, Danish and Malay merchants against the Dutch company's monopoly; the company, allied with Arung Palakka of Bone, conquers it (Treaty of Bongaya, 1667; fall of Somba Opu, 1669), and Bugis and Makassarese sailors and soldiers scatter across the archipelago.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya, The Heritage of Arung Palakka (1981); Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce vol. 2 (1993)

upsert.boundary: The Malacca sultanate, about 1400 to 1511
upsert.description: Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, founds Malacca where the monsoons of the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea meet, wins Ming protection during Zheng He's visits and turns Muslim; its harbour masters serve merchants from Gujarat, Tamil country, Java, China and the Ryukyus, Malay becomes the language of trade across the islands, and Tomé Pires writes that whoever is lord of Malacca has his hand on the throat of Venice.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Cortesão (ed.), The Suma Oriental of Tomé Pires (1944)

upsert.boundary: Britain takes Penang and founds Singapore, 1786 to 1819
upsert.description: The East India Company takes Penang from the sultan of Kedah (1786) and Raffles founds Singapore as a free port (1819); the Anglo-Dutch treaty of 1824 divides the Malay world along the Strait of Malacca, the north to Britain and the south to the Netherlands, a line that still divides Malaysia from Indonesia.
provenance: sources to check: Turnbull, A History of Modern Singapore (3rd ed. 2009)

upsert.boundary: Sa Huynh jar burials and the jade trade of the South China Sea, about 500 BCE to 100 CE
upsert.description: On the central Vietnamese coast, people bury their dead in great jars with ear ornaments of a style found around the South China Sea; the nephrite of many comes from Taiwan, worked in the Philippines and Vietnam and traded as far as Thailand and Borneo, one of the oldest maritime trades of jade.
provenance: sources to check: Hung et al. 2007, PNAS 104
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam, the Philippines, Borneo, Thailand)

upsert.boundary: Singapore's rise, 1965 to 2025
upsert.description: Expelled from Malaysia with no hinterland, water or army, Lee Kuan Yew's People's Action Party government courts foreign manufacturers, builds public flats that house over 80% of the people by the 1980s, a compulsory savings fund and English-medium schools, and governs as a dominant-party state with tight limits on dissent. By the 2010s Singapore's income per head is among the highest in the world, its port among the busiest, and it is the region's financial centre.
provenance: sources to check: Huff, The Economic Growth of Singapore (1994); Lee Kuan Yew, From Third World to First (2000), as a participant's account

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's wealth and exchange groups. Wealth: the land transfers of the Great Mahele, the Native Land Court, Indian Removal and South Africa's Natives Land Act name the concentration of wealth (h.standing.wealth), whose rise from 1820 to 1910 they are part of; United Fruit's concessions, Haiti's indemnity, Chávez's oil spending and Singapore's rise name the output, trade, state revenue and poverty they move. Exchange: the port powers and trading states (Carthage, Aksum, Funan, the isthmus ports, Sa Huynh's jade, Srivijaya, the Swahili coast, Malacca, Zheng He is in the next batch, the Portuguese in Asia, Havana's fleets, Makassar, Penang and Singapore) name trade between peoples (h.exchange) and, where they took territory, colonial rule; the Beaver Wars name war between polities, Dahomey and Dutch Brazil the slave trade, the Macassan trepangers primary goods, the rubber boom primary goods, compulsion and the Putumayo killings. The forager and early networks (ostrich-eggshell beads, Bismarck obsidian, Australia's routes, Poverty Point, Hopewell, the kula ring, the hiri voyages, Yap's stone money) and Mansa Musa's pilgrimage observe trade (observation_process_ids): they show it, they do not move the world share. Every Event is restated whole from the current model, with only process_ids or observation_process_ids extended.

upsert.boundary: A San-like toolkit at Border Cave, about 44,000 years ago
upsert.description: Digging-stick weights, a poison applicator, beeswax hafting, bone arrowheads and ostrich-eggshell beads like those San foragers used in the twentieth century: a way of life that lasted more than forty thousand years.
provenance: sources to check: d'Errico et al. 2012, PNAS 109

upsert.boundary: Camels make the Sahara crossable, about 100 BCE to 300 CE
upsert.description: Dromedaries, spreading west from Egypt and the Horn, let traders cross the desert in caravans, which later carry the gold trade.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the timing is uncertain
sources to check: Bulliet, The Camel and the Wheel (1975)

upsert.boundary: Fishers and hunters of the green Sahara, about 9000 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: Communities along the Sahara's lakes and rivers fish with bone harpoons, make wavy-line pottery and bury their dead in cemeteries such as Gobero in Niger and early Khartoum: a settled foraging life that the drying later ends.
provenance: sources to check: Sereno et al. 2008, PLoS ONE 3 (Gobero)

upsert.boundary: Shellfish and ochre at Pinnacle Point, about 164,000 years ago
upsert.description: In a cave on South Africa's south coast, people living through the cold of the penultimate glacial collect shellfish and use ground ochre: the oldest known systematic use of the sea's foods, on a coast that may have been a refuge for a shrunken population.
provenance: sources to check: Marean et al. 2007, Nature 449

upsert.boundary: The Norse in Greenland and Vinland, about 985 to 1450
upsert.description: Norse farmers settle south-west Greenland (about 985) and reach Newfoundland, where L'Anse aux Meadows is occupied in 1021; the Greenland colonies die out by about 1450 as the climate cools and trade with Norway fails.
provenance: sources to check: Kuitems et al. 2022, Nature 601 (L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021); Arneborg, in The Viking World (2008)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Greenland, Canada); Europe (Northern Europe)

upsert.boundary: Gunditjmara eel aquaculture at Budj Bim, from about 6,600 years ago
upsert.description: In the young lava fields of south-western Victoria, the Gunditjmara cut channels and weirs to trap and hold short-finned eels and build stone houses beside them, a system some 6,600 years old in its earliest parts and still worked when settlers came; it has been a World Heritage site since 2019. Whether such practices amount to agriculture, as some recent books argue, or to skilled management of wild resources, as their critics answer, is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the age of the oldest channels and the 'agriculture' debate are open
sources to check: McNiven et al. 2012, Journal of Archaeological Science 39; Pascoe, Dark Emu (2014); Sutton and Walshe, Farmers or Hunter-Gatherers? (2021)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (south-western Victoria)

upsert.boundary: New tools, new places and more people, about 4000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Across mainland Australia small backed blades and points spread, seed-grinding grows, sites multiply and people settle harsher country, as rainfall becomes less reliable with the strengthening of El Nino. Whether this was an 'intensification' driven by society and population growth or a response to a more variable climate is a long debate.
provenance: sources to check: Lourandos, Continent of Hunter-Gatherers (1997); Hiscock (2008); Williams et al. 2015, Quaternary Science Reviews 123
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (mainland Australia)

upsert.boundary: Zheng He's voyages, 1405 to 1433
upsert.description: The Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He leads seven fleets of up to 250 ships and some 27,000 men for the Yongle emperor to South-east Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, collecting tribute and giraffes; after 1433 the court ends the voyages and later restricts private overseas trade.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; fleet sizes come from Ming sources and may be inflated
sources to check: Dreyer, Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty (2007)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern, South-eastern, Southern and Western Asia); Africa (Eastern Africa)

upsert.boundary: El Fin del Mundo: Clovis hunters in Sonora, about 13,400 years ago
upsert.description: At a spring in the Sonoran desert, hunters with Clovis points kill and butcher gomphotheres, elephant relatives that lived on in Mexico after they had vanished farther north. Among the oldest securely dated Clovis sites, it puts Clovis people in Mexico as early as anywhere in the north.
provenance: sources to check: Sanchez et al. 2014, PNAS 111

upsert.boundary: Cuba's Special Period, 1991 to 2000
upsert.description: When Soviet aid and trade end, Cuba's economy shrinks by about a third between 1990 and 1993; food and fuel run short, Cubans lose weight, and an epidemic of optic neuropathy follows malnutrition. The government legalizes the dollar and opens to tourism and foreign investment; tens of thousands flee by raft in 1994.
provenance: sources to check: Pérez (2015); Franco et al. 2013, BMJ 346

upsert.boundary: First contact in the New Guinea highlands, 1930 to 1939
upsert.description: Gold prospectors, among them Michael and Dan Leahy with the patrol officer Jim Taylor (1933), walk into the Wahgi and other highland valleys and find about a million people, gardeners in dense populations whom no outsider had known of; the Leahys' film records the meeting, and government patrols, missions and coffee follow.
provenance: sources to check: Connolly and Anderson, First Contact (1987)

upsert.boundary: Folsom bison hunters, about 12,800 to 11,900 years ago
upsert.description: On the Great Plains and in the Rockies, hunters with finely fluted Folsom points kill herds of an extinct, larger bison; at the Folsom site in New Mexico in 1927 a point found between bison ribs proved that people had lived in the Americas in the Ice Age. As mammoths disappear, bison become the plains hunters' staple, as they remain until the 1880s.
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Plains)

upsert.boundary: Hohokam canals in the Salt and Gila valleys, about 450 to 1450
upsert.description: In the Sonoran Desert around modern Phoenix, the Hohokam dig hundreds of kilometres of canals, the largest irrigation system in pre-Columbian North America, grow maize, beans, squash and cotton, build ball courts like Mesoamerica's and trade shell from the Gulf of California; their towns are largely abandoned by about 1450, after floods and droughts.
provenance: sources to check: Fish and Fish (eds.), The Hohokam Millennium (2007)

upsert.boundary: Horses reach the Plains peoples, about 1680 to 1750
upsert.description: Horses taken in the Pueblo Revolt and traded and raided north from New Mexico reach the northern plains by about 1730. Comanche, Lakota, Cheyenne, Crow, Blackfoot and others become mounted bison hunters and warriors: farmers and foragers move onto the grasslands, wealth in horses divides rich from poor, and new powers rise. Guns arrive from the east at the same time, and epidemics follow both.
provenance: sources to check: Hämäläinen 2003, Journal of American History 90; Ewers, The Horse in Blackfoot Indian Culture (1955)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Great Plains)

upsert.boundary: Ranked fishing societies of the north-west coast, about 1800 BCE to 1774
upsert.description: From the Columbia River to south-east Alaska, peoples who live on salmon, shellfish, sea mammals and cedar settle in plank-house villages and come to rank people as nobles, commoners and slaves, raise carved poles and give away wealth at potlatch feasts: unequal, complex societies of foragers, which accounts tying rank to farming did not expect. Spanish and British ships arrive in 1774 and 1778, and smallpox in the 1770s.
provenance: sources to check: Ames and Maschner, Peoples of the Northwest Coast (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Pacific north-west)

upsert.boundary: Cook's Pacific voyages, 1768 to 1779
upsert.description: James Cook observes the transit of Venus from Tahiti, charts New Zealand and the east coast of Australia (1770), crosses the Antarctic Circle and is killed in Hawaii (1779); his maps and reports open the Pacific to British settlement, trade and missions.
provenance: sources to check: Beaglehole, The Life of Captain James Cook (1974); Salmond, The Trial of the Cannibal Dog (2003)
upsert.region: Oceania (Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: Europeans enter the Pacific, 1521 to 1768
upsert.description: Magellan crosses the Pacific (1521); the Manila galleons cross it yearly from 1565; Spain conquers Guam and the Marianas in wars and epidemics that cut the Chamorro by nine-tenths; Tasman (1642) and Dutch captains chart Tasmania, New Zealand and the west of Australia.
provenance: sources to check: Spate, The Spanish Lake (1979)
upsert.region: Oceania (Micronesia: Guam; Australia and New Zealand); Europe

upsert.boundary: Hoabinhian foragers of the mainland, about 22,000 to 4,000 years ago
upsert.description: Foragers who flake river pebbles on one side live in the rock shelters and hills of Vietnam, Laos, Thailand and Malaysia; ancient genomes show they are related to today's Semang of the Malay peninsula and to the Onge of the Andamans, and that their descendants mixed with the farmers who came from the north.
provenance: sources to check: McColl et al. 2018, Science 361; Higham, Early Mainland Southeast Asia (2014)

upsert.boundary: Deep-sea fishing at Jerimalai in Timor, about 42,000 years ago
upsert.description: Bones of tuna and other open-sea fish from 42,000 years ago, and a shell fish-hook from about 23,000 to 16,000 years ago, show island foragers fishing the deep sea, the oldest evidence of open-ocean fishing.
provenance: sources to check: O'Connor, Ono and Clarkson 2011, Science 334

changes.value: Widen, the breadth check's provisioning and connection groups. Provisioning: the horse on the Plains makes farmers and foragers into mounted, mobile bison hunters (mobile foragers, foraging); the north-west coast's ranked foragers name hereditary rank, bondage and settling; the green Sahara's fishers and Budj Bim's stone houses name settling down (mobile foragers); Australia's mid-Holocene growth names its people and the reach of Oceania's land; the Hohokam canals name cropland; Cuba's Special Period the Americas' output; Folsom and El Fin del Mundo the end of the Ice Age's great game (the wild animals). Jerimalai and Pinnacle Point observe animal foods, Border Cave and the Hoabinhians observe foraging (and Border Cave's beads lasting ornament): they show those states, they do not move them. Connection: camels make the Sahara a freight route and its herders camel nomads; the Norse add and then lose range in Greenland; Zheng He's voyages and their end move trade; the New Guinea highland patrols bring about a million people under a state and absorb their polities; Cook's arrival in Hawai'i begins its people's collapse; Spain's conquest of the Marianas cuts the Chamorro by nine tenths and puts them under colonial rule. Every Event is restated whole from the current model, with only process_ids or observation_process_ids extended.

Fill the gaps the coverage report names after the breadth links of r377 and r378: trade and its three parts in the first two centuries CE, colonial rule and its five areas in the 1780s, and the concentration of wealth from 1820 to 1850. Wholes and parts are given values at the same dates so the declared sums hold.

points.note: Zero before 1415, as the parent is by definition.
Portugal's forts on Africa's Atlantic coast, Elmina among them (1482).
Doubles with France's conquest of Algeria (from 1830).
Jumps: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882).
The Scramble's conquests: most of West, East and southern Africa comes under European rule.
Britain's sack of Benin (1897) ends one of the last independent kingdoms of the forest coast, after Dahomey (1894), Asante and Madagascar (1896).
Almost all of Africa but Ethiopia and Liberia is partitioned: Africa now holds about a fifth of the colonized.
Egypt's nominal independence (1922) takes it out of the count.
Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1935 to 1936).
Africa becomes most of colonial rule as South Asia leaves it (1947 to 1948).
Falls by two thirds: the year of Africa (1960) and the independences of 1961.
Falls by two thirds: Portugal's African colonies become independent (1974 to 1975).
Zimbabwe (1980) is independent; Namibia is what remains.
Namibia's independence (1990) leaves only small islands.
Zero before Castile rules Hispaniola (1493 to 1496).
Castile begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over their numbers.
Hispaniola's Taínos have mostly died; Cuba, Puerto Rico and Darién add few.
Central Mexico under Spanish rule after Tenochtitlan falls: almost all of colonial rule is now in the Americas.
The Andes join after Pizarro takes the Inca empire.
Halves without a colony lost: epidemics, war and forced labour kill the colonized (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
Spanish America near its demographic low.
Recovery: Spanish America's people grow again, and the sugar islands, Brazil and the English mainland colonies fill with settlers and enslaved Africans.
The Americas are now the smaller part: Bengal makes Asia the larger.
The thirteen colonies leave the count when they rebel (1776), about 2.8 million people.
Haiti's independence (1804) takes Saint-Domingue out.
Argentina, Chile and Gran Colombia's core are independent; Mexico, Peru, Central America, Brazil and the Caribbean remain.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822): the part falls by almost two thirds.
Peru and Upper Peru leave (1824 to 1825); Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Caribbean colonies, the Guianas and British North America remain.
British North America leaves the count as responsible government comes (1848 to 1855).
Spain takes back the Dominican Republic (1861 to 1865). Maximilian's Mexico (1864 to 1867) is a client empire on the spot, not counted.
Cuba and Puerto Rico pass from Spain to the United States (1898); Hawaii is annexed. Cuba under American occupation until 1902 is still counted.
Cuba's independence (1902) takes it out.
Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana become French départements with deputies in Paris (1946) and leave the count.
Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago leave (August 1962).
Guyana (May 1966) leaves; Barbados follows at the month's end.
Suriname (1975) leaves; the Bahamas and Grenada already have (1973, 1974).
Belize, Antigua and St Kitts leave (1981 to 1983): Puerto Rico is most of what remains.

With Hong Kong and Macau returned, the Americas are almost all of colonial rule: Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands and the British and Dutch Caribbean. The lower band carries the UN's list, which has left Puerto Rico out since 1953.
About 3.7 million people, 3.2 million of them in Puerto Rico.
Zero before the Portuguese in India (1498 to 1510).
Cabral's first factory at Cochin; no territory yet.
Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515) under Portugal.
Spain's Philippines (from 1565) bring the part to about a seventh of colonial rule.
The Dutch company's Batavia (1619), Amboina and Formosa's coast (1624).
The Dutch company rules Java's north coast and the Priangan; Madras, Bombay, Calcutta and Pondicherry are company towns.
Bengal, Bihar and Orissa under the East India Company after Plassey: Asia becomes most of colonial rule, as it stays until 1948.
Penang ceded by the Sultan of Kedah to Francis Light for the Company (1786), a few thousand people; Bengal's growth is the larger change.
Mysore falls (1799) and Britain takes the Dutch Ceylon coast (1796). The parent's remainder here implies some 70 million people, above a count of about 55 million: the parent may be high at 1800.
Doubles after the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818): the Company is paramount over most of India, its princely states counted with it.
India, the Dutch Indies, Indochina, the Philippines (American from 1898), Ceylon, Malaya and Taiwan: about 365 million people.
Korea, a Japanese protectorate from 1905, is already counted before its annexation (1910).
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces.
Manchukuo (1932), a puppet state whose counting is debated, adds about 1.4 points.
South-east Asia passes from European and American to Japanese rule without changing the count.
Japan's empire ends: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave, and Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence.
The Philippines become independent (July 1946).
India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon leave (1947 to 1948): the part falls by six sevenths in two years, and Africa becomes the larger part.
Indonesia's independence (December 1949).

After Geneva (1954) Indochina is out. This is the parent's remainder; a count of what is left (Malaya, Singapore, Hong Kong, Aden, Cyprus, the Borneo territories, Goa, Macau, Timor and the Gulf protectorates) gives about 0.6%, so either the parent or Africa's part is about half a point high here; the band reaches down to the count.
Malaya (1957) and Cyprus (1960) are out.
Singapore and the Borneo states join Malaysia (1963) and West New Guinea passes to Indonesia (1963).
Aden leaves (November 1967).
Hong Kong and Macau are almost all that remains, growing faster than the world.
Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China: no colonial rule from overseas is left in Asia.
Zero before Portugal takes Ceuta (1415).
All of colonial rule in 1450: Ceuta, Madeira, the Azores and the first Canaries, which belong to Europe by today's borders.
Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496).
Britain takes Malta (1800).
The Ionian Islands become a British protectorate (1815).
The Atlantic islands send deputies to the Cortes of Madrid and Lisbon (1820 to 1822) and leave the count; Malta and the Ionian Islands remain.
Britain cedes the Ionian Islands to Greece (1864).
Italy takes the Dodecanese (1912).
Italy's Albania (1939 to 1943) is military occupation and not counted.
The Dodecanese pass to Greece (1947).
Malta's independence (September 1964) leaves Gibraltar.
Gibraltar's 34,000 people.
Zero before Spain rules the Marianas (1668).
Spain's mission to Guam (1668) brings the Chamorros of the Marianas under its rule.
The Spanish–Chamorro wars and epidemics cut the Chamorros from tens of thousands to a few thousand by about 1710.
Before the First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove (January 1788) the only colonial rule in Oceania is Spain's in the Marianas.
New South Wales (1788) adds about a thousand convicts and soldiers.
The Australian colonies' settlers grow, and Britain claims New Zealand (1840).

The peak before self-government: the Victorian gold rush has not yet begun, but the Australian colonies hold about 400,000 settlers and convicts, and New Zealand about 25,000 settlers beside the Māori counted under the Crown's rule; all still governed from London.

Responsible government in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia (1855 to 1857) and New Zealand (1856) takes them out by the parent's definition; Aboriginal Australians and most Māori, with no vote, are a debated exception the band does not carry. Western Australia, the Marianas and Tahiti remain.
Fiji is ceded to Britain (1874).
Britain and Germany divide eastern New Guinea (1884) and Germany takes the Marshall Islands (1885); their rule reaches the coasts.
Samoa divided (1899), the Carolines and Marianas sold to Germany (1899), Guam to the United States (1898), the Solomons and the Gilberts British (1892 to 1893).
Patrols reach New Guinea's highlands (from 1933), about a million people never contacted before; how fast they count as ruled is a matter of judgment.

New Guinea's highland valleys, reached by patrols from 1933, are counted as administered by about 1940, which with Fiji, the Solomons, New Caledonia and Japan's mandated islands brings the part to about two million people. How much of the highlands counted as ruled by 1940 is a judgment; the band carries it.
Western Samoa becomes independent (1962).
Fiji and Tonga's protectorate end (1970).
Papua New Guinea becomes independent (September 1975): the part falls by three quarters.
The Solomons, Tuvalu (1978) and Kiribati (1979) are independent; Vanuatu follows in 1980.

New Caledonia and French Polynesia, Guam, the Northern Marianas, American Samoa, Wallis and Futuna and Tokelau. The French territories elect deputies to Paris but are on the UN's list of territories to decolonize (New Caledonia from 1986, French Polynesia from 2013); the lower band leaves them out.

Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.
Penang (1786) and New South Wales (1788) add a few thousand people each; the share keeps rising on the growth of the Company's India, not on these new footholds.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882), about eight million people; the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) follows.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
Between Madagascar and Asante (1896) and Benin (1897), the conquest of Africa's coasts and their hinterlands is nearly complete; on the line between 1895 and 1900.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan (January 1956), Morocco and Tunisia (March 1956) become independent, about 23 million people; Ghana and Malaya follow in 1957.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.
Portugal's African empire, Rhodesia and small territories, with Hong Kong; their numbers grow while their count of territories does not, until the independences of 1974 and 1975.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
Shell beads and finished tools passed between bands.
Textiles and metalwork from the first cities' workshops.
Chinese silk, Roman glass and fine pottery, Indian cloth.
Silk, Indian cotton cloth and Roman glass and metalware at the trade's height.
Song porcelain and silk carried by sea to South-east Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Indian cotton cloth floods European and West African markets (the calico craze).
British machine-made cotton goods replace Indian cloth in world markets.
Lend-lease arms and machines are much of wartime trade.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now, as Europe's and Japan's industries trade with one another.
East Asia's export manufacturing and the trade in parts between factories.
Global value chains: a phone's parts cross many borders before it is sold.
Goods hold up in the pandemic (medical supplies, electronics for home working) while travel stops.
The goods boom of the pandemic's second year.
On the path between the pandemic's goods boom and 2025.
Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
Pepper, spices, incense and the grain fleets of Egypt.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
Peru's guano (from 1840) joins cotton, grain and timber as the industrial cities draw on the world's farms, forests and mines; on the path between 1820 and 1850.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Grain, beef, coffee and sugar from the Americas and wool from Australia flow to Europe as freight rates fall; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Refrigerated meat and butter join grain, wool, coffee and sugar; on the path between 1880 and 1890.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Japan's purchases of Australian wool, coal and iron ore under the commerce agreement of 1957 begin to turn Oceania's primary exports toward Asia; on the path between 1954 and 1960.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Commodity prices recover from the pandemic's low.
Oil, gas, grain and fertilizer prices jump in 2022 with the war in Ukraine; primary goods' share of trade's value rises with them.
Zero: nothing is sold between bands apart from goods.
Shipping and caravan services begin to be paid apart from the goods they carry: a sliver.
Italian merchant banks and the carrying trade of Venice and Genoa sell finance and freight.
Dutch shipping carries much of Europe's trade: the Republic sells freight and insurance.
Steamship freight, marine insurance and London's finance: about a twelfth of trade.
Travel, shipping and finance resume after the war: about an eighth of trade.
Travel stops in the pandemic: services fall about a fifth while goods hold.
Travel still mostly closed; digital and business services grow.
Travel recovers from the pandemic; digital services keep growing.
About a quarter of trade: travel recovered, business and digital services growing fastest.
Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.

The Roman trade with India at its height: by Strabo about 120 ships a year sail from Myos Hormos, the Muziris papyrus prices one cargo at about 7 million sesterces, and Han silk reaches Rome through Parthia and the Kushans. A small rise over the value at 1, within the band.
The Antonine plague (from 165) kills perhaps a tenth of the Roman Empire's people and the trade begins to ebb; whether it was the turn in the Indian Ocean trade or only a pause is debated.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The ASEAN free trade area (1992) and NAFTA (1994) begin and the former Soviet bloc opens to trade; the sum of its three parts on their paths.
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).
Goods trade rebounds from the pandemic while travel is still closed; the sum of its three parts.
Trade recovers from the pandemic and its value peaks as energy and food prices jump after Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the sum of its three parts.

Foragers' material wealth (tools, ornaments) and relational wealth (ties to others) are shared fairly evenly: wealth Ginis about 0.25 to 0.35 in Borgerhoff Mulder and others' comparison, a top-tenth share of about a quarter.
Rich burials such as Sungir's (about 32,000 years ago) show that some foragers could concentrate prestige goods, rarely and briefly.
Rises with farming: stored grain, fields and herds can be held and handed down, and house sizes begin to diverge.
Draft animals, the plough and states: Kohler and others find Old World house-size Ginis near 0.6 by the Bronze Age, above the New World's, where there were no large draft animals.
The Roman senatorial and Han landlord elites: Scheidel's agrarian empires, where the richest tenth hold most land and slaves.
Falls: the collapse of Roman rule in the West destroys the great senatorial fortunes (Scheidel's leveller of state failure).
Falls: the Black Death kills a third or more in Europe and the Near East, land becomes cheap and labour dear, and wealth inequality falls for a century (Alfani's and Scheidel's plague leveller).
Plantations, colonial fortunes and the first industrial capital; from here the gap between countries adds to the gap within them.

Britain abolishes slavery (1833 to 1838) and pays the slave-owners 20 million pounds, about two fifths of a year's government spending: their wealth in people becomes wealth in government bonds rather than vanishing, and the freed get nothing. The richest tenth's share is not cut by it.

Indian Removal (1830 to 1850) turns some 25 million acres of Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole land into land sold to settlers and planters: the expansion of cotton slavery that follows concentrates wealth in the American South.

The Great Mahele (1848) divides Hawaiian land among the crown, the government and the chiefs and, after 1850, lets foreigners buy it; within two generations most of it is held by a few planters. On the world's scale this is small; the rise goes on with industrial and colonial capital.
The peak: on the eve of 1914 the richest tenth hold about nine tenths of wealth in Britain and France (Piketty's series), while most of the world's people own almost nothing.
On the eve of the war wealth concentration is at its peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from destroyed capital, taxes and inflation.
Falls: the war destroys capital and raises taxes and inflation.
The crash wipes out paper fortunes in the United States, where the top tenth's share falls after 1929, and Mexico's land reform resumes; at world scale the share barely moves.
The great levelling of the world wars: destruction, inflation, high taxes and expropriation in Japan, Europe and Eastern Europe.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) and the Soviet bloc's expropriations take the wealth of the landlords and owners.
Bolivia's revolution (1952 to 1953) takes the great tin mines and the haciendas, as China's land reform has done on a far larger scale.
Turns up: privatisation, financial deregulation and rising asset prices.
The privatisation of Soviet-bloc property after 1991 creates new fortunes.
The World Inequality Report 2022 puts the richest tenth's share of world wealth at about 76%, as recalled.

upsert.reason: Sketched before 1995 from the comparative wealth Ginis of foragers and farmers, Kohler and others' house-size Ginis, the agrarian estimates in Scheidel's Great Leveler and Piketty's series for Europe and the United States, all as recalled; from 1995 near the World Inequality Database's world top-tenth share.
