Fill the remaining stretches the coverage report names after the breadth links: wholes and parts at the same dates where sums are declared (colonial rule, settling down, range, output by area, trade). Also correct the bands of the share living under a state at 1930, 1940, 1950, 1960 and 1970, which an earlier pass set as plus or minus a tenth and so ran above 100%, a bound the measure cannot pass.

points.note: Zero before 1415, as the parent is by definition.
Portugal's forts on Africa's Atlantic coast, Elmina among them (1482).
Freetown is founded for freed Black Britons (1787), a few hundred people.
Doubles with France's conquest of Algeria (from 1830).
Jumps: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882).
The Scramble's conquests: most of West, East and southern Africa comes under European rule.
Britain's sack of Benin (1897) ends one of the last independent kingdoms of the forest coast, after Dahomey (1894), Asante and Madagascar (1896).
Almost all of Africa but Ethiopia and Liberia is partitioned: Africa now holds about a fifth of the colonized.
Egypt's nominal independence (1922) takes it out of the count.
Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1935 to 1936).
Africa becomes most of colonial rule as South Asia leaves it (1947 to 1948).
Falls by two thirds: the year of Africa (1960) and the independences of 1961.
Falls by two thirds: Portugal's African colonies become independent (1974 to 1975).
Zimbabwe (1980) is independent; Namibia is what remains.
Namibia's independence (1990) leaves only small islands.
Zero before Castile rules Hispaniola (1493 to 1496).
Castile begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over their numbers.
Hispaniola's Taínos have mostly died; Cuba, Puerto Rico and Darién add few.
Central Mexico under Spanish rule after Tenochtitlan falls: almost all of colonial rule is now in the Americas.
The Andes join after Pizarro takes the Inca empire.
Halves without a colony lost: epidemics, war and forced labour kill the colonized (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
Spanish America near its demographic low.
Recovery: Spanish America's people grow again, and the sugar islands, Brazil and the English mainland colonies fill with settlers and enslaved Africans.
The Americas are now the smaller part: Bengal makes Asia the larger.
The thirteen colonies leave the count when they rebel (1776), about 2.8 million people.
Haiti's independence (1804) takes Saint-Domingue out.
Argentina, Chile and Gran Colombia's core are independent; Mexico, Peru, Central America, Brazil and the Caribbean remain.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822): the part falls by almost two thirds.
Peru and Upper Peru leave (1824 to 1825); Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Caribbean colonies, the Guianas and British North America remain.
British North America leaves the count as responsible government comes (1848 to 1855).
Spain takes back the Dominican Republic (1861 to 1865). Maximilian's Mexico (1864 to 1867) is a client empire on the spot, not counted.
Cuba and Puerto Rico pass from Spain to the United States (1898); Hawaii is annexed. Cuba under American occupation until 1902 is still counted.
Cuba's independence (1902) takes it out.
Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana become French départements with deputies in Paris (1946) and leave the count.
Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago leave (August 1962).
Guyana (May 1966) leaves; Barbados follows at the month's end.
Suriname (1975) leaves; the Bahamas and Grenada already have (1973, 1974).
Belize, Antigua and St Kitts leave (1981 to 1983): Puerto Rico is most of what remains.

With Hong Kong and Macau returned, the Americas are almost all of colonial rule: Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands and the British and Dutch Caribbean. The lower band carries the UN's list, which has left Puerto Rico out since 1953.
About 3.7 million people, 3.2 million of them in Puerto Rico.
Zero before the Portuguese in India (1498 to 1510).
Cabral's first factory at Cochin; no territory yet.
Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515) under Portugal.
Spain's Philippines (from 1565) bring the part to about a seventh of colonial rule.
The Dutch company's Batavia (1619), Amboina and Formosa's coast (1624).
The Dutch company rules Java's north coast and the Priangan; Madras, Bombay, Calcutta and Pondicherry are company towns.
Bengal, Bihar and Orissa under the East India Company after Plassey: Asia becomes most of colonial rule, as it stays until 1948.
Penang ceded by the Sultan of Kedah to Francis Light for the Company (1786), a few thousand people; Bengal's growth is the larger change.
Mysore falls (1799) and Britain takes the Dutch Ceylon coast (1796). The parent's remainder here implies some 70 million people, above a count of about 55 million: the parent may be high at 1800.
Doubles after the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818): the Company is paramount over most of India, its princely states counted with it.
India, the Dutch Indies, Indochina, the Philippines (American from 1898), Ceylon, Malaya and Taiwan: about 365 million people.
Korea, a Japanese protectorate from 1905, is already counted before its annexation (1910).
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces.
Manchukuo (1932), a puppet state whose counting is debated, adds about 1.4 points.
South-east Asia passes from European and American to Japanese rule without changing the count.
Japan's empire ends: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave, and Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence.
The Philippines become independent (July 1946).
India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon leave (1947 to 1948): the part falls by six sevenths in two years, and Africa becomes the larger part.
Indonesia's independence (December 1949).

After Geneva (1954) Indochina is out. This is the parent's remainder; a count of what is left (Malaya, Singapore, Hong Kong, Aden, Cyprus, the Borneo territories, Goa, Macau, Timor and the Gulf protectorates) gives about 0.6%, so either the parent or Africa's part is about half a point high here; the band reaches down to the count.
Malaya (1957) and Cyprus (1960) are out.
Singapore and the Borneo states join Malaysia (1963) and West New Guinea passes to Indonesia (1963).
Aden leaves (November 1967).
Hong Kong and Macau are almost all that remains, growing faster than the world.
Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China: no colonial rule from overseas is left in Asia.
Zero before Portugal takes Ceuta (1415).
All of colonial rule in 1450: Ceuta, Madeira, the Azores and the first Canaries, which belong to Europe by today's borders.
Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496).
Britain takes Malta (1800).
The Ionian Islands become a British protectorate (1815).
The Atlantic islands send deputies to the Cortes of Madrid and Lisbon (1820 to 1822) and leave the count; Malta and the Ionian Islands remain.
Britain cedes the Ionian Islands to Greece (1864).
Italy takes the Dodecanese (1912).
Italy's Albania (1939 to 1943) is military occupation and not counted.
The Dodecanese pass to Greece (1947).
Malta's independence (September 1964) leaves Gibraltar.
Gibraltar's 34,000 people.
Zero before Spain rules the Marianas (1668).
Spain's mission to Guam (1668) brings the Chamorros of the Marianas under its rule.
The Spanish–Chamorro wars and epidemics cut the Chamorros from tens of thousands to a few thousand by about 1710.
Before the First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove (January 1788) the only colonial rule in Oceania is Spain's in the Marianas.
New South Wales (1788) adds about a thousand convicts and soldiers.
The Australian colonies' settlers grow, and Britain claims New Zealand (1840).

The peak before self-government: the Victorian gold rush has not yet begun, but the Australian colonies hold about 400,000 settlers and convicts, and New Zealand about 25,000 settlers beside the Māori counted under the Crown's rule; all still governed from London.

Responsible government in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia (1855 to 1857) and New Zealand (1856) takes them out by the parent's definition; Aboriginal Australians and most Māori, with no vote, are a debated exception the band does not carry. Western Australia, the Marianas and Tahiti remain.
Fiji is ceded to Britain (1874).
Britain and Germany divide eastern New Guinea (1884) and Germany takes the Marshall Islands (1885); their rule reaches the coasts.
Samoa divided (1899), the Carolines and Marianas sold to Germany (1899), Guam to the United States (1898), the Solomons and the Gilberts British (1892 to 1893).
Patrols reach New Guinea's highlands (from 1933), about a million people never contacted before; how fast they count as ruled is a matter of judgment.

New Guinea's highland valleys, reached by patrols from 1933, are counted as administered by about 1940, which with Fiji, the Solomons, New Caledonia and Japan's mandated islands brings the part to about two million people. How much of the highlands counted as ruled by 1940 is a judgment; the band carries it.
Western Samoa becomes independent (1962).
Fiji and Tonga's protectorate end (1970).
Papua New Guinea becomes independent (September 1975): the part falls by three quarters.
The Solomons, Tuvalu (1978) and Kiribati (1979) are independent; Vanuatu follows in 1980.

New Caledonia and French Polynesia, Guam, the Northern Marianas, American Samoa, Wallis and Futuna and Tokelau. The French territories elect deputies to Paris but are on the UN's list of territories to decolonize (New Caledonia from 1986, French Polynesia from 2013); the lower band leaves them out.

Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.
Penang (1786) and New South Wales (1788) add a few thousand people each; the share keeps rising on the growth of the Company's India, not on these new footholds.
The abolition committee forms in London (1787) and the First Fleet sails for Botany Bay: neither moves the share yet, which climbs on India's growth under the Company.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882), about eight million people; the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) follows.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
Between Madagascar and Asante (1896) and Benin (1897), the conquest of Africa's coasts and their hinterlands is nearly complete; on the line between 1895 and 1900.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan (January 1956), Morocco and Tunisia (March 1956) become independent, about 23 million people; Ghana and Malaya follow in 1957.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.
Portugal's African empire, Rhodesia and small territories, with Hong Kong; their numbers grow while their count of territories does not, until the independences of 1974 and 1975.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.
The Pleistocene's large mammals on every continent: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, diprotodons and the herds of the savannas and steppes, perhaps 20 to 25 Mt C.

Sahul's megafauna (diprotodons, giant kangaroos, Genyornis) vanish soon after people arrive, about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago; whether hunting, fire or drying climate decided it is debated (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction). A small part of the world's wild mass.
The glacial maximum: the mammoth steppe from France to the Yukon holds great herds of grazers even as forests shrink.

The Americas lose most of their large mammal genera between about 11,000 and 9,000 BCE, as Clovis hunters spread and the Younger Dryas cold returns; hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.

In the Younger Dryas cold (from about 10,900 BCE) the Americas' mammoths, mastodons, horses and camels are going; Clovis and then Folsom hunters (from about 10,800 BCE) turn to bison, and the African Humid Period greens the Sahara for its animals. The loss runs on through the cold, so the value lies between 11,000 and 10,000 BCE.

After the end-Pleistocene extinctions: the Americas lose about three quarters of their large mammal genera between 13,000 and 11,000 years ago, and northern Eurasia its mammoths, woolly rhinos and giant deer, as people spread and the climate swings at the glacial's end. Hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.
From here fields and pastures slowly take land from wild herds; the loss is gradual for six thousand years.
Most of it now in the bison of North America (perhaps 30 to 60 million), the savanna herds of Africa and the wild ungulates of Asia's steppes and forests.
The slaughter of the bison for hides begins with the railways across the plains.
The bison are down to under a thousand (1889), and rinderpest, brought to the Horn of Africa in 1887, kills up to nine in ten of East Africa's buffalo and wildebeest within a decade.
Tropical forest cleared for fields and pasture, and bushmeat hunting, take wild mammals down by about a third in half a century while livestock doubles.

Bar-On and colleagues (2018): wild land mammals about 0.003 Gt C, against 0.06 for humans and 0.1 for livestock; Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) about 20 Mt of wet mass, the same order. As recalled, to be checked.

upsert.reason: Pleistocene level from the reconstructions of megafaunal biomass (Barnosky 2008; Bar-On and colleagues 2018 put it near 0.02 Gt C), the present from Bar-On and colleagues and Greenspoon and colleagues (2023), as recalled; the path between is sketched from the dated extinctions and the nineteenth-century slaughters.

points.note: Shell beads and finished tools passed between bands.
Textiles and metalwork from the first cities' workshops.
Chinese silk, Roman glass and fine pottery, Indian cloth.
Silk, Indian cotton cloth and Roman glass and metalware at the trade's height.
Song porcelain and silk carried by sea to South-east Asia and the Indian Ocean.
Indian cotton cloth floods European and West African markets (the calico craze).
British machine-made cotton goods replace Indian cloth in world markets.
Lend-lease arms and machines are much of wartime trade.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now, as Europe's and Japan's industries trade with one another.
East Asia's export manufacturing and the trade in parts between factories.
Global value chains: a phone's parts cross many borders before it is sold.
Goods hold up in the pandemic (medical supplies, electronics for home working) while travel stops.
The goods boom of the pandemic's second year.
On the path between the pandemic's goods boom and 2025.
Stone, shells and ochre carried between bands: most of what passes between peoples.
Obsidian from Anatolia carried across the Levant and Mesopotamia.
The Bronze Age's tin and copper, carried from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the cities that made bronze.
Grain, wine and oil across the Mediterranean, pepper and spices from India: about three fifths of trade.
Pepper, spices, incense and the grain fleets of Egypt.
American silver begins to flow to Europe and, through it and the Manila galleons, to China.
Sugar and tobacco from the Atlantic plantations, tea from China, grain and timber from the Baltic.
Peru's guano (from 1840) joins cotton, grain and timber as the industrial cities draw on the world's farms, forests and mines; on the path between 1820 and 1850.
The great specialization: grain, cotton, wool, meat and minerals from the Americas, Australia, India and Russia for Europe's manufactures.
The American Civil War's cotton famine raises raw cotton's price.
Grain, beef, coffee and sugar from the Americas and wool from Australia flow to Europe as freight rates fall; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Refrigerated meat and butter join grain, wool, coffee and sugar; on the path between 1880 and 1890.
Primary prices collapse in the Depression, and with them primary producers' share of trade.
War trade is mostly arms and machines.
Japan's purchases of Australian wool, coal and iron ore under the commerce agreement of 1957 begin to turn Oceania's primary exports toward Asia; on the path between 1954 and 1960.
Manufactures pass primary goods about now.
The oil price quadruples in 1973 to 1974: fuels jump to about a fifth of merchandise trade.
The second oil shock: primary goods back to two fifths of trade.
After the oil price collapse of 1986 manufactures dominate trade.
The commodity boom driven by China's demand for ores, oil and soy.
The oil price collapses in the pandemic.
Commodity prices recover from the pandemic's low.
Oil, gas, grain and fertilizer prices jump in 2022 with the war in Ukraine; primary goods' share of trade's value rises with them.
Zero: nothing is sold between bands apart from goods.
Shipping and caravan services begin to be paid apart from the goods they carry: a sliver.
Italian merchant banks and the carrying trade of Venice and Genoa sell finance and freight.
Dutch shipping carries much of Europe's trade: the Republic sells freight and insurance.
Steamship freight, marine insurance and London's finance: about a twelfth of trade.
Travel, shipping and finance resume after the war: about an eighth of trade.
Travel stops in the pandemic: services fall about a fifth while goods hold.
Travel still mostly closed; digital and business services grow.
Travel recovers from the pandemic; digital services keep growing.
About a quarter of trade: travel recovered, business and digital services growing fastest.
Shells and stone carried hundreds of kilometres, but a tiny share of output.
Obsidian networks across Anatolia and the Levant.

The Roman trade with India at its height: by Strabo about 120 ships a year sail from Myos Hormos, the Muziris papyrus prices one cargo at about 7 million sesterces, and Han silk reaches Rome through Parthia and the Kushans. A small rise over the value at 1, within the band.
The Antonine plague (from 165) kills perhaps a tenth of the Roman Empire's people and the trade begins to ebb; whether it was the turn in the Indian Ocean trade or only a pause is debated.

The Arab conquests (from 632) join the Sasanian and much of the Byzantine trading world under one rule, and Srivijaya (from 671) comes to hold the Malacca strait for the trade between China and India. The share stays about one percent. Pirenne's thesis that Islam cut the Mediterranean's trade is set against the alternative that the trade had already shrunk with the Roman west, and that the caliphate's own trade grew: the band carries both.
Mongol-era overland routes broken; Indian Ocean trade growing; the Ming voyages begin in 1405.
The Portuguese Indies trade and the first Atlantic crossings add to Eurasia's trade.
The first globalization's peak, on the eve of the war.
War and blockade shrink trade.
On the eve of the crash world trade is near its interwar peak; the fall through 1930 to the low of the mid-1930s follows the slump, the tariffs and the currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
World trade has fallen by about two thirds in value since 1929, behind tariffs and currency blocs (ev.interwar-crisis).
Wartime blockade and shipping losses shrink trade.
Trade still depressed by the war; the postwar order rebuilds it (ev.postwar-order).
The ASEAN free trade area (1992) and NAFTA (1994) begin and the former Soviet bloc opens to trade; the sum of its three parts on their paths.
The 2001 slump cuts trade; China joins the WTO in December (ev.as.china-wto).
Goods trade rebounds from the pandemic while travel is still closed; the sum of its three parts.
Trade recovers from the pandemic and its value peaks as energy and food prices jump after Russia's invasion of Ukraine; the sum of its three parts.
All people forage and move camp with the seasons.
The Natufians and the Jomon settle: the first foragers counted as settled.
The green Sahara's lake fishers and the Levant's late Natufian successors are among the foragers who settle.
Falls as farming villages grow far denser than foragers; about nine in ten of the remaining foragers still move.
Herders are now about two in five of the mobile, a little more than the parent's note (a third) says, because this split counts some foragers as settled.
Epidemics and conquest in the Americas take the land and lives of many mobile foragers; the share of remaining foragers who move falls below nine in ten.
Settlers take foragers' lands in North America, Australia, Siberia and southern Africa.
Small bands still move camp to forage for part or all of the year: in the Kalahari, the Congo basin, among the Hadza, in Amazonia and the Andaman Islands, and the sea nomads of South-east Asia.
No domestic animals, so no herders.
Begins: goat and sheep herders of the Zagros and Taurus may already move between seasonal pastures; whether any households were fully mobile this early is debated.
On the path between its neighbours: cattle herding begins in the eastern Sahara and sheep and goat herders move with farmers into Europe.
Cattle herders range across the green Sahara, the largest mobile herding population of the age.
Rises: the Yamnaya move with ox-wagons and herds across the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and their descendants spread east and west; the Sahara's herders move south as it dries.

Dips from 3000 BCE: the Yamnaya's descendants settle into mixed farming across Europe, the farming valleys of Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus and China grow faster than the steppe, and the dry spell of about 2200 BCE (the 4.2 ka event) presses on the herders of the drying Sahara and the steppe.
The camel is domesticated in Arabia, opening the deserts to herders.
Mounted nomadism on the steppe: herders ride, range far and raid settled states.
The Xiongnu unite the eastern steppe and press Han China.
Huns and Avars in the west, the Rouran and Turks in the east; camel-herding Berbers cross the Sahara.
The Mongols unite the steppe: perhaps one or two million herders build the largest land empire.
Up a little: the Black Death kills more of the settled, crowded peoples than of the herders.
Herders pass mobile foragers as the larger part of the mobile between 1600 and 1650.
The Qing destroy the Dzungars (1755 to 1758) and Russia advances on the Kazakh steppe: states begin to settle and tax the herders.
Russian peasants settle the Kazakh steppe and France conquers the Sahara's herders; rinderpest kills most of East Africa's cattle in the 1890s.
Falls faster: Soviet collectivization forces the Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Turkmen nomads to settle (1928 to 1934); the famine that follows kills perhaps a third of the Kazakhs.
Mongolia's herders are collectivized, Tibet's herds taken into communes, and new states in the Middle East and Africa push herders to settle.
The Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s drive many herders into towns and camps; Africa's fast-growing herding peoples keep the share from falling faster.
Perhaps 10 to 60 million people: estimates differ because many households now move only part of the family with the herds.
No settled markets to serve.
Begins with the first cities and states: smiths, traders and entertainers who move among settled people; how many lived without a fixed home is unknown.
The Roma, who left India centuries before, reach the Balkans by about 1300; Banjara carriers supply the Delhi Sultanate's armies.

Most of this share is South Asia's carrier and service nomads: Banjara caravans of tens of thousands of bullocks, nomadic smiths, traders and entertainers; Europe's Roma and Travellers and the Middle East's Dom are fewer.
Turns down: railways take the Banjara carrying trade, and India's Criminal Tribes Act (1871) brands many nomadic castes as criminal and forces them to settle.
Nazi Germany and its allies murder perhaps 200,000 to 500,000 Roma and Sinti (the Porajmos), many of them travelling families; the estimate is debated.
Most of India's nomadic castes, the Roma and the Travellers are now settled; some still travel for part of the year.
All people are mobile foragers, moving camp with the seasons.
Some glacial-age winter settlements on the Russian plain were reoccupied for months, but their people still moved.
Turns down: the Natufians of the Levant settle in stone houses about 12,500 BCE, harvesting wild cereals before they farm; the Jomon of Japan settle about the same time.

Farming villages in the Fertile Crescent, millet farmers in north China and the gardeners of Kuk in New Guinea begin to grow denser than foragers, and fishers settle by the lakes of the green Sahara; the fall from 96 at 9500 BCE toward 82 at 7900 BCE is taken as steady, though it may have come later and faster.
Farming villages in south-west Asia, China and New Guinea hold a growing share, because farmers live far denser than foragers.
Herders begin to move with their animals on the steppe and in the Sahara as it dries; pastoral nomadism will keep a share mobile after foraging shrinks.
Mounted nomadism on the steppe (the Scythians and their neighbours): herders now move on horseback over great ranges and threaten settled states.
The Mongols unite the steppe; about a third of the mobile are now herders rather than foragers.
The Qing destroy the Dzungar state (1755 to 1758) and Russia advances on the Kazakh steppe: the last great nomad powers end, and settled states begin to fence and tax the herders.
Turns down faster: Soviet collectivization forces the Kazakh and other Central Asian nomads to settle, 1928 to 1934, and the famine that follows kills perhaps a third of the Kazakhs.
The Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s drive many herders into towns and camps.

Mobile herders in the Sahel, the Horn of Africa, Arabia, Iran, Central Asia, Mongolia and Tibet, and a few foraging bands; estimates of mobile pastoralists differ by a factor of two, since many herders now move only part of the household.

upsert.reason: Mobile foragers from the model's foraging share, taking about 7% of foragers as sedentary after 12,500 BCE; pastoral nomads sketched at 2 to 3% of humanity from mounted nomadism to 1500 (steppe, Arabia, Sahara, East Africa, Tibet), falling to about 1% by 1900 and about 0.3% now, as estimates of mobile pastoralists put them (some 30 to 40 million today, as recalled).

points.note: All of range is African: Homo sapiens from Jebel Irhoud to Florisbad, in patches between deserts and other hominins' lands, about half of Africa's land.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara hyperarid, people in the wetter east, south and coasts.
Termination II ends the penultimate glacial: the monsoon reaches the Sahara again and rivers and lakes open it, so Africa's part rises by half in a few thousand years.
The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes: Africa's part nearly doubles, close to the whole continent.
The glacial returns and the Sahara dries.
Holds while the dispersal fills Asia, Sahul and Europe: the dispersal added land elsewhere, it did not empty Africa.
The glacial maximum's aridity: the Sahara and the Kalahari spread, the rainforest shrinks to refuges.
The African Humid Period begins (from about 10,500 BCE): the first lakes and grass return to the Sahara before the Younger Dryas ends, and hunters follow them north.
The African Humid Period: lakes and grassland across the Sahara as far as Lake Mega-Chad, hunters and then cattle herders across it.
Africa's highest: almost all of its land within range.
The African Humid Period has ended: the herders withdraw to the Nile, the Sahel and the oases, and the Sahara's core empties, about 2.8 points of the world's land given up in a thousand years.
The camel spreads across the Sahara from about the first centuries CE and lets nomads use more of the desert between the oases.
Voyagers from Borneo have settled Madagascar, about 0.4 points of the world's land.
Motor tracks, oil and gas fields (Hassi Messaoud, 1956) and mines carry regular use into parts of the Sahara's core that only caravans had crossed.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Africa's land (about 30.3 million km2), the Sahara's green and dry phases, and the dated Events of the account; the Sahara's hyperarid core, about 2 to 3 points of the world's land, is outside range in dry phases.

points.note: Claims of people in the Americas before the glacial maximum (Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico, about 30,000 years ago) are debated; the band keeps them open.

The footprints at White Sands, New Mexico (about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago), put people south of the ice during the glacial maximum; the dates are debated but have held against two later tests. Their numbers and reach are unknown, so the part is small and the band wide.
The peopling of the Americas proper begins: a coastal route along the Pacific is open as the Cordilleran ice retreats from the coast.
Monte Verde in southern Chile (about 12,500 BCE) and the Paisley Caves in Oregon (about 12,300 BCE): people reach both ends of the hemisphere within a thousand years.
Clovis hunters spread across North America within about three centuries (from about 11,100 BCE), the fastest gain in range in the account.
Peopled to Tierra del Fuego; the Laurentide ice still covers much of Canada, and the Arctic islands and Greenland stay empty.
The Laurentide ice is almost gone and hunters follow the caribou north across Canada; the high Arctic and Greenland remain outside range.
The first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola, about 0.1 points of the world's land.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic to Greenland's ice-free coasts, about two points of the world's land that no one had lived on: the last large gain in range.

Unchanged: the Norse settlements of south-west Greenland (from 985) use a few tens of thousands of square kilometres, about 0.02 points, and Late Dorset people already hunt in the north-west; the Norse are gone by about 1450.
Polynesians settle Hawai'i (about 1000 to 1200), which by 2026 borders is part of the United States and so of this part; the Thule Inuit spread across the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland.
The epidemics after 1492 empty parts of the Americas for a time, the Mississippi and Amazon floodplains and the Caribbean's islands among them: the one area whose range falls in the historical era.
Weather stations, airfields and mines on Canada's Arctic islands (Resolute, 1947; Alert, 1950) and Greenland's bases bring the high Arctic's last empty land into regular use.
Nearly all the Americas' ice-free land: the Atacama's core and the emptiest Arctic islands are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from the Americas' ice-free land (about 38.7 million km2), the account's dated Events of their peopling (White Sands, Monte Verde, the Paisley Caves, Clovis, the Paleo-Inuit) and the epidemics after 1492.

points.note: No one reaches Antarctica for almost all of human history.
Cook crosses the Antarctic Circle (1773) and circles the continent without seeing it.
Antarctica is first sighted (January 1820); sealers land on the South Shetlands the next summer.
Sealers work the South Shetlands and the Peninsula's islands each summer until the fur seals are nearly gone (by the 1830s).
Sealers' seasonal camps on the South Shetland beaches.
Argentina's station on Laurie Island (1904), the first held year round, and the whalers' station at Deception Island (from 1906).
Britain's Operation Tabarin (1944) sets up the first permanent bases on the Antarctic Peninsula.
The IGY's fifty stations, from McMurdo to Vostok, bring most of the coastal oases and the dry valleys within regular reach.
The treaty (December 1959) keeps the IGY's stations open for science under shared rules.
The International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958) and the treaty that followed put some forty stations on the continent and field parties into the dry valleys.
About seventy stations and the field science of the treaty's members reach most of the ice-free ground at least in summer.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Antarctica's ice-free area (about 45,000 km2 as recalled) and the dates of sealing, the first stations and the treaty's science.

points.note: The Misliya jaw (about 185,000 years ago) puts Homo sapiens in the Levant for a time: a first, small excursion out of Africa.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant (Skhul and Qafzeh) and greens Arabia's interior, where lakes and stone tools of African type appear.
The glacial returns: Arabia dries, and the Levant goes back to the Neanderthals by about 90,000 years ago.
A few groups hold on in Arabia's south and east (Jebel Faya); whether others reached India before Toba is debated.
The dispersal: people move along southern Asia from Arabia through India to Sunda within a few thousand years.
Eastern and central Asia are entered: north China, Mongolia's steppe, the Altai (where people meet the Denisovans) and the Tibetan margins.
The glacial maximum dries Central Asia and north China into desert and loess; people withdraw from the Mongolian plateau and the high steppe, while Sundaland's lowlands, then dry land, stay in range.
The early Holocene monsoon greens Arabia and the Thar again, and the steppe and north China are reoccupied.
Asia's highest before the modern era: Arabia's interior has lakes, hunters and then herders.
Arabia's humid phase has ended with Africa's: the Rub' al Khali and the Nafud empty, and herders keep to their edges and the oases.
Barley farmers and yak herders settle the high Tibetan plateau year round (from about 1600 BCE), while the drying of Central Asia's lowlands takes back about as much.
Oil camps and roads reach Arabia's interior and the Taklamakan's rim; the Rub' al Khali's core stays outside regular use.
About 86% of Asia's land in range; the empty quarter, the Taklamakan's core and the highest Tibetan and Karakoram ground are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Asia's land without Russia (about 31.5 million km2), the Levant's and Arabia's green phases, the dispersal's dates and the deserts and high plateaus that stay outside range.

points.note: A skull at Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) has been read as Homo sapiens, which would be a brief excursion; the reading is debated, and Europe is otherwise the Neanderthals' for another 160,000 years.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley (about 54,000 years ago) holds a Homo sapiens tooth between Neanderthal layers: a first, short-lived foothold.
Homo sapiens spreads from the Balkans (Bacho Kiro, about 45,000 years ago) across Europe and into western Siberia (Ust'-Ishim), meeting the last Neanderthals.
People live at the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and across the Russian plain: under M49 all of Russia is Europe, so Siberia's peopling is this part's.

The glacial maximum: ice covers Scandinavia and the north of Britain and Russia, polar desert spreads across Siberia's north, and people hold refuges in Iberia, southern France, Italy, the Balkans, the Russian plain's south and southern Siberia.
The Bølling warmth (from about 12,700 BCE): Magdalenian and Hamburgian hunters follow the reindeer north across Germany and Poland, and Siberia's north is reoccupied.
The Scandinavian ice has melted and hunters live in the north of Norway and Finland and on the Arctic coasts; Zhokhov Island in the New Siberian Islands is used about 6000 BCE.
Herders and hunters push into the drier steppe and the northern taiga: a quarter of a point over a millennium.
Iceland, settled from about 870, is mostly taken in by 900.
Norse settlers have made Iceland's ice-free land (about 0.07 points of the world's) part of range since about 870.
Russia's Arctic coasts and Kamchatka gain posts and hunting camps, and Svalbard's coasts hold whalers' and trappers' stations.
The Soviet Northern Sea Route, Gulag camps and mines (Vorkuta, Norilsk, Kolyma) bring the far north and Siberia's interior into regular use.
About 86% of Europe's land with Russia in range; the high Arctic islands' interiors and the emptiest tundra are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Europe's land with all of Russia (about 23.4 million km2), the dates of Homo sapiens' arrival, the ice sheets and polar deserts of the glacial maximum and the Arctic's late settlement.

points.note: Madjedbebe in northern Australia has been dated to about 65,000 years ago, which would put people in Sahul here; many read the site's layers as mixed and prefer about 50,000. The account follows the later date (ev.oc.sahul-arrival) and keeps the earlier one in the band.
People cross the Wallacean straits to Sahul, the longest sea crossings anyone had made, and land in New Guinea and northern Australia.
Within a few thousand years people live across Australia's coasts and rivers (Lake Mungo by about 42,000 years ago) and New Guinea's highlands.
Tasmania, then joined to the mainland, and the Bismarcks and Solomons of Near Oceania are reached.

The glacial maximum dries Australia's interior into dune fields: Aboriginal people withdraw to refuges on the coasts, the ranges and the rivers, giving up perhaps two fifths of the continent for several thousand years.
The interior is reoccupied as the climate eases; Tasmania is cut off by the rising sea about 12,000 years ago and stays inhabited.
Lapita voyagers reach Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa (about 1100 to 800 BCE), the first people in Remote Oceania.
East Polynesia's settlement, by the short chronology from about 900 to 1000, adds islands too small to show; New Zealand, about 0.2 points, is still empty until about 1280.
East Polynesia is settled from the Society Islands to Rapa Nui (about 1000 to 1200): many islands, little land.
East Polynesians settle Aotearoa (about 1280), the last large land on Earth to be peopled, about 0.2 points of the world's land.
The First Fleet (1788) brings settlers to land already within Aboriginal range: colonization changes who holds the land, not how much of it is held.
Unchanged since Aotearoa's settlement: every later change in Oceania (colonization, dispossession, the cities) is a change in who holds the land and how densely, not how much of it is held.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Oceania's land (about 8.5 million km2), the debated date of Sahul's peopling, the glacial maximum's desert refuges and the dates of Lapita's and the Polynesians' voyages.

points.note: Homo sapiens across Africa (Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Florisbad in the south, Omo in Ethiopia), but in patches between deserts and other hominins' lands: about a tenth of today's ice-free land, Africa being under a quarter of it.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and people hold the wetter east and south of Africa and its coasts.

The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes and opens the Levant and Arabia: the first time Homo sapiens holds land outside Africa for long (Skhul and Qafzeh). Range doubles in a few thousand years.
The glacial returns: the Sahara dries and the Levant goes back to the Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia.
The dispersal: people spread along southern Asia from Arabia to Sunda in a few thousand years, adding about seven million km2.

The largest gain in range in the account: in about ten thousand years people take in Sahul, Europe, eastern and northern Asia; WaveOfAdvance#4cec's fronts on land and long sea crossings to Sahul (the card's long-distance jumps) together.
People live as far north as the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and in Japan, Tibet's margins and Tasmania.

The glacial maximum begins: the ice sheets advance, the steppe of Siberia and the north European plain turn to polar desert and Australia's interior dries; people begin to withdraw to refuges in southern Europe, the Russian plain's south, the Altai and the Australian coasts, and range falls toward its glacial low of about a third of the land by 21,000 BCE.

Corrected from 50. The deglaciation begins to open the north: Magdalenian hunters spread from Iberia and southern France toward the Paris Basin and Germany, and Siberia's south is reoccupied. People are probably already south of the ice in the Americas (White Sands), but most of the Americas' peopling comes after 13,000 BCE (Monte Verde about 12,500 BCE, Clovis about 11,100 BCE). The earlier value read '14,500 years ago' as 14,500 BCE.
Corrected from 53, for the same reason as at -14600.
Corrected from 57. The Bølling warmth (from about 12,700 BCE) carries hunters north across Europe and the Russian plain; the Americas are entered along the Pacific coast and the ice-free corridor.
Corrected from 62: Monte Verde in Chile and the Paisley Caves in Oregon are occupied, but much of the Americas' interior is not yet reached.
Corrected from 66.
Corrected from 70. Clovis hunters spread across North America in a few centuries; the Younger Dryas (from about 10,950 BCE) brings the cold back to the north and dries the Sahara.

Corrected from 82. Late in the Younger Dryas: the Americas are peopled to Tierra del Fuego, but the Sahara is still dry and the north still cold; the Holocene's warmth and the African Humid Period lift range again from 9700 BCE.
Near its prehistoric peak: the Sahara and Arabia are grassland with lakes, hunters and then herders live across them, and the Laurentide ice is almost gone.
The Sahara's grasslands are already thinning at their edges; Varna's chiefs and the Balkan copper towns live inside a range that farming filled but did not widen.

Two moves nearly cancel: the first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola (about 0.1% of the land), while the African Humid Period ends and the Sahara's herders begin to withdraw to the Nile, the Sahel and the oases, the largest loss of range since the glacial maximum, played out over the next thousand years.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic to Greenland's ice-free coasts, adding about three million km2 of tundra no one had lived on.

Holds: the first millennium BCE adds no new land. The Axial age's schools and cities change how people think and live inside a range already near its Holocene extent; only the Paleo-Inuit's later Dorset phase and the herders' spread into the drier steppe move it by fractions.
Voyagers from Borneo have settled Madagascar (about 0.4% of the land), the last large uninhabited land of the Old World tropics.
Iceland is settled from about 870; East Polynesia's islands and the Norse fjords of Greenland (from 985) are tiny in the world's land, and gunpowder changes nothing here.
East Polynesians reach Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land to be peopled; Iceland (about 870) and the eastern Pacific islands came just before.
Dips a little: epidemics after 1492 leave parts of the Americas, the Mississippi and Amazon floodplains among them, all but empty for a time; the survivors' ranges still cover most of the land.

Weather stations, mines and bases on the high Arctic islands and the ice-free coasts of Antarctica add the last fractions; the empty cores of the Sahara, the Rub' al Khali and the Taklamakan remain outside regular use.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the archaeology and genomics of each region's first peopling and abandonments, as recalled (Africa's Middle Stone Age sites, the green Sahara corridors, the dispersal through Arabia and southern Asia, Sahul by about 50,000 years ago, Europe by 45,000, Arctic Siberia by 32,000, the Americas by about 16,000 at the latest, the glacial maximum's refuges, the Holocene Sahara and its desiccation, the Paleo-Inuit, Remote Oceania and Aotearoa), with the areas of regions and deserts. The boundary of 'regular use' is soft; the band carries it.

points.note: All of humanity's output is made in Africa until Homo sapiens settles western Asia in the Last Interglacial; output per person is the forager level (h.provisioning).
Asia's first farmers now make more than Africa's foragers and herders: Africa's output passes below Asia's between 9500 and 7900 BCE.
Egypt unified (ev.af.egypt-unification): the Nile valley's output per person near the world's, the rest of Africa below it.
Africa's output stalls between 1800 and 1820 while its people's share falls: the Atlantic slave trade's last peak and the wars of the Sokoto jihad and the Mfecane.
Conquest and colonial rule: Africa's share of world output falls toward its low of under 4%, though mines and cash crops raise its output in absolute terms.
Africa's lost decades begin: debt, falling commodity prices and wars hold its output per person flat or falling from about 1980 to 1995 while its people grow fastest.
Africa's output has grown faster than the world's since 2000, but at about 5% of world output it is a quarter of its share of people.
No people live in the Americas until about 16,000 years ago (the White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, put a few earlier).
People are south of the ice (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago): the Americas' first output, a few tens of thousands of foragers.
The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya kingdoms, Moche and Tiwanaku raise the Americas' output per person a little toward the world's.

On the eve of contact the Americas make about a twelfth of world output, the Aztec and Inca states and their tributaries most of it; the size depends on the contact population, which is debated (see h.region-americas).
The Aztec and Inca states fall; smallpox has already run through Mexico and the Andes. Output shrinks with the people, at the rate between 1520 and 1550.
Potosí is found (1545) and the cocoliztli strikes New Spain (1545 to 1548): silver rises as people die.

The Columbian collapse (ev.columbian-exchange, VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd): the Americas' output falls by two fifths from 1520 to 1550 and by two thirds to 1600 with its people, though the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas becomes the most valuable thing the Americas send out.
The nadir: the Americas make under 2% of world output.
The United States' output per person is already more than twice the world's; with Latin America's near the world's, the Americas' output per person is about 1.4 times it.
Spanish America's wars of independence end with its economies smaller than in 1810, while the United States grows; on the path from 1820 to 1850.
Latin America stagnates under the caudillos while the United States grows by canals and cotton; the Americas' output doubles from 1820 to 1850, almost all of the gain in the north.
The Americas pass a tenth of world output, the United States most of it.

Between 1870 and 1890 on a constant growth rate: the United States grows fast after the Civil War despite the depression of 1873, Argentina's export boom begins, and the slave economies of Cuba and Brazil end in the 1880s. About 13.6% of world output, up from 11.3% in 1870.
The First World War: the Americas' output rises while Europe's falls.
The bank panics of 1930 and 1931 and the collapse of commodity prices take the Americas' output down a tenth from 1929; Latin America's export economies turn to making their own goods.
The Depression's trough: the Americas' output falls about a fifth from 1929 (ev.nam.depression), more than any other area's.
The war economy: the Americas' output passes Europe's for the first time, the United States making about two fifths of the world's manufactures.
Demobilization: American output falls about a tenth from its wartime peak.
Latin America's lost decade (ev.am.debt-crisis): its output per person falls while Northern America's grows, so the Americas' output grows slower than the world's.
No Homo sapiens lives in Asia before the Last Interglacial; the Denisovans and other archaic humans are not counted.
The dispersal out of Africa (ev.era.dispersal): Asia's output grows with its people, at the forager level per person.
Farming in the Fertile Crescent and then China: Asia's output passes Africa's and keeps about three fifths of the world's or more for the next nine thousand years.
Han China and the Indian kingdoms: Asia makes about seven tenths of world output, close to its share of people (Maddison about 74% as recalled).
Song China's commercial economy at its height: Asia's output per person a little above the world's.
The Mongol wars, the Yuan collapse and the Black Death in western Asia: Asia's output falls from 1300 to 1400 with its people.
Ming China and the Indian kingdoms: Asia makes about 62% of world output, near Maddison's figure as recalled.
The seventeenth-century crisis: the Ming–Qing wars and famines hold Asia's output near flat from 1600 to 1650.
Asia makes about 57% of world output with 65% of its people: the Great Divergence has begun but is still small (MalthusianTrap#0f6b binds Asia as it bound everyone).
Europe's output has passed Asia's for the first time since antiquity, between 1870 and 1890: Asia grows slowly while the El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 cut India's and north China's people.
Japan's war in China from 1937: Asia's output falls from 1936 to 1940.
China's famine of the Great Leap Forward: Asia makes under a quarter of world output, near its lowest share.

Japan grows about a tenth a year and Singapore, independent from 1965, begins its rise, while the American war in Vietnam escalates; China's Cultural Revolution (from 1966) will cut its output in 1967 and 1968.
China's reform (from 1978), Japan's boom and the Asian tigers: Asia's output about equals Europe's and the Americas'.
Asia's output has passed Europe's and the Americas' in the 1990s, for the first time since about 1880.
Asia makes about half of world output, near its share before 1820, though its output per person is still under the world's.
Neanderthals hold Europe and are not counted; Homo sapiens arrives about 45,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum drives Europe's foragers into southern refuges; its output falls with its people.
The Roman peace: the Mediterranean's output per person about a sixth above the world's, Europe's north below it.

Rome's fall in the west (ev.eu.rome-fall): cities shrink, trade and coin fail and people fall, so Europe's output falls by about two fifths from 200 to 610 and its output per person drops below the world's.
The high-medieval peak: Europe's output more than doubles from 1000 with its people and its towns.
After the Black Death: Europe's output about an eighth below 1300's though output per person is higher, fewer people working the same land (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
Atlantic trade and the Dutch and English economies: Europe's output per person is about two fifths above the world's.
Coal and steam (Sunbound#c94c): Europe's output per person reaches about 1.75 times the world's.
Europe's output passes Asia's for the first time since antiquity, between 1870 and 1890.
Europe's output falls about a tenth from 1913 with the war.
The war's last year: occupied, bombed and fought-over Europe makes about a seventh less than in 1940; Germany's output collapses in 1945.
The postwar boom: Western Europe's recovery and the Soviet Union's growth carry Europe's output back above the Americas'.
The Soviet bloc's collapse: Eastern Europe's output falls about two fifths between 1989 and 1998, so Europe's output grows slowly through the 1990s (ev.eu.soviet-collapse).
No people in Sahul until about 50,000 years ago on the later dates (65,000 on Madjedebe's, debated).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) and wool: Oceania's output more than doubles in a decade.
Australia's settlers are among the richest people on Earth; Oceania's output per person about twice the world's, though its first peoples are falling (ev.oc.depopulation).
Frozen meat and butter (the Dunedin, 1882) join wool and gold as Oceania's exports; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Wool and wheat prices collapse in the Depression: Australia's and New Zealand's output falls about a sixth.
The Australia-Japan commerce agreement (1957) begins the turn of Oceania's trade from Britain to Asia; on the path between 1954 and 1960.
France's nuclear tests at Moruroa begin (1966); they move Polynesia's politics and health, not the area's output.
Britain joins the European Community (1973), ending New Zealand's assured market, while Panguna's copper (from 1972) lifts Papua New Guinea's exports; on the path between 1970 and 1975.

points.note: Uruk-period polities, if counted as states.
The Han and Roman empires at their height, with the Parthians, Kushans and Satavahanas, hold most of the world's people; the share falls only as the Han breaks up after 184.
The southern Maya kingdoms fail while new states form in South-east Asia (Angkor, 802) and the Abbasid and Carolingian realms hold; the share barely moves.

The Tang and Abbasid realms fragment but their people stay under states; the southern Maya kingdoms fail; Polynesians settle eastern islands without states. The share under a state barely moves between 770 and 1000.
The Triple Alliance forms in the valley of Mexico; the Ming, Timurid and Ottoman states hold most of Asia's people.
Pachacuti begins the Inca conquests: within a century about ten million Andean people come under one state.
Band corrected: the earlier band ran to 108%, above what a share can be.

Leahy's and Taylor's patrol into the Wahgi (1933) finds about a million highlanders, some 0.05% of humanity, who come under the Australian administration over the next two decades; Japan's conquest of Manchuria (1931) changes which state rules, not whether one does.
Band corrected: the earlier band ran to 109%.

Starts: some 300,000 people in forager bands of about 35, each answering to no one; the band size and the population are both uncertain by a factor of several.
Falls a little with people in the deepest part of the penultimate glacial.
Flat through the Last Glacial Maximum: no more people, so no more bands.
At the Holocene's start, about 130,000 bands: the number of autonomous units grows with people for as long as everyone lives in bands.
Farming multiplies people faster than it enlarges their units: autonomous villages of a hundred or two join the bands, and the count passes a third of a million.

Peaks in the late Bronze Age at about three quarters of a million: states hold a quarter of humanity, but the people outside them, in bands, villages and chiefdoms, are still most and still growing. Carneiro's order of magnitude, about 600,000 in 1000 BCE, lies inside the band.
Falls: the Han, Roman, Parthian and Kushan empires hold six in ten people, and the units left outside them are larger chiefdoms and tribes.
Falls by a quarter: the Black Death and the Mongol and Timurid wars cut people while states (Ming, Ottoman, Vijayanagara, Mali, the Aztec and Inca beginnings) hold three in four of those left.
Falls: the Americas' chiefdoms and villages die with their people after 1492 or come under Spain and Portugal, and Russia's conquest of Siberia reaches the Pacific (1639).

Falls fast: the Scramble for Africa, the conquests of the American West, Patagonia and Siberia's last peoples, and the Dutch, British and French advance in South-east Asia bring hundreds of thousands of stateless villages and bands under states between 1870 and 1900.

Set directly from here on: what remains outside states is the New Guinea highlands' clans (perhaps a million people), the Amazon's villages, interior Borneo, the Sahara's and Arabia's tribes and the Afghan frontier; the model's share under a state (98%) would leave twice as many people outside states, a tension to resolve in a later pass.

The highland patrols begin to bring the clans of the Wahgi and neighbouring valleys, several thousand autonomous groups, under one administration; the count falls fastest in New Guinea through the 1930s.
Patrols and gold prospectors reach the New Guinea highlands' valleys (the Wahgi, 1933), whose clans had been the largest population on Earth outside any state.
Postwar patrols and missions in New Guinea, the Amazon and Borneo bring most remaining groups under some administration; the count of all autonomous units falls toward that of states.
States now make up half or more of all autonomous units; the rest are uncontacted groups in Amazonia, western New Guinea and the Andamans, perhaps a hundred or two.
Rises: the Soviet Union's breakup makes fifteen states of one, and Yugoslavia's four more.

About 197 states, recognized or not, and perhaps a hundred uncontacted peoples who answer to no state in practice; whether those count as autonomous polities is a matter of definition the band carries.

Foragers' material wealth (tools, ornaments) and relational wealth (ties to others) are shared fairly evenly: wealth Ginis about 0.25 to 0.35 in Borgerhoff Mulder and others' comparison, a top-tenth share of about a quarter.
Rich burials such as Sungir's (about 32,000 years ago) show that some foragers could concentrate prestige goods, rarely and briefly.
Rises with farming: stored grain, fields and herds can be held and handed down, and house sizes begin to diverge.
Draft animals, the plough and states: Kohler and others find Old World house-size Ginis near 0.6 by the Bronze Age, above the New World's, where there were no large draft animals.
The Roman senatorial and Han landlord elites: Scheidel's agrarian empires, where the richest tenth hold most land and slaves.
Falls: the collapse of Roman rule in the West destroys the great senatorial fortunes (Scheidel's leveller of state failure).
Falls: the Black Death kills a third or more in Europe and the Near East, land becomes cheap and labour dear, and wealth inequality falls for a century (Alfani's and Scheidel's plague leveller).
Plantations, colonial fortunes and the first industrial capital; from here the gap between countries adds to the gap within them.

Spanish America's new republics free the children of slaves (from 1821) and end slavery only slowly, to 1854; Indian Removal is about to begin. Nothing yet turns the slow rise in the richest tenth's share.

Britain abolishes slavery (1833 to 1838) and pays the slave-owners 20 million pounds, about two fifths of a year's government spending: their wealth in people becomes wealth in government bonds rather than vanishing, and the freed get nothing. The richest tenth's share is not cut by it.

Indian Removal (1830 to 1850) turns some 25 million acres of Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole land into land sold to settlers and planters: the expansion of cotton slavery that follows concentrates wealth in the American South.

The Great Mahele (1848) divides Hawaiian land among the crown, the government and the chiefs and, after 1850, lets foreigners buy it; within two generations most of it is held by a few planters. On the world's scale this is small; the rise goes on with industrial and colonial capital.
The peak: on the eve of 1914 the richest tenth hold about nine tenths of wealth in Britain and France (Piketty's series), while most of the world's people own almost nothing.
On the eve of the war wealth concentration is at its peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from destroyed capital, taxes and inflation.
Falls: the war destroys capital and raises taxes and inflation.
The crash wipes out paper fortunes in the United States, where the top tenth's share falls after 1929, and Mexico's land reform resumes; at world scale the share barely moves.
The great levelling of the world wars: destruction, inflation, high taxes and expropriation in Japan, Europe and Eastern Europe.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) and the Soviet bloc's expropriations take the wealth of the landlords and owners.
Bolivia's revolution (1952 to 1953) takes the great tin mines and the haciendas, as China's land reform has done on a far larger scale.
Turns up: privatisation, financial deregulation and rising asset prices.
The privatisation of Soviet-bloc property after 1991 creates new fortunes.
The World Inequality Report 2022 puts the richest tenth's share of world wealth at about 76%, as recalled.

The Roman trade with India at its height: by Strabo about 120 ships a year sail from Myos Hormos, the Muziris papyrus prices one cargo at about 7 million sesterces, and Han silk reaches Rome through Parthia and the Kushans. A small rise over the value at 1, within the band.
The Antonine plague (from 165) kills perhaps a tenth of the Roman Empire's people and the trade begins to ebb; whether it was the turn in the Indian Ocean trade or only a pause is debated.

The Arab conquests (from 632) join the Sasanian and much of the Byzantine trading world under one rule, and Srivijaya (from 671) comes to hold the Malacca strait for the trade between China and India. The share stays about one percent. Pirenne's thesis that Islam cut the Mediterranean's trade is set against the alternative that the trade had already shrunk with the Roman west, and that the caliphate's own trade grew: the band carries both.

Gains and losses about cancel at world scale.

upsert.lens: To follow the parts of understanding that move apart: the time spent being taught (schooling), the command of number (numeracy), the making of new knowledge (discovery) and, added now, language, which the last record of this carve named as still without a home. The breadth check names the society group's Events of residential schools and the stolen generations, which took children from their languages, and the model holds the spread of whole language families with farmers and herders (Bantu, Austronesian, Pama-Nyungan, the steppe migrations) linked to nothing that follows language. Range: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, followed as world measures of adults, of all living people or of the world's languages.

Open the language part of the understanding carve (r384) as a count of living languages, from the origin of Homo sapiens to 2025, on the same dates as the population series. Deep values scale with the number of people and the size of forager speech communities (about one language per 1,500 people, as Aboriginal Australia and New Guinea suggest); the floor of 1500 is today's count plus the losses documented since; the recent fall follows the catalogues' counts and measured rates of loss.

points.note: Perhaps 300,000 people in scattered groups across Africa. If they spoke languages as people do now, as the gradual view of language's origin holds, a few hundred communities of a thousand or two each; under the late view, that fully modern language arose only some 100,000 to 50,000 years ago, there were none in this sense, so the band runs to zero.
Dips with the people in the depth of the penultimate glacial: communities that die out or merge take their tongues with them.
By now even the late view grants full language; the lower band leaves zero.
Rises with the dispersal out of Africa: each group that moves into new land drifts into a tongue of its own within a thousand or two years.
The Last Glacial Maximum empties the northern ranges; their communities retreat south, and some vanish.
People enter the Americas: a few founding tongues begin to divide over a new hemisphere, which will hold some two thousand languages by 1492.

About 4.4 million foragers on every continent but Antarctica. At one language per 1,500 people, as Aboriginal Australia (about 250 languages for perhaps 750,000 people) and New Guinea suggest, some 3,000 languages. The alternative, that the world's languages were most numerous now, before farmers' and herders' language families spread over the foragers', needs speech communities of a few hundred and puts the count near today's: the upper band carries it.

The great spreads begin: steppe herders carry Indo-European west (from 3000 BCE), Austronesian farmers leave Taiwan, Bantu farmers leave the Cameroon borderlands soon after. Each absorbs many forager tongues, but each also splits into hundreds as it spreads (Bantu into about 500, Austronesian into about 1,200), so with the farmers of the tropics multiplying the count goes on rising.

Pama-Nyungan has spread over seven eighths of Australia, replacing or absorbing the languages there; Akkadian is the language of rule over the Sumerian cities, and Sumerian is dying as a spoken tongue.

Levels off: in the empires Latin, Greek, Aramaic, Chinese and the Prakrits replace many tongues, while Bantu, Austronesian, Amazonian and New Guinean communities go on dividing theirs. Whether the world's count peaked about now or before farming spread is the debate the band carries.
Latin has replaced Gaulish, Iberian and Etruscan in the western provinces; Bantu speakers reach Natal; Malagasy begins on Madagascar.

Turns down slowly: after the conquests Arabic replaces Aramaic, Coptic and much of Berber, Turkic spreads over Iranian-speaking Central Asia, and Chinese moves south; East Polynesia's settlement adds only a few.

The floor is today's count, about 7,150, plus the losses that can be traced since: about a thousand in the Americas, which held some two thousand languages at contact and keep about a thousand, more than a hundred in Australia, and several hundred in Africa, Asia, Europe and the Pacific. Languages that vanished unrecorded raise the upper band.
The Taino languages of the Greater Antilles are dying with their speakers.
Falls: smallpox and conquest destroy whole peoples of the Caribbean, Mexico and the Andes' margins, and their tongues with them, while Nahuatl and Quechua spread as the missions' common languages.
Settlers' frontiers in North America, Australia, southern Africa and Siberia: the Tasmanian languages and many of California's die within a generation of the frontier's arrival.
Residential and mission schools in North America and Australia punish children for speaking their own languages; the loss shows a generation later, as the last who learned them die.

The fall quickens: the last speakers of many Australian, North American and Siberian languages die, children no longer learning them after the schools of the decades before, and national languages spread with radio and mass schooling.
Revivals begin, Maori language nests from 1982 and Hawaiian immersion schools from 1984: they keep languages from dying, but do not add to the count.

Ethnologue counts about 7,160 living languages and Glottolog a few hundred more by its own rules; about two fifths are endangered, and some two dozen are the first language of half of humanity. Losses run at roughly one language every one to three months (Bromham and colleagues, 2022), faster than the long average since 1500 of about three a year.
