upsert.boundary: The Bantu expansion, about 2500 BCE to 500 CE
upsert.description: Farmers speaking Bantu languages move out of the borderlands of Cameroon and Nigeria, through the rainforest to the Great Lakes by about 500 BCE, and on to the Limpopo and Natal by about 300 to 500 CE, with yams and oil palm, then cereals, cattle and iron. They absorb or displace most foragers. Some 350 million Africans speak Bantu languages today.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its routes are argued from languages, archaeology and genomes together
sources to check: Vansina 1995, Journal of African History 36; Grollemund et al. 2015, PNAS 112; Patin et al. 2017, Science 356
upsert.region: Africa: Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa, from Western Africa

upsert.boundary: The Dutch Cape Colony, 1652 to 1806
upsert.description: The Dutch East India Company's supply station at the Cape grows into a colony of settlers and enslaved people from Asia and Africa; the Khoekhoe lose their land and, in the smallpox of 1713, most of their people; trekboer herders push the frontier east until it meets the Xhosa. Britain takes the colony in 1806.
provenance: sources to check: Ross, A Concise History of South Africa (2nd ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: Ibn Battuta's travels, 1325 to 1354
upsert.description: A scholar from Tangier travels about 120,000 kilometres through the Islamic world and beyond, from Mecca to India, China, the Swahili coast and Mali, and dictates the Rihla: a portrait of a connected Afro-Eurasia before and during the Black Death.
provenance: sources to check: Dunn, The Adventures of Ibn Battuta (1986)
upsert.region: Africa: Northern Africa (Morocco), Western Africa (Mali), Eastern Africa; Asia; Southern Europe (al-Andalus)

upsert.boundary: The New Laws and the Valladolid debate, 1542 to 1551
upsert.description: Pressed by Bartolomé de las Casas, Spain bans the enslavement of Native Americans and limits the encomienda; at Valladolid Las Casas and Sepúlveda debate whether conquest is just: an early argument over universal rights, followed by forced labour under other names.
provenance: sources to check: Hanke, All Mankind Is One (1974)

upsert.boundary: The Taíno of the Greater Antilles destroyed, 1493 to 1520
upsert.description: Forced into gold mining and farm labour under the encomienda, hit by war, famine and, from 1518, smallpox, the Taíno of Hispaniola fall from perhaps several hundred thousand to a few thousand within a generation; the Spanish raid the Bahamas and the mainland for slaves to replace them.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Hispaniola's 1492 population is estimated from about 100,000 to several million
sources to check: Reséndez, The Other Slavery (2016); Livi Bacci 2003, Hispanic American Historical Review 83
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica)

upsert.boundary: The race to the South Pole, December 1911 to January 1912
upsert.description: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party, using dogs and skis, reaches the South Pole on 14 December 1911; Robert Falcon Scott's British party arrives on 17 January 1912 and dies on the return march.
provenance: sources to check: Huntford, Scott and Amundsen (1979)

upsert.boundary: The Waitangi Tribunal and the Maori renaissance, from 1975
upsert.description: The land march of 1975 and the occupation of Bastion Point (1977 to 1978) come with the Waitangi Tribunal (1975), empowered from 1985 to hear claims back to 1840; Crown settlements from the 1990s return land and money to iwi such as Tainui and Ngai Tahu, and kohanga reo (1982) and Maori-language schools revive te reo, an official language since 1987.
provenance: sources to check: Walker, Ka Whawhai Tonu Matou (1990); Orange, The Treaty of Waitangi (2nd ed. 2011)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Pama-Nyungan languages spread across most of Australia, about 4000 to 2000 BCE
upsert.description: One language family, Pama-Nyungan, spreads from the Gulf country across seven-eighths of the continent, displacing or absorbing others everywhere but the north; a phylogenetic study dates its origin about 6,000 years ago. Whether it spread with migrating people or by people changing language, with little movement, is debated: Aboriginal genomes show deep regional continuity.
provenance: exploring: its date and manner of spread are debated
sources to check: Bouckaert et al. 2018, Nature Ecology and Evolution 2; Malaspinas et al. 2016, Nature 538

upsert.boundary: The 'social laboratory': arbitration, pensions and labour parties, about 1890 to 1910
upsert.description: After the great strikes of 1890 to 1894, the colonies and then the Commonwealth build compulsory arbitration courts (New Zealand 1894), old-age pensions (New Zealand 1898, Australia 1908) and, in the Harvester judgment (1907), a legal basic wage for a family; Australia has the world's first national Labor government (1904), and observers from Europe and America come to study the 'social laboratory'.
provenance: sources to check: Castles, The Working Class and Welfare (1985); Macintyre (2016)

upsert.boundary: The Austronesian expansion, about 3000 BCE to 1300 CE
upsert.description: Rice- and millet-farming speakers of Austronesian languages sail from Taiwan into the Philippines and Indonesia, then east into the Pacific and west to Madagascar, in outrigger and double canoes; by 1300 their languages are spoken across more than half the globe's longitude, from Madagascar to Rapa Nui.
provenance: sources to check: Bellwood, First Islanders (2017); Gray, Drummond and Greenhill 2009, Science 323
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern Asia: Taiwan; South-eastern Asia); Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia, New Zealand); Africa (Eastern Africa: Madagascar)

upsert.boundary: Herders from the steppe move into Europe, about 3000 to 2300 BCE
upsert.description: Yamnaya-descended herders with wagons, and perhaps plague, move west from the Pontic steppe; their descendants of the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker cultures replace most of the ancestry of central and northern Europe, in Britain some 90% within a few centuries, and probably carry the Indo-European languages.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the role of plague is debated
sources to check: Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522; Olalde et al. 2018, Nature 555; Rasmussen et al. 2015, Cell 163
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern, Central, Northern and Western Europe)

upsert.boundary: Boarding and residential schools for Native children, 1879 to 1996
upsert.description: The United States, from the Carlisle school (1879), and Canada, through church-run residential schools made compulsory in 1920, take Native children from their families to strip them of their languages and religions; about 150,000 children pass through Canada's schools, the last of which closes in 1996, and thousands die in them. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2015) calls the system cultural genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada, Final Report (2015); Adams, Education for Extinction (1995)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States and Canada)

upsert.boundary: Māori Aotearoa before Cook, about 1280 to 1769
upsert.description: Polynesian settlers adapt to a cool, large land: they hunt moa and seals, then grow kumara and fern root, build fortified pā and form iwi and hapū that compete for land and mana, developing a Māori culture distinct from the tropical Pacific's.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Binney and Harris, Tangata Whenua (2014)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Pacific Islanders recruited for the Queensland cane fields, 1863 to 1906
upsert.description: Some 62,000 men and women from Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands are recruited, many by deception or force ('blackbirding'), to work on Queensland's sugar plantations; most are deported under the White Australia policy after 1906.
upsert.region: Oceania (Melanesia: Vanuatu, Solomon Islands; Australia and New Zealand: Australia)

upsert.boundary: The stolen generations, about 1910 to 1970
upsert.description: Under government policies of 'protection' and assimilation, perhaps one in ten to one in three Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are taken from their families and raised in institutions or by white families; a national apology follows in 2008.
provenance: sources to check: Bringing Them Home report (1997)

upsert.boundary: The Hawaiian renaissance and sovereignty movement, from 1970
upsert.description: Native Hawaiians revive voyaging, hula and the Hawaiian language, banned as a medium of schooling since 1896: immersion preschools (Punana Leo, from 1984) bring back a language that only a few hundred children still spoke; protests end the navy's bombing of Kaho'olawe (1990), the United States apologizes for the overthrow of the kingdom (1993), and the stand against a telescope on Mauna Kea (2019) draws thousands.
provenance: sources to check: Trask, From a Native Daughter (1993); Wilson and Kamana 2001, in Hinton and Hale (eds.), The Green Book of Language Revitalization
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: Palmares, about 1605 to 1695
upsert.description: In the hills of Alagoas, people who escaped Pernambuco's sugar estates build a federation of quilombo villages, perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 strong at its height, that defeats Dutch and Portuguese expeditions for most of a century; it falls to a bandeirante army in 1694, and its leader Zumbi is killed in 1695. The day of his death, 20 November, is Black Consciousness Day in Brazil.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its numbers are uncertain
sources to check: Anderson 1996, Journal of Latin American Studies 28

Widen, the breadth check's society group and the new language measure. Society: the New Laws free enslaved Native Americans in law (bondage); the Cape Colony brings the Cape under the Company with enslaved labour (colonial rule in Africa, bondage); Palmares is people escaping bondage; blackbirding is compelled work and migration into Australia; the social laboratory's arbitration courts and basic wage set the terms of work for an employer; Maori Aotearoa extends Oceania's range and its people; residential schools and the stolen generations take children from their languages (living languages). Language: the Bantu, Austronesian, Pama-Nyungan and steppe spreads carry language families over foragers' tongues, and the Taino die with theirs. The Hawaiian and Maori revivals and Ibn Battuta's travels and the race to the South Pole show a state without changing it, and are observations. The Atlantic slave trade near its peak, about 80,000 people a year, and serfdom extended to Ukraine (1783), while the American Revolution opens the age of revolutions whose language of liberty will be turned against slavery.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery in 1794, while the cotton gin (1793) begins the expansion of slavery in the United States and the slave trade still runs near its peak.

Haiti's independence (1804) ends slavery for about half a million people, while Usman dan Fodio's jihad (from 1804) founds the Sokoto caliphate on plantation slavery; at world scale the share drifts down.

Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees about 800,000 people in the Caribbean, the Cape and Mauritius, and Spanish America's republics free theirs slowly by law; the world share keeps drifting down.

A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.

No one reaches Antarctica for almost all of human history.
Cook crosses the Antarctic Circle (1773) and circles the continent without seeing it.
Antarctica is first sighted (January 1820); sealers land on the South Shetlands the next summer.
Sealers work the South Shetlands and the Peninsula's islands each summer until the fur seals are nearly gone (by the 1830s).
Sealers' seasonal camps on the South Shetland beaches.
Argentina's station on Laurie Island (1904), the first held year round, and the whalers' station at Deception Island (from 1906).
Unchanged: Amundsen's and Scott's parties reach the Pole and leave no station; the land in use is still the whalers' shore stations and Laurie Island.
Britain's Operation Tabarin (1944) sets up the first permanent bases on the Antarctic Peninsula.
The IGY's fifty stations, from McMurdo to Vostok, bring most of the coastal oases and the dry valleys within regular reach.
The treaty (December 1959) keeps the IGY's stations open for science under shared rules.
The International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958) and the treaty that followed put some forty stations on the continent and field parties into the dry valleys.
About seventy stations and the field science of the treaty's members reach most of the ice-free ground at least in summer.

The alternative, that the world's languages were most numerous now, before farmers' and herders' language families spread over the foragers', needs speech communities of a few hundred and puts the count near today's: the upper band carries it.

The great spreads begin: steppe herders carry Indo-European west (from 3000 BCE), Austronesian farmers leave Taiwan, Bantu farmers leave the Cameroon borderlands soon after. Each absorbs many forager tongues, but each also splits into hundreds as it spreads (Bantu into about 500, Austronesian into about 1,200), so with the farmers of the tropics multiplying the count goes on rising.

Pama-Nyungan has spread over seven eighths of Australia, replacing or absorbing the languages there; Akkadian is the language of rule over the Sumerian cities, and Sumerian is dying as a spoken tongue.

Levels off: in the empires Latin, Greek, Aramaic, Chinese and the Prakrits replace many tongues, while Bantu, Austronesian, Amazonian and New Guinean communities go on dividing theirs. Whether the world's count peaked about now or before farming spread is the debate the band carries.
Latin has replaced Gaulish, Iberian and Etruscan in the western provinces; Bantu speakers reach Natal; Malagasy begins on Madagascar.

Turns down slowly: after the conquests Arabic replaces Aramaic, Coptic and much of Berber, Turkic spreads over Iranian-speaking Central Asia, and Chinese moves south; East Polynesia's settlement adds only a few.

The floor is today's count, about 7,150, plus the losses that can be traced since: about a thousand in the Americas, which held some two thousand languages at contact and keep about a thousand, more than a hundred in Australia, and several hundred in Africa, Asia, Europe and the Pacific. Languages that vanished unrecorded raise the upper band.
The Taino languages of the Greater Antilles are dying with their speakers.
Falls: smallpox and conquest destroy whole peoples of the Caribbean, Mexico and the Andes' margins, and their tongues with them, while Nahuatl and Quechua spread as the missions' common languages.
Settlers' frontiers in North America, Australia, southern Africa and Siberia: the Tasmanian languages and many of California's die within a generation of the frontier's arrival.

Carlisle (1879) opens the boarding schools; the abolitions in Cuba and Brazil free people whose African languages survive by now mostly in ritual, as Lucumi in Cuba and the songs of Candomble in Bahia.
Residential and mission schools in North America and Australia punish children for speaking their own languages; the loss shows a generation later, as the last who learned them die.

The fall quickens: the last speakers of many Australian, North American and Siberian languages die, children no longer learning them after the schools of the decades before, and national languages spread with radio and mass schooling.

Papua New Guinea becomes independent (1975) with more than 800 languages, about a ninth of the world's, and uses Tok Pisin, Hiri Motu and English to govern them; the Waitangi Tribunal (1975) opens the Maori renaissance. Neither changes the count, which falls by several languages a year.
Tuvalu's parting from Kiribati follows the line between Polynesian Tuvaluan and Micronesian Gilbertese; it changes no language's survival.
Revivals begin, Maori language nests from 1982 and Hawaiian immersion schools from 1984: they keep languages from dying, but do not add to the count.

Ethnologue counts about 7,160 living languages and Glottolog a few hundred more by its own rules; about two fifths are endangered, and some two dozen are the first language of half of humanity. Losses run at roughly one language every one to three months (Bromham and colleagues, 2022), faster than the long average since 1500 of about three a year.

upsert.reason: Before writing no language is recorded: deep values are the number of people divided by the size of forager speech communities, with bands that also carry the debate over when language began. After 1500 they are today's count plus the losses that can be traced.

upsert.lens: To follow the two halves of the hemisphere whose migrants rise and fall apart, which one share hides: the Africans of the slave trade and the Iberian settlers in Latin America and the Caribbean for three centuries, the mass migration to the United States and Canada after 1845, the European migrants to Argentina and Brazil whose count rose while the United States' quotas cut the north's, and since 1965 the north's climb and, lately, Venezuela's exodus. The deepen check names this process (14 Events, values mostly sketched). Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living Homo sapiens, over the two parts of the Americas in the UN M49 standard (Northern America, 021; Latin America and the Caribbean, 419) by 2026 borders.

changes.value: Open the two parts of the carve of r393 at every date of the whole, so that they sum to it. The whole is left as it is; each date's split follows the people of each half before 1492, the colonies' and the slave trade's counts after, the national censuses from 1850 (the United States, Canada, Argentina, Brazil) and the UN's migrant stock from 1960, as recalled. Bands are the whole's, widened by the uncertainty of the split.

points.note: Claims of people in South America this early (Pedra Furada) are contested; the band allows a few.
Monte Verde in southern Chile is occupied about 14,500 years ago: people have reached the far south within a few centuries, or earlier.
The Aztec and Inca states move conquered peoples; the Inca mitmaq resettle whole communities across today's lines from Ecuador to Chile.
The first Spanish settlers and enslaved Africans reach Hispaniola and Cuba.
Iberian settlers and Africans in Mexico, Peru, Brazil and the islands, as the Americas' own peoples die of epidemics: nearly all the hemisphere's migrants.
Brazil's gold rush begins (1690s) with Portuguese migrants and more enslaved Africans.
The slave trade at its height lands 60,000 to 80,000 Africans a year in Brazil and the Caribbean, where the African-born stay most of the enslaved because deaths outrun births.
Saint-Domingue's revolution ends imports there; Cuba and Brazil take more.
Brazil ends its slave trade (1850): its African-born, the largest group of migrants in Latin America, begin to age out.
The low point: the African-born of Brazil and Cuba are dying, and the European mass migration to the south has only begun.
Italians and Spaniards pour into Argentina and Uruguay, Italians and Portuguese into Sao Paulo's coffee lands.
Argentina's census of 1914 counts 2.4 million foreign-born, three in ten of its people, the highest share of any large country.
Europe's displaced people and Spain's and Italy's poor sail again for Buenos Aires, Sao Paulo and Caracas.
About six million by the UN's count, a third of the hemisphere's migrants: the south's highest share since the 1840s.
About seven million: the European-born of the old migration die out, and Latin America now sends more people north than it receives.
The low point as a share of humanity, about six and a half million.
Jumps: about five million Venezuelans have left since 2015, most of them to Colombia, Peru, Brazil, Chile and Ecuador; the UN counts about 15 million migrants in Latin America and the Caribbean.
About 17 million, with nearly eight million Venezuelans abroad.
All of the hemisphere's movers, if the White Sands footprints' dates hold, are in what is now Northern America.
The first Americans come from Beringia along the coast or the ice-free corridor; most of the hemisphere's people are still in the north, though Monte Verde in Chile is already occupied.
With the hemisphere peopled to Tierra del Fuego, its movers follow its people, about a third of them north of the Rio Grande.
Falls as a part of the whole as Mesoamerica's and the Andes' farmers grow far denser than the north's foragers.
Cahokia and the Mississippian towns draw people from across the mid-continent.
A few thousand Europeans at St Augustine, in New Mexico and on the St Lawrence: almost all the hemisphere's newcomers are in the Spanish and Portuguese lands.
Virginia, Maryland, New England and New Netherland hold some fifty thousand colonists, most of them born in England, against several hundred thousand Africans and Iberians in the south.
German, Scots-Irish and English settlers and enslaved Africans in the thirteen colonies: about a fifth of the hemisphere's migrants.
The United States has ended its slave trade (1808): its African-born age out, while Brazil and Cuba still import; the north holds about a third.
The Irish famine emigration begins: the north's part rises past half.
The United States counts 2.24 million foreign-born and British North America about half a million: two thirds of the hemisphere's migrants.
The United States counts 5.6 million foreign-born: four fifths of the hemisphere's migrants, the north's highest share before 1990.
The United States' 13.5 million foreign-born and Canada's 1.6 million: the north's peak as a share of humanity until the 1990s.
Turns down: the quota acts of 1921 and 1924 cut arrivals by four fifths, and the foreign-born age.
The United States counts 10.3 million foreign-born (1950) and Canada 2.1 million.
The trough: about 12.5 million by the UN's count, the European-born of the great migration dying out.
The Hart-Celler Act ends the national-origins quotas.
About 28 million by the UN's count.
About 40 million: 86% of the hemisphere's migrants, the north's highest share.
About 59 million by the UN's count; growth slows as arrivals from Mexico fall after 2007.
About 61 million: a fifth of the world's migrants, a slightly smaller share of humanity than in 2020.

changes.value: Check the parts against the whole: migrants living in the Americas (h.connection.migration.americas) is, by its parts' own definitions, the sum of migrants living in Northern America and in Latin America and the Caribbean, in the same unit (% of all living people), and the two M49 halves cover the hemisphere without overlap (MECE#ae19). Declared a sum so the report compares them at every date; the 2025 value is re-recorded unchanged to carry the declaration. At r394 the parts already sum to the whole at every one of the 86 dates.

upsert.boundary: The California gold rush, 1848 to 1855
upsert.description: About 300,000 people pour into California from across the world; the Native Californian population, already halved under Spanish missions, falls from perhaps 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killing, disease and starvation.
provenance: sources to check: Madley, An American Genocide (2016)

upsert.boundary: Latin American migration to the United States, from 1965
upsert.description: The 1965 immigration act ends national-origin quotas, and the end of the Bracero programme (1964) pushes Mexican labour migration outside the law; Mexicans, then Cubans, Dominicans, Central Americans, Colombians and Venezuelans move north, and the Hispanic share of the United States rises from about 4% (1960) to about 19% (2020), some 62 million people. Remittances become a mainstay of Mexico's and Central America's economies, while enforcement and the politics of the border harden from the 1990s.
provenance: sources to check: Massey, Durand and Malone, Beyond Smoke and Mirrors (2002); Pew Research Center, Hispanic population estimates
upsert.region: The Americas: Latin America and the Caribbean to Northern America

upsert.boundary: Venezuela's collapse and exodus, from 2013
upsert.description: Falling oil prices, price controls and Maduro's authoritarian rule shrink Venezuela's economy by about three quarters; nearly eight million people, about a quarter of the population, leave, the largest displacement in the Americas' modern history.
provenance: sources to check: R4V Inter-Agency Coordination Platform reports (2024)
upsert.region: The Americas: South America (Venezuela, Colombia, Peru)

upsert.boundary: The great European emigration, 1815 to 1914
upsert.description: Some 50 to 55 million Europeans, Irish, British, Germans, Scandinavians, Italians, Poles, Jews and others, leave for the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, driven by land hunger, famine and persecution and drawn by wages, cheap land and steamships.
provenance: sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)
upsert.region: Europe; Americas; Oceania (Australia and New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852
upsert.description: Potato blight destroys the crop of a people who live on it; about a million die of hunger and disease and over a million emigrate, while food is exported and relief is grudging; Ireland's population falls by a quarter and keeps falling for a century.
provenance: sources to check: Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond (1999)

upsert.boundary: Indentured labour from India and China, 1838 to 1917
upsert.description: After emancipation, planters bring workers bound by contracts of five years or more: about 240,000 Indians to British Guiana, about 145,000 to Trinidad, others to Suriname, Jamaica and the French islands; about 125,000 Chinese to Cuba (1847 to 1874) and about 100,000 to Peru's guano islands and plantations. Their descendants are the largest group in Guyana and Trinidad today.
provenance: sources to check: Northrup, Indentured Labor in the Age of Imperialism (1995); Hu-DeHart 1993, Slavery and Abolition 14
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean and South America; Asia: Southern and Eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: The great immigration, 1880 to 1924
upsert.description: About 25 million immigrants arrive in the United States, most from southern and eastern Europe (Italians, Poles, Jews from the Russian empire), others from Scandinavia, Germany, Ireland, Mexico and, until the exclusion act of 1882, China; by 1910 about one American in seven was born abroad. Canada takes another three million, many of them to the prairies. They work the mines, mills and building sites of the industrial cities.
provenance: sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)

upsert.boundary: The United States restricts immigration, 1921 to 1924
upsert.description: Quota acts limit arrivals by national origin to a small share of each group's numbers in the census of 1890, cutting immigration from southern and eastern Europe by about nine tenths and barring Asians altogether; Mexicans and Canadians stay outside the quotas. Mass immigration to the United States ends for forty years.
provenance: sources to check: Ngai, Impossible Subjects (2004)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Polynesian diaspora, from 1962
upsert.description: Samoans, Tongans, Cook Islanders and Niueans migrate to New Zealand, Australia and the United States for work; by the 2000s more Cook Islanders and Niueans live in New Zealand than at home, and remittances are among the largest shares of national income in the world for Tonga and Samoa.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, remittance data; Lee and Francis (eds.), Migration and Transnationalism (2009)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: Hawai'i's sugar plantations and their workers, 1850 to 1946
upsert.description: Planters bring some 400,000 contract workers from China, Japan, Portugal, Korea and the Philippines; by 1900 Japanese are the largest group in the islands and Native Hawaiians, about 40,000, a minority; the reciprocity treaty with the United States (1875), renewed in 1887 in return for Pearl Harbor, gives Hawaiian sugar free entry.
provenance: sources to check: Takaki, Pau Hana (1983)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (Hawai'i); the Americas: Northern America by 2026 borders

upsert.boundary: Argentina's export boom and mass immigration, 1880 to 1914
upsert.description: Railways built with British capital open the pampas, taken from their Indigenous peoples in the Conquest of the Desert (1878 to 1885), to wheat and to cattle shipped as chilled beef; about four million immigrants arrive, mostly Italians and Spaniards, and by 1914 a third of the people of Argentina are foreign-born. Growth puts Argentina among the ten or so richest countries per person by 1913 on Maddison's figures, a ranking some economists think overstated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the ranking is debated
sources to check: Della Paolera and Taylor (eds.), A New Economic History of Argentina (2003); Maddison Project Database

upsert.boundary: Coffee makes São Paulo, 1850 to 1930
upsert.description: Coffee spreads from the Paraíba valley onto the red soils of São Paulo, and Brazil grows most of the world's coffee, at first with enslaved labour and, after the slave trade's end (1850) and abolition (1888), with about two million subsidized immigrants from Italy, Portugal, Spain and Japan. Coffee money builds São Paulo's railways and first factories, and the collapse of its price in 1929 helps bring Vargas to power.
provenance: sources to check: Holloway, Immigrants on the Land (1980); Dean, The Industrialization of São Paulo (1969)

upsert.boundary: Re-education camps and the boat people, 1975 to 1996
upsert.description: After the fall of Saigon the victors send hundreds of thousands of former officials and officers to re-education camps, and from 1978, as Vietnam turns on its ethnic Chinese and on private trade, people flee by sea. About 800,000 reach Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Hong Kong and the Philippines, and many die at sea of storms and pirates, estimates running from tens of thousands to 200,000 or more. Most are resettled in the United States, Canada, Australia and France under the Geneva agreements of 1979 and the Comprehensive Plan of Action (1989), which ends in 1996.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths at sea are unknown and debated
sources to check: Robinson, Terms of Refuge (1998); UNHCR, The State of the World's Refugees 2000
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam and the countries of first asylum), Eastern Asia (Hong Kong)

upsert.boundary: The transatlantic slave trade, 1501 to 1867.
upsert.description: About 12.5 million Africans are embarked for the Americas, of whom about 10.7 million survive the crossing; the plantations they are forced to work grow the sugar and the cotton of the Atlantic economy.
provenance: inferred: the voyages database's totals, as recalled

Northern America: the California gold rush, the Irish famine's emigrants, the great immigration of 1880 to 1924, the quota acts that ended it, Latin American migration north from 1965, the boat people resettled in the United States and Canada, and, by 2026 borders, Hawai'i's plantation workers and the Polynesians who moved to the United States. Latin America and the Caribbean: Venezuela's exodus (to Colombia, Peru, Brazil, Chile and Ecuador), the indentured Indians and Chinese of the Caribbean, Guyana and Peru, Argentina's boom and Sao Paulo's coffee migrants. Both halves: the great European emigration of 1815 to 1914 (the United States and Canada, Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay) and the Atlantic slave trade, nine tenths of whose survivors were landed in Brazil and the Caribbean and about a twentieth in the thirteen colonies and the United States. Every other field of each Event is restated as the model holds it at r394, read back from an export of the model.

upsert.lens: To follow who keeps the makers of art, which one number hides: for five thousand years nearly all were kept by rulers, nobles and temples; markets of buyers and paying audiences grew from the Song cities, the Renaissance workshops, Edo's theatres and the printed book until they kept most makers by about 1820; and after 1917 and 1945 public bodies (the Soviet and Chinese state troupes, Europe's subsidized theatres and orchestras, the state broadcasters) kept a quarter or more, until the Soviet system's end. The deepen check names this process first (16 Events, every value sketched). Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living Homo sapiens: zero before anyone was kept for the arts, and the kept makers of chiefdoms, temple states, empires, markets and modern states after.

changes.value: Opens the three parts of the carve of the arts' makers (carve.concept.humanity.wants.play.makers, r397) at every date of h.play.makers, so that they sum to it: kept by patrons, living from markets, kept by public bodies. Each date's split is a share of the parent's value, the market part taken as the remainder so the sum holds exactly; the shares are sketched from what is recalled of courts, temples, markets and state arts systems (Blanning, The Triumph of Music; Baumol and Bowen; Scherer, Quarter Notes and Bank Notes; Soviet and Chinese arts administration), not from any series, and share one foundation with the parent (EvidenceDependence#23ca). Bands are the parent's band times the share, widened for the split.

points.note: Begins: musicians and jewellers who sell their work or play for hire in Mesopotamia's cities beside the temple and palace dependants.
Greek vase painters, sculptors and travelling poets and players sell to many buyers across the Mediterranean.
A tenth of all makers: Rome's actors, mimes, charioteers and copyists' workshops, and the entertainers of Han cities, paid by crowds and buyers.
Falls with the cities of the western empire and their theatres.
Rises with the Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds: about a sixth of all makers.
London's and Madrid's commercial theatres, Antwerp's and later Amsterdam's open picture market, printed books' authors and printed images: three makers in ten live from buyers and audiences.
Edo's and Osaka's kabuki and puppet theatres and the ukiyo-e print trade join Europe's markets.
Markets now keep more makers than patrons do: public concerts, publishers of music and novels, theatres run for profit.
Music halls, vaudeville, the illustrated press and the first professional sport.
Hollywood's studios, commercial radio's singers and bands, the record companies and sport as a profession: three quarters of all makers.
War takes performers into the forces and closes commercial theatres across occupied Europe and Asia.
Falls as a share while the communist states take their theatres, studios and troupes into public hands; it still keeps most makers.
Rises as the post-Soviet states and China's reformed troupes push makers onto the market.
The pandemic falls on market makers: closed venues and cancelled seasons cost freelance performers most of a year's work, while salaried public makers keep their posts.
About three quarters of all makers: the self-employed, the film, music, games and publishing industries and professional sport.

upsert.reason: The parent's value less the patrons' and public bodies' parts at each date: zero before about 2200 BCE, a few per cent in antiquity, a sixth in the Song cities, a third by 1650, most of all makers from about 1820, three quarters now.

points.note: Zero, as the parent: no forager band keeps anyone to make art.
If anyone was kept to carve Göbekli Tepe's pillars, it was by the leaders of the feasts that raised them: patrons, not buyers.
Chiefs keep the first craftsmen of fine things: Varna's goldsmiths, Ubaid's temple painters.
Every kept maker is a dependant of a temple or palace workshop in Sumer and Egypt.
Dips with the palaces of the Bronze Age collapse.

Near the level it keeps for the next seventeen centuries: the Han court's Music Bureau, Rome's imperial and senatorial households and the temples of every empire keep about 450 to 475 makers per million people.
Falls with Rome's western patrons; the Gupta, Sasanian and southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Its peak per person, barely above the first century's: the Mughal, Safavid, Ottoman and Ming ateliers and Europe's courts and churches.
Falls: the French Revolution ends the court's and the Church's patronage in France, and secularization strips German and Austrian monasteries and prince-bishops of theirs.
Britain's punitive expedition sacks Benin City and ends the royal guilds of casters and carvers.
The Russian, Austrian, German and Ottoman courts are gone; the Russian revolution ends aristocratic patronage across a sixth of the world's land.
India's princely states are merged into the republic (1947 to 1949) and their courts' musicians and painters lose their keepers.
About a twentieth of all makers: church musicians, royal and princely households, private patrons and foundations' commissions.

upsert.reason: The parent's value times the patrons' share: all of it until markets appear, nine tenths in antiquity, three quarters in 1500, half by 1800, a tenth by 1950, a twentieth now.

Rome's public games and theatres, paid partly from the treasury, partly by magistrates who count as patrons here.
The western cities' public games and theatres close.
Town musicians and civic painters of Europe's and Asia's self-governing cities: a fiftieth of all makers.
Court theatres begin to become national ones (Vienna's Burgtheater, 1776) and academies take state salaries.
Germany's and Austria's municipal theatres and orchestras, Europe's conservatories and academies: about a sixteenth of all makers.
Rises: the Soviet state takes the theatres, conservatories and studios into public hands (1919), and Germany's and Austria's court theatres become state theatres.
The New Deal's Federal Art, Music, Theatre and Writers' Projects employ about 40,000 makers (1935 to 1939), and the Soviet and fascist states' arts administrations grow.
Jumps: Eastern Europe's new regimes and the People's Republic of China (1949) take theatres, studios and troupes into public hands, and Western Europe's arts councils and public broadcasters grow.
Near its peak share, three tenths of all makers: China's thousands of state troupes, the Soviet bloc's theatres, studios and artists' unions, and Europe's subsidized stages and broadcasters.
The Cultural Revolution disbands or purges China's troupes and sends their members to the countryside, leaving the eight model works.
Falls: the Soviet system's end cuts state theatres, studios and unions across Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, and China begins to turn its troupes into enterprises.
Holds through the pandemic: salaried makers of state theatres, orchestras and broadcasters keep their posts while freelance performers lose their work.
About a sixth of all makers: public broadcasters, state and municipal theatres, orchestras and troupes, most of them in Europe and East Asia.

changes.value: Check the parts against the whole: the arts' makers (h.play.makers) is, by its parts' own definitions, the sum of makers kept by patrons, living from markets and kept by public bodies, in the same unit (people per million), each maker placed once by the source of most of their income (MECE#ae19). Declared a sum so the report compares them at every date; the 2025 value is re-recorded unchanged to carry the declaration.

Values inside two Events the arts' makers and its parts will be linked to, where the series held no date: the French Revolution (1789.35 to 1799.86), valued at 1795, and the Soviet Union's breakup (1991.62 to 1991.98), valued at 1991.8. Whole and parts at the same dates so the declared sum holds; each lies on the path between its neighbours except where the Event turns it.

points.note: Zero by the measure's definition: no forager band keeps anyone to make art. The beads, engravings and paintings of the Stone Age were made by people whose main work was getting food.
Sunghir's burials, with thousands of ivory beads that took thousands of hours to make, show great effort spent on ornament, but nothing shows anyone kept for the work.

Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars (from about 9500 BCE) are raised by foragers' communal labour, perhaps with a few carvers who did little else; whether anyone was kept for the work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Chiefdoms begin to keep craftsmen: the goldsmiths behind Varna's graves (about 4500 BCE), the builders and painters of Ubaid Mesopotamia's temples.
The temple and palace workshops of Sumer and Egypt keep the first full-time sculptors, painters, musicians and goldsmiths; perhaps a fifth of humanity now lives under such courts.
Minoan Crete's palaces keep fresco painters, seal-cutters and goldsmiths beside Egypt's and Mesopotamia's workshops.
Olmec rulers at San Lorenzo keep the sculptors of the colossal heads: makers of art are now kept in the Americas too.
The tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, the Shang bronze-casters, the palace painters of Crete and the Olmec sculptors: courts on three continents now keep makers of art.
Greek cities' festivals keep poets, actors and sculptors, and the Persian, Indian and Chinese courts their musicians and craftsmen.

Rome's theatres, games and workshops and the Han court's Music Bureau, about 800 musicians before 7 BCE: a few makers in every thousand people of the great cities, about one in two thousand people worldwide.
Gupta India's court poets, dramatists and temple sculptors (Kalidasa wrote about 400) rise as Rome's western patrons fail.
Falls with Rome in the west: theatres, games and the patrons who paid for them close; Gupta India, Sasanian Iran and the southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds, beside the courts of the Abbasids, the Fatimids and Heian Japan.
The Black Death and the Mongol wars kill makers and patrons alike.
The workshops of Italy and the Netherlands, the Mughal and Safavid ateliers, Ming porcelain and printed images: art is made for markets as well as for patrons.
Between 1789 and 1800 on the line; inside it the Revolution moves makers from the court and the Church to the market and the new state's festivals.
Theatres, music halls, the illustrated press and the publishers' authors grow with the cities of the industrial world.
Cinema: the picture houses' actors and pit musicians, and the first professional footballers and boxers.
Hollywood's studios, radio's orchestras and singers, and sport as a profession.
War takes performers into the forces and closes theatres in occupied Europe and Asia.
The pandemic closes theatres, concert halls and stadiums; live performers lose most of a year's work.
About twenty million people of some 3.6 billion workers: artists, musicians, actors, writers, dancers, players of sport and makers of art wares.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned: zero among foragers by definition; a few hundred per million under the agrarian states' courts and temples, bounded by the surplus that keeps them (SurplusBound#7fe3); a few thousand per million now. The 2025 value rests on the recalled count of about 30 million jobs in the cultural and creative industries in 2013 (UNESCO and EY), of which the makers themselves are perhaps two thirds; to be checked. Where the line falls between a maker of art wares and a maker of ordinary goods moves every value before 1900 by a factor of two either way.

upsert.boundary: Britain sacks Benin City, 1897
upsert.description: A punitive expedition burns Benin City, exiles the oba and carries off thousands of bronzes and ivories to London, now argued over in claims for their return.
provenance: sources to check: Hicks, The Brutish Museums (2020)

upsert.boundary: Ife's bronze and terracotta heads, about 1100 to 1450
upsert.description: The Yoruba city of Ile-Ife, sacred as the place of creation, casts naturalistic heads in copper alloy and terracotta of a skill that astonished the Europeans who first saw them in 1910.
provenance: sources to check: Blier, Art and Risk in Ancient Yoruba (2015)

upsert.boundary: The bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu, about 850 to 950
upsert.description: Intricate cast bronzes, beads from as far as Egypt or India, and a burial of a titled man in south-eastern Nigeria show wealth, craft and long-distance trade in the forest centuries before Benin.
provenance: sources to check: Shaw, Unearthing Igbo-Ukwu (1977)

upsert.boundary: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela, about 1181 to 1221
upsert.description: Under the Zagwe king Lalibela, eleven churches are carved down into the volcanic rock as a New Jerusalem, at a time when Jerusalem itself had fallen to Saladin.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the churches may have been cut over a longer span
sources to check: Phillipson, Ancient Churches of Ethiopia (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Nok culture of central Nigeria, about 900 BCE to 1 CE
upsert.description: Farmers on the Jos plateau make life-size terracotta heads and figures, the oldest large sculpture south of the Sahara, and smelt iron from about 500 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Breunig and Rupp 2016, Journal of African Archaeology 14

upsert.boundary: Paracas and Nazca, about 800 BCE to 600 CE
upsert.description: On Peru's south coast, Paracas weavers make some of the finest textiles of antiquity and Nazca people draw the giant lines and figures on the desert floor and tap groundwater with spiral wells.
provenance: sources to check: Silverman and Proulx, The Nasca (2002)

upsert.boundary: The Olmec, about 1600 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: On the Gulf coast of Mexico, at San Lorenzo and La Venta, rulers carve colossal stone heads and jade figures; Olmec symbols, the ballgame and perhaps the calendar spread across Mesoamerica.
provenance: sources to check: Pool, Olmec Archaeology and Early Mesoamerica (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Gupta age, about 320 to 550
upsert.description: The Guptas rule north India in an age remembered as classical: Sanskrit drama and poetry (Kālidāsa), the temples and sculpture of Hinduism's devotional cults, the university at Nalanda, and Aryabhata's astronomy; Hun invasions bring it down.
provenance: sources to check: Thapar, Early India (2002)

upsert.boundary: Heian Japan, 794 to 1185
upsert.description: From Heian-kyō (Kyoto), a court aristocracy dominated by the Fujiwara develops the kana scripts and a literature written largely by women, above all Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji (about 1008), while warrior clans grow in the provinces until the Genpei War (1180 to 1185).
provenance: sources to check: Morris, The World of the Shining Prince (1964)

upsert.boundary: The Mughal empire, 1526 to 1857
upsert.description: Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, defeats the last Delhi sultan at Panipat (1526); Akbar (1556 to 1605) builds an empire of perhaps 100 million people with a salaried nobility and tolerance among faiths; Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal; Aurangzeb extends it furthest but leaves it at war, and after his death in 1707 it breaks into successor states, Maratha power and in the end British rule; the British depose the last emperor in 1857.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; population an estimate
sources to check: Richards, The Mughal Empire (1993)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan)

upsert.boundary: Mao's People's Republic, 1949 to 1976
upsert.description: The Communist Party unifies China, carries out a land reform in which perhaps a million or more landlords are killed, collectivizes farming, launches the Great Leap Forward and its famine and then the Cultural Revolution; it also roughly doubles life expectancy and spreads basic schooling. Religion is suppressed and the state teaches atheism.
provenance: sources to check: Dikötter, The Tragedy of Liberation (2013); MacFarquhar (ed.), The Politics of China (3rd ed. 2011)

upsert.boundary: Song China and its commercial revolution, 960 to 1279
upsert.description: The Song govern through officials chosen by examination, print books in great numbers, issue the first government paper money and grow early-ripening Champa rice; China's population passes 100 million, and Kaifeng and later Hangzhou hold a million people or more, the largest cities in the world. Iron and coal, the compass at sea and gunpowder weapons grow with them, and Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism becomes the orthodoxy of later dynasties. The north falls to the Jurchen in 1127 and the south to the Mongols in 1279.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; city populations are estimates
sources to check: Elvin, The Pattern of the Chinese Past (1973); Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule (2009)

upsert.boundary: Tokugawa Japan, 1603 to 1868
upsert.description: The Tokugawa shoguns keep two and a half centuries of peace from Edo, make the lords spend alternate years at court, expel missionaries, persecute Christians and close the country to all but Dutch and Chinese traders at Nagasaki (1639); Edo grows to a million people, literacy spreads, and kabuki, ukiyo-e and haiku flourish.
provenance: sources to check: Totman, Early Modern Japan (1993)

upsert.boundary: Radio and television, 1920 to 1990
upsert.description: From the first commercial radio broadcasts (1920) radio reaches most homes in rich countries by the 1930s and is used by Hitler and Roosevelt alike; television spreads from the 1950s, and by 1990 most of humanity is regularly reached by broadcast media.
provenance: sources to check: Briggs and Burke, A Social History of the Media (3rd ed. 2009)

upsert.boundary: Athenian democracy and the classical age, 508 to 322 BCE
upsert.description: Cleisthenes' reforms give power to the assembly of citizens; Athens leads the Greeks against Persia, builds the Parthenon and stages the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, until Macedon ends its democracy in 322 BCE. Women, slaves and foreigners have no vote.
provenance: sources to check: Ober, The Rise and Fall of Classical Greece (2015)

upsert.boundary: The French Revolution, 1789 to 1799
upsert.description: Bankrupt after its wars, the monarchy calls the Estates-General; the Third Estate makes itself a National Assembly, Parisians storm the Bastille, the assembly abolishes feudal privileges and declares the Rights of Man; the king is executed (1793), the Terror follows, and war with Europe's monarchies brings Napoleon to power (1799).
provenance: sources to check: Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (2nd ed. 2002)

upsert.boundary: Minoan Crete, about 2000 to 1450 BCE
upsert.description: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, painted with frescoes of bull-leaping, store and redistribute goods recorded in Linear A, still undeciphered; Mycenaean Greeks take over Knossos around 1450 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Shelmerdine (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Aegean Bronze Age (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Renaissance, about 1350 to 1550
upsert.description: In the Italian cities, Petrarch and the humanists recover classical texts, Florence's Brunelleschi masters perspective and builds the cathedral dome, and Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael paint and sculpt for popes and bankers; through print and travel the movement spreads north.
provenance: sources to check: Burke, The European Renaissance (1998)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Italy; Western and Northern Europe)

upsert.boundary: The Russian revolutions and civil war, 1917 to 1922
upsert.description: Wartime collapse brings down the tsar (February 1917); Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power (October), take Russia out of the war and win a civil war of terror, famine and epidemics that kills perhaps eight to ten million, founding the Soviet Union (December 1922), a one-party state that persecutes religion.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, Russia in Revolution (2017)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus); Asia (Central Asia)

upsert.boundary: The Soviet Union breaks up, 1991
upsert.description: After a failed hard-line coup (August 1991) the republics declare independence one by one, and the Soviet Union is dissolved on 26 December 1991 into fifteen states.
provenance: sources to check: Plokhy, The Last Empire (2014)

The 16 Events that named h.play.makers now also name the part they move: patrons for the courts, temples and chiefs who kept makers (Minoan Crete, the Olmec, Nok, Dong Son, Paracas and Nazca, the Gupta, Borobudur, Igbo-Ukwu, Heian, Lalibela, Ife, Rapa Nui) and for Benin's royal guilds ended in 1897; patrons and markets for the Renaissance, whose artists worked for popes and bankers and, through print, for buyers; public bodies for the Festival of Pacific Arts, which governments stage; markets for rugby, whose players became professionals. upsert.lens: To follow who does the killing, which one rate hides: before states every massacre was the work of raiding parties of bands and villages; states took most of it over, by conquest massacres and terror, and the twentieth century's peaks are nearly all states' work; groups that are not states take a larger part again where states fail or break up (Partition, the Lord's Resistance Army, the Islamic State, Boko Haram). The deepen check names this process (17 Events, values mostly sketched). Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living Homo sapiens: the massacres of foragers' camps and farmers' villages, the sacks and deportations of the first states and empires, and the genocides, politicides and militia killings of the modern world.

Each date's split is the states' share of the parent's value, the non-state part taken as the remainder so the sum holds exactly. The shares are sketched from which organizations carried out the massacres the parent's notes name (the Assyrian and Mongol sacks, the Dzungar, Herero and Armenian genocides, the Holocaust, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Rwanda for states; forager and village raids, Vikings, rebel armies, pogroms, Partition, the Islamic State for groups that are not states), with militias a government arms and directs counted with the state, as UCDP and Rummel would; they share the parent's foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca). A tenth of all makers: Rome's actors, mimes, charioteers and copyists' workshops, and the entertainers of Han cities, paid by crowds and buyers.
Falls with the cities of the western empire and their theatres.

Edo's and Osaka's kabuki and puppet theatres and the ukiyo-e print trade join Europe's markets.
Markets now keep more makers than patrons do: public concerts, publishers of music and novels, theatres run for profit.
Music halls, vaudeville, the illustrated press and the first professional sport.
Hollywood's studios, commercial radio's singers and bands, the record companies and sport as a profession: three quarters of all makers.
War takes performers into the forces and closes commercial theatres across occupied Europe and Asia.
Falls as a share while the communist states take their theatres, studios and troupes into public hands; it still keeps most makers.
Rises as the post-Soviet states and China's reformed troupes push makers onto the market.

About three quarters of all makers: the self-employed, the film, music, games and publishing industries and professional sport.

Falls with the cities of the western empire and their theatres.
Rises with the Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds: about a sixth of all makers.
London's and Madrid's commercial theatres, Antwerp's and later Amsterdam's open picture market, printed books' authors and printed images: three makers in ten live from buyers and audiences.
Edo's and Osaka's kabuki and puppet theatres and the ukiyo-e print trade join Europe's markets.
Markets now keep more makers than patrons do: public concerts, publishers of music and novels, theatres run for profit.
Music halls, vaudeville, the illustrated press and the first professional sport.
Hollywood's studios, commercial radio's singers and bands, the record companies and sport as a profession: three quarters of all makers.
War takes performers into the forces and closes commercial theatres across occupied Europe and Asia.
Falls as a share while the communist states take their theatres, studios and troupes into public hands; it still keeps most makers.
Rises as the post-Soviet states and China's reformed troupes push makers onto the market.
The pandemic falls on market makers: closed venues and cancelled seasons cost freelance performers most of a year's work, while salaried public makers keep their posts.
About three quarters of all makers: the self-employed, the film, music, games and publishing industries and professional sport.

upsert.reason: The parent's value less the patrons' and public bodies' parts at each date: zero before about 2200 BCE, a few per cent in antiquity, a sixth in the Song cities, a third by 1650, most of all makers from about 1820, three quarters now.

points.note: Zero, as the parent: no forager band keeps anyone to make art.
If anyone was kept to carve Göbekli Tepe's pillars, it was by the leaders of the feasts that raised them: patrons, not buyers.
Chiefs keep the first craftsmen of fine things: Varna's goldsmiths, Ubaid's temple painters.
Every kept maker is a dependant of a temple or palace workshop in Sumer and Egypt.
Dips with the palaces of the Bronze Age collapse.

Near the level it keeps for the next seventeen centuries: the Han court's Music Bureau, Rome's imperial and senatorial households and the temples of every empire keep about 450 to 475 makers per million people.
Falls with Rome's western patrons; the Gupta, Sasanian and southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Its peak per person, barely above the first century's: the Mughal, Safavid, Ottoman and Ming ateliers and Europe's courts and churches.
Falling: the Revolution abolishes the court, confiscates the Church's lands and closes the chapels and choir schools that kept France's musicians, painters and sculptors.
Falls: the French Revolution ends the court's and the Church's patronage in France, and secularization strips German and Austrian monasteries and prince-bishops of theirs.
Britain's punitive expedition sacks Benin City and ends the royal guilds of casters and carvers.
On the eve of the February revolution, which ends the Russian court's and aristocracy's patronage.
The February revolution: the Imperial Theatres and the court's orchestras and choirs pass to the state, and the aristocracy's patronage ends with its estates.
The Russian, Austrian, German and Ottoman courts are gone; the Russian revolution ends aristocratic patronage across a sixth of the world's land.
India's princely states are merged into the republic (1947 to 1949) and their courts' musicians and painters lose their keepers.
About a twentieth of all makers: church musicians, royal and princely households, private patrons and foundations' commissions.

upsert.reason: The parent's value times the patrons' share: all of it until markets appear, nine tenths in antiquity, three quarters in 1500, half by 1800, a tenth by 1950, a twentieth now.

points.note: Begins: the Greek cities' civic festivals pay poets, choruses, musicians and sculptors from public funds and liturgies.
Cleisthenes' reforms: Athens's City Dionysia, whose tragic contests began about 534 BCE, is paid for by the city and its liturgies.
Rome's public games and theatres, paid partly from the treasury, partly by magistrates who count as patrons here.
The western cities' public games and theatres close.
Town musicians and civic painters of Europe's and Asia's self-governing cities: a fiftieth of all makers.
Court theatres begin to become national ones (Vienna's Burgtheater, 1776) and academies take state salaries.
The republic's festivals, the Conservatoire (1795) and the Louvre's public museum (1793) keep some makers on public funds.
Germany's and Austria's municipal theatres and orchestras, Europe's conservatories and academies: about a sixteenth of all makers.
Rises: the Soviet state takes the theatres, conservatories and studios into public hands (1919), and Germany's and Austria's court theatres become state theatres.
The New Deal's Federal Art, Music, Theatre and Writers' Projects employ about 40,000 makers (1935 to 1939), and the Soviet and fascist states' arts administrations grow.
Jumps: Eastern Europe's new regimes and the People's Republic of China (1949) take theatres, studios and troupes into public hands, and Western Europe's arts councils and public broadcasters grow.
Near its peak share, three tenths of all makers: China's thousands of state troupes, the Soviet bloc's theatres, studios and artists' unions, and Europe's subsidized stages and broadcasters.
The Cultural Revolution disbands or purges China's troupes and sends their members to the countryside, leaving the eight model works.
The Soviet Union's breakup ends the union-wide state system of theatres, studios, conservatories and creative unions; budgets collapse in the 1990s.
Falls: the Soviet system's end cuts state theatres, studios and unions across Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, and China begins to turn its troupes into enterprises.
Holds through the pandemic: salaried makers of state theatres, orchestras and broadcasters keep their posts while freelance performers lose their work.
About a sixth of all makers: public broadcasters, state and municipal theatres, orchestras and troupes, most of them in Europe and East Asia.

upsert.reason: The parent's value times the public bodies' share: none before the Greek cities' festivals, a few per cent until 1900, a tenth by 1930, a quarter to three tenths from 1950 to 1990, under a fifth now.

points.note: Zero by the measure's definition: no forager band keeps anyone to make art. The beads, engravings and paintings of the Stone Age were made by people whose main work was getting food.
Sunghir's burials, with thousands of ivory beads that took thousands of hours to make, show great effort spent on ornament, but nothing shows anyone kept for the work.

Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars (from about 9500 BCE) are raised by foragers' communal labour, perhaps with a few carvers who did little else; whether anyone was kept for the work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Chiefdoms begin to keep craftsmen: the goldsmiths behind Varna's graves (about 4500 BCE), the builders and painters of Ubaid Mesopotamia's temples.
The temple and palace workshops of Sumer and Egypt keep the first full-time sculptors, painters, musicians and goldsmiths; perhaps a fifth of humanity now lives under such courts.
Minoan Crete's palaces keep fresco painters, seal-cutters and goldsmiths beside Egypt's and Mesopotamia's workshops.
Olmec rulers at San Lorenzo keep the sculptors of the colossal heads: makers of art are now kept in the Americas too.
The tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, the Shang bronze-casters, the palace painters of Crete and the Olmec sculptors: courts on three continents now keep makers of art.
Greek cities' festivals keep poets, actors and sculptors, and the Persian, Indian and Chinese courts their musicians and craftsmen.

Rome's theatres, games and workshops and the Han court's Music Bureau, about 800 musicians before 7 BCE: a few makers in every thousand people of the great cities, about one in two thousand people worldwide.
Gupta India's court poets, dramatists and temple sculptors (Kalidasa wrote about 400) rise as Rome's western patrons fail.
Falls with Rome in the west: theatres, games and the patrons who paid for them close; Gupta India, Sasanian Iran and the southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds, beside the courts of the Abbasids, the Fatimids and Heian Japan.
The Black Death and the Mongol wars kill makers and patrons alike.
The workshops of Italy and the Netherlands, the Mughal and Safavid ateliers, Ming porcelain and printed images: art is made for markets as well as for patrons.
Between 1789 and 1800 on the line; inside it the Revolution moves makers from the court and the Church to the market and the new state's festivals.
Theatres, music halls, the illustrated press and the publishers' authors grow with the cities of the industrial world.
Cinema: the picture houses' actors and pit musicians, and the first professional footballers and boxers.
Hollywood's studios, radio's orchestras and singers, and sport as a profession.
War takes performers into the forces and closes theatres in occupied Europe and Asia.
The pandemic closes theatres, concert halls and stadiums; live performers lose most of a year's work.
About twenty million people of some 3.6 billion workers: artists, musicians, actors, writers, dancers, players of sport and makers of art wares.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned: zero among foragers by definition; a few hundred per million under the agrarian states' courts and temples, bounded by the surplus that keeps them (SurplusBound#7fe3); a few thousand per million now. The 2025 value rests on the recalled count of about 30 million jobs in the cultural and creative industries in 2013 (UNESCO and EY), of which the makers themselves are perhaps two thirds; to be checked. Where the line falls between a maker of art wares and a maker of ordinary goods moves every value before 1900 by a factor of two either way.

changes.value: Check the parts against the whole: one-sided killing (h.war.one-sided) is, by its parts' own definitions, the sum of killing by states and killing by groups that are not states, in the same unit (deaths per 100,000 a year, averaged to the next date), each massacre counted once by the organization that carried it out (MECE#ae19). Declared a sum so the report compares them at every date; the 2025 value is re-recorded unchanged to carry the declaration.

upsert.boundary: The war in Darfur, 2003 to 2010
upsert.description: The Sudanese government and Janjaweed militias answer a rebellion with massacres of Fur, Masalit and Zaghawa villagers; perhaps 200,000 to 300,000 die and two million flee.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is uncertain
sources to check: Flint and de Waal, Darfur: A New History of a Long War (2008)

upsert.boundary: The genocide of the Herero and Nama, 1904 to 1908
upsert.description: After the Herero and Nama rise against German South West Africa, General von Trotha orders the Herero driven into the desert; perhaps 80% of the Herero and half of the Nama die in the desert and in camps. Germany acknowledged it as genocide in 2021.
provenance: sources to check: Olusoga and Erichsen, The Kaiser's Holocaust (2010)

upsert.boundary: The genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda, April to July 1994
upsert.description: After the president's plane is shot down, Hutu Power militias and soldiers kill about 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about a hundred days, while the UN withdraws; the Rwandan Patriotic Front's victory ends it, and a million and more Hutu flee into the Congo.
provenance: sources to check: Des Forges, Leave None to Tell the Story (Human Rights Watch, 1999)

upsert.boundary: Civil wars in Central America, 1979 to 1996
upsert.description: The Sandinista revolution in Nicaragua (1979) and the American-backed Contra war, El Salvador's civil war, and Guatemala's war, in which the army's campaigns against Maya villages are judged genocide; about 300,000 die in all.
provenance: sources to check: Commission for Historical Clarification, Guatemala: Memory of Silence (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central America (Nicaragua, El Salvador, Guatemala)

upsert.boundary: The California gold rush, 1848 to 1855
upsert.description: About 300,000 people pour into California from across the world; the Native Californian population, already halved under Spanish missions, falls from perhaps 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killing, disease and starvation.
provenance: sources to check: Madley, An American Genocide (2016)

upsert.boundary: The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1917
upsert.description: The Ottoman government deports the Armenians of Anatolia toward the Syrian desert; through massacre, death marches and starvation perhaps a million or more die, and Assyrian and Greek Christians are also killed in great numbers.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; totals range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million
sources to check: Suny, 'They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else' (2015)

upsert.boundary: The Mongols sack Baghdad, February 1258
upsert.description: Hulagu's army takes Baghdad, kills the last Abbasid caliph and a great part of the city's people, ending the caliphate that had reigned there for five centuries.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is unknown
sources to check: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

upsert.boundary: Bangladesh's war of independence, 1971
upsert.description: When Pakistan's army cracks down on East Bengal after the Awami League wins the 1970 election, hundreds of thousands to perhaps three million people are killed and ten million flee to India; India intervenes in December and Bangladesh becomes independent.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is fiercely disputed
sources to check: Raghavan, 1971 (2013); Bass, The Blood Telegram (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Cultural Revolution, 1966 to 1976
upsert.description: Mao mobilizes students as Red Guards against party officials, teachers and 'old' culture; schools and universities close, millions are persecuted and sent to the countryside, and perhaps one to two million die, before the arrest of the Gang of Four ends it in October 1976.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths are very uncertain
sources to check: MacFarquhar and Schoenhals, Mao's Last Revolution (2006)

upsert.boundary: Japan's war in China and the Pacific, 1931 to 1945
upsert.description: Japan seizes Manchuria (1931), invades China proper (1937), massacring civilians at Nanjing, and in 1941 attacks Pearl Harbor and conquers South-east Asia; perhaps 15 to 20 million Chinese and millions more across Asia die. Defeat at sea, the firebombing of its cities, the atomic bombs and the Soviet attack end the war in August 1945.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Chinese deaths are very uncertain
sources to check: Mitter, China's War with Japan 1937–1945 (2013); Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Japan, Korea), South-eastern Asia; Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia); Americas (Northern America: Hawaii)

upsert.boundary: Independence and the partition of India, 1947
upsert.description: Britain hands power to two states, India and Pakistan (East and West), at midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947; as the borders cut through Punjab and Bengal, about 15 million people flee across them and perhaps 200,000 to two million are killed in communal violence.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is very uncertain
sources to check: Khan, The Great Partition (2007)

upsert.boundary: Europe's postwar expulsions, 1944 to 1950
upsert.description: As borders move west, some 12 to 14 million Germans flee or are expelled from Poland, Czechoslovakia and the east, and millions of Poles, Ukrainians and others are moved; perhaps half a million or more die.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths are disputed
sources to check: Douglas, Orderly and Humane (2012)

upsert.boundary: Stalin's Great Terror, 1936 to 1938
upsert.description: The NKVD arrests over 1.5 million people and shoots about 680,000, party leaders, officers, kulaks, national minorities and ordinary people alike, while the Gulag camps hold millions.
provenance: sources to check: Khlevniuk, The History of the Gulag (2004); Conquest, The Great Terror (1968)

upsert.boundary: The Yugoslav wars, 1991 to 2001
upsert.description: Yugoslavia breaks apart in wars in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Kosovo and North Macedonia; some 130,000 to 140,000 die, millions are displaced by 'ethnic cleansing', and Bosnian Serb forces murder about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica (1995), a genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Glenny, The Fall of Yugoslavia (3rd ed. 1996); ICTY judgments

upsert.boundary: The Amazon rubber boom, 1879 to 1912
upsert.description: Demand for tyres and insulation makes wild Amazonian rubber one of the world's most valuable commodities; Manaus builds an opera house, Brazil takes Acre from Bolivia, and tappers, many of them indebted migrants from the drought-stricken north-east, spread up every river. In the Putumayo the Peruvian Amazon Company's agents enslave and kill tens of thousands of Indigenous people. Plantations in Malaya and Ceylon, grown from seeds taken from Brazil in 1876, undercut it after 1910.
provenance: sources to check: Weinstein, The Amazon Rubber Boom (1983); Goodman, The Devil and Mr Casement (2009)

upsert.boundary: The expulsion of the Rohingya, 2016 to 2017
upsert.description: After attacks by a small Rohingya armed group on border posts (October 2016 and August 2017), Myanmar's army and local mobs burn hundreds of Rohingya villages in northern Rakhine, killing thousands, at least 6,700 in the first month by one survey, and raping women. About 740,000 Rohingya, whom Myanmar had denied citizenship since 1982, flee to Bangladesh, where some 900,000 or more live in camps around Cox's Bazar; the Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar is before the International Court of Justice.
provenance: sources to check: UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar, report (2018); Médecins Sans Frontières mortality surveys (2017)

upsert.boundary: The 11 September attacks, 2001
upsert.description: Al-Qaeda hijackers fly airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, killing nearly 3,000 people; the United States responds with the invasion of Afghanistan and a global war on terrorism.
provenance: sources to check: The 9/11 Commission Report (2004)

changes.value: Observe the parts of one-sided killing (carve r404, parts r405, sum r408): the 17 Events that name h.war.one-sided now also name the part for the organization that carried out the killing. States: the Mongol sack of Baghdad, the Herero and Nama genocide, the Armenian genocide, Japan's massacres in China, Stalin's Great Terror, the deaths in the postwar expulsions, the Cultural Revolution's killings (mostly by state-directed militias and the army), Bangladesh in 1971, Guatemala's and El Salvador's armies in the Central American wars, Rwanda's genocide (government, army and the ruling party's militias), Darfur (the government and the Janjaweed it armed) and the Rohingya's expulsion (Myanmar's army). Every other field of each Event is restated as the model holds it, read back from an export of the model (r394, and r396 for the gold rush).

(1) Killing by a group's own rule: judicial and customary executions (and among foragers the collective killing of a dangerous member), the sacrifice of retainers and captives (Ur's royal tombs, Kerma, the Shang, the Aztec temples), and killings by police. It passes the tests once the frame is deliberate killing: necessary (the witch-hunts' 40,000 to 60,000 executions, Tudor and Qing justice, the Aztec sacrifices, the abolition of the death penalty in most countries since 1960 have no home), independent (it fell in Europe after 1750 on its own timetable) and universal (every society puts some of its members to death). It is not followed now for one reason only: the carve divides violent death as the parent measures it, homicide plus war (h.safety), and that measure leaves these deaths out, so a part opened under it would not be part of what its parent counts; widening h.safety is a change to an existing measure, which this pass leaves as it is. Political mass executions (the Great Terror, the Khmer Rouge's) are already counted under one-sided killing (h.war.one-sided.states), and policy famines under hunger. The measure that would follow the rest is named for the pass that widens h.safety: killing by a group's own rule, per 100,000 living people a year, sketched at perhaps 1 to 5 among foragers (Boehm and Wrangham on collective execution), higher in the first states with retainer and captive sacrifice, about 4 per 100,000 of the world's people from the Aztec sacrifices alone in the fifteenth century, a European peak about 1550 to 1650, and under 0.5 since 1950 (a few thousand executions a year, most in China and Iran, and some tens of thousands of police killings). Carved again because the breadth check names this carve's open completeness: the first record (r104) left fresh water, the nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, and aerosols and novel entities without a home, and the nutrient cycles had passed all three tests but waited for a measure. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, followed as global measures; the parent's own measure is global mean temperature against 1850 to 1900.

scale.semantic_role: The nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixed by people: Reactive nitrogen fixed by people's activities in a year, in teragrams (million tonnes) of nitrogen: biological fixation by sown legumes and paddy rice beyond what the land's wild plants would fix, industrial ammonia synthesis (Haber-Bosch, from 1913) and nitrogen oxides from burning fuel. The land's own biological fixation, about 60 to 120 Tg N a year, is the background it is read against; the planetary boundary for industrial and intentional fixation is put at about 60 to 80 Tg N a year (Steffen and colleagues 2015). Mined guano and nitrates are not fixation: they are counted among the Earth's stores.
