changes.value: Opens the nitrogen cycle, the part the re-recorded carve of the Earth as setting promoted (carve.concept.dim.earth, r411 and r412), as nitrogen fixed by people in Tg N a year, on the same dates as the Earth's stores. Zero before farming; a slow rise with sown pulses from about 9700 BCE and paddy rice from about 5000 BCE, roughly with the farmed area and people; Europe's legume rotations from 1650; about 15 Tg in 1860 and about 187 Tg in 2005 as Galloway and colleagues reckon them (as recalled, to be checked); Haber-Bosch from 1913 and the green revolution from 1960 carry most of the rise. Values are recalled or reasoned, tagged sketch before 1850 and inferred after, and share one foundation with the farmland and food series (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Zero: foragers sow nothing, and their fires fix next to no nitrogen.
Begins: lentils, peas, chickpeas and bitter vetch are sown with the first wheat and barley in the Fertile Crescent.
Paddy rice in the Yangtze valley, whose flooded fields' cyanobacteria fix nitrogen, and pulses wherever farming has spread.
Roman and Han farmers rotate beans and vetches with grain; China's paddies spread south. Still a twentieth or less of the land's own fixation.
Falls a little as fields are abandoned after the Black Death and the Mongol wars.
Clover and turnip rotations spread from the Low Countries and England: Europe's fields fix more nitrogen and feed more animals.
About 15 Tg in 1860 as Galloway and colleagues reckon it, nearly all from crops; guano and Chilean nitrate, imported by the hundred thousand tonnes, are mined, not fixed.
Haber-Bosch: BASF's plant at Oppau (1913) and the wartime Leuna works make ammonia for Germany's explosives once the British blockade cuts off Chilean nitrate.
War plants turned to fertilizer: synthetic nitrogen use climbs steeply from the late 1940s.
Passes the planetary boundary for intentional fixation (about 60 to 80 Tg N a year), as Steffen and colleagues put it.
The green revolution's high-yielding wheat and rice need fertilizer: about as much nitrogen fixed by people as by all the land's wild plants and microbes.
About 156 Tg by Galloway and colleagues' reckoning for 1990, with combustion: more than twice the land's own fixation at its lower estimates.
About 187 Tg in 2005 by Galloway and colleagues (2008): Haber-Bosch about 120, crops about 40, combustion about 25.
About 210 Tg: perhaps half of the nitrogen in the world's food crops comes from Haber-Bosch, and about half of what is applied runs off into rivers, coasts and the air.

upsert.boundary: Europe's agricultural revolution, about 1650 to 1850
upsert.description: First in the Low Countries and England, then across Europe, farmers grow clover and turnips in new rotations that feed more animals and fix nitrogen, enclose open fields and adopt the potato; yields roughly double, and the share of workers needed to grow food falls, from about three-quarters toward a third in England by 1800.

sources to check: Overton, Agricultural Revolution in England (1996); Allen, Enclosure and the Yeoman (1992)

upsert.boundary: The green revolution, 1960 to 2000.
upsert.description: High-yielding wheat and rice, with fertilizer and irrigation, double and triple cereal yields across Asia and Latin America; food per person rises while population doubles.

upsert.boundary: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer, from 1913 to now.
upsert.description: The Haber–Bosch process fixes nitrogen from the air: from the first plant at Oppau in 1913 to over 100 million tonnes of fixed nitrogen a year, on which perhaps two fifths to a half of the food people eat depends.

changes.value: Opens the two parts the re-recorded carve of how people get it added (carve.concept.humanity.means, r418): wealth held, as years of world output, and organized belief, as people kept to serve a faith per 1,000, on the Earth's and the stores' grid of dates with values at the starts of the Events they will be linked to. Wealth: about a third of a year's output among foragers, five to six years in the agrarian empires as land and herds, near Piketty's world series from 1870 (about 5 in 1870, 4.7 in 1910, 2.4 in 1950, 4.4 in 2010) and the World Inequality Database's world wealth-to-income ratio of about 5.5 to 6 now, as recalled. Organized belief: none among foragers, temple households from the first states, the sangha and the monasteries at their height in the medieval centuries (perhaps eight per 1,000 of all people), five centuries of decline through the Reformation, the revolutions and secularization to about 1.4 now (some eleven million people), as recalled. Every value shares one foundation with its neighbours (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Zero: foragers' shamans and ritual elders also hunt and gather; no one is kept to serve the sacred.
Begins, perhaps: the enclosures of Gobekli Tepe and Neolithic shrines may have had keepers fed by the feasts' builders; unknown.
Eridu's temple and the chiefdoms' priests.
The temple households of Sumer and Egypt's priesthood: in the first states a temple can be the largest owner of land and keeper of people.
Egypt's New Kingdom temples hold perhaps a tenth of its land and keep tens of thousands; Amun's priesthood rivals the throne.
The Buddha's and Mahavira's orders of monks and nuns, the first communities kept wholly by believers' alms, beside the Brahmins, the magi and the Greek temples.
Buddhist monks begin to carry the dharma into Han China.
Christian monasticism begins in Egypt's desert (Antony, then Pachomius's communities about 320).

Rises most: China's Buddhist monasteries under the Northern Wei and the southern courts, perhaps a million or more monks and nuns by the claims of the time, and Christian monasteries from Egypt to Ireland.

Near its peak: Europe's clergy and religious perhaps one or two in every hundred people, holding a fifth to a quarter of its land; Theravada monasteries in every mainland village; Tibet's monasteries; the ulama and Sufi orders.
Falls: the Reformation dissolves the monasteries of England, Scandinavia and Protestant Germany and turns their lands to crowns and nobles.
Catholic Europe's Counter-Reformation clergy and Tibet's monasteries, where perhaps a sixth of men are monks, hold the level.
Falls: the French Revolution abolishes the religious orders and sells the Church's lands, and the secularizations of Joseph II and Napoleon follow.
The Soviet state closes churches and monasteries and kills or exiles tens of thousands of clergy.
Falls: China's new state laicizes monks and nuns and takes temple lands; after 1959 Tibet's monasteries are emptied.
The Cultural Revolution closes every temple, church and mosque in China.

About eleven million: Catholic priests, sisters and brothers about a million, Protestant pastors two to three million, imams and ulama one to two million, Buddhist monks and nuns one to two million, Hindu temple priests one to three million, and others.
A forager band's tools, ornaments, shelters and canoes: a few months of what it gets in a year. What foragers hold in skills and ties is real wealth but not counted here.
Rises with the first fields, stores and houses: farmers hold what foragers did not, land made fertile, granaries and herds.
Irrigated land, temples, granaries and herds: the first states sit on stocks of several years' harvest.
Land is most of it: the Roman and Han estates; a large estate's price was some twenty to thirty years of its rent, and rents a third to a half of the harvest.
Falls: after the Black Death land is plentiful and labour scarce, so land's value falls against what the survivors produce.
Britain's and France's wealth is about seven years of national income, mostly land (Piketty); Asia's agrarian empires perhaps four to five.
About five years by Piketty's world series: land's share falls as railways, factories and housing rise.
Falls: war destroys capital and war finance turns savings into government debt that inflation will erase; the Russian revolution expropriates the property of a sixth of the world's land.
The Depression wipes out share and property values.

The low: the world wars' destruction, inflation, nationalizations, rent controls and the communist revolutions' expropriations (China's from 1949) leave the world's wealth at about two and a half years of output.
Rises with privatization in the former communist states, falling interest rates and housing booms.
Peaks before the financial crisis, at the top of the housing and credit boom.
Near-zero interest rates lift asset prices while the pandemic cuts output.
About five and a half years of world output, near the World Inequality Database's global estimate, and back near where it stood before 1914.

The Buddha's and Mahavira's orders of monks and nuns, the first communities kept wholly by believers' alms, beside the Brahmins, the magi and the Greek temples.
Buddhist monks begin to carry the dharma into Han China.
Christian monasticism begins in Egypt's desert (Antony, then Pachomius's communities about 320).

Rises most: China's Buddhist monasteries under the Northern Wei and the southern courts, perhaps a million or more monks and nuns by the claims of the time, and Christian monasteries from Egypt to Ireland.

Falls: the Tang emperor Wuzong's Huichang suppression (842 to 845) destroys some 4,600 monasteries and returns about 260,000 monks and nuns to lay life, a large part of all the people kept for faiths in a China that held a quarter of humanity; the sangha recovers under the Song.

Near its peak: Europe's clergy and religious perhaps one or two in every hundred people, holding a fifth to a quarter of its land; Theravada monasteries in every mainland village; Tibet's monasteries; the ulama and Sufi orders.
Falls: the Reformation dissolves the monasteries of England, Scandinavia and Protestant Germany and turns their lands to crowns and nobles.
Catholic Europe's Counter-Reformation clergy and Tibet's monasteries, where perhaps a sixth of men are monks, hold the level.
Falls: the French Revolution abolishes the religious orders and sells the Church's lands, and the secularizations of Joseph II and Napoleon follow.
The Soviet state closes churches and monasteries and kills or exiles tens of thousands of clergy.
Falls: China's new state laicizes monks and nuns and takes temple lands; after 1959 Tibet's monasteries are emptied.
The Cultural Revolution closes every temple, church and mosque in China.

About eleven million: Catholic priests, sisters and brothers about a million, Protestant pastors two to three million, imams and ulama one to two million, Buddhist monks and nuns one to two million, Hindu temple priests one to three million, and others.
A forager band's tools, ornaments, shelters and canoes: a few months of what it gets in a year. What foragers hold in skills and ties is real wealth but not counted here.
Rises with the first fields, stores and houses: farmers hold what foragers did not, land made fertile, granaries and herds.
Irrigated land, temples, granaries and herds: the first states sit on stocks of several years' harvest.
Land is most of it: the Roman and Han estates; a large estate's price was some twenty to thirty years of its rent, and rents a third to a half of the harvest.
The Black Death kills a third or more of Eurasia's western and central peoples; land loses value against what the survivors can make and earn.
Falls: after the Black Death land is plentiful and labour scarce, so land's value falls against what the survivors produce.
Britain's and France's wealth is about seven years of national income, mostly land (Piketty); Asia's agrarian empires perhaps four to five.
About five years by Piketty's world series: land's share falls as railways, factories and housing rise.
Falls: war destroys capital and war finance turns savings into government debt that inflation will erase; the Russian revolution expropriates the property of a sixth of the world's land.
The Depression wipes out share and property values.
War spreads to the Pacific: bombing and fighting destroy housing, factories and transport from Europe to China, and governments borrow on a scale that inflation will later erase.

The low: the world wars' destruction, inflation, nationalizations, rent controls and the communist revolutions' expropriations (China's from 1949) leave the world's wealth at about two and a half years of output.
Rises with privatization in the former communist states, falling interest rates and housing booms.
Peaks before the financial crisis, at the top of the housing and credit boom.
Near-zero interest rates lift asset prices while the pandemic cuts output.
About five and a half years of world output, near the World Inequality Database's global estimate, and back near where it stood before 1914.

upsert.boundary: Christian monasticism in the Egyptian desert, about 270 to 451
upsert.description: Antony withdraws to the desert and Pachomius founds the first communal monasteries (about 320); the practice spreads to Syria, Byzantium and the West. At Chalcedon (451) Egypt's church parts from Rome and Constantinople, becoming the Coptic church.
provenance: sources to check: Brown, The Rise of Western Christendom (2nd ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Buddhism spreads to China, Korea and Japan, about 65 to 600
upsert.description: Merchants and monks carry Buddhism along the Silk Roads and the sea routes; after the Han fall it wins converts at every level of Chinese society; Korea's kingdoms adopt it in the 300s and 500s and Japan in 538 or 552; by 600 it is the largest tradition of East Asia's courts and monasteries.
provenance: sources to check: Zürcher, The Buddhist Conquest of China (1959)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Korea, Japan), Central Asia

upsert.boundary: The Cultural Revolution, 1966 to 1976
upsert.description: Mao mobilizes students as Red Guards against party officials, teachers and 'old' culture; schools and universities close, millions are persecuted and sent to the countryside, and perhaps one to two million die, before the arrest of the Gang of Four ends it in October 1976.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths are very uncertain
sources to check: MacFarquhar and Schoenhals, Mao's Last Revolution (2006)

upsert.boundary: Mao's People's Republic, 1949 to 1976
upsert.description: The Communist Party unifies China, carries out a land reform in which perhaps a million or more landlords are killed, collectivizes farming, launches the Great Leap Forward and its famine and then the Cultural Revolution; it also roughly doubles life expectancy and spreads basic schooling. Religion is suppressed and the state teaches atheism.
provenance: sources to check: Dikötter, The Tragedy of Liberation (2013); MacFarquhar (ed.), The Politics of China (3rd ed. 2011)

upsert.boundary: The Buddha and Mahavira, about 500 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: In the cities of the Ganges plain, the Buddha teaches the end of suffering through the middle way and the eightfold path, and Mahavira the non-violence of Jainism; both found orders of monks and nuns that reject the authority of the Vedas and the priests.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Buddha's dates vary by about a century
sources to check: Gethin, The Foundations of Buddhism (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Tang dynasty, 618 to 907
upsert.description: The Tang rule from Chang'an, a city of perhaps a million people and among the largest in the world, over an empire reaching into Central Asia; they recruit some officials by examination, codify law, patronize Buddhism until the persecution of 845, and host Sogdian, Persian and Arab merchants. The poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu marks its height. After the An Lushan rebellion regional governors hold real power, and the dynasty ends in 907.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Chang'an's population is an estimate
sources to check: Lewis, China's Cosmopolitan Empire (2009)

upsert.boundary: The French Revolution, 1789 to 1799
upsert.description: Bankrupt after its wars, the monarchy calls the Estates-General; the Third Estate makes itself a National Assembly, Parisians storm the Bastille, the assembly abolishes feudal privileges and declares the Rights of Man; the king is executed (1793), the Terror follows, and war with Europe's monarchies brings Napoleon to power (1799).
provenance: sources to check: Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (2nd ed. 2002)

upsert.boundary: The Russian revolutions and civil war, 1917 to 1922
upsert.description: Wartime collapse brings down the tsar (February 1917); Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power (October), take Russia out of the war and win a civil war of terror, famine and epidemics that kills perhaps eight to ten million, founding the Soviet Union (December 1922), a one-party state that persecutes religion.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, Russia in Revolution (2017)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus); Asia (Central Asia)

upsert.boundary: The global financial crisis, 2007 to 2009
upsert.description: Losses on American mortgage securities freeze credit; Lehman Brothers fails (September 2008), banks are rescued across the rich world, world output falls in 2009 for the first time since 1945, and Europe's debt crisis follows.

upsert.boundary: The crash and the Great Depression in the United States, 1929 to 1933
upsert.description: After the stock market crash of October 1929, banks fail in waves (about 9,000 by 1933), the money supply shrinks by about a third, prices fall and output falls by about a quarter; a quarter of workers are unemployed by 1933. The gold standard and the collapse of American lending and imports carry the slump around the world. Why it was so deep is argued: the monetary contraction and bank failures, the gold standard, debt and falling demand each have their advocates.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weights of its causes are debated
sources to check: Friedman and Schwartz, A Monetary History of the United States (1963); Eichengreen, Golden Fetters (1992); Bernanke 1983, American Economic Review 73
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Reformation, 1517 to 1648.
upsert.description: Protestant churches ask every believer to read scripture; Protestant lands, and Catholic ones competing with them, open schools.

upsert.boundary: Pagan unites the Irrawaddy valley, 1044 to 1287
upsert.description: Anawrahta unites the Irrawaddy basin and, by tradition after conquering the Mon of Thaton, makes Theravada Buddhism the court's religion; his successors build over ten thousand temples and monasteries on the plain of Bagan, about two thousand of which still stand, and the Burmese language is first written; the kingdom breaks up after Mongol attacks (1287).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Thaton conquest story is doubted
sources to check: Aung-Thwin, Pagan: The Origins of Modern Burma (1985); Lieberman, Strange Parallels vol. 1 (2003)

upsert.boundary: Theravada Buddhism becomes the mainland's religion, about 1050 to 1450
upsert.description: Monks ordained in Sri Lanka's reformed Theravada lineage spread from Pagan to Sukhothai, Lan Na, Cambodia and Laos; village monasteries teach boys to read and write, and by the 1400s Theravada has displaced the Mahayana and Hindu cults of the courts, even at Angkor.
provenance: sources to check: Swearer, The Buddhist World of Southeast Asia (2nd ed. 2010)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia)

upsert.boundary: The First World War, 1914 to November 1918.
upsert.description: About 9 to 10 million soldiers and some 7 million civilians die.

upsert.boundary: The Second World War, September 1939 to September 1945.
upsert.description: With the Sino-Japanese war already under way, it kills about 70 to 85 million, most of them civilians, the largest share in the Soviet Union and China. Governments take over a third or more of national output.

changes.value: Widen and observe the two parts the carve of how people get it added at r418 (opened r419 to r422). Organized belief: the Buddha's and Mahavira's orders of monks and nuns, Christian monasticism in Egypt's desert, Buddhism's spread to East Asia with its monasteries, the Tang (patrons of Buddhism until the persecution of 845), Pagan's ten thousand temples and monasteries, the Theravada monasteries of the mainland, the Reformation (the monasteries dissolved), the French Revolution (the orders abolished and the Church's lands sold), the Russian revolutions and Mao's China (churches, temples and monasteries closed) and the Cultural Revolution (every place of worship in China shut). upsert.boundary: The carve of staying alive and well (r121) left the years lived in ill health and disability, and mental health, without a home. Both pass necessity and independence, but neither has a world reading before the Global Burden of Disease study's series from 1990 (healthy life expectancy, disability-adjusted life years, the burden of depression and anxiety); before that, a value would be life expectancy times a guessed fraction, a restatement of survival rather than a reading of ill health. The body's condition in earlier centuries is read through stature (h.health) and the causes of death, which carry what can be said. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611, AbsenceEvidence#10a3: that the past left few records of suffering is no evidence of its absence). Reopen if healthy life expectancy is opened from 1990 with a sketched course before it bounded by stature and morbidity studies of past populations (skeletal lesions, enamel defects), which bioarchaeology can supply.

upsert.boundary: The carve of beauty and play (r363) left three things without a measured home. (1) The forms that leave no lasting trace before writing (music, dance, story) are in every population but no world measure can read them across the span; their makers, once kept, are counted among the arts' makers (now divided by who keeps them, r397), and their audiences, once copied, in mass media. (2) What people spend on feasts, festivals and entertainment has household-budget readings only from about 1900. (3) Games and sport: their paid players are counted among the arts' makers (markets, since the codification of football and rugby), the hours played are leisure, and organized contests with fixed rules and audiences are a kind many populations lack. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611, AbsenceEvidence#10a3); reopen if festival and holy days a year are opened as a count beside leisure hours, which has readings for the medieval calendars and the Protestant cuts in them.

upsert.boundary: The carve of standing (r150) left women's standing against men and esteem (how people feel they stand) without a measured home. Women's standing passes necessity and independence, but no world measure of it reaches back before the 1990s (the gender development and inequality indices) or, for law, before V-Dem's women's civil liberties index from 1789; parts of it are already read elsewhere (women's vote under voice, women's age at marriage, plural unions). Esteem is a reading of persons with no world series at all. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611). The candidate most worth opening is women's legal standing, the share of the world's women living where married women can own property and sue in their own name, which has a clear course (coverture's laws repealed from 1839 to the 1970s, Islamic and customary law's own rules) and Events in the account (the women's vote, Seneca Falls); it would sit under freedom beside voice.

upsert.boundary: The carve of sustenance and comfort (r129) left clothing and household goods without a measured home. Clothing: a world series of textile fibre per person exists from about 1900; before that, cotton's spread and the industrial revolution's cheap cloth are well told but would be sketched as one number per person with bands wider than the change, and its comfort is mostly warmth, which energy already carries. Household goods: the consumer and industrious revolutions are read in probate inventories and household surveys for some places and times only. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611); reopen if fibre per person is opened from 1900 with its earlier course bounded by Europe's and China's textile output (Riello, Broadberry), which would also give the cotton revolution's Events (Lancashire, the cotton gin, India's handloom collapse) a measure to move.

upsert.boundary: The carve of understanding (r384) left knowledge held in store (books, archives, libraries: knowledge kept outside heads) as a frontier part, for universality uncertain. It passes necessity and independence (book production rose apart from literacy), but a world series of books or titles per person can be read only from about 1450 in Europe (Buringh and van Zanden) and for Song and later China in pieces; before printing, manuscripts and tablets are counted only for a few libraries; and after 2000 books are a falling share of what is stored, so one measure would change its meaning midway (MetricReading#56a9: one definition must hold over the series). Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611). The candidate, if opened, is new titles printed per million people a year from 1450, with Europe's and China's series summed and the rest of the world sketched; Printing in East Asia and printing with movable type in Europe, already Events of the account, would name it.

upsert.boundary: The stopped pass linked the exchange group's other Events (r377). One remains: mobile money in Africa, from M-Pesa in 2007. It changes how payments move and who can make them (Kenya's households reached by a phone-based account, and the remittances sent home that way), which no measure of the account follows: trade between peoples (h.exchange) does not see it, the share online (h.internet) does not count the feature phones it runs on, and its effect on extreme poverty, about 2% of Kenyan households by Suri and Jack's study, does not show at world scale. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611). The measure that would follow it is the share of the world's adults with an account at a bank or a mobile-money provider (the World Bank's Findex, from 2011: about half then, three quarters by 2021), which would also take the savings banks and credit societies of earlier centuries as its older kinds.

upsert.boundary: Still Bay and Howiesons Poort, about 77,000 to 59,000 years ago.
upsert.description: In southern Africa people make hafted microliths, heat-treat stone, engrave ochre and wear shell beads, then the toolkits fade and return: an instance of CumulativeCulture#4f93, held where populations were large and connected and lost where they were not. It shows the skills that later let small groups live in new lands.
provenance: exploring: whether these industries mark a change that made the dispersal possible is argued, not settled

changes.value: Widen: Still Bay and Howiesons Poort, the one Event within Africa's Middle Stone Age that named no process, now observes image and ornament (h.play.images): its engraved ochre, engraved ostrich eggshell and shell beads show southern Africa's populations making lasting art, then losing and regaining the toolkits, the flicker that measure's bands hold. It observes rather than moves the share, since the change it shows is local and comes and goes within the stretch. Other fields restated as the model holds them, read back from an export at r394.

upsert.boundary: The first farmers, 9700 to 3500 BCE
upsert.description: Wheat, barley, sheep and goats in south-west Asia, millet and rice in China, squash and maize in Mesoamerica, taro and bananas in New Guinea, and later crops in the Andes and Africa; farming peoples expand into Europe, South Asia and East Asia and replace or absorb foragers. Villages grow into towns such as Çatalhöyük; copper is smelted; by the era's end irrigation farmers crowd the Mesopotamian plain.
provenance: sources to check: Bellwood, First Farmers (2005); Larson et al. 2014, PNAS 111 (domestication)
upsert.region: Western, Eastern and Southern Asia, Europe, the Americas, Melanesia and Africa

changes.value: Widen: the era of the first farmers (9700 to 3500 BCE), the one Event within the agrarian age that named no process, now names what it changes at world scale: farmland (h.farmland) and the share living by foraging (h.foraging) and without a fixed dwelling (h.habitat.mobile), which farming's spread raises and lowers, and nitrogen fixed by people (h.earth.nitrogen), which begins with its sown pulses and paddy rice. Other fields restated as the model holds them, read back from an export at r394.

upsert.boundary: Wild cereal stands spread across the Levant and the Zagros, about 14,700 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: As the world warms and carbon dioxide rises, the wild ancestors of einkorn, emmer and barley, with lentils, peas and flax, grow densely within reach of people who also live among wild sheep, goats, cattle and pigs: more domesticable species together than anywhere else.
provenance: inferred: the founder crops' wild ranges and their deglacial expansion, as recalled

changes.value: Widen: the spread of wild cereal stands across the Levant and the Zagros (about 12,700 to 9700 BCE), the one Event within the Earth's lifecycle that named no process, now observes what its description names: the warming (h.earth, global temperature) and the rise of carbon dioxide (h.co2) under which the founder crops' wild ancestors grew densely within people's reach. It shows those states rather than moving them. Other fields restated as the model holds them, read back from an export at r394.

upsert.boundary: The one Event within the Earth's lifecycle that named no process, the spread of wild cereal stands across the Levant and the Zagros (about 12,700 to 9700 BCE), now observes global temperature (h.earth) and carbon dioxide (h.co2) (r440), the warming and the rising carbon dioxide under which the founder crops' ancestors grew densely within people's reach. Reopen when the parent is recorded as a series, or when the epidemics are read decade by decade for central Mexico and the Andes, where the counts of tributaries allow it.

upsert.reason: Wari had built the first highland empire, with roads, administrative centres, storehouses and knotted-cord records, and Tiwanaku a state cult around Lake Titicaca, which the Inca claimed as their origin. The Inca took up road, storehouse, khipu and rotational labour from that inheritance; without it they would have had to invent an imperial apparatus as Wari did, and an empire built in one century would be less likely.

provenance: exploring: Gupta and later courts and temples kept astronomers whose calendars and horoscopes demanded long calculations; Aryabhata wrote at Kusumapura under that patronage. Without it the method would likely have spread more slowly among merchants and astronomers but would still have come.

The four outcomes the open questions name as at the top of an importance scale with only one linked cause: the Classic Maya, the Inca empire, the place-value decimal system with zero and the founder crops of the Fertile Crescent. Each is asked against a stated contrast (ContrastClass#7398); causes present in both outcome and contrast, such as maize for the Maya, are left out because they do not choose between them. Readings are sketches from recalled scholarship; where the causal claim itself is debated the reading is tagged exploring and the debate stated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). Differences do not sum: the causes act together.

Opens the three parts of the metal-ores carve (r447) at every date of the parent and declares metal ores their sum. Each part is the parent's value times a sketched share of the ore tonnage, each tonne counted under the metal that gives most of its value: before 1900 the shares rest on recalled histories of mining (copper first, iron from about 1000 BCE, the Roman and Spanish-American silver, the gold rushes); from 1950 on recalled production and ore grades (iron ore about 3 Gt, copper about 23 Mt of metal from ore near 0.6%, gold about 3,600 t from ore near 1.5 g/t in 2025). Bands take the parent's band times the share, widened by about a third for the share's own doubt.

Rises: heap leaching with cyanide from the 1980s makes gold ores of one gram a tonne worth mining, in Nevada, Australia and Peru.
About 2.5 Gt: some 3,600 tonnes of gold a year from ores near 1.5 grams a tonne, with primary silver ores; about a quarter of the whole.

upsert.reason: The parent times the sketched share of precious ores: a tenth to a fifth in the Bronze Age, perhaps two-fifths in Rome's mines, a third in the silver century, a tenth to a quarter from 1850 to 1980, and near a quarter since heap leaching made gold ores of one gram a tonne worth mining.

points.note: Native copper is hammered into beads and awls at Çayönü in Anatolia, too little to count.
Copper is smelted from ore in the Balkans (Belovode, Pločnik) and Iran: the first ore taken for metal.
Arsenical and then tin bronze; copper from Oman, Feinan and Cyprus is traded across thousands of kilometres.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant; ores need no long trade, so more is dug.
Rome's mines (Rio Tinto, the lead and silver of Spain, the gold of Las Médulas) and the Han's iron: lead in Greenland's ice peaks in the first century, a level not seen again until the Middle Ages.
Rome's western mines close and the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China's iron industry, perhaps 100,000 tonnes of iron a year about 1080 on Hartwell's much-argued estimate, and Europe's silver mines (Goslar, Kutná Hora later).
The silver century: Potosí's and Zacatecas's ore, refined with mercury from 1573, and Japan's silver, with Sweden's iron and copper.
Iron for rails, ships and machines: about 4.5 Mt of pig iron in 1850, and the gold rushes of California and Victoria.
The steel century begins: about 40 Mt of pig iron, copper for electricity, and the Witwatersrand's gold reef, crushed by the million tonnes.
War production holds up iron and copper while building stops.
Ores per person grow two and a half times from 1950 to 1970, and grades fall: copper ore near 1% means a hundred tonnes dug for each tonne of metal.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries' steel use stops growing.
China's steel and the commodity boom of 2003 to 2014: iron ore mined doubles within a decade.
About 10 Gt of ore a year, iron ore about a quarter of it by mass and copper ore much of the rest.

upsert.boundary: Diamonds at Kimberley and gold on the Witwatersrand, 1867 to 1899
upsert.description: Diamonds found in 1867 and the world's richest gold reef in 1886 turn southern Africa into a mining economy: Johannesburg grows from nothing to 100,000 people in a decade, migrant workers from across the region live in compounds under pass laws, and by the late 1890s the Rand produces about a quarter of the world's gold.
provenance: sources to check: Feinstein, An Economic History of South Africa (2005)

upsert.boundary: Iron smelting begins in West and Central Africa, about 800 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: Furnaces at Taruga and Nok in Nigeria, in Cameroon, and at Urewe sites around Lake Victoria smelt iron, perhaps invented in Africa, perhaps learned from the north; iron hoes and axes later open the forests and savannas to farming.
provenance: exploring: whether African iron-working was invented independently is debated
sources to check: Alpern 2005, History in Africa 32; Holl 2009, Journal of World Prehistory 22
upsert.region: Africa: Western, Middle and Eastern Africa

upsert.boundary: Brazil's gold rush, 1695 to 1760
upsert.description: Gold and then diamonds in Minas Gerais draw hundreds of thousands of Portuguese and many more enslaved Africans inland; Rio de Janeiro becomes the colony's capital (1763), and Brazilian gold flows through Lisbon to Britain.
provenance: sources to check: Boxer, The Golden Age of Brazil (1962)

upsert.boundary: The California gold rush, 1848 to 1855
upsert.description: About 300,000 people pour into California from across the world; the Native Californian population, already halved under Spanish missions, falls from perhaps 150,000 to about 30,000 by 1870 through killing, disease and starvation.
provenance: sources to check: Madley, An American Genocide (2016)

upsert.boundary: The silver of Potosí, 1545 to 1650
upsert.description: A mountain of silver found in the Andes in 1545 makes Potosí one of the largest cities of the world by 1600; after 1573 the mita forces Andean villages to send men to its mines, where mercury refining kills many. Its silver pays Spain's wars and, through Manila, buys China's goods.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Lane, Potosí (2019)

upsert.boundary: Song China and its commercial revolution, 960 to 1279
upsert.description: The Song govern through officials chosen by examination, print books in great numbers, issue the first government paper money and grow early-ripening Champa rice; China's population passes 100 million, and Kaifeng and later Hangzhou hold a million people or more, the largest cities in the world. Iron and coal, the compass at sea and gunpowder weapons grow with them, and Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism becomes the orthodoxy of later dynasties. The north falls to the Jurchen in 1127 and the south to the Mongols in 1279.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; city populations are estimates
sources to check: Elvin, The Pattern of the Chinese Past (1973); Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Tarascan state, about 1350 to 1530
upsert.description: From Tzintzuntzan by Lake Pátzcuaro, the Purépecha kings build a state in western Mexico that works copper and bronze and defeats an Aztec invasion (1478), the one neighbour the Triple Alliance never conquered; its last king submits to the Spanish in 1522 and is executed in 1530.
provenance: sources to check: Pollard, Taríacuri's Legacy (1993)

upsert.boundary: The silver frontier: Zacatecas and the Chichimeca war, 1546 to 1600
upsert.description: Silver strikes at Zacatecas (1546) and Guanajuato draw Spaniards, Indigenous workers and enslaved Africans north into the lands of the nomadic peoples the Spanish called Chichimecas, who fight a forty-year war of raids on the silver roads (1550 to 1590), ended by gifts of food and goods and by settling Tlaxcalan colonists among them. New Spain's silver soon rivals Potosí's.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico (1971); Powell, Soldiers, Indians and Silver (1952)

upsert.boundary: The Panguna mine on Bougainville, 1972 to 1989
upsert.description: One of the world's largest open-pit copper and gold mines provides nearly half of Papua New Guinea's exports while its tailings poison the Jaba river; landowners' anger over the damage and the sharing of its wealth closes it in 1989.
provenance: sources to check: Regan, Light Intervention (2010)

upsert.boundary: Copper smelted, then bronze, about 5000 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Smelting copper from ore begins in the Balkans and Iran by about 5000 BCE; arsenical and then tin bronze follows in south-west Asia, giving harder tools and weapons and a trade in metal and tin across thousands of kilometres.
provenance: sources to check: Radivojević et al. 2010, Journal of Archaeological Science 37; Roberts, Thornton and Pigott 2009, Antiquity 83
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Eastern Europe: the Balkans); Asia (Western and Southern Asia)

upsert.boundary: Old Copper: native copper worked around Lake Superior, about 4000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers of the upper Great Lakes dig pure native copper from veins and glacial drift and cold-hammer and anneal it into spear points, knives, awls and fishhooks, among the earliest metalworking anywhere; recent dates would push its start back to about 7500 BCE, which is disputed. They never smelt ore, and copper later becomes a material of ornament and exchange, reaching the Hopewell across half a continent.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dates are disputed
sources to check: Pompeani et al. 2021, Quaternary International; Martin, Wonderful Power (1999)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the upper Great Lakes)

upsert.boundary: The United States becomes the largest industrial economy, 1870 to 1913
upsert.description: Steel from Carnegie's mills, oil from Rockefeller's refineries, electricity from Edison's and Westinghouse's systems, the corporation, the research laboratory and mass distribution make the United States the world's largest manufacturer by about 1890 and the maker of about a third of the world's manufactures by 1913, with the highest output per worker. A continental market, cheap land, abundant coal, iron and oil, immigrant labour and secure property all played a part; how much each mattered is argued.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weights of its causes are debated
sources to check: Gordon, The Rise and Fall of American Growth (2016); Wright 1990, American Economic Review 80; Bairoch 1982, Journal of European Economic History 11
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the United States)

upsert.boundary: The gold rushes of Australia and New Zealand, 1851 to 1900
upsert.description: Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria (1851), Otago (1861) and Western Australia (1890s) draws hundreds of thousands of migrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese; Victoria's population grows sevenfold in a decade and Melbourne becomes one of the richest cities in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Blainey, The Rush That Never Ended (5th ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Andean metalworking begins, about 1500 BCE
upsert.description: Smiths of the southern Peruvian highlands hammer gold into thin foil (Waywaka, about 1500 BCE); later Andean smiths smelt copper, alloy it with arsenic and then tin into bronze, and gild and silver copper by chemical means. In the Andes metal serves rank and ritual far more than work.
provenance: sources to check: Aldenderfer et al. 2008, PNAS 105; Lechtman 1984, Technology and Culture 25

upsert.boundary: British Malaya: tin, rubber and migrant workers, 1874 to 1941
upsert.description: The Pangkor treaty (1874) puts British residents beside the Malay sultans; Chinese miners make Malaya the world's largest producer of tin, and from about 1900 Tamil workers from India tap rubber on estates that make it the largest producer of rubber too; by 1931 Malays are fewer than half of the peninsula's people, the plural society that independent Malaysia inherits.
provenance: sources to check: Andaya and Andaya, A History of Malaysia (3rd ed. 2017); Drabble, An Economic History of Malaysia (2000)

upsert.boundary: Bronze working spreads on the mainland, from about 1100 BCE
upsert.description: Copper is mined at Phu Lon and Khao Wong Prachan and cast with tin into axes, bangles and bells at Ban Chiang, Ban Non Wat and Non Nok Tha; richer burials show rank growing. Ban Chiang's bronze was once dated to 3600 BCE; the dates are now much later, and a gap remains between the shorter and longer chronologies.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the chronology is debated
sources to check: Higham et al. 2015, Journal of World Prehistory 28; White and Hamilton 2014, in Roberts and Thornton (eds.), Archaeometallurgy in Global Perspective

upsert.lens: To follow the two lands whose peopling differs by sixty thousand years, which one share hides: Australia peopled about 50,000 years ago and holding its foragers' numbers through the Holocene; Aotearoa New Zealand empty until Polynesian voyagers about 1280; then the dispossession of Aboriginal Australians and Maori and the settler societies built on their lands. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for the people of the subregion; a land may stand at zero before anyone lives there, as New Zealand does before about 1280.

changes.value: Opens the two parts of the Australia and New Zealand carve (r451) at every date of the parent and declares the parent their sum. New Zealand is zero before about 1280; after that each part is the parent times its share of the subregion's people, from recalled estimates: Aboriginal Australians about 750,000 before 1788 (300,000 to over a million), Maori about 100,000 at contact (85,000 to 150,000), and the colonial and national censuses and the UN's estimates after. The parts follow the parent as it stands, including its shortfall against the UN from 1950 to 2010, noted on the carve.

points.note: Zero: no people in Australia yet.
Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Begins: people cross the sea from Sunda to Sahul.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply, so the share falls.

The First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove. Aboriginal Australians perhaps 750,000, from 300,000 to over a million on the estimates; as a share of the parent this holds about 500,000, the gap being the parent's.
Falls: the smallpox of 1789 kills perhaps half the Eora around Sydney; whether it came from the First Fleet's stores or from Makassan trepangers in the north is debated.
About 405,000 settlers and convicts, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession.
Rises most: Victoria's gold rush more than doubles the settlers within a decade.
About 3.8 million at Federation (1901); the Immigration Restriction Act begins the White Australia policy.
The postwar migration programme brings Britons and the displaced of Europe ('populate or perish').
The White Australia policy ends (1973); migration from Asia grows.
Rises with the parent, whose values from 1950 to 2010 run a little below the UN's estimates (about 0.42% in 1960 against 0.398 here); see the carve's synthesis.
About 27 million; about three in ten born overseas, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples 3.2% at the 2021 census.

upsert.reason: The whole of the parent before about 1280; after that the parent less New Zealand's part.

points.note: Zero: no people reach Aotearoa New Zealand before Polynesian voyagers about 1280.
Still empty. Radiocarbon dates on rat-gnawed seeds and the earliest sites put first settlement about 1250 to 1300; an older claim of about 800, from dates on rat bones, is now rejected.
Begins: Polynesian voyagers from the Society and Cook Islands settle Aotearoa about 1280, a founding population of perhaps a few hundred.
Grows fast on moa and seals, and on kumara where it will grow; the moa are gone by about 1450.
About 100,000 Maori at Cook's visits (1769) on the usual estimate, between perhaps 85,000 and 150,000; here the parent's share times that against Australia's numbers.
A larger share of the subregion as Aboriginal numbers fall; the Musket Wars among iwi armed with traded guns (about 1807 to 1845) kill perhaps 20,000.
The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and organized settlement begin; Maori perhaps 80,000 after the Musket Wars and new diseases.
Falls: Maori about 60,000, settlers about 25,000.
Rises most: Otago's gold rush from 1861 and assisted migration; settlers outnumber Maori from about 1858, and the New Zealand Wars (1845 to 1872) take Maori land.
Vogel's assisted immigration of the 1870s; Maori at their lowest, about 42,000 in 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills about 9,000, Maori at about seven times the settlers' rate.
Falls: emigration to Australia after 1976 and slowing births.
About 5.3 million, a sixth of the subregion's people; Maori about a sixth of New Zealand's, Pasifika peoples about a twelfth.

upsert.reason: Zero before about 1280; then the parent times New Zealand's share of the subregion's people, wider before the censuses of the 1850s.

Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago (ev.oc.lake-mungo).
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off (ev.anz.tasmanian-isolation) and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply.

Interpolated. From about 4000 BCE backed blades, seed-grinding and new sites spread across mainland Australia and Pama-Nyungan languages spread from the Gulf country. Many read these as signs of more people, but the share still falls because farmers elsewhere multiply faster.
Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land reached by people.

The First Fleet (ev.oc.first-fleet). As a share of the parent's 0.2% this holds about 570,000 people, against the usual estimates of about 750,000 Aboriginal Australians (from 300,000 to over a million) and about 100,000 Maori; the gap is the parent's (h.region-oceania), whose early-modern level is debated, and the band now reaches the usual estimates.
About 470,000 settlers, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 and Maori to 60,000, from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession (ev.oc.depopulation).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) more than double Australia's settlers in a decade.
Assisted passages from Britain and the displaced of Europe: migration keeps Australia's and New Zealand's share level while the world grows faster than ever.
The postwar migration programmes, 'populate or perish', hold the share steady while the world grows fastest.
About 33 million; immigration, from Asia above all since the 1970s, carries most of the growth.

upsert.reason: Declared the sum of Australia and New Zealand, which share its unit and hold every person in the subregion once.

upsert.boundary: Convict transportation to Australia, 1788 to 1868
upsert.description: Britain transports about 162,000 convicts, one in six of them women, to New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land and, last, Western Australia (to 1868); assigned to settlers and public works, most stay when freed, and their labour builds the colonies' roads, farms and towns.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987); Nicholas (ed.), Convict Workers (1988)

upsert.boundary: Convict and settler colonies, 1788 to 1901
upsert.description: Britain founds convict colonies at Sydney (1788) and Hobart (1803) and annexes New Zealand (1840); pastoralists take Aboriginal land across the south-east, and frontier wars and epidemics follow; Maori fight the New Zealand Wars. Gold (from 1851) brings mass migration; the colonies win self-government, the secret ballot and manhood suffrage in the 1850s, and New Zealand gives women the vote in 1893.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre, A Concise History of Australia (4th ed. 2016); Belich, Making Peoples (1996)

upsert.boundary: Federation, dominions and the world wars, 1901 to 1945
upsert.description: Australia federates (1901) behind the White Australia policy and New Zealand becomes a dominion (1907); both build arbitration courts, pensions and Labour governments; they lose about 60,000 and 18,000 dead in the First World War and are shaken by the Depression, and Japan's advance in 1942 turns them from Britain toward the United States.
provenance: sources to check: Macintyre (2016); King, The Penguin History of New Zealand (2003)

upsert.boundary: The first Australians, about 65,000 or 50,000 to 30,000 years ago
upsert.description: People cross from Wallacea to Sahul's northern shores and spread across the continent: the coasts, the rivers of the south-east, the arid interior and, by about 40,000 years ago, Tasmania, joined to the mainland while the sea was low. They grind the edges of stone axes, bury their dead with ochre at Lake Mungo, and within some thousands of years of their arrival the giant marsupials, birds and reptiles are gone. When the first people came is debated: luminescence dates at Madjedbebe put them there by 65,000 years ago, while most secure sites are about 50,000 years old.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the start of the era is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature 547 (Madjedbebe); O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS 115; Hiscock, Archaeology of Ancient Australia (2008)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Australia, with Tasmania)

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum's deserts and refuges, about 30,000 to 12,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the last glacial deepens, Australia's interior dries, dunes spread and lakes such as Mungo empty; people withdraw from much of the arid interior to refuges in the ranges, along rivers and on the coastal plains then exposed, and their numbers may fall. Tasmania's hunters live on wallaby at the southern edge of the inhabited world. From about 18,000 years ago the climate eases and the seas rise.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how far people left the deserts is debated
sources to check: Smith, The Archaeology of Australia's Deserts (2013); Williams et al. 2013, Quaternary Science Reviews 61

upsert.boundary: Holocene Australia, about 12,000 years ago to 1280
upsert.description: The rising sea cuts off Tasmania and then New Guinea and drowns the coastal plains. In a warmer and, from about 5,000 years ago, more variable climate, Aboriginal societies change: small backed tools spread, seed-grinding and eel-trapping grow, the Pama-Nyungan languages spread across most of the continent, and about 3,500 years ago the dingo arrives from island South-east Asia. Aotearoa New Zealand, the subregion's other land, has no people yet.
provenance: sources to check: Mulvaney and Kamminga, Prehistory of Australia (1999); Hiscock (2008)

upsert.boundary: Migration, Asia and the first peoples' rights, 1945 to 2025
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish' millions of migrants arrive, first from Britain and Europe and, after White Australia ends (1973), from Asia; trade turns from Britain to Japan and China; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people win citizenship rights, land rights and native title, and Maori a tribunal for Treaty claims and a revival of their language; both countries grow rich on minerals, farm exports and services.

upsert.boundary: Aboriginal Australia and Maori Aotearoa, about 1280 to 1788
upsert.description: East Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa, the last large land on Earth to be peopled; within two centuries the moa are gone, and Maori live from gardens of kumara, fern root and the sea, building fortified pa and forming iwi and hapu. Across the Tasman, hundreds of Aboriginal nations keep their country by law, ceremony and fire; Makassan fishermen visit the north coast from about 1720, and Dutch and English ships chart the west and south from 1606.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Binney and Harris, Tangata Whenua (2014); Mulvaney and Kamminga (1999)

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum: Aboriginal people withdraw to refuges, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the continent cools and dries, dunes advance and inland lakes fail; people leave much of the arid interior for refuges in the ranges, along rivers and on the broad coastal plains then exposed, and their numbers may fall by half or more before they reoccupy the deserts as the climate eases. How far the deserts were abandoned and how far numbers fell are debated: radiocarbon dates used as a proxy for population are read both ways.
provenance: exploring: the size of the fall is debated
sources to check: Williams et al. 2013, Quaternary Science Reviews 61; Smith, The Archaeology of Australia's Deserts (2013)

upsert.boundary: New tools, new places and more people, about 4000 to 1000 BCE
upsert.description: Across mainland Australia small backed blades and points spread, seed-grinding grows, sites multiply and people settle harsher country, as rainfall becomes less reliable with the strengthening of El Nino. Whether this was an 'intensification' driven by society and population growth or a response to a more variable climate is a long debate.
provenance: sources to check: Lourandos, Continent of Hunter-Gatherers (1997); Hiscock (2008); Williams et al. 2015, Quaternary Science Reviews 123
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (mainland Australia)

upsert.boundary: The Musket Wars in Aotearoa, about 1807 to 1842
upsert.description: Iwi who obtain muskets from traders, above all Ngapuhi under Hongi Hika after his visit to England in 1820, raid their rivals the length of the North Island; perhaps 20,000 die and tens of thousands are enslaved or driven from their lands before the guns spread to every side; the displacements shape the land claims the Crown later meets.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is debated
sources to check: Crosby, The Musket Wars (1999); Ballara, Taua (2003)
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Aotearoa New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Smallpox at Sydney, 1789
upsert.description: Fifteen months after the First Fleet, smallpox breaks out among the Eora and their neighbours around Port Jackson (April 1789), killing perhaps half of them or more, while almost no colonists fall ill; it spreads inland along the rivers. Whether it came from variolous matter carried by the fleet's surgeons or with Makassan visitors in the north is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the source of the virus is debated
sources to check: Campbell, Invisible Invaders (2002); Warren 2014, Journal of Australian Colonial History 16
upsert.region: Oceania: Australia and New Zealand (Sydney and New South Wales)

upsert.boundary: Māori Aotearoa before Cook, about 1280 to 1769
upsert.description: Polynesian settlers adapt to a cool, large land: they hunt moa and seals, then grow kumara and fern root, build fortified pā and form iwi and hapū that compete for land and mana, developing a Māori culture distinct from the tropical Pacific's.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Binney and Harris, Tangata Whenua (2014)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Oceania's indigenous peoples decimated, 1788 to 1920
upsert.description: Smallpox, measles, influenza, venereal disease, violence and the loss of land cut Aboriginal Australians from perhaps 800,000 to under 100,000, Māori to about 42,000 (1896) and Hawaiians from some 300,000 to about 40,000 (1890), and many smaller island peoples by more; populations recover only in the 1900s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; pre-contact numbers are uncertain
sources to check: Butlin, Our Original Aggression (1983); Pool, Te Iwi Maori (1991)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand; Polynesia; Melanesia)

upsert.boundary: The First Fleet founds a convict colony at Sydney, January 1788
upsert.description: Eleven British ships land some 1,400 convicts, marines and officials at Sydney Cove (26 January 1788) on the land of the Gadigal people; Britain will send about 160,000 convicts to Australia by 1868.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: Australia); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: The gold rushes of Australia and New Zealand, 1851 to 1900
upsert.description: Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria (1851), Otago (1861) and Western Australia (1890s) draws hundreds of thousands of migrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese; Victoria's population grows sevenfold in a decade and Melbourne becomes one of the richest cities in the world.

points.note: News moves at the pace of a walker or runner passing it on; fire and smoke signals carry only a few agreed meanings.
Royal messengers of Egypt and Sumer carry written orders by boat and on foot.
Couriers with horses and chariots carry the letters of the Amarna age between Egypt, Babylon and the Hittites.
The Achaemenid relay riders carry the king's messages from Sardis to Susa, some 2,700 km, in about a week, as Herodotus tells it.
Augustus's cursus publicus and the Han relay posts.
The Tang relay posts and the Abbasid barid.
The Mongol yam: urgent riders change horses at stations and cover 300 to 400 km a day.
The Taxis postal relays in Europe from about 1490; the Ming courier stations.
Before Chappe's semaphore (1794): the jump to 1800 is its first line's, so the riders' speed holds until here.

Jumps: Chappe's semaphore line from Paris to Lille (1794) passes a message 230 km in minutes to an hour; lines spread across France, Britain and Sweden. Words now outrun riders for the first time on a regular service.
Jumps again: the electric telegraph (Cooke and Wheatstone 1837, Morse 1844) carries messages across a continent in minutes, slowed by relaying and copying.
The transatlantic cable (1866): London to New York in minutes instead of ten days.

Interpolated between the transatlantic cable and the world network, within the band. A message crosses a cable in minutes, but news passes through several relaying stations and offices: word of Krakatoa's eruption (27 August 1883) went by cable from Batavia and reached London's newspapers within hours.
A cable network girdles the world; news reaches the antipodes in hours.
Radio telegraphy and radio telephony connect continents without relays.
Communications satellites (1962) and direct long-distance dialling.
Fibre-optic cables carry signals near the speed of light in glass.

Reaches the limit: transoceanic fibre cables (from TAT-8 in 1988 to the round-the-world FLAG cable in 1997) replace satellite hops, whose round trip to geostationary orbit added about a quarter of a second, and messages cross the world at nearly the speed of light in glass.
At the limit: light in fibre travels about 200,000 km a second. From here what changes is who can send and receive, read in being online (h.internet) and mass media (h.media).

upsert.reason: From the recorded speeds of relay posts (Herodotus on the Persian riders, the Mongol yam, European posts), the semaphore and telegraph lines, and the latency of cable, radio and fibre networks, as recalled; orders of magnitude after 1850.

changes.value: Check the parts against the whole. Eight wholes that earlier passes meant to declare the sum of their parts carry no declaration in the model: range (r338), migration (r343 and r344), discovery (r348), migrants living in the Americas (r395), the arts' makers (r399), one-sided killing (r408), metal ores (r448) and Australia and New Zealand (r452). Each of those revisions re-recorded a value with process.aggregate through life_values_record, which does not change an existing process, as r231 had already found; only r232 and r370, which restated the process through life_model_revise, took. Each whole is restated here with scale.aggregate = sum and everything else as it was, so the values report compares its parts with it at every date. Each is the sum of its parts by the parts' own definitions, in the same unit (MECE#ae19: one criterion per carve, where the people, land or researchers are, who keeps the makers, who kills, which metal, which land). Energy for warmth, light and work (h.warmth) is left undeclared: its unit counts food, which its three parts do not, so it is the parts plus food energy (h.food in kcal a day times 365 days times 4,184 J), not their sum.

Correction left open by the last pass (claude.closing.fill-widen-pass-5): Oceania's share and its parts from 1950 to 2025 against the UN's World Population Prospects as recalled (2022 and 2024 revisions; to be checked there, so tagged inferred). Australia ran about 5% under the UN from 1955 to 1980 (0.324 against about 0.341 in 1960), dipped without cause at 2006 and 2010 and rose without cause at 2014; New Zealand ran 2 to 7% under; Micronesia and Polynesia ran a fifth to a third under from 1950 to 1980 (Polynesia's dip to 0.006 at 1965 had no cause). Each part is set from the recalled national counts over the recalled world total (2.499 billion in 1950, 3.695 in 1970, 5.316 in 1990, 6.986 in 2010, about 8.19 in 2025), and Oceania is set to their sum, now declared (r458). Because the five M49 areas divide all people, Oceania's rise of up to 0.03 points is taken from Asia and from Southern Asia, its largest subregion, at their own dates from 1950 (interpolated): a change far inside both bands, which keeps the five areas at 100 and Asia equal to its subregions. points.note: Tools at Jwalapuram lie beneath the Toba ash, about 74,000 years old; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated, so the share is small with a band to zero.
The dispersal out of Africa fills the subcontinent's coasts and river valleys; South Asia holds the largest share of the people outside Africa from now until farming.
Farming at Mehrgarh, on the edge of the Indus plain, from about 7000 BCE.
The Harappan cities at their height, perhaps five million people in the Indus valley.
Farming spreads through the Ganges valley with iron; Southern Asia becomes Asia's largest part for the next two thousand years on most reconstructions.

India's people in 1 CE are the widest debate in this series: McEvedy and Jones about 35 million, Maddison 75 million; this value takes about 60 million for the subcontinent, with Iran and Afghanistan about 7.
Rises as Eastern Asia's falls under the Mongol conquest, which reached Iran but held India only at its edge.
Mughal India grows while China falls in the Ming-Qing transition: for a few decades Southern Asia holds more of humanity than Eastern Asia.
Interpolated: the Mughal empire has broken into successor states; the Company's victory at Plassey (1757) comes two years later.
India grows more slowly than Qing China through the eighteenth century, after the Mughal break-up and the famine of 1770 in Bengal.
The famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 kill perhaps 12 to 30 million in British India, and plague arrives from 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills perhaps 12 to 17 million in India, its largest toll anywhere.
The Bengal famine of 1943 kills about two to three million, yet deaths are falling elsewhere in India and its share rises.
About 2001 Southern Asia's share passes Eastern Asia's, since its births fell later and more slowly; India itself passes China in 2023.
Close to its peak share: India's fertility is now below replacement, so Southern Asia's share levels off as Africa's keeps rising.

Between the Last Interglacial values on either side: Homo sapiens in the Levant and Arabia, all of Asia's people in Western Asia.
Toba erupts in Sumatra (ev.toba); whether it thinned the few Homo sapiens then in Asia is debated.
Between Toba and the dispersal; set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's interpolated value.

Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. The date is debated: genomes put the main dispersal about 60,000 to 50,000 years ago, while finds in Arabia, the Levant and China suggest earlier, smaller exits from about 120,000 years ago that left little or no trace in living people (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). This series follows the genomic date.
Between -44000 and -37000, set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's, Europe's and Oceania's interpolated values.

Interpolated, in the pandemic: COVID-19's excess deaths fall on Asia roughly in proportion to its people, so they move its share little; India's own toll for 2020 and 2021 is debated, about 4.7 million on the WHO's estimate against about half a million officially counted. Child mortality (h.child-survival) and farmland (h.farmland) declare that they are the sum of their parts, but the values report never compares them, because the parts' unit strings differ from the parent's ('% of live births' against '% dying before age 5'; '% of ice-free land' against '% of ice-free land as crops or pasture'). upsert.description: An Event of the era of revolutions, industry and empire.

upsert.boundary: Asiatic cholera's first three pandemics, 1817 to 1860.
upsert.description: Cholera, long endemic in the Ganges delta, spreads in 1817 along the routes of trade, pilgrimage and armies: the first pandemic reaches South-east Asia, China, Japan, Arabia and the Caspian (to 1824); the second reaches Russia (1830), Europe and North America (1832), killing about 18,000 in Paris and over 30,000 in Britain; the third (1846 to 1860) is the deadliest, in Russia over a million dead and in London the outbreak of 1854 that John Snow traced to the Broad Street pump. India bears most of the toll: perhaps 15 million deaths from 1817 to 1860 on a commonly cited estimate, whose basis is weak and whose range is wide. Across about 1.1 to 1.3 billion people the pandemics add a few tens of deaths per 100,000 a year to infection's thousands, but they fall on the new industrial cities, where they show what dirty water does and set off the sanitary movement.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Indian toll is debated (about 15 million from 1817 to 1860 is the usual figure, resting on later colonial extrapolation)

changes.value: Fill, before values: the coverage report names 1820 to 1850 as the coarsest stretch of the survival measures, and the account has no Event for what moved infection deaths in it. Asiatic cholera leaves the Ganges delta in 1817 and in three pandemics to 1860 reaches every inhabited region but Oceania; it is the stretch's new killer and the spur to the sanitary reforms the account already holds (ev.sanitation, whose description begins 'After the cholera epidemics'). The Event names infection deaths, placed in the Earth as a whole and in Southern Asia, where it began and killed most; filed in the era of revolutions, industry and empire; judged on the scales for everyone, for population, for Asia and for Europe.
