Fill: the coverage report names 1820 to 1850 as the coarsest stretch of the survival and household measures, which held only their 1820 and 1850 values, and 1500 to 1600 and 1972 to 1980 for other kinds of human. Values at 1832, when cholera's second pandemic reaches Europe and North America (ev.cholera-pandemics, added at r461), and at 1840, between it and the Irish famine. They are guessed within the values around them and their bands: the world's survival barely moves in these decades (life expectancy near 30), with smallpox vaccination spreading and cholera added. Injury is the exception: its 1850 value was lowered to the level of early registration data (about one death in twenty-five), while the agrarian values before it rest on wider sketches; the new values stand on the line between, and the note says the step is a change of estimate. Other kinds of human stay at zero, as at every date since about 40,000 years ago.

points.note: Ethnographic foragers reaching fifteen live on about 37 to 43 years (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled); the model's life expectancy of 30 with child mortality of 45% would imply about 45, so one of those two existing values, most likely the forager child mortality, is too high: ethnographic foragers lose about a quarter to a third of children before five.
Held from the deep forager reading: remaining years at 15 for mobile foragers, from the ethnographic range of recent foragers (about 37 to 43) widened for the deep past; no evidence turns it here.
Farmers' adults live shorter lives than foragers': crowd diseases from livestock and crowding, worse teeth and bones in the skeletons (Armelagos's first epidemiological transition).
Roman tombstones and Egyptian census returns give adults of fifteen some 30 to 35 more years: crowded cities and malaria kill adults as well as children.
The Justinianic plague kills adults as freely as children.
The Black Death at its height kills people of every age in the year it passes (ev.black-death).

Smallpox reaches the Caribbean (1518) and Mexico (1520) and kills adults as well as children, but in about a tenth of humanity: a fall of several years there moves the world's figure by under half a year, inside the band.
The Taiping war and the American Civil War kill young men above all.
On the eve of the First World War: the fall to 1918 is the war's and the influenza's, so the series holds until here and drops after.
The 1918 influenza kills young adults above all, with the war's dead: adult survival falls by a sixth in a year while child mortality barely moves.
The war's deadliest years and the famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
War deaths and the war's famines last into 1945 (Vietnam, Java, the Dutch hunger winter, the battles for Germany, Okinawa and Manila), so adult survival is still near the 1944 low.
The war ends in August and September 1945: young men stop dying in battle and the occupied lands' famines end, so adult survival jumps.
On the postwar rise; the lower value at 1960 is the Great Leap famine's dip, not the trend.
The Great Leap Forward famine holds adult survival down in 1959 to 1961.
Recovering from the Great Leap famine of 1959 to 1961.
Slowed by AIDS in eastern and southern Africa and by the mortality crisis of Russian and Ukrainian men after 1991.
COVID-19's first year: excess deaths in 2020 are under a third of the pandemic's toll, so adult survival falls about halfway to the 2021 trough.
COVID-19 kills adults, the old above all (ev.covid).
About 33 births a year per 1,000 people, of whom perhaps one in twelve dies in the first month, and about one mother in a hundred births.
Held: deaths of mothers and newborns around birth, scaled from natural fertility of about six births per woman and recent forager neonatal loss.
Farmers have more births, closer together, and so more deaths at birth per head.
Semmelweis shows in 1847 that childbed fever is carried by doctors' hands; antisepsis reaches maternity wards only after 1870.
Sulfa drugs cut deaths from puerperal fever in rich countries by half within a few years.
About five million newborns and half a million mothers die a year, as the UN's child-mortality group and maternal-mortality group count them.
About 2.3 million newborns and 260,000 mothers a year, more than half of each in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Few live long enough to die of them; the old who do are often recorded as dying of a last infection.
Held: degenerative deaths at older ages in the few who reach them; low because few live past 60, not because the old do not die of them.
As infections retreat in the industrial countries more people reach the ages of heart disease and cancer; cigarettes spread after 1880.

Heart disease and lung cancer peak in rich countries; their fall afterwards, with less smoking and treated blood pressure, is matched by the poor world's ageing, so the world rate per head holds near five hundred.
About 42 million deaths, three in four of all, by the Global Burden of Disease's count, as recalled.
Rising per head as the world ages, though each age's rate keeps falling.
About two thirds of foragers' deaths are from illness, mostly respiratory and gut infections and parasites (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled).

Held: infection in small mobile bands without crowd diseases, mostly gut, respiratory and wound infections and parasites in children; the largest share of forager deaths, as in recent forager mortality studies.
Villages, stored grain, livestock and standing water bring crowd diseases and parasites: infections rise with farming, the first epidemiological transition (Armelagos).
Malaria in Italy's lowlands, gut infections in Rome's crowded city: about seven in ten deaths are infections.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), probably smallpox, which killed perhaps a tenth of the Roman Empire's people.
The Justinianic plague (ev.justinian-plague), the first pandemic of Yersinia pestis.
The plague recurs until about 750 and then vanishes from the Mediterranean for six centuries; infection deaths fall back to their agrarian level.
The Black Death at its height (ev.black-death): the infection death rate more than doubles for the years it passes.
Plague returns every decade or two after 1348.
Smallpox reaches the Caribbean in 1518 and Mexico in 1520; the Americas' epidemics raise the world's infection deaths toward the 1550 value, though the Americas hold about a tenth of humanity.
Smallpox, measles and cocoliztli in the Americas (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd) add deaths, though the Americas are a tenth of humanity.
Jenner's vaccine (1796) begins the retreat of smallpox; plague has left Europe.

Cholera's second pandemic reaches Russia, Europe and North America (ev.cholera-pandemics). Its deaths, most of them in India, add a few tens per 100,000 a year to infection's thousands, while vaccination keeps smallpox falling, so the total barely moves.
Cholera pandemics in the new industrial cities; sanitation's retreat of infection begins in Britain after the 1848 Public Health Act.
Germ theory, clean water and sewers cut infection deaths in Europe and North America; most of the world has not yet begun.
Before the influenza: the 1918 value is the pandemic's spike, not a trend, so the fall since 1900 continues to here; wartime typhus in Serbia and the east adds little at the world's scale.
The 1918 influenza kills perhaps 25 to 50 million in little more than a year, most in India and China (ev.flu-1918).
The influenza has passed by 1920 and the long fall of infection deaths resumes.
Sulfa drugs, from 1935, the first antibacterial medicines.
Penicillin, streptomycin and DDT spread after the war: infection deaths fall faster than at any time before.
About 1967 chronic disease passes infection as the world's leading cause of death.
Smallpox is declared eradicated (1980); the Expanded Programme on Immunization reaches most children by 1990.
HIV/AIDS climbs toward its peak of about two million deaths a year (2004).
COVID-19's first year: about four to five million excess deaths in 2020 on the WHO's estimate, under a third of the pandemic's toll, which peaks in 2021.
COVID-19: about 15 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 on the WHO's estimate, most of them in 2021 (ev.covid).
Hunting, falls, drowning, snakebite and burns: about one forager death in fifteen.
Held: accidents, falls, drowning, animal attack among mobile hunters; violence is counted in h.safety, not here.

On the line between the agrarian sketch (about 210) and the level of early registration data at 1850 (about 140). The step is a change of estimate, not of the world: European registers count injury as about one death in twenty-five, foragers' and some agrarian peoples' accident shares are higher, and which holds for the agrarian world is debated, so the bands overlap.

Revised down from the agrarian level: the share of deaths from injury in early registration data (England, Sweden) is about one in twenty-five, lower than the forager and agrarian sketches assumed; the earlier values stay as they are with their wide bands.
Mines, railways and factories: industrial accidents peak in the late nineteenth century.
Road deaths peak in rich countries about 1970, then fall with seat belts and safer cars, while they rise in the poor world.
About 1.2 million road deaths, 700,000 suicides, and falls and drownings: the Global Burden of Disease's injuries without interpersonal violence and war, as recalled.
Early farming villages: denser settlement and zoonoses lowered life expectancy below foragers'.
The Antonine plague and the Han collapse.
Just after the first wave; during 1348–1350 period life expectancy in the stricken regions fell far lower.
Plague returned every decade or two after 1348; life expectancy below both 1300 and 1500.
Riley's world estimate for 1800 is about 28.5, as recalled.
Cholera reaches Europe and North America (ev.cholera-pandemics) while vaccination keeps smallpox falling: the world's life expectancy hardly moves.
Before the First World War and the 1918 influenza.
The influenza year, about five years below 1910.
The war widens to the Soviet Union and, in December, the Pacific.
The war at its deadliest and Bengal's famine (1943): period life expectancy keeps falling toward the 1944 low.
The war's deadliest stretch, with the Bengal and Henan famines of 1942-44: period life expectancy dips below 1940's.
War deaths and the famines of Bengal (1943), Henan (1942–43), Vietnam and the Netherlands (1944–45) hold life expectancy down until the war ends.
The war ends in August 1945; deaths fall at once.
Peace, sulfa drugs, penicillin and DDT: life expectancy rises fast after the war.
Revised from 50: the Great Chinese Famine pulls world life expectancy down in 1959–1961.
Recovered from the Chinese famine and rising fast with vaccines and antibiotics in the poor world.
The COVID-19 trough.

Most foragers reckon descent through both parents and live in flexible bands; some (Aboriginal Australians, many Amazonian and North American peoples) have clans and moieties: about three in ten, guessed from ethnographic foragers.
Farming makes land and herds property worth holding in common by descent: lineages and clans spread with farmers.
About three in five people live under clans or lineages: China's, India's, the Middle East's tribes, Africa's lineages, the Celtic and Germanic kindreds.

Western Christendom's kin groups dissolve under the Church's bans on cousin marriage and its rules on inheritance (Goody), from about 600 to 1500; the debated root of Europe's individualism and of its guilds, communes and universities (Henrich; Greif; critics stress institutions and the state instead).
South China's lineages, with their halls, estates and genealogies, are at their strongest from the Song to the Qing, while western Europe's kin groups are nearly gone.
Europe's and North America's fast-growing populations, with nuclear families, lower the world's share slowly.
Soviet collectivization and settlement break the clans of Central Asia's herders.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) takes the lineages' estates and ends their courts; collectivization and, from 1966, the attacks on ancestral halls finish them as corporate groups for a generation.
Held near a third: south China's lineages revive after 1980 and Africa's growing share of humanity lives mostly in lineage societies, against cities and schooling everywhere.
About a quarter to a third: much of sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East's and Central and South Asia's tribes and castes, and rural south China.
Nearly half of foragers' child deaths come after weaning, at about two to four: hunger, infections and accidents.
In agrarian populations the crowd diseases of childhood (later measles and smallpox) kill most at these ages.
The plague's returns in the decades after the Black Death kill children above all.
Smallpox vaccination (Jenner, 1796) begins to cut deaths at these ages where it spreads.
Vaccination keeps cutting smallpox deaths at these ages where it reaches; cholera kills adults more than young children.
The wartime famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam kill weaned children most.
Measles vaccine (1963) and the smallpox eradication campaign (1967 to 1977) cut deaths at these ages fastest of the three.
Malaria in sub-Saharan Africa keeps deaths at one to four high as other ages fall.
Insecticide-treated nets and new vaccines (pneumococcal, rotavirus) halve these deaths in fifteen years.
About 9 per 1,000 births, a quarter of deaths before five, from about two fifths for most of history.
About a quarter of foragers' child deaths: infections of the breastfed infant.
Farming raises infancy's deaths: cereal gruels as weaning food, crowding and dirty water.
The urban penalty: infants in the industrial cities die of diarrhoea and dirty water faster than in the countryside.
Clean water, sewers and safer milk begin to cut infancy's deaths in Europe and North America.
Oral rehydration salts, adopted widely from the late 1970s, cut infants' deaths from diarrhoea.
About 10 per 1,000 births.
About a quarter of foragers' deaths before five come in the first month: birth, prematurity and the infections of the newborn.
The first month falls least of the three: its deaths yield to skilled birth care, not to clean water or vaccines.
About 37 per 1,000 births, two fifths of all deaths before five (UN Inter-agency Group, as recalled).
About 17 per 1,000 births, nearly half of all deaths before five: prematurity, birth asphyxia and newborn infections.

Corrected from 45: with life expectancy at 30 and adults of fifteen living on about 41 more years (h.alive.adult), the share dying before five must be about 42%, since life expectancy is roughly the survivors to fifteen times (15 plus their remaining years) plus the short lives of the rest; ethnographic foragers lose about a quarter to two fifths of their children before five (Gurven and Kaplan, as recalled). Check: recompute life expectancy from the three at any forager date.
Corrected from 45.1, as at the forager dates: farming begins and child mortality starts to rise with crowding and new diseases.
Corrected from 46 to fit life expectancy of 29 and adults living on about 40 years.
Corrected from 47: life expectancy of 27 with adults living on about 37 years fits about 44% dying before five.
Corrected from 46.5; from here the earlier values already fit life expectancy and adult survival within a point.
The flu year.
The wartime famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam raise children's deaths.
Before the war cuts births.
War and flu cut births.
The Depression lowers births in the industrial countries.
Wartime separations and famine lower births.
Wartime separations lower births for a few years.
The postwar baby boom in the rich world.
The world's fertility is near its postwar peak; the transition begins in East Asia and Latin America (ev.fertility-transition).
The fertility transition is under way in East Asia and Latin America (ev.fertility-transition).

Homo sapiens shares the Earth with about seven other kinds of human: the early Neanderthals in Europe, the Denisovans in Asia, Homo erectus in Java, the small hominins of Flores and Luzon, Homo naledi in southern Africa and the archaic people of Kabwe. Lineages known only from genomes (the 'ghost' archaics in West Africans' ancestry) are in the upper band.
Homo naledi's last known date is about 236,000 years ago.
The last Homo erectus, at Ngandong on the Solo River, dies out about 108,000 years ago as Java's open woodland turns to rainforest, before Homo sapiens arrives.
The Toba eruption (about 74,000 years ago) leaves no sign of ending any lineage: Neanderthals, Denisovans and the island hominins of Flores and Luzon all outlast it.
Homo floresiensis's last dates at Liang Bua and Homo luzonensis's at Callao Cave are about 50,000 years ago, close to Homo sapiens' arrival in Wallacea; whether the arrival ended them is debated.

Homo sapiens is the only human on Earth, on the latest reading of Denisovan admixture into Papuans (about 30,000 years ago); the Red Deer Cave people of southern China (about 14,000 years ago), once proposed as archaic, are now read as Homo sapiens, and stay in the upper band.
At the glacial maximum Homo sapiens is the only human on Earth; the upper band keeps open a late Denisovan population in New Guinea or Wallacea that the admixture dates allow.
No other kind of human is known to be alive as the glacial maximum begins.
The first Neanderthal recognized as another kind of human (the Feldhofer skeleton, 1856, named in 1864) changes what people know, not the count: the lineage ended about 40,000 years ago.
Homo sapiens alone; about 2% of the genome of every population outside Africa is Neanderthal, and up to about 5% of Papuans' and Aboriginal Australians' is Denisovan.

upsert.reason: Counted from the hominin fossil and genomic record as recalled: Homo naledi (335,000 to 236,000 years ago), Kabwe (about 300,000), Homo erectus at Ngandong (117,000 to 108,000, the last), Homo floresiensis (to about 50,000), Homo luzonensis (known 67,000 to 50,000; hominins on Luzon since 700,000), Neanderthals (to about 40,000) and Denisovans (admixture into Papuans as late as about 30,000 years ago on one reading). Sources to check: Berger and colleagues 2017 (eLife); Rizal and colleagues 2020 (Nature 577); Sutikna and colleagues 2016 (Nature 532); Détroit and colleagues 2019 (Nature 568); Higham and colleagues 2014 (Nature 512); Jacobs and colleagues 2019 (Cell 177).

points.note: Early Upper Palaeolithic people were tall.
Heights fell with the first farming diets and village disease.
The low point of the farming transition's heights.
After the Black Death, survivors ate better where land was plentiful; European skeletal heights rose.

Band narrowed from the ±20% placeholder at 1800 (131 to 197 cm): national height series for the early 1800s, from about 160 cm in parts of Asia to about 170 in North America, bound the world mean within a few centimetres.
Heights fall in Britain's and the United States' fast-growing cities in the 1830s and 1840s (the 'antebellum puzzle'), but the world's mean, mostly Asian and rural, holds.
Early industrial cities: heights stalled or fell where they grew fastest.
Foragers marry and part easily: among the Hadza and the !Kung a third or more of first marriages end in separation (Blurton Jones and colleagues; Howell, as recalled), with little property to divide.
Falls slowly as farmers outnumber foragers: land, herds and bridewealth bind marriages and kin enforce them.
Rome's elite divorce and remarry freely; most Romans, and most Chinese and Indians, do not.
The Church moves toward indissoluble marriage in the west (made a sacrament, divorce barred by the twelfth century); Islamic law lets husbands divorce easily, and many Muslim societies divorce often.
Down with the collapse of the Americas' peoples, many of whom parted easily.
Lowest: China, India and Christian Europe, most of humanity, almost never divorce; Tokugawa Japan's villages, Java and the Malay world, and many African and Muslim societies divorce often.
Western countries begin to allow civil divorce (England 1857, France 1884); Meiji Japan's code of 1898 lowers its high divorce.
Soviet Russia makes divorce a matter of registration (1917 to 1936), the easiest in the world; wartime marriages end after the war.
Jumps: wartime marriages end in a wave of divorces in the United States and Europe in 1946 and 1947.
China's Marriage Law (1950) lets women divorce: a wave of divorces follows to 1953. Java and Malaya divorce at among the world's highest rates, about half of marriages.
Divorce falls in Java and the Malay world, where marriage becomes later and chosen, while it has not yet risen in the West.
The divorce revolution: California's no-fault law (1969) and its followers across the West; women's earnings and the pill make leaving possible.
About two in five first marriages end in divorce in the United States, northern Europe and the Soviet Union; under one in fifty in India.
China's divorce rate climbs after the 2003 rules make divorce a matter of registration.

Turns level: China's divorces fall after the 2021 cooling-off period, and Western divorce has fallen since about 1990 as people marry later and fewer marry. World divorce is measured unevenly, and periods and cohorts give different shares; the band carries both.

Most foraging societies allow a man more than one wife, but few manage it: a few to a fifth of married women, more where older men control marriages, as among many Aboriginal Australians (Marlowe's forager sample, as recalled).
Rises with farming: where wealth is in land, herds and the labour of wives and children, more men take more wives; polygyny is commonest among hoe farmers and herders in the ethnographic record.
Turns down as states grow: in Egypt and Mesopotamia most men have one wife, kings and the rich add secondary wives and concubines.
Greek cities and Rome allow one wife only; whether socially imposed monogamy spread because it eased competition among men (Henrich, Boyd and Richerson) or for other reasons is debated.
Han China: one principal wife, with concubines for the rich (counted here as plural unions, which is debated, since concubines were not wives in law); India permits more wives but few take them.
Islam permits up to four wives; few men can afford more than one, a few in a hundred marriages in most Muslim societies, and conversion does not lower Africa's polygyny.
Most of it now in sub-Saharan Africa, where a third or more of married women share a husband; China's, India's and the Muslim world's elites add a little.
The United States forces the Mormon church to give up plural marriage (1890).
Turkey bans polygamy (1926).
China's Marriage Law (1950) bans concubinage; India's Hindu Marriage Act (1955) makes Hindu marriage monogamous.

Level since 1900: Africa's growing share of humanity balances the fall of polygyny within Africa, where the share of married women in polygynous unions falls from about two in five in West Africa toward a quarter or a third.

Pew (2020) finds about 2% of the world's people living in polygamous households, most in West and Central Africa (over a third of people in Burkina Faso, Mali and Nigeria's north, as recalled); as a share of married women it is a little higher.
Raised from 17.2 so the series no longer dips between 1300 (17.5) and 1500 (18).
The European marriage pattern begins to set in (ev.eu.marriage-pattern), among too few people to move the world mean much.

changes.value: Values at 1815, where the coverage report found eight processes passing over three Events between 1808.2 and 1820 once the cholera Event was added (Latin America's wars of independence, the cholera pandemics, the great emigration's start, the Congress of Vienna, the Erie Canal). The parts of colonial rule and of migration are given values at the same date so they still sum to their wholes.

points.note: Zero before 1415, as the parent is by definition.
Portugal's forts on Africa's Atlantic coast, Elmina among them (1482).
Freetown is founded for freed Black Britons (1787), a few hundred people.
Doubles with France's conquest of Algeria (from 1830).
Jumps: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882).
The Scramble's conquests: most of West, East and southern Africa comes under European rule.
Britain's sack of Benin (1897) ends one of the last independent kingdoms of the forest coast, after Dahomey (1894), Asante and Madagascar (1896).
Almost all of Africa but Ethiopia and Liberia is partitioned: Africa now holds about a fifth of the colonized.
Egypt's nominal independence (1922) takes it out of the count.
Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1935 to 1936).
Africa becomes most of colonial rule as South Asia leaves it (1947 to 1948).
Falls by two thirds: the year of Africa (1960) and the independences of 1961.
Falls by two thirds: Portugal's African colonies become independent (1974 to 1975).
Zimbabwe (1980) is independent; Namibia is what remains.
Namibia's independence (1990) leaves only small islands.
Zero before Castile rules Hispaniola (1493 to 1496).
Castile begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over their numbers.
Hispaniola's Taínos have mostly died; Cuba, Puerto Rico and Darién add few.
Central Mexico under Spanish rule after Tenochtitlan falls: almost all of colonial rule is now in the Americas.
The Andes join after Pizarro takes the Inca empire.
Halves without a colony lost: epidemics, war and forced labour kill the colonized (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
Spanish America near its demographic low.
Recovery: Spanish America's people grow again, and the sugar islands, Brazil and the English mainland colonies fill with settlers and enslaved Africans.
The Americas are now the smaller part: Bengal makes Asia the larger.
The thirteen colonies leave the count when they rebel (1776), about 2.8 million people.
Haiti's independence (1804) takes Saint-Domingue out.
The Río de la Plata (1810), Paraguay (1811) and much of Venezuela and New Granada at war rule themselves: the part falls slowly before the decisive years after 1817.
Argentina, Chile and Gran Colombia's core are independent; Mexico, Peru, Central America, Brazil and the Caribbean remain.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822): the part falls by almost two thirds.
Peru and Upper Peru leave (1824 to 1825); Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Caribbean colonies, the Guianas and British North America remain.
British North America leaves the count as responsible government comes (1848 to 1855).
Spain takes back the Dominican Republic (1861 to 1865). Maximilian's Mexico (1864 to 1867) is a client empire on the spot, not counted.
Cuba and Puerto Rico pass from Spain to the United States (1898); Hawaii is annexed. Cuba under American occupation until 1902 is still counted.
Cuba's independence (1902) takes it out.
Martinique, Guadeloupe and French Guiana become French départements with deputies in Paris (1946) and leave the count.
Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago leave (August 1962).
Guyana (May 1966) leaves; Barbados follows at the month's end.
Suriname (1975) leaves; the Bahamas and Grenada already have (1973, 1974).
Belize, Antigua and St Kitts leave (1981 to 1983): Puerto Rico is most of what remains.

With Hong Kong and Macau returned, the Americas are almost all of colonial rule: Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands and the British and Dutch Caribbean. The lower band carries the UN's list, which has left Puerto Rico out since 1953.
About 3.7 million people, 3.2 million of them in Puerto Rico.
Zero before the Portuguese in India (1498 to 1510).
Cabral's first factory at Cochin; no territory yet.
Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515) under Portugal.
Spain's Philippines (from 1565) bring the part to about a seventh of colonial rule.
The Dutch company's Batavia (1619), Amboina and Formosa's coast (1624).
The Dutch company rules Java's north coast and the Priangan; Madras, Bombay, Calcutta and Pondicherry are company towns.
Bengal, Bihar and Orissa under the East India Company after Plassey: Asia becomes most of colonial rule, as it stays until 1948.
Penang ceded by the Sultan of Kedah to Francis Light for the Company (1786), a few thousand people; Bengal's growth is the larger change.
Mysore falls (1799) and Britain takes the Dutch Ceylon coast (1796). The parent's remainder here implies some 70 million people, above a count of about 55 million: the parent may be high at 1800.
Doubles after the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818): the Company is paramount over most of India, its princely states counted with it.
India, the Dutch Indies, Indochina, the Philippines (American from 1898), Ceylon, Malaya and Taiwan: about 365 million people.
Korea, a Japanese protectorate from 1905, is already counted before its annexation (1910).
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces.
Manchukuo (1932), a puppet state whose counting is debated, adds about 1.4 points.
South-east Asia passes from European and American to Japanese rule without changing the count.
Japan's empire ends: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave, and Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence.
The Philippines become independent (July 1946).
India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon leave (1947 to 1948): the part falls by six sevenths in two years, and Africa becomes the larger part.
Indonesia's independence (December 1949).

After Geneva (1954) Indochina is out. This is the parent's remainder; a count of what is left (Malaya, Singapore, Hong Kong, Aden, Cyprus, the Borneo territories, Goa, Macau, Timor and the Gulf protectorates) gives about 0.6%, so either the parent or Africa's part is about half a point high here; the band reaches down to the count.
Malaya (1957) and Cyprus (1960) are out.
Singapore and the Borneo states join Malaysia (1963) and West New Guinea passes to Indonesia (1963).
Aden leaves (November 1967).
Hong Kong and Macau are almost all that remains, growing faster than the world.
Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China: no colonial rule from overseas is left in Asia.
Zero before Portugal takes Ceuta (1415).
All of colonial rule in 1450: Ceuta, Madeira, the Azores and the first Canaries, which belong to Europe by today's borders.
Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496).
Britain takes Malta (1800).
The Ionian Islands become a British protectorate (1815), beside Malta.
The Ionian Islands become a British protectorate (1815).
The Atlantic islands send deputies to the Cortes of Madrid and Lisbon (1820 to 1822) and leave the count; Malta and the Ionian Islands remain.
Britain cedes the Ionian Islands to Greece (1864).
Italy takes the Dodecanese (1912).
Italy's Albania (1939 to 1943) is military occupation and not counted.
The Dodecanese pass to Greece (1947).
Malta's independence (September 1964) leaves Gibraltar.
Gibraltar's 34,000 people.
Zero before Spain rules the Marianas (1668).
Spain's mission to Guam (1668) brings the Chamorros of the Marianas under its rule.
The Spanish–Chamorro wars and epidemics cut the Chamorros from tens of thousands to a few thousand by about 1710.
Before the First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove (January 1788) the only colonial rule in Oceania is Spain's in the Marianas.
New South Wales (1788) adds about a thousand convicts and soldiers.
The Australian colonies' settlers grow, and Britain claims New Zealand (1840).

The peak before self-government: the Victorian gold rush has not yet begun, but the Australian colonies hold about 400,000 settlers and convicts, and New Zealand about 25,000 settlers beside the Māori counted under the Crown's rule; all still governed from London.

Responsible government in New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia (1855 to 1857) and New Zealand (1856) takes them out by the parent's definition; Aboriginal Australians and most Māori, with no vote, are a debated exception the band does not carry. Western Australia, the Marianas and Tahiti remain.
Fiji is ceded to Britain (1874).
Britain and Germany divide eastern New Guinea (1884) and Germany takes the Marshall Islands (1885); their rule reaches the coasts.
Samoa divided (1899), the Carolines and Marianas sold to Germany (1899), Guam to the United States (1898), the Solomons and the Gilberts British (1892 to 1893).
Patrols reach New Guinea's highlands (from 1933), about a million people never contacted before; how fast they count as ruled is a matter of judgment.

New Guinea's highland valleys, reached by patrols from 1933, are counted as administered by about 1940, which with Fiji, the Solomons, New Caledonia and Japan's mandated islands brings the part to about two million people. How much of the highlands counted as ruled by 1940 is a judgment; the band carries it.
Western Samoa becomes independent (1962).
Fiji and Tonga's protectorate end (1970).
Papua New Guinea becomes independent (September 1975): the part falls by three quarters.
The Solomons, Tuvalu (1978) and Kiribati (1979) are independent; Vanuatu follows in 1980.

New Caledonia and French Polynesia, Guam, the Northern Marianas, American Samoa, Wallis and Futuna and Tokelau. The French territories elect deputies to Paris but are on the UN's list of territories to decolonize (New Caledonia from 1986, French Polynesia from 2013); the lower band leaves them out.

Zero by definition before 1415: this measure follows the modern colonial empires ruled from overseas. Earlier rule over provinces and colonies across the sea (Athens, Carthage, Rome's provinces before 212, Venice and Genoa) is a different kind and outside it; counted, Rome's overseas provinces alone would put about a tenth of humanity under such rule around 100 CE.
Portugal's Ceuta (1415), Madeira and the Azores, and Castile's Canaries: a few tens of thousands of people.
Columbus's landfall changes nothing yet: the Atlantic islands and a few African forts.

Castile completes the conquest of the Canaries (Tenerife, 1496) and begins ruling the Taínos of Hispaniola; the band carries the debate over Hispaniola's numbers, from about 100,000 to several million.
Hispaniola under Spanish rule, with the Atlantic islands and the first Portuguese forts in Africa and India.

The fall of Tenochtitlan (ev.am.aztec-fall): central Mexico comes under Spanish rule, some 6 to 12 million people after the smallpox of 1520; the band carries the debate over the contact population (Borah and Cook's high counts against the low ones).
Pizarro takes the Inca empire (ev.am.inca-fall): the Andes join New Spain under colonial rule.

The colonial share falls by almost half from 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost: the colonized die of epidemics, war and forced labour (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd), while the Philippines (from 1565) add few.
The Dutch East India Company is chartered (1602) with powers of war, but its territory is still a few forts; the share holds.
Jamestown (1607) and Quebec (1608) are founded: a few hundred settlers each, among Native nations not yet under their rule.
The first English, French and Dutch colonies in North America and the Dutch company's first posts in Java (Batavia, 1619) add few people; Spanish America is near its demographic low.
The Dutch take Pernambuco (1630) and Formosa's coast; the English settle Barbados and Massachusetts. Each adds tens of thousands, not millions.

Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) bring Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, some 25 million people, under the East India Company: the colonial share doubles. Whether Bengal is colonial from 1757 or only from 1765 is a matter of definition; the band carries both.

On the eve of the American Revolution: the Company's Bengal, Spanish and Portuguese America and the Caribbean, with the thirteen colonies' 2.5 million (about 0.3% of humanity) still counted. Their independence takes them out, and India's annexations put more in, so the share still rises to 1780.
The thirteen colonies have rebelled (1776) and leave the count; India's coastal presidencies and Awadh's subsidiary alliance add more than they take away.
Penang (1786) and New South Wales (1788) add a few thousand people each; the share keeps rising on the growth of the Company's India, not on these new footholds.
The abolition committee forms in London (1787) and the First Fleet sails for Botany Bay: neither moves the share yet, which climbs on India's growth under the Company.

The Congress of Vienna (1815) returns Java to the Dutch and keeps the Cape, Ceylon and Malta British; Spanish America is at war, its de facto independent parts out of the count; the Company's India grows by conquest, before the Maratha war of 1817 to 1818 nearly doubles it.

After the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817 to 1818) the Company is paramount over most of India; Spanish America's independence (1810 to 1825) takes away about 15 million people but India adds about 100 million: nearly a fifth of humanity under colonial rule.
Mexico, Central America and Brazil leave colonial rule (1821 to 1822); Peru and Upper Peru stay Spanish until 1824 to 1825.
The first Anglo-Burmese war begins (1824) and will add Arakan and Assam; Ayacucho ends Spanish rule in Peru at the year's end.
Mexico, Central America, Peru and Brazil leave colonial rule between 1821 and 1826, about 15 million people, while the Company's India stays: the share dips from 1820.
France takes Algeria from 1830 and the Dutch tighten their hold on Java after the Java War; with India's growth the share climbs back toward a fifth by 1850.
The Indian rebellion (1857 to 1858) and its suppression; the Crown's takeover and France's first moves on Indochina (1858) change who rules, not how many are ruled.
The Crown takes India from the Company after the rising of 1857 (ev.as.british-raj); the share is unchanged by it.
Britain's residents in the Malay states (1874) and the Dutch war in Aceh (from 1873) extend rule a little; India's growth carries most of the rise.
On the eve of the scramble for Africa (from 1881).
Lower Burma, Cochinchina and the Malay states are under European rule and India's people grow; the scramble for Africa has not yet begun.
France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain occupies Egypt (1882), about eight million people; the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) follows.
After the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885), Tonkin and Annam (1883 to 1885) and Upper Burma (1885) the share climbs; most of Africa's conquest is still to come.
Most of Africa has been partitioned on paper and is being conquered, and Japan takes Taiwan (1895); the share climbs toward its pre-1914 level.
Between Madagascar and Asante (1896) and Benin (1897), the conquest of Africa's coasts and their hinterlands is nearly complete; on the line between 1895 and 1900.
The Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1900) brings almost all of Africa under European rule; with India, Indonesia and Indochina, three in ten of all people live in colonies.
Japan annexes Korea (1910, about 13 million people) and France makes Morocco a protectorate (1912); the colonial share is near its pre-war height before the war's changes.
Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide happen inside a sovereign Ottoman state; Germany's African and Pacific colonies are being taken by the Allies, a change of rulers that leaves the count unchanged.

The war moves Germany's colonies to new rulers without changing their count; Sykes–Picot (1916) plans the Arab provinces' division, which adds them only as Britain and France occupy them in 1917 and 1918.
Britain and France occupy the Ottoman Arab provinces, soon League mandates.
Japan's Manchukuo (1932) and Italy's conquest of Ethiopia (1936) add about 50 million; without Manchukuo, a puppet state whose counting is debated, the share is about 30.7%.
The colonial share's peak, about a third of humanity, most of it in British India.
The day Japan's attacks begin: the share is unchanged; see 1941.95.
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor, Malaya and the Philippines (8 December 1941); the colonies change hands over the next months without changing how many people are ruled from abroad.

Japan's conquest of South-east Asia moves about 150 million people from European and American to Japanese colonial rule; the share hardly changes. Japan's occupation of eastern China is military occupation and not counted.

Japan's surrender ends its empire: Korea, Taiwan and Manchuria leave colonial rule; Indonesia and Vietnam declare independence, contested by the Dutch and the French until 1949 and 1954 (counted at half for Indonesia).
India and Pakistan (August 1947, ev.as.partition), Burma and Ceylon (1948): the colonial share falls from about 28% to 11% in two years, the largest fall of rule from overseas ever.
Sudan (January 1956), Morocco and Tunisia (March 1956) become independent, about 23 million people; Ghana and Malaya follow in 1957.
Sudan, Morocco and Tunisia (1956), Ghana (March 1957) and Malaya (August 1957) leave colonial rule, about 40 million people; Algeria's war goes on.
On the eve of the Year of Africa (ev.af.year-of-africa): seventeen African states become independent during 1960.
Most of Africa is independent; what remains are Portugal's colonies, Rhodesia, the High Commission territories, Algeria until July and small islands.
Algeria (July 1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago (August) leave colonial rule, about 13 million people, 0.4% of humanity.
Uganda (October 1962), Kenya and Zanzibar (1963), Malawi, Zambia and Malta (1964) and the Borneo states joining Malaysia (1963): about 25 million more.
Portugal's African empire, Rhodesia and small territories, with Hong Kong; their numbers grow while their count of territories does not, until the independences of 1974 and 1975.

Before Portugal's empire ends in 1974 to 1975 after the Carnation Revolution (Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola); Rhodesia after its declaration of independence (1965) is still counted, its majority without a vote.

Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China; what remains is Puerto Rico and small territories, counted because their people have no vote in the government that rules them. The UN's list of non-self-governing territories has left Puerto Rico out since 1953, an alternative reading that would halve the value.
About five million people, most of them in Puerto Rico.

Foragers carry their goods when they move camp and carry home what they kill and gather: a few tonne-km a person a year. Obsidian and shells travel hundreds of kilometres by exchange, but in tiny amounts.
Farmers carry harvests, stores and building stuff, but rarely far.
Donkeys are domesticated in north-east Africa and carry loads.
The wheel and the sail: carts on land, sailing boats on the Nile and the Gulf.
Rome's grain fleet carries some hundreds of thousands of tonnes from Egypt and Africa each year; the empire's sea trade lifts its average to several times the world's.
Falls: Mediterranean shipping shrinks with the Western empire, as shipwreck counts show.
Song China's Grand Canal and coastal junks move rice, salt and iron in bulk.
Dutch and English merchant fleets, and coal shipped from Newcastle to London.
Peace at sea after 1815 restores the Atlantic and Asian trades that the wars and blockades had cut; the Erie Canal is begun (1817).
Turns up steeply: railways and steamships cut the cost of moving bulk goods by most of its cost on roads.
Railways spread across North America, Mexico (the Porfiriato), Argentina and India and steamships take over bulk freight once the Suez Canal opens (1869): freight per person grows at about 9% a year.
Refrigerated ships (the Dunedin, 1882) begin carrying meat and butter halfway round the world, beside grain, coal and cotton.
On the eve of the First World War world trade and shipping stand at their prewar peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from submarine sinkings and blockade.
Submarine warfare sinks a fifth of the world's merchant tonnage.
Supertankers and bulk carriers: oil and ore cross oceans in unprecedented tonnages; the container ship spreads from 1956.
Dips: the oil shocks cut long-haul tanker trade in the early 1980s.
China's trade boom carries ore and coal in and containers out.
COVID-19's first year: world trade volume falls about a twentieth in 2020 and recovers in 2021.
About 130 trillion tonne-km a year, three quarters of it by sea (UNCTAD and the International Transport Forum, as recalled).

upsert.reason: Before 1850 sketched from loads and distances (a forager's camp moves, a farmer's surplus carried to market, Roman, Song and Dutch shipping); 1850 to 1950 from railway and shipping statistics as recalled; after 1970 from UNCTAD's seaborne tonne-miles and the International Transport Forum's land freight, as recalled.

points.note: All of humanity's movers live in Africa, the only area Homo sapiens holds.
Falls as a share of humanity, not in Africa: the dispersal puts a growing part of humanity, and so of its movers, in Asia, Sahul and Europe.
The Arab conquest of North Africa (from 640) and the Berber and Arab movements that follow add settlers born in Arabia and across today's lines.
About two million: Europeans in Algeria, South Africa and Egypt, Indians in Natal and East Africa, and the first labour migrants to the Rand's mines from Mozambique and beyond.

Rises with the postwar labour migrations of the colonial economies (Burkinabé and Malians to the Gold Coast's and Côte d'Ivoire's cocoa, Mozambicans and Malawians to the mines and farms of the south) and with Europeans settling in the Rhodesias and Kenya.
About nine million by the UN's count for Africa in 1960: labour migrants between the new states and the last of the settlers.
Algeria's independence sends about 900,000 pieds-noirs to France in a year.
About 16 million, the UN's count for Africa in 1990, swollen by refugees from Mozambique's, Ethiopia's and Sudan's wars.
About 29 million, most of them from neighbouring countries: South Sudan's and Sudan's refugees in Uganda, Chad and Egypt, and workers in South Africa and Côte d'Ivoire.

upsert.reason: Before 1850 the part follows Africa's share of humanity and its many small cells on today's map; then colonial settlers and labour migrants; from 1990 the UN's count for Africa.

points.note: Claims of people in South America this early (Pedra Furada) are contested; the band allows a few.
Monte Verde in southern Chile is occupied about 14,500 years ago: people have reached the far south within a few centuries, or earlier.
The Aztec and Inca states move conquered peoples; the Inca mitmaq resettle whole communities across today's lines from Ecuador to Chile.
The first Spanish settlers and enslaved Africans reach Hispaniola and Cuba.
Iberian settlers and Africans in Mexico, Peru, Brazil and the islands, as the Americas' own peoples die of epidemics: nearly all the hemisphere's migrants.
Brazil's gold rush begins (1690s) with Portuguese migrants and more enslaved Africans.
The slave trade at its height lands 60,000 to 80,000 Africans a year in Brazil and the Caribbean, where the African-born stay most of the enslaved because deaths outrun births.
Saint-Domingue's revolution ends imports there; Cuba and Brazil take more.
Brazil ends its slave trade (1850): its African-born, the largest group of migrants in Latin America, begin to age out.
The low point: the African-born of Brazil and Cuba are dying, and the European mass migration to the south has only begun.
Italians and Spaniards pour into Argentina and Uruguay, Italians and Portuguese into Sao Paulo's coffee lands.
Argentina's census of 1914 counts 2.4 million foreign-born, three in ten of its people, the highest share of any large country.
Europe's displaced people and Spain's and Italy's poor sail again for Buenos Aires, Sao Paulo and Caracas.
About six million by the UN's count, a third of the hemisphere's migrants: the south's highest share since the 1840s.
About seven million: the European-born of the old migration die out, and Latin America now sends more people north than it receives.
The low point as a share of humanity, about six and a half million.
Jumps: about five million Venezuelans have left since 2015, most of them to Colombia, Peru, Brazil, Chile and Ecuador; the UN counts about 15 million migrants in Latin America and the Caribbean.
About 17 million, with nearly eight million Venezuelans abroad.
All of the hemisphere's movers, if the White Sands footprints' dates hold, are in what is now Northern America.
The first Americans come from Beringia along the coast or the ice-free corridor; most of the hemisphere's people are still in the north, though Monte Verde in Chile is already occupied.
With the hemisphere peopled to Tierra del Fuego, its movers follow its people, about a third of them north of the Rio Grande.
Falls as a part of the whole as Mesoamerica's and the Andes' farmers grow far denser than the north's foragers.
Cahokia and the Mississippian towns draw people from across the mid-continent.
A few thousand Europeans at St Augustine, in New Mexico and on the St Lawrence: almost all the hemisphere's newcomers are in the Spanish and Portuguese lands.
Virginia, Maryland, New England and New Netherland hold some fifty thousand colonists, most of them born in England, against several hundred thousand Africans and Iberians in the south.
German, Scots-Irish and English settlers and enslaved Africans in the thirteen colonies: about a fifth of the hemisphere's migrants.
The United States has ended its slave trade (1808): its African-born age out, while Brazil and Cuba still import; the north holds about a third.
The Irish famine emigration begins: the north's part rises past half.
The United States counts 2.24 million foreign-born and British North America about half a million: two thirds of the hemisphere's migrants.
The United States counts 5.6 million foreign-born: four fifths of the hemisphere's migrants, the north's highest share before 1990.
The United States' 13.5 million foreign-born and Canada's 1.6 million: the north's peak as a share of humanity until the 1990s.
Turns down: the quota acts of 1921 and 1924 cut arrivals by four fifths, and the foreign-born age.
The United States counts 10.3 million foreign-born (1950) and Canada 2.1 million.
The trough: about 12.5 million by the UN's count, the European-born of the great migration dying out.
The Hart-Celler Act ends the national-origins quotas.
About 28 million by the UN's count.
About 40 million: 86% of the hemisphere's migrants, the north's highest share.
About 59 million by the UN's count; growth slows as arrivals from Mexico fall after 2007.
About 61 million: a fifth of the world's migrants, a slightly smaller share of humanity than in 2020.
If the White Sands footprints' dates hold, a few people live south of the ice; how many, and how far they moved, is unknown.
The Americas are peopled to Tierra del Fuego: a tenth of humanity's movers now live there, at forager rates.
The Aztec and Inca states move conquered peoples (the Inca mitmaq resettled whole communities across today's lines from Ecuador to Chile).
The first Spanish settlers and the first enslaved Africans reach the Caribbean.
Iberian settlers and enslaved Africans arrive as the Americas' own peoples die of epidemics: the foreign-born become a growing share of a shrinking population.
The Atlantic slave trade at its height brings about 60,000 to 80,000 Africans a year to Brazil and the Caribbean, where deaths are so high that the African-born stay most of the enslaved.

Britain and the United States end their slave trades (1807 and 1808): the African-born begin to age out of the count in North America and the British Caribbean, though Brazil and Cuba import for decades more.
The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born (1850), with Irish and Germans arriving by the hundred thousand a year.
About twenty million: the United States' 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina's 2.4 million, Canada's 1.6 million, Brazil's and the rest; nearly half of the world's migrants live in the Americas.
The United States' quota acts (1921 and 1924) cut arrivals by four fifths; the foreign-born age and die faster than new ones come.
Near its low: about nineteen million by the UN's count for Northern and Latin America, the old European-born dying out faster than new arrivals replace them.
The United States' Hart-Celler Act (1965) ends the national-origins quotas; arrivals from Latin America and Asia begin the climb of the next sixty years.
Vietnam's first refugees reach the United States (about 130,000 in 1975).
About 35 million by the UN's count: 28 million in Northern America and 7 million in Latin America and the Caribbean.
About 78 million: some 61 million in Northern America (the United States alone about a fifth of the world's migrants) and 17 million in Latin America, swollen by Venezuela's exodus.

upsert.reason: Zero before the Americas are peopled; then foragers' movers; from 1500 the Spanish and Portuguese settlers and the enslaved; from 1850 the censuses of the United States, Canada, Argentina and Brazil as recalled; from 1990 the UN's counts for Northern America and Latin America together.

points.note: The few Homo sapiens of the Levant (Misliya) carry the first movers outside Africa.
The dispersal along southern Asia: a growing share of humanity, and of its movers, lives in Asia.
Assyria deports whole peoples across its empire (Israelites, Arameans, Babylonians), perhaps several million over three centuries.
The Mongol empire moves artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand: Persian craftsmen to Karakorum, Central Asians to Yuan China.
About nine million: the Chinese and Indians of Malaya, Burma, Siam and the Indies, Russians settled in today's Kazakhstan and Central Asia, Japanese in Korea and Taiwan.

Japan's empire at its height: about two million Koreans in Japan, Japanese settlers in Korea, Manchuria and Taiwan, and the Soviet deportees (Volga Germans, Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Koreans) in Kazakhstan and Central Asia.
Japan's surrender begins the repatriation of some six million Japanese and the return of most Koreans from Japan.
Partition's refugees in India and Pakistan, about ten million by December 1947.

Partition (1947 to 1948): about fourteen million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee: Asia's part rises by two fifths in two years.
About 35 million by the UN's count for Asia in 1960 with the Soviet republics' movers added: Partition's refugees still the largest group.
Falls as Partition's generation dies and Asia's population grows faster than its migrants.
Afghanistan's war puts some five million refugees in Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia, Egypt and the Philippines.
About 48 million, the UN's count for Asia in 1990.
Asia's low share: most Afghan refugees have gone home and Asia's population has grown by half since 1970.
About 92 million: the Gulf states (where most residents were born abroad), Syria's refugees in Turkey, Lebanon and Jordan, and Afghans and Rohingya in their neighbours.

upsert.reason: From the first excursions into the Levant on; deportations, nomads and captives in the agrarian millennia; the Nanyang Chinese and Indians, Koreans in Japan and Russians in Central Asia; Partition; the Gulf; from 1990 the UN's count for Asia.

points.note: Homo sapiens has reached Europe and western Siberia, a land of many small cells on today's map.
The steppe herders' descendants spread across Europe (the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker peoples), crossing today's lines by the hundred thousand.
Rome's wars begin to fill Italy with captives from Carthage, Spain and Greece.
Perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria: Europe holds about two fifths of the world's migrants.
The migration period: Goths, Vandals, Franks, Saxons and Lombards settle inside the old Roman frontier, while Rome's slave imports end.
The Irish famine sends hundreds of thousands to Britain's cities, which by 2026 borders are another country.

About twelve million, most of them moves inside empires that today's borders divide: Czechs and Galicians in Vienna, Poles of Posen in the Ruhr, Ukrainians, Poles and Balts in Russia's cities; besides them Italians in France and the Irish in Britain.
The war adds about eight million prisoners of war held abroad and millions of refugees (Belgians in Britain and France, Serbs, Poles and Balts driven into Russia).
Germany brings in millions of foreign workers and prisoners, and the Soviet Union deports Poles and Balts into Russia.
At the war's height Germany holds about 7.5 million foreign civilian workers and 2 million prisoners at work: Europe holds two fifths of the world's migrants.
The expulsions: some twelve million Germans born in today's Poland, Czechia and Russia's Kaliningrad are driven west into today's Germany and Austria while most forced labourers go home.

About 23 million by the UN's count for Europe in 1960 with the Soviet republics' movers added; guest workers from Italy, Spain, Turkey and Yugoslavia begin to replace the war's displaced in the count.
About 49 million by the UN's count for Europe in 1990, a third of them people born in one Soviet republic living in another.
About 94 million: movers inside the European Union, Ukraine's refugees since 2022, Syrians, Turks and Africans in the west, and Central Asians in Russia.

upsert.reason: Zero before Homo sapiens reaches Europe; Rome's captives and the migration period; the moves across today's lines inside the Habsburg, German and Russian empires; the wars' forced labour and expulsions; the guest workers and the European Union; from 1990 the UN's count for Europe.

points.note: Sahul is reached; its peoples live in what are now three countries (Australia, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia's Papua), so few moves cross today's lines.
The rising sea cuts New Guinea from Australia (about 6500 BCE) and farming begins in New Guinea's highlands: Oceania's share of humanity falls as the farming lands of Asia grow.
The First Fleet (1788) lands about 1,400 people at Sydney Cove, the first of some 160,000 convicts sent to Australia by 1868.
Free settlers and transported convicts make the British-born a growing share of the Australian colonies and, from 1840, of New Zealand.
The Victorian gold rush (from 1851) more than doubles Australia's people in a decade, most of the newcomers born in Britain, Ireland, China and the Americas.
About 1.4 million: the British- and Irish-born of Australia and New Zealand and the Indians of Fiji; the White Australia policy (1901) keeps out most others.
The Depression stops immigration and the British-born of the gold rushes and the 1910s die out: Australia's foreign-born fall to about a tenth of its people by 1947, their lowest.
Australia's Department of Immigration is founded (July 1945) and the postwar scheme planned; arrivals begin in 1947.
Australia's postwar scheme (from 1947) brings displaced persons, Britons, Italians and Greeks: about two million arrivals by 1970.
About 4.7 million by the UN's count for Oceania in 1990.
About ten million, nearly all in Australia (three in ten Australians were born abroad) and New Zealand.

upsert.reason: Zero before Sahul is reached; Sahul's foragers; from 1788 the convicts, gold rushes, indentured and labour-trade workers and the postwar schemes; from 1990 the UN's count for Oceania.

points.note: All people are foragers in Africa. With countries by 2026 borders as cells about 750 km across, a forager whose home lies a few tens of kilometres from where they were born crosses one of today's lines perhaps one time in twenty, adults far more often than children: about one person in fifty. Reasoned from forager residence and marriage distances, not counted.
The green Sahara and the Levant open longer ranges across many of today's borders; the reading barely moves.

Eases: a growing share of humanity lives in Asia and Sahul, in what are now large countries (Australia, India, China, Indonesia's islands, Russia), where a forager's moves cross fewer of today's lines. The dispersal itself adds little: its fronts advance by births where people already live (WaveOfAdvance#4cec), not by people living far from their birthplace.

The agrarian floor: most people die within a few kilometres of where they were born; nomads crossing today's lines with their herds, deportees (the Assyrians move whole peoples), soldiers, slaves and traders make up the rest.

Rome's wars carry captives from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria to Italy: perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, nearly half a percent of humanity alone; Han settlers and soldiers in Korea and northern Vietnam add a little.

The migration period moves Goths, Vandals, Franks and Saxons from beyond the Rhine and Danube into the Roman west, a few hundred thousand people born in one of today's countries and living in another; as Rome's slave imports end, the share holds.
The Mongol conquests move artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand, and the empire's posts carry merchants from Venice to Khanbaliq: a small rise.

About two million people born in Africa are enslaved in the Americas, a fifth of a percent of humanity, as the Atlantic trade passes its peak; Europeans born in Europe in the Americas, Asians in other Asian countries and Europe's own movers make up the rest.
The great European emigration begins with the peace (ev.eu.emigration), but its numbers are small until the 1830s; the African-born enslaved in the Americas still make up the largest group of movers.
Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees about 800,000 people, many born in Africa, but frees them where they live: it changes their status, not the share living outside their country of birth.
The first indentured Indians reach British Guiana (1838) and Mauritius, beginning the indenture that replaces enslaved labour on the sugar colonies.

The Irish famine (from 1845) sends about a million and a half people to Britain and North America by 1852, and the California gold rush (from 1848) draws Chinese, Chileans, Mexicans and Europeans: the turn into the age of mass migration.

Turns up: the Irish famine's emigrants, the gold rushes of California and Australia, and the first indentured Indians and Chinese begin the age of mass migration. The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born in 1850.

Indentured Indians begin arriving in Fiji (1879) as they had in Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana; the European emigration to the Americas, slowed by the depression of the 1870s, picks up again at the decade's end.

Cuba's gradual abolition (1880 to 1886) and Brazil's (1888) end the Atlantic world's slave societies; their places on the plantations are taken by immigrants from Spain, Italy, Portugal, China and India.
The United States' Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) is the first law to bar a people by origin; the European flow it does not touch reaches about 800,000 arrivals that year.

The great immigration to the United States, Argentina and Brazil from southern and eastern Europe begins about 1880; Brazil's abolition (May 1888) and its subsidized Italian immigration that follows add to it.

The peak of the age of mass migration: the United States counts 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina 2.4 million (three in ten of its people), Canada 1.6 million; Indians and Chinese in South-east Asia, Russians in Central Asia and Europe's own movers between today's countries add as many again: some 40 to 45 million people, about 2.5% of humanity.
Falls back: the United States' quota acts (1921 to 1924) cut its immigration by four fifths, and the Depression stops and reverses movement; emigrants of 1900 to 1914 die or return.

Rises with the war: Germany puts millions of foreign workers and prisoners to work in the Reich, the Soviet Union deports Poles, Balts, Volga Germans, Chechens and others across today's lines, and Japan moves Koreans to its mines.

At its wartime height Germany holds about 7.5 million foreign civilian workers and 2 million prisoners of war at work, and about 2 million Koreans live in Japan: forced labour lifts the share living outside their country of birth to near its postwar level.

The war's last year moves people both ways: the Germans of the east begin to flee and be expelled, and forced labourers in the Reich and Koreans in Japan are at their peak, so the share holds near its wartime high.

The war's end starts the largest movement home in history: some ten million forced labourers and prisoners leave the Reich, while expellees from the east and Japanese repatriated from the empire take their place in the count.
Most of the forced labourers and displaced persons go home, while the Germans expelled from the east and the Japanese repatriated replace them in the count: the share holds.
Most of Partition's crossings come between August and December 1947: about ten million people are already living on the other side of the new lines by the year's end.
Partition: about 14 million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan in 1947 and 1948, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee Israel's war of independence.

Partition moves about 14 million people across the new lines of India, Pakistan and East Pakistan (now Bangladesh), and 12 to 14 million Germans have been expelled from the east: the share living outside their country of birth stands near its highest until the 2010s.
The UN's estimate of about 76 million international migrants (2.5%) counts the countries of 1960; by 2026 borders the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants (about 15 million) are added.
The United States' Hart-Celler Act (October 1965) ends the national-origin quotas; its effect on the count comes over the next decades.
The low after the postwar displacement: the displaced of the 1940s die or are counted among the natives' children, and humanity grows faster than the migrants' numbers.
Afghanistan's war sends some five million refugees into Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia and the Arab world.

The UN's count for the countries of 2020: about 153 million. The Soviet Union's breakup makes some 25 million people international migrants overnight in the UN's own series; by 2026 borders they were counted all along, so this series has no jump here.

upsert.reason: Sketched before 1850 from forager residence and marriage distances (Hill and colleagues 2011; Marlowe 2004), farmers' village exogamy, and the numbers carried by slave trades, conquests and settlement; 1850 to 1960 from the receiving countries' censuses as recalled (the United States, Argentina, Brazil, Canada, Australia) and McKeown's global migration (2004); from 1960 the UN's international migrant stock (UN DESA), adjusted to 2026 borders before 1990 by adding the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants. Sources to check: UN DESA International Migrant Stock 2024; McKeown 2004, Journal of World History 15; Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998).

points.note: No states: every autonomous unit is a band.
The first: Uruk and its neighbours on the lower Euphrates, if counted as states.
Some thirty Sumerian city-states, Egypt unified under one king, Elam and the cities of upper Mesopotamia and Syria.
Falls: Akkad unites Mesopotamia's city-states under one king (about 2334 to 2154 BCE).

The Zhou conquer the Shang (1046 BCE) and enfeoff kinsmen and allies in vassal states that will become the independent states of the Spring and Autumn period; after the Bronze Age collapse the Levant and Anatolia hold Aramaean, Neo-Hittite and Phoenician city-states.
Rises: the Zhou's vassals become the independent states of the Spring and Autumn period (about 150), the Greek poleis multiply, and the Ganges plain's janapadas and the Phoenician cities form.
The Greek world alone holds about a thousand poleis, of which several hundred answer to no one; how many of the smallest to count as states is the largest uncertainty, carried by the band.
Falls by two thirds: Qin unites the Warring States (221), the Hellenistic kingdoms and Rome absorb the poleis, and the Maurya empire most of the subcontinent (Warsift#b01b).
Rises: the western Roman provinces become kingdoms, China is divided, and the Maya city-states multiply.
Falls: the Mongol conquests absorb the states of China, Central Asia, Iran and Rus'.

Europe's roughly five hundred more or less autonomous units (Tilly's count, the Holy Roman Empire's principalities among them), Japan's warring daimyo, the sultanates of India and the Malay world, Africa's kingdoms and the Americas' states: several hundred in all.

Falls by two fifths: the Holy Roman Empire's some 250 principalities, free cities and church lands are mediatized (1803) and the Empire dissolved (1806), leaving about forty German states; Napoleon annexes much of Italy and the Low Countries.

The Congress of Vienna restores the Italian states and the Netherlands and sets the German Confederation at thirty-nine states: Europe's count recovers from Napoleon's annexations while Latin America's first republics are not yet secure.
About eighteen new Latin American states (1810 to 1826) offset the last Maratha states and Ceylon's Kandy coming under British rule (1815 to 1818).
Falls: Italy (1861 to 1870) and Germany (1871) unify, some thirty states becoming two.
Falls to its low: the Scramble for Africa (1881 to 1914) ends almost every African kingdom but Ethiopia and Liberia, and Burma, Vietnam and the last Indian and Malay states come under colonial rule.
Rises: from the fallen Russian, Austro-Hungarian, German and Ottoman empires come Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, the Baltic states, Austria and Hungary (Versailles, 1919).
Falls: Germany, the Soviet Union, Italy and Japan absorb Austria, Czechoslovakia, Albania, Poland and the Baltic states.
The occupied states are restored as the war ends.
India and Pakistan become independent (August 1947): two states holding a sixth of humanity, the first of decolonization's great steps.
Jumps: the year of Africa, seventeen new states in 1960.
Germany reunites and the two Yemens join; Namibia becomes independent.
Jumps: fifteen states from the Soviet Union and four from Yugoslavia.
The 193 members of the United Nations, the Holy See and the states that govern themselves without general recognition (Taiwan, Kosovo and a few others).
