Fill: the report names 1820 to 1850 as the coarsest stretch of most measures, which hold only their 1820 and 1850 values; the stretch holds the first railways (1825 to 1830), the electric telegraph (1837 to 1844), the penny press, Europe's coal take-off and the first great emigration. Values at 1830 and 1840 for the Earth's measures, food, farmland, births by order, the Earth's stores, world output by area, settlement, faith, force and wealth, each guessed on the path between its neighbours with what these decades changed, and wholes set so their parts still sum to them. All recalled or reasoned, sharing one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: News moves at the pace of a walker or runner passing it on; fire and smoke signals carry only a few agreed meanings.
Royal messengers of Egypt and Sumer carry written orders by boat and on foot.
Couriers with horses and chariots carry the letters of the Amarna age between Egypt, Babylon and the Hittites.
The Achaemenid relay riders carry the king's messages from Sardis to Susa, some 2,700 km, in about a week, as Herodotus tells it.
Augustus's cursus publicus and the Han relay posts.
The Tang relay posts and the Abbasid barid.
The Mongol yam: urgent riders change horses at stations and cover 300 to 400 km a day.
The Taxis postal relays in Europe from about 1490; the Ming courier stations.
Before Chappe's semaphore (1794): the jump to 1800 is its first line's, so the riders' speed holds until here.

Jumps: Chappe's semaphore line from Paris to Lille (1794) passes a message 230 km in minutes to an hour; lines spread across France, Britain and Sweden. Words now outrun riders for the first time on a regular service.

Still the optical telegraph: Chappe's semaphore lines in France and the new Prussian line (1832) pass a short message hundreds of kilometres in minutes in clear daylight; elsewhere the fastest regular message rides a horse or a ship.
The first electric telegraphs run along British railways (Cooke and Wheatstone, 1838 to 1839); the long lines that make the jump come after Morse's line of 1844.
Jumps again: the electric telegraph (Cooke and Wheatstone 1837, Morse 1844) carries messages across a continent in minutes, slowed by relaying and copying.
The transatlantic cable (1866): London to New York in minutes instead of ten days.

Interpolated between the transatlantic cable and the world network, within the band. A message crosses a cable in minutes, but news passes through several relaying stations and offices: word of Krakatoa's eruption (27 August 1883) went by cable from Batavia and reached London's newspapers within hours.
A cable network girdles the world; news reaches the antipodes in hours.
Radio telegraphy and radio telephony connect continents without relays.
Communications satellites (1962) and direct long-distance dialling.
Fibre-optic cables carry signals near the speed of light in glass.

Reaches the limit: transoceanic fibre cables (from TAT-8 in 1988 to the round-the-world FLAG cable in 1997) replace satellite hops, whose round trip to geostationary orbit added about a quarter of a second, and messages cross the world at nearly the speed of light in glass.
At the limit: light in fibre travels about 200,000 km a second. From here what changes is who can send and receive, read in being online (h.internet) and mass media (h.media).

upsert.reason: From the recorded speeds of relay posts (Herodotus on the Persian riders, the Mongol yam, European posts), the semaphore and telegraph lines, and the latency of cable, radio and fibre networks, as recalled; orders of magnitude after 1850.

points.note: Almost every woman who lives through her childbearing years has a first child; about 8% have none.
War and the flu postpone marriages and first births.
Postponed marriages and first births make the start of the baby boom.
Childlessness and postponement rise in East Asia and Europe.

First births fall below 0.9 per woman: in South Korea, China and southern Europe many women now have none (DemographicTransition#6e31's failure mode 'end assumed': births need not settle at replacement).
About two thirds of all births are third and later children, held below the biological maximum by long breastfeeding and birth spacing of three to four years.
Farming shortens birth intervals with earlier weaning onto cereal foods: more later births per woman.
The peak of later births per woman, before family limitation begins anywhere but in France.
France's couples are already limiting later births, a century before most of the world; the world's third and later births barely move.
Family limitation spreads from France across Europe and North America: couples stop after two or three.
War and the flu cut births of every order.
The last peak: later births per woman, high across Asia, Africa and Latin America and in the rich world's baby boom.
The transition: later births fall by a fifth in five years as East Asia and Latin America stop at two or three, a generation after children's deaths began to fall (DemographicTransition#6e31).
Under two thirds of a later birth per woman, most of them in sub-Saharan Africa: about nine tenths of the fall from five children per woman in 1965 to 2.2 now came here.
China's one-child policy (1979 to 1980) begins to cut second births, the first time they fall at world scale.
About 0.7 second births per woman: one-child families common in East Asia and southern and eastern Europe.
Zero: foragers sow nothing, and their fires fix next to no nitrogen.
Begins: lentils, peas, chickpeas and bitter vetch are sown with the first wheat and barley in the Fertile Crescent.
Paddy rice in the Yangtze valley, whose flooded fields' cyanobacteria fix nitrogen, and pulses wherever farming has spread.
Roman and Han farmers rotate beans and vetches with grain; China's paddies spread south. Still a twentieth or less of the land's own fixation.
Falls a little as fields are abandoned after the Black Death and the Mongol wars.
Clover and turnip rotations spread from the Low Countries and England: Europe's fields fix more nitrogen and feed more animals.
Peruvian guano reaches European farms from 1840, but adds hundredths of a teragram; clover rotations and the spread of legumes and rice carry the total.
About 15 Tg in 1860 as Galloway and colleagues reckon it, nearly all from crops; guano and Chilean nitrate, imported by the hundred thousand tonnes, are mined, not fixed.
BASF's first Haber-Bosch plant opens at Oppau in September 1913; its output is still a rounding error beside the crops' fixation.
Haber-Bosch: BASF's plant at Oppau (1913) and the wartime Leuna works make ammonia for Germany's explosives once the British blockade cuts off Chilean nitrate.
War plants turned to fertilizer: synthetic nitrogen use climbs steeply from the late 1940s.
Passes the planetary boundary for intentional fixation (about 60 to 80 Tg N a year), as Steffen and colleagues put it.
The green revolution's high-yielding wheat and rice need fertilizer: about as much nitrogen fixed by people as by all the land's wild plants and microbes.
About 156 Tg by Galloway and colleagues' reckoning for 1990, with combustion: more than twice the land's own fixation at its lower estimates.
About 187 Tg in 2005 by Galloway and colleagues (2008): Haber-Bosch about 120, crops about 40, combustion about 25.
About 210 Tg: perhaps half of the nitrogen in the world's food crops comes from Haber-Bosch, and about half of what is applied runs off into rivers, coasts and the air.
Bitumen from seeps in Mesopotamia and the Dead Sea, for mortar, caulking and inlay: fossil carbon taken in tiny amounts.
Song China begins to burn coal: Kaifeng heats with it and the north's iron furnaces run on it as the forests near the cities give out.
Falls back after the Jurchen and Mongol conquests of north China.
England's coal grows several times over in half a century as wood grows dear around London.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
About 40 to 45 million tonnes of coal, most of it British; Belgium's and the Ruhr's mines open with the railways.
Drake's well (1859) begins oil's century; coal is already over 100 Mt a year.
About 760 Mt of coal and 20 Mt of oil: fuel is nearly half of all that is dug.

Dips in the war's last year with the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores): the mines of northern France and Belgium occupied, Russia's output collapsed. Corrected at r376 from 0.74, which the seam with that energy showed too high (17.4 GJ a head at about 26 GJ a tonne is about 0.67 t).

Mines wrecked and flooded in Europe and Asia in the last year of the war. Corrected at r376 from 0.72: the energy drawn from stores (about 22 GJ a head) at about 28.5 GJ a tonne, with oil's share rising, needs about 0.77 t.
Oil and gas join coal: fossil fuels per person grow by about 70% to 1973.
Corrected at r376 from 1.30: the energy drawn from stores (about 44 GJ a head) at about 32 GJ a tonne needs about 1.38 t; coal about 2.7 Gt, oil 1.55 Gt, gas 0.5 Gt.
After the oil shocks fossil fuels per person fall back and stay flat for twenty years.
China's coal grows about two and a half times between 2000 and 2013.
The pandemic year's dip, below the 2014 level per person.
About 9 Gt of coal, 4.4 Gt of oil and 3 Gt of gas: some 16 Gt a year.

upsert.reason: From recalled world output of coal and lignite, crude oil and natural gas (gas at about 0.72 tonnes per thousand cubic metres) divided by the world's people; before 1800 from the scale of English and Chinese coal mining. It must turn with the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores), which counts the same fuels in GJ.

points.note: Zero: no ore is dug before smelting.
Native copper is hammered at Çayönü, not dug as ore; too little to count.
Begins: copper is smelted from ore in the Balkans (Belovode, Pločnik) and Iran, the first ore dug for metal.
Arsenical and then tin bronze; copper from Oman, Feinan and Cyprus traded across thousands of kilometres.
Falls as a share as iron takes over tools and weapons, though copper for bronze still grows.
Rome's copper and lead (Rio Tinto, Cyprus, Britain's lead) and the Han's coin copper.
Falls: Rome's western mines close.
Song copper for coin, perhaps over ten thousand tonnes of metal a year about 1080, some of it won by precipitating copper from mine water onto iron.
Sweden's Falun and Japan's copper mines lead the world.
Cornwall's copper and tin, smelted at Swansea.
Falls as a share as iron ore grows fivefold; Chile's and Michigan's copper, Cornwall's tin, Spain's lead.
Copper for electricity from the mines of Montana, Arizona and Chile.
Rises most: porphyry copper ores near 1%, a hundred tonnes of ore for each tonne of metal, and bauxite for aluminium; as large as iron ore.
About half the ore dug: copper's grades keep falling, so the ore dug grows faster than the copper won.
Rises again: copper ore near 0.6% copper, and Indonesia's nickel laterites from 2020.
About 5 Gt: copper ore about 4 Gt, with bauxite and nickel, zinc and lead ores; the metals of the energy transition.

upsert.reason: The parent times the sketched share of copper and the other base metals: nearly all the ore before iron, a third or less from the Iron Age to 1820, a sixth to a third from 1850 to 1945, and the largest share since about 1950 as copper's grade falls.

points.note: Zero: no ore is dug before smelting.
Zero: the first ore smelted is copper; iron's ores need hotter, more reducing fires.
Begins: Anatolia's smiths smelt iron from ore in small amounts.
Rises most: bloomery iron spreads from Anatolia and the Levant; its ores lie almost everywhere, so a quarter of the ore dug is soon for iron.
Han China's state iron monopoly from 117 BCE, and the bloomeries of Rome's provinces.
Holds better than the other ores after Rome's western mines close: iron is smelted locally from local ores, and becomes the largest share.
Song China's iron, perhaps 100,000 tonnes a year about 1080 on Hartwell's much-argued estimate, from some 250,000 tonnes of ore.
Europe's blast furnaces, spreading from the Low Countries and Sweden, cast iron for guns.
Coke smelting spreads in Britain after 1750, and the Urals' charcoal furnaces make Russia the largest iron maker.
Hot blast (Neilson, 1828) cuts the coal needed per tonne of iron, and the first railways want rails: iron ore grows fastest of the ores.
Rises most: about 4.5 Mt of pig iron, or some 11 Mt of ore, for rails, ships and machines; more than half the ore dug is now for iron.
Bessemer and open-hearth steel; the ores of Lorraine, Bilbao and the Mesabi Range.
Falls: the postwar slump of 1920 and 1921 cuts steel.
Rearmament: steel for war.
Falls below half the ore dug for the first time since about 1840, as copper ore grows faster.
Falls per person: rich countries' steel use stops growing after the oil shocks.
Rises most: China's steel; iron ore mined roughly doubles from 2003 to 2013.
About 3 Gt of ore as mined, a little over a quarter of the whole; China's steel output has levelled off.

upsert.reason: The parent times iron's sketched share of the ore tonnage: zero before about 1500 BCE, a quarter to two-fifths from the Iron Age to 1800, above half from the coke furnace to the 1940s, a quarter to a third since.

points.note: Zero: no ore is dug before smelting.
Begins: gold is worked at Varna, mostly from river gravels.
Silver is won from lead ores by cupellation in Anatolia and Mesopotamia.
Egypt's gold from Nubia and the Eastern Desert.
Rises: Laurion's silver-lead ore, worked hard from 483 BCE to pay for Athens's fleet, with Lydian and Achaemenid gold.

Its largest share of the ore dug in this account, perhaps two-fifths: Rome's silver at Rio Tinto and in Spain's lead-silver mines, and the gold of Las Médulas, worked by bringing down hillsides with water.
Falls most: Rome's western mines close and the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Europe's silver mines: Goslar's Rammelsberg, and Freiberg from 1168.
Central Europe's silver boom (Schwaz, Joachimsthal), with new drainage and the liquation of copper-silver ores.
Rises: Potosí's silver from 1545 and Zacatecas's from 1546.
The silver century: Potosí's and Zacatecas's ore, refined with mercury from 1573, and Japan's silver; precious ores perhaps a third of the ore dug.
Brazil's gold from Minas Gerais, from 1695.
Mexico's silver at its colonial peak.
Mexico's and Peru's silver mines, flooded and wrecked in the independence wars, recover slowly; the Urals' gold placers grow.
Siberia's gold rush of the 1830s and 1840s makes Russia the largest gold producer before California.

Rises: the gold rushes of California (1848) and Victoria (1851). This part counts ore and gravel worked as far as the parent does; the rushes washed perhaps tens of millions of tonnes of gravel a year, so it is the most uncertain here.
The Witwatersrand's gold reef, crushed by the million tonnes at about ten grams a tonne, and the Klondike.
Rises: gold's dollar price is raised by 69% in 1934, and gold mines expand while other mining slumps.
Falls: gold mining is cut in the war for labour and materials.
Recovers after the war.
Rises: heap leaching with cyanide from the 1980s makes gold ores of one gram a tonne worth mining, in Nevada, Australia and Peru.
About 2.5 Gt: some 3,600 tonnes of gold a year from ores near 1.5 grams a tonne, with primary silver ores; about a quarter of the whole.

upsert.reason: The parent times the sketched share of precious ores: a tenth to a fifth in the Bronze Age, perhaps two-fifths in Rome's mines, a third in the silver century, a tenth to a quarter from 1850 to 1980, and near a quarter since heap leaching made gold ores of one gram a tonne worth mining.

points.note: Native copper is hammered into beads and awls at Çayönü in Anatolia, too little to count.
Copper is smelted from ore in the Balkans (Belovode, Pločnik) and Iran: the first ore taken for metal.
Arsenical and then tin bronze; copper from Oman, Feinan and Cyprus is traded across thousands of kilometres.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant; ores need no long trade, so more is dug.
Rome's mines (Rio Tinto, the lead and silver of Spain, the gold of Las Médulas) and the Han's iron: lead in Greenland's ice peaks in the first century, a level not seen again until the Middle Ages.
Rome's western mines close and the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China's iron industry, perhaps 100,000 tonnes of iron a year about 1080 on Hartwell's much-argued estimate, and Europe's silver mines (Goslar, Kutná Hora later).
The silver century: Potosí's and Zacatecas's ore, refined with mercury from 1573, and Japan's silver, with Sweden's iron and copper.
Iron for rails, ships and machines: about 4.5 Mt of pig iron in 1850, and the gold rushes of California and Victoria.
The steel century begins: about 40 Mt of pig iron, copper for electricity, and the Witwatersrand's gold reef, crushed by the million tonnes.
War production holds up iron and copper while building stops.
Ores per person grow two and a half times from 1950 to 1970, and grades fall: copper ore near 1% means a hundred tonnes dug for each tonne of metal.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries' steel use stops growing.
China's steel and the commodity boom of 2003 to 2014: iron ore mined doubles within a decade.
About 10 Gt of ore a year, iron ore about a quarter of it by mass and copper ore much of the rest.

upsert.reason: Declared the sum of its three parts, which share its unit and count each tonne of ore once.

points.note: Flint, chert and ochre: the first draw on the Earth's stores is stone for tools and colour, a few kilograms per person a year.
Mud brick and lime plaster for the first villages (Çatalhöyük, Jericho): earth for building becomes the largest draw on the stores and stays so.
Cities of mud brick and the first monuments of stone (the pyramids from about 2600 BCE).
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the Han's walls, roads and tombs.
Building in stone and brick collapses in the western Roman lands.
Europe's cathedrals and castles and Song China's cities build in stone and brick.

Nearly flat at about half a tonne a head for sixty years while fossil fuels and ores per person grow tenfold: the first industrial century digs fuel and ore; building in stone and brick grows with Europe's and America's cities, but not faster than the world's people.
War halts building: the dip in the whole falls mostly on building materials. Was 0.285 before the fossil correction of r376.
Cement and aggregate for reconstruction and growth: building minerals per person grow about 5% a year for twenty years.
Keeps rising after the oil shocks, while fuels and ores per person stall: Asia's and the Gulf's building.
China's building boom: its cement, and the sand and gravel poured with it, drive two thirds of the rise.
About 55 Gt a year, two thirds of all that is dug: sand, gravel and crushed stone for concrete and roads above all.

upsert.reason: The remainder of the whole once fossil fuels and metal ores are counted; all of it before smelting. After 1950 it rests on recalled cement output and the usual ratios of aggregate to cement; before, on reasoning about building.

points.note: Stone for tools and ochre for colour: a few kilograms per person a year.
Natufian and early Neolithic stone houses, mortars and querns.
Villages of mud brick and lime plaster, as at Çatalhöyük and Jericho; lime is burned from stone. Earth for building is the first large draw on the stores.
Cities of mud brick, copper and then bronze smelted from ores.
Iron, smelted from ores found almost everywhere, spreads from Anatolia and the Levant.
Roman concrete, brick and stone and the mines of Spain: lead in Greenland's ice reaches a peak in the first century CE not matched again until the Middle Ages (as recalled from the ice-core studies).
Western Roman building and mining collapse; the lead in Greenland's ice falls back.
Song China burns coal for iron, and Europe builds in stone.
Potosí's silver and Britain's first coal boom, small against the stone and earth of building.
Coal begins to count: Britain mines about 15 Mt a year, most of the world's.
Raised from 0.85 so that building minerals, opened as a part at r369, do not fall per person while railways, ports and cities grow.

Krausmann and colleagues: about 7 Gt of materials taken in 1900, about a quarter of it coal, ores and building minerals (about 1.75 Gt, or 1.06 tonnes a head); the rest is harvested biomass, not counted here. Raised from 1.0 to the figure this note gives, so the three parts opened at r369 sum to it.
Raised from 1.2 with 1900.
Mines and cities wrecked in Europe and Asia: extraction per person dips in the last year of the war.
Reconstruction and the long boom: steel, cement and oil per person grow about 4% a year from 1950.
The great acceleration: oil, cement and steel for reconstruction and for growth, faster than people.
Flat for twenty years after the oil shocks, as rich countries build less and use energy better.
China's building boom: it poured more cement in 2011 to 2013 than the United States in the whole twentieth century, and coal and iron ore follow.
The UNEP International Resource Panel counts about 100 Gt taken in 2020, three quarters of it non-metallic minerals, fossil fuels and metal ores.

upsert.reason: From 1900 Krausmann and colleagues' material flows (about 7 Gt of materials in 1900, a quarter of it minerals and fuels) and the UNEP International Resource Panel's (about 100 Gt in 2020, three quarters minerals and fuels), as recalled; before 1900 sketched from building, mining and toolmaking.

points.note: About half a billion tonnes of carbon by models of the unfished ocean (Bianchi and colleagues 2021, Jennings and Collingridge 2015, as recalled); how glacial seas changed it is unknown, so it is held level until fishing.
Rome's fisheries and fish-sauce works, China's and the Mediterranean's coastal fishing: large locally, too small to move the world's fish.
Europe's herring and cod fisheries grow (the Hanseatic herring of the Baltic); river fish decline with mills and dams.
European fleets fish the cod of the Newfoundland banks.
Turns down: steam trawlers work the North Sea from 1881 and soon find fewer fish per hour of trawling, the first industrial depletion.
The war keeps trawlers in port and North Sea stocks recover a little.
The second war again halts much fishing, and the North Sea's stocks recover.
World catches about 20 million tonnes of wet weight a year; from here sonar, synthetic nets, diesel trawlers and factory freezers carry fishing to every ocean.
World catch rises from about 20 to 30 million tonnes of wet weight between 1950 and 1955, mostly from stocks not yet fished down.
Peru's anchoveta fishery, the world's largest, lands some 12 million tonnes and collapses in 1972 with El Niño and overfishing.
The Newfoundland cod collapse follows (1992): a moratorium ends a fishery of five centuries.
World catches peak: about 86 million tonnes as reported, about 130 by Pauly and Zeller's reconstruction with unreported catch; both fall slowly after.

Debated: stock assessments (Hilborn and colleagues, the RAM Legacy database) find assessed stocks in North America, Europe and Oceania stable or rebuilding since about 2000; catch reconstructions and whole-ocean models (Pauly and Zeller; Christensen and colleagues 2014; Bianchi and colleagues 2021) find fish of fishable size about halved since 1900, predatory fish down by about two thirds. The band carries both readings.

Before whaling: perhaps four to five times today's mass, most of it in the great baleen and sperm whales; read back from population models of the whales before exploitation, which disagree widely. How glacial seas changed it is unknown; held level.
Coastal peoples hunt seals and stranded or small whales from the Arctic to Korea (the Bangudae petroglyphs); a local taking, too small to move the world's mass.
Basque whalers hunt right whales in the Bay of Biscay; the Thule Inuit hunt bowheads across the Arctic. Still local.
Basque whalers at Red Bay in Labrador take thousands of bowhead and right whales: the first whaling across an ocean.
Turns down: Dutch and English fleets hunt the bowheads of Spitsbergen from 1611 for oil and baleen.
American sperm whaling grows from Nantucket after 1712.
Sealers kill millions of fur seals on the southern islands, from Juan Fernández to South Georgia, for skins sold in Canton, and elephant seals for oil.
American, British and French whalers work the sperm-whale grounds of the Pacific and the right whales of the south; the fur seals of the sub-Antarctic are nearly gone.
The American whaling fleet at its height, some 700 ships about 1846; bowheads of the Bering Sea hunted from 1848, gray whales in their Baja lagoons in the 1850s.
Petroleum from 1859 begins to replace whale oil for lamps, but whaling does not end.
Svend Foyn's harpoon cannon and steam catchers (1868) open the fast rorquals, the blue and fin whales, to hunting.
Antarctic whaling begins from South Georgia (1904).
Falls fastest: factory ships with stern slipways (from 1925) process whales at sea; the 1930/31 season takes some 37,000 whales, most of them blue whales.
The war halts most whaling from 1940 to 1945, a short respite.
The Antarctic quota of 16,000 blue-whale units a season (from 1946) is filled every year with fin and humpback whales as blue whales grow scarce.
Fin whales now the main catch; the Soviet fleets secretly take some 180,000 whales beyond what they report (1948 to 1973).
Lowest: blue whales a few per cent of their former numbers, fin and sei whales a small fraction.
The International Whaling Commission's moratorium on commercial whaling, adopted in 1982, takes effect in 1986.

Recovering: humpback, gray, southern right whales and fur seals have come back in many seas, blue whales much less. Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) put wild marine mammals near 40 Mt of wet mass, about 6 Mt C; Bar-On and colleagues (2018) about 4 Mt C. As recalled, to be checked.
The Pleistocene's large mammals on every continent: mammoths, mastodons, giant ground sloths, diprotodons and the herds of the savannas and steppes, perhaps 20 to 25 Mt C.

Sahul's megafauna (diprotodons, giant kangaroos, Genyornis) vanish soon after people arrive, about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago; whether hunting, fire or drying climate decided it is debated (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction). A small part of the world's wild mass.
The glacial maximum: the mammoth steppe from France to the Yukon holds great herds of grazers even as forests shrink.

The Americas lose most of their large mammal genera between about 11,000 and 9,000 BCE, as Clovis hunters spread and the Younger Dryas cold returns; hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.

In the Younger Dryas cold (from about 10,900 BCE) the Americas' mammoths, mastodons, horses and camels are going; Clovis and then Folsom hunters (from about 10,800 BCE) turn to bison, and the African Humid Period greens the Sahara for its animals. The loss runs on through the cold, so the value lies between 11,000 and 10,000 BCE.

After the end-Pleistocene extinctions: the Americas lose about three quarters of their large mammal genera between 13,000 and 11,000 years ago, and northern Eurasia its mammoths, woolly rhinos and giant deer, as people spread and the climate swings at the glacial's end. Hunting and climate share the cause in a debated measure.
From here fields and pastures slowly take land from wild herds; the loss is gradual for six thousand years.
Most of it now in the bison of North America (perhaps 30 to 60 million), the savanna herds of Africa and the wild ungulates of Asia's steppes and forests.
The plains bison, perhaps 30 million, are hunted for robes for eastern markets, before the rail-borne slaughter of the 1870s.
The slaughter of the bison for hides begins with the railways across the plains.
The bison are down to under a thousand (1889), and rinderpest, brought to the Horn of Africa in 1887, kills up to nine in ten of East Africa's buffalo and wildebeest within a decade.
Tropical forest cleared for fields and pasture, and bushmeat hunting, take wild mammals down by about a third in half a century while livestock doubles.

Bar-On and colleagues (2018): wild land mammals about 0.003 Gt C, against 0.06 for humans and 0.1 for livestock; Greenspoon and colleagues (2023) about 20 Mt of wet mass, the same order. As recalled, to be checked.

upsert.reason: Pleistocene level from the reconstructions of megafaunal biomass (Barnosky 2008; Bar-On and colleagues 2018 put it near 0.02 Gt C), the present from Bar-On and colleagues and Greenspoon and colleagues (2023), as recalled; the path between is sketched from the dated extinctions and the nineteenth-century slaughters.

points.note: MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c, a warm substage of the penultimate interglacial complex.
Penultimate glacial (MIS 6).
Deepest MIS 6.
Last Interglacial peak, warmer than pre-industrial.
MIS 5d.
MIS 5b.
Entering MIS 4.
Toba erupts (ev.toba). A volcanic winter of a few years is argued by some and doubted by others; the slide into the MIS 4 cold stage is orbital, not volcanic.
End of the MIS 4 cold stage.
MIS 3, near Heinrich event 4.
Last Glacial Maximum.
Deglaciation under way, before the Bølling warming.
About 14,000 years ago, the Bølling–Allerød warm interval of the deglaciation.
Start of the Younger Dryas: a pause in global warming, a deep cold in the north Atlantic.
Revised from -1.5: about 12,000 years ago, inside the Younger Dryas; global reconstructions of the deglaciation (Shakun and others, as recalled) reach Holocene levels only about 10,000 years ago.
The Holocene begins.
Early Holocene, near the 8.2 ka cold event.
The 4.2 ka event: drought more than global cooling.
Medieval warmth, regional more than global.
Entering the Little Ice Age.
Maunder Minimum, the coldest part of the Little Ice Age.
The Maunder minimum, deep in the Little Ice Age (ev.little-ice-age).
Just before Tambora: the 1810s are already cool after an unidentified eruption of 1809.
Tambora's sulphate (ev.sea.tambora) cools the Earth by about a quarter to half a degree for a year: 1816 is the year without a summer.
The sulphate washes out within two or three years and the temperature recovers toward the cool decade's level.
After Tambora (1815) and the cold 1810s.
Cosigüina's eruption (1835) cools the late 1830s, the last cold spell of the Little Ice Age before the warming that begins about 1850.
Just before Krakatoa, on the line from 1870 to 1890.
Krakatoa's haze (ev.sea.krakatoa) cools the world by about two tenths of a degree in 1884.
Recovering after Krakatoa; the 1880s stay cool.
The cool mid-1950s: a long La Niña from 1954 to 1956 and rising sulphate aerosols hold the mean slightly below 1950s average.
Aerosols and the Agung eruption of 1963 hold temperature flat (ev.aerosols).
Just before Pinatubo, on the line from 1990 to 1996.
Pinatubo's sulphate spreads through the stratosphere from June 1991; the cooling deepens into 1992.

Corrected from 0.42: Pinatubo's sulphate (ev.sea.pinatubo) cools the world by about 0.2 to 0.3 degrees in 1992's annual mean and up to half a degree at the monthly peak, as climate models predicted beforehand; the instrumental record runs about two tenths below the line from 1990 to 1996 in 1992 despite an El Nino. Check: the annual global means of 1990 to 1994.
The aerosol clears and warming resumes.
Derived as in the first pass: cube root of the life, literacy and income terms.
The wartime dip in life expectancy (h.alive) pulls the index down.

upsert.reason: Derived as the first pass defined it: the cube root of ((life expectancy - 20)/65) x max(literacy, 0.5%) x (ln(output per person/100)/ln 750), from the values at the same date.

points.note: Zero: no fields before farming.
The first sown fields of the Fertile Crescent.
About 1.7 million km2 of fields in the Roman and Han worlds' time, about two fifths of farmland.
The high-medieval clearing at its height in Europe and China.
Falls after the Black Death: deserted villages and abandoned fields, some of them turned to grazing.
The Americas' fields begin to be abandoned as their farmers die; cropland falls for a generation while the world's pasture grows.
The great ploughing: the American and Canadian prairies, the Russian steppe, the pampas and Australia's wheat belt, about 1870 to 1914.
About 12 million km2. From here yields, not new fields, carry most of the gain in food (the Green Revolution).
About 16 million km2, growing slowly with soy and oil palm in the tropics while temperate fields are abandoned.
Zero: no herds before herding.
Sheep, goats and then cattle herded beside the first fields.
Pastoralism spreads over the steppe and the Sahel as the Sahara dries: pasture becomes as large as the fields.
The horse-riding pastoralists of the Eurasian steppe: pasture is about three fifths of farmland for the next two thousand years.
After the Black Death, fields are turned to grazing (England's sheep walks): pasture holds while cropland falls.
Spanish cattle, sheep and horses spread over the emptied lands of Mexico and the pampas.
The herding frontier opens: from here pasture grows faster than cropland until about 1950.
Australia's sheep runs, the pampas' cattle and the Cape's and Siberia's frontiers.
The squatters' sheep spread over south-eastern Australia's grasslands (ev.anz.wool-frontier), and the pampas, the Cape and Siberia's steppe frontier are grazed.
The American West's open range and the cattle drives.
Rangeland in Latin America and Africa, and ranches cleared from tropical forest, carry most of the growth after 1950.
Pasture's peak, about 34 million km2: grazing land then shrinks as poor rangeland is abandoned and herds are fed more grain.
About 33 million km2, two thirds of farmland.
Deserted villages and abandoned fields after the plague: below 1300 (4.5).
American fields begin to be abandoned as their farmers die.
Within SurplusBound#7fe3: about one in five working outside food-getting.

Perhaps a third of foragers' energy. Debated: Cordain's survey of the ethnographic atlas puts most foragers above half, Marlowe and others find warm-climate foragers nearer a quarter to a third; glacial-age hunters of the cold steppe ate more meat. The band carries both.
Falls as farming spreads: farmers' diets narrow to grain, with meat and milk about a tenth of energy; early farmers' skeletons are shorter and their teeth worse (h.health).
Turns up: after the Black Death land is plentiful and labour dear, and Europeans and Near Easterners eat more meat than before or for centuries after (Abel's age of meat).
Falls again as Europe's population recovers and grain displaces meat.
Refrigerated ships bring Argentine, Australian and New Zealand meat to Europe from 1880, and dairying spreads.
Wartime shortages cut meat and fat first.
Rises with incomes from here: Popkin's nutrition transition, from the rich countries in the 1950s and 1960s to China after 1980.
About a sixth of all calories.
Fruit, nuts and honey: perhaps a quarter of foragers' energy; honey alone is about a sixth of the Hadza's.
Falls as farming narrows the diet to staples.
Olive oil, wine, fruit and vegetables in the Mediterranean; sesame and other oils in India and China.
Rises: Caribbean and Brazilian slave plantations make sugar cheap enough for Europe's working households (Mintz's Sweetness and Power).
Rises most from here: vegetable oils, sugar and fruit carry most of the world's gain in calories since 1960; palm and soybean oil above all after 1970.
About a third of all calories: oils about a tenth, sugar about a twelfth.
Foragers' tubers, wild seeds and staple nuts: perhaps two fifths of their energy, less in cold climates.
Wild grains ground at Ohalo II by the Sea of Galilee about 23,000 years ago: seeds were eaten long before they were sown.
Rises as farming spreads: grain, rice, millet and roots become three quarters of farmers' energy.
Maize, potatoes and cassava begin to spread from the Americas through Eurasia and Africa.
Wartime famines take hold: Henan (1942 to 1943), Bengal (1943), occupied Java and the Burma–Siam railway's camps, while Mexico's wheat programme starts.
Flat per person from here: the Green Revolution's higher yields feed more people at the same staple ration, and the gain in calories goes to animal and other foods.
About half of all calories, most of them cereals.
More land per survivor after the plague; better diets than in 1300 (1950).
Before wartime shortages.
Wartime shortages.
Wartime shortages and the famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
Wartime shortages and famines.
The postwar food crisis of 1946–47 in Europe and Asia.
The green revolution's new wheats reach India and Pakistan (ev.green-revolution).
The MIS 8 glacial: forest retreats before MIS 7's warm stages.
MIS 7c, a warm substage of the penultimate interglacial complex: forest spreads, then retreats into the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) begins: forest retreats.
The deepest MIS 6: forest at its glacial low.
Termination II (ev.termination-ii): forest spreads with the Last Interglacial's warmth, then retreats as ice returns.
The Last Interglacial ends about 116,000 years ago (ev.eu.eemian); forest retreats in the cold of MIS 5d.
MIS 5c, a warm substage: forest spreads again before MIS 5b's cold. Band narrowed from 18 to 72, an artefact of an earlier interpolation.
MIS 5b, a cold substage: forest retreats.
Revised from 45: inside the Younger Dryas (ev.younger-dryas) forest is no larger than at the Holocene's start; the 45 sat above both neighbours with no cause.
Holocene optimum; the Sahara green.
Regrowth on abandoned fields after the plague.
All people forage and move camp with the seasons.
The Natufians and the Jomon settle: the first foragers counted as settled.
The green Sahara's lake fishers and the Levant's late Natufian successors are among the foragers who settle.
Falls as farming villages grow far denser than foragers; about nine in ten of the remaining foragers still move.
Herders are now about two in five of the mobile, a little more than the parent's note (a third) says, because this split counts some foragers as settled.
Epidemics and conquest in the Americas take the land and lives of many mobile foragers; the share of remaining foragers who move falls below nine in ten.
Indian Removal (1830) and the wool frontier push foragers and hunters off their lands in North America and Australia.
Settlers take foragers' lands in North America, Australia, Siberia and southern Africa.
Small bands still move camp to forage for part or all of the year: in the Kalahari, the Congo basin, among the Hadza, in Amazonia and the Andaman Islands, and the sea nomads of South-east Asia.
No domestic animals, so no herders.
Begins: goat and sheep herders of the Zagros and Taurus may already move between seasonal pastures; whether any households were fully mobile this early is debated.
On the path between its neighbours: cattle herding begins in the eastern Sahara and sheep and goat herders move with farmers into Europe.
Cattle herders range across the green Sahara, the largest mobile herding population of the age.
Rises: the Yamnaya move with ox-wagons and herds across the Pontic-Caspian steppe, and their descendants spread east and west; the Sahara's herders move south as it dries.

Dips from 3000 BCE: the Yamnaya's descendants settle into mixed farming across Europe, the farming valleys of Egypt, Mesopotamia, the Indus and China grow faster than the steppe, and the dry spell of about 2200 BCE (the 4.2 ka event) presses on the herders of the drying Sahara and the steppe.
The camel is domesticated in Arabia, opening the deserts to herders.
Mounted nomadism on the steppe: herders ride, range far and raid settled states.
The Xiongnu unite the eastern steppe and press Han China.
Huns and Avars in the west, the Rouran and Turks in the east; camel-herding Berbers cross the Sahara.
The Mongols unite the steppe: perhaps one or two million herders build the largest land empire.
Up a little: the Black Death kills more of the settled, crowded peoples than of the herders.
Herders pass mobile foragers as the larger part of the mobile between 1600 and 1650.
The Qing destroy the Dzungars (1755 to 1758) and Russia advances on the Kazakh steppe: states begin to settle and tax the herders.
Russian peasants settle the Kazakh steppe and France conquers the Sahara's herders; rinderpest kills most of East Africa's cattle in the 1890s.
Falls faster: Soviet collectivization forces the Kazakh, Kyrgyz and Turkmen nomads to settle (1928 to 1934); the famine that follows kills perhaps a third of the Kazakhs.
Mongolia's herders are collectivized, Tibet's herds taken into communes, and new states in the Middle East and Africa push herders to settle.
The Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s drive many herders into towns and camps; Africa's fast-growing herding peoples keep the share from falling faster.
Perhaps 10 to 60 million people: estimates differ because many households now move only part of the family with the herds.
No settled markets to serve.
Begins with the first cities and states: smiths, traders and entertainers who move among settled people; how many lived without a fixed home is unknown.
The Roma, who left India centuries before, reach the Balkans by about 1300; Banjara carriers supply the Delhi Sultanate's armies.

Most of this share is South Asia's carrier and service nomads: Banjara caravans of tens of thousands of bullocks, nomadic smiths, traders and entertainers; Europe's Roma and Travellers and the Middle East's Dom are fewer.
Turns down: railways take the Banjara carrying trade, and India's Criminal Tribes Act (1871) brands many nomadic castes as criminal and forces them to settle.
Nazi Germany and its allies murder perhaps 200,000 to 500,000 Roma and Sinti (the Porajmos), many of them travelling families; the estimate is debated.
Most of India's nomadic castes, the Roma and the Travellers are now settled; some still travel for part of the year.
All people are mobile foragers, moving camp with the seasons.
Some glacial-age winter settlements on the Russian plain were reoccupied for months, but their people still moved.
Turns down: the Natufians of the Levant settle in stone houses about 12,500 BCE, harvesting wild cereals before they farm; the Jomon of Japan settle about the same time.

Farming villages in the Fertile Crescent, millet farmers in north China and the gardeners of Kuk in New Guinea begin to grow denser than foragers, and fishers settle by the lakes of the green Sahara; the fall from 96 at 9500 BCE toward 82 at 7900 BCE is taken as steady, though it may have come later and faster.
Farming villages in south-west Asia, China and New Guinea hold a growing share, because farmers live far denser than foragers.
Herders begin to move with their animals on the steppe and in the Sahara as it dries; pastoral nomadism will keep a share mobile after foraging shrinks.
Mounted nomadism on the steppe (the Scythians and their neighbours): herders now move on horseback over great ranges and threaten settled states.
The Mongols unite the steppe; about a third of the mobile are now herders rather than foragers.
The Qing destroy the Dzungar state (1755 to 1758) and Russia advances on the Kazakh steppe: the last great nomad powers end, and settled states begin to fence and tax the herders.
Turns down faster: Soviet collectivization forces the Kazakh and other Central Asian nomads to settle, 1928 to 1934, and the famine that follows kills perhaps a third of the Kazakhs.
The Sahel droughts of the 1970s and 1980s drive many herders into towns and camps.

Mobile herders in the Sahel, the Horn of Africa, Arabia, Iran, Central Asia, Mongolia and Tibet, and a few foraging bands; estimates of mobile pastoralists differ by a factor of two, since many herders now move only part of the household.

upsert.reason: Mobile foragers from the model's foraging share, taking about 7% of foragers as sedentary after 12,500 BCE; pastoral nomads sketched at 2 to 3% of humanity from mounted nomadism to 1500 (steppe, Arabia, Sahara, East Africa, Tibet), falling to about 1% by 1900 and about 0.3% now, as estimates of mobile pastoralists put them (some 30 to 40 million today, as recalled).

points.note: Penultimate glacial; numbers in Africa possibly reduced.
Deepest part of the penultimate glacial.
Last Interglacial: a green Sahara and Arabia open early ranges beyond Africa.
Around the Toba eruption; the genetic case for a bottleneck then is weak, so no dip is drawn.
The dispersal out of Africa under way.
Last Glacial Maximum: northern ranges abandoned.
The Americas entered about now.
Geometric growth from 4.4 million at -10000 to 18 million at -5000 gives about 12 million; set a little lower because farming populations grew fastest after -6000.
Rome and Han China near their peaks, about 65 and 56 million.
After the Antonine plague and as the Han collapsed.
Recovering from the Justinianic plague; Tang China after the An Lushan rebellion.
Song China past 100 million; Europe's high-medieval growth.
After the Black Death and the Ming–Yuan transition: below both 1300 (390 million) and 1500 (461 million). McEvedy and Jones's order of magnitude, as recalled.
Eurasia grows, but the Americas lose millions in the first smallpox epidemic: the world adds less than its trend.
Before the war: about 1.8 billion.
Growth near its all-time peak of about 2% a year: deaths have fallen, births not yet (DemographicTransition#6e31).
Gravettian aggregation sites such as Dolní Věstonice.
Jericho's first settlement grows beside its spring.
Large PPNB villages such as Abu Hureyra or Jericho.
Çatalhöyük near its peak (7100–5700 BCE). Larger than the -5000 value (5): the largest settlements shrank before the Tripolye megasites and Uruk.
The Tripolye megasites and early Uruk.
Ur.
Babylon or Linzi.
Rome or Chang'an.
Rome, past its peak.
Daxing-Chang'an, rebuilt by the Sui, as the Tang take it (ev.as.tang).
Chang'an under the Tang; Baghdad just founded.
Kaifeng becomes the Song capital (ev.as.song).
Hangzhou after the fall of Kaifeng.
Nanjing, the early Ming capital, in Chandler's estimate as recalled; Cairo and Vijayanagara next.
London overtakes Beijing.
London, about 1.66 million at the census of 1831 with its suburbs, is now the largest city by a clear margin over Beijing.
Greater Tokyo.
Tokyo.
Akkad or Old Kingdom Egypt.
New Kingdom Egypt and the Shang each rule a few million as the Bronze Age collapse begins.
Before the Achaemenid empire: Assyria, Egypt and the Zhou each rule a few million.
Cyrus takes the Median kingdom (ev.as.achaemenid); Lydia and Babylon fall to him within twelve years.
Darius rules from the Indus to Egypt and Thrace: the Achaemenid empire holds perhaps a fifth of humanity (ev.as.achaemenid).
The Achaemenid empire.
Alexander takes the Achaemenid empire whole (334 to 330 BCE): the largest polity changes hands, not size.
Ashoka's Maurya empire, over most of the subcontinent, is the largest; its people are estimated from about 15 to 50 million, a wide debate the band carries.
Qin unifies China (ev.as.qin) as the Maurya empire declines after Ashoka: each holds perhaps a sixth to a fifth of humanity.
Han China.
Rome, about 65 million of 245.
Rome, with the Han breaking up.
Rome's western half has fallen (ev.eu.rome-fall) and China is divided between north and south: no polity holds more than about a seventh of humanity.
Sui China, whose census of 609 counts about 46 million.
Tang China.
The Northern Song, perhaps 80 million of 295 million, before the Jin take the north (ev.as.song).
Southern Song after losing the north to the Jin.
The Southern Song, with the Jin close behind.
Yuan China after the fall of the Song.
Revised from 28: Yuan China holds about the same quarter of humanity as at 1279; the 28 was the coarse fill's value and rose with no cause.
Ming China, about 80 million of 350 million; the 1393 census count of 60 million is taken as an undercount.
Qing China at its population peak.
Qing China, about 410 million on the debated official counts, still holds over a third of humanity on the eve of the Opium War.
Qing China and the British Empire about equal.
India passes China as the most populous state about April 2023, on the UN's estimate (ev.as.india-most-populous): the largest polity changes, but its share holds near 17.7% across the change.

Foragers' spirits and ancestors rarely judge conduct between people: moralizing high gods are rare among foragers in the cross-cultural samples (Swanson's, and Peoples and Marlowe's). Debated: Purzycki and others find local gods that care about some conduct, which would raise this; the band allows it.
Early farmers' ancestor cults and shrines, as at Catalhoyuk, show no sign of gods that judge conduct.

The first states: Egypt's Maat and Mesopotamia's sun god as judge. Whether these count as moralizing gods is debated; the Seshat coding that placed them early was part of a study retracted in 2021 over its treatment of missing data.
Egypt's judgment of the dead spreads beyond the king in the Coffin Texts.
The Zhou claim Heaven's mandate (about 1046 BCE): Heaven judges rulers by their virtue.

Rises most between 800 and 500 BCE: karma taught as a law repaying conduct (the Upanishads, the Buddha, Mahavira), Zoroaster's judging god, the Hebrew prophets, Confucius's Heaven. Whether this Axial Age is a break or a gradual growth is debated (Jaspers and Bellah against Mullins and others), as is why: Baumard and Boyer's affluence against the Big Gods case that such beliefs let large societies cooperate (Norenzayan).
Buddhist judgment of the dead enters Chinese folk religion; Christianity in the Mediterranean.
Enlightenment unbelief and deism are a few among the educated of Europe; the world share barely moves.
The peak: nearly all of humanity in traditions that teach judged conduct, before state atheism.
Turns down: the Soviet state teaches unbelief from 1917.
China's new state teaches unbelief from 1949.
The trough: China's Cultural Revolution closes temples and churches; Western Europe's young stop believing as well as attending.
Turns up: belief revives in the former Soviet lands and in China after the Cultural Revolution, and the Muslim and African Christian shares grow.
Unbelief grows in Europe, East Asia and the Americas while belief holds in Muslim and African populations (Pew and Gallup surveys, as recalled); the two nearly cancel.

upsert.reason: Sketched: before 1900 from the share of people in traditions coded as having moralizing high gods or broad supernatural punishment (Swanson; Peoples and Marlowe; Norenzayan's Big Gods; the Seshat moralizing-gods data and their critics, as recalled), counting part of the local and Chinese traditions; after 1900 lowered by the unaffiliated and by unbelief within traditions as surveys show.

points.note: No tradition open to every people exists before the Buddha; foragers' traditions are bound to their band and land.
The first states' traditions are bound to their city, king and land; Akhenaten's Aten cult (about 1350 BCE) does not seek converts abroad.
The Buddha's teaching begins in the Ganges plain, open to any who join the order whatever their birth: the first tradition of this kind.
Turns up: Ashoka's patronage and his missions to Sri Lanka, Gandhara and the Hellenistic kings carry the teaching beyond its first people.
Buddhism reaches China along the Silk Roads; Christians are still a few hundred thousand in the Roman Empire.
Turns up: the Roman Empire becomes Christian between Constantine's conversion (312) and Theodosius's decrees (380), and Buddhism spreads through China.
Islam enters the count after 610; most conquered peoples convert only slowly over the next three centuries.
Northern and Eastern Europe baptized from the 960s; conversion in Iran and the Near East passes the half.
The Black Death kills Christians and Muslims around the Mediterranean in greater shares than East Asian Buddhists; the sum barely moves.
The survivors in the Spanish Americas are baptized; the gain is small because so many of them die.
Turns up faster: Europe's and the Americas' Christian peoples grow faster than Asia's, and missions spread in Africa and Oceania.
Turns flat: Buddhists fall under state atheism after 1917 and 1949 while Christians grow in Africa and Muslims by births; the sum holds near 53 to 55 until 1970.
Rises again, mainly by the higher birth rates of Muslim and African Christian populations, not by conversion.
Christians about 31% and Muslims about 24.5% of humanity, Buddhists about 6% (Pew Research Center's Global Religious Futures estimates, as recalled).

upsert.reason: The sum of the model's Buddhist, Christian and Muslim shares at each date; its band carries theirs.

points.note: On the eve of the Cultural Revolution, which closes China's temples and churches.
All of humanity's output is made in Africa until Homo sapiens settles western Asia in the Last Interglacial; output per person is the forager level (h.provisioning).
Asia's first farmers now make more than Africa's foragers and herders: Africa's output passes below Asia's between 9500 and 7900 BCE.
Egypt unified (ev.af.egypt-unification): the Nile valley's output per person near the world's, the rest of Africa below it.
Africa's output stalls between 1800 and 1820 while its people's share falls: the Atlantic slave trade's last peak and the wars of the Sokoto jihad and the Mfecane.
Conquest and colonial rule: Africa's share of world output falls toward its low of under 4%, though mines and cash crops raise its output in absolute terms.
Africa's lost decades begin: debt, falling commodity prices and wars hold its output per person flat or falling from about 1980 to 1995 while its people grow fastest.
Africa's output has grown faster than the world's since 2000, but at about 5% of world output it is a quarter of its share of people.
No people live in the Americas until about 16,000 years ago (the White Sands footprints, if their dates hold, put a few earlier).
People are south of the ice (Monte Verde by about 14,500 years ago): the Americas' first output, a few tens of thousands of foragers.
The Classic: Teotihuacan, the Maya kingdoms, Moche and Tiwanaku raise the Americas' output per person a little toward the world's.

On the eve of contact the Americas make about a twelfth of world output, the Aztec and Inca states and their tributaries most of it; the size depends on the contact population, which is debated (see h.region-americas).
The Aztec and Inca states fall; smallpox has already run through Mexico and the Andes. Output shrinks with the people, at the rate between 1520 and 1550.
Potosí is found (1545) and the cocoliztli strikes New Spain (1545 to 1548): silver rises as people die.

The Columbian collapse (ev.columbian-exchange, VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd): the Americas' output falls by two fifths from 1520 to 1550 and by two thirds to 1600 with its people, though the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas becomes the most valuable thing the Americas send out.
The nadir: the Americas make under 2% of world output.
The United States' output per person is already more than twice the world's; with Latin America's near the world's, the Americas' output per person is about 1.4 times it.
Spanish America's wars of independence end with its economies smaller than in 1810, while the United States grows; on the path from 1820 to 1850.
Latin America stagnates under the caudillos while the United States grows by canals and cotton; the Americas' output doubles from 1820 to 1850, almost all of the gain in the north.
The Americas pass a tenth of world output, the United States most of it.

Between 1870 and 1890 on a constant growth rate: the United States grows fast after the Civil War despite the depression of 1873, Argentina's export boom begins, and the slave economies of Cuba and Brazil end in the 1880s. About 13.6% of world output, up from 11.3% in 1870.
The First World War: the Americas' output rises while Europe's falls.
The bank panics of 1930 and 1931 and the collapse of commodity prices take the Americas' output down a tenth from 1929; Latin America's export economies turn to making their own goods.
The Depression's trough: the Americas' output falls about a fifth from 1929 (ev.nam.depression), more than any other area's.
The war economy: the Americas' output passes Europe's for the first time, the United States making about two fifths of the world's manufactures.
Demobilization: American output falls about a tenth from its wartime peak.
Latin America's lost decade (ev.am.debt-crisis): its output per person falls while Northern America's grows, so the Americas' output grows slower than the world's.
No Homo sapiens lives in Asia before the Last Interglacial; the Denisovans and other archaic humans are not counted.
The dispersal out of Africa (ev.era.dispersal): Asia's output grows with its people, at the forager level per person.
Farming in the Fertile Crescent and then China: Asia's output passes Africa's and keeps about three fifths of the world's or more for the next nine thousand years.
Han China and the Indian kingdoms: Asia makes about seven tenths of world output, close to its share of people (Maddison about 74% as recalled).
Song China's commercial economy at its height: Asia's output per person a little above the world's.
The Mongol wars, the Yuan collapse and the Black Death in western Asia: Asia's output falls from 1300 to 1400 with its people.
Ming China and the Indian kingdoms: Asia makes about 62% of world output, near Maddison's figure as recalled.
The seventeenth-century crisis: the Ming–Qing wars and famines hold Asia's output near flat from 1600 to 1650.
Asia makes about 57% of world output with 65% of its people: the Great Divergence has begun but is still small (MalthusianTrap#0f6b binds Asia as it bound everyone).
Europe's output has passed Asia's for the first time since antiquity, between 1870 and 1890: Asia grows slowly while the El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 cut India's and north China's people.
Japan's war in China from 1937: Asia's output falls from 1936 to 1940.
China's famine of the Great Leap Forward: Asia makes under a quarter of world output, near its lowest share.

Japan grows about a tenth a year and Singapore, independent from 1965, begins its rise, while the American war in Vietnam escalates; China's Cultural Revolution (from 1966) will cut its output in 1967 and 1968.
China's reform (from 1978), Japan's boom and the Asian tigers: Asia's output about equals Europe's and the Americas'.
Asia's output has passed Europe's and the Americas' in the 1990s, for the first time since about 1880.
Asia makes about half of world output, near its share before 1820, though its output per person is still under the world's.
Zero: foragers' shamans and ritual elders also hunt and gather; no one is kept to serve the sacred.
Begins, perhaps: the enclosures of Gobekli Tepe and Neolithic shrines may have had keepers fed by the feasts' builders; unknown.
Eridu's temple and the chiefdoms' priests.
The temple households of Sumer and Egypt's priesthood: in the first states a temple can be the largest owner of land and keeper of people.
Egypt's New Kingdom temples hold perhaps a tenth of its land and keep tens of thousands; Amun's priesthood rivals the throne.
The Buddha's and Mahavira's orders of monks and nuns, the first communities kept wholly by believers' alms, beside the Brahmins, the magi and the Greek temples.
Buddhist monks begin to carry the dharma into Han China.
Christian monasticism begins in Egypt's desert (Antony, then Pachomius's communities about 320).

Rises most: China's Buddhist monasteries under the Northern Wei and the southern courts, perhaps a million or more monks and nuns by the claims of the time, and Christian monasteries from Egypt to Ireland.

Falls: the Tang emperor Wuzong's Huichang suppression (842 to 845) destroys some 4,600 monasteries and returns about 260,000 monks and nuns to lay life, a large part of all the people kept for faiths in a China that held a quarter of humanity; the sangha recovers under the Song.

Near its peak: Europe's clergy and religious perhaps one or two in every hundred people, holding a fifth to a quarter of its land; Theravada monasteries in every mainland village; Tibet's monasteries; the ulama and Sufi orders.
Falls: the Reformation dissolves the monasteries of England, Scandinavia and Protestant Germany and turns their lands to crowns and nobles.
Catholic Europe's Counter-Reformation clergy and Tibet's monasteries, where perhaps a sixth of men are monks, hold the level.
Falls: the French Revolution abolishes the religious orders and sells the Church's lands, and the secularizations of Joseph II and Napoleon follow.
The Soviet state closes churches and monasteries and kills or exiles tens of thousands of clergy.
Falls: China's new state laicizes monks and nuns and takes temple lands; after 1959 Tibet's monasteries are emptied.
The Cultural Revolution closes every temple, church and mosque in China.

About eleven million: Catholic priests, sisters and brothers about a million, Protestant pastors two to three million, imams and ulama one to two million, Buddhist monks and nuns one to two million, Hindu temple priests one to three million, and others.
Neanderthals hold Europe and are not counted; Homo sapiens arrives about 45,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum drives Europe's foragers into southern refuges; its output falls with its people.
The Roman peace: the Mediterranean's output per person about a sixth above the world's, Europe's north below it.

Rome's fall in the west (ev.eu.rome-fall): cities shrink, trade and coin fail and people fall, so Europe's output falls by about two fifths from 200 to 610 and its output per person drops below the world's.
The high-medieval peak: Europe's output more than doubles from 1000 with its people and its towns.
After the Black Death: Europe's output about an eighth below 1300's though output per person is higher, fewer people working the same land (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
Atlantic trade and the Dutch and English economies: Europe's output per person is about two fifths above the world's.
Coal and steam (Sunbound#c94c): Europe's output per person reaches about 1.75 times the world's.
Europe's output passes Asia's for the first time since antiquity, between 1870 and 1890.
Europe's output falls about a tenth from 1913 with the war.
The war's last year: occupied, bombed and fought-over Europe makes about a seventh less than in 1940; Germany's output collapses in 1945.
The postwar boom: Western Europe's recovery and the Soviet Union's growth carry Europe's output back above the Americas'.
The Soviet bloc's collapse: Eastern Europe's output falls about two fifths between 1989 and 1998, so Europe's output grows slowly through the 1990s (ev.eu.soviet-collapse).
Starts: a heavy thrusting or thrown spear delivers a few hundred joules, the most any weapon can.
Bows and arrows, by about 64,000 years ago in southern Africa, reach farther but strike with less energy than a spear; the frontier does not move.
The spear-thrower, from about 20,000 years ago, throws a dart harder and farther than an arm alone.
The first states' sieges: rams swung or pushed by many men against city gates.
Assyria's wheeled siege engines with heavy rams.
Jumps: torsion catapults, from Syracuse about 400 BCE, and the Hellenistic stone-throwers that hurl stones of a talent (about 26 kg) or more at city walls.
Falls a little: the great torsion engines go out of use with Rome's armies, and the traction trebuchet, coming west from China, throws lighter stones.
The counterweight trebuchet, in the Mediterranean world from the twelfth century, throws stones of a hundred kilograms and more.
Jumps a hundredfold: the Jin's iron-cased thunder-crash bombs, packed with gunpowder, at Kaifeng (1232) against the Mongols (ev.gunpowder).
Jumps: gunpowder mines of a ton or so under fortress walls, as Pedro Navarro's at Naples (1503), release a thousand times the energy of the great bombards' balls.
Paixhans' shell guns (adopted by France, 1837) fire explosive shells flat at ships, the end of the wooden warship, but a single shot's energy stays near that of the heaviest mortars.
Still the black-powder mine: the Union's mine at Petersburg (1864) holds about four tonnes.
High explosives (dynamite, guncotton, lyddite) replace black powder in mines and shells.
Jumps: the largest of the mines under Messines ridge (June 1917) holds about 40 tonnes of ammonal.
Jumps about five hundredfold: the atomic bombs on Hiroshima (about 15 kilotons) and Nagasaki (about 21) (ev.as.hiroshima).
Jumps thirtyfold: the hydrogen bomb in service, the Mark 17 of 10 to 15 megatons, the yield Castle Bravo tested (ev.mic.castle-bravo).
Its peak: the American B41 of 25 megatons enters service; the Soviet Tsar Bomba's 50 megatons (1961) is tested, not deployed.
Falls: the B41 is retired as accurate missiles make yield less needed; the largest left are Soviet warheads of about 20 megatons on the heaviest missiles.

Falls: the single-warhead heavy missiles are replaced by multiple smaller warheads; the American B53 of 9 megatons is about the largest left. When the last 20-megaton Soviet warheads left service is uncertain, and the band holds it.
The B53 retired (1997): the largest warheads in service are China's of about 4 to 5 megatons on the DF-5.
Starts: bands give perhaps a hundredth of their effort to raids, feuds and the weapons kept for them, an order of magnitude the band carries.
Chiefs keep retinues and villages build palisades: a little more of output goes to force.
Rises: the Warring States' conscript armies, the Punic wars and the Maurya army take more of output than any earlier states.
The Roman and Han armies each take about half their states' revenue: perhaps 2 to 3% of their output.
The military revolution: bastion forts, gunpowder armies and navies take a growing share of states' revenue, three quarters or more in Europe's wars.
The Seven Years' War, fought in Europe, the Americas and India.
The Napoleonic wars' peak: Britain spends a fifth or more of its output on war, France and its satellites as much, mostly on credit.
Falls with the peace after 1815: armies are cut and the concert of Europe keeps the great powers from war.
The American Civil War and the Taiping war.
The naval race and the European armies' growth before 1914.
Jumps sixfold: the war economies of 1915 to 1918 give a third to a half of the belligerents' output to war, financed mostly by borrowing and money creation.
Falls with demobilization.
Rearmament: Germany, the Soviet Union and Japan arm first, Britain and France after 1936.
The peak: the belligerents, three quarters of world output, give two fifths to three quarters of theirs to the war (the United States about two fifths, the Soviet Union and Germany more than half).
Falls fast with demobilization after August 1945.
The Korean War and the Cold War's rearmament: the United States spends about 14% of its output, the Soviet Union more.
The American war in Vietnam.
The last Cold War build-up, American and Soviet.
Turns down: the Cold War ends and the Soviet Union's spending collapses with it.
The peace dividend: a third less of output goes to force than in 1990.
The wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, and output's fall in 2009.
Rising again with Russia's war on Ukraine and rearmament in Europe and Asia: SIPRI puts the world's military burden at about 2.5% of output in 2024.
In bands the men who fight in raids and feuds also hunt and gather: almost no one is kept under arms, though most men may fight.
Chiefs begin to keep retinues of fighting men, but most fighting is still done by farmers and herders between seasons.
The first states keep guards and standing troops; Sargon of Akkad later boasts of 5,400 men who eat daily before him.
Chariot armies of Egypt, the Hittites and Shang China: specialists kept at great cost.
Assyria keeps the first great standing army.

The Warring States of China field conscript armies of hundreds of thousands; Rome mobilizes a large share of its citizens against Carthage; the Mauryan army is reported at hundreds of thousands. The share under arms in states peaks before unification.

Rome's legions and auxiliaries, about 300,000 to 400,000 of some 60 million, and Han China's standing and frontier forces of the same order: about one in two hundred people in the states, almost none beyond them.
Song China keeps more than a million soldiers, about one in a hundred of its people, the largest standing army of its age.
The Mongols make every adult man a soldier of the decimal army, a small people wholly under arms.
The military revolution: gunpowder and the bastion fort make European armies grow tenfold in two centuries; the Ottoman, Mughal and Ming armies are as large or larger.
Louis XIV's France keeps about 400,000 men, and the Qing banners and Green Standard about 800,000.
The Napoleonic peak: the levée en masse of 1793 and conscription put about six million under arms in Europe at once.
The Taiping and Qing armies of millions and the American Civil War's, about 1.5 million under arms at once in 1864.
On the eve of mobilization (August 1914): within weeks some twenty million men are called up, the jump to 1916.
The First World War: about 40 million under arms at the height, from conscript armies of a size no earlier war had seen.
Demobilized in the West; the Red Army of the Russian Civil War still about five million.
The invasion of the Soviet Union (June 1941): some 8 to 9 million under arms on the Eastern Front alone, and Japan's and the Allies' mobilization still rising.
The Second World War: about 70 million under arms at the height, the Soviet Union and the United States about 12 million each, Germany about 10, China, Japan and Britain about 5 to 6 each.
Japan surrenders in August and September 1945; demobilization has barely begun, so the fall to 1946 comes after.
Demobilization: tens of millions sent home within a year.
The Korean war and the Cold War's rearmament.
The World Bank counts about 29 million in armed forces, paramilitary included, at the Cold War's end.
Armies cut by about a quarter after the Cold War, in Russia above all.
About 27 to 28 million under arms; Russia's and Ukraine's wartime mobilization adds about a million, against a falling share elsewhere.
No people in Sahul until about 50,000 years ago on the later dates (65,000 on Madjedebe's, debated).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) and wool: Oceania's output more than doubles in a decade.
Australia's settlers are among the richest people on Earth; Oceania's output per person about twice the world's, though its first peoples are falling (ev.oc.depopulation).
Frozen meat and butter (the Dunedin, 1882) join wool and gold as Oceania's exports; on the path between 1870 and 1890.
Wool and wheat prices collapse in the Depression: Australia's and New Zealand's output falls about a sixth.
The Australia-Japan commerce agreement (1957) begins the turn of Oceania's trade from Britain to Asia; on the path between 1954 and 1960.
France's nuclear tests at Moruroa begin (1966); they move Polynesia's politics and health, not the area's output.
Britain joins the European Community (1973), ending New Zealand's assured market, while Panguna's copper (from 1972) lifts Papua New Guinea's exports; on the path between 1970 and 1975.
A forager band's tools, ornaments, shelters and canoes: a few months of what it gets in a year. What foragers hold in skills and ties is real wealth but not counted here.
Rises with the first fields, stores and houses: farmers hold what foragers did not, land made fertile, granaries and herds.
Irrigated land, temples, granaries and herds: the first states sit on stocks of several years' harvest.
Land is most of it: the Roman and Han estates; a large estate's price was some twenty to thirty years of its rent, and rents a third to a half of the harvest.
The Black Death kills a third or more of Eurasia's western and central peoples; land loses value against what the survivors can make and earn.
Falls: after the Black Death land is plentiful and labour scarce, so land's value falls against what the survivors produce.
Britain's and France's wealth is about seven years of national income, mostly land (Piketty); Asia's agrarian empires perhaps four to five.
About five years by Piketty's world series: land's share falls as railways, factories and housing rise.
Falls: war destroys capital and war finance turns savings into government debt that inflation will erase; the Russian revolution expropriates the property of a sixth of the world's land.
The Depression wipes out share and property values.
War spreads to the Pacific: bombing and fighting destroy housing, factories and transport from Europe to China, and governments borrow on a scale that inflation will later erase.

The low: the world wars' destruction, inflation, nationalizations, rent controls and the communist revolutions' expropriations (China's from 1949) leave the world's wealth at about two and a half years of output.
Rises with privatization in the former communist states, falling interest rates and housing booms.
Peaks before the financial crisis, at the top of the housing and credit boom.
Near-zero interest rates lift asset prices while the pandemic cuts output.
About five and a half years of world output, near the World Inequality Database's global estimate, and back near where it stood before 1914.
Derived: output per person times people.

Output per person (2,560) times people (1.83 billion), before the war.
Output per person (2,450) times people (1.84 billion).
Output per person (2,950) times people (2.066 billion): the interwar peak on the eve of the crash.
Output per person (2,650) times people (2.13 billion): the Depression's trough.
Output per person (3,050) times people (2.21 billion).
Output per person (3,200) times people (2.345 billion): the war economies' peak.
Output per person (3,150) times people (2.36 billion).
Output per person (3,100) times people (2.38 billion).
Output per person (5,050) times people (3.34 billion).
Output per person (6,600) times people (4.15 billion).

upsert.reason: Derived: output per person times the number of people, at the same date.

points.note: Before print.
Gutenberg's press is being built; nothing printed reaches anyone regularly yet (ev.printing).
The steam press and the penny papers (the New York Sun, 1833) bring daily news to clerks and artisans in the cities of Britain, France and the United States.
Radio reaches most households in the industrial countries.
About four fifths of foragers' small output is food; the rest is tools, clothing and shelter, and services barely counted.
Farming feeds more people per hectare, not more per person: food-getting per person barely moves for five thousand years while its share of output begins to fall (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
After the Black Death the survivors farm the best land: food output per person rises with output per person.
Turns flat: from here food-getting per person grows far more slowly than output, so its share falls from about half to a third by 1900.
The new farmlands of the Americas, Russia and Australia feed Europe's cities by rail and steamship.
War cuts harvests in Europe and Russia.
Food output holds through the Depression while prices collapse: farmers keep producing, so the fall in output per person is industry's and services'.
The war's trough: occupied Europe, the Soviet Union and Asia harvest far less, and famine strikes Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
Food-getting falls below a tenth of world output. Value added grows more slowly than harvests, because fertilizer, fuel and machines bought from industry are counted there.
About 5% of world output (World Bank value added at market prices is about 4%, more at purchasing power).

upsert.reason: Sector shares of world output: about 80% food-getting for foragers (output counted as subsistence, mostly food), 55 to 65% in agrarian economies (Broadberry's and others' sectoral reconstructions for England, China and India, as recalled, averaged toward the more agrarian majority), about a third by 1900, a fifth by 1950, and from the World Bank's value-added shares after 1960, raised somewhat for purchasing power.

points.note: Healing, teaching and ritual among foragers are done unpaid within the band; output counts little of them.
Turns up: temples, scribes, officials and long-distance traders of the first cities.
Services pass making in this sketch about now; whether agrarian services outweighed crafts is uncertain (England in 1381 had more industry than services), and the bands overlap.
Song China's commercial revolution: merchants, shippers, brokers and paper money.
Railways, shipping, banking and city trades grow with industry.
Services pass food-getting in world output about now.
Services reach half of world output.
About two thirds of world output.

upsert.reason: The remainder of output: about 5% for foragers, whose services are unpaid and barely counted; a fifth to a quarter in agrarian economies (trade, transport, housing, government, religion, servants); about a third by 1900, two fifths by 1950 and two thirds now.

points.note: Song China's commercial peak.
MalthusianTrap#0f6b: fewer people on the same land.
MalthusianTrap#0f6b: a disaster that removes people raises output per person until numbers recover. Between 1300 (850) and 1500 (1000), but post-plague, so not below the 1300 level.
1913, the pre-war peak of the first globalization.
The war's last year: output per person below 1910's.
The interwar peak, on the eve of the crash: output per person then falls about a tenth to 1932 (ev.interwar-crisis), a dip the series' dates did not show.
The Depression's trough: world output per person about a tenth below 1929, by Maddison's reconstruction as recalled; recovery to 1936 is fastest in the Soviet Union, Japan and Germany.
Wartime mobilization: American and Soviet output peaks in 1944 while occupied Europe and Asia fall back.
Output per person no higher than in 1940: the war's destruction and demobilization.
The MIS 8 glacial: the sea falls to about 90 m below today before MIS 7's warm stages.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: ice sheets shrink and the sea rises to within a few tens of metres of today's before falling into the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) builds its ice sheets: the sea falls about 70 m.
Rising to the Last Interglacial highstand, several metres above today.

The Last Interglacial highstand: about 6 to 9 m above today between about 126,000 and 117,000 years ago (Dutton and colleagues, as recalled; its size debated), with Greenland about 2 m and Antarctica, above all West Antarctica, about 3 m of it (h.sea.greenland, h.sea.antarctic).
The Last Interglacial ends about 116,000 years ago (ev.eu.eemian); ice builds again in MIS 5d and the sea falls.
The MIS 4 cold stage: ice sheets grow and the sea falls to about 80 m below today.
Just before meltwater pulse 1A.
Just after meltwater pulse 1A.

upsert.reason: The Last Interglacial highstand, missing from the values though the note at -127000 names it.

Fill, second batch of the 1820 to 1850 stretch: foraging, the four forests, range and its six areas, and the regional shares with their subregions at 1830 and 1840. The five areas are set to sum to 100 at both dates (Africa as the remainder of the others, which agrees with its own path from 10.2 to 8.8 within a few hundredths), each area to the sum of its subregions, Oceania to its four, the forests to forest and range's areas to range.
