Africa's share falls because the world's other peoples grow faster while the Atlantic trade to Brazil and Cuba peaks and the East African trade grows; Northern America's rises fastest with births and the first mass emigration from Europe.

points.note: Before cultivation; some sedentary foragers harvesting wild cereals.
Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent (ev.as.fertile-crescent); foragers are still almost everyone.

Cultivation has begun in several centres at once: the Fertile Crescent's pre-pottery Neolithic, squash in Oaxaca, millet in north China, manioc and squash in south-western Amazonia, and soon the New Guinea highlands. Farmers are still a few in a hundred; the fall quickens only as their villages multiply, so the value lies between 98 at 9500 BCE and 92 at 7900 BCE.

Squash and maize in Mexico, millet in north China, manioc in Amazonia and the New Guinea highlands all begin about now, beside the Fertile Crescent's villages; the Holocene's warm, stable climate made cultivation possible in many places at once.
Pre-pottery Neolithic farming in the Fertile Crescent; early cultivation in China.

Rice in the Yangtze valley, Mehrgarh in Baluchistan and farmers leaving Anatolia for Europe: farming's area grows several-fold, and because farmers live far more densely, their share of people grows faster than their share of land.

Farming established in south-west Asia, Anatolia, the Yellow and Yangtze valleys and arriving in Greece; farmers already perhaps a quarter of all people because their densities were far higher. WaveOfAdvance#4cec for the spread into Europe.

Bantu-speaking farmers begin to move out of West Africa's borderlands, and rice and millet farmers and Austronesian seafarers reach South-east Asia: the last great farming expansions into lands held by foragers.

Maize becomes the eastern woodlands' staple and Polynesian farmers settle the eastern Pacific, while herders and farmers keep pressing into the remaining foragers' lands in Africa and northern Eurasia.
The boreal forest moves most with the glacial cycles: it shrinks to refugia south of the ice at glacial maxima and reaches beyond today's treeline in the warmest interglacials.
The MIS 8 glacial: ice covers much of the boreal range and the forest shrinks south of it.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: the boreal forest spreads north again.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) begins: the forest retreats before the ice.
The deepest MIS 6: the boreal forest at a glacial low, in refugia south of the ice.
Termination II under way: the ice melts and the forest follows it north.
The Last Interglacial: boreal forest reaches farther north than now.
The Last Interglacial has ended; the cold of MIS 5d pushes the treeline south.
MIS 5c, a warm substage: the forest spreads again.
MIS 5b, a cold substage: the forest retreats.
Glacial maximum: ice sheets cover most of the boreal forest's range in North America and Scandinavia, and steppe-tundra most of Siberia's; conifers survive south of the ice.
Rises most: the boreal forest follows the melting ice north.
The boreal forest follows the melting ice north: nearly all of the rise from the end of the Younger Dryas to the early Holocene's widest reach comes before here (the note at 7900 BCE).
The ice sheets are nearly gone and the early Holocene's summers are warmer than now: the boreal forest reaches its widest, beyond today's northern treeline.
The Neoglacial cooling pushes the northern treeline south from its mid-Holocene reach.
Logging and fire begin to cut into Scandinavia's, Russia's and Canada's boreal forests; most of it still stands.
About 27% of all forest in FAO's 2020 assessment as recalled; larger fires since 2000 in Siberia and Canada.
Termination II under way.
Turns down: farmers and herders clear the Mediterranean hills, the Ganges plain and southern China; goats and ploughs keep much of it open.
Southern China's rice frontier spreads under the Song.
Qing China's hill frontier: maize and sweet potato carry farmers up the forested hills of the south.
About 11% of all forest in FAO's 2020 assessment as recalled.
The MIS 8 glacial: temperate trees retreat to southern refugia.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: temperate forest spreads north.
Termination II under way: temperate trees spread out of their refugia.
The Last Interglacial: temperate forest reaches its widest, with hippos in the Thames.
The Last Interglacial has ended; MIS 5d's cold thins the temperate forest.
MIS 5c, a warm substage: temperate forest spreads again.
Glacial maximum: temperate trees survive in southern refugia, in Iberia, Italy, the Balkans, the Caucasus, southern China and the south-eastern United States.
Turns down for four thousand years: farmers clear Europe's and northern China's temperate forests.
Forest returns on abandoned land in the post-Roman West while clearing goes on in China; the world share holds.
The high-medieval clearances leave Europe's lowlands largely open.
Turns up briefly: forest returns on fields abandoned after the Black Death.
Europe's wood shortage and the colonists' clearing of eastern North America begin.
Settlers clear the forests of Ohio, Indiana and Upper Canada along the new canals.
Falls fastest in the nineteenth century: the clearing of the American Midwest's and Ontario's forests and of Russia's mixed forest.
Regrowth on abandoned farms in New England and planting in Europe begin about now, but clearing in China and the Soviet Union outweighs them for decades.
The world's temperate forest bottoms out about 1950 to 1976: regrowth in Europe and North America is offset by clearing in China and the Soviet Union until China's planting after 1978.
Turns up: the forest transition reaches China, whose planting from 1978 adds tens of millions of hectares, and continues in Europe and North America.
About 16% of all forest in FAO's 2020 assessment as recalled.
Split from the parent's forest share: in glacial times by how far each domain moves with the ice, tropical forest least; from about 4000 BCE by where people cleared.
The MIS 8 glacial: drier tropics shrink the rainforest a little.
MIS 7c, a warm and wet substage: the rainforest spreads.
Termination II under way: the tropics grow wetter.
The Last Interglacial: tropical forest at its widest, wetter than now in Africa's monsoon belt.

Glacial maximum: drier tropics shrink the rainforest, while the exposed Sunda shelf adds lowland forest. Whether Amazonia broke into refugia (Haffer) or stayed mostly forested (Colinvaux) is debated; the band holds both.

Turns up: fields and gardens of the Americas return to forest as most of their people die (the Great Dying); Koch and others put the regrowth at about 56 million hectares by 1600, and whether it drew down enough carbon to help cool the Little Ice Age is debated.
Turns down: plantations, railways and settlers begin clearing tropical forest in India, Java, Brazil's Atlantic forest and West Africa.
Falls fastest from here: roads, chainsaws, cattle, soy, oil palm and settlement programmes open Amazonia, Indonesia, the Congo basin and West Africa.
About 45% of all forest, about 1.8 billion hectares, in FAO's Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020 as recalled.
All of range is African: Homo sapiens from Jebel Irhoud to Florisbad, in patches between deserts and other hominins' lands, about half of Africa's land.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara hyperarid, people in the wetter east, south and coasts.
Termination II ends the penultimate glacial: the monsoon reaches the Sahara again and rivers and lakes open it, so Africa's part rises by half in a few thousand years.
The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes: Africa's part nearly doubles, close to the whole continent.
The glacial returns and the Sahara dries.
Holds while the dispersal fills Asia, Sahul and Europe: the dispersal added land elsewhere, it did not empty Africa.
The glacial maximum's aridity: the Sahara and the Kalahari spread, the rainforest shrinks to refuges.
The African Humid Period begins (from about 10,500 BCE): the first lakes and grass return to the Sahara before the Younger Dryas ends, and hunters follow them north.
The African Humid Period: lakes and grassland across the Sahara as far as Lake Mega-Chad, hunters and then cattle herders across it.
Africa's highest: almost all of its land within range.
The African Humid Period has ended: the herders withdraw to the Nile, the Sahel and the oases, and the Sahara's core empties, about 2.8 points of the world's land given up in a thousand years.
The camel spreads across the Sahara from about the first centuries CE and lets nomads use more of the desert between the oases.
Voyagers from Borneo have settled Madagascar, about 0.4 points of the world's land.
Motor tracks, oil and gas fields (Hassi Messaoud, 1956) and mines carry regular use into parts of the Sahara's core that only caravans had crossed.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Africa's land (about 30.3 million km2), the Sahara's green and dry phases, and the dated Events of the account; the Sahara's hyperarid core, about 2 to 3 points of the world's land, is outside range in dry phases.

points.note: Claims of people in the Americas before the glacial maximum (Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico, about 30,000 years ago) are debated; the band keeps them open.

The footprints at White Sands, New Mexico (about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago), put people south of the ice during the glacial maximum; the dates are debated but have held against two later tests. Their numbers and reach are unknown, so the part is small and the band wide.
The peopling of the Americas proper begins: a coastal route along the Pacific is open as the Cordilleran ice retreats from the coast.
Monte Verde in southern Chile (about 12,500 BCE) and the Paisley Caves in Oregon (about 12,300 BCE): people reach both ends of the hemisphere within a thousand years.
Clovis hunters spread across North America within about three centuries (from about 11,100 BCE), the fastest gain in range in the account.
Peopled to Tierra del Fuego; the Laurentide ice still covers much of Canada, and the Arctic islands and Greenland stay empty.
The Laurentide ice is almost gone and hunters follow the caribou north across Canada; the high Arctic and Greenland remain outside range.
The first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola, about 0.1 points of the world's land.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic to Greenland's ice-free coasts, about two points of the world's land that no one had lived on: the last large gain in range.

Unchanged: the Norse settlements of south-west Greenland (from 985) use a few tens of thousands of square kilometres, about 0.02 points, and Late Dorset people already hunt in the north-west; the Norse are gone by about 1450.
Polynesians settle Hawai'i (about 1000 to 1200), which by 2026 borders is part of the United States and so of this part; the Thule Inuit spread across the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland.
The epidemics after 1492 empty parts of the Americas for a time, the Mississippi and Amazon floodplains and the Caribbean's islands among them: the one area whose range falls in the historical era.
Weather stations, airfields and mines on Canada's Arctic islands (Resolute, 1947; Alert, 1950) and Greenland's bases bring the high Arctic's last empty land into regular use.
Nearly all the Americas' ice-free land: the Atacama's core and the emptiest Arctic islands are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from the Americas' ice-free land (about 38.7 million km2), the account's dated Events of their peopling (White Sands, Monte Verde, the Paisley Caves, Clovis, the Paleo-Inuit) and the epidemics after 1492.

points.note: The Misliya jaw (about 185,000 years ago) puts Homo sapiens in the Levant for a time: a first, small excursion out of Africa.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant (Skhul and Qafzeh) and greens Arabia's interior, where lakes and stone tools of African type appear.
The glacial returns: Arabia dries, and the Levant goes back to the Neanderthals by about 90,000 years ago.
A few groups hold on in Arabia's south and east (Jebel Faya); whether others reached India before Toba is debated.
The dispersal: people move along southern Asia from Arabia through India to Sunda within a few thousand years.
Eastern and central Asia are entered: north China, Mongolia's steppe, the Altai (where people meet the Denisovans) and the Tibetan margins.
The glacial maximum dries Central Asia and north China into desert and loess; people withdraw from the Mongolian plateau and the high steppe, while Sundaland's lowlands, then dry land, stay in range.
The early Holocene monsoon greens Arabia and the Thar again, and the steppe and north China are reoccupied.
Asia's highest before the modern era: Arabia's interior has lakes, hunters and then herders.
Arabia's humid phase has ended with Africa's: the Rub' al Khali and the Nafud empty, and herders keep to their edges and the oases.
Barley farmers and yak herders settle the high Tibetan plateau year round (from about 1600 BCE), while the drying of Central Asia's lowlands takes back about as much.
Oil camps and roads reach Arabia's interior and the Taklamakan's rim; the Rub' al Khali's core stays outside regular use.
About 86% of Asia's land in range; the empty quarter, the Taklamakan's core and the highest Tibetan and Karakoram ground are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Asia's land without Russia (about 31.5 million km2), the Levant's and Arabia's green phases, the dispersal's dates and the deserts and high plateaus that stay outside range.

points.note: A skull at Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) has been read as Homo sapiens, which would be a brief excursion; the reading is debated, and Europe is otherwise the Neanderthals' for another 160,000 years.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley (about 54,000 years ago) holds a Homo sapiens tooth between Neanderthal layers: a first, short-lived foothold.
Homo sapiens spreads from the Balkans (Bacho Kiro, about 45,000 years ago) across Europe and into western Siberia (Ust'-Ishim), meeting the last Neanderthals.
People live at the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and across the Russian plain: under M49 all of Russia is Europe, so Siberia's peopling is this part's.

The glacial maximum: ice covers Scandinavia and the north of Britain and Russia, polar desert spreads across Siberia's north, and people hold refuges in Iberia, southern France, Italy, the Balkans, the Russian plain's south and southern Siberia.
The Bølling warmth (from about 12,700 BCE): Magdalenian and Hamburgian hunters follow the reindeer north across Germany and Poland, and Siberia's north is reoccupied.
The Scandinavian ice has melted and hunters live in the north of Norway and Finland and on the Arctic coasts; Zhokhov Island in the New Siberian Islands is used about 6000 BCE.
Herders and hunters push into the drier steppe and the northern taiga: a quarter of a point over a millennium.
Iceland, settled from about 870, is mostly taken in by 900.
Norse settlers have made Iceland's ice-free land (about 0.07 points of the world's) part of range since about 870.
Russia's Arctic coasts and Kamchatka gain posts and hunting camps, and Svalbard's coasts hold whalers' and trappers' stations.
The Soviet Northern Sea Route, Gulag camps and mines (Vorkuta, Norilsk, Kolyma) bring the far north and Siberia's interior into regular use.
About 86% of Europe's land with Russia in range; the high Arctic islands' interiors and the emptiest tundra are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Europe's land with all of Russia (about 23.4 million km2), the dates of Homo sapiens' arrival, the ice sheets and polar deserts of the glacial maximum and the Arctic's late settlement.

points.note: Madjedbebe in northern Australia has been dated to about 65,000 years ago, which would put people in Sahul here; many read the site's layers as mixed and prefer about 50,000. The account follows the later date (ev.oc.sahul-arrival) and keeps the earlier one in the band.
People cross the Wallacean straits to Sahul, the longest sea crossings anyone had made, and land in New Guinea and northern Australia.
Within a few thousand years people live across Australia's coasts and rivers (Lake Mungo by about 42,000 years ago) and New Guinea's highlands.
Tasmania, then joined to the mainland, and the Bismarcks and Solomons of Near Oceania are reached.

The glacial maximum dries Australia's interior into dune fields: Aboriginal people withdraw to refuges on the coasts, the ranges and the rivers, giving up perhaps two fifths of the continent for several thousand years.
The interior is reoccupied as the climate eases; Tasmania is cut off by the rising sea about 12,000 years ago and stays inhabited.
Lapita voyagers reach Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa (about 1100 to 800 BCE), the first people in Remote Oceania.
East Polynesia's settlement, by the short chronology from about 900 to 1000, adds islands too small to show; New Zealand, about 0.2 points, is still empty until about 1280.
East Polynesia is settled from the Society Islands to Rapa Nui (about 1000 to 1200): many islands, little land.
East Polynesians settle Aotearoa (about 1280), the last large land on Earth to be peopled, about 0.2 points of the world's land.
The First Fleet (1788) brings settlers to land already within Aboriginal range: colonization changes who holds the land, not how much of it is held.
Unchanged since Aotearoa's settlement: every later change in Oceania (colonization, dispossession, the cities) is a change in who holds the land and how densely, not how much of it is held.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Oceania's land (about 8.5 million km2), the debated date of Sahul's peopling, the glacial maximum's desert refuges and the dates of Lapita's and the Polynesians' voyages.

points.note: Homo sapiens across Africa (Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Florisbad in the south, Omo in Ethiopia), but in patches between deserts and other hominins' lands: about a tenth of today's ice-free land, Africa being under a quarter of it.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and people hold the wetter east and south of Africa and its coasts.

The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes and opens the Levant and Arabia: the first time Homo sapiens holds land outside Africa for long (Skhul and Qafzeh). Range doubles in a few thousand years.
The glacial returns: the Sahara dries and the Levant goes back to the Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia.
The dispersal: people spread along southern Asia from Arabia to Sunda in a few thousand years, adding about seven million km2.

The largest gain in range in the account: in about ten thousand years people take in Sahul, Europe, eastern and northern Asia; WaveOfAdvance#4cec's fronts on land and long sea crossings to Sahul (the card's long-distance jumps) together.
People live as far north as the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and in Japan, Tibet's margins and Tasmania.

The glacial maximum begins: the ice sheets advance, the steppe of Siberia and the north European plain turn to polar desert and Australia's interior dries; people begin to withdraw to refuges in southern Europe, the Russian plain's south, the Altai and the Australian coasts, and range falls toward its glacial low of about a third of the land by 21,000 BCE.

Corrected from 50. The deglaciation begins to open the north: Magdalenian hunters spread from Iberia and southern France toward the Paris Basin and Germany, and Siberia's south is reoccupied. People are probably already south of the ice in the Americas (White Sands), but most of the Americas' peopling comes after 13,000 BCE (Monte Verde about 12,500 BCE, Clovis about 11,100 BCE). The earlier value read '14,500 years ago' as 14,500 BCE.
Corrected from 53, for the same reason as at -14600.
Corrected from 57. The Bølling warmth (from about 12,700 BCE) carries hunters north across Europe and the Russian plain; the Americas are entered along the Pacific coast and the ice-free corridor.
Corrected from 62: Monte Verde in Chile and the Paisley Caves in Oregon are occupied, but much of the Americas' interior is not yet reached.
Corrected from 66.
Corrected from 70. Clovis hunters spread across North America in a few centuries; the Younger Dryas (from about 10,950 BCE) brings the cold back to the north and dries the Sahara.

Corrected from 82. Late in the Younger Dryas: the Americas are peopled to Tierra del Fuego, but the Sahara is still dry and the north still cold; the Holocene's warmth and the African Humid Period lift range again from 9700 BCE.
Near its prehistoric peak: the Sahara and Arabia are grassland with lakes, hunters and then herders live across them, and the Laurentide ice is almost gone.
The Sahara's grasslands are already thinning at their edges; Varna's chiefs and the Balkan copper towns live inside a range that farming filled but did not widen.

Two moves nearly cancel: the first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola (about 0.1% of the land), while the African Humid Period ends and the Sahara's herders begin to withdraw to the Nile, the Sahel and the oases, the largest loss of range since the glacial maximum, played out over the next thousand years.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic to Greenland's ice-free coasts, adding about three million km2 of tundra no one had lived on.

Holds: the first millennium BCE adds no new land. The Axial age's schools and cities change how people think and live inside a range already near its Holocene extent; only the Paleo-Inuit's later Dorset phase and the herders' spread into the drier steppe move it by fractions.
Voyagers from Borneo have settled Madagascar (about 0.4% of the land), the last large uninhabited land of the Old World tropics.
Iceland is settled from about 870; East Polynesia's islands and the Norse fjords of Greenland (from 985) are tiny in the world's land, and gunpowder changes nothing here.
East Polynesians reach Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land to be peopled; Iceland (about 870) and the eastern Pacific islands came just before.
Dips a little: epidemics after 1492 leave parts of the Americas, the Mississippi and Amazon floodplains among them, all but empty for a time; the survivors' ranges still cover most of the land.

Weather stations, mines and bases on the high Arctic islands and the ice-free coasts of Antarctica add the last fractions; the empty cores of the Sahara, the Rub' al Khali and the Taklamakan remain outside regular use.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the archaeology and genomics of each region's first peopling and abandonments, as recalled (Africa's Middle Stone Age sites, the green Sahara corridors, the dispersal through Arabia and southern Asia, Sahul by about 50,000 years ago, Europe by 45,000, Arctic Siberia by 32,000, the Americas by about 16,000 at the latest, the glacial maximum's refuges, the Holocene Sahara and its desiccation, the Paleo-Inuit, Remote Oceania and Aotearoa), with the areas of regions and deserts. The boundary of 'regular use' is soft; the band carries it.

points.note: Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years old: the oldest Homo sapiens fossils yet found are in Northern Africa.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and Northern Africa's people shrink to the Nile and the coasts.
The Last Interglacial's monsoon greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes; people spread into it from the south and east (the green Sahara corridors).
The green Sahara at its widest: Northern Africa's share peaks before the drier phases after 115,000 years ago shrink it again.
The glacial maximum: the Sahara at its driest; people hold on along the Nile and the Maghreb's coasts (the Iberomaurusians).
The African Humid Period greens the Sahara with lakes and grassland from about 12,500 years ago; hunters and then herders spread into it.
The Sahara dries after about 3500 BCE and its herders crowd into the Nile valley, where Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.
Interpolated: the Nile valley fills as herders leave the drying Sahara, and its first states form before Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.

The Middle Kingdom reunites Egypt after the First Intermediate Period, a century of divided rule that came with the low Nile floods of the 4.2-kiloyear drought. How many died in it is unknown, and the series keeps a straight line through it.
Roman Egypt, perhaps four to seven million, and Roman Africa's grain lands: Northern Africa holds about two fifths of the continent's people.

Interpolated: the Arab conquest (640 to 709) brings Egypt and the Maghreb into the caliphate, while the Justinianic plague's returns (541 to about 750) keep the Mediterranean's numbers down, Egypt's among them.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Egypt's people, and its returns keep Egypt's numbers down for two centuries.
The low point: Egypt perhaps four million, after plague's returns and famine; the Maghreb about six.
Egypt's people double in the nineteenth century, with cotton and the end of plague, to about ten million.
Egypt passes 118 million; with Sudan and the Maghreb the region holds a third of a billion.
Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, about 230,000 years ago.
The dispersal out of Africa probably leaves from Eastern Africa, across the Bab el-Mandeb or the Sinai.
Aksum in the Ethiopian highlands; Bantu-speaking farmers reach the Great Lakes.
Great Zimbabwe and the Swahili coast's towns at their height.
Eastern Africa has become Sub-Saharan Africa's largest part as the Atlantic trade drains the west; the Indian Ocean and Red Sea trades take fewer.
The east African slave trade to Zanzibar's clove plantations and the Gulf peaks in the 1860s and 1870s.
The rinderpest panzootic from 1887 kills most cattle, and Ethiopia's great famine (1888 to 1892) perhaps a third of its people.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985 kills perhaps 400,000 to a million, a dent the region's growth fills within a year.
The Rwandan genocide (1994) kills perhaps 500,000 to 800,000.
Ethiopia passes 130 million, Tanzania 70, Kenya 57: Eastern Africa now holds about one person in sixteen.
Bantu-speaking farmers begin to move south and east from the Cameroon grassfields.
The Kingdom of Kongo forms on the lower Congo, about 1390.
West-Central Africa, Kongo and Angola above all, becomes the largest single source of the Atlantic slave trade, about 5.7 million of its 12.5 million.

The Congo Free State's regime of forced rubber collection (1885 to 1908), with sleeping sickness and smallpox: its losses are debated, from a few million to ten, and the region's share falls by a third in twenty years.
The low point: about 26 million, a share less than half of 1750's.
The Congo wars (1996 to 2003): their excess deaths are debated, from under a million to over five, most from hunger and disease.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo passes 110 million, with births above six per woman, the highest of any large country.
The south coast's shellfish and Pinnacle Point's ochre: a refuge through the penultimate glacial, on Marean's argument, one candidate for where the species weathered it.
Blombos Cave's engraved ochre and shell beads, Still Bay and Howiesons Poort.
Foragers only, while farmers elsewhere multiply: the San's share of humanity shrinks for ten thousand years.
Khoe herders with sheep have arrived; Bantu-speaking farmers follow within a few centuries.
Mapungubwe on the Limpopo, about 1220 to 1290, the first kingdom of the region.
Smallpox from the Cape (1713) devastates the Khoe; the Dutch colony grows slowly.
The wars and migrations of the Mfecane (about 1815 to 1840) on the highveld; their scale is debated.
The mineral revolution: diamonds at Kimberley (1867) and gold on the Witwatersrand (1886) draw migrants and settlers.
The peak share: AIDS cuts life expectancy in South Africa and Botswana by a decade or more in the 2000s, and births fall faster than elsewhere in Africa.
Pearl millet domesticated in the Sahel about 2500 BCE; yams and oil palm in the forest margins.
The Nok culture's iron and terracottas on the Jos plateau.
The empire of Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade; Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes.
The Mali empire at its height, Ife's and Benin's cities in the forest.
Interpolated: Benin under Ewuare and the rise of Songhay; Portuguese ships reach the coast from the 1440s, before the Atlantic slave trade grows.

The Bights of Benin and Biafra and the Gold Coast lose tens of thousands a year to the Atlantic trade: on Manning's estimates Western Africa's numbers stand still from about 1700 to 1850, while the rest of the world's grow.
The Nigerian civil war (1967 to 1970): perhaps one to two million Biafrans die, most of hunger.
Nigeria, about 230 million, is half of the region; Niger's births are the world's highest, near seven per woman.

Homo sapiens lives only in Africa; how it was spread across the continent is debated: an eastern or southern cradle, or a pan-African web of populations linked by migration, with Jebel Irhoud in the north among the oldest.
The penultimate glacial dries the Sahara: Northern Africa empties toward the coasts and the Nile.
The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara: Northern Africa's share rises to perhaps a sixth (the Aterian).
The low point: about 14 million south of the Sahara against about 9 million in Egypt, the Maghreb and Nubia, on recalled reconstructions.
Bantu-speaking farmers with iron have reached the far south-east, and Sub-Saharan Africa grows faster than the Mediterranean world in decline.
Untouched or barely touched by the Black Death, so its share rises as Eurasia's and Egypt's people fall; whether plague reached south of the Sahara is debated.
The Atlantic slave trade at its height, about 80,000 people a year carried off, most of them young adults, while Eurasia's numbers grow: the region's share falls for a century and a half.
The low point: conquest, rinderpest, sleeping sickness and the Congo Free State's regime cut numbers in the 1890s, while Europe and Asia grow.
Births still near five per woman while deaths have fallen: the region's share has more than doubled since 1950 and is now the world's fastest-growing (DemographicTransition#6e31).
Pinnacle Point's shellfish and ochre (ev.af.pinnacle-point): Homo sapiens lives only in Africa.
As the Last Interglacial opens the Levant, a small share of humanity lives beyond Africa (ev.era.last-interglacial).
Early ventures into the Levant (Misliya, Skhul, Qafzeh).
Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. Africa's share falls not because Africa's people fall but because those who left multiply in Asia (ev.era.dispersal).

Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. The dispersal's descendants fill Asia, reach Sahul and, from about 45,000 years ago, enter Europe, while Africa's own numbers grow slowly; Africa's share keeps falling though its people do not.
Durand's ranges and McEvedy's differ most for Africa: 10 to 19% in 1500.
Kept so the five shares sum to 100 at 1518.
Kept so the five shares sum to 100 at 1521.

Falls as the world's other peoples grow faster: the Atlantic trade carries its last great numbers to Brazil and Cuba, the East African trade to Zanzibar's plantations and Arabia grows, and Africa's own numbers grow slowly.
The Berlin Conference (ev.af.berlin-conference): the partition begins; the losses to conquest, rinderpest and famine come after it.
Homo sapiens reaches the steppe and its oases after the coasts, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago; Neanderthals and Denisovans were there before.

Homo sapiens spreads onto the steppe and into the oases of Central Asia after the southern coasts, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, meeting the Neanderthals and Denisovans already there; the share triples from a tiny base.
The cold, dry glacial maximum thins the steppe's people.
Farming reaches the foot of the Kopet Dag at Jeitun, about 6000 BCE.
The oasis towns of the Bactria-Margiana complex, and herders spreading over the steppe with horses and wagons.
Samanid Bukhara and Samarkand, among the richest oases of the Islamic world.
The Mongol destruction of Khwarazm's and Transoxiana's cities (1219 to 1221); some oases never regain their numbers.
The Black Death passes through the steppe on its way west.
Flat across the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933, which killed about one and a half to two million, some two fifths of the Kazakhs, and drove many into China.
The Virgin Lands campaign brings settlers to Kazakhstan, and high fertility in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
After the Soviet Union's end, Russians and Germans leave Kazakhstan by the million and births fall: the share dips.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Central Asia's part of it: the oases of Sogdiana, Bactria's north and Khwarazm, and the Kazakh steppe.

points.note: Zero on the usual account; the Fuyan Cave teeth, dated 80,000 to 120,000 years, would put a few Homo sapiens in south China already, a claim that is debated.
The dispersal along the southern coasts reaches Eastern Asia last of Asia's subregions; Tianyuan, near Beijing, is about 40,000 years old.
Millet farming in the Yellow River valley and rice in the Yangtze valley multiply Eastern Asia's people (Peiligang, Cishan, then Yangshao).
The low point of Eastern Asia's share before the Zhou states grow: Western Zhou China held perhaps 10 to 20 million, while India's Ganges valley and Western Asia's empires were as large.
The Han census of 2 CE counts 59.6 million registered people, about a quarter of humanity.

The Han collapse after the Yellow Turban rising (184): registered people fall from 56 million (157) to 16 million (280). Much of that fall is people lost to registration, not to death; how much is a debate, and this value takes a loss of about a sixth.
China reunited under the Sui, whose register of 609 counts about 46 million.

Tang China at its height, just before the An Lushan rebellion (755 to 763). The register of 754 counts about 53 million and that of 764 about 17 million. Most historians read the fall as a collapse of registration, with real losses of some millions; a minority reading, popular in lists of the deadliest wars, takes it as some 36 million dead. This series takes the first reading, so the share stays on its line to 770; the second would put a fall of several points here (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

Interpolated: the late Tang loses its hold, Huang Chao's rebellion (875 to 884) sacks Guangzhou and Chang'an, and the dynasty ends in 907; the Five Dynasties follow in the north until the Song reunite China from 960.
Song China passes 100 million with early-ripening rice, the densest farming the world had seen.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin and the Song (1211 to 1279): north China's registers fall by perhaps two thirds, and Eastern Asia's share by about seven points.
Rises only because Europe's and Western Asia's people fall in the Black Death.
Interpolated: late Ming China grows with the silver trade (from 1571) and Japan is unified by war; Japan's invasions of Korea (1592 to 1598) come after.
Late Ming China, perhaps 160 million, with New World crops beginning to spread.
The Ming-Qing transition: rebellion, conquest, famine and epidemics cut China's people by perhaps a sixth to a quarter between the 1620s and the 1650s, a loss whose size is debated.
Eastern Asia's peak share: Qing China near 380 million, more than a third of humanity, with Japan and Korea.
The Taiping war (1850 to 1864) and the Nian and Hui risings: China loses perhaps 20 to 30 million in war, famine and plague, and Eastern Asia's share falls four points in fifteen years.
Down again after the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, while Europe, the Americas and South-eastern Asia grow faster.

Interpolated, on the eve of the Great Leap Forward's famine. On the UN's estimates China's share of humanity peaks about 1958 and the famine of 1959 to 1961, 15 to 45 million dead on the debated counts, takes about half a point from it by 1961. This series shows the dip only faintly (26.85 at 1960 against 26.87 here), because Eastern Asia's subregion values are held to sum to Asia's and Asia's to the world's; a truer dip would raise this value by about 0.3 to 0.4 and needs Asia's and the other regions' 1958 values revised with it. Left for the next pass.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward (1959 to 1961) costs China 15 to 45 million deaths on the debated estimates; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Births fall first in Eastern Asia: Japan from the 1950s, then China's 'later, longer, fewer' campaign of the 1970s and the one-child policy from 1980 (DemographicTransition#6e31).
China's population has fallen since 2022; Eastern Asia's share is back to where it stood in the first millennium BCE.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Eastern Asia's part of it; China dominates the part at every date.

points.note: Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and the last Homo erectus live here; archaic humans are not counted.
The Lida Ajer teeth in Sumatra, about 73,000 to 63,000 years old, would put Homo sapiens here before the main dispersal; debated.
Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. The dispersal reaches South-east Asia on its way to Sahul, along coasts now drowned by the sea; the date is debated, as at Asia's value here.
At the glacial maximum the low sea exposes Sundaland, a warm lowland joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the mainland: a refuge, when the north was cold and dry.
The seas rise and begin to drown Sundaland; the region's share falls as its lowland shrinks.
Foragers still, while farmers multiply in Eastern and Southern Asia: rice farming arrives from the north only from about 2500 BCE, and the Austronesians reach the Philippines about 2200 BCE.

Interpolated: the Pyu cities and the isthmus ports trade with India and China, but the region's foragers and small farming chiefdoms grow more slowly than the Han and the Mauryan successor states, so its share falls.
The low point: perhaps five million, thinly spread through forest, with dense rice farming only in a few deltas and in northern Vietnam.
Anthony Reid's estimate of about 22 million for the region in 1600, as recalled.
Interpolated: Britain's first war in Burma opens the colonial century (ev.sea.era.colonial); the Java War and the Cultivation System follow, and the region's faster growth begins about 1850.

The turn: from here the region grows faster than the world for a century and a half, as Java's people multiply from under 5 million in 1815 to about 28 million in 1900 and the deltas of Burma, Siam and Cochinchina are cleared for rice.
Interpolated: the rice frontiers of the Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya and Mekong deltas open, and France begins its conquest of Indochina (1858); the region's growth outpaces the world's.
Japan invades (ev.sea.japanese-occupation). The region has grown a little faster than the world since 1936; from here its growth stops for four years.

The famine in northern Vietnam begins. Its dead are debated: about two million in Vietnamese accounts, about one million in some others. Hunger and forced labour in Java kill on a similar scale on some estimates, and the battle of Manila (February to March 1945) kills about 100,000 civilians; most of these deaths fall in the next eight months.
Flat through Japan's occupation: forced labour, the famine in northern Vietnam (about one to two million dead, 1944 to 1945) and hunger in Java hold the region's growth to nothing for four years.

Revised from 6.37, recorded earlier in this pass: the famine in northern Vietnam peaks in spring 1945 and the battle of Manila is fought in February and March, so at Japan's surrender the share is still at its wartime level. The August Revolution and Indonesia's proclamation open wars of independence (ev.sea.august-revolution, ev.as.indonesia-independence); the famines end, and the region grows again at about 2% a year against the world's 1 to 1.5%.
Revised from 6.43 with the value at 1945.63.

After the killings in Indonesia (ev.sea.indonesia-1965): about half a million dead, on estimates from 400,000 to a million or more, take about two hundredths of a point from the region's share, which its births keep rising.
Saigon falls and the Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh; the note at 1976 gives the scale of their effect on the share.

The fall of Saigon (1975), the Khmer Rouge's killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people (1975 to 1979) and the flight of the boat people: grave for the countries, a few hundredths of a point for the region's share, which keeps rising with Indonesia's and the Philippines' births.
The peak share: births have fallen to about replacement in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the share now eases.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times South-eastern Asia's part of it; from 1600 Reid's estimates for the region as recalled, and Java's nineteenth-century growth.

points.note: Tools at Jwalapuram lie beneath the Toba ash, about 74,000 years old; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated, so the share is small with a band to zero.
The dispersal out of Africa fills the subcontinent's coasts and river valleys; South Asia holds the largest share of the people outside Africa from now until farming.
Farming at Mehrgarh, on the edge of the Indus plain, from about 7000 BCE.
The Harappan cities at their height, perhaps five million people in the Indus valley.
Farming spreads through the Ganges valley with iron; Southern Asia becomes Asia's largest part for the next two thousand years on most reconstructions.

India's people in 1 CE are the widest debate in this series: McEvedy and Jones about 35 million, Maddison 75 million; this value takes about 60 million for the subcontinent, with Iran and Afghanistan about 7.
Rises as Eastern Asia's falls under the Mongol conquest, which reached Iran but held India only at its edge.
Mughal India grows while China falls in the Ming-Qing transition: for a few decades Southern Asia holds more of humanity than Eastern Asia.
Interpolated: the Mughal empire has broken into successor states; the Company's victory at Plassey (1757) comes two years later.
India grows more slowly than Qing China through the eighteenth century, after the Mughal break-up and the famine of 1770 in Bengal.
The famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 kill perhaps 12 to 30 million in British India, and plague arrives from 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills perhaps 12 to 17 million in India, its largest toll anywhere.
The Bengal famine of 1943 kills about two to three million, yet deaths are falling elsewhere in India and its share rises.
About 2001 Southern Asia's share passes Eastern Asia's, since its births fell later and more slowly; India itself passes China in 2023.
Close to its peak share: India's fertility is now below replacement, so Southern Asia's share levels off as Africa's keeps rising.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Southern Asia's part of it; the Indian subcontinent dominates the part, with Iran beside it.

points.note: The Misliya jaw, about 180,000 years old, is an early venture into the Levant that left no lasting population; counted as zero.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant and Arabia to Homo sapiens (Skhul and Qafzeh); for fifty thousand years all of Asia's people live here.
The glacial returns and the Levant's Homo sapiens give way to Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia (the Al Wusta finger bone, about 86,000 years old).
The glacial maximum dries Arabia and the Iranian plateau; Western Asia's people shrink into the Levant and the Zagros foothills.
The Natufians settle in villages in the Levant before farming.
The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent: Western Asia's share grows faster than any other region's for four thousand years.
The first cities of Mesopotamia (Uruk).
Western Asia's peak share, perhaps one in six of all people; from here it falls for four thousand years as farming spreads to larger lands.

Western Asia's people hold near 20 million through the Hellenistic and Roman-Parthian centuries while Han China, India and Mediterranean Europe grow, so its share falls by a third between 500 and 90 BCE.
Late Roman Anatolia and Syria and Sasanian Iraq at their fullest, before the plague of 541.
Iraq's irrigation decays after the ninth century, and Western Asia's share keeps falling.

Interpolated. The Mongols have beaten the Seljuks of Rum at Köse Dağ (1243) and overrun Armenia and Georgia, but most of the fall to 1300 comes after this date, with the sack of Baghdad (1258) and the wars between the Ilkhans and the Mamluks. The value is kept on the line between its neighbours so Asia's subregions still sum to Asia; the band holds the later timing.
The Mongols sack Baghdad (1258) and Iraq's canals are not rebuilt.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Syria's and Iraq's people.
The low point after the plague's returns and Timur's sacks of Baghdad and Damascus (1400 to 1401).
On the eve of the Armenian genocide and Gallipoli. Most of Western Asia's wartime losses, from massacre, deportation, war and the famine in Lebanon and Syria, come after this date.
The low point: war, the Armenian genocide, the Assyrian and Greek deportations and famine in Lebanon and Syria cost Anatolia and the Levant several million people from 1914 to 1922.
Rising fastest of Asia's parts: high fertility in Iraq and Yemen, and millions of workers drawn to the Gulf's oil states.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Western Asia's part of it, which holds all of Asia's people before the dispersal and the first farmers after it.

points.note: The Denisovans and other archaic humans are not counted; Homo sapiens has not yet left Africa for good.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant to Homo sapiens, Skhul and Qafzeh soon after (ev.era.last-interglacial); Misliya's earlier venture left no lasting population.
Between the Last Interglacial values on either side: Homo sapiens in the Levant and Arabia, all of Asia's people in Western Asia.
Toba erupts in Sumatra (ev.toba); whether it thinned the few Homo sapiens then in Asia is debated.
Between Toba and the dispersal; set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's interpolated value.

Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. The dispersal out of Africa (ev.era.dispersal): the ancestors of all living non-Africans leave Africa and spread along southern Asia, and their numbers grow fast in lands without other Homo sapiens, so Asia's share triples in a few thousand years. The date is debated: genomes put the main dispersal about 60,000 to 50,000 years ago, while finds in Arabia, the Levant and China suggest earlier, smaller exits from about 120,000 years ago that left little or no trace in living people (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). This series follows the genomic date.
Between -44000 and -37000, set so the regional shares sum to 100 with Africa's, Europe's and Oceania's interpolated values.
Farming in south-west Asia and China multiplies Asia's numbers first.

Interpolated, in the Axial age: the Buddha and Mahavira teach in the Ganges cities, the Achaemenid empire rules from the Indus to Egypt and attacks Greece, and Dong Son's bronze drums are cast; Asia's share edges up as the Ganges valley and China's warring states grow.
The Seljuks begin their conquest of Iran (1037). Through the eleventh century Song China's growth balances the easing shares of Southern and Western Asia, so Asia's share holds near 64%.
The Mongol conquests begin (ev.mongol-conquests); China's losses to them and to the Yuan collapse carry Asia's share down toward 1400.
Interpolated: the Mongols attack Dai Viet and sack Baghdad within months; most of Asia's fall from 1206 to 1300 comes from north China's losses.
China's own losses in the Yuan collapse bring Asia's share down after 1353.
Interpolated: the Portuguese take Malacca and the Safavids rule Iran; the Ottomans take Egypt in 1517. Asia's share edges up as the Americas' begins to fall.
Revised from 60.8 with the Americas' share, which no longer falls before smallpox reaches the mainland, so the five shares still sum to 100.
Rises only because the Americas' share falls, mid-epidemic in central Mexico.
Revised from 61.3 with the Americas' share, so the five shares still sum to 100. Rises only because the Americas' share falls.

Interpolated. Britain's first war in Burma and the Java War (some 200,000 Javanese dead) open the colonial century in South-east Asia. Asia's share eases because Europe's and the Americas' people grow faster, not because Asia's fall.

Interpolated. The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 kill perhaps 5 to 10 million in India and 9 to 13 million in north China on the usual estimates; Asia's share falls fastest in these decades, as Europe's and the Americas' people multiply while Asia's are cut back. The straight line spreads a loss that was concentrated in 1876 to 1879.
Asia's lowest share in two thousand years.

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor and its conquest of South-east Asia (ev.sea.japanese-occupation, ev.oc.pacific-war): Asia's share holds near 55% through the war. China's war dead and the famines of Henan (1942 to 1943), Bengal (1943), Java and northern Vietnam (1944 to 1945) are set against Europe's heavier losses for its size and Southern and Western Asia's growth; the share moves by hundredths, not points.

The fall of Saigon and the Khmer Rouge's victory. Their killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people, 1.5 to 2 million by 1979, takes about a twentieth of a point from Asia's share; Asia's births keep the share rising.
Vietnam takes Phnom Penh and ends the Khmer Rouge's rule, and China's war on Vietnam follows. Asia's share keeps rising: its deaths have fallen faster than its births.
The Indian Ocean tsunami kills about 230,000, a few thousandths of a point of humanity; Asia's share stands near its peak as births fall across East and South-east Asia.

Interpolated, in the pandemic: COVID-19's excess deaths fall on Asia roughly in proportion to its people, so they move its share little; India's own toll for 2020 and 2021 is debated, about 4.7 million on the WHO's estimate against about half a million officially counted. Asia's share keeps easing because its births fall while Africa's stay high.
India overtakes China as the most populous country (ev.as.india-most-populous); Asia's share keeps easing as Africa's grows.
The first Homo sapiens in Europe come in from the south-east: Bacho Kiro in Bulgaria about 46,000 years ago, Kostenki on the Don about 42,000.
The Gravettian mammoth hunters of Moravia and the Russian plain.
The glacial maximum empties the northern plain; people hold on in the Carpathian basin and the Ukrainian steppe.
The Cucuteni-Trypillia towns of Ukraine and Moldova, some of fifteen thousand people, the largest settlements in Europe.
Dacians, Thracians, Sarmatians, Balts and Slavs beyond Rome's frontier: about a fifth of Europe's people.
The Black Death strikes Eastern Europe less hard than the west and south; Poland is said to have escaped the worst of it.
Eastern Europe becomes Europe's largest part: Russia's peasants spread over the black-earth steppe and beyond the Volga.
Eastern Europe's peak share, more than a tenth of humanity, as the Russian Empire's births stay high while its deaths fall.
War, revolution, the civil war and the famine of 1921 cost the Russian lands perhaps 15 to 20 million lives between 1914 and 1922.
The Holodomor and the Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933 kill perhaps five to seven million, about four million of them in Ukraine.
The Second World War's deadliest ground: the Soviet Union loses about 27 million and Poland about six, Jews and others murdered in the Holocaust among them (ev.eu.eastern-front, ev.eu.holocaust).
After the Soviet Union's end births collapse and deaths rise among Russian and Ukrainian men: the region's numbers fall in absolute terms from 1993.
Russia's war on Ukraine from 2022 kills and scatters Ukraine's people; how many left Eastern Europe and how many remain in Poland and the rest of it is uncertain, so the band is wider.
Under the ice: Britain north of the Thames, Ireland and Scandinavia are covered or polar desert at the glacial maximum.
Hunters return to Britain and the Baltic as the ice retreats (the Creswellian and Hamburgian).
Doggerland drowns and Britain becomes an island, about 6500 BCE.
Foragers still, while farmers fill the Balkans and the Danube valley: the north's share of Europe falls until farming arrives about 4000 BCE.
Roman Britain at its fullest, perhaps two to three million.
The Viking age: raids and settlement in Britain, Ireland and Normandy move people within the region and out of it more than they change its share.
England near its medieval peak, perhaps four and a half to five million before the famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death kills perhaps four in ten in England and Scandinavia.
Britain's industrial towns grow fastest in Europe; Ireland loses a million to the famine of 1845 to 1852 and as many to emigration, yet the subregion's share rises.
Northern Europe's peak share: from here falling births and the emigration of Britons, Irish and Scandinavians overseas hold it back.
Immigration keeps the British and Nordic numbers growing while their births are below replacement.
Apidima in Greece, about 210,000 years old, may be an early Homo sapiens venture that left no descendants; counted as zero.
The glacial refuges of Iberia, Italy and the Balkans hold almost half of Europe's people at the glacial maximum.
Europe's first farmers arrive from Anatolia in Thessaly and Macedonia, about 6500 BCE, and spread along the Mediterranean coasts.

Minoan Crete at its height and the first Mycenaean shaft graves. The eruption of Thera is dated about 1600 BCE by radiocarbon and about 1500 BCE by the older archaeological chronology, a standing debate; it devastates Aegean coasts but leaves no mark on a share this coarse.
Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.
Interpolated: Rome expels its kings (509 BCE) and Cleisthenes' reforms follow at Athens (508 BCE); Greek cities and colonies keep growing.
Greek cities and colonies, Etruscan and Latin Italy, Phoenician and Iberian Spain.
Interpolated: after the Peloponnesian War and Alexander's conquests, which draw Greek settlers east, Rome unites Italy by 264 BCE; the Punic Wars follow.
Augustan Italy, Iberia and Greece: perhaps 15 million, almost half of Europe's people, the Roman Empire's heart.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), which struck the Mediterranean hardest.

Interpolated: the third-century crisis and the plague of Cyprian (249 to about 262) have lowered the Mediterranean's numbers; Constantine founds Constantinople (330), and the western empire's fall is still to come.
The western empire's fall: Italy's and Spain's cities shrink, and the Mediterranean loses its lead in Europe.
The Justinianic plague and the Gothic wars in Italy (535 to 554).
The Black Death kills perhaps half of Italy's and Spain's people in towns like Florence and Siena.
Plague in northern Italy (1629 to 1631) and Spain's seventeenth-century crisis.
Mass emigration from Italy, Spain and Portugal to the Americas holds the share nearly flat.
Italy and Spain now have the lowest births in the world, about 1.2 children per woman, and the Yugoslav wars (1991 to 1999) scatter the Balkans' people.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley may hold a brief Homo sapiens presence about 54,000 years ago, among Neanderthals; debated, and with no lasting population.
The Aurignacians of the Danube and the Swabian Jura, with the first figurines and flutes, and Chauvet's paintings about 36,000 years ago.
South-west France, the Franco-Cantabrian refuge, holds Western Europe's people at the glacial maximum; the north and the Alps are empty.
The Linear Pottery farmers spread from the Danube across the loess of Germany and northern France, about 5500 to 5000 BCE.
Celtic Gaul before Caesar's conquest, perhaps six to eight million.
Late Roman Gaul and the Rhineland, after the third-century crisis and before the Rhine frontier breaks at the end of 406.
The high-medieval clearing of forests in France and Germany: Western Europe becomes Europe's largest part.
France perhaps 17 to 20 million, the most populous kingdom in Christendom, before the great famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death (ev.black-death).
Interpolated: France's wars of religion (from 1562) and the Dutch revolt (from 1568) kill hundreds of thousands, yet Western Europe's numbers keep pace with the world's.

Interpolated: the Thirty Years' War begins (1618). Most of Germany's losses to war, plague and hunger, perhaps a third of its people, fall in the 1630s; the value is kept on the line between its neighbours so Europe's parts still sum to Europe, and the band holds a later fall.
The Thirty Years War (1618 to 1648) costs Germany perhaps a third of its people, in some regions more than half, to war, plague and hunger.
The French Revolution begins. France's births have begun to fall, and its wars from 1792 to 1815 kill about a million and a half French soldiers on most estimates, so Western Europe's share eases.
France's births begin to fall a century before the rest of Europe's, and Western Europe's share eases from here.

Interpolated: industry spreads from Britain to Belgium, northern France and the Rhineland, and the first factory laws pass; Western Europe's share holds while France's births stay low and Germany's rise.
The Western Front: France and Germany each lose more than a million and a half soldiers.
Some twelve million Germans expelled from the east arrive in the occupied zones, 1945 to 1950.
Immigration, the refugees of 2015 and of Ukraine since 2022 among them, keeps Germany's and France's numbers rising while their births stay low.
Neanderthals hold Europe; archaic humans are not counted, and Apidima's skull, if it is an early sapiens, left no lasting population.
Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) may be an early sapiens venture with no descendants; counted as zero.
Glacial maximum: retreat to southern refugia.
The Roman peak.
After the Antonine plague.
After the first wave of the Justinianic plague.
High-medieval growth: about 70 million.
The Black Death: from about 74 to 50 million.
Europe's peak share, a quarter of humanity.
The war's deadliest years in Europe, the Holocaust and the war in the east (ev.eu.holocaust, ev.eu.eastern-front): Europe's share falls by about a tenth of a point a year.
Europe's war dead and the expulsions after it lower its share.
The postwar boom begins. Europe's births rise in the baby boom, but deaths fall faster in Asia, Africa and Latin America, so Europe's share falls by about a quarter of a point a year.
Interpolated: Europe's share falls by about 0.16 points a year through the 1950s.
Zero: no people in Australia yet.
Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Begins: people cross the sea from Sunda to Sahul.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply, so the share falls.

The First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove. Aboriginal Australians perhaps 750,000, from 300,000 to over a million on the estimates; as a share of the parent this holds about 500,000, the gap being the parent's.
Falls: the smallpox of 1789 kills perhaps half the Eora around Sydney; whether it came from the First Fleet's stores or from Makassan trepangers in the north is debated.
Settlers pass 70,000 as the squatters' wool frontier opens, while smallpox (1789 and 1829 to 1831) and the frontier wars cut Aboriginal numbers.
About 405,000 settlers and convicts, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession.
Rises most: Victoria's gold rush more than doubles the settlers within a decade.
About 3.8 million at Federation (1901); the Immigration Restriction Act begins the White Australia policy.
About 8.2 million: postwar immigration and the baby boom begin to lift Australia's share.
The postwar migration programme brings Britons and the displaced of Europe ('populate or perish'); with the baby boom Australia grows faster than the world.
Australia's peak share since 1950, about 11.4 million: from here the world's growth, at its fastest ever, outpaces Australia's as births fall after the boom.
The White Australia policy ends (1973); migration from Asia grows, but slower intakes and falling births let the share ease.
The low point of Australia's share: from the mid-2000s the mining boom draws record immigration, and Australia again grows faster than the world.
About 27 million; about three in ten born overseas, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples 3.2% at the 2021 census.

upsert.reason: The whole of the parent before about 1280; after that the parent less New Zealand's part.

points.note: Zero: no people reach Aotearoa New Zealand before Polynesian voyagers about 1280.
Still empty. Radiocarbon dates on rat-gnawed seeds and the earliest sites put first settlement about 1250 to 1300; an older claim of about 800, from dates on rat bones, is now rejected.
Begins: Polynesian voyagers from the Society and Cook Islands settle Aotearoa about 1280, a founding population of perhaps a few hundred.
Grows fast on moa and seals, and on kumara where it will grow; the moa are gone by about 1450.
About 100,000 Maori at Cook's visits (1769) on the usual estimate, between perhaps 85,000 and 150,000; here the parent's share times that against Australia's numbers.
A larger share of the subregion as Aboriginal numbers fall; the Musket Wars among iwi armed with traded guns (about 1807 to 1845) kill perhaps 20,000.
The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and organized settlement begin; Maori perhaps 80,000 after the Musket Wars and new diseases.
Falls: Maori about 60,000, settlers about 25,000.
Rises most: Otago's gold rush from 1861 and assisted migration; settlers outnumber Maori from about 1858, and the New Zealand Wars (1845 to 1872) take Maori land.
Vogel's assisted immigration of the 1870s; Maori at their lowest, about 42,000 in 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills about 9,000, Maori at about seven times the settlers' rate.
New Zealand's peak share since 1950, about 2.6 million at the height of its baby boom and assisted migration; it falls from here as births drop and New Zealanders leave for Australia.
Falls: emigration to Australia after 1976, net losses in most years to 1990, and slowing births.
The low point: from 2014 net migration turns strongly positive, New Zealanders returning from Australia and arrivals from Asia, and the share rises.
About 5.3 million, a sixth of the subregion's people; Maori about a sixth of New Zealand's, Pasifika peoples about a twelfth.

upsert.reason: Zero before about 1280; then the parent times New Zealand's share of the subregion's people, wider before the censuses of the 1850s.

points.note: Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago (ev.oc.lake-mungo).
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off (ev.anz.tasmanian-isolation) and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply.

Interpolated. From about 4000 BCE backed blades, seed-grinding and new sites spread across mainland Australia and Pama-Nyungan languages spread from the Gulf country. Many read these as signs of more people, but the share still falls because farmers elsewhere multiply faster.
Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land reached by people.

The First Fleet (ev.oc.first-fleet). As a share of the parent's 0.2% this holds about 570,000 people, against the usual estimates of about 750,000 Aboriginal Australians (from 300,000 to over a million) and about 100,000 Maori; the gap is the parent's (h.region-oceania), whose early-modern level is debated, and the band now reaches the usual estimates.
About 470,000 settlers, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 and Maori to 60,000, from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession (ev.oc.depopulation).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) more than double Australia's settlers in a decade.
The sum of Australia (about 8.2 million) and New Zealand (about 1.9 million).
Assisted passages from Britain and the displaced of Europe: migration and the baby boom carry Australia's and New Zealand's share up while the world grows faster than ever.
The subregion's peak share since 1950: both lands' booms end, and from here the world outgrows them.
The low point: the mining boom's immigration into Australia and, from 2014, New Zealand's returning migrants lift the share again.
About 32.5 million; immigration, from Asia above all since the 1970s, carries most of the growth.

upsert.reason: Declared the sum of Australia and New Zealand, which share its unit and hold every person in the subregion once.

points.note: The Ivane valley in the highlands about 49,000 years ago, and the Bismarck islands by about 45,000 (ev.mel.ivane, ev.mel.near-oceania).
Gardens at Kuk Swamp: New Guinea's highlanders cultivate taro and bananas, one of the world's independent inventions of farming (ev.oc.new-guinea-farming).
Lapita potters in the Bismarck archipelago, about 1350 BCE (ev.oc.lapita).
The sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands from the Americas, and highland valleys grow dense (ev.mel.sweet-potato) (DensityRatchet#2ace).
Australia and New Zealand pass Melanesia, about 1868: for the first time since farming began, most of Oceania's people do not live in Melanesia.
Measles kills about a quarter of Fiji's people in 1875 (ev.mel.fiji-measles), and labour recruiting takes tens of thousands to Queensland and Fiji.
The highland valleys, with perhaps a million people, are first entered by outsiders in 1933 (ev.mel.highlands-contact).

Papua New Guinea's count is disputed: the UN's model gives about 10.5 million, while a 2021 study for the government suggested about 17, which would raise this share by half; the band reaches toward it.
Voyagers from the Philippines cross some 2,000 kilometres of open sea to the Marianas, about 1500 BCE, the longest sea crossing yet made (ev.mic.marianas).
Nan Madol on Pohnpei, the Saudeleur capital of basalt islets, at its height.
The Spanish-Chamorro wars and epidemics (1668 to 1695) cut the Marianas' people from perhaps 40,000 or more to under 5,000, too few to move the subregion's share by a thousandth.
Smallpox on Pohnpei (1854) kills perhaps half its people.
Japanese settlers in the South Seas Mandate outnumber the islanders by 1940; they are deported after 1945.
About 155,000: Guam with its American base, Kiribati, the Carolines, the Marshalls, the Marianas, Palau and Nauru.

Micronesia's peak share: high births on Kiribati and in the Federated States, and workers drawn to Guam and the Northern Marianas' garment factories; from the 1990s the compacts of free association let islanders move to the United States.
About 540,000 people; emigration to Guam, Hawai'i and the United States under the compacts of free association holds the numbers nearly flat as the world grows.
Lapita voyagers reach Tonga and Samoa, about 850 BCE (ev.pol.tonga-samoa-lapita); then the long pause of nearly two thousand years.
The voyages east begin: the Society Islands and the Marquesas are settled about 1000 to 1100 (ev.oc.polynesia-settlement).
Wallis (1767) and Cook (1769) at Tahiti: contact brings venereal disease, tuberculosis and dysentery.
The Marquesas lose perhaps nine in ten of their people in the nineteenth century, and Tahiti's fall to about a fifth of Cook's estimate (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The Peruvian slave raids of 1862 to 1863 carry off about 3,600 islanders, a third of Rapa Nui's people among them, and the smallpox of the few returned kills more (ev.pol.slave-raids).
The low point, about a third of the pre-contact numbers.
The influenza of 1918 kills about a fifth of Western Samoa's people (ev.pol.samoa-influenza) (Twinflow#9474).

About 240,000 in Samoa, Tonga, French Polynesia, American Samoa, the Cook Islands, Tuvalu, Wallis and Futuna and Niue: numbers have recovered from the low of about 1900 and grow fast with falling deaths.

Polynesia's peak share since contact: from the 1960s Samoans, Tongans and Cook Islanders leave in large numbers for New Zealand, the United States and Australia, so the islands grow slower than the world.
About 700,000 at home; more Samoans and Tongans now live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States than in their islands (ev.pol.diaspora).

Sahul before people on the later arrival, about 50,000 years ago; luminescence dates at Madjedebe of about 65,000 years would put people here already. The two accounts are debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Zero here takes the later arrival in Sahul (about 50,000 years); Madjedebe's 65,000 would make it positive.

Interpolated: Sahul's first people reach New Guinea's highlands (the Ivane valley) and Arnhem Land's ground-edge axes by about 49,000 years ago. When they first arrived is debated, about 65,000 years ago on Madjedebe's dates or about 50,000 on others; this series takes the later date, and the band carries both.
Sahul's first people spread across the continent and New Guinea (ev.oc.sahul-arrival, ev.oc.lake-mungo).
Interpolated: people reach Tasmania across the Bass Strait land bridge and the Bismarcks and Solomons by sea, and bury their dead at Lake Mungo; Sahul's share rises as its people fill the continent.
Sahul's people keep growing as they settle its margins and highlands after the megafauna are gone (ev.oc.megafauna-extinction).

Interpolated: Australia's mid-Holocene changes (new tools, Pama-Nyungan's spread, eel traps at Budj Bim) and New Guinea's gardens add people, but farmers elsewhere multiply faster, so Oceania's share keeps falling.

Interpolated: Lapita voyagers reach the Bismarcks and then Remote Oceania, and voyagers from Island South-east Asia settle Palau and the Marianas; new islands add people, but too few to turn the share.

The value stands but is debated: the usual pre-contact estimates (Aboriginal Australians from about 300,000 to over a million, Maori about 100,000, Melanesia one to two million, Polynesia and Micronesia some hundreds of thousands) sum to about 2 to 3.5 million, 0.4 to 0.7% of the world's people in 1500 and 0.25 to 0.35% in 1788, against this series' 0.2%, about 0.9 to 2 million (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). The band now carries both; moving the value needs Asia's and Europe's shares rebalanced with it.

The First Fleet lands at Sydney (ev.oc.first-fleet); smallpox and the frontier wars begin to cut Aboriginal numbers while settlers are still few. The usual pre-contact estimates would put Oceania at 0.25 to 0.35% here; the band carries them.
The Musket Wars begin in Aotearoa (1807) and Hawai'i's kapu falls (1819); Oceania's share holds near 0.2%, a level that is debated (see the note at 1500).
Before gold is found: about 2.5 million people in Oceania, some 0.47 million of them settlers in Australia and New Zealand and about 2 million islanders and first peoples.
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) nearly double Australia's settlers in four years.
Corrected from 0.2, which left the gold rushes out: settlers reach about 1.1 million against roughly 2 million first peoples and islanders.
Corrected from 0.2: Otago's rush (1861) adds New Zealand's settlers to Australia's.
Corrected from 0.2: about 1.6 million settlers.
Corrected from 0.22: about 1.9 million settlers, while the first peoples keep falling (ev.oc.depopulation).

Corrected from 0.3: about 3.8 million settlers after the 1880s boom and Western Australia's rush, on the way to the 0.4% of 1900. The few hundredths of a point come from Asia's and Europe's shares, within their bands, and are not rebalanced here.
About 12.7 million: the sum of Australia and New Zealand, Melanesia, Micronesia and Polynesia.
Oceania's share stands near its postwar high from 1965 to 1975: Australia's and New Zealand's immigration and baby booms keep pace with the world's fastest growth.

Oceania's low point after 1950: Australia's and New Zealand's births and intakes are low while Africa and South Asia grow fast; from the mid-2000s Australia's mining-boom immigration and Melanesia's growth lift the share.
About 46 million; the band reaches up for Papua New Guinea's disputed count.

changes.value: Fill, third batch of the 1820 to 1850 stretch: homicide and safety, politics, revenue, faiths, schooling, voice, standing, toil, literacy and numeracy, languages, discovery by area, energy and the number ever born, at 1830 and 1840 where they had nothing between 1820 and 1850. Wholes are set to the sum of their parts (the arts' makers, revenue, schooling, toil, discovery), energy for warmth to its parts plus food energy, and the eight faiths to 100. Safety's 1820 value is corrected from 16.5 to 17.5, the sum of homicide (10.5) and war (7) at that date; safety has no aggregate declared because war is averaged to the next date, so the report does not compare them.

points.note: Homo sapiens shares the Earth with about seven other kinds of human: the early Neanderthals in Europe, the Denisovans in Asia, Homo erectus in Java, the small hominins of Flores and Luzon, Homo naledi in southern Africa and the archaic people of Kabwe. Lineages known only from genomes (the 'ghost' archaics in West Africans' ancestry) are in the upper band.
Homo naledi's last known date is about 236,000 years ago.
The last Homo erectus, at Ngandong on the Solo River, dies out about 108,000 years ago as Java's open woodland turns to rainforest, before Homo sapiens arrives.
The Toba eruption (about 74,000 years ago) leaves no sign of ending any lineage: Neanderthals, Denisovans and the island hominins of Flores and Luzon all outlast it.
Homo floresiensis's last dates at Liang Bua and Homo luzonensis's at Callao Cave are about 50,000 years ago, close to Homo sapiens' arrival in Wallacea; whether the arrival ended them is debated.

Homo sapiens is the only human on Earth, on the latest reading of Denisovan admixture into Papuans (about 30,000 years ago); the Red Deer Cave people of southern China (about 14,000 years ago), once proposed as archaic, are now read as Homo sapiens, and stay in the upper band.
At the glacial maximum Homo sapiens is the only human on Earth; the upper band keeps open a late Denisovan population in New Guinea or Wallacea that the admixture dates allow.
No other kind of human is known to be alive as the glacial maximum begins.
The first Neanderthal recognized as another kind of human (the Feldhofer skeleton, 1856, named in 1864) changes what people know, not the count: the lineage ended about 40,000 years ago.
Homo sapiens alone; about 2% of the genome of every population outside Africa is Neanderthal, and up to about 5% of Papuans' and Aboriginal Australians' is Denisovan.

upsert.reason: Counted from the hominin fossil and genomic record as recalled: Homo naledi (335,000 to 236,000 years ago), Kabwe (about 300,000), Homo erectus at Ngandong (117,000 to 108,000, the last), Homo floresiensis (to about 50,000), Homo luzonensis (known 67,000 to 50,000; hominins on Luzon since 700,000), Neanderthals (to about 40,000) and Denisovans (admixture into Papuans as late as about 30,000 years ago on one reading). Sources to check: Berger and colleagues 2017 (eLife); Rizal and colleagues 2020 (Nature 577); Sutikna and colleagues 2016 (Nature 532); Détroit and colleagues 2019 (Nature 568); Higham and colleagues 2014 (Nature 512); Jacobs and colleagues 2019 (Cell 177).

points.note: Roman Italy perhaps a third enslaved; most of the world far less.
Serfdom loosening in western Europe after the plague and tightening in the east; slavery across the Islamic world, Africa and South-east Asia.
Enslavement in the Caribbean and the first Atlantic shipments of Africans add little at world scale yet.

Brazil's first sugar mills (from the 1530s) and the New Laws (1542) pull opposite ways, but at world scale neither moves the share: enslaved Native and African people in the Americas number a few hundred thousand, against tens of millions held in bondage across Eurasia and Africa, and the New Laws free some thousands in law while forced labour goes on under other names.
Brazil's sugar slavery grows and the first enslaved Africans reach Virginia (1619), while serfdom tightens in Russia and Poland; at world scale the share in bondage holds near 9%.

The sugar revolution begins in Barbados; Russia's Ulozhenie (1649) binds its peasants for good. Growth in Atlantic slavery and eastern serfdom is offset by a world population still recovering from the 1600s' crises.

The Atlantic slave trade near its peak, about 80,000 people a year, and serfdom extended to Ukraine (1783), while the American Revolution opens the age of revolutions whose language of liberty will be turned against slavery.

The enslaved of Saint-Domingue free themselves (1791 to 1793) and France abolishes slavery in 1794, while the cotton gin (1793) begins the expansion of slavery in the United States and the slave trade still runs near its peak.

Haiti's independence (1804) ends slavery for about half a million people, while Usman dan Fodio's jihad (from 1804) founds the Sokoto caliphate on plantation slavery; at world scale the share drifts down.

Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees about 800,000 people in the Caribbean, the Cape and Mauritius, and Spanish America's republics free theirs slowly by law; the world share keeps drifting down.
Russian serfdom ends in 1861, American slavery in 1865, Brazilian in 1888.
A year after Russia's emancipation; the United States still holds about four million in slavery.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs in 1861 (ev.russian-emancipation) and the United States about 4 million by 1865 (ev.us-civil-war): together about two points of humanity in six years.
Soviet collectivization and the camps of the Great Terror.
German, Japanese and Soviet forced labour at its height.
German and Japanese forced labour and the Soviet camps at their height.
The Axis camps are opened; the Soviet camps remain.
Mostly the Soviet camps and colonial forced labour.
London's Metropolitan Police (1829) and the new police of other European and American cities; homicide keeps its slow European fall while frontier and plantation societies stay violent.
Steady at world scale: rising rates in the United States and Latin America from the late 1960s are offset by falls elsewhere; the drug trade's violence grows only later.

The world rate stops falling in the early 1990s: Latin America's homicide epidemic (ev.lac.homicide), with Colombia near its peak and Brazil's rates rising, and Russia's killings after the Soviet collapse offset the long decline elsewhere.
No network exists: computers are single machines; ARPANET is twelve years away.
The integrated circuit is invented (1958 to 1959); no network yet.
Cheap smartphones and mobile data bring most of Asia and much of Africa online (ev.internet).
None before 1945.
Starts: three bombs built by August 1945, the test at Alamogordo and the two dropped on Japan; one or two more cores by the year's end (ev.nuclear-weapons).
The Soviet Union tests its first bomb (1949) and begins its stockpile.
