The arms race at its fastest: the American stockpile grows by several thousand a year (SecurityDilemma#a61b).
The peak: about 70,000 warheads, two thirds of them Soviet.
Falls: the INF treaty (1987) and then START cut the arsenals; tactical weapons are withdrawn as the Cold War ends.

A third fewer than in 1990: START I (signed 1991) cuts the strategic arsenals and both sides withdraw most tactical weapons, while the Soviet weapons in Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan are moved to Russia.
About 12,200 warheads in nine states, about nine in ten Russian or American; China's arsenal is the one growing fast.

Pigments ground at Olorgesailie and Kapthurin, about 300,000 years ago, may have coloured bodies or objects, but no lasting ornament or image of this age is known; how many populations made what has not survived is unknown.
Pierced shells at Bizmoune in Morocco (about 142,000 to 150,000 years ago), the oldest known ornaments; one site is a lower bound, not a census.
Blombos's ochre-mixing kit (about 100,000 years ago) and shell beads at Skhul, Qafzeh and in North Africa: lasting art is made in several regions, though the record holds only a handful of sites.
Blombos's beads and engraved ochre (about 75,000 years ago) and the Still Bay: in southern Africa ornament and image are made widely for a few thousand years.
The record flickers: the Still Bay's and Howiesons Poort's engraving come and go in southern Africa, as models of cultural loss in small, scattered populations predict (CumulativeCulture#4f93).

Ostrich-eggshell beads spread across eastern and southern Africa and the first known figurative painting is made in Sulawesi (at least 51,200 years ago): the share nears half as the dispersal carries the practice.
The Aurignacian ivories, flutes and Chauvet in Europe, hand stencils and animals in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo: most of humanity now lives in populations that make lasting art.
Sahul's people are drawing on rock by now (Nawarla Gabarnmang, about 28,000 years ago): one more continent's populations in the count.
Every living population makes lasting images and ornament, printed and plastic among them.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned from the dated sites, which are a lower bound on the practice, not a census of it (AbsenceEvidence#10a3). Three readings are argued and the bands hold all of them (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): a gradual emergence across Africa from about 300,000 years ago, thinly recorded (McBrearty and Brooks 2000), which would put the early values far too low; a late change in minds or society about 50,000 years ago (Klein), which would put them too high; and a demographic reading in which the practice is kept or lost with population density and connection (Powell, Shennan and Thomas 2009; CumulativeCulture#4f93), which predicts the flickering record of southern Africa. A distinguishing test: if density decides, the oldest ornaments should cluster where and when genomes and site counts show the densest Middle Stone Age populations.

points.note: Begins: musicians and jewellers who sell their work or play for hire in Mesopotamia's cities beside the temple and palace dependants.
Greek vase painters, sculptors and travelling poets and players sell to many buyers across the Mediterranean.
A tenth of all makers: Rome's actors, mimes, charioteers and copyists' workshops, and the entertainers of Han cities, paid by crowds and buyers.
Falls with the cities of the western empire and their theatres.
Rises with the Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds: about a sixth of all makers.
London's and Madrid's commercial theatres, Antwerp's and later Amsterdam's open picture market, printed books' authors and printed images: three makers in ten live from buyers and audiences.
Edo's and Osaka's kabuki and puppet theatres and the ukiyo-e print trade join Europe's markets.
Markets now keep more makers than patrons do: public concerts, publishers of music and novels, theatres run for profit.
The steam press, lithography and the subscription concert: novelists, illustrators and virtuosi live from sales and tickets.
Music halls, vaudeville, the illustrated press and the first professional sport.
Hollywood's studios, commercial radio's singers and bands, the record companies and sport as a profession: three quarters of all makers.
War takes performers into the forces and closes commercial theatres across occupied Europe and Asia.
Falls as a share while the communist states take their theatres, studios and troupes into public hands; it still keeps most makers.
Rises as the post-Soviet states and China's reformed troupes push makers onto the market.
The pandemic falls on market makers: closed venues and cancelled seasons cost freelance performers most of a year's work, while salaried public makers keep their posts.
About three quarters of all makers: the self-employed, the film, music, games and publishing industries and professional sport.

upsert.reason: The parent's value less the patrons' and public bodies' parts at each date: zero before about 2200 BCE, a few per cent in antiquity, a sixth in the Song cities, a third by 1650, most of all makers from about 1820, three quarters now.

points.note: Zero, as the parent: no forager band keeps anyone to make art.
If anyone was kept to carve Göbekli Tepe's pillars, it was by the leaders of the feasts that raised them: patrons, not buyers.
Chiefs keep the first craftsmen of fine things: Varna's goldsmiths, Ubaid's temple painters.
Every kept maker is a dependant of a temple or palace workshop in Sumer and Egypt.
Dips with the palaces of the Bronze Age collapse.

Near the level it keeps for the next seventeen centuries: the Han court's Music Bureau, Rome's imperial and senatorial households and the temples of every empire keep about 450 to 475 makers per million people.
Falls with Rome's western patrons; the Gupta, Sasanian and southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Its peak per person, barely above the first century's: the Mughal, Safavid, Ottoman and Ming ateliers and Europe's courts and churches.
Falling: the Revolution abolishes the court, confiscates the Church's lands and closes the chapels and choir schools that kept France's musicians, painters and sculptors.
Falls: the French Revolution ends the court's and the Church's patronage in France, and secularization strips German and Austrian monasteries and prince-bishops of theirs.
Britain's punitive expedition sacks Benin City and ends the royal guilds of casters and carvers.
On the eve of the February revolution, which ends the Russian court's and aristocracy's patronage.
The February revolution: the Imperial Theatres and the court's orchestras and choirs pass to the state, and the aristocracy's patronage ends with its estates.
The Russian, Austrian, German and Ottoman courts are gone; the Russian revolution ends aristocratic patronage across a sixth of the world's land.
India's princely states are merged into the republic (1947 to 1949) and their courts' musicians and painters lose their keepers.
About a twentieth of all makers: church musicians, royal and princely households, private patrons and foundations' commissions.

upsert.reason: The parent's value times the patrons' share: all of it until markets appear, nine tenths in antiquity, three quarters in 1500, half by 1800, a tenth by 1950, a twentieth now.

points.note: Begins: the Greek cities' civic festivals pay poets, choruses, musicians and sculptors from public funds and liturgies.
Cleisthenes' reforms: Athens's City Dionysia, whose tragic contests began about 534 BCE, is paid for by the city and its liturgies.
Rome's public games and theatres, paid partly from the treasury, partly by magistrates who count as patrons here.
The western cities' public games and theatres close.
Town musicians and civic painters of Europe's and Asia's self-governing cities: a fiftieth of all makers.
Court theatres begin to become national ones (Vienna's Burgtheater, 1776) and academies take state salaries.
The republic's festivals, the Conservatoire (1795) and the Louvre's public museum (1793) keep some makers on public funds.
Germany's and Austria's municipal theatres and orchestras, Europe's conservatories and academies: about a sixteenth of all makers.
Rises: the Soviet state takes the theatres, conservatories and studios into public hands (1919), and Germany's and Austria's court theatres become state theatres.
The New Deal's Federal Art, Music, Theatre and Writers' Projects employ about 40,000 makers (1935 to 1939), and the Soviet and fascist states' arts administrations grow.
Jumps: Eastern Europe's new regimes and the People's Republic of China (1949) take theatres, studios and troupes into public hands, and Western Europe's arts councils and public broadcasters grow.
Near its peak share, three tenths of all makers: China's thousands of state troupes, the Soviet bloc's theatres, studios and artists' unions, and Europe's subsidized stages and broadcasters.
The Cultural Revolution disbands or purges China's troupes and sends their members to the countryside, leaving the eight model works.
The Soviet Union's breakup ends the union-wide state system of theatres, studios, conservatories and creative unions; budgets collapse in the 1990s.
Falls: the Soviet system's end cuts state theatres, studios and unions across Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, and China begins to turn its troupes into enterprises.
Holds through the pandemic: salaried makers of state theatres, orchestras and broadcasters keep their posts while freelance performers lose their work.
About a sixth of all makers: public broadcasters, state and municipal theatres, orchestras and troupes, most of them in Europe and East Asia.

upsert.reason: The parent's value times the public bodies' share: none before the Greek cities' festivals, a few per cent until 1900, a tenth by 1930, a quarter to three tenths from 1950 to 1990, under a fifth now.

points.note: Zero by the measure's definition: no forager band keeps anyone to make art. The beads, engravings and paintings of the Stone Age were made by people whose main work was getting food.
Sunghir's burials, with thousands of ivory beads that took thousands of hours to make, show great effort spent on ornament, but nothing shows anyone kept for the work.

Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars (from about 9500 BCE) are raised by foragers' communal labour, perhaps with a few carvers who did little else; whether anyone was kept for the work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Chiefdoms begin to keep craftsmen: the goldsmiths behind Varna's graves (about 4500 BCE), the builders and painters of Ubaid Mesopotamia's temples.
The temple and palace workshops of Sumer and Egypt keep the first full-time sculptors, painters, musicians and goldsmiths; perhaps a fifth of humanity now lives under such courts.
Minoan Crete's palaces keep fresco painters, seal-cutters and goldsmiths beside Egypt's and Mesopotamia's workshops.
Olmec rulers at San Lorenzo keep the sculptors of the colossal heads: makers of art are now kept in the Americas too.
The tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, the Shang bronze-casters, the palace painters of Crete and the Olmec sculptors: courts on three continents now keep makers of art.
Greek cities' festivals keep poets, actors and sculptors, and the Persian, Indian and Chinese courts their musicians and craftsmen.

Rome's theatres, games and workshops and the Han court's Music Bureau, about 800 musicians before 7 BCE: a few makers in every thousand people of the great cities, about one in two thousand people worldwide.
Gupta India's court poets, dramatists and temple sculptors (Kalidasa wrote about 400) rise as Rome's western patrons fail.
Falls with Rome in the west: theatres, games and the patrons who paid for them close; Gupta India, Sasanian Iran and the southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds, beside the courts of the Abbasids, the Fatimids and Heian Japan.
The Black Death and the Mongol wars kill makers and patrons alike.
The workshops of Italy and the Netherlands, the Mughal and Safavid ateliers, Ming porcelain and printed images: art is made for markets as well as for patrons.
Between 1789 and 1800 on the line; inside it the Revolution moves makers from the court and the Church to the market and the new state's festivals.
Theatres, music halls, the illustrated press and the publishers' authors grow with the cities of the industrial world.
Cinema: the picture houses' actors and pit musicians, and the first professional footballers and boxers.
Hollywood's studios, radio's orchestras and singers, and sport as a profession.
War takes performers into the forces and closes theatres in occupied Europe and Asia.
The pandemic closes theatres, concert halls and stadiums; live performers lose most of a year's work.
About twenty million people of some 3.6 billion workers: artists, musicians, actors, writers, dancers, players of sport and makers of art wares.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned: zero among foragers by definition; a few hundred per million under the agrarian states' courts and temples, bounded by the surplus that keeps them (SurplusBound#7fe3); a few thousand per million now. The 2025 value rests on the recalled count of about 30 million jobs in the cultural and creative industries in 2013 (UNESCO and EY), of which the makers themselves are perhaps two thirds; to be checked. Where the line falls between a maker of art wares and a maker of ordinary goods moves every value before 1900 by a factor of two either way.

points.note: Wartime hours (h.toil) cut leisure in the belligerents.
Uruk-period polities, if counted as states.
The Han and Roman empires at their height, with the Parthians, Kushans and Satavahanas, hold most of the world's people; the share falls only as the Han breaks up after 184.
The southern Maya kingdoms fail while new states form in South-east Asia (Angkor, 802) and the Abbasid and Carolingian realms hold; the share barely moves.

The Tang and Abbasid realms fragment but their people stay under states; the southern Maya kingdoms fail; Polynesians settle eastern islands without states. The share under a state barely moves between 770 and 1000.
The Triple Alliance forms in the valley of Mexico; the Ming, Timurid and Ottoman states hold most of Asia's people.
Pachacuti begins the Inca conquests: within a century about ten million Andean people come under one state.
Band corrected: the earlier band ran to 108%, above what a share can be.

Leahy's and Taylor's patrol into the Wahgi (1933) finds about a million highlanders, some 0.05% of humanity, who come under the Australian administration over the next two decades; Japan's conquest of Manchuria (1931) changes which state rules, not whether one does.
Band corrected: the earlier band ran to 109%.
Band corrected: the earlier band ran to 104%.
Band corrected: the earlier band ran to 105%.
Band corrected: the earlier band ran to 105%.
Starts: some 300,000 people in forager bands of about 35, each answering to no one; the band size and the population are both uncertain by a factor of several.
Falls a little with people in the deepest part of the penultimate glacial.
Flat through the Last Glacial Maximum: no more people, so no more bands.
At the Holocene's start, about 130,000 bands: the number of autonomous units grows with people for as long as everyone lives in bands.
Farming multiplies people faster than it enlarges their units: autonomous villages of a hundred or two join the bands, and the count passes a third of a million.

Peaks in the late Bronze Age at about three quarters of a million: states hold a quarter of humanity, but the people outside them, in bands, villages and chiefdoms, are still most and still growing. Carneiro's order of magnitude, about 600,000 in 1000 BCE, lies inside the band.
Falls: the Han, Roman, Parthian and Kushan empires hold six in ten people, and the units left outside them are larger chiefdoms and tribes.
Falls by a quarter: the Black Death and the Mongol and Timurid wars cut people while states (Ming, Ottoman, Vijayanagara, Mali, the Aztec and Inca beginnings) hold three in four of those left.
Falls: the Americas' chiefdoms and villages die with their people after 1492 or come under Spain and Portugal, and Russia's conquest of Siberia reaches the Pacific (1639).

Falls fast: the Scramble for Africa, the conquests of the American West, Patagonia and Siberia's last peoples, and the Dutch, British and French advance in South-east Asia bring hundreds of thousands of stateless villages and bands under states between 1870 and 1900.

Set directly from here on: what remains outside states is the New Guinea highlands' clans (perhaps a million people), the Amazon's villages, interior Borneo, the Sahara's and Arabia's tribes and the Afghan frontier; the model's share under a state (98%) would leave twice as many people outside states, a tension to resolve in a later pass.

The highland patrols begin to bring the clans of the Wahgi and neighbouring valleys, several thousand autonomous groups, under one administration; the count falls fastest in New Guinea through the 1930s.
Patrols and gold prospectors reach the New Guinea highlands' valleys (the Wahgi, 1933), whose clans had been the largest population on Earth outside any state.
Postwar patrols and missions in New Guinea, the Amazon and Borneo bring most remaining groups under some administration; the count of all autonomous units falls toward that of states.
States now make up half or more of all autonomous units; the rest are uncontacted groups in Amazonia, western New Guinea and the Andamans, perhaps a hundred or two.
Rises: the Soviet Union's breakup makes fifteen states of one, and Yugoslavia's four more.

About 197 states, recognized or not, and perhaps a hundred uncontacted peoples who answer to no state in practice; whether those count as autonomous polities is a matter of definition the band carries.

The Roman world's own cults, counted here, still hold almost all of its people.
The empire's temples lose most of their people between Constantine (312) and Theodosius's ban on sacrifice (391).
The Greco-Roman cults have given way to Christianity (h.religion-4); local traditions are now those of sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas, northern Europe, the steppe, Arabia and the islands.
Rises a little to 1400 as the Black Death and the Mongol wars shrink Eurasia's people while the Americas and Africa, where local traditions hold, are spared.
Local traditions lose most in the Americas, where their people die and the survivors are baptized.
The first Protestant missions land on Tahiti (1797); the conversions of the Pacific that follow move well under a tenth of a point of humanity, so the share keeps its slow drift.

The first Vedic communities in the Punjab.
The Upanishads (ev.as.upanishads) and the Vedic religion of the Ganges plain.
Brahmanical religion spreads through the Ganges plain and south India after the Mauryas, as South Asia's share of humanity grows.
Holds: Theravada displaces the Hindu court cults of the mainland, from Pagan to Angkor, but those courts' followers are a fraction of a point of humanity beside India's own people.
The Buddha's teaching begins in the Ganges plain (ev.as.sramana).
The Buddha's own lifetime.
Ashoka's accession (ev.as.ashoka): Buddhism is still a minority movement of the Ganges plain; his patronage carries it across India and beyond.
After Ashoka; spreading to Central Asia.
Buddhism reaches China, by tradition under Emperor Ming (ev.as.buddhism-east).
Falls slowly: Buddhism's decline in India outweighs Theravada's spread across the mainland's villages from Pagan.

No Christians yet: Jesus's movement begins about 30 (ev.christianity-rise).
About 200,000 Christians in the Roman Empire by Hopkins's and Stark's reconstructions, near 0.1% of humanity; the upper band keeps the higher line of the World Christian Database.

After Constantine's conversion (312) the churches grow fastest: Stark's model has about 34 million Christians in 350, more than half the empire, from about 6 million in 300. Faster growth after 312 than before (MacMullen) and Stark's steady 40% a decade give similar values here.

Most of the Roman world has become Christian since Constantine (312) and Theodosius (380), with Armenia, Georgia, Aksum and the Church of the East in Persia: about a fifth of humanity. Stark's model has 34 million Christians already by 350; the World Christian Database about 22% at 500.
Nubia converts (540s to 570s), but the Justinianic plague (from 541) falls hardest on the Christian Mediterranean: the share holds.

The Arab conquests put Syria, Egypt, North Africa and Spain under Muslim rule, but their Christians convert to Islam only slowly over the next three centuries (Bulliet), so the share falls little yet.
Conversion to Islam in Egypt, Syria, Iraq and al-Andalus, fastest in the ninth and tenth centuries, takes the share to its low.
Latin Europe's people grow faster than the world's, and the north is now baptized.
The Church of the East in Asia shrinks after the Mongol conversions to Islam; the Black Death (1347 to 1351) falls hardest on Europe, so the share falls to 17% by 1400.
The Reformation (1517) divides Western Christianity without changing its share.
Revolutionary France's dechristianization (1793 to 1794) is reversed within a decade and the Pacific missions begin (1797); the Christian share holds near 22%.
Christians grow fastest of the faiths: Europe's and the Americas' populations outgrow Asia's, and the Second Great Awakening and the missionary societies spread churches on the frontiers.
Muhammad's first revelation, by tradition in 610 (ev.islam-rise): the Muslim community is a few followers in Mecca.
The caliphate's subjects were mostly not yet Muslim; conversion ran over the next three centuries.
Israelite religion and Zoroastrianism (ev.as.israel-bible, ev.as.zoroastrianism) separate from the local traditions they grew out of.
Zoroastrianism becomes the Achaemenid court's religion and Judaism takes its lasting shape in the Babylonian exile and return (ev.as.zoroastrianism, ev.as.israel-bible).
Jews of Judah and the diaspora, and Zoroastrians under the Achaemenids. The anchor of 0 at -1000 leaves Israelite religion among local traditions, a choice that could be revisited.
The Jewish diaspora spreads across the Hellenistic and Roman world, and Zoroastrianism holds Parthian Iran (ev.as.parthia).
Christianity absorbs much of the Roman world's Jewish and pagan population (ev.christianity-rise), and Buddhism and Christianity grow faster than Judaism and Zoroastrianism.
Jews expelled from Spain (1492) and Portugal (1496) move within the world, not out of their faith; Guru Nanak's teaching begins about 1499. The share holds.
Before most of the Holocaust's killing (ev.eu.holocaust).

By early 1943 most of the Holocaust's victims are dead: the death camps of Operation Reinhard and the shootings in the east killed most of them in 1942 (ev.eu.holocaust), so the Jewish share is already near its 1944 low.
By 1944 about five of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust are dead (ev.eu.holocaust): the Jewish share of humanity falls from about 0.7% to under 0.5%.

Revised from 1.95: the series did not subtract the Holocaust's six million dead, about a quarter of a point of humanity, which its own note recorded. The other seven shares rise in proportion by less than their rounding.

The Russian revolution (ev.eu.russian-revolution); state atheism follows from 1918.
The People's Republic is proclaimed (ev.as.prc); its campaigns against religion follow.
Zero: no states.
Tolls on goods moving through the first states: a twentieth of their revenue.
Han China's salt and iron monopolies, from 117 BCE, and Rome's harbour and frontier duties.
After the An Lushan rebellion the Tang raise about half their cash revenue from the salt monopoly.
Song China's commercial taxes and monopolies of salt, tea and wine pass its land tax: the first state to live mostly on goods.
Below the Song's height after the Mongol conquest of China.

England's excise state after 1688: by 1750 customs and excise are about three quarters of British revenue (Brewer's fiscal-military state). War between the European powers rewarded the states that could raise more (Warsift#b01b).
Customs and excise carry the nineteenth-century states (the United States lived on its tariff until 1913); the Qing add the lijin transit tax from 1853.
The Soviet turnover tax, levied on goods, pays most of a state that takes about a third of its economy's output.
Value-added tax spreads across Europe after 1967 from France's of 1954, and later to most of the world.
About three tenths of revenue, more in poorer countries, which lean on VAT and customs.
Zero until Britain's income tax of 1799: earlier levies on movables and tithes on produce are counted with land and goods.
Pitt's income tax, 1799, to pay for the war with revolutionary France.
Britain repeals its income tax in 1816: back to about zero.
Peel brings Britain's income tax back in 1842.
The Union's income tax of 1862, for the Civil War.
The American wartime income tax lapses (1872).
Prussia's income tax of 1891 and Bismarck's social insurance from 1883; Japan's income tax of 1887.

About a tenth of all years of school; women now outnumber men in higher education in most countries.

Rectangular mud-brick houses of the first farmers; at Catalhoyuk a main room of about 25 m² with storerooms for a household of five to eight.

Greek houses of the eighth century BCE have a median floor of about 45 m²; by the fourth century several times that (Morris's house-size series), a rise that was not general across the agrarian world.
Crowded insulae in Rome and the cities beside large peasant and villa houses; Han Chinese farmhouses of a few rooms.
After Rome's fall houses in the West are smaller and of timber; whether the world average fell is unknown.
Turns up: the Black Death leaves the same houses to fewer people.
After the plagues, peasants in western Europe and the Near East have more room and better houses, as wages are high.
Turns down: the industrial cities pack workers into cellars, courts and back-to-backs at a few square metres each.
Turns down: bombing and fighting destroy a fifth of Germany's dwellings, much of Japan's cities and of the western Soviet Union; tens of millions are homeless.
The bombing of Germany and Japan and the fighting in the Philippines and Europe destroy dwellings faster than any are built; the GI Bill's houses come after the war.
Turns up for good: mass housing in Europe, the Soviet Union and Japan, suburbs in North America.
China's housing reform of 1998 starts the largest building boom in history: urban floor space per person there rises from about 8 m² in 1978 to near 40 m² by 2020.

The world's buildings hold about 240 billion m² of floor, roughly three quarters of it dwellings (UN Environment's Global Status Reports for Buildings and Construction, as recalled): about 22 m² a person, from over 60 in the United States to under 10 in much of Africa and South Asia.

upsert.reason: Sketched from house floors in the archaeological record and household sizes before 1950, and from housing statistics and the global buildings floor-area estimates after; the band is wide because no one has summed dwelling space for the world before the late twentieth century.

The war sends the United States' chemists and physicists into war research and leaves it a National Research Council; American industry's laboratories (General Electric, Bell, DuPont) grow fastest of any.

Europe's and Japan's science lies in ruins while the American wartime laboratories stand: the Americas' share of the world's researchers jumps to about two fifths, and German and other European scientists come west.
Flat as a share of humanity's researchers falls: the United States' research staff grows slowly after 2000 while China's triples.

points.note: Uruk's temple scribes, the first people who may have kept records and calendars as their main work.
Babylon's astronomical diaries, Ionia's natural philosophers (Miletus is in Türkiye, so Asia's), the Hundred Schools and India's grammarians: Asia holds about two thirds of the world's inquiry.
Holds while the west's schools close: Aryabhata (499), China's astronomical bureau and Constantinople's scholars carry on, so Asia's share rises to three quarters.
Baghdad's House of Wisdom and its successors, Bukhara (Ibn Sina), al-Biruni, and Song China's bureaus and academies.
The Mongol conquest destroys Baghdad (1258) but its khans found the Maragha observatory (1259): Asia's part falls, Europe's grows.
Meiji Japan's Imperial University (1877) and its institutes make Japan Asia's first modern research system.

Asia passes Europe and becomes the area with the most researchers, as China's research staff triples between 1996 and 2010.
About 5.7 million, nearly half the world's researchers: China most of all, then Japan, Korea and India.

Caliphal Córdoba's astronomers and physicians (Spain, so Europe's) and the first cathedral schools.
Toledo's translators carry Arabic and Greek science into Latin.
Europe passes Asia in people kept for inquiry, as printing and the universities multiply and the scientific revolution begins (Copernicus, Vesalius, 1543).
The research university spreads from Humboldt's Berlin (1810): Liebig's teaching laboratory at Giessen (1826) trains chemists by research, and Faraday works at the Royal Institution.
Germany's universities and chemical firms, France's grandes écoles and Britain's laboratories hold about seven in ten of the world's researchers.

About three million, a quarter of the world's: the European Union's two million, Britain's, Russia's and the rest.

points.note: No forager makes inquiry their main work: zero by the measure's definition, not a judgment that foragers learned nothing new. Most of what people discovered for 300,000 years was found by people whose main work was something else.
The first temple scribes of Uruk keep accounts and calendars; whether any had inquiry as their main work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Rising toward the Axial age: Assyria's and Babylon's scholars, Egypt's temple priests, and the first Greek and Indian thinkers who make inquiry their work.

Babylon's astronomers keep their diaries of the sky, Ionia's philosophers argue about nature, the Hundred Schools teach in China and India's grammarians and physicians write: a few hundred people in a world of 160 million.
The Museum of Alexandria (from about 280 BCE) pays perhaps a hundred scholars at a time, the first institution kept for inquiry; with Babylon, Han China and India, about one person in a million.
Falls: the western schools close with Rome's fall in the west, while India's astronomers (Aryabhata, 499) and China's carry on with fewer patrons.
Rises with the patrons: Baghdad's House of Wisdom and its astronomers, Cordoba, Cairo and Song China's bureaus keep several hundred scholars between them.
Bologna's law school (from 1088), then Paris and Oxford, begin the universities; for a century they teach far more than they discover, so the measure barely moves.

The Royal Society (1660) and the Académie des sciences (1666) give natural philosophy members and journals; perhaps two thousand people in Europe, the Ottoman world, India, China and Japan make inquiry their main work.

The research university (Berlin's model, from 1810) and the industrial laboratory (Edison's, 1876; the German chemical firms') make research a paid profession: some fifty thousand people, doubling about every fifteen years, as Price measured the growth of science.

The First World War brings chemists, physicists and engineers into war research (gas, sound-ranging, aircraft) and leaves states with research councils (Britain's in 1916, the United States' National Research Council in 1916).

War research at its height: the Manhattan Project employs some 130,000 people (most of them builders and operators, not researchers), radar laboratories such as MIT's Radiation Laboratory several thousand scientists, and Germany, Britain, the Soviet Union and Japan their own programmes.
War research (radar, the bomb, penicillin) leaves states paying for science: the United States, the Soviet Union and Europe hold about half a million researchers between them.

The International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958) puts some 60,000 scientists from 67 countries into one programme; Sputnik (October 1957) sets off the United States' National Defense Education Act and NASA, and research staff grow fastest of any time.
Rises little in the 1990s: the former Soviet Union's research staff falls by about half while Asia's grows.

upsert.reason: Before 1900 reasoned from the institutions that kept people for inquiry (Babylon's astronomers, the Museum of Alexandria, the Han and Tang bureaus, the House of Wisdom, Maragha and Samarkand, the seventeenth century's academies and their membership), with wide bands; 1900 to 1990 from the growth of the scientific workforce (Price 1963) and national research statistics as recalled (the United States' National Science Foundation, the Soviet Union's scientific workers); from 1990 UNESCO's researchers per million, as recalled, to be checked (UNESCO Science Report 2021).

points.note: Perhaps 300,000 people in scattered groups across Africa. If they spoke languages as people do now, as the gradual view of language's origin holds, a few hundred communities of a thousand or two each; under the late view, that fully modern language arose only some 100,000 to 50,000 years ago, there were none in this sense, so the band runs to zero.
Dips with the people in the depth of the penultimate glacial: communities that die out or merge take their tongues with them.
By now even the late view grants full language; the lower band leaves zero.
Rises with the dispersal out of Africa: each group that moves into new land drifts into a tongue of its own within a thousand or two years.
The Last Glacial Maximum empties the northern ranges; their communities retreat south, and some vanish.
People enter the Americas: a few founding tongues begin to divide over a new hemisphere, which will hold some two thousand languages by 1492.

About 4.4 million foragers on every continent but Antarctica. At one language per 1,500 people, as Aboriginal Australia (about 250 languages for perhaps 750,000 people) and New Guinea suggest, some 3,000 languages. The alternative, that the world's languages were most numerous now, before farmers' and herders' language families spread over the foragers', needs speech communities of a few hundred and puts the count near today's: the upper band carries it.

The great spreads begin: steppe herders carry Indo-European west (from 3000 BCE), Austronesian farmers leave Taiwan, Bantu farmers leave the Cameroon borderlands soon after. Each absorbs many forager tongues, but each also splits into hundreds as it spreads (Bantu into about 500, Austronesian into about 1,200), so with the farmers of the tropics multiplying the count goes on rising.

Pama-Nyungan has spread over seven eighths of Australia, replacing or absorbing the languages there; Akkadian is the language of rule over the Sumerian cities, and Sumerian is dying as a spoken tongue.

Levels off: in the empires Latin, Greek, Aramaic, Chinese and the Prakrits replace many tongues, while Bantu, Austronesian, Amazonian and New Guinean communities go on dividing theirs. Whether the world's count peaked about now or before farming spread is the debate the band carries.
Latin has replaced Gaulish, Iberian and Etruscan in the western provinces; Bantu speakers reach Natal; Malagasy begins on Madagascar.

Turns down slowly: after the conquests Arabic replaces Aramaic, Coptic and much of Berber, Turkic spreads over Iranian-speaking Central Asia, and Chinese moves south; East Polynesia's settlement adds only a few.

The floor is today's count, about 7,150, plus the losses that can be traced since: about a thousand in the Americas, which held some two thousand languages at contact and keep about a thousand, more than a hundred in Australia, and several hundred in Africa, Asia, Europe and the Pacific. Languages that vanished unrecorded raise the upper band.
The Taino languages of the Greater Antilles are dying with their speakers.
Falls: smallpox and conquest destroy whole peoples of the Caribbean, Mexico and the Andes' margins, and their tongues with them, while Nahuatl and Quechua spread as the missions' common languages.
Settlers' frontiers in North America, Australia, southern Africa and Siberia: the Tasmanian languages and many of California's die within a generation of the frontier's arrival.

Carlisle (1879) opens the boarding schools; the abolitions in Cuba and Brazil free people whose African languages survive by now mostly in ritual, as Lucumi in Cuba and the songs of Candomble in Bahia.
Residential and mission schools in North America and Australia punish children for speaking their own languages; the loss shows a generation later, as the last who learned them die.

The fall quickens: the last speakers of many Australian, North American and Siberian languages die, children no longer learning them after the schools of the decades before, and national languages spread with radio and mass schooling.

Papua New Guinea becomes independent (1975) with more than 800 languages, about a ninth of the world's, and uses Tok Pisin, Hiri Motu and English to govern them; the Waitangi Tribunal (1975) opens the Maori renaissance. Neither changes the count, which falls by several languages a year.
Tuvalu's parting from Kiribati follows the line between Polynesian Tuvaluan and Micronesian Gilbertese; it changes no language's survival.
Revivals begin, Maori language nests from 1982 and Hawaiian immersion schools from 1984: they keep languages from dying, but do not add to the count.

Ethnologue counts about 7,160 living languages and Glottolog a few hundred more by its own rules; about two fifths are endangered, and some two dozen are the first language of half of humanity. Losses run at roughly one language every one to three months (Bromham and colleagues, 2022), faster than the long average since 1500 of about three a year.

upsert.reason: Before writing no language is recorded: deep values are the number of people divided by the size of forager speech communities, with bands that also carry the debate over when language began. After 1500 they are today's count plus the losses that can be traced.

points.note: Foragers count, but nobody reckons ages in years without a calendar of years, so this measure reads about zero.
Writing, calendars and temple accounts in Mesopotamia and Egypt: ages begin to be reckoned by scribes and officials.
Qin and Han household registers record each person's age: China's numeracy runs ahead of the rest of the world's and of its own literacy.
Roman tombstones round ages to multiples of five: perhaps a third to a half of commemorated Romans knew their age; Han China's registers count more.
Lower with the end of Roman administration in the west and the Chinese registers' collapse in the age of division.
The numeracy revolution of north-western Europe (Baten): age heaping falls there from about 1500, with trade, Protestant schooling and parish registers; Qing China and Japan are as numerate or more.
Numeracy far ahead of literacy (12%): most people reckon and know their age without reading.
Mass schooling spreads numeracy with literacy in Europe, the Americas and Japan; South Asia and Africa lag.
Almost every adult knows their age: the age-heaping measure saturates, and numeracy's differences now lie in skills it cannot read (PISA's and PIAAC's tests).
No writing until about 3300 BCE.
Writing appears about 3300 BCE.
Gutenberg's press begins; its effect on literacy comes over the next centuries (ev.printing).
Printed books are cheap in Europe by now; literacy creeps up there.
Literacy is high in north-west Europe and North America, low almost everywhere else (ev.mass-schooling).
Literacy campaigns in China, the Soviet Union's completed, and the first schooled generations of the new states.
No state, so no elections of rulers.

Rises: the Greek poleis choose their magistrates in assemblies or councils, Carthage elects its suffetes, and the gana-sangha republics of the Ganges plain choose their leaders in councils of clan heads; together perhaps half a percent of humanity, the Ganges republics the largest and least certain part.

Rome expels its kings and elects consuls (509), and Cleisthenes gives Athens' assembly its power (508): with the poleis and the Ganges republics about one person in a hundred lives where rulers are chosen by contested votes, however narrow the electorate.

Rises: Greek democracies and oligarchies, the Roman Republic, Carthage's elected magistrates and the gana-sangha republics of the Ganges plain, whose councils of clan heads chose their leaders; how competitive the last were is uncertain.
Roman Italy, with citizenship for all free Italians; the provinces are ruled, not represented.
Falls: the Republic gives way to the Principate.
Venice elects its doge.
The Italian communes elect their consuls.
Most Italian communes have fallen to lords (signori).
Rises: Poland-Lithuania's nobles elect their kings from 1573, and the Dutch Republic governs itself from 1581.
Britain's Parliament becomes supreme after 1688, its ministries resting on contested elections among a few percent of men.
The new United States.
Falls: Poland-Lithuania is partitioned (1795) and Napoleon takes power (1799).

The July Revolution (1830) makes France's chamber, chosen by about 170,000 voters, the master of its government, and Belgium's constitution (1831) follows; the United Kingdom, the United States and a few others already choose rulers in contested elections.
France's Second Republic, with Belgium, the Netherlands, Piedmont, Denmark, Switzerland and Latin America's competitive oligarchies.
Falls: Louis-Napoleon's coup of December 1851 ends the Second Republic.
Rises: France's Third Republic (1870) and parliamentary government in united Italy.
The Weimar Republic and the new republics of central Europe.
Mussolini's dictatorship and Poland's coup of 1926.
Falls: Hitler's dictatorship from 1933.
Germany occupies most of Europe's democracies.
Liberated western Europe is under provisional governments; its first postwar elections follow from October 1945 into 1946, the rise to 1946.
Liberated western Europe and the Philippines hold elections.
Rises most: India, Japan and West Germany choose their governments in competitive elections.

Ghana and Malaya become independent with elected governments (1957), about 13 million people. Indonesia's parliamentary democracy ends from 1957 under Guided Democracy; if its 1955 election counts it among competitive polities, about three points of humanity leave, which the 1960 value's lower band carries.

Burma's army takes power (1962) and Brazil's (1964), about 100 million people leaving competitive elections, while new African and Caribbean states hold their first elections; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Marcos's martial law (1972) takes the Philippines, about 1% of humanity, out of competitive elections; Chile's and Uruguay's coups follow in 1973.
India's Emergency (June 1975) has not yet begun: the fall to 1976 comes with it.
Falls: India's Emergency suspends elections (1975 to 1977), with juntas in Chile, Argentina and Uruguay; indices differ on India, hence the band.
India's election of March 1977 ends the Emergency and the Congress party loses power.
Before the revolutions of late 1989 the rise to 1990 has not yet come: most of it is Eastern Europe's free elections of 1990.
Rises: multiparty elections in Eastern Europe and Latin America's return to elected government.
Indonesia's first free election since 1955 (1999).
Falls slowly as elections lose their competitiveness in several large countries; whether some (India, Turkey) still count is debated, which the band carries.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the populations of republics, competitive oligarchies and parliamentary regimes at each date (as recalled), divided by the world's people.

points.note: No state, so no national elections: bands decide by consensus, which the parent's measure does not count.
The first states have assemblies of elders and citizens (Mesopotamian city assemblies, as Jacobsen argued), but no elections of rulers by a franchise that can be counted.
Citizens of Athens after 508 BCE and of other Greek democracies and the Roman Republic: a few hundred thousand men in a world of some sixty million adults.
Rome extends citizenship to Italy after the Social War (89 BCE): about a million adult men may vote, if they come to Rome.
Falls: under Augustus the Roman assemblies lose their elections to the Senate and the emperor (by 14 CE).
Iceland's Althing and Venice's popular assembly.
The Italian communes' councils, the Swiss cantons and the county electors of England's Commons.
England's forty-shilling freeholders (1430).
The nobles of Poland-Lithuania, perhaps a tenth of its people, vote in their dietines and elect the king.
Rises: some five to six million Frenchmen vote for the Estates-General, and the new American states widen their franchises.
Napoleon's plebiscites are open to all Frenchmen: votes without a choice of rulers, counted here because the measure is the formal right.
Under Napoleon's empire the plebiscite franchise holds until the Restoration of 1814 cuts the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers; the fall to 1820 comes then.
Falls: the restored French monarchy limits the vote to about a hundred thousand taxpayers.
Rises again: the American states drop property qualifications for white men in the 1820s, and Britain's Reform Act (1832) adds about 300,000 voters.
Jumps: the Second Republic gives every French man the vote (March 1848), about nine million voters, one in seventy of the world's adults.
France adopts manhood suffrage in 1848; most white American men vote.
Britain's Second Reform Act (1867) and the German Reich's manhood suffrage (1871).
New Zealand (1893) and South Australia (1894) give women the vote.
Before the war about a tenth of adults may vote; the great widening comes from 1917 to 1920, in Soviet Russia, Britain, Germany and the United States.
Rises most: women vote in Britain (1918), Germany (1919), the United States (1920) and Soviet Russia, where the franchise excludes only the 'former people'.
The Soviet constitution of 1936 grants universal suffrage in single-candidate elections.
Women vote in France (1944), Italy and Japan (1946).
India's constitution of 1950 gives all adults the vote.
Bolivia's revolution gives the vote to all adults (1952), most of them Indigenous and unable to read; China's elections of 1953 and 1954 are still to come.

China's first elections under its 1953 electoral law, held through 1953 and 1954 with universal suffrage for the lowest people's congresses, add about a quarter of the world's adults to the formal franchise: most of the rise to 1955.
China's first national elections under the constitution of 1954, with universal suffrage for the lowest people's congresses; formal right, not a choice of rulers.
Switzerland gives women the federal vote in 1971, nearly the last democracy to do so.
Myanmar's coup and the Taliban's return end national elections for some ninety million people.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the dates of franchise laws and the adult populations they covered (as recalled from the suffrage histories and V-Dem's suffrage indicator), divided by the world's adults.

points.note: Athens' democracy (508 BCE) excludes women, slaves and foreigners: not broad suffrage.
Athenian democracy excluded women, slaves and foreigners: not broad suffrage.
England's settlement makes Parliament supreme, but its electorate is a few percent of men: not broad suffrage.
The French Revolution: the suffrage of 1792 is men's only and soon suspended.
No polity yet joins competitive elections to a broad suffrage under this measure's definition; the United States' white-manhood suffrage excludes the enslaved, women and most free Black men.
Women vote in New Zealand, Australia, Finland and Norway: about one person in a hundred lives under broad suffrage.
Women's suffrage in Britain, Germany, Canada and the new republics of 1918.
Germany, Austria, Spain and others have fallen out of democracy since 1930 (ev.interwar-crisis).
Most of continental Europe's democracies are under occupation.
France and Italy begin to be liberated.
At the war's end: the Western democracies, Australasia and a few others, about a twelfth of humanity; most of Asia and Africa are colonies or dictatorships.
Japan's first election with women voting (April 1946) and Italy's referendum and constituent election (June 1946).

India's first general election (October 1951 to February 1952), with universal adult suffrage, puts about a seventh of humanity under elected government: most of the rise from 1950 to 1960 happens here, not evenly through the decade.
India's democracy (ev.india-democracy, elections from 1951-52) and the new states of decolonization (ev.decolonization) double the share.
Decolonization ends with most new states under one-party or military rule; the share is held up by India, which declares its Emergency in June 1975.
India's Emergency (1975–77) suspends elections and liberties; indices differ on whether India still counts, hence the wide band.
India's Emergency ends with the election of March 1977, which the opposition wins: the share returns to its level before the Emergency.
Peru (1980), Bolivia (1982), Argentina (1983), Uruguay and Brazil (1985) return to elected government (ev.lac.democratic-transitions), with Turkey (1983): most of the rise from 30% since 1980.
Before People Power, little changed since Brazil's and Uruguay's returns to civilian rule in 1985.
People Power (ev.sea.people-power) restores elected government to some 56 million Filipinos, about 1.1% of humanity.
Before the revolutions of 1989: the third wave has reached southern Europe, Latin America, South Korea and the Philippines.
Eastern Europe and some former Soviet republics hold free elections as the Soviet Union dissolves (ev.cold-war-end).
After the democratizations of 1989–1994, India counted throughout.
Before Suharto's fall, little changed since 1996.
Indonesia's first free election since 1955 (June 1999, ev.sea.reformasi) adds about 3.4% of humanity, and Nigeria's return to civilian rule (May 1999) about 2%.
Pakistan's coup (October 1999) takes back about 2.3 points of the 1999 rise.
Foragers near subsistence: most put staying fed and alive first, the rest family and the sacred. Nothing is measured; the band is wide.
Penultimate glacial: harsher ranges, read as slightly more survival-first.
The Last Interglacial opens wider, wetter ranges.
The Last Glacial Maximum approaches: people retreat to refugia.
Early farmers: shorter, sicker and more exposed to harvest failure than foragers (DensityRatchet#2ace), yet with more stores and more ritual life; read as no net change.
The axial-age traditions make salvation and right conduct a first want for some; small at world scale.
The Little Ice Age and the famines of the early 1300s.
After the Black Death survivors eat better (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
The seventeenth-century crisis: war, cold and famine from China to Europe.
Industrial north-west Europe and North America begin to move away from survival-first; most of the world does not yet.
War and famine push survival back to first for many.
Western Europe's postwar boom begins (ev.eu.postwar-boom): there survival stops being the first want; most of the world is not yet touched.
The postwar escape from extreme poverty begins (h.sustenance).
Values surveys begin to cover enough of the world to read this, as recalled.
China's escape from poverty moves the world total most.
COVID-19 and its slump push some back toward survival-first; read as a pause rather than a turn.
About one person in five still puts survival first: more than the 8.5% in extreme poverty, since many above that line still live close to it.

upsert.reason: Sketch until 1980: survival-first is read as tracking how close people lived to subsistence, with a floor of family and faith and security that every society also puts first for some. From 1985, exploring: the survival end of the survival/self-expression axis in values surveys, as recalled, not checked.

points.note: Zero: no machine harnesses water, wind or sun before the watermill.
The first watermills, in the Greek east about the third century BCE, then Han China's water-powered trip hammers and bellows.
Roman mills spread (Barbegal's sixteen wheels, about 100 CE).
The medieval mill economy: Domesday Book counts about 6,000 mills in England (1086); mills grind, full and saw across Europe and Song China.
The post windmill spreads in Europe from the late twelfth century.
Dutch windmills drain the polders and saw timber for the Golden Age's ships.
Water power's height as a mill power: New England's and Lancashire's mill towns before steam took over.
Mills decline as steam replaces them; hydroelectricity begins in the 1880s and holds the total.
Hydroelectricity's first large plants (Niagara, 1895).
Hydroelectricity about 340 TWh a year.
Hydroelectricity about 1,750 TWh.
Wind and solar begin to count: about 380 TWh together beside hydro's 3,450.
Wind and solar about 2,450 TWh, beside hydro's 4,350.
Wind and solar, about 5,000 TWh, pass hydroelectricity's 4,400: the flows have doubled per person since 2010, though they are still about a fifteenth of the stores.

upsert.reason: Mills from recalled counts (Domesday, Kander and colleagues' water and wind for Europe), hydro, wind and solar from recalled world generation (Energy Institute, IEA), at 3.6 PJ a TWh.

points.note: Fire for cooking, warmth and light beside about 3.4 GJ of food: about 110 kg of wood a person a year, held flat across the forager span for want of any world measure.
Rises with the warming after the glacial maximum and the first settled foragers (the Natufians), who heat houses and parch wild grain.
Farming begins: houses, lime plaster and parched and cooked grain need more fuel per person than foraging did.
Pottery kilns and plaster across the farming world.

Copper smelting and the first towns. The parent's note here names draught animals, whose feed this part does not count: the feed of working animals is a frontier part of the carve, outside the parent's accounting.
Iron smelting spreads; charcoal for iron becomes one of the largest fuel uses of the iron ages.
Roman and Han cities, baths, kilns and smelters: about 12 GJ a person, about 0.8 tonnes of wood, near the most a land-bound economy reaches before 1500 (Sunbound#c94c).
The medieval clearing of Europe's and China's forests: fuel per person near its pre-industrial height before the Black Death.
Flat per person: wood shortages in England, the Low Countries and north China push households toward coal and peat.
The burned harvest per person peaks between 1840 and 1870 at about 18 GJ, with North America's wood-burning frontier, Russia's forests and the world's cooking fires.
From here the burned harvest per person falls: coal replaces wood in the industrial world while the world's total of burned biomass stays near 23 EJ and population grows.
The stores pass the burned harvest between 1900 and 1905 by these values (12.4 against 14.1 GJ a person in 1900); the date is usually given as about 1900, within a decade either way.
About 10 GJ a person as kerosene, coal and electricity replace wood in cities; the world's total of burned biomass still grows, about 25 EJ.
About 7 GJ a person: traditional biomass for about two billion people's cooking, with modern bioenergy; its world total, about 60 EJ, is the largest ever.

upsert.reason: The parent minus food, flows and stores; checked against recalled world biomass totals (about 23 EJ in 1870 and 1900, 25 in 1950, 48 in 2000, 60 now).

points.note: Zero: no population burns coal, oil or gas as fuel before the Bronze Age.
Coal burned at a Bronze Age site in Xinjiang about 1600 BCE is the earliest known fuel use of a store; the world's use per person rounds to zero.
Coal begins to be burned in Han China, for iron working where wood was short, and later in Roman Britain: a few thousandths of a GJ a person.
Roman Britain's coal burning ends with Roman rule; China's continues on a small scale.
Song China's coal: Kaifeng's households and the northern iron industry turn to coal as the north China plain is cleared of trees (Hartwell's estimates, as recalled).
Below the late eleventh-century Song peak: the Jurchen conquest of the north in 1127 and the wars that followed cut the northern iron and coal economy back.
England's sea coal (about 2 to 3 million tonnes a year) and the Dutch peat that fuelled the Golden Age.
Britain's coal, about 5 million tonnes; the stores are still under 2% of the world's energy.
About 15 million tonnes of coal, most of it British.
Steam's coal: Britain, Belgium, the German lands and the United States.

Drake's well opens the oil age, though coal carries the rise. The value sits at the top of the recalled range (about 2.6) so that the burned harvest stays smooth beneath the parent's jump from 23 to 24.5 GJ.
About 770 million tonnes of coal and 20 million tonnes of oil.
Coal's pre-war peak, about 1.3 billion tonnes in 1913.
Dips in the war's last year: the mines of northern France and Belgium occupied, Russia's output collapsed.
Oil about a fifth of fossil energy; the Depression then cuts coal by about a fifth by 1932, a trough no value here records.
The wartime peak of fuel burning.

Falls by about a tenth as Germany's and Japan's mines, railways and industry collapse at the war's end (world coal about 1.2 against 1.45 billion tonnes a year earlier, as recalled); oil rises a little.
Postwar recovery: coal about 1.5 to 1.8 billion tonnes and oil about half a billion.
Oil passes coal about this time.
Slower after the 1973 oil shock. Recalled fuel totals put it nearer 56; the value is set by the parent's sum, which runs low here (see the carve's synthesis).
The second oil shock: the stores' use per person peaks for a generation.
Falls after the oil shocks as recession, efficiency and the turn from oil cut use per person.
Flat through the 1990s: the collapse of Soviet and East European industry offsets Asia's growth.
China's coal boom from 2002 lifts the world's use per person for the first time since 1979.
COVID-19's lockdowns cut oil use by about a tenth for the year.
About 64 GJ a person: oil, coal and gas in roughly equal thirds, nuclear heat about a twentieth.

upsert.reason: From recalled world fuel totals (Smil; the Energy Institute's Statistical Review; the IEA), converted at about 24 GJ a tonne of coal and 42 a tonne of oil, nuclear as reactor heat; set within the band where the parent's sum required.

points.note: Draught animals not yet; more fuel for cooking, pottery and houses.
Draught animals, the plough and copper smelting.
Sunbound#c94c: energy per person creeps up through mills and better use of land, not by much.
The coal age's pre-war peak.

Lowered from 39: fuel burning fell by about a tenth as Germany's and Japan's mines, railways and industry collapsed at the war's end (world coal about 1.2 against 1.45 billion tonnes a year earlier, as recalled); the stores (h.warmth.stores) carry the dip.
Lowered from 39 with the war's-end dip; recovery begins.
Lowered from 39: recovery from the war's-end dip.
Lowered from 39.4: recovery; by 1948 the earlier path is regained.

upsert.reason: Lowered at the end of the Second World War, where the carve's parts show a dip in fuel burning that the parent had smoothed over.

points.note: Births before 300,000 years ago, from the emergence of Homo sapiens about 320,000 years ago at a few hundred thousand people. Revised from 0.01.
The Bureau's account has about 47 billion by 1 CE.

Checked 2026-10-11 against the usual estimate of about 117 billion (Population Reference Bureau). That estimate counts 46 billion births between 8000 BCE and 1 CE and 26 billion between 1 and 1200 by assuming 80 and 60 births per 1,000 a year; in a population that barely grows that means a life expectancy of about 12.5 and 17 years. This model's life expectancy is 25 to 30 in those periods, as palaeodemography and ancient censuses put it, which gives 35 to 40 births per 1,000 and about 22 billion by 1 CE. After 1650 the two accounts agree within a few billion. Raising this value to 117 would contradict the model's own life expectancy before 1650; so it stays, with both accounts inside the band.

upsert.reason: Integral of humanity times a crude birth rate consistent with the model's life expectancy; the upper band holds the Population Reference Bureau's account (about 117 billion by 2022).

changes.value: Fill, last of the 1820 to 1850 stretch: the six contributions to sea level at 1830 and 1840, summing to sea level at both dates. The mountain glaciers make their last Little Ice Age advance in these decades, so they hold a little more water at 1830 than at 1820; the ice sheets and the ocean's warmth barely move.

points.note: Starting value in a glacial stage (MIS 8) about 60 m below today; Antarctica's share is set at about a tenth of each glacial fall, as reconstructions of the last cycle give it.
Grows with the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: shrinks toward its interglacial size.
Grows again in the penultimate glacial (MIS 6).
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: by the start of the Last Interglacial Antarctica already holds less ice than today.

The Last Interglacial: about 3 m from Antarctica, above all a retreat of West Antarctica, the largest share of the highstand; how much, and whether East Antarctica's marine basins retreated too, is debated.
Glacial inception (MIS 5d): regrows as the world cools after about 116,000 years ago.
MIS 4: grows quickly with the northern sheets.
About 12.5 m at the glacial maximum, the most debated of the parts: reconstructions run from about 5 to 20 m.
Antarctica lags: still near its glacial size while the northern sheets have begun to melt.
A few metres to meltwater pulse 1A; some reconstructions give it much more (debated).
After the northern sheets are gone, Antarctica's slow retreat supplies most of the last 3.5 m of the Holocene rise, ending about 4,000 years ago.
Losing ice since the 1990s, faster since about 2010 as West Antarctica's glaciers speed up: about 1 cm of sea level since 2000.
Starting value, set at about a fiftieth of the glacial fall: mountain glaciers and ice caps, the Patagonian ice among them.
Advance in the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: retreat.
Advance again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: retreat to interglacial size.
Smaller than today in the Last Interglacial's warmth.
Advance at the glacial inception.
MIS 4: advance.
The mountain glaciers and ice caps of the glacial maximum, the Patagonian ice sheet among them: about 2.5 m (debated).
Retreat from the glacial maximum; the Patagonian ice thins.
Mid-Holocene glaciers about as small as in 2000, many smaller.
The neoglacial: glaciers grow back after about 4,000 years ago.
The cold of the sixth and seventh centuries (the Late Antique Little Ice Age).
Medieval warmth: glaciers smaller than in the Little Ice Age.
The Little Ice Age: glaciers advance in the Alps, Scandinavia and elsewhere from about 1550.
The Little Ice Age's last advances, about 1820 to 1850: glaciers hold about 8.5 cm of sea level more than in 2000.
The glaciers' last Little Ice Age advance (the Alpine glaciers reach their modern maximum about 1850 to 1855): they hold slightly more water than in 1820.
Retreat begins about 1850, the start of the modern rise.
About 2 cm since 2000; glaciers were the largest part of the rise from 1900 to 1990.
Starting value, set at about a fortieth of the glacial fall: in glacials Greenland's ice reaches out over its continental shelf.
Grows with the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: shrinks toward its present size.
Grows again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: northern summers peak and Greenland melts past its present size.
About 2 m smaller than today in the Last Interglacial (estimates from about 1 to 3.5).
Regrows after about 116,000 years ago as northern summers cool.
MIS 4: grows with the cold stage.
Larger at the glacial maximum, out to the edge of the continental shelf: about 3 m.
Begins to retreat from the shelf with the deglaciation.
Slightly smaller than in 2000 in the mid-Holocene warmth (debated), then regrowing in the neoglacial cooling to the Little Ice Age.
The neoglacial: Greenland's ice regrows past its 2000 size.
The Arctic warming of the 1920s to 1940s melts Greenland faster than any time until the 1990s.
Near balance from about 1970 to 1995.
About 2 cm of sea level since 2000, a fifth of the rise.
Pluvial lakes fill in the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: the pluvial lakes shrink.
They fill again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial's pluvial lakes.
Termination II: the pluvial lakes empty.
The Last Interglacial's green Sahara held lakes too; no estimate is recalled.
MIS 4's pluvial lakes.
The pluvial lakes of the glacial maximum, Lake Bonneville and Lake Lahontan in the American Great Basin among them, hold a few tenths of a metre.
Lake Agassiz forms at the Laurentide's southern edge as the pluvial lakes of the west shrink.
Lake Agassiz near its largest and the lakes of the green Sahara (mega-Chad among them) full: about half a metre of sea level held on land.
Lake Agassiz drains into Hudson Bay about 8,200 years ago; the Sahara's lakes are still full.
The Sahara dries and its lakes give their water back.
Before the great dams: land holds about a centimetre of sea level less than in 2000, because reservoirs have since held back more than pumped groundwater has released.
The great dam-building decades begin: reservoirs hold back about 3 cm of sea level by 2000 while groundwater pumping returns part of it.
Groundwater pumped from the aquifers of India, China, the Middle East and the American plains has outrun the dams since about 2000.
The northern sheets carry about five sixths of every glacial fall of the sea; the shares of the other parts are set from the last glacial cycle's reconstructions and scaled to each stage.
MIS 8: the northern sheets grow to a full glacial, about 75 m of sea level.
MIS 7c: most of the northern ice melts.
MIS 6, the penultimate glacial, builds the northern sheets again after MIS 7's warm substages.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6): the Eurasian ice sheet larger than at the last maximum and the North American smaller (debated); together about 92 m.
Termination II: nearly all of it gone by the start of the Last Interglacial.
Gone: the Last Interglacial, like today, has no northern ice outside Greenland.
Ice returns in MIS 5d.
MIS 4: the northern sheets grow quickly.
Toward the last glacial maximum: the Laurentide and Fennoscandian sheets reach their greatest extent between about 26,000 and 19,000 years ago.

The last glacial maximum: the Laurentide, Cordilleran, Fennoscandian, British-Irish and Barents-Kara sheets hold about 104 m of sea level (most reconstructions 90 to 115), most of the 125 m fall that exposed Beringia and Doggerland.
Retreat begins after about 19,000 years ago, slowly at first.

Meltwater pulse 1A, about 14,600 years ago (between -13000 and -12000 here): about 15 to 20 m of sea level in four centuries. Most reconstructions credit the collapse of the ice saddle between the Laurentide and Cordilleran sheets; others give Antarctica a large share (debated). Here the northern sheets give about 16 m and Antarctica about 2.5.
The Laurentide's last domes collapse over Hudson Bay; Lake Agassiz drains about 8,200 years ago.
Gone: the last Laurentide ice in Labrador and Nunavut melted about 6,700 years ago; zero from here on.
Starting value: a glacial ocean colder than today's, set at about a fiftieth of the glacial fall.
Cools in the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: warms.
Cools again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: warms to interglacial temperatures and past today's.
A warmer ocean in the Last Interglacial: about half a metre of the highstand.
Cools at the glacial inception.
MIS 4: cools.
A colder ocean takes less room: about 2.5 m at the glacial maximum.
Warms through the deglaciation.
The neoglacial cooling: the ocean colder than in 2000.
The ocean's warming takes up again after mid-century and speeds up from about 1970.
About 3.7 cm since 2000, the largest single part of the recent rise.

upsert.lens: The deepen check names it first (10 Events move it, 2 at the top of an importance scale, every value a sketch). One number hides where in the hemisphere range was gained and lost: the southern continents fill within a few thousand years of the first arrivals, while the north waits on the ice and gains its last land in the Arctic thousands of years later, and the losses after 1492 fall mostly on the islands and the floodplains of the south. The carve is to give each first peopling, abandonment and return a home in the part of the land it changed, and to let each part's land area bound its own curve. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all resident Homo sapiens, over the land of the Americas by 2026 borders, divided as the UN M49 standard divides it.

points.note: Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico (stone tools about 30,000 years ago) would put people here before the glacial maximum; whether its stones are tools is debated, so the value stays at zero with the band open.

Monte Verde in southern Chile (about 12,500 BCE): people reach the far south within about a millennium of the first secure Pacific coast sites, faster than a front could walk (a coastal spread by jumps).
Peopled to Tierra del Fuego: South America and Mexico near their ceiling, except the high Andes' ice, the Patagonian ice sheet's remnants and the islands.
The first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola, about 0.1 points of the world's land.
Archaic and then Saladoid (from about 500 BCE) islanders spread through Puerto Rico and the Lesser Antilles; the Bahamas wait until about 700 CE.

The Lucayans of the Bahamas are carried off as slaves and the islands are empty by 1520; Hispaniola's and Cuba's Taino die of war, forced labour and smallpox (1518): the islands are the first land in the account to fall out of range.
The epidemics empty the Amazon's floodplain chiefdoms and parts of northern Mexico and the Caribbean for a time; the forest grows back over them.
The Trans-Amazonian highway (from 1970) and Brazil's frontier settlement bring forest emptied since the epidemics back into regular use, along with the ranches and roads of the Chaco and Patagonia.
Nearly all of Latin America's ice-free land; the Atacama's core and the Andes' highest ground are the rest.
Bluefish Caves in the Yukon (cut-marked bones about 24,000 years ago, debated) would put people in eastern Beringia before the glacial maximum; the band keeps it open.
The White Sands footprints (about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago) put people south of the ice in New Mexico; their reach is unknown.
The Pacific coast opens as the Cordilleran ice pulls back; Cooper's Ferry in Idaho (about 16,000 years ago) and Swan Point in Alaska.
Clovis hunters spread across the unglaciated south of North America within about three centuries.
South of the ice nearly all of North America is lived on; the Laurentide ice still covers much of Canada.
The Laurentide ice is almost gone and hunters follow the caribou north across Canada; the high Arctic and Greenland stay outside range.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic islands to Greenland's ice-free coasts, about two points of the world's land no one had lived on: Northern America's, and the Americas', last large gain.
Unchanged: the Norse farms of south-west Greenland (from 985) use a few tens of thousands of square kilometres, and Late Dorset people already hunt in the north-west.
Polynesians settle Hawai'i (about 1000 to 1200), part of the United States by 2026 borders, and the Thule Inuit spread from Alaska across the Arctic to Greenland.
After de Soto's entrada (1539 to 1543) and the epidemics that followed, the Mississippian chiefdoms of the south-east and parts of the Mississippi valley are emptied for a time.
Settlers' farms and the mounted peoples of the Plains bring land emptied after the epidemics back into regular use.
Weather stations, airfields and mines on Canada's Arctic islands (Resolute, 1947; Alert, 1950) and Greenland's bases bring the high Arctic's last empty land into regular use.
Nearly all of Northern America's ice-free land; the emptiest Arctic islands are the rest.

upsert.boundary: Monte Verde in southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago
upsert.description: A camp of wooden huts by a creek, with mastodon meat, seaweed and medicinal plants, preserved under peat: the site that broke the 'Clovis first' account.
provenance: sources to check: Dillehay et al. 2008, Science 320; Dillehay et al. 2015, PLoS ONE 10

upsert.boundary: The Norse in Greenland and Vinland, about 985 to 1450
upsert.description: Norse farmers settle south-west Greenland (about 985) and reach Newfoundland, where L'Anse aux Meadows is occupied in 1021; the Greenland colonies die out by about 1450 as the climate cools and trade with Norway fails.
provenance: sources to check: Kuitems et al. 2022, Nature 601 (L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021); Arneborg, in The Viking World (2008)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (Greenland, Canada); Europe (Northern Europe)

upsert.boundary: People spread through the Americas, about 16,000 to 13,000 years ago
upsert.description: Descendants of a population that lived isolated in Beringia move south, probably along the Pacific coast first, then through an ice-free corridor; within a few thousand years they reach Tierra del Fuego. Genomes show one main founding population, splitting early into northern and southern branches.
provenance: sources to check: Moreno-Mayar et al. 2018, Science 362; Braje et al. 2017, Science 357

upsert.boundary: Footprints at White Sands, about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago
upsert.description: Human footprints in the dried lake beds of New Mexico, beside those of mammoths and giant sloths, dated by seeds, pollen and quartz to the height of the last glacial: if the dates hold, people lived south of the ice sheets thousands of years before Clovis.
provenance: exploring: the dates are contested but have held up to repeated testing
sources to check: Bennett et al. 2021, Science 373; Pigati et al. 2023, Science 382

upsert.boundary: The first people reach Cuba and Hispaniola, about 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Foragers cross open sea to the Greater Antilles, the first settlement in the Americas of islands out of sight of the mainland; their flaked-stone tools resemble those of Belize and Yucatán, which suggests a crossing from Central America, but a route from South America is also argued, and the evidence fits both. Ground sloths and other island animals disappear in the millennia after people arrive.
provenance: inferred: the arrival as recalled; its source is debated
sources to check: Keegan and Hofman, The Caribbean before Columbus (2017); Steadman et al. 2005, PNAS 102
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (Cuba and Hispaniola)

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum and the peopling of the Americas, about 26,000 to 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: Ice sheets at their greatest drive people from the far north into refugia. Dogs are domesticated, pottery appears in East Asia, and people enter the Americas. As the world warms after about 19,000 years ago, the Natufians of the Levant settle in villages and harvest wild cereals; the Younger Dryas cold closes the age.
provenance: sources to check: Clark et al. 2009, Science 325 (the Last Glacial Maximum); Wu et al. 2012, Science 336 (Xianrendong pottery)

upsert.boundary: The ice-free corridor opens, about 13,800 to 12,600 years ago
upsert.description: As the Laurentide and Cordilleran ice sheets pull apart east of the Rockies, a corridor of meltwater lakes and bare ground opens from Alaska to the plains; on one reading of its plant and animal DNA it could support people along its whole length only from about 12,600 years ago, on another bison used it by 13,000. Either way it opened after people were at Monte Verde and the Paisley Caves, which is why most now think the first people came south along the Pacific coast, though the coastal sites lie drowned under the risen sea.
provenance: exploring: when the corridor could support people, and so which route came first, is debated
sources to check: Pedersen et al. 2016, Nature 537; Heintzman et al. 2016, PNAS 113

upsert.boundary: People at the Paisley Caves, about 14,300 years ago
upsert.description: In caves above a vanished lake in Oregon, dried human faeces dated about 14,300 years ago carry Native American mitochondrial DNA, and stemmed points lie in layers as old as Clovis: people lived in the Great Basin before the Clovis hunters spread. Questions about contamination of the samples have been raised and answered; most now accept the dates.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; contamination of the samples has been argued and answered
sources to check: Gilbert et al. 2008, Science 320; Jenkins et al. 2012, Science 337

upsert.boundary: The first Arctic peoples cross to Greenland, about 2500 BCE
upsert.description: Hunters of the Arctic Small Tool tradition, with tiny chipped blades, bows and skin tents, move from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland within a few centuries (Saqqaq, Independence I). A 4,000-year-old Saqqaq genome shows they came from Siberia in a migration separate from that of other Native Americans; their Dorset successors hold the high Arctic until the Thule arrive.
provenance: sources to check: Rasmussen et al. 2010, Nature 463; Raghavan et al. 2014, Science 345
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the Arctic and Greenland)

upsert.boundary: Polynesians settle the eastern Pacific, about 900 to 1300
upsert.description: After a pause of nearly two thousand years in Samoa and Tonga, voyagers navigating by stars, swells and birds settle the Society Islands and the Marquesas, then within a few centuries Hawaii, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa New Zealand (about 1280), the last large land on Earth to be peopled.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates follow the 'short chronology'
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108
