The ten Events that name it now also name the part they change: Northern America for White Sands, the Paisley Caves, the ice-free corridor, the Paleo-Inuit, the Norse and Polynesia's settlement (Hawai'i); Latin America and the Caribbean for Monte Verde and the Greater Antilles; both for the peopling of the Americas and the glacial maximum's era. Each Event is restated whole from the record read at r469, with only process_ids changed.

upsert.lens: The deepen check names it (19 Events move it). One number hides who holds the claim on the worker, and that changed apart from how much: the first states' corvée, Rome's slaves, Europe's serfs, the Atlantic slavery of the eighteenth century, Russia's serfs freed in 1861, colonial forced labour after 1885, the Soviet, German and Japanese camps, and today's forced labour, mostly private and by debt. The carve is to give each abolition, imposition and camp system a home in the part of compulsion it changed, so the parent's long rise and fall can be read as different systems replacing one another. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, over the work of all the world's workers; every hour of compelled work, wherever and whenever it is done.

Opens the three parts of the carve of work under compulsion (carve.concept.humanity.wants.sustenance.toil.compelled, r471 and r472) at every date of the parent, each the parent's value times the share held by private masters, by lords and creditors, and by rulers, so the three sum to it; bands are the parent's band times the same share. The shares are sketched from the recalled history of slavery, serfdom, corvée and the camps (to check against the Cambridge World History of Slavery, Blum on European serfdom, the ILO's estimates of forced labour since 2005 and Applebaum and Khlevniuk on the Gulag) and share one foundation with the parent (EvidenceDependence#23ca). The parent is left as it was.

points.note: The dependants of Uruk's temples and great households, fed on rations and bound to work for them.
Rome's tenants are bound to the land by law (the colonate), and in China great families hold dependent tenants: bound work grows as slavery held by masters falls.
High medieval serfdom at its height in western Europe, before the Black Death, with dependent tenants across Asia.
After the Black Death labour is scarce and labour dues fade in western Europe as lords commute them to rents.
The second serfdom east of the Elbe: Polish, Prussian and Bohemian lords raise labour dues to grow grain for the Baltic trade.
Russia's Law Code of 1649 binds its peasants to their lords for good.
The revolutions of 1848 end labour dues in the Habsburg lands; Russia's serfs remain.
Russia frees about 23 million serfs (1861); their dues end in stages, the 'temporarily obligated' peasants owing labour until they redeem their land.
Indenture carries Indians and Chinese to the Caribbean, Mauritius, Natal and Fiji, and debt peonage binds workers on Mexico's haciendas.
About a third of today's compelled hours: debt bondage in South Asia's brick kilns, quarries and farms, and recruitment debts that bind migrant workers, as recalled from the ILO's estimates.
Captives of raids kept to work by their captors in the first farming villages and among settled foragers: the first compelled work is held by masters, before any ruler can compel.
Chattel slavery spreads with the Greek cities and Carthage: Athens's silver mines at Laurion work thousands of slaves.
The ancient peak of slavery held by masters: perhaps a third of Roman Italy's people are slaves, captured in the wars of conquest and worked on latifundia and in mines.
Falls as Rome's conquests end and estates turn to tenants bound to the land (the colonate), whose hours belong to the bound.
Slaves in the Islamic world, Byzantium and Africa, and the Viking and Slav slave trades, hold the part steady while western Europe's slaves become serfs.
The Atlantic trade begins to carry Africans to Brazil's sugar engenhos; slavery in the Ottoman and Mughal lands and in Africa itself goes on.

The largest part of compelled work for the first time since Rome: the Atlantic trade at its height (some 80,000 people a year), the Caribbean's and Brazil's plantations, and slavery in Africa, the Ottoman lands and India.
Saint-Domingue's enslaved free themselves (1791 to 1793); the cotton gin (1793) opens the United States' second slavery.
Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees some 800,000, while the cotton South, Cuba and Brazil grow.
The United States' four million enslaved are freed (1865): the part loses about a third.
Cuba (1886) and Brazil (1888) end slavery, the last in the Americas; slavery inside Africa, perhaps millions in the Sokoto caliphate and the Sudan, ends only slowly under colonial rule.
Rises as the camps close: trafficking for labour and sex, held by private exploiters, grows with migration and the end of the Soviet bloc, and becomes the largest part.
About half of today's compelled hours: the ILO's private forced labour without debt and its forced commercial sexual exploitation (about 6 million people), as recalled from its 2022 estimates.
The first states: Uruk's rulers call out labour for walls, canals and temples, and from here the ruler's corvée is the largest part of compelled work for three thousand years.
Egypt's corvée on the pyramids and canals and the Akkadian and Ur III labour gangs: half of compelled work.
Qin's and Han's labour service, a month or more a year for every adult man, on walls, roads and canals.
The Sui dig the Grand Canal with millions of conscripted labourers (605 to 610).
The Inca mit'a at its height in the Andes; Ming China's labour service is being converted to silver.
Falls: China's Single Whip reform (1581) turns most labour service into a silver tax, though the Spanish mita drafts Andeans to Potosí from 1573.
Turns up: the Dutch Cultivation System (from 1830) makes Java's villagers grow export crops for the colonial state, and Egypt's corvée digs Muhammad Ali's canals.
Colonial forced labour grows as the private owners' part ends: rubber quotas in Leopold's Congo, corvée in French Africa and Indochina, porterage for every colonial army.
War labour: some eight million prisoners of war, deportees from occupied Belgium and Poland, and porters and labour corps from Africa, India and China.
The Gulag grows past a million prisoners with collectivization's deportations; colonial labour codes still compel work in Africa.
The peak of rulers' compulsion: about thirteen million foreign workers and prisoners in Germany, the Gulag's camps and labour armies, and Japan's romusha and conscripted Koreans and Chinese.
The Gulag is emptied after Stalin's death (1953), while China's laogai camps grow.
The Khmer Rouge drive Cambodia's towns into forced agricultural cooperatives (1975 to 1979).
About a seventh of today's compelled hours: the ILO's state-imposed forced labour (about 3.9 million people), in prisons and compulsory labour schemes, as recalled from its 2022 estimates.

upsert.boundary: The movement to abolish the slave trade and slavery, 1787 to 1888.
upsert.description: From the London committee of 1787 and the Haitian revolution of 1791 to Brazil's Golden Law of 1888: Britain abolishes the trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1834, and its navy suppresses the Atlantic trade.

upsert.boundary: Cash crops, mines and migrant labour: the colonial economy, about 1900 to 1950
upsert.description: Railways from ports to mines and plantations; head and hut taxes payable in coin push men into wage work far from home; the Gold Coast becomes the world's largest cocoa grower by 1911, Nigeria and Senegal export groundnuts, the Copperbelt opens in the 1920s; forced labour persists in many colonies into the 1940s.
provenance: sources to check: Austin, African Economic History (1987, 2nd ed.); Frankema and van Waijenburg 2012, Journal of Economic History 72
upsert.region: Africa: Western, Middle, Eastern and Southern Africa

upsert.boundary: Leopold II's Congo Free State, 1885 to 1908
upsert.description: The Belgian king rules the Congo basin as his own property; to meet rubber quotas his agents and the Force Publique take hostages, burn villages and cut off hands. Violence, flight, famine and sleeping sickness kill perhaps millions; an international campaign forces Belgium to annex it (1908).
provenance: exploring: the death toll is contested; Hochschild's ten million is not well founded, and demographers give wide ranges
sources to check: Hochschild, King Leopold's Ghost (1998); Vansina, Being Colonized (2010)
upsert.region: Africa: Middle Africa (Democratic Republic of the Congo)

upsert.boundary: Brazil abolishes slavery, May 1888
upsert.description: The Golden Law frees the last enslaved people in the Americas, about 700,000; the empire falls to a republic the next year.
provenance: sources to check: Conrad, The Destruction of Brazilian Slavery 1850–1888 (1972)

upsert.boundary: The silver of Potosí, 1545 to 1650
upsert.description: A mountain of silver found in the Andes in 1545 makes Potosí one of the largest cities of the world by 1600; after 1573 the mita forces Andean villages to send men to its mines, where mercury refining kills many. Its silver pays Spain's wars and, through Manila, buys China's goods.
provenance: sources to check: Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984); Lane, Potosí (2019)

upsert.boundary: The Baptist War and emancipation in the British Caribbean, 1831 to 1838
upsert.description: In the Baptist War of Christmas 1831, perhaps 60,000 enslaved people in Jamaica strike and rise under Samuel Sharpe; its brutal suppression helps push Parliament to abolish slavery (1833, in force 1834). About 670,000 people in the British Caribbean are freed after an 'apprenticeship' of unpaid labour that ends in 1838; the owners, not the enslaved, receive £20 million in compensation, about two fifths of the government's yearly spending.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The Problem of Freedom (1992); Draper, The Price of Emancipation (2010)
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: Slavery ends in Cuba, 1880 to 1886
upsert.description: A law of 1880 turns Cuba's remaining enslaved people into 'apprentices' (the patronato) bound to their masters; many buy or win their freedom early, and the system ends in October 1886, two years before Brazil's abolition. Puerto Rico had abolished slavery in 1873.
provenance: sources to check: Scott, Slave Emancipation in Cuba (1985)

upsert.boundary: Lords, serfs and the manor, about 800 to 1350
upsert.description: Across western Europe most peasants hold land from a lord in return for labour, rents and dues, tied to the manor as serfs, while a warrior aristocracy holds land for military service; serfdom fades in the west after the Black Death but deepens in the east.
provenance: sources to check: Bloch, Feudal Society (1939); Wickham, Medieval Europe (2016)

upsert.boundary: Spanish America abolishes slavery, 1821 to 1854
upsert.description: The new republics first free the children of the enslaved (free-womb laws) and the slaves who fought for independence, then abolish slavery outright: Chile (1823), Central America (1824), Mexico (1829), Uruguay (1842), Colombia (1851), Argentina (1853), Venezuela and Peru (1854). Owners are usually compensated; the freed are not.
provenance: sources to check: Andrews, Afro-Latin America 1800-2000 (2004)

upsert.boundary: Cotton and the second slavery in the United States, 1793 to 1860
upsert.description: After the cotton gin (1793) short-staple cotton spreads across the Deep South to Texas; about a million enslaved people are sold or marched west in the domestic slave trade, their families broken at auction. The enslaved population grows, mostly by births, from 0.7 million in 1790 to 3.95 million in 1860, and raw cotton becomes the largest American export and the main fibre of Britain's mills. How the planters raised output per worker, by the whip as Baptist argues or by better cotton seed as Olmstead and Rhode answer, is debated.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the source of the rise in output per worker is debated
sources to check: Baptist, The Half Has Never Been Told (2014); Olmstead and Rhode 2018, Explorations in Economic History 67; Berlin, Generations of Captivity (2003)
upsert.region: The Americas: Northern America (the US South)

upsert.boundary: Pacific Islanders recruited for the Queensland cane fields, 1863 to 1906
upsert.description: Some 62,000 men and women from Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands are recruited, many by deception or force ('blackbirding'), to work on Queensland's sugar plantations; most are deported under the White Australia policy after 1906.
upsert.region: Oceania (Melanesia: Vanuatu, Solomon Islands; Australia and New Zealand: Australia)

upsert.boundary: Russia emancipates its serfs, March 1861.
upsert.description: About 23 million privately held serfs become free in law, with land they must buy back over 49 years; the state peasants follow in 1866.

upsert.boundary: Peru's guano age, 1840 to 1880
upsert.description: Bird droppings piled on the Chincha islands become the richest fertilizer of Europe and North America; Peru's state earns most of its revenue from them for forty years, dug by about 100,000 Chinese indentured labourers in brutal conditions, and borrows against them until the deposits run out and the state defaults (1876). The Atacama's nitrates follow, and with them war.
provenance: sources to check: Gootenberg, Between Silver and Guano (1989); Cushman, Guano and the Opening of the Pacific World (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Amazon rubber boom, 1879 to 1912
upsert.description: Demand for tyres and insulation makes wild Amazonian rubber one of the world's most valuable commodities; Manaus builds an opera house, Brazil takes Acre from Bolivia, and tappers, many of them indebted migrants from the drought-stricken north-east, spread up every river. In the Putumayo the Peruvian Amazon Company's agents enslave and kill tens of thousands of Indigenous people. Plantations in Malaya and Ceylon, grown from seeds taken from Brazil in 1876, undercut it after 1910.
provenance: sources to check: Weinstein, The Amazon Rubber Boom (1983); Goodman, The Devil and Mr Casement (2009)

upsert.boundary: Viceroy Toledo's reforms, 1569 to 1581
upsert.description: Francisco de Toledo tours the viceroyalty, resettles about 1.5 million Andean people into some 800 Spanish-style towns, fixes their tribute, organizes the mita that sends a seventh of the men of sixteen highland provinces to Potosí each year, brings in mercury amalgamation that multiplies the silver output, and executes the last Inca of Vilcabamba, Túpac Amaru (1572).
provenance: sources to check: Stern, Peru's Indian Peoples and the Challenge of Spanish Conquest (1982); Bakewell, Miners of the Red Mountain (1984)

upsert.boundary: The Burma–Siam railway, 1942 to 1943
upsert.description: To supply its army in Burma, Japan builds a 415-kilometre railway from Ban Pong in Thailand to Thanbyuzayat in Burma with about 60,000 Allied prisoners of war and perhaps 200,000 or more Asian labourers, Tamils, Malays, Burmese, Javanese and Chinese. About 12,000 of the prisoners and perhaps 70,000 to 90,000 or more of the Asian labourers die of overwork, cholera, starvation and beatings.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Asian labourers' numbers and deaths are uncertain
sources to check: Kratoska (ed.), The Thailand–Burma Railway 1942–1946 (2006)

upsert.boundary: The Cultivation System in Java, 1830 to 1870
upsert.description: Villages must grow coffee, sugar, indigo and other export crops on part of their land or give labour to the government, which pays them little and sells the crops in Amsterdam; the surplus sent home pays for about a third of the Dutch state's revenue in the 1850s, while rice land is squeezed and famines strike Cirebon (1844) and Demak and Grobogan (1849 to 1850).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how much it impoverished Java is debated
sources to check: Elson, Village Java under the Cultivation System (1994); Fasseur, The Politics of Colonial Exploitation (1992)

upsert.boundary: Forced labour and hunger in occupied Java, 1943 to 1945
upsert.description: The occupation government conscripts millions of Javanese as romusha, labourers for railways, airfields and fortifications in Java and across the region, some 270,000 of them sent beyond Java, of whom few return; it requisitions rice at fixed prices, and hunger spreads through 1944 and 1945. Estimates of the deaths from hunger and forced labour run from several hundred thousand to over two million; the figures are poorly documented and contested.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; numbers mobilized and dead are contested
sources to check: Sato, War, Nationalism and Peasants: Java under the Japanese Occupation (1994); Ricklefs (2008)

points.note: The first states: Uruk's rulers call out labour for walls, canals and temples, and from here the ruler's corvée is the largest part of compelled work for three thousand years.
Egypt's corvée on the pyramids and canals and the Akkadian and Ur III labour gangs: half of compelled work.
Qin's and Han's labour service, a month or more a year for every adult man, on walls, roads and canals.
The Sui dig the Grand Canal with millions of conscripted labourers (605 to 610).
The Inca mit'a at its height in the Andes; Ming China's labour service is being converted to silver.
Falls: China's Single Whip reform (1581) turns most labour service into a silver tax, though the Spanish mita drafts Andeans to Potosí from 1573.
Turns up: the Dutch Cultivation System (from 1830) makes Java's villagers grow export crops for the colonial state, and Egypt's corvée digs Muhammad Ali's canals.
Colonial forced labour grows as the private owners' part ends: rubber quotas in Leopold's Congo, corvée in French Africa and Indochina, porterage for every colonial army.
War labour: some eight million prisoners of war, deportees from occupied Belgium and Poland, and porters and labour corps from Africa, India and China.
The Gulag grows past a million prisoners with collectivization's deportations; colonial labour codes still compel work in Africa.
The peak of rulers' compulsion: about thirteen million foreign workers and prisoners in Germany, the Gulag's camps and labour armies, and Japan's romusha and conscripted Koreans and Chinese.

Germany's surrender (May 1945) and Japan's (August) free some fifteen million foreign workers, prisoners and romusha from the Axis camps and labour programmes (ev.sea.java-romusha ends); the Soviet camps and the labour of German and Japanese prisoners of war remain.
The Gulag is emptied after Stalin's death (1953), while China's laogai camps grow.
The Khmer Rouge drive Cambodia's towns into forced agricultural cooperatives (1975 to 1979).
About a seventh of today's compelled hours: the ILO's state-imposed forced labour (about 3.9 million people), in prisons and compulsory labour schemes, as recalled from its 2022 estimates.

upsert.lens: The deepen check names it (24 Events move it, 4 at the top of an importance scale). One count hides where states were made and unmade, and by what: Europe's hundreds of principalities fall by war, mediatization and unification; the Americas' states appear only after 1776; Africa's kingdoms are conquered from outside in the Scramble and return as some fifty states after 1956; Asia's are absorbed by the Mongols, the Qing, the Mughals and the colonial empires and multiply again after 1945; Oceania's appear from 1845. The carve is to give each formation, conquest and independence a home in the area it changed, and to test whether the count's long fall follows one path everywhere. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, every state on Earth, placed by the UN M49 area (by 2026 borders) in which its seat of government lies.

points.note: The proto-kingdoms of Upper Egypt (Naqada, Hierakonpolis, This) and Nubia's A-Group.
Egypt united under one king (about 3100 BCE), with Ta-Seti in Lower Nubia.
Egypt's First Intermediate Period splits the kingdom among rival nomarchs and dynasties; Kerma rules Upper Nubia.
Kush rises at Napata, and Phoenicians found Carthage (814 BCE) and the other cities of the Libyan coast.
Carthage and its sister cities, the Greek cities of Cyrenaica, Kush and the Berber kingdoms; Egypt is under Persia.
Ghana, Kanem and Gao in the Sahel, the Nubian kingdoms, Ethiopia's highland kingdom, the Aghlabids, Idrisids and Tulunids as the Abbasid west breaks away.
Mali at its height, the Solomonic kingdom, Kanem, Great Zimbabwe, the Swahili city-states and the Hausa and Yoruba cities.

Africa's count at its height: Oyo, Dahomey, Asante, Benin, the Hausa states, Bornu, Funj, Ethiopia, Morocco, the regencies of the Maghreb, Kongo's successor states, Lunda and the Swahili and Malagasy kingdoms.
France has taken Algeria (1830 to 1847); Sokoto has absorbed the Hausa states and the Zulu kingdom has risen; Liberia is independent (1847).
The Scramble begins: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain Egypt (1882).
Falls by half in a decade: after the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) European armies and companies conquer the kingdoms of West Africa, the Congo basin and East Africa.
Almost every African state is conquered: Ethiopia (which defeats Italy at Adwa, 1896), Liberia, Morocco, Darfur, Wadai and, until 1903, Sokoto remain.
The low point: Ethiopia and Liberia alone, after Morocco's protectorate (1912) and Darfur's conquest (1916).
The year of Africa: Sudan, Morocco, Tunisia (1956), Ghana (1957) and Guinea (1958) are followed by seventeen states in 1960.
Portugal's revolution (1974) frees Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Angola.
Namibia becomes independent (March 1990).
South Sudan becomes independent (2011), the 54th.
Caral and the towns of Peru's Norte Chico raise platform mounds, but whether they are states is debated; they are not counted.
The Olmec centres (San Lorenzo, then La Venta) are counted as chiefdoms, not states, on the usual reading; some argue for an early state.
The first states of the Americas: Monte Albán in Oaxaca and the first Maya kingdoms of the Preclassic (Nakbe, El Mirador).
Classic Maya city-states multiply under their divine kings, beside Teotihuacan, Monte Albán and the Moche of the Peruvian coast.
The Late Classic peak: some sixty Maya kingdoms with emblem glyphs, with Tiwanaku and Wari in the Andes.
The Classic Maya collapse: the southern lowland kingdoms are abandoned one by one in the ninth century.
The Tepanec war (1426 to 1428) makes the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, which will absorb most of central Mexico's city-states.
Spain conquers the Aztec (1521) and Inca (1532 to 1572) states and most of the Maya kingdoms; the Itza of Petén hold out.
The low point: Nojpetén, the last Maya kingdom, falls in 1697; what remains is the hard-to-count polities of the Plains, the Arauco frontier and the Amazon.
The United States declares independence (1776).
Haiti becomes independent (1804).
Paraguay, the Río de la Plata and Chile govern themselves, and Kamehameha has united the Kingdom of Hawai'i (1810).
Mexico, the Central American federation, Gran Colombia, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil and Uruguay: the independences of 1810 to 1828.
The Central American federation (1841) and Gran Colombia (1830) break into their parts; the Dominican Republic leaves Haiti (1844).
Hawai'i is annexed by the United States (1898), and the count of the Americas' de facto independent polities is now the twenty republics with the United States, Canada's dominion not yet counted.
Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago become independent (1962), the first of the Caribbean's independences.
With Belize, Antigua and Barbuda (1981) and Saint Kitts and Nevis (1983), the Americas reach their 35 states of today.
The first states: Uruk and its neighbours on the lower Euphrates, if counted as states.
Akkad unites Mesopotamia's city-states under one king.
The Zhou enfeoff kinsmen and allies in vassal states; the Levant fills with Aramaean, Neo-Hittite and Phoenician city-states after the Bronze Age collapse.
The Zhou's vassals become the independent states of the Spring and Autumn period, and the Ganges plain's janapadas form.

Fewer than in 800 BCE: Persia has absorbed the Near East's kingdoms and China's states are falling to a few warring powers, but the Ionian poleis, India's janapadas and republics and southern Arabia's kingdoms remain.
Qin unites the Warring States (221 BCE) and the Maurya hold most of the subcontinent; Hellenistic kingdoms and India's successor states remain.
The Abbasid caliphate breaks into emirates and the Tang fall into the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms.
Falls by nearly half: the Mongols absorb the Jin, the Xi Xia, the Song, Khwarazm, the Abbasids and the states of Central Asia and Iran.
Japan's Sengoku: after the Ōnin war (1467 to 1477) the daimyo rule their domains as independent lords; the Malay and Indian sultanates multiply.
Hideyoshi unites Japan (1590) and the Mughals take the Deccan's sultanates.
The Qing conquer the Ming and the southern Ming states; the Mughal empire is at its widest.
The Mughal empire's successor states (Hyderabad, Awadh, Bengal, the Marathas) rule for themselves after 1707.
The East India Company's victory at Plassey (1757) begins the British conquest of India.
The last Maratha states and Kandy (1815 to 1818) come under British rule.
Burma (1885), Vietnam (1884) and the last Malay and Central Asian states fall to Britain, France and Russia.
Japan annexes Korea (1910): Asia's independent states are the Ottoman Empire, Persia, Afghanistan, China, Japan, Siam, Nepal, Bhutan and a few Arabian states.
India and Pakistan become independent (August 1947), after the Philippines, Syria, Lebanon and Jordan.
Bangladesh (1971) and the Gulf states (Bahrain, Qatar, the Emirates, 1971) are independent.
Falls: South Vietnam is absorbed by the North (1975, united 1976) and Sikkim by India (1975).
The two Yemens unite (May 1990).
Jumps: the five Central Asian republics and the three of the Caucasus become independent as the Soviet Union breaks up (1991).
Timor-Leste becomes independent (May 2002).
Some 48: the UN's Asian members with Taiwan and the State of Palestine, counted as states that govern themselves; the count of the latter is debated.
The first states of Europe: Crete's palaces (from about 1950 BCE) and the Mycenaean kingdoms of mainland Greece.
Falls: the Mycenaean palaces are destroyed in the Bronze Age collapse (about 1200 to 1150 BCE).

The Greek poleis of the mainland, the islands, Magna Graecia, Sicily and the Black Sea, with the Etruscan and Latin cities: most of the world's states sit in Europe for the only time in history; how many of the smallest poleis to count is the largest uncertainty.
Falls by four fifths: Macedon and the leagues absorb the poleis, and Rome the Italian and Sicilian cities.
Rome holds the Mediterranean; Europe's other states are its client kingdoms, Bosporus and the Thracian and Dacian kingdoms.
The western Roman provinces become Visigothic, Frankish, Ostrogothic, Burgundian, Vandal and Anglo-Saxon kingdoms.
The Carolingian empire breaks into its kingdoms and great principalities, and Scandinavian, Slav and Magyar states form.

Europe's peak since the poleis: some five hundred more or less autonomous units on Tilly's count, of which perhaps three hundred and seventy answer to no one in practice, most of them the Holy Roman Empire's principalities, free cities and church lands.
The Peace of Westphalia (1648) confirms the Empire's three hundred or so estates in their rights to make war and treaties.
Poland's first partition (1772); by 1795 Poland-Lithuania is gone.
Falls by two thirds: the Empire's principalities, free cities and church lands are mediatized (1803) and the Empire dissolved (1806); Napoleon annexes Italy and the Low Countries.
Italy unifies (1859 to 1861), its states becoming one kingdom.
Germany unifies (1866 to 1871), some twenty-five states becoming one empire.
Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Finland, the Baltic states, Austria and Hungary come out of the fallen empires (Versailles, 1919).
Germany, the Soviet Union and Italy absorb Austria, Czechoslovakia, Albania, Poland and the Baltic states, and Germany occupies Denmark, Norway, the Low Countries and France.
The occupied states are restored as the war ends, though the Baltic states stay in the Soviet Union.
Germany reunites (October 1990).
Jumps: the Baltic states, Ukraine, Belarus and Moldova leave the Soviet Union, and Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Macedonia leave Yugoslavia.
Serbia and Montenegro part (2006).
Kosovo declares independence (2008), recognized by about half the world's states.
The Tu'i Tonga's maritime chiefdom (from about 1200) is sometimes called an empire; it is counted here as a paramount chiefdom, not a state, and the band keeps it open.
George Tupou I unites Tonga (1845) and Cakobau's Bau dominates eastern Fiji: Oceania's first states.
Fiji has been ceded to Britain (1874); Tonga becomes a British protected state in 1900.

Australia and New Zealand, self-governing dominions since 1901 and 1907, become independent in law with the Statute of Westminster (1931; adopted 1942 and 1947): when to count them is a convention, here from 1931.
Western Samoa becomes independent (1962), the first of the Pacific island states.
Papua New Guinea becomes independent (September 1975).
Palau becomes independent in free association with the United States (1994), the last.
The fourteen UN members of Oceania; the Cook Islands and Niue, self-governing in free association with New Zealand, are not counted.

upsert.boundary: The Berlin conference, November 1884 to February 1885
upsert.description: Fourteen states, no African among them, agree how claims to African coasts will be recognized and give the Congo basin to King Leopold's association.
provenance: sources to check: Förster, Mommsen and Robinson (eds.), Bismarck, Europe and Africa (1988)

upsert.boundary: Liberia founded and independent, 1822 to 1847
upsert.description: The American Colonization Society settles freed Black Americans at Monrovia (1822); Liberia declares independence in 1847, ruled by the settlers' descendants over the indigenous majority.
provenance: sources to check: Clegg, The Price of Liberty (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Scramble for Africa, 1881 to 1914
upsert.description: France takes Tunisia (1881) and Britain Egypt (1882); the Berlin conference (1884 to 1885) sets rules for claiming the rest; with machine guns, quinine and African soldiers, Britain, France, Germany, Belgium's king, Portugal, Italy and Spain partition almost the whole continent by 1914. Peoples who had lived without states, perhaps a third or more of Africans, come under colonial governments.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the share of Africans living without states before conquest is a rough guess
sources to check: Pakenham, The Scramble for Africa (1991); Vansina, Being Colonized (2010)

upsert.boundary: The year of Africa, 1960
upsert.description: Seventeen countries become independent in one year, fourteen of them French colonies, with Nigeria and the Congo; by 1965 most of the continent is independent.
provenance: sources to check: Cooper, Africa since 1940 (2nd ed. 2019)

upsert.boundary: Latin America's wars of independence, 1808 to 1826
upsert.description: After Napoleon seizes Spain (1808), juntas and armies across Spanish America fight for independence: Hidalgo's rising in Mexico (1810), Bolívar in the north and San Martín in the south, until Ayacucho (1824) and the fall of Callao (1826); Brazil separates from Portugal peacefully as an empire (1822). About eighteen new states emerge.
provenance: sources to check: Lynch, The Spanish American Revolutions 1808–1826 (2nd ed. 1986)
upsert.region: The Americas: Central and South America

upsert.boundary: The American Revolution, 1775 to 1783
upsert.description: Thirteen colonies rebel against British taxation and rule, declare independence (July 1776) and, with French help, win at Saratoga and Yorktown; the Treaty of Paris (1783) recognizes the United States.
provenance: sources to check: Wood, The Radicalism of the American Revolution (1992)

upsert.boundary: Israel's founding and the war of 1948
upsert.description: After the UN votes to partition Palestine (November 1947), civil war breaks out; Israel declares independence (May 1948) and defeats the armies of its Arab neighbours; about 700,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled, the Nakba, and hundreds of thousands of Jews later leave or are driven from Arab countries.

upsert.boundary: Qin unifies China, 221 to 206 BCE
upsert.description: The First Emperor conquers the last of the warring states and imposes one script, one coinage, standard weights, axle widths and laws, ruled through appointed officials in commanderies rather than nobles; the dynasty falls soon after his death, but the unified empire endures.
provenance: sources to check: Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires: Qin and Han (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Zhou overthrow the Shang, 1046 BCE
upsert.description: At Muye the Zhou defeat the last Shang king and justify it by the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that heaven grants rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from the wicked, which every later Chinese dynasty invokes.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the date follows the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project
sources to check: Shaughnessy, in The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)

upsert.boundary: The British Caribbean's independence, 1962 to 1983
upsert.description: After the West Indies Federation breaks up (1962), Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago become independent (1962), then Barbados and, on the mainland, Guyana (1966), the Bahamas (1973), Grenada (1974) and the smaller islands, the last St Kitts and Nevis (1983); most remain parliamentary democracies on the Westminster model. Anguilla, the Cayman Islands and others stay British.
upsert.region: The Americas: the Caribbean (the British islands)

upsert.boundary: The Ottomans take Constantinople, 6 April to 29 May 1453
upsert.description: After a siege of seven weeks in which great bronze cannon batter the land walls, Mehmed II takes the city and ends the Byzantine empire, the last remnant of Rome; as Istanbul it becomes the Ottoman capital.
provenance: sources to check: Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453 (1965); Crowley, Constantinople: The Last Great Siege (2005)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Turkey); Europe (Southern Europe: the Byzantine state)

upsert.boundary: Decolonization, 1945 to 1975.
upsert.description: From Indonesia and India to Angola and Mozambique, about eighty colonies become independent states; some keep elected government, many do not.

upsert.boundary: The Congress of Vienna, 1814 to 1815
upsert.description: The victorious powers redraw Europe's map and set up a concert of great powers that keeps a general peace for almost a century, broken by limited wars.
provenance: sources to check: Schroeder, The Transformation of European Politics 1763–1848 (1994)

upsert.boundary: The fiscal-military state, about 1550 to 1815
upsert.description: Gunpowder fortresses, standing armies and navies multiply the cost of war; Europe's states that tax, borrow and administer most survive and absorb the rest (Warsift#b01b), so that the five hundred or so polities of 1500 shrink to about thirty by 1900, and Britain, France, Prussia, Austria and Russia emerge as great powers.

upsert.lens: The deepen check names Polynesia first (15 Events move it, 3 at the top of an importance scale, 68% of its values sketched or wide). One share hides two island worlds peopled two thousand years apart: Tonga and Samoa from about 880 BCE, alone through the 'long pause', and the Society Islands, the Marquesas, the Cooks and the Tuamotus from about 1025. The losses after contact fell far harder on the east (the Marquesas lost nine in ten), and since 1960 the east has grown fastest while Samoans and Tongans emigrate. The carve is to give each settlement, loss and recovery a home in the island world it changed, and to let each part's own clock bound its curve. Range: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for the people of the subregion; a part stands at zero before its first landfall.

changes.value: Opens the two parts of the carve of Polynesia (carve.concept.humanity.oceania.polynesia, r479) at every date of the parent, so that they sum to it, and corrects the parent where reading it for the carve showed three errors. (1) It held 0.003 at 1200 BCE, 0.006 at 1000 BCE and 0.008 at 800 BCE, before or just after the first landfall in Tonga about 880 BCE: set to 0, 0 and 0.002, with the 0.006 points moved to Melanesia at the same dates, where the Lapita people of those centuries lived, so Oceania is unchanged. (2) It held 0.022 from 1500 to 1788 and 0.02 at 1800, so Polynesia's numbers rose from about 176,000 in 1767 to 198,000 in 1800 while contact began cutting Tahiti's; raised from 1600 to 1791 to reach about 215,000 in 1767 (usual estimates about 180,000 to over 300,000), with Oceania raised by the same amounts; and 1865 and 1870 smoothed (a rise of a tenth in five years that nothing explains). (3) It held 0.006 from 1910 to 1945 and 0.0097 at 1950, a seam left when an earlier pass set the values from 1950 from the UN's counts: raised from 1910 to 1945 from the colonial censuses as recalled, with Oceania raised by the same amounts. The few thousandths of a point added to Oceania are not taken from Asia's share, whose band dwarfs them, as the 1890 correction did. The parts are split by recalled counts of each island group: West Polynesia holds all of Polynesia from 880 BCE to about 1025, a little under half on the eve of contact, two thirds by 1900 and about 57% now. All recalled or reasoned and sharing one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca); sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2017); McArthur, Island Populations of the Pacific (1967); Rallu (1990); the UN's World Population Prospects.

points.note: The Ivane valley in the highlands about 49,000 years ago, and the Bismarck islands by about 45,000 (ev.mel.ivane, ev.mel.near-oceania).

Raised from 0.19 by the 0.006 points the Polynesian series had placed in Tonga and Samoa before their first landfall: the Lapita people of these centuries live in Fiji, Vanuatu and New Caledonia (ev.oc.lapita).
The sweet potato reaches the New Guinea highlands from the Americas, and highland valleys grow dense (ev.mel.sweet-potato) (DensityRatchet#2ace).
Australia and New Zealand pass Melanesia, about 1868: for the first time since farming began, most of Oceania's people do not live in Melanesia.
Measles kills about a quarter of Fiji's people in 1875 (ev.mel.fiji-measles), and labour recruiting takes tens of thousands to Queensland and Fiji.
The highland valleys, with perhaps a million people, are first entered by outsiders in 1933 (ev.mel.highlands-contact).

points.note: No one lives in East Polynesia before the voyages after the long pause, about 1025 by the short chronology.
Empty by the short chronology; the older 'long chronology', with East Polynesia settled from about 300 to 800, is now held by few, and the band leaves room for it (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Still empty by the short chronology, whose radiocarbon dates on short-lived plant remains put the first landfall in the Society Islands about 1025 to 1120 (ev.pol.society-islands).

Voyagers from Samoa settle the Society Islands about 1025 to 1120 and within a century the Cooks, the Marquesas, the Australs and the Tuamotus (ev.oc.polynesia-settlement): founding groups of a few hundred growing at 2 to 3% a year.
The east's islands fill: the Marquesan valleys and the Society Islands' chiefdoms build marae and terraces (ev.pol.era.chiefdoms), and their numbers draw level with the west's.

On the eve of contact, about 120,000 people, more than half of Polynesia's: the Marquesas perhaps 35,000 to 100,000, the Society Islands 35,000 to 70,000 (Cook's 204,000 for Tahiti is rejected), the Cooks about 17,000, the Tuamotus, Australs and Mangareva some 20,000 (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Wallis (1767), Bougainville and Cook (1769) at Tahiti bring venereal disease, tuberculosis and dysentery (ev.oc.cook-voyages): the east's numbers begin to fall (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
Tahiti holds about 16,000 at the missionaries' count of 1797; whalers and traders reach the Marquesas, whose fall begins (ev.pol.marquesas).
Peruvian slavers take most of Tongareva's people in the northern Cooks (ev.pol.slave-raids), and smallpox reaches the Marquesas (1863).

The low point: about 37,000 in French Polynesia and the Cooks, perhaps a third of the east's numbers at contact; the Marquesas fall on to about 2,000 by the 1920s, while Tahiti, with Chinese and European settlers, begins to grow.
About 77,000: French Polynesia about 62,000 and the Cooks about 15,000.

France's nuclear testing centre at Moruroa and Fangataufa (1963 to 1996) brings work, money and migrants to Tahiti: French Polynesia grows faster than any other part of Polynesia, while Cook Islanders leave for New Zealand.
About 297,000: French Polynesia about 280,000, whose growth has slowed since the testing centre closed, and the Cook Islands about 15,000, most of whose people now live in New Zealand.

Lapita potters from Fiji land at Nukuleka in Tonga about 880 BCE and reach Samoa soon after (ev.pol.tonga-samoa-lapita): a few hundred settlers, the first people of Polynesia.

The west's peak share: from the 1960s Samoans and Tongans leave in large numbers for New Zealand, the United States and Australia (ev.pol.diaspora).
About 395,000 at home (Samoa about 220,000, Tonga about 104,000, American Samoa about 45,000); more Samoans and Tongans now live abroad than in their islands.

upsert.boundary: Chiefdoms and island states, about 1200 to 1767
upsert.description: On every high island chiefs build marae and ahu; the Tu'i Tonga's maritime chiefdom reaches Samoa, 'Uvea and Fiji; Hawai'i's paramount chiefs rule irrigated taro lands and fishponds through land divisions and kapu; Rapa Nui's clans raise the moai; voyaging between distant archipelagos grows rarer. Europeans pass by: Mendana in the Marquesas (1595), Le Maire and Schouten (1616), Roggeveen at Rapa Nui (1722).
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, How Chiefs Became Kings (2010)

upsert.boundary: Colonial rule and resistance, 1900 to 1962
upsert.description: Samoa is divided between Germany and the United States (1899) and New Zealand takes the German part (1914); influenza kills a fifth of Western Samoans in 1918, and the Mau movement demands self-rule; Tonga remains a protected kingdom; Pearl Harbor (1941) brings the Pacific war; Hawai'i becomes an American state (1959).
provenance: sources to check: Meleisea, Lagaga (1987); Campbell (1989)

upsert.boundary: Contact, missions, island kingdoms and annexation, 1767 to 1900
upsert.description: Wallis (1767), Bougainville and Cook bring Tahiti into Europe's imagination; diseases cut island peoples by half or more; Protestant missions convert Tahiti, Tonga, Samoa and Hawai'i; chiefs with muskets build kingdoms (Kamehameha's Hawai'i, Pomare's Tahiti, Tupou's Tonga); France annexes Tahiti, Peruvian slavers take a third of Rapa Nui's people (1862), and Hawai'i's monarchy is overthrown (1893) and annexed by the United States (1898).
provenance: sources to check: Denoon et al. (1997); Campbell, A History of the Pacific Islands (1989)

upsert.boundary: Island nations, territories and the diaspora, 1962 to 2025
upsert.description: Samoa (1962), Tonga (1970) and Tuvalu (1978) become independent, and the Cook Islands and Niue self-governing in free association with New Zealand; France tests nuclear weapons at Moruroa until 1996; more Cook Islanders and Niueans, and very many Samoans and Tongans, come to live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States; the voyaging canoe Hokule'a revives navigation without instruments; the atolls face rising seas.
provenance: sources to check: Campbell (1989); Denoon et al. (1997)

upsert.boundary: The great voyages east, about 900 to 1200
upsert.description: Voyagers in double-hulled canoes, navigating by stars, swells and birds, settle the Society and Cook Islands, then the Marquesas, Hawai'i and Rapa Nui, carrying taro, breadfruit, pigs, dogs, chickens and the Pacific rat. The dating is debated: a short chronology puts the Society Islands about 1025 and the remotest islands about 1200, a longer one centuries earlier.
provenance: exploring: the chronology of East Polynesian settlement is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108; Kirch (2017)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia (East Polynesia, with Hawai'i and Rapa Nui)

upsert.boundary: The Marquesas lose nine-tenths of their people, 1790s to 1920
upsert.description: With whalers, traders and the French (1842) come venereal disease, tuberculosis, smallpox (1863), opium, alcohol and wars fought with muskets; the islanders fall from perhaps 50,000 or more at contact to about 2,000 by the 1920s, the steepest fall of any Polynesian people.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the population at contact is debated, from about 35,000 to over 100,000
sources to check: Dening, Islands and Beaches (1980); Rallu, Les populations océaniennes aux XIXe et XXe siècles (1990)

upsert.boundary: Influenza in Samoa, November 1918
upsert.description: New Zealand's administration lets the steamer Talune land passengers with influenza at Apia; about 8,500 die, a fifth of Western Samoa's people, while American Samoa, under strict quarantine, has no deaths: one of the clearest tests of quarantine in the pandemic.
provenance: sources to check: Tomkins 1992, Social History of Medicine 5; Shanks et al. 2012

upsert.boundary: Peruvian slave raids, 1862 to 1863
upsert.description: Ships from Callao kidnap or lure some 3,500 Polynesians and Micronesians from Rapa Nui, Tuvalu, Tokelau, the Cook Islands, Niue and Kiribati to work in Peru; most die of disease within a year, and the few returned bring smallpox to Rapa Nui, whose people fall to 111 by 1877, taking much of its knowledge with them, perhaps including the reading of the rongorongo script.
provenance: sources to check: Maude, Slavers in Paradise (1981)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia, Micronesia (Kiribati); the Americas: South America (Peru, and Rapa Nui by 2026 borders)

upsert.boundary: Voyagers settle the Society Islands, about 1025 to 1120
upsert.description: After the long pause, canoes from Samoa reach the Society Islands; radiocarbon dates on short-lived plant remains put the first settlement about 1025 to 1120, and Ra'iatea, with the marae of Taputapuatea, becomes a centre from which voyagers go on to the remoter islands. Other scholars date the settlement centuries earlier.
provenance: exploring: the short chronology is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108; Kirch (2017)

upsert.boundary: Lapita voyagers reach Tonga and Samoa, about 880 to 800 BCE
upsert.description: Potters from Fiji settle Nukuleka in Tonga about 880 BCE, a date fixed by uranium in their coral tools, and soon Samoa, where the Mulifanua site now lies under the lagoon: the first people of what becomes Polynesia.
provenance: sources to check: Burley et al. 2012, PLOS ONE 7; Kirch (2017)

changes.value: Opens the five parts of the carve of migrants living in Oceania by area of birth (carve.concept.humanity.means.connection.migration.oceania, r482) at every date of the parent, so that they sum to it, and corrects the parent against the birthplace counts of Australia's and New Zealand's censuses as recalled (Australia's overseas-born 63% of its people in 1861, 32% in 1891, 23% in 1901, 17% in 1911, 10% in 1947, 20% in 1971; New Zealand's about a third in 1901 and 15% in 1945). The parent ran a third too low from the gold rush to 1890 (0.05 in 1859 against about 0.068), anticipated the rush at 1850, and ran a fifth to a half too high from 1910 to 1960 (0.08 against 0.053 to 0.067), when the gold-rush generation died out and the White Australia policy held immigration down. World migration, the declared sum of its five areas, is moved by the same amounts at the same dates (at most 0.03 points, inside its band). The parts: before 1788 Oceania's own peoples crossing today's borders (seven in ten) and people born in western New Guinea, which M49 counts in Asia (three in ten); from 1788 the Europe-born; the Chinese of the gold rushes, Fiji's girmitiyas and Micronesia's Japanese; Asia's rise after 1973 to half of all migrants. points.note: Before people reach Sahul, about 50,000 years ago, no one lives in Oceania.

Sahul's first people come from Wallacea, in what M49 counts as Asia, and their descendants move across what are now the borders of western New Guinea (Indonesia, so Asia), Papua New Guinea and Australia: about three in ten of the movers living east of today's lines were born west of them.

Some 40,000 Chinese come to the Victorian and New South Wales goldfields (ev.oc.gold-rushes); Victoria's poll tax (1855) and the riots at Lambing Flat (1861) begin the exclusion that the White Australia policy completes.
The first girmitiyas reach Fiji from India (May 1879; ev.mel.girmit).
About 40,000 India-born girmitiyas in Fiji at the height of indenture, while the Chinese of Australia dwindle under the White Australia policy (ev.anz.white-australia).
Indenture ends (1916 to 1920) and the India-born of Fiji begin to die out, while Japan's South Seas Mandate (1920) opens Micronesia to Japanese settlers.
About 85,000 Japanese and Okinawans live in the South Seas Mandate, outnumbering the islanders.
The battles of Saipan, Tinian and Guam (June to August 1944) kill thousands of Japanese settlers.
The Japanese of Micronesia are repatriated to Japan in 1945 and 1946.
The White Australia policy is relaxed (1966): Asians with skills may settle.
The White Australia policy ends (1973; ev.anz.white-australia); Lebanese fleeing the civil war (from 1975) and Turks come first.
Vietnamese boat people are resettled from 1978 (ev.sea.boat-people).
About 5.2 million, half of Oceania's migrants: Indians, Chinese, Filipinos and Vietnamese above all.

points.note: All people are foragers in Africa. With countries by 2026 borders as cells about 750 km across, a forager whose home lies a few tens of kilometres from where they were born crosses one of today's lines perhaps one time in twenty, adults far more often than children: about one person in fifty. Reasoned from forager residence and marriage distances, not counted.
The green Sahara and the Levant open longer ranges across many of today's borders; the reading barely moves.

Eases: a growing share of humanity lives in Asia and Sahul, in what are now large countries (Australia, India, China, Indonesia's islands, Russia), where a forager's moves cross fewer of today's lines. The dispersal itself adds little: its fronts advance by births where people already live (WaveOfAdvance#4cec), not by people living far from their birthplace.

The agrarian floor: most people die within a few kilometres of where they were born; nomads crossing today's lines with their herds, deportees (the Assyrians move whole peoples), soldiers, slaves and traders make up the rest.

Rome's wars carry captives from Gaul, Greece, Thrace, Asia Minor and Syria to Italy: perhaps a million foreign-born slaves live in Italy at the Republic's end, nearly half a percent of humanity alone; Han settlers and soldiers in Korea and northern Vietnam add a little.

The migration period moves Goths, Vandals, Franks and Saxons from beyond the Rhine and Danube into the Roman west, a few hundred thousand people born in one of today's countries and living in another; as Rome's slave imports end, the share holds.
The Mongol conquests move artisans, conscripts and captives across Asia by the hundred thousand, and the empire's posts carry merchants from Venice to Khanbaliq: a small rise.

About two million people born in Africa are enslaved in the Americas, a fifth of a percent of humanity, as the Atlantic trade passes its peak; Europeans born in Europe in the Americas, Asians in other Asian countries and Europe's own movers make up the rest.
The great European emigration begins with the peace (ev.eu.emigration), but its numbers are small until the 1830s; the African-born enslaved in the Americas still make up the largest group of movers.
Britain's emancipation (1834 to 1838) frees about 800,000 people, many born in Africa, but frees them where they live: it changes their status, not the share living outside their country of birth.
The first indentured Indians reach British Guiana (1838) and Mauritius, beginning the indenture that replaces enslaved labour on the sugar colonies.

The Irish famine (from 1845) sends about a million and a half people to Britain and North America by 1852, and the California gold rush (from 1848) draws Chinese, Chileans, Mexicans and Europeans: the turn into the age of mass migration.

Turns up: the Irish famine's emigrants, the gold rushes of California and Australia, and the first indentured Indians and Chinese begin the age of mass migration. The United States counts 2.2 million foreign-born in 1850.

Indentured Indians begin arriving in Fiji (1879) as they had in Mauritius, Trinidad and Guyana; the European emigration to the Americas, slowed by the depression of the 1870s, picks up again at the decade's end.

Cuba's gradual abolition (1880 to 1886) and Brazil's (1888) end the Atlantic world's slave societies; their places on the plantations are taken by immigrants from Spain, Italy, Portugal, China and India.
The United States' Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) is the first law to bar a people by origin; the European flow it does not touch reaches about 800,000 arrivals that year.

The great immigration to the United States, Argentina and Brazil from southern and eastern Europe begins about 1880; Brazil's abolition (May 1888) and its subsidized Italian immigration that follows add to it.

The peak of the age of mass migration: the United States counts 13.5 million foreign-born, Argentina 2.4 million (three in ten of its people), Canada 1.6 million; Indians and Chinese in South-east Asia, Russians in Central Asia and Europe's own movers between today's countries add as many again: some 40 to 45 million people, about 2.5% of humanity.
Falls back: the United States' quota acts (1921 to 1924) cut its immigration by four fifths, and the Depression stops and reverses movement; emigrants of 1900 to 1914 die or return.

Rises with the war: Germany puts millions of foreign workers and prisoners to work in the Reich, the Soviet Union deports Poles, Balts, Volga Germans, Chechens and others across today's lines, and Japan moves Koreans to its mines.

At its wartime height Germany holds about 7.5 million foreign civilian workers and 2 million prisoners of war at work, and about 2 million Koreans live in Japan: forced labour lifts the share living outside their country of birth to near its postwar level.

The war's last year moves people both ways: the Germans of the east begin to flee and be expelled, and forced labourers in the Reich and Koreans in Japan are at their peak, so the share holds near its wartime high.

The war's end starts the largest movement home in history: some ten million forced labourers and prisoners leave the Reich, while expellees from the east and Japanese repatriated from the empire take their place in the count.
Most of the forced labourers and displaced persons go home, while the Germans expelled from the east and the Japanese repatriated replace them in the count: the share holds.
Most of Partition's crossings come between August and December 1947: about ten million people are already living on the other side of the new lines by the year's end.
Partition: about 14 million people cross the new lines between India, Pakistan and East Pakistan in 1947 and 1948, and some 700,000 Palestinians flee Israel's war of independence.

Partition moves about 14 million people across the new lines of India, Pakistan and East Pakistan (now Bangladesh), and 12 to 14 million Germans have been expelled from the east: the share living outside their country of birth stands near its highest until the 2010s.
The UN's estimate of about 76 million international migrants (2.5%) counts the countries of 1960; by 2026 borders the Soviet Union's inter-republic migrants (about 15 million) are added.
The United States' Hart-Celler Act (October 1965) ends the national-origin quotas; its effect on the count comes over the next decades.
The low after the postwar displacement: the displaced of the 1940s die or are counted among the natives' children, and humanity grows faster than the migrants' numbers.
Afghanistan's war sends some five million refugees into Pakistan and Iran, and the Gulf's oil boom draws millions of workers from South Asia and the Arab world.

The UN's count for the countries of 2020: about 153 million. The Soviet Union's breakup makes some 25 million people international migrants overnight in the UN's own series; by 2026 borders they were counted all along, so this series has no jump here.

points.note: No one lives in Polynesia before the first landfall in Tonga, about 880 BCE.
Lapita potters from Fiji land at Nukuleka in Tonga about 880 BCE and reach Samoa soon after (ev.pol.tonga-samoa-lapita): a few hundred settlers, the first people of Polynesia.
Tonga and Samoa fill with the descendants of the first few hundred settlers: growing at about 1% a year, they number perhaps ten thousand by 500 BCE (ev.pol.era.ancestral).
The long pause: Tonga, Samoa, 'Uvea and Futuna hold all of Polynesia's people for nearly two thousand years (ev.pol.era.ancestral).
Voyagers from Samoa settle the Society Islands about 1025 to 1120 (ev.pol.society-islands); the west's share eases as the east fills and the world grows.
On the eve of contact: about 95,000 to 100,000 people, Samoa perhaps 40,000 to 60,000 and Tonga 25,000 to 40,000; the west now holds a little under half of Polynesia's people.
Tonga's civil wars begin (1799) and last half a century, but Samoa sees few outsiders before the missions of 1830, so the west's numbers hold near 100,000 while the east's fall.
Peruvian slavers take people from Tuvalu, Tokelau and Niue (ev.pol.slave-raids); Tokelau loses nearly half its people.
About 70,000: the west's low point, some two thirds of its numbers at contact.
The influenza of November 1918 kills about 8,500 in Western Samoa, a fifth of its people, while American Samoa's quarantine keeps it out (ev.pol.samoa-influenza); numbers recover within a few years.
About 169,000: Samoa 82,000, Tonga 50,000, American Samoa 19,000 and the smaller islands 18,000; falling deaths make the west grow at about 3% a year.
The west's peak share: from the 1960s Samoans and Tongans leave in large numbers for New Zealand, the United States and Australia (ev.pol.diaspora).
About 395,000 at home (Samoa about 220,000, Tonga about 104,000, American Samoa about 45,000); more Samoans and Tongans now live abroad than in their islands.

About 210,000: Samoa, Tonga and French Polynesia grow at 2 to 3% a year as deaths fall, so the share rises toward the UN's count of 1950.

upsert.boundary: Convict transportation to Australia, 1788 to 1868
upsert.description: Britain transports about 162,000 convicts, one in six of them women, to New South Wales, Van Diemen's Land and, last, Western Australia (to 1868); assigned to settlers and public works, most stay when freed, and their labour builds the colonies' roads, farms and towns.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987); Nicholas (ed.), Convict Workers (1988)

upsert.boundary: The White Australia policy, 1901 to 1973
upsert.description: The Immigration Restriction Act (December 1901) bars non-Europeans through a dictation test in any European language, and the Pacific Island Labourers Act deports most Melanesian workers; New Zealand adopts similar rules. The policy is relaxed from 1966 and ended by the Whitlam government in 1973.
provenance: sources to check: Tavan, The Long, Slow Death of White Australia (2005)

upsert.boundary: The great European emigration, 1815 to 1914
upsert.description: Some 50 to 55 million Europeans, Irish, British, Germans, Scandinavians, Italians, Poles, Jews and others, leave for the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, driven by land hunger, famine and persecution and drawn by wages, cheap land and steamships.
provenance: sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)
upsert.region: Europe; Americas; Oceania (Australia and New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Indian indentured labour in Fiji, 1879 to 1916
upsert.description: To work the sugar plantations without disturbing Fijian villages, the colonial government brings 60,965 Indians under five-year contracts (girmit); most stay, and by 1946 Indo-Fijians outnumber indigenous Fijians, while most land stays in Fijian hands: the root of the political conflicts after independence.

upsert.boundary: The central Pacific campaign, November 1943 to August 1945
upsert.description: American forces cross Micronesia island by island: Tarawa (November 1943), Kwajalein and Enewetak (February 1944), the carrier raid that wrecks the fleet anchorage at Truk, then Saipan, Guam and Tinian (June to August 1944), where about 30,000 Japanese soldiers and thousands of Japanese, Okinawan, Korean and Chamorro civilians die, hundreds of them by suicide at Saipan's northern cliffs, and Peleliu (September to November 1944). From the Marianas, B-29s burn Japan's cities, and from Tinian the Enola Gay carries the atomic bomb to Hiroshima.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; civilian deaths on Saipan are uncertain
sources to check: Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985); Peattie, Nan'yo (1988); Poyer, Falgout and Carucci, The Typhoon of War (2001)
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (Kiribati, the Marshalls, the Carolines, the Marianas, Palau)

upsert.boundary: Guam and the Northern Marianas under the United States, from 1950
upsert.description: The Organic Act (1950) makes Guam's Chamorros United States citizens under a civilian government while the armed forces hold about a third of the island; the Northern Marianas choose commonwealth status (approved 1975, in force 1986); Japanese tourism, and garment factories that bring tens of thousands of Asian workers to Saipan (1980s to 2009), remake both economies, and Chamorro activists press for decolonization and against the build-up of bases.
provenance: sources to check: Rogers, Destiny's Landfall (1995); Hezel, Strangers in Their Own Land (1995)
upsert.region: Oceania: Micronesia (Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands)

upsert.boundary: Japan's South Seas Mandate, 1914 to 1944
upsert.description: Japan seizes Germany's islands (October 1914) and rules them under a League of Nations mandate (1920); sugar plantations on Saipan and Tinian draw Japanese, Okinawan and Korean settlers, some 80,000 by 1940, outnumbering the islanders; the islands are fortified and become battlefields from 1943.

upsert.boundary: Pacific Islanders recruited for the Queensland cane fields, 1863 to 1906
upsert.description: Some 62,000 men and women from Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands are recruited, many by deception or force ('blackbirding'), to work on Queensland's sugar plantations; most are deported under the White Australia policy after 1906.
upsert.region: Oceania (Melanesia: Vanuatu, Solomon Islands; Australia and New Zealand: Australia)

upsert.boundary: The gold rushes of Australia and New Zealand, 1851 to 1900
upsert.description: Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria (1851), Otago (1861) and Western Australia (1890s) draws hundreds of thousands of migrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese; Victoria's population grows sevenfold in a decade and Melbourne becomes one of the richest cities in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Blainey, The Rush That Never Ended (5th ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Postwar migration remakes Australia and New Zealand, from 1945
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish', Australia takes millions of migrants from Britain, then southern and eastern Europe; the White Australia policy ends (1973) and migrants from Asia follow, until nearly a third of Australians are born overseas; Oceania grows from about 13 to 46 million people.
provenance: sources to check: Jupp, From White Australia to Woomera (2nd ed. 2007); Australian Bureau of Statistics

upsert.boundary: The Polynesian diaspora, from 1962
upsert.description: Samoans, Tongans, Cook Islanders and Niueans migrate to New Zealand, Australia and the United States for work; by the 2000s more Cook Islanders and Niueans live in New Zealand than at home, and remittances are among the largest shares of national income in the world for Tonga and Samoa.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, remittance data; Lee and Francis (eds.), Migration and Transnationalism (2009)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: Re-education camps and the boat people, 1975 to 1996

sources to check: Robinson, Terms of Refuge (1998); UNHCR, The State of the World's Refugees 2000

Most of the forced labourers and displaced persons go home, while the Germans expelled from the east and the Japanese repatriated replace them in the count: the share holds.

upsert.boundary: The Congo wars, 1996 to 2003
upsert.description: Rwanda and Uganda invade to pursue the génocidaires and overthrow Mobutu (1997); in the second war, from 1998, nine African states and many militias fight over the Congo and its minerals. Excess deaths are counted in millions, mostly from disease and hunger, though the highest estimates are disputed.

sources to check: Prunier, Africa's World War (2009); Stearns, Dancing in the Glory of Monsters (2011)

upsert.boundary: The Mexican Revolution, 1910 to 1920
upsert.description: Madero's revolt against Díaz opens a decade of civil war (Villa, Zapata, Carranza, Obregón); perhaps one to two million die or flee, and the 1917 constitution promises land reform and national control of oil and minerals.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll is contested
sources to check: Knight, The Mexican Revolution (1986)

upsert.boundary: The An Lushan rebellion, 755 to 763
upsert.description: A frontier general of Sogdian and Turkic descent rebels and takes both Tang capitals; the war and its famines cut the registered population from about 53 million to 17 million, though much of that fall is people lost to the census rather than dead. The Tang survive but lose Central Asia and control of the provinces.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is much disputed
sources to check: Twitchett (ed.), The Cambridge History of China vol. 3 (1979)

upsert.boundary: China's civil war, 1927 to 1949
upsert.description: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists turn on their Communist allies (1927); the Communists survive the Long March (1934 to 1935) and grow during the war with Japan, then defeat the Nationalists in 1946 to 1949; Mao proclaims the People's Republic in October 1949 and the Nationalists withdraw to Taiwan.
provenance: sources to check: Westad, Decisive Encounters (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Russian revolutions and civil war, 1917 to 1922
upsert.description: Wartime collapse brings down the tsar (February 1917); Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power (October), take Russia out of the war and win a civil war of terror, famine and epidemics that kills perhaps eight to ten million, founding the Soviet Union (December 1922), a one-party state that persecutes religion.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, Russia in Revolution (2017)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus); Asia (Central Asia)

upsert.boundary: Europe's wars of religion, 1562 to 1648
upsert.description: Catholics and Protestants fight across Europe: the French Wars of Religion (1562 to 1598), the Dutch Revolt against Spain (from 1568) and finally the Thirty Years' War, entangled with the rivalries of dynasties.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The French Wars of Religion (2nd ed. 2005); Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009)

upsert.boundary: The fall of the Han and the Three Kingdoms, 184 to 280.
upsert.description: The Yellow Turban rising, warlord wars and the Three Kingdoms: China's registered population falls from about 56 million to about 16 million, partly a collapse of registration, partly real loss. Jin reunifies China in 280.

upsert.boundary: The late Ming crisis, about 1550 to 1650.
upsert.description: After a century of growth China holds perhaps 150 to 200 million people; degree-holders multiply faster than offices, the Wanli court's finances fail, the defence of Liaodong against the Jurchen needs new land taxes, and the silver on which taxes are paid stops arriving in the 1630s. The structural-demographic cycle's state crisis, in the decades before the collapse.

Check the parts against the whole, and observe the parts. Fighting over who rules (h.war.within.government) is, by its parts' own definitions, the sum of the deaths in wars for the centre fought in Asia, Europe, the Americas, Africa and Oceania (opened at r487 to r492), all per 100,000 of all people a year averaged to the next date, so it is declared their sum through life_model_revise, everything else as it was. The nine Events that name it now also name the area they were fought in: Asia for the Han's fall, An Lushan, the late Ming crisis, the Taiping and China's civil war; Europe for the wars of religion and the Russian revolutions and civil war; the Americas for the Mexican Revolution; Africa for the Congo wars. Each Event is restated whole from the record read at r485, with only process_ids changed.

upsert.boundary: Postwar migration remakes Australia and New Zealand, from 1945
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish', Australia takes millions of migrants from Britain, then southern and eastern Europe; the White Australia policy ends (1973) and migrants from Asia follow, until nearly a third of Australians are born overseas; Oceania grows from about 13 to 46 million people.
provenance: sources to check: Jupp, From White Australia to Woomera (2nd ed. 2007); Australian Bureau of Statistics

upsert.boundary: George Tupou I unites Tonga and gives it a constitution, 1845 to 1875

provenance: sources to check: Lātūkefu, Church and State in Tonga (1974)

upsert.boundary: Missions convert the peoples of the Americas, 1524 to 1650
upsert.description: Franciscans arrive in Mexico in 1524, then Dominicans, Augustinians and Jesuits; millions are baptized, temples are destroyed and churches built on them, and an Indigenous Catholicism forms around saints and the Virgin of Guadalupe. upsert.boundary: The British Raj, 1858 to 1947
upsert.description: The Crown rules India through a viceroy, a small civil service and princely allies; railways, canals and telegraphs are built, and English education creates a new middle class, while India's income per head barely grows, famines kill tens of millions and India's taxes and trade surplus help pay for Britain's empire.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Raj's economic effect is debated
sources to check: Roy, The Economic History of India 1857–2010 (4th ed. 2020); Tomlinson, The Economy of Modern India (2013)
