upsert.boundary: Land reform in East and South Asia, 1946 to 1956
upsert.description: Under American occupation Japan buys out its landlords and sells the land to tenants (1946 to 1950); South Korea (1949 to 1950) and Taiwan (1949 to 1953) follow, China's Communists take the landlords' land by force (1950 to 1952), and India's states abolish the zamindari estates through the 1950s. Land taxes and rents fixed in money melt in the war's inflation, and states turn to taxes on incomes and goods.
provenance: sources to check: Kawagoe, in Hayami and Godo (eds.) (1999); Studwell, How Asia Works (2013)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (Japan, Korea, Taiwan, China), Southern Asia (India)

upsert.boundary: Mao's People's Republic, 1949 to 1976
upsert.description: The Communist Party unifies China, carries out a land reform in which perhaps a million or more landlords are killed, collectivizes farming, launches the Great Leap Forward and its famine and then the Cultural Revolution; it also roughly doubles life expectancy and spreads basic schooling. Religion is suppressed and the state teaches atheism.
provenance: sources to check: Dikötter, The Tragedy of Liberation (2013); MacFarquhar (ed.), The Politics of China (3rd ed. 2011)

upsert.boundary: The Buddha and Mahavira, about 500 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: In the cities of the Ganges plain, the Buddha teaches the end of suffering through the middle way and the eightfold path, and Mahavira the non-violence of Jainism; both found orders of monks and nuns that reject the authority of the Vedas and the priests.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Buddha's dates vary by about a century
sources to check: Gethin, The Foundations of Buddhism (1998)

upsert.boundary: Jesus and the rise of Christianity, about 30 to 380
upsert.description: Jesus of Nazareth is crucified in Jerusalem about 30 CE; his followers, Paul above all, spread the faith through the cities of the Roman empire; despite persecutions it grows to perhaps a tenth of the empire's people by 300; Constantine converts (312) and Theodosius makes it the state religion (380).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; growth figures follow Stark's estimates, which are debated
sources to check: Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996); MacCulloch, A History of Christianity (2009)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Judea, Syria, Anatolia); Europe (Southern Europe); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt, Carthage)

upsert.boundary: The COVID-19 pandemic, 2020 to May 2023.
upsert.description: About 15 to 20 million excess deaths; world life expectancy falls by nearly two years by 2021 and recovers by 2023.

upsert.boundary: Decolonization, 1945 to 1975.
upsert.description: From Indonesia and India to Angola and Mozambique, about eighty colonies become independent states; some keep elected government, many do not.

upsert.boundary: The divorce revolution, 1965 to 1990
upsert.description: California's no-fault law (1969), England's Divorce Reform Act (1969), Italy's divorce law (1970) and Spain's (1981) make divorce available or easy; in the West, and in the Soviet Union and eastern Europe, a third to a half of the marriages of the 1970s end in divorce, against a few in a hundred two generations before.
provenance: sources to check: Phillips, Putting Asunder (1988); Goode, World Changes in Divorce Patterns (1993)

upsert.boundary: The Western Church's marriage rules and Europe's kindreds, about 500 to 1200
upsert.description: The Latin Church forbids marriage between cousins to the sixth and then the seventh degree, and between in-laws and godkin, discourages adoption and remarriage of widows, and claims bequests; over these centuries the clans and lineages of much of western Europe give way to small households and to lordship, parish and guild. Whether the Church's rules caused this, or states, manors and towns did, is debated.
provenance: exploring: the thesis (Goody 1983; Schulz, Bahrami-Rad, Beauchamp and Henrich 2019) that the Church's marriage rules dissolved Europe's kin groups is debated; critics point to kindreds already weak in late Rome, and to states, manors and towns (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)
sources to check: Goody, The Development of the Family and Marriage in Europe (1983); Schulz et al., Science 366 (2019)

upsert.boundary: The Congress of Vienna, 1814 to 1815
upsert.description: The victorious powers redraw Europe's map and set up a concert of great powers that keeps a general peace for almost a century, broken by limited wars.
provenance: sources to check: Schroeder, The Transformation of European Politics 1763–1848 (1994)

upsert.boundary: The Holocaust, 1941 to 1945
upsert.description: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murder about six million Jews, two-thirds of Europe's Jews, by mass shootings in the east and in the gas chambers of Auschwitz, Treblinka and other death camps; Roma, disabled people and millions of Soviet prisoners and Polish civilians are also murdered.
provenance: sources to check: Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (3rd ed. 2003); Friedländer, The Years of Extermination (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933
upsert.description: Forced collectivization and grain requisitions starve some five to seven million people, about four million in Ukraine, where the regime seals off the starving villages, and more than a million Kazakhs, nearly 40% of them.
provenance: sources to check: Davies and Wheatcroft, The Years of Hunger (2004); Applebaum, Red Famine (2017); Cameron, The Hungry Steppe (2018)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Ukraine, Russia); Asia (Central Asia: Kazakhstan)

upsert.boundary: Napoleon's wars, 1799 to 1815
upsert.description: Napoleon seizes power, crowns himself emperor and conquers most of continental Europe, spreading his Civil Code and abolishing the Holy Roman Empire, until the retreat from Moscow (1812) and defeat at Leipzig and Waterloo (1815); some three to six million die.
provenance: sources to check: Bell, The First Total War (2007)

upsert.boundary: The age of great dams and hydroelectricity, 1930 to 2012
upsert.description: Hoover (1936), Grand Coulee (1942), the Soviet Union's Volga and Dnieper dams, Aswan's High Dam (1970), Itaipu (1984) and the Three Gorges (2003 to 2012) lead some 50,000 large dams built by 2000; hydroelectricity grows from about 100 to about 3,500 terawatt-hours a year, and the reservoirs hold back about three centimetres of sea level, while tens of millions of people are moved from the valleys they flood.
provenance: sources to check: World Commission on Dams, Dams and Development (2000); Chao, Wu and Li, Science 320 (2008)

upsert.boundary: The green revolution, 1960 to 2000.
upsert.description: High-yielding wheat and rice, with fertilizer and irrigation, double and triple cereal yields across Asia and Latin America; food per person rises while population doubles.

upsert.boundary: Groundwater mining for irrigation, from about 1960
upsert.description: Tube wells and electric pumps in India's Punjab, the North China Plain, the Middle East and the American High Plains draw down aquifers faster than rain refills them; the water pumped out ends in the sea, and since about 2000 it outweighs what new reservoirs hold back.
provenance: sources to check: Wada et al., Geophysical Research Letters 37 (2010); Shah, Taming the Anarchy (2009)
upsert.region: Asia (Southern, Eastern and Western Asia); the Americas (Northern America)

upsert.boundary: The internet, from 1969
upsert.description: From ARPANET (1969) and TCP/IP (1983) through the World Wide Web, invented at CERN (1989 to 1991), and the smartphone (2007), the internet reaches about two-thirds of humanity by 2024, joining people, markets and knowledge in one network.
provenance: sources to check: Abbate, Inventing the Internet (1999); ITU, Facts and Figures 2024
upsert.region: Americas (Northern America); Europe; Asia; then everywhere

upsert.boundary: Muhammad, the Arab conquests and the Umayyad caliphate, 610 to 750
upsert.description: In Mecca and Medina Muhammad preaches submission to one God and unites the tribes of Arabia (610 to 632); within a century his successors conquer the Sasanian empire, Byzantine Syria and Egypt, North Africa and Spain, and reach the Indus and Central Asia. The Umayyad caliphs rule from Damascus one of the largest empires yet; conversion to Islam among the conquered, slow at first, follows over the next centuries. The Abbasid revolution ends Umayyad rule in 750.
provenance: sources to check: Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010); Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Arabia, the Levant, Iraq; Southern Asia: Iran; Central Asia); Africa (Northern Africa); Europe (Southern Europe: Iberia)

upsert.boundary: Watermills and windmills spread, about 900 to 1300
upsert.description: Watermills grind grain, full cloth, saw timber and work forge bellows across Europe, the Islamic world and Song China; Domesday Book counts about 6,000 mills in England (1086), and the post windmill appears in England and Flanders in the 1180s. Mechanical power from water and wind roughly doubles per person, though it stays a few hundredths of a gigajoule a year, against hundreds of times more from fuel wood and food.
provenance: sources to check: Langdon, Mills in the Medieval Economy (2004); Lucas, Wind, Water, Work (2006)

upsert.boundary: Monogamy made law, 1926 to 1956
upsert.description: Turkey's civil code (1926) abolishes polygamy, China's Marriage Law (1950) bans concubinage, India's Hindu Marriage Act (1955) makes Hindu marriage monogamous, and Tunisia's Code of Personal Status (1956) bans polygamy; the plural unions of Asia's elites fade within a generation, while polygyny remains common in much of Africa.
provenance: sources to check: Goode, World Revolution and Family Patterns (1963); Diamant, Revolutionizing the Family (2000)
upsert.region: Asia (Western, Eastern and Southern Asia); Africa (Northern Africa: Tunisia)

upsert.boundary: Oceania becomes Christian, 1797 to about 1900
upsert.description: London Missionary Society missionaries land on Tahiti from the Duff (1797); after Pomare II's victory at Fei Pi (1815) Tahiti turns Christian, followed by Hawai'i (from 1820), Tonga and Samoa (1820s and 1830s), Fiji (1850s) and, largely through Pacific Islander teachers, much of Melanesia; Marsden preaches in New Zealand from 1814. Missions bring writing in the islanders' own languages; today about nine in ten Pacific Islanders are Christian.
provenance: sources to check: Garrett, To Live Among the Stars (1982)
upsert.region: Oceania: Polynesia, Melanesia, Micronesia, Australia and New Zealand

upsert.boundary: Clearing tropical forest, 1950 to now.
upsert.description: Cattle, soy, oil palm, smallholders and logging clear forest in Amazonia, south-east Asia and central Africa.

changes.value: Widen: sixteen processes were observed by no Event. Where an existing Event plainly moves one, it now names it: China's People's Republic and the Soviet famine (kin groups beyond the household, broken by land reform, collectivization and the Kazakhs' forced settlement); Napoleon's wars, the Congress of Vienna and decolonization (colonial rule in Europe: Malta taken in 1800, the Ionian Islands' protectorate of 1815, Malta's independence of 1964); the Raj and the Holocaust (peripatetic trades: the Criminal Tribes Act and railways, the murder of Roma and Sinti); COVID-19 (the development index, which fell in 2020 and 2021); the Buddha and Mahavira, the rise of Christianity and of Islam (belief in a moral order and the share in faiths that seek converts), and the missions of the Americas and Oceania (that share); the green revolution (value added in food-getting); the internet (services trade and services output); tropical clearing (other foods: oil palm and soy). Where none did, new Events are added from what the series' own notes already name, each placed and contained by the account's conventions: the medieval mills (flows harnessed by machines), the great dams (flows and water held on land), groundwater mining (water held on land), the divorce revolution (how marriages end), monogamy laws across Asia (plural unions), the Western Church's marriage rules and Europe's kindreds (kin groups, a debated thesis tagged exploring), and the land reforms of East and South Asia (revenue from land and wealth's concentration). Existing Events are restated whole from the records read at r495, with only process_ids changed.

Fill: the report names 1870 to 1890 as the coarsest stretch of the survival and household measures, which held only their 1870 and 1890 values while hunger already has values at the El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879. Values at 1877, the famines' peak, and 1885, between them and Ethiopia's famine and the rinderpest of 1888: the famines' excess deaths are counted under hunger (by its definition, whatever their proximate disease), so they lower life expectancy by about a year in their years and lift child and adult deaths a little, while infection, chronic disease and injury go on along their paths (cholera's fifth pandemic from 1881, industrial accidents rising). Child mortality is kept the sum of its three age bands. All recalled or reasoned, sharing one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Ethnographic foragers reaching fifteen live on about 37 to 43 years (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled); the model's life expectancy of 30 with child mortality of 45% would imply about 45, so one of those two existing values, most likely the forager child mortality, is too high: ethnographic foragers lose about a quarter to a third of children before five.
Held from the deep forager reading: remaining years at 15 for mobile foragers, from the ethnographic range of recent foragers (about 37 to 43) widened for the deep past; no evidence turns it here.
Farmers' adults live shorter lives than foragers': crowd diseases from livestock and crowding, worse teeth and bones in the skeletons (Armelagos's first epidemiological transition).
Roman tombstones and Egyptian census returns give adults of fifteen some 30 to 35 more years: crowded cities and malaria kill adults as well as children.
The Justinianic plague kills adults as freely as children.
The Black Death at its height kills people of every age in the year it passes (ev.black-death).

Smallpox reaches the Caribbean (1518) and Mexico (1520) and kills adults as well as children, but in about a tenth of humanity: a fall of several years there moves the world's figure by under half a year, inside the band.
The Taiping war and the American Civil War kill young men above all.
On the eve of the First World War: the fall to 1918 is the war's and the influenza's, so the series holds until here and drops after.
The 1918 influenza kills young adults above all, with the war's dead: adult survival falls by a sixth in a year while child mortality barely moves.
The war's deadliest years and the famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
War deaths and the war's famines last into 1945 (Vietnam, Java, the Dutch hunger winter, the battles for Germany, Okinawa and Manila), so adult survival is still near the 1944 low.
The war ends in August and September 1945: young men stop dying in battle and the occupied lands' famines end, so adult survival jumps.
On the postwar rise; the lower value at 1960 is the Great Leap famine's dip, not the trend.
The Great Leap Forward famine holds adult survival down in 1959 to 1961.
Recovering from the Great Leap famine of 1959 to 1961.
Slowed by AIDS in eastern and southern Africa and by the mortality crisis of Russian and Ukrainian men after 1991.
COVID-19's first year: excess deaths in 2020 are under a third of the pandemic's toll, so adult survival falls about halfway to the 2021 trough.
COVID-19 kills adults, the old above all (ev.covid).
About 33 births a year per 1,000 people, of whom perhaps one in twelve dies in the first month, and about one mother in a hundred births.
Held: deaths of mothers and newborns around birth, scaled from natural fertility of about six births per woman and recent forager neonatal loss.
Farmers have more births, closer together, and so more deaths at birth per head.
Semmelweis shows in 1847 that childbed fever is carried by doctors' hands; antisepsis reaches maternity wards only after 1870.
Sulfa drugs cut deaths from puerperal fever in rich countries by half within a few years.
About five million newborns and half a million mothers die a year, as the UN's child-mortality group and maternal-mortality group count them.
About 2.3 million newborns and 260,000 mothers a year, more than half of each in Sub-Saharan Africa.
Few live long enough to die of them; the old who do are often recorded as dying of a last infection.
Held: degenerative deaths at older ages in the few who reach them; low because few live past 60, not because the old do not die of them.
As infections retreat in the industrial countries more people reach the ages of heart disease and cancer; cigarettes spread after 1880.

Heart disease and lung cancer peak in rich countries; their fall afterwards, with less smoking and treated blood pressure, is matched by the poor world's ageing, so the world rate per head holds near five hundred.
About 42 million deaths, three in four of all, by the Global Burden of Disease's count, as recalled.
Rising per head as the world ages, though each age's rate keeps falling.
About two thirds of foragers' deaths are from illness, mostly respiratory and gut infections and parasites (Gurven and Kaplan's comparison, as recalled).

Held: infection in small mobile bands without crowd diseases, mostly gut, respiratory and wound infections and parasites in children; the largest share of forager deaths, as in recent forager mortality studies.
Villages, stored grain, livestock and standing water bring crowd diseases and parasites: infections rise with farming, the first epidemiological transition (Armelagos).
Malaria in Italy's lowlands, gut infections in Rome's crowded city: about seven in ten deaths are infections.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), probably smallpox, which killed perhaps a tenth of the Roman Empire's people.
The Justinianic plague (ev.justinian-plague), the first pandemic of Yersinia pestis.
The plague recurs until about 750 and then vanishes from the Mediterranean for six centuries; infection deaths fall back to their agrarian level.
The Black Death at its height (ev.black-death): the infection death rate more than doubles for the years it passes.
Plague returns every decade or two after 1348.
Smallpox reaches the Caribbean in 1518 and Mexico in 1520; the Americas' epidemics raise the world's infection deaths toward the 1550 value, though the Americas hold about a tenth of humanity.
Smallpox, measles and cocoliztli in the Americas (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd) add deaths, though the Americas are a tenth of humanity.
Jenner's vaccine (1796) begins the retreat of smallpox; plague has left Europe.

Cholera's second pandemic reaches Russia, Europe and North America (ev.cholera-pandemics). Its deaths, most of them in India, add a few tens per 100,000 a year to infection's thousands, while vaccination keeps smallpox falling, so the total barely moves.
Cholera pandemics in the new industrial cities; sanitation's retreat of infection begins in Britain after the 1848 Public Health Act.
The famines' excess deaths count under hunger whatever their proximate disease; infection holds its path between cholera's fourth pandemic (to 1875) and its fifth (from 1881).
Germ theory, clean water and sewers cut infection deaths in Europe and North America; most of the world has not yet begun.
Before the influenza: the 1918 value is the pandemic's spike, not a trend, so the fall since 1900 continues to here; wartime typhus in Serbia and the east adds little at the world's scale.
The 1918 influenza kills perhaps 25 to 50 million in little more than a year, most in India and China (ev.flu-1918).
The influenza has passed by 1920 and the long fall of infection deaths resumes.
Sulfa drugs, from 1935, the first antibacterial medicines.
Penicillin, streptomycin and DDT spread after the war: infection deaths fall faster than at any time before.
About 1967 chronic disease passes infection as the world's leading cause of death.
Smallpox is declared eradicated (1980); the Expanded Programme on Immunization reaches most children by 1990.
HIV/AIDS climbs toward its peak of about two million deaths a year (2004).
COVID-19's first year: about four to five million excess deaths in 2020 on the WHO's estimate, under a third of the pandemic's toll, which peaks in 2021.
COVID-19: about 15 million excess deaths in 2020 and 2021 on the WHO's estimate, most of them in 2021 (ev.covid).
Hunting, falls, drowning, snakebite and burns: about one forager death in fifteen.
Held: accidents, falls, drowning, animal attack among mobile hunters; violence is counted in h.safety, not here.

On the line between the agrarian sketch (about 210) and the level of early registration data at 1850 (about 140). The step is a change of estimate, not of the world: European registers count injury as about one death in twenty-five, foragers' and some agrarian peoples' accident shares are higher, and which holds for the agrarian world is debated, so the bands overlap.

Revised down from the agrarian level: the share of deaths from injury in early registration data (England, Sweden) is about one in twenty-five, lower than the forager and agrarian sketches assumed; the earlier values stay as they are with their wide bands.
Mines, railways and factories: industrial accidents peak in the late nineteenth century.
Road deaths peak in rich countries about 1970, then fall with seat belts and safer cars, while they rise in the poor world.
About 1.2 million road deaths, 700,000 suicides, and falls and drownings: the Global Burden of Disease's injuries without interpersonal violence and war, as recalled.
Early farming villages: denser settlement and zoonoses lowered life expectancy below foragers'.
The Antonine plague and the Han collapse.
Just after the first wave; during 1348–1350 period life expectancy in the stricken regions fell far lower.
Plague returned every decade or two after 1348; life expectancy below both 1300 and 1500.
Riley's world estimate for 1800 is about 28.5, as recalled.
Cholera reaches Europe and North America (ev.cholera-pandemics) while vaccination keeps smallpox falling: the world's life expectancy hardly moves.
The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 in India, north China and Brazil (ev.as.el-nino-famines) cut world life expectancy by about a year in their years.
Recovers after the rains of 1879; Koch's discoveries (1882 to 1884) do not yet reach mortality outside Europe's cities.
Before the First World War and the 1918 influenza.
The influenza year, about five years below 1910.
The war widens to the Soviet Union and, in December, the Pacific.
The war at its deadliest and Bengal's famine (1943): period life expectancy keeps falling toward the 1944 low.
The war's deadliest stretch, with the Bengal and Henan famines of 1942-44: period life expectancy dips below 1940's.
War deaths and the famines of Bengal (1943), Henan (1942–43), Vietnam and the Netherlands (1944–45) hold life expectancy down until the war ends.
The war ends in August 1945; deaths fall at once.
Peace, sulfa drugs, penicillin and DDT: life expectancy rises fast after the war.
Revised from 50: the Great Chinese Famine pulls world life expectancy down in 1959–1961.
Recovered from the Chinese famine and rising fast with vaccines and antibiotics in the poor world.
The COVID-19 trough.

Most foragers reckon descent through both parents and live in flexible bands; some (Aboriginal Australians, many Amazonian and North American peoples) have clans and moieties: about three in ten, guessed from ethnographic foragers.
Farming makes land and herds property worth holding in common by descent: lineages and clans spread with farmers.
About three in five people live under clans or lineages: China's, India's, the Middle East's tribes, Africa's lineages, the Celtic and Germanic kindreds.

Western Christendom's kin groups dissolve under the Church's bans on cousin marriage and its rules on inheritance (Goody), from about 600 to 1500; the debated root of Europe's individualism and of its guilds, communes and universities (Henrich; Greif; critics stress institutions and the state instead).
South China's lineages, with their halls, estates and genealogies, are at their strongest from the Song to the Qing, while western Europe's kin groups are nearly gone.
Europe's and North America's fast-growing populations, with nuclear families, lower the world's share slowly.
Soviet collectivization and settlement break the clans of Central Asia's herders.
China's land reform (1950 to 1952) takes the lineages' estates and ends their courts; collectivization and, from 1966, the attacks on ancestral halls finish them as corporate groups for a generation.
Held near a third: south China's lineages revive after 1980 and Africa's growing share of humanity lives mostly in lineage societies, against cities and schooling everywhere.
About a quarter to a third: much of sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East's and Central and South Asia's tribes and castes, and rural south China.
Nearly half of foragers' child deaths come after weaning, at about two to four: hunger, infections and accidents.
In agrarian populations the crowd diseases of childhood (later measles and smallpox) kill most at these ages.
The plague's returns in the decades after the Black Death kill children above all.
Smallpox vaccination (Jenner, 1796) begins to cut deaths at these ages where it spreads.
Vaccination keeps cutting smallpox deaths at these ages where it reaches; cholera kills adults more than young children.
Famine kills young children above all: ages one to four rise a little above their path in the famine years.
The wartime famines of Bengal, Henan and Vietnam kill weaned children most.
Measles vaccine (1963) and the smallpox eradication campaign (1967 to 1977) cut deaths at these ages fastest of the three.
Malaria in sub-Saharan Africa keeps deaths at one to four high as other ages fall.
Insecticide-treated nets and new vaccines (pneumococcal, rotavirus) halve these deaths in fifteen years.
About 9 per 1,000 births, a quarter of deaths before five, from about two fifths for most of history.
About a quarter of foragers' child deaths: infections of the breastfed infant.
Farming raises infancy's deaths: cereal gruels as weaning food, crowding and dirty water.
The urban penalty: infants in the industrial cities die of diarrhoea and dirty water faster than in the countryside.
Clean water, sewers and safer milk begin to cut infancy's deaths in Europe and North America.
Oral rehydration salts, adopted widely from the late 1970s, cut infants' deaths from diarrhoea.
About 10 per 1,000 births.
About a quarter of foragers' deaths before five come in the first month: birth, prematurity and the infections of the newborn.
The first month falls least of the three: its deaths yield to skilled birth care, not to clean water or vaccines.
About 37 per 1,000 births, two fifths of all deaths before five (UN Inter-agency Group, as recalled).
About 17 per 1,000 births, nearly half of all deaths before five: prematurity, birth asphyxia and newborn infections.
