Fill: the report names 1870 to 1890 as the coarsest stretch of the range people live on and use, by area, and of the share in towns and cities. 1880 is filled on the line between its neighbours, wholes kept the sum of their parts (range = the six areas; the Americas = Latin America and the Caribbean + Northern America). The range barely moves now: by 1870 almost all ice-free land is lived on or used, and the frontiers of settlement change who uses land, not whether it is used.

points.note: All of range is African: Homo sapiens from Jebel Irhoud to Florisbad, in patches between deserts and other hominins' lands, about half of Africa's land.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara hyperarid, people in the wetter east, south and coasts.
Termination II ends the penultimate glacial: the monsoon reaches the Sahara again and rivers and lakes open it, so Africa's part rises by half in a few thousand years.
The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes: Africa's part nearly doubles, close to the whole continent.
The glacial returns and the Sahara dries.
Holds while the dispersal fills Asia, Sahul and Europe: the dispersal added land elsewhere, it did not empty Africa.
The glacial maximum's aridity: the Sahara and the Kalahari spread, the rainforest shrinks to refuges.
The African Humid Period begins (from about 10,500 BCE): the first lakes and grass return to the Sahara before the Younger Dryas ends, and hunters follow them north.
The African Humid Period: lakes and grassland across the Sahara as far as Lake Mega-Chad, hunters and then cattle herders across it.
Africa's highest: almost all of its land within range.
The African Humid Period has ended: the herders withdraw to the Nile, the Sahel and the oases, and the Sahara's core empties, about 2.8 points of the world's land given up in a thousand years.
The camel spreads across the Sahara from about the first centuries CE and lets nomads use more of the desert between the oases.
Voyagers from Borneo have settled Madagascar, about 0.4 points of the world's land.
Motor tracks, oil and gas fields (Hassi Messaoud, 1956) and mines carry regular use into parts of the Sahara's core that only caravans had crossed.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Africa's land (about 30.3 million km2), the Sahara's green and dry phases, and the dated Events of the account; the Sahara's hyperarid core, about 2 to 3 points of the world's land, is outside range in dry phases.

points.note: Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico (stone tools about 30,000 years ago) would put people here before the glacial maximum; whether its stones are tools is debated, so the value stays at zero with the band open.

Monte Verde in southern Chile (about 12,500 BCE): people reach the far south within about a millennium of the first secure Pacific coast sites, faster than a front could walk (a coastal spread by jumps).
Peopled to Tierra del Fuego: South America and Mexico near their ceiling, except the high Andes' ice, the Patagonian ice sheet's remnants and the islands.
The first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola, about 0.1 points of the world's land.
Archaic and then Saladoid (from about 500 BCE) islanders spread through Puerto Rico and the Lesser Antilles; the Bahamas wait until about 700 CE.

The Lucayans of the Bahamas are carried off as slaves and the islands are empty by 1520; Hispaniola's and Cuba's Taino die of war, forced labour and smallpox (1518): the islands are the first land in the account to fall out of range.
The epidemics empty the Amazon's floodplain chiefdoms and parts of northern Mexico and the Caribbean for a time; the forest grows back over them.
The Trans-Amazonian highway (from 1970) and Brazil's frontier settlement bring forest emptied since the epidemics back into regular use, along with the ranches and roads of the Chaco and Patagonia.
Nearly all of Latin America's ice-free land; the Atacama's core and the Andes' highest ground are the rest.
Bluefish Caves in the Yukon (cut-marked bones about 24,000 years ago, debated) would put people in eastern Beringia before the glacial maximum; the band keeps it open.
The White Sands footprints (about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago) put people south of the ice in New Mexico; their reach is unknown.
The Pacific coast opens as the Cordilleran ice pulls back; Cooper's Ferry in Idaho (about 16,000 years ago) and Swan Point in Alaska.
Clovis hunters spread across the unglaciated south of North America within about three centuries.
South of the ice nearly all of North America is lived on; the Laurentide ice still covers much of Canada.
The Laurentide ice is almost gone and hunters follow the caribou north across Canada; the high Arctic and Greenland stay outside range.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic islands to Greenland's ice-free coasts, about two points of the world's land no one had lived on: Northern America's, and the Americas', last large gain.
Unchanged: the Norse farms of south-west Greenland (from 985) use a few tens of thousands of square kilometres, and Late Dorset people already hunt in the north-west.
Polynesians settle Hawai'i (about 1000 to 1200), part of the United States by 2026 borders, and the Thule Inuit spread from Alaska across the Arctic to Greenland.
After de Soto's entrada (1539 to 1543) and the epidemics that followed, the Mississippian chiefdoms of the south-east and parts of the Mississippi valley are emptied for a time.
Settlers' farms and the mounted peoples of the Plains bring land emptied after the epidemics back into regular use.
Weather stations, airfields and mines on Canada's Arctic islands (Resolute, 1947; Alert, 1950) and Greenland's bases bring the high Arctic's last empty land into regular use.
Nearly all of Northern America's ice-free land; the emptiest Arctic islands are the rest.
Claims of people in the Americas before the glacial maximum (Chiquihuite Cave in Mexico, about 30,000 years ago) are debated; the band keeps them open.

The footprints at White Sands, New Mexico (about 23,000 to 21,000 years ago), put people south of the ice during the glacial maximum; the dates are debated but have held against two later tests. Their numbers and reach are unknown, so the part is small and the band wide.
The peopling of the Americas proper begins: a coastal route along the Pacific is open as the Cordilleran ice retreats from the coast.
Monte Verde in southern Chile (about 12,500 BCE) and the Paisley Caves in Oregon (about 12,300 BCE): people reach both ends of the hemisphere within a thousand years.
Clovis hunters spread across North America within about three centuries (from about 11,100 BCE), the fastest gain in range in the account.
Peopled to Tierra del Fuego; the Laurentide ice still covers much of Canada, and the Arctic islands and Greenland stay empty.
The Laurentide ice is almost gone and hunters follow the caribou north across Canada; the high Arctic and Greenland remain outside range.
The first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola, about 0.1 points of the world's land.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic to Greenland's ice-free coasts, about two points of the world's land that no one had lived on: the last large gain in range.

Unchanged: the Norse settlements of south-west Greenland (from 985) use a few tens of thousands of square kilometres, about 0.02 points, and Late Dorset people already hunt in the north-west; the Norse are gone by about 1450.
Polynesians settle Hawai'i (about 1000 to 1200), which by 2026 borders is part of the United States and so of this part; the Thule Inuit spread across the Arctic from Alaska to Greenland.
The epidemics after 1492 empty parts of the Americas for a time, the Mississippi and Amazon floodplains and the Caribbean's islands among them: the one area whose range falls in the historical era.
Weather stations, airfields and mines on Canada's Arctic islands (Resolute, 1947; Alert, 1950) and Greenland's bases bring the high Arctic's last empty land into regular use.
Nearly all the Americas' ice-free land: the Atacama's core and the emptiest Arctic islands are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from the Americas' ice-free land (about 38.7 million km2), the account's dated Events of their peopling (White Sands, Monte Verde, the Paisley Caves, Clovis, the Paleo-Inuit) and the epidemics after 1492.

points.note: No one reaches Antarctica for almost all of human history.
Cook crosses the Antarctic Circle (1773) and circles the continent without seeing it.
Antarctica is first sighted (January 1820); sealers land on the South Shetlands the next summer.
Sealers work the South Shetlands and the Peninsula's islands each summer until the fur seals are nearly gone (by the 1830s).
Sealers' seasonal camps on the South Shetland beaches.
Argentina's station on Laurie Island (1904), the first held year round, and the whalers' station at Deception Island (from 1906).
Unchanged: Amundsen's and Scott's parties reach the Pole and leave no station; the land in use is still the whalers' shore stations and Laurie Island.
Britain's Operation Tabarin (1944) sets up the first permanent bases on the Antarctic Peninsula.
The IGY's fifty stations, from McMurdo to Vostok, bring most of the coastal oases and the dry valleys within regular reach.
The treaty (December 1959) keeps the IGY's stations open for science under shared rules.
The International Geophysical Year (1957 to 1958) and the treaty that followed put some forty stations on the continent and field parties into the dry valleys.
About seventy stations and the field science of the treaty's members reach most of the ice-free ground at least in summer.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Antarctica's ice-free area (about 45,000 km2 as recalled) and the dates of sealing, the first stations and the treaty's science.

points.note: The Misliya jaw (about 185,000 years ago) puts Homo sapiens in the Levant for a time: a first, small excursion out of Africa.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant (Skhul and Qafzeh) and greens Arabia's interior, where lakes and stone tools of African type appear.
The glacial returns: Arabia dries, and the Levant goes back to the Neanderthals by about 90,000 years ago.
A few groups hold on in Arabia's south and east (Jebel Faya); whether others reached India before Toba is debated.
The dispersal: people move along southern Asia from Arabia through India to Sunda within a few thousand years.
Eastern and central Asia are entered: north China, Mongolia's steppe, the Altai (where people meet the Denisovans) and the Tibetan margins.
The glacial maximum dries Central Asia and north China into desert and loess; people withdraw from the Mongolian plateau and the high steppe, while Sundaland's lowlands, then dry land, stay in range.
The early Holocene monsoon greens Arabia and the Thar again, and the steppe and north China are reoccupied.
Asia's highest before the modern era: Arabia's interior has lakes, hunters and then herders.
Arabia's humid phase has ended with Africa's: the Rub' al Khali and the Nafud empty, and herders keep to their edges and the oases.
Barley farmers and yak herders settle the high Tibetan plateau year round (from about 1600 BCE), while the drying of Central Asia's lowlands takes back about as much.
Oil camps and roads reach Arabia's interior and the Taklamakan's rim; the Rub' al Khali's core stays outside regular use.
About 86% of Asia's land in range; the empty quarter, the Taklamakan's core and the highest Tibetan and Karakoram ground are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Asia's land without Russia (about 31.5 million km2), the Levant's and Arabia's green phases, the dispersal's dates and the deserts and high plateaus that stay outside range.

points.note: A skull at Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) has been read as Homo sapiens, which would be a brief excursion; the reading is debated, and Europe is otherwise the Neanderthals' for another 160,000 years.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley (about 54,000 years ago) holds a Homo sapiens tooth between Neanderthal layers: a first, short-lived foothold.
Homo sapiens spreads from the Balkans (Bacho Kiro, about 45,000 years ago) across Europe and into western Siberia (Ust'-Ishim), meeting the last Neanderthals.
People live at the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and across the Russian plain: under M49 all of Russia is Europe, so Siberia's peopling is this part's.

The glacial maximum: ice covers Scandinavia and the north of Britain and Russia, polar desert spreads across Siberia's north, and people hold refuges in Iberia, southern France, Italy, the Balkans, the Russian plain's south and southern Siberia.
The Bølling warmth (from about 12,700 BCE): Magdalenian and Hamburgian hunters follow the reindeer north across Germany and Poland, and Siberia's north is reoccupied.
The Scandinavian ice has melted and hunters live in the north of Norway and Finland and on the Arctic coasts; Zhokhov Island in the New Siberian Islands is used about 6000 BCE.
Herders and hunters push into the drier steppe and the northern taiga: a quarter of a point over a millennium.
Iceland, settled from about 870, is mostly taken in by 900.
Norse settlers have made Iceland's ice-free land (about 0.07 points of the world's) part of range since about 870.
Russia's Arctic coasts and Kamchatka gain posts and hunting camps, and Svalbard's coasts hold whalers' and trappers' stations.
The Soviet Northern Sea Route, Gulag camps and mines (Vorkuta, Norilsk, Kolyma) bring the far north and Siberia's interior into regular use.
About 86% of Europe's land with Russia in range; the high Arctic islands' interiors and the emptiest tundra are the rest.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Europe's land with all of Russia (about 23.4 million km2), the dates of Homo sapiens' arrival, the ice sheets and polar deserts of the glacial maximum and the Arctic's late settlement.

points.note: Madjedbebe in northern Australia has been dated to about 65,000 years ago, which would put people in Sahul here; many read the site's layers as mixed and prefer about 50,000. The account follows the later date (ev.oc.sahul-arrival) and keeps the earlier one in the band.
People cross the Wallacean straits to Sahul, the longest sea crossings anyone had made, and land in New Guinea and northern Australia.
Within a few thousand years people live across Australia's coasts and rivers (Lake Mungo by about 42,000 years ago) and New Guinea's highlands.
Tasmania, then joined to the mainland, and the Bismarcks and Solomons of Near Oceania are reached.

The glacial maximum dries Australia's interior into dune fields: Aboriginal people withdraw to refuges on the coasts, the ranges and the rivers, giving up perhaps two fifths of the continent for several thousand years.
The interior is reoccupied as the climate eases; Tasmania is cut off by the rising sea about 12,000 years ago and stays inhabited.
Lapita voyagers reach Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa (about 1100 to 800 BCE), the first people in Remote Oceania.
East Polynesia's settlement, by the short chronology from about 900 to 1000, adds islands too small to show; New Zealand, about 0.2 points, is still empty until about 1280.
East Polynesia is settled from the Society Islands to Rapa Nui (about 1000 to 1200): many islands, little land.
East Polynesians settle Aotearoa (about 1280), the last large land on Earth to be peopled, about 0.2 points of the world's land.
The First Fleet (1788) brings settlers to land already within Aboriginal range: colonization changes who holds the land, not how much of it is held.
Unchanged since Aotearoa's settlement: every later change in Oceania (colonization, dispossession, the cities) is a change in who holds the land and how densely, not how much of it is held.

upsert.reason: Reasoned from Oceania's land (about 8.5 million km2), the debated date of Sahul's peopling, the glacial maximum's desert refuges and the dates of Lapita's and the Polynesians' voyages.

points.note: Homo sapiens across Africa (Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Florisbad in the south, Omo in Ethiopia), but in patches between deserts and other hominins' lands: about a tenth of today's ice-free land, Africa being under a quarter of it.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and people hold the wetter east and south of Africa and its coasts.

The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes and opens the Levant and Arabia: the first time Homo sapiens holds land outside Africa for long (Skhul and Qafzeh). Range doubles in a few thousand years.
The glacial returns: the Sahara dries and the Levant goes back to the Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia.
The dispersal: people spread along southern Asia from Arabia to Sunda in a few thousand years, adding about seven million km2.

The largest gain in range in the account: in about ten thousand years people take in Sahul, Europe, eastern and northern Asia; WaveOfAdvance#4cec's fronts on land and long sea crossings to Sahul (the card's long-distance jumps) together.
People live as far north as the Yana River in Arctic Siberia (about 32,000 years ago) and in Japan, Tibet's margins and Tasmania.

The glacial maximum begins: the ice sheets advance, the steppe of Siberia and the north European plain turn to polar desert and Australia's interior dries; people begin to withdraw to refuges in southern Europe, the Russian plain's south, the Altai and the Australian coasts, and range falls toward its glacial low of about a third of the land by 21,000 BCE.

Corrected from 50. The deglaciation begins to open the north: Magdalenian hunters spread from Iberia and southern France toward the Paris Basin and Germany, and Siberia's south is reoccupied. People are probably already south of the ice in the Americas (White Sands), but most of the Americas' peopling comes after 13,000 BCE (Monte Verde about 12,500 BCE, Clovis about 11,100 BCE). The earlier value read '14,500 years ago' as 14,500 BCE.
Corrected from 53, for the same reason as at -14600.
Corrected from 57. The Bølling warmth (from about 12,700 BCE) carries hunters north across Europe and the Russian plain; the Americas are entered along the Pacific coast and the ice-free corridor.
Corrected from 62: Monte Verde in Chile and the Paisley Caves in Oregon are occupied, but much of the Americas' interior is not yet reached.
Corrected from 66.
Corrected from 70. Clovis hunters spread across North America in a few centuries; the Younger Dryas (from about 10,950 BCE) brings the cold back to the north and dries the Sahara.

Corrected from 82. Late in the Younger Dryas: the Americas are peopled to Tierra del Fuego, but the Sahara is still dry and the north still cold; the Holocene's warmth and the African Humid Period lift range again from 9700 BCE.
Near its prehistoric peak: the Sahara and Arabia are grassland with lakes, hunters and then herders live across them, and the Laurentide ice is almost gone.
The Sahara's grasslands are already thinning at their edges; Varna's chiefs and the Balkan copper towns live inside a range that farming filled but did not widen.

Two moves nearly cancel: the first people cross to Cuba and Hispaniola (about 0.1% of the land), while the African Humid Period ends and the Sahara's herders begin to withdraw to the Nile, the Sahel and the oases, the largest loss of range since the glacial maximum, played out over the next thousand years.
The Paleo-Inuit cross the Canadian Arctic to Greenland's ice-free coasts, adding about three million km2 of tundra no one had lived on.

Holds: the first millennium BCE adds no new land. The Axial age's schools and cities change how people think and live inside a range already near its Holocene extent; only the Paleo-Inuit's later Dorset phase and the herders' spread into the drier steppe move it by fractions.
Voyagers from Borneo have settled Madagascar (about 0.4% of the land), the last large uninhabited land of the Old World tropics.
Iceland is settled from about 870; East Polynesia's islands and the Norse fjords of Greenland (from 985) are tiny in the world's land, and gunpowder changes nothing here.
East Polynesians reach Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land to be peopled; Iceland (about 870) and the eastern Pacific islands came just before.
Dips a little: epidemics after 1492 leave parts of the Americas, the Mississippi and Amazon floodplains among them, all but empty for a time; the survivors' ranges still cover most of the land.

Weather stations, mines and bases on the high Arctic islands and the ice-free coasts of Antarctica add the last fractions; the empty cores of the Sahara, the Rub' al Khali and the Taklamakan remain outside regular use.

upsert.reason: Sketched from the archaeology and genomics of each region's first peopling and abandonments, as recalled (Africa's Middle Stone Age sites, the green Sahara corridors, the dispersal through Arabia and southern Asia, Sahul by about 50,000 years ago, Europe by 45,000, Arctic Siberia by 32,000, the Americas by about 16,000 at the latest, the glacial maximum's refuges, the Holocene Sahara and its desiccation, the Paleo-Inuit, Remote Oceania and Aotearoa), with the areas of regions and deserts. The boundary of 'regular use' is soft; the band carries it.

points.note: Jericho, if a walled village counts as a town.
Çatalhöyük and a few large villages, if counted as towns.
Uruk growing; the Tripolye megasites.
Plague hit towns hardest.

War industries draw workers to cities in Europe, North America and Japan, and the Great Migration of Black Americans from the rural South to northern cities begins (1916); Gallipoli and the Armenian genocide kill but barely move the world's urban share.

changes.value: Fill: the report names 1870 to 1890 as the coarsest stretch of health, homicide, humanity, the internet, the largest city and polity, marriage and its parts, and belief. 1880 is filled for each, near the line between its neighbours unless an Event moves it. Recalled (London's census of 1881, China's population after the Taiping war) or interpolated (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Early Upper Palaeolithic people were tall.
Heights fell with the first farming diets and village disease.
The low point of the farming transition's heights.
After the Black Death, survivors ate better where land was plentiful; European skeletal heights rose.

Band narrowed from the ±20% placeholder at 1800 (131 to 197 cm): national height series for the early 1800s, from about 160 cm in parts of Asia to about 170 in North America, bound the world mean within a few centimetres.
Heights fall in Britain's and the United States' fast-growing cities in the 1830s and 1840s (the 'antebellum puzzle'), but the world's mean, mostly Asian and rural, holds.
Early industrial cities: heights stalled or fell where they grew fastest.
London's Metropolitan Police (1829) and the new police of other European and American cities; homicide keeps its slow European fall while frontier and plantation societies stay violent.
Steady at world scale: rising rates in the United States and Latin America from the late 1960s are offset by falls elsewhere; the drug trade's violence grows only later.

The world rate stops falling in the early 1990s: Latin America's homicide epidemic (ev.lac.homicide), with Colombia near its peak and Brazil's rates rising, and Russia's killings after the Soviet collapse offset the long decline elsewhere.
Penultimate glacial; numbers in Africa possibly reduced.
Deepest part of the penultimate glacial.
Last Interglacial: a green Sahara and Arabia open early ranges beyond Africa.
Around the Toba eruption; the genetic case for a bottleneck then is weak, so no dip is drawn.
The dispersal out of Africa under way.
Last Glacial Maximum: northern ranges abandoned.
The Americas entered about now.
Geometric growth from 4.4 million at -10000 to 18 million at -5000 gives about 12 million; set a little lower because farming populations grew fastest after -6000.
Rome and Han China near their peaks, about 65 and 56 million.
After the Antonine plague and as the Han collapsed.
Recovering from the Justinianic plague; Tang China after the An Lushan rebellion.
Song China past 100 million; Europe's high-medieval growth.
After the Black Death and the Ming–Yuan transition: below both 1300 (390 million) and 1500 (461 million). McEvedy and Jones's order of magnitude, as recalled.
Eurasia grows, but the Americas lose millions in the first smallpox epidemic: the world adds less than its trend.
A little under the line: the El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 kill perhaps 15 to 25 million in India, north China and Brazil.
Before the war: about 1.8 billion.
Growth near its all-time peak of about 2% a year: deaths have fallen, births not yet (DemographicTransition#6e31).
No network exists: computers are single machines; ARPANET is twelve years away.
The integrated circuit is invented (1958 to 1959); no network yet.
Cheap smartphones and mobile data bring most of Asia and much of Africa online (ev.internet).
Gravettian aggregation sites such as Dolní Věstonice.
Jericho's first settlement grows beside its spring.
Large PPNB villages such as Abu Hureyra or Jericho.
Çatalhöyük near its peak (7100–5700 BCE). Larger than the -5000 value (5): the largest settlements shrank before the Tripolye megasites and Uruk.
The Tripolye megasites and early Uruk.
Ur.
Babylon or Linzi.
Rome or Chang'an.
Rome, past its peak.
Daxing-Chang'an, rebuilt by the Sui, as the Tang take it (ev.as.tang).
Chang'an under the Tang; Baghdad just founded.
Kaifeng becomes the Song capital (ev.as.song).
Hangzhou after the fall of Kaifeng.
Nanjing, the early Ming capital, in Chandler's estimate as recalled; Cairo and Vijayanagara next.
London overtakes Beijing.
London, about 1.66 million at the census of 1831 with its suburbs, is now the largest city by a clear margin over Beijing.
London, with about 4.8 million in its 1881 census area.
Greater Tokyo.
Tokyo.
Akkad or Old Kingdom Egypt.
New Kingdom Egypt and the Shang each rule a few million as the Bronze Age collapse begins.
Before the Achaemenid empire: Assyria, Egypt and the Zhou each rule a few million.
Cyrus takes the Median kingdom (ev.as.achaemenid); Lydia and Babylon fall to him within twelve years.
Darius rules from the Indus to Egypt and Thrace: the Achaemenid empire holds perhaps a fifth of humanity (ev.as.achaemenid).
The Achaemenid empire.
Alexander takes the Achaemenid empire whole (334 to 330 BCE): the largest polity changes hands, not size.
Ashoka's Maurya empire, over most of the subcontinent, is the largest; its people are estimated from about 15 to 50 million, a wide debate the band carries.
Qin unifies China (ev.as.qin) as the Maurya empire declines after Ashoka: each holds perhaps a sixth to a fifth of humanity.
Han China.
Rome, about 65 million of 245.
Rome, with the Han breaking up.
Rome's western half has fallen (ev.eu.rome-fall) and China is divided between north and south: no polity holds more than about a seventh of humanity.
Sui China, whose census of 609 counts about 46 million.
Tang China.
The Northern Song, perhaps 80 million of 295 million, before the Jin take the north (ev.as.song).
Southern Song after losing the north to the Jin.
The Southern Song, with the Jin close behind.
Yuan China after the fall of the Song.
Revised from 28: Yuan China holds about the same quarter of humanity as at 1279; the 28 was the coarse fill's value and rose with no cause.
Ming China, about 80 million of 350 million; the 1393 census count of 60 million is taken as an undercount.
Qing China at its population peak.
Qing China, about 410 million on the debated official counts, still holds over a third of humanity on the eve of the Opium War.
Qing China, still the largest, though its share falls after the Taiping war and the northern famine; the British Empire's share rises with India's growth.
Qing China and the British Empire about equal.
India passes China as the most populous state about April 2023, on the UN's estimate (ev.as.india-most-populous): the largest polity changes, but its share holds near 17.7% across the change.
Foragers marry and part easily: among the Hadza and the !Kung a third or more of first marriages end in separation (Blurton Jones and colleagues; Howell, as recalled), with little property to divide.
Falls slowly as farmers outnumber foragers: land, herds and bridewealth bind marriages and kin enforce them.
Rome's elite divorce and remarry freely; most Romans, and most Chinese and Indians, do not.
The Church moves toward indissoluble marriage in the west (made a sacrament, divorce barred by the twelfth century); Islamic law lets husbands divorce easily, and many Muslim societies divorce often.
Down with the collapse of the Americas' peoples, many of whom parted easily.
Lowest: China, India and Christian Europe, most of humanity, almost never divorce; Tokugawa Japan's villages, Java and the Malay world, and many African and Muslim societies divorce often.
Western countries begin to allow civil divorce (England 1857, France 1884); Meiji Japan's code of 1898 lowers its high divorce.
Soviet Russia makes divorce a matter of registration (1917 to 1936), the easiest in the world; wartime marriages end after the war.
Jumps: wartime marriages end in a wave of divorces in the United States and Europe in 1946 and 1947.
China's Marriage Law (1950) lets women divorce: a wave of divorces follows to 1953. Java and Malaya divorce at among the world's highest rates, about half of marriages.
Divorce falls in Java and the Malay world, where marriage becomes later and chosen, while it has not yet risen in the West.
The divorce revolution: California's no-fault law (1969) and its followers across the West; women's earnings and the pill make leaving possible.
About two in five first marriages end in divorce in the United States, northern Europe and the Soviet Union; under one in fifty in India.
China's divorce rate climbs after the 2003 rules make divorce a matter of registration.

Turns level: China's divorces fall after the 2021 cooling-off period, and Western divorce has fallen since about 1990 as people marry later and fewer marry. World divorce is measured unevenly, and periods and cohorts give different shares; the band carries both.

Most foraging societies allow a man more than one wife, but few manage it: a few to a fifth of married women, more where older men control marriages, as among many Aboriginal Australians (Marlowe's forager sample, as recalled).
Rises with farming: where wealth is in land, herds and the labour of wives and children, more men take more wives; polygyny is commonest among hoe farmers and herders in the ethnographic record.
Turns down as states grow: in Egypt and Mesopotamia most men have one wife, kings and the rich add secondary wives and concubines.
Greek cities and Rome allow one wife only; whether socially imposed monogamy spread because it eased competition among men (Henrich, Boyd and Richerson) or for other reasons is debated.
Han China: one principal wife, with concubines for the rich (counted here as plural unions, which is debated, since concubines were not wives in law); India permits more wives but few take them.
Islam permits up to four wives; few men can afford more than one, a few in a hundred marriages in most Muslim societies, and conversion does not lower Africa's polygyny.
Most of it now in sub-Saharan Africa, where a third or more of married women share a husband; China's, India's and the Muslim world's elites add a little.
The United States forces the Mormon church to give up plural marriage (1890).
Turkey bans polygamy (1926).
China's Marriage Law (1950) bans concubinage; India's Hindu Marriage Act (1955) makes Hindu marriage monogamous.

Level since 1900: Africa's growing share of humanity balances the fall of polygyny within Africa, where the share of married women in polygynous unions falls from about two in five in West Africa toward a quarter or a third.

Pew (2020) finds about 2% of the world's people living in polygamous households, most in West and Central Africa (over a third of people in Burkina Faso, Mali and Nigeria's north, as recalled); as a share of married women it is a little higher.
Raised from 17.2 so the series no longer dips between 1300 (17.5) and 1500 (18).
The European marriage pattern begins to set in (ev.eu.marriage-pattern), among too few people to move the world mean much.

Foragers' spirits and ancestors rarely judge conduct between people: moralizing high gods are rare among foragers in the cross-cultural samples (Swanson's, and Peoples and Marlowe's). Debated: Purzycki and others find local gods that care about some conduct, which would raise this; the band allows it.
Early farmers' ancestor cults and shrines, as at Catalhoyuk, show no sign of gods that judge conduct.

The first states: Egypt's Maat and Mesopotamia's sun god as judge. Whether these count as moralizing gods is debated; the Seshat coding that placed them early was part of a study retracted in 2021 over its treatment of missing data.
Egypt's judgment of the dead spreads beyond the king in the Coffin Texts.
The Zhou claim Heaven's mandate (about 1046 BCE): Heaven judges rulers by their virtue.

Rises most between 800 and 500 BCE: karma taught as a law repaying conduct (the Upanishads, the Buddha, Mahavira), Zoroaster's judging god, the Hebrew prophets, Confucius's Heaven. Whether this Axial Age is a break or a gradual growth is debated (Jaspers and Bellah against Mullins and others), as is why: Baumard and Boyer's affluence against the Big Gods case that such beliefs let large societies cooperate (Norenzayan).
Buddhist judgment of the dead enters Chinese folk religion; Christianity in the Mediterranean.
Enlightenment unbelief and deism are a few among the educated of Europe; the world share barely moves.
The peak: nearly all of humanity in traditions that teach judged conduct, before state atheism.
Turns down: the Soviet state teaches unbelief from 1917.
China's new state teaches unbelief from 1949.
The trough: China's Cultural Revolution closes temples and churches; Western Europe's young stop believing as well as attending.
Turns up: belief revives in the former Soviet lands and in China after the Cultural Revolution, and the Muslim and African Christian shares grow.
Unbelief grows in Europe, East Asia and the Americas while belief holds in Muslim and African populations (Pew and Gallup surveys, as recalled); the two nearly cancel.

upsert.reason: Sketched: before 1900 from the share of people in traditions coded as having moralizing high gods or broad supernatural punishment (Swanson; Peoples and Marlowe; Norenzayan's Big Gods; the Seshat moralizing-gods data and their critics, as recalled), counting part of the local and Chinese traditions; after 1900 lowered by the unaffiliated and by unbelief within traditions as surveys show.

changes.value: Fill: the report names 1870 to 1890 as the coarsest stretch of tradition, regular worship, the people kept to serve a faith, force, wealth held, mass media, lasting art and the arts' makers with their three parts. 1880 is filled for each near the line between its neighbours, the arts' makers kept the sum of markets, patrons and public bodies. Interpolated, with what the decade's Events did (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: No tradition open to every people exists before the Buddha; foragers' traditions are bound to their band and land.
The first states' traditions are bound to their city, king and land; Akhenaten's Aten cult (about 1350 BCE) does not seek converts abroad.
The Buddha's teaching begins in the Ganges plain, open to any who join the order whatever their birth: the first tradition of this kind.
Turns up: Ashoka's patronage and his missions to Sri Lanka, Gandhara and the Hellenistic kings carry the teaching beyond its first people.
Buddhism reaches China along the Silk Roads; Christians are still a few hundred thousand in the Roman Empire.
Turns up: the Roman Empire becomes Christian between Constantine's conversion (312) and Theodosius's decrees (380), and Buddhism spreads through China.
Islam enters the count after 610; most conquered peoples convert only slowly over the next three centuries.
Northern and Eastern Europe baptized from the 960s; conversion in Iran and the Near East passes the half.
The Black Death kills Christians and Muslims around the Mediterranean in greater shares than East Asian Buddhists; the sum barely moves.
The survivors in the Spanish Americas are baptized; the gain is small because so many of them die.
Turns up faster: Europe's and the Americas' Christian peoples grow faster than Asia's, and missions spread in Africa and Oceania.
Missions follow colonial rule into Africa and Asia, and Europe's and the Americas' Christians grow fastest by births.
Turns flat: Buddhists fall under state atheism after 1917 and 1949 while Christians grow in Africa and Muslims by births; the sum holds near 53 to 55 until 1970.
Rises again, mainly by the higher birth rates of Muslim and African Christian populations, not by conversion.
Christians about 31% and Muslims about 24.5% of humanity, Buddhists about 6% (Pew Research Center's Global Religious Futures estimates, as recalled).

upsert.reason: The sum of the model's Buddhist, Christian and Muslim shares at each date; its band carries theirs.

points.note: On the eve of the Cultural Revolution, which closes China's temples and churches.
Zero: foragers' shamans and ritual elders also hunt and gather; no one is kept to serve the sacred.
Begins, perhaps: the enclosures of Gobekli Tepe and Neolithic shrines may have had keepers fed by the feasts' builders; unknown.
Eridu's temple and the chiefdoms' priests.
The temple households of Sumer and Egypt's priesthood: in the first states a temple can be the largest owner of land and keeper of people.
Egypt's New Kingdom temples hold perhaps a tenth of its land and keep tens of thousands; Amun's priesthood rivals the throne.
The Buddha's and Mahavira's orders of monks and nuns, the first communities kept wholly by believers' alms, beside the Brahmins, the magi and the Greek temples.
Buddhist monks begin to carry the dharma into Han China.
Christian monasticism begins in Egypt's desert (Antony, then Pachomius's communities about 320).

Rises most: China's Buddhist monasteries under the Northern Wei and the southern courts, perhaps a million or more monks and nuns by the claims of the time, and Christian monasteries from Egypt to Ireland.

Falls: the Tang emperor Wuzong's Huichang suppression (842 to 845) destroys some 4,600 monasteries and returns about 260,000 monks and nuns to lay life, a large part of all the people kept for faiths in a China that held a quarter of humanity; the sangha recovers under the Song.

Near its peak: Europe's clergy and religious perhaps one or two in every hundred people, holding a fifth to a quarter of its land; Theravada monasteries in every mainland village; Tibet's monasteries; the ulama and Sufi orders.
Falls: the Reformation dissolves the monasteries of England, Scandinavia and Protestant Germany and turns their lands to crowns and nobles.
Catholic Europe's Counter-Reformation clergy and Tibet's monasteries, where perhaps a sixth of men are monks, hold the level.
Falls: the French Revolution abolishes the religious orders and sells the Church's lands, and the secularizations of Joseph II and Napoleon follow.
The Soviet state closes churches and monasteries and kills or exiles tens of thousands of clergy.
Falls: China's new state laicizes monks and nuns and takes temple lands; after 1959 Tibet's monasteries are emptied.
The Cultural Revolution closes every temple, church and mosque in China.

About eleven million: Catholic priests, sisters and brothers about a million, Protestant pastors two to three million, imams and ulama one to two million, Buddhist monks and nuns one to two million, Hindu temple priests one to three million, and others.
In bands the men who fight in raids and feuds also hunt and gather: almost no one is kept under arms, though most men may fight.
Chiefs begin to keep retinues of fighting men, but most fighting is still done by farmers and herders between seasons.
The first states keep guards and standing troops; Sargon of Akkad later boasts of 5,400 men who eat daily before him.
Chariot armies of Egypt, the Hittites and Shang China: specialists kept at great cost.
Assyria keeps the first great standing army.

The Warring States of China field conscript armies of hundreds of thousands; Rome mobilizes a large share of its citizens against Carthage; the Mauryan army is reported at hundreds of thousands. The share under arms in states peaks before unification.

Rome's legions and auxiliaries, about 300,000 to 400,000 of some 60 million, and Han China's standing and frontier forces of the same order: about one in two hundred people in the states, almost none beyond them.
Song China keeps more than a million soldiers, about one in a hundred of its people, the largest standing army of its age.
The Mongols make every adult man a soldier of the decimal army, a small people wholly under arms.
The military revolution: gunpowder and the bastion fort make European armies grow tenfold in two centuries; the Ottoman, Mughal and Ming armies are as large or larger.
Louis XIV's France keeps about 400,000 men, and the Qing banners and Green Standard about 800,000.
The Napoleonic peak: the levée en masse of 1793 and conscription put about six million under arms in Europe at once.
The Taiping and Qing armies of millions and the American Civil War's, about 1.5 million under arms at once in 1864.
Armies demobilize after the Russo-Turkish war (1877 to 1878) but conscription keeps Europe's standing armies large.
On the eve of mobilization (August 1914): within weeks some twenty million men are called up, the jump to 1916.
The First World War: about 40 million under arms at the height, from conscript armies of a size no earlier war had seen.
Demobilized in the West; the Red Army of the Russian Civil War still about five million.
The invasion of the Soviet Union (June 1941): some 8 to 9 million under arms on the Eastern Front alone, and Japan's and the Allies' mobilization still rising.
The Second World War: about 70 million under arms at the height, the Soviet Union and the United States about 12 million each, Germany about 10, China, Japan and Britain about 5 to 6 each.
Japan surrenders in August and September 1945; demobilization has barely begun, so the fall to 1946 comes after.
Demobilization: tens of millions sent home within a year.
The Korean war and the Cold War's rearmament.
The World Bank counts about 29 million in armed forces, paramilitary included, at the Cold War's end.
Armies cut by about a quarter after the Cold War, in Russia above all.
About 27 to 28 million under arms; Russia's and Ukraine's wartime mobilization adds about a million, against a falling share elsewhere.
A forager band's tools, ornaments, shelters and canoes: a few months of what it gets in a year. What foragers hold in skills and ties is real wealth but not counted here.
Rises with the first fields, stores and houses: farmers hold what foragers did not, land made fertile, granaries and herds.
Irrigated land, temples, granaries and herds: the first states sit on stocks of several years' harvest.
Land is most of it: the Roman and Han estates; a large estate's price was some twenty to thirty years of its rent, and rents a third to a half of the harvest.
The Black Death kills a third or more of Eurasia's western and central peoples; land loses value against what the survivors can make and earn.
Falls: after the Black Death land is plentiful and labour scarce, so land's value falls against what the survivors produce.
Britain's and France's wealth is about seven years of national income, mostly land (Piketty); Asia's agrarian empires perhaps four to five.
About five years by Piketty's world series: land's share falls as railways, factories and housing rise.
Falls: war destroys capital and war finance turns savings into government debt that inflation will erase; the Russian revolution expropriates the property of a sixth of the world's land.
The Depression wipes out share and property values.
War spreads to the Pacific: bombing and fighting destroy housing, factories and transport from Europe to China, and governments borrow on a scale that inflation will later erase.

The low: the world wars' destruction, inflation, nationalizations, rent controls and the communist revolutions' expropriations (China's from 1949) leave the world's wealth at about two and a half years of output.
Rises with privatization in the former communist states, falling interest rates and housing booms.
Peaks before the financial crisis, at the top of the housing and credit boom.
Near-zero interest rates lift asset prices while the pandemic cuts output.
About five and a half years of world output, near the World Inequality Database's global estimate, and back near where it stood before 1914.
Before print.
Gutenberg's press is being built; nothing printed reaches anyone regularly yet (ev.printing).
The steam press and the penny papers (the New York Sun, 1833) bring daily news to clerks and artisans in the cities of Britain, France and the United States.
Rotary presses and cheap wood-pulp paper make the penny daily, but readers are still mostly in Europe, North America and Japan.
Radio reaches most households in the industrial countries.

Pigments ground at Olorgesailie and Kapthurin, about 300,000 years ago, may have coloured bodies or objects, but no lasting ornament or image of this age is known; how many populations made what has not survived is unknown.
Pierced shells at Bizmoune in Morocco (about 142,000 to 150,000 years ago), the oldest known ornaments; one site is a lower bound, not a census.
Blombos's ochre-mixing kit (about 100,000 years ago) and shell beads at Skhul, Qafzeh and in North Africa: lasting art is made in several regions, though the record holds only a handful of sites.
Blombos's beads and engraved ochre (about 75,000 years ago) and the Still Bay: in southern Africa ornament and image are made widely for a few thousand years.
The record flickers: the Still Bay's and Howiesons Poort's engraving come and go in southern Africa, as models of cultural loss in small, scattered populations predict (CumulativeCulture#4f93).

Ostrich-eggshell beads spread across eastern and southern Africa and the first known figurative painting is made in Sulawesi (at least 51,200 years ago): the share nears half as the dispersal carries the practice.
The Aurignacian ivories, flutes and Chauvet in Europe, hand stencils and animals in the caves of Sulawesi and Borneo: most of humanity now lives in populations that make lasting art.
Sahul's people are drawing on rock by now (Nawarla Gabarnmang, about 28,000 years ago): one more continent's populations in the count.
Every living population makes lasting images and ornament, printed and plastic among them.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned from the dated sites, which are a lower bound on the practice, not a census of it (AbsenceEvidence#10a3). Three readings are argued and the bands hold all of them (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): a gradual emergence across Africa from about 300,000 years ago, thinly recorded (McBrearty and Brooks 2000), which would put the early values far too low; a late change in minds or society about 50,000 years ago (Klein), which would put them too high; and a demographic reading in which the practice is kept or lost with population density and connection (Powell, Shennan and Thomas 2009; CumulativeCulture#4f93), which predicts the flickering record of southern Africa. A distinguishing test: if density decides, the oldest ornaments should cluster where and when genomes and site counts show the densest Middle Stone Age populations.

points.note: Begins: musicians and jewellers who sell their work or play for hire in Mesopotamia's cities beside the temple and palace dependants.
Greek vase painters, sculptors and travelling poets and players sell to many buyers across the Mediterranean.
A tenth of all makers: Rome's actors, mimes, charioteers and copyists' workshops, and the entertainers of Han cities, paid by crowds and buyers.
Falls with the cities of the western empire and their theatres.
Rises with the Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds: about a sixth of all makers.
London's and Madrid's commercial theatres, Antwerp's and later Amsterdam's open picture market, printed books' authors and printed images: three makers in ten live from buyers and audiences.
Edo's and Osaka's kabuki and puppet theatres and the ukiyo-e print trade join Europe's markets.
Markets now keep more makers than patrons do: public concerts, publishers of music and novels, theatres run for profit.
The steam press, lithography and the subscription concert: novelists, illustrators and virtuosi live from sales and tickets.
Music halls, vaudeville, the illustrated press and the first professional sport.
Hollywood's studios, commercial radio's singers and bands, the record companies and sport as a profession: three quarters of all makers.
War takes performers into the forces and closes commercial theatres across occupied Europe and Asia.
Falls as a share while the communist states take their theatres, studios and troupes into public hands; it still keeps most makers.
Rises as the post-Soviet states and China's reformed troupes push makers onto the market.
The pandemic falls on market makers: closed venues and cancelled seasons cost freelance performers most of a year's work, while salaried public makers keep their posts.
About three quarters of all makers: the self-employed, the film, music, games and publishing industries and professional sport.

upsert.reason: The parent's value less the patrons' and public bodies' parts at each date: zero before about 2200 BCE, a few per cent in antiquity, a sixth in the Song cities, a third by 1650, most of all makers from about 1820, three quarters now.

points.note: Zero, as the parent: no forager band keeps anyone to make art.
If anyone was kept to carve Göbekli Tepe's pillars, it was by the leaders of the feasts that raised them: patrons, not buyers.
Chiefs keep the first craftsmen of fine things: Varna's goldsmiths, Ubaid's temple painters.
Every kept maker is a dependant of a temple or palace workshop in Sumer and Egypt.
Dips with the palaces of the Bronze Age collapse.

Near the level it keeps for the next seventeen centuries: the Han court's Music Bureau, Rome's imperial and senatorial households and the temples of every empire keep about 450 to 475 makers per million people.
Falls with Rome's western patrons; the Gupta, Sasanian and southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Its peak per person, barely above the first century's: the Mughal, Safavid, Ottoman and Ming ateliers and Europe's courts and churches.
Falling: the Revolution abolishes the court, confiscates the Church's lands and closes the chapels and choir schools that kept France's musicians, painters and sculptors.
Falls: the French Revolution ends the court's and the Church's patronage in France, and secularization strips German and Austrian monasteries and prince-bishops of theirs.
Britain's punitive expedition sacks Benin City and ends the royal guilds of casters and carvers.
On the eve of the February revolution, which ends the Russian court's and aristocracy's patronage.
The February revolution: the Imperial Theatres and the court's orchestras and choirs pass to the state, and the aristocracy's patronage ends with its estates.
The Russian, Austrian, German and Ottoman courts are gone; the Russian revolution ends aristocratic patronage across a sixth of the world's land.
India's princely states are merged into the republic (1947 to 1949) and their courts' musicians and painters lose their keepers.
About a twentieth of all makers: church musicians, royal and princely households, private patrons and foundations' commissions.

upsert.reason: The parent's value times the patrons' share: all of it until markets appear, nine tenths in antiquity, three quarters in 1500, half by 1800, a tenth by 1950, a twentieth now.

points.note: Begins: the Greek cities' civic festivals pay poets, choruses, musicians and sculptors from public funds and liturgies.
Cleisthenes' reforms: Athens's City Dionysia, whose tragic contests began about 534 BCE, is paid for by the city and its liturgies.
Rome's public games and theatres, paid partly from the treasury, partly by magistrates who count as patrons here.
The western cities' public games and theatres close.
Town musicians and civic painters of Europe's and Asia's self-governing cities: a fiftieth of all makers.
Court theatres begin to become national ones (Vienna's Burgtheater, 1776) and academies take state salaries.
The republic's festivals, the Conservatoire (1795) and the Louvre's public museum (1793) keep some makers on public funds.
Germany's and Austria's municipal theatres and orchestras, Europe's conservatories and academies: about a sixteenth of all makers.
Rises: the Soviet state takes the theatres, conservatories and studios into public hands (1919), and Germany's and Austria's court theatres become state theatres.
The New Deal's Federal Art, Music, Theatre and Writers' Projects employ about 40,000 makers (1935 to 1939), and the Soviet and fascist states' arts administrations grow.
Jumps: Eastern Europe's new regimes and the People's Republic of China (1949) take theatres, studios and troupes into public hands, and Western Europe's arts councils and public broadcasters grow.
Near its peak share, three tenths of all makers: China's thousands of state troupes, the Soviet bloc's theatres, studios and artists' unions, and Europe's subsidized stages and broadcasters.
The Cultural Revolution disbands or purges China's troupes and sends their members to the countryside, leaving the eight model works.
The Soviet Union's breakup ends the union-wide state system of theatres, studios, conservatories and creative unions; budgets collapse in the 1990s.
Falls: the Soviet system's end cuts state theatres, studios and unions across Eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union, and China begins to turn its troupes into enterprises.
Holds through the pandemic: salaried makers of state theatres, orchestras and broadcasters keep their posts while freelance performers lose their work.
About a sixth of all makers: public broadcasters, state and municipal theatres, orchestras and troupes, most of them in Europe and East Asia.

upsert.reason: The parent's value times the public bodies' share: none before the Greek cities' festivals, a few per cent until 1900, a tenth by 1930, a quarter to three tenths from 1950 to 1990, under a fifth now.

points.note: Zero by the measure's definition: no forager band keeps anyone to make art. The beads, engravings and paintings of the Stone Age were made by people whose main work was getting food.
Sunghir's burials, with thousands of ivory beads that took thousands of hours to make, show great effort spent on ornament, but nothing shows anyone kept for the work.

Göbekli Tepe's carved pillars (from about 9500 BCE) are raised by foragers' communal labour, perhaps with a few carvers who did little else; whether anyone was kept for the work is unknown, so the value starts barely above zero.
Chiefdoms begin to keep craftsmen: the goldsmiths behind Varna's graves (about 4500 BCE), the builders and painters of Ubaid Mesopotamia's temples.
The temple and palace workshops of Sumer and Egypt keep the first full-time sculptors, painters, musicians and goldsmiths; perhaps a fifth of humanity now lives under such courts.
Minoan Crete's palaces keep fresco painters, seal-cutters and goldsmiths beside Egypt's and Mesopotamia's workshops.
Olmec rulers at San Lorenzo keep the sculptors of the colossal heads: makers of art are now kept in the Americas too.
The tomb-builders of Deir el-Medina, the Shang bronze-casters, the palace painters of Crete and the Olmec sculptors: courts on three continents now keep makers of art.
Greek cities' festivals keep poets, actors and sculptors, and the Persian, Indian and Chinese courts their musicians and craftsmen.

Rome's theatres, games and workshops and the Han court's Music Bureau, about 800 musicians before 7 BCE: a few makers in every thousand people of the great cities, about one in two thousand people worldwide.
Gupta India's court poets, dramatists and temple sculptors (Kalidasa wrote about 400) rise as Rome's western patrons fail.
Falls with Rome in the west: theatres, games and the patrons who paid for them close; Gupta India, Sasanian Iran and the southern Chinese courts keep theirs.
Song cities' entertainment quarters, where storytellers, puppeteers, actors and musicians play to paying crowds, beside the courts of the Abbasids, the Fatimids and Heian Japan.
The Black Death and the Mongol wars kill makers and patrons alike.
The workshops of Italy and the Netherlands, the Mughal and Safavid ateliers, Ming porcelain and printed images: art is made for markets as well as for patrons.
Between 1789 and 1800 on the line; inside it the Revolution moves makers from the court and the Church to the market and the new state's festivals.
Theatres, music halls, the illustrated press and the publishers' authors grow with the cities of the industrial world.
Cinema: the picture houses' actors and pit musicians, and the first professional footballers and boxers.
Hollywood's studios, radio's orchestras and singers, and sport as a profession.
War takes performers into the forces and closes theatres in occupied Europe and Asia.
The pandemic closes theatres, concert halls and stadiums; live performers lose most of a year's work.
About twenty million people of some 3.6 billion workers: artists, musicians, actors, writers, dancers, players of sport and makers of art wares.

upsert.reason: Recalled and reasoned: zero among foragers by definition; a few hundred per million under the agrarian states' courts and temples, bounded by the surplus that keeps them (SurplusBound#7fe3); a few thousand per million now. The 2025 value rests on the recalled count of about 30 million jobs in the cultural and creative industries in 2013 (UNESCO and EY), of which the makers themselves are perhaps two thirds; to be checked. Where the line falls between a maker of art wares and a maker of ordinary goods moves every value before 1900 by a factor of two either way.

Fill: the report names 1870 to 1890 as the coarsest stretch of leisure, the three sectors of output, hereditary rank and Africa's subregions. 1880 is filled for each, wholes kept the sum of their parts: food-getting + making + services = the 1,730 of output per person recorded at 1880 a little under the line (the long depression from 1873), and Africa = Northern + Sub-Saharan, Sub-Saharan = its four subregions, with Africa's share given 1880 too. Interpolated, with what the decade's Events did (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Wartime hours (h.toil) cut leisure in the belligerents.
About four fifths of foragers' small output is food; the rest is tools, clothing and shelter, and services barely counted.
Farming feeds more people per hectare, not more per person: food-getting per person barely moves for five thousand years while its share of output begins to fall (MalthusianTrap#0f6b).
After the Black Death the survivors farm the best land: food output per person rises with output per person.
Turns flat: from here food-getting per person grows far more slowly than output, so its share falls from about half to a third by 1900.
The new farmlands of the Americas, Russia and Australia feed Europe's cities by rail and steamship.
War cuts harvests in Europe and Russia.
Food output holds through the Depression while prices collapse: farmers keep producing, so the fall in output per person is industry's and services'.
The war's trough: occupied Europe, the Soviet Union and Asia harvest far less, and famine strikes Bengal, Henan and Vietnam.
Food-getting falls below a tenth of world output. Value added grows more slowly than harvests, because fertilizer, fuel and machines bought from industry are counted there.
About 5% of world output (World Bank value added at market prices is about 4%, more at purchasing power).

upsert.reason: Sector shares of world output: about 80% food-getting for foragers (output counted as subsistence, mostly food), 55 to 65% in agrarian economies (Broadberry's and others' sectoral reconstructions for England, China and India, as recalled, averaged toward the more agrarian majority), about a third by 1900, a fifth by 1950, and from the World Bank's value-added shares after 1960, raised somewhat for purchasing power.

points.note: Stone tools, wooden spears, skins and shelters: about a sixth of foragers' output.
Pottery, weaving, houses and the first copper: farmers make more things than foragers.
Bronze, monumental building and specialist craftsmen in the first states.
The collapse of Roman manufacturing and trade in the West: pottery, coins and buildings become cruder and fewer.
Song China's iron output, perhaps over 100,000 tonnes a year by 1078 as Hartwell reconstructed it, is not matched until the eighteenth century.
Turns up: the industrial revolution's cotton mills, iron and steam spread from Britain.
A little under the line: the long depression after the panic of 1873 slows Europe's and America's industry until the mid-1880s.
Steel, chemicals and electricity: the second industrial revolution in Germany and the United States.
Making passes food-getting in world output about now.
Ford's moving assembly line and the Haber–Bosch process begin in 1913, on the eve of the war.
World industrial production falls by about a third from 1929 to 1932, by the League of Nations' index as recalled: the Depression is above all industry's collapse.
Peak of war production: American and Soviet factories make arms on a scale never seen.
Demobilization: war production stops and factories convert.
Industry's share of world output near its peak, about 37%.
Turns flat: deindustrialization in the old industrial countries and the collapse of Soviet-bloc industry after 1989.
Turns up again: China becomes the world's workshop.
About 28% of world output.

upsert.reason: Industry's share of world output: about 15% for foragers' tools, clothing and shelters, 16 to 22% in agrarian economies, a third by 1950 and its peak about 37% in the 1960s, about 28% now (World Bank value added after 1960, as recalled).

points.note: Healing, teaching and ritual among foragers are done unpaid within the band; output counts little of them.
Turns up: temples, scribes, officials and long-distance traders of the first cities.
Services pass making in this sketch about now; whether agrarian services outweighed crafts is uncertain (England in 1381 had more industry than services), and the bands overlap.
Song China's commercial revolution: merchants, shippers, brokers and paper money.
Railways, shipping, banking and city trades grow with industry.
Services pass food-getting in world output about now.
Services reach half of world output.
About two thirds of world output.

upsert.reason: The remainder of output: about 5% for foragers, whose services are unpaid and barely counted; a fifth to a quarter in agrarian economies (trade, transport, housing, government, religion, servants); about a third by 1900, two fifths by 1950 and two thirds now.

points.note: Rich child burials such as Sungir hint at inherited status in a few groups.
A few sedentary complex foragers, such as the early Natufians, may have had inherited status.
Meiji Japan abolishes the samurai and outcaste estates (1871), and the fall goes on as legal estates end elsewhere; India's castes, a fifth of humanity, stay.
Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, about 315,000 years old: the oldest Homo sapiens fossils yet found are in Northern Africa.
The penultimate glacial's driest phase: the Sahara is hyperarid and Northern Africa's people shrink to the Nile and the coasts.
The Last Interglacial's monsoon greens the Sahara with rivers and lakes; people spread into it from the south and east (the green Sahara corridors).
The green Sahara at its widest: Northern Africa's share peaks before the drier phases after 115,000 years ago shrink it again.
The glacial maximum: the Sahara at its driest; people hold on along the Nile and the Maghreb's coasts (the Iberomaurusians).
The African Humid Period greens the Sahara with lakes and grassland from about 12,500 years ago; hunters and then herders spread into it.
The Sahara dries after about 3500 BCE and its herders crowd into the Nile valley, where Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.
Interpolated: the Nile valley fills as herders leave the drying Sahara, and its first states form before Egypt is unified about 3100 BCE.

The Middle Kingdom reunites Egypt after the First Intermediate Period, a century of divided rule that came with the low Nile floods of the 4.2-kiloyear drought. How many died in it is unknown, and the series keeps a straight line through it.
Roman Egypt, perhaps four to seven million, and Roman Africa's grain lands: Northern Africa holds about two fifths of the continent's people.

Interpolated: the Arab conquest (640 to 709) brings Egypt and the Maghreb into the caliphate, while the Justinianic plague's returns (541 to about 750) keep the Mediterranean's numbers down, Egypt's among them.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Egypt's people, and its returns keep Egypt's numbers down for two centuries.
The low point: Egypt perhaps four million, after plague's returns and famine; the Maghreb about six.
Egypt's people double in the nineteenth century, with cotton and the end of plague, to about ten million.
Egypt passes 118 million; with Sudan and the Maghreb the region holds a third of a billion.
Omo Kibish in Ethiopia, about 230,000 years ago.
The dispersal out of Africa probably leaves from Eastern Africa, across the Bab el-Mandeb or the Sinai.
Aksum in the Ethiopian highlands; Bantu-speaking farmers reach the Great Lakes.
Great Zimbabwe and the Swahili coast's towns at their height.
Eastern Africa has become Sub-Saharan Africa's largest part as the Atlantic trade drains the west; the Indian Ocean and Red Sea trades take fewer.
The east African slave trade to Zanzibar's clove plantations and the Gulf peaks in the 1860s and 1870s.
The rinderpest panzootic from 1887 kills most cattle, and Ethiopia's great famine (1888 to 1892) perhaps a third of its people.
The Ethiopian famine of 1983 to 1985 kills perhaps 400,000 to a million, a dent the region's growth fills within a year.
The Rwandan genocide (1994) kills perhaps 500,000 to 800,000.
Ethiopia passes 130 million, Tanzania 70, Kenya 57: Eastern Africa now holds about one person in sixteen.
Bantu-speaking farmers begin to move south and east from the Cameroon grassfields.
The Kingdom of Kongo forms on the lower Congo, about 1390.
West-Central Africa, Kongo and Angola above all, becomes the largest single source of the Atlantic slave trade, about 5.7 million of its 12.5 million.
Before the Free State, the Zanzibari ivory and slave raiders of Tippu Tip push into the eastern Congo in the 1870s, with smallpox along their roads.

The Congo Free State's regime of forced rubber collection (1885 to 1908), with sleeping sickness and smallpox: its losses are debated, from a few million to ten, and the region's share falls by a third in twenty years.
The low point: about 26 million, a share less than half of 1750's.
The Congo wars (1996 to 2003): their excess deaths are debated, from under a million to over five, most from hunger and disease.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo passes 110 million, with births above six per woman, the highest of any large country.
The south coast's shellfish and Pinnacle Point's ochre: a refuge through the penultimate glacial, on Marean's argument, one candidate for where the species weathered it.
Blombos Cave's engraved ochre and shell beads, Still Bay and Howiesons Poort.
Foragers only, while farmers elsewhere multiply: the San's share of humanity shrinks for ten thousand years.
Khoe herders with sheep have arrived; Bantu-speaking farmers follow within a few centuries.
Mapungubwe on the Limpopo, about 1220 to 1290, the first kingdom of the region.
Smallpox from the Cape (1713) devastates the Khoe; the Dutch colony grows slowly.
The wars and migrations of the Mfecane (about 1815 to 1840) on the highveld; their scale is debated.
The mineral revolution: diamonds at Kimberley (1867) and gold on the Witwatersrand (1886) draw migrants and settlers.
The peak share: AIDS cuts life expectancy in South Africa and Botswana by a decade or more in the 2000s, and births fall faster than elsewhere in Africa.
Pearl millet domesticated in the Sahel about 2500 BCE; yams and oil palm in the forest margins.
The Nok culture's iron and terracottas on the Jos plateau.
The empire of Ghana and the trans-Saharan gold trade; Igbo-Ukwu's bronzes.
The Mali empire at its height, Ife's and Benin's cities in the forest.
Interpolated: Benin under Ewuare and the rise of Songhay; Portuguese ships reach the coast from the 1440s, before the Atlantic slave trade grows.

The Bights of Benin and Biafra and the Gold Coast lose tens of thousands a year to the Atlantic trade: on Manning's estimates Western Africa's numbers stand still from about 1700 to 1850, while the rest of the world's grow.
The Nigerian civil war (1967 to 1970): perhaps one to two million Biafrans die, most of hunger.
Nigeria, about 230 million, is half of the region; Niger's births are the world's highest, near seven per woman.

Homo sapiens lives only in Africa; how it was spread across the continent is debated: an eastern or southern cradle, or a pan-African web of populations linked by migration, with Jebel Irhoud in the north among the oldest.
The penultimate glacial dries the Sahara: Northern Africa empties toward the coasts and the Nile.
The Last Interglacial greens the Sahara: Northern Africa's share rises to perhaps a sixth (the Aterian).
The low point: about 14 million south of the Sahara against about 9 million in Egypt, the Maghreb and Nubia, on recalled reconstructions.
Bantu-speaking farmers with iron have reached the far south-east, and Sub-Saharan Africa grows faster than the Mediterranean world in decline.
Untouched or barely touched by the Black Death, so its share rises as Eurasia's and Egypt's people fall; whether plague reached south of the Sahara is debated.
The Atlantic slave trade at its height, about 80,000 people a year carried off, most of them young adults, while Eurasia's numbers grow: the region's share falls for a century and a half.
The low point: conquest, rinderpest, sleeping sickness and the Congo Free State's regime cut numbers in the 1890s, while Europe and Asia grow.
Births still near five per woman while deaths have fallen: the region's share has more than doubled since 1950 and is now the world's fastest-growing (DemographicTransition#6e31).
Pinnacle Point's shellfish and ochre (ev.af.pinnacle-point): Homo sapiens lives only in Africa.
As the Last Interglacial opens the Levant, a small share of humanity lives beyond Africa (ev.era.last-interglacial).
Early ventures into the Levant (Misliya, Skhul, Qafzeh).
Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. Africa's share falls not because Africa's people fall but because those who left multiply in Asia (ev.era.dispersal).

Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. The dispersal's descendants fill Asia, reach Sahul and, from about 45,000 years ago, enter Europe, while Africa's own numbers grow slowly; Africa's share keeps falling though its people do not.
Durand's ranges and McEvedy's differ most for Africa: 10 to 19% in 1500.
Kept so the five shares sum to 100 at 1518.
Kept so the five shares sum to 100 at 1521.

Falls as the world's other peoples grow faster: the Atlantic trade carries its last great numbers to Brazil and Cuba, the East African trade to Zanzibar's plantations and Arabia grows, and Africa's own numbers grow slowly.
The Berlin Conference (ev.af.berlin-conference): the partition begins; the losses to conquest, rinderpest and famine come after it.
