Fill: the report names 1870 to 1890 as the coarsest stretch of the subregions' shares of humanity in the Americas, Asia and Europe. 1880 is filled on the line between 1870 and 1890, which keeps each area the sum of its subregions (the Americas' 7.24 at 1880 already recorded; Asia's 60.84 as its own line gives it between 1874.05 and 1883.65; Europe 23.4). The El Niño famines of 1876 to 1879 would put Asia's share about 0.6 of a point lower at 1880 and the other areas' higher, inside every band; Asia's note already says the line spreads that loss, and a later pass can give 1876 and 1880 their own values across all areas at once.

points.note: The first islanders: Banwari Trace on Trinidad, then Cuba and Hispaniola by about 4000 BCE.
Saladoid farmers and potters move up the island chain from the Orinoco.
The Taíno and their neighbours, perhaps two and a half million on the middle estimates; Hispaniola alone has been put anywhere from a few hundred thousand to eight million.
War, forced labour and earlier disease have killed most of the Greater Antilles' Taíno before smallpox arrives in December 1518; Hispaniola's census of 1514 finds about 26,000 left.
Smallpox, from December 1518, kills perhaps a third to a half of the Taíno left in the Greater Antilles.
The low point: the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles, a few Spanish towns and the first enslaved Africans, perhaps a third of a million.
Barbados's sugar boom of the 1640s begins the sugar islands' growth on enslaved Africans.
Saint-Domingue alone holds half a million enslaved people, the most valuable colony in the world.
The Haitian Revolution (1791 to 1804) costs perhaps 150,000 to 350,000 lives.
Cuba's Ten Years' War (1868 to 1878) and the end of slavery; indentured workers from India and China come to Trinidad, Guyana and Cuba.
The Caribbean's peak share: from here emigration to North America and Europe and early-falling births hold its growth below the world's.
Squash domesticated at Guilá Naquitz by about 8000 BCE; teosinte becomes maize over the next millennia.
The Olmec centres of the Gulf coast.
Teotihuacan, perhaps 100,000 people, and the Classic Maya cities near their height.
The Classic Maya collapse (ev.am.maya-collapse): the southern lowland cities empty between about 800 and 950, as droughts strike and wars multiply; the share dips while the Andes' rises.
About 21 million, on a middle reading: central Mexico alone has been put at 25 million by Borah and Cook and at 6 to 12 million by their critics, the sharpest of the contact-population debates.

Revised from 4.21: smallpox reaches the mainland only in spring 1520, so at the start of the year central Mexico's numbers are still near their 1518 level (Cholula's massacre in October 1519 kills some thousands); the losses come between here and 1521.
Mid-epidemic: about half of the epidemic's deaths in central Mexico.
Smallpox in 1520 and the siege of Tenochtitlan (ev.smallpox-americas): perhaps a third of central Mexico dies within a year (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The cocoliztli of 1545 to 1548 (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1545), perhaps the deadliest single epidemic in Mexico's history; whether it was an introduced Salmonella or a native haemorrhagic fever is debated.
The second cocoliztli (ev.cam.cocoliztli-1576) kills perhaps two million.
Perhaps one in ten of central Mexico's people of 1519 remain; New Spain's whole population is about three million, Spaniards, Africans and mixed included.
Flat through the Mexican Revolution (ev.am.mexican-revolution): perhaps one to two million die or flee in 1910 to 1920, and Mexico's people barely grow.
Zero on the usual account; the White Sands footprints in New Mexico, dated 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, would make it a small positive share. Their dating is debated (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
People south of the ice in the far north-west and the Pacific coast (Paisley Caves, Cooper's Ferry) and in the east (Page-Ladson), soon after the ice-free corridor and the coast open.
The Clovis hunters spread across the continent within a few centuries.
Archaic foragers; from here the farming centres of Mesoamerica and the Andes grow faster, and Northern America's part of the hemisphere falls for six thousand years.
Maize farming spreads through the eastern woodlands and the Mississippian towns begin.
Cahokia empties and the Great Drought (1276 to 1299) drives the Ancestral Puebloans from the Four Corners.

Perhaps 4 to 5 million north of Mexico on middle estimates; the range runs from about 2 million (Ubelaker) to 18 million (Dobyns), with Thornton's 7 million between, a debate this value does not settle.
The Native nations' losses begin in earnest after de Soto's entrada (1539 to 1543) and the first coastal epidemics; the settlers are not yet a thousand.
The epidemics among the north-eastern nations of 1616 to 1640 and the Huron losses of the 1630s (ev.nam.northeast-epidemics) (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
The low point: about a million Native people and a quarter of a million colonists and enslaved Africans.
The British colonies double every 25 years or so, the fastest growth then known, as Franklin and Malthus both noted.
The census of 1880 counts 50 million in the United States; immigration from Germany, Britain, Ireland and Scandinavia peaks in the early 1880s.
Immigration is cut by the quota acts of 1921 and 1924, and the share rises more slowly.
Northern America's peak share, with the baby boom; from here births fall below the world's and the share declines.
Immigration keeps the decline slow: about one in seven of its people was born abroad.
Homo sapiens reaches the steppe and its oases after the coasts, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago; Neanderthals and Denisovans were there before.

Homo sapiens spreads onto the steppe and into the oases of Central Asia after the southern coasts, about 50,000 to 45,000 years ago, meeting the Neanderthals and Denisovans already there; the share triples from a tiny base.
The cold, dry glacial maximum thins the steppe's people.
Farming reaches the foot of the Kopet Dag at Jeitun, about 6000 BCE.
The oasis towns of the Bactria-Margiana complex, and herders spreading over the steppe with horses and wagons.
Samanid Bukhara and Samarkand, among the richest oases of the Islamic world.
The Mongol destruction of Khwarazm's and Transoxiana's cities (1219 to 1221); some oases never regain their numbers.
The Black Death passes through the steppe on its way west.
Flat across the Kazakh famine of 1930 to 1933, which killed about one and a half to two million, some two fifths of the Kazakhs, and drove many into China.
The Virgin Lands campaign brings settlers to Kazakhstan, and high fertility in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
After the Soviet Union's end, Russians and Germans leave Kazakhstan by the million and births fall: the share dips.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Central Asia's part of it: the oases of Sogdiana, Bactria's north and Khwarazm, and the Kazakh steppe.

points.note: Zero on the usual account; the Fuyan Cave teeth, dated 80,000 to 120,000 years, would put a few Homo sapiens in south China already, a claim that is debated.
The dispersal along the southern coasts reaches Eastern Asia last of Asia's subregions; Tianyuan, near Beijing, is about 40,000 years old.
Millet farming in the Yellow River valley and rice in the Yangtze valley multiply Eastern Asia's people (Peiligang, Cishan, then Yangshao).
The low point of Eastern Asia's share before the Zhou states grow: Western Zhou China held perhaps 10 to 20 million, while India's Ganges valley and Western Asia's empires were as large.
The Han census of 2 CE counts 59.6 million registered people, about a quarter of humanity.

The Han collapse after the Yellow Turban rising (184): registered people fall from 56 million (157) to 16 million (280). Much of that fall is people lost to registration, not to death; how much is a debate, and this value takes a loss of about a sixth.
China reunited under the Sui, whose register of 609 counts about 46 million.

Tang China at its height, just before the An Lushan rebellion (755 to 763). The register of 754 counts about 53 million and that of 764 about 17 million. Most historians read the fall as a collapse of registration, with real losses of some millions; a minority reading, popular in lists of the deadliest wars, takes it as some 36 million dead. This series takes the first reading, so the share stays on its line to 770; the second would put a fall of several points here (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

Interpolated: the late Tang loses its hold, Huang Chao's rebellion (875 to 884) sacks Guangzhou and Chang'an, and the dynasty ends in 907; the Five Dynasties follow in the north until the Song reunite China from 960.
Song China passes 100 million with early-ripening rice, the densest farming the world had seen.
The Mongol conquest of the Jin and the Song (1211 to 1279): north China's registers fall by perhaps two thirds, and Eastern Asia's share by about seven points.
Rises only because Europe's and Western Asia's people fall in the Black Death.
Interpolated: late Ming China grows with the silver trade (from 1571) and Japan is unified by war; Japan's invasions of Korea (1592 to 1598) come after.
Late Ming China, perhaps 160 million, with New World crops beginning to spread.
The Ming-Qing transition: rebellion, conquest, famine and epidemics cut China's people by perhaps a sixth to a quarter between the 1620s and the 1650s, a loss whose size is debated.
Eastern Asia's peak share: Qing China near 380 million, more than a third of humanity, with Japan and Korea.
The Taiping war (1850 to 1864) and the Nian and Hui risings: China loses perhaps 20 to 30 million in war, famine and plague, and Eastern Asia's share falls four points in fifteen years.
On the line: the north China famine of 1876 to 1879 (9 to 13 million dead) makes the real fall steeper here and flatter afterwards.
Down again after the North China famine of 1876 to 1879, while Europe, the Americas and South-eastern Asia grow faster.

Interpolated, on the eve of the Great Leap Forward's famine. On the UN's estimates China's share of humanity peaks about 1958 and the famine of 1959 to 1961, 15 to 45 million dead on the debated counts, takes about half a point from it by 1961. This series shows the dip only faintly (26.85 at 1960 against 26.87 here), because Eastern Asia's subregion values are held to sum to Asia's and Asia's to the world's; a truer dip would raise this value by about 0.3 to 0.4 and needs Asia's and the other regions' 1958 values revised with it. Left for the next pass.
The famine of the Great Leap Forward (1959 to 1961) costs China 15 to 45 million deaths on the debated estimates; the share dips and recovers by 1965.
Births fall first in Eastern Asia: Japan from the 1950s, then China's 'later, longer, fewer' campaign of the 1970s and the one-child policy from 1980 (DemographicTransition#6e31).
China's population has fallen since 2022; Eastern Asia's share is back to where it stood in the first millennium BCE.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Eastern Asia's part of it; China dominates the part at every date.

points.note: Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and the last Homo erectus live here; archaic humans are not counted.
The Lida Ajer teeth in Sumatra, about 73,000 to 63,000 years old, would put Homo sapiens here before the main dispersal; debated.
Value unchanged; reason added in the review pass. The dispersal reaches South-east Asia on its way to Sahul, along coasts now drowned by the sea; the date is debated, as at Asia's value here.
At the glacial maximum the low sea exposes Sundaland, a warm lowland joining Sumatra, Java and Borneo to the mainland: a refuge, when the north was cold and dry.
The seas rise and begin to drown Sundaland; the region's share falls as its lowland shrinks.
Foragers still, while farmers multiply in Eastern and Southern Asia: rice farming arrives from the north only from about 2500 BCE, and the Austronesians reach the Philippines about 2200 BCE.

Interpolated: the Pyu cities and the isthmus ports trade with India and China, but the region's foragers and small farming chiefdoms grow more slowly than the Han and the Mauryan successor states, so its share falls.
The low point: perhaps five million, thinly spread through forest, with dense rice farming only in a few deltas and in northern Vietnam.
Anthony Reid's estimate of about 22 million for the region in 1600, as recalled.
Interpolated: Britain's first war in Burma opens the colonial century (ev.sea.era.colonial); the Java War and the Cultivation System follow, and the region's faster growth begins about 1850.

The turn: from here the region grows faster than the world for a century and a half, as Java's people multiply from under 5 million in 1815 to about 28 million in 1900 and the deltas of Burma, Siam and Cochinchina are cleared for rice.
Interpolated: the rice frontiers of the Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya and Mekong deltas open, and France begins its conquest of Indochina (1858); the region's growth outpaces the world's.
Japan invades (ev.sea.japanese-occupation). The region has grown a little faster than the world since 1936; from here its growth stops for four years.

The famine in northern Vietnam begins. Its dead are debated: about two million in Vietnamese accounts, about one million in some others. Hunger and forced labour in Java kill on a similar scale on some estimates, and the battle of Manila (February to March 1945) kills about 100,000 civilians; most of these deaths fall in the next eight months.
Flat through Japan's occupation: forced labour, the famine in northern Vietnam (about one to two million dead, 1944 to 1945) and hunger in Java hold the region's growth to nothing for four years.

Revised from 6.37, recorded earlier in this pass: the famine in northern Vietnam peaks in spring 1945 and the battle of Manila is fought in February and March, so at Japan's surrender the share is still at its wartime level. The August Revolution and Indonesia's proclamation open wars of independence (ev.sea.august-revolution, ev.as.indonesia-independence); the famines end, and the region grows again at about 2% a year against the world's 1 to 1.5%.
Revised from 6.43 with the value at 1945.63.

After the killings in Indonesia (ev.sea.indonesia-1965): about half a million dead, on estimates from 400,000 to a million or more, take about two hundredths of a point from the region's share, which its births keep rising.
Saigon falls and the Khmer Rouge take Phnom Penh; the note at 1976 gives the scale of their effect on the share.

The fall of Saigon (1975), the Khmer Rouge's killing and starving of perhaps a quarter of Cambodia's people (1975 to 1979) and the flight of the boat people: grave for the countries, a few hundredths of a point for the region's share, which keeps rising with Indonesia's and the Philippines' births.
The peak share: births have fallen to about replacement in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia, and the share now eases.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times South-eastern Asia's part of it; from 1600 Reid's estimates for the region as recalled, and Java's nineteenth-century growth.

points.note: Tools at Jwalapuram lie beneath the Toba ash, about 74,000 years old; whether their makers were Homo sapiens is debated, so the share is small with a band to zero.
The dispersal out of Africa fills the subcontinent's coasts and river valleys; South Asia holds the largest share of the people outside Africa from now until farming.
Farming at Mehrgarh, on the edge of the Indus plain, from about 7000 BCE.
The Harappan cities at their height, perhaps five million people in the Indus valley.
Farming spreads through the Ganges valley with iron; Southern Asia becomes Asia's largest part for the next two thousand years on most reconstructions.

India's people in 1 CE are the widest debate in this series: McEvedy and Jones about 35 million, Maddison 75 million; this value takes about 60 million for the subcontinent, with Iran and Afghanistan about 7.
Rises as Eastern Asia's falls under the Mongol conquest, which reached Iran but held India only at its edge.
Mughal India grows while China falls in the Ming-Qing transition: for a few decades Southern Asia holds more of humanity than Eastern Asia.
Interpolated: the Mughal empire has broken into successor states; the Company's victory at Plassey (1757) comes two years later.
India grows more slowly than Qing China through the eighteenth century, after the Mughal break-up and the famine of 1770 in Bengal.
On the line: the Indian famine of 1876 to 1878 (6 to 10 million dead) makes the real fall steeper here and flatter afterwards.
The famines of 1876 to 1878 and 1896 to 1902 kill perhaps 12 to 30 million in British India, and plague arrives from 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills perhaps 12 to 17 million in India, its largest toll anywhere.
The Bengal famine of 1943 kills about two to three million, yet deaths are falling elsewhere in India and its share rises.
About 2001 Southern Asia's share passes Eastern Asia's, since its births fell later and more slowly; India itself passes China in 2023.
Close to its peak share: India's fertility is now below replacement, so Southern Asia's share levels off as Africa's keeps rising.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Southern Asia's part of it; the Indian subcontinent dominates the part, with Iran beside it.

points.note: The Misliya jaw, about 180,000 years old, is an early venture into the Levant that left no lasting population; counted as zero.
The Last Interglacial opens the Levant and Arabia to Homo sapiens (Skhul and Qafzeh); for fifty thousand years all of Asia's people live here.
The glacial returns and the Levant's Homo sapiens give way to Neanderthals; a few hold on in Arabia (the Al Wusta finger bone, about 86,000 years old).
The glacial maximum dries Arabia and the Iranian plateau; Western Asia's people shrink into the Levant and the Zagros foothills.
The Natufians settle in villages in the Levant before farming.
The first farmers of the Fertile Crescent: Western Asia's share grows faster than any other region's for four thousand years.
The first cities of Mesopotamia (Uruk).
Western Asia's peak share, perhaps one in six of all people; from here it falls for four thousand years as farming spreads to larger lands.

Western Asia's people hold near 20 million through the Hellenistic and Roman-Parthian centuries while Han China, India and Mediterranean Europe grow, so its share falls by a third between 500 and 90 BCE.
Late Roman Anatolia and Syria and Sasanian Iraq at their fullest, before the plague of 541.
Iraq's irrigation decays after the ninth century, and Western Asia's share keeps falling.

Interpolated. The Mongols have beaten the Seljuks of Rum at Köse Dağ (1243) and overrun Armenia and Georgia, but most of the fall to 1300 comes after this date, with the sack of Baghdad (1258) and the wars between the Ilkhans and the Mamluks. The value is kept on the line between its neighbours so Asia's subregions still sum to Asia; the band holds the later timing.
The Mongols sack Baghdad (1258) and Iraq's canals are not rebuilt.
The Black Death kills perhaps a third of Syria's and Iraq's people.
The low point after the plague's returns and Timur's sacks of Baghdad and Damascus (1400 to 1401).
On the eve of the Armenian genocide and Gallipoli. Most of Western Asia's wartime losses, from massacre, deportation, war and the famine in Lebanon and Syria, come after this date.
The low point: war, the Armenian genocide, the Assyrian and Greek deportations and famine in Lebanon and Syria cost Anatolia and the Levant several million people from 1914 to 1922.
Rising fastest of Asia's parts: high fertility in Iraq and Yemen, and millions of workers drawn to the Gulf's oil states.

upsert.reason: Asia's share times Western Asia's part of it, which holds all of Asia's people before the dispersal and the first farmers after it.

points.note: The first Homo sapiens in Europe come in from the south-east: Bacho Kiro in Bulgaria about 46,000 years ago, Kostenki on the Don about 42,000.
The Gravettian mammoth hunters of Moravia and the Russian plain.
The glacial maximum empties the northern plain; people hold on in the Carpathian basin and the Ukrainian steppe.
The Cucuteni-Trypillia towns of Ukraine and Moldova, some of fifteen thousand people, the largest settlements in Europe.
Dacians, Thracians, Sarmatians, Balts and Slavs beyond Rome's frontier: about a fifth of Europe's people.
The Black Death strikes Eastern Europe less hard than the west and south; Poland is said to have escaped the worst of it.
Eastern Europe becomes Europe's largest part: Russia's peasants spread over the black-earth steppe and beyond the Volga.
Eastern Europe's peak share, more than a tenth of humanity, as the Russian Empire's births stay high while its deaths fall.
War, revolution, the civil war and the famine of 1921 cost the Russian lands perhaps 15 to 20 million lives between 1914 and 1922.
The Holodomor and the Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933 kill perhaps five to seven million, about four million of them in Ukraine.
The Second World War's deadliest ground: the Soviet Union loses about 27 million and Poland about six, Jews and others murdered in the Holocaust among them (ev.eu.eastern-front, ev.eu.holocaust).
After the Soviet Union's end births collapse and deaths rise among Russian and Ukrainian men: the region's numbers fall in absolute terms from 1993.
Russia's war on Ukraine from 2022 kills and scatters Ukraine's people; how many left Eastern Europe and how many remain in Poland and the rest of it is uncertain, so the band is wider.
Under the ice: Britain north of the Thames, Ireland and Scandinavia are covered or polar desert at the glacial maximum.
Hunters return to Britain and the Baltic as the ice retreats (the Creswellian and Hamburgian).
Doggerland drowns and Britain becomes an island, about 6500 BCE.
Foragers still, while farmers fill the Balkans and the Danube valley: the north's share of Europe falls until farming arrives about 4000 BCE.
Roman Britain at its fullest, perhaps two to three million.
The Viking age: raids and settlement in Britain, Ireland and Normandy move people within the region and out of it more than they change its share.
England near its medieval peak, perhaps four and a half to five million before the famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death kills perhaps four in ten in England and Scandinavia.
Britain's industrial towns grow fastest in Europe; Ireland loses a million to the famine of 1845 to 1852 and as many to emigration, yet the subregion's share rises.
Northern Europe's peak share: from here falling births and the emigration of Britons, Irish and Scandinavians overseas hold it back.
Immigration keeps the British and Nordic numbers growing while their births are below replacement.
Apidima in Greece, about 210,000 years old, may be an early Homo sapiens venture that left no descendants; counted as zero.
The glacial refuges of Iberia, Italy and the Balkans hold almost half of Europe's people at the glacial maximum.
Europe's first farmers arrive from Anatolia in Thessaly and Macedonia, about 6500 BCE, and spread along the Mediterranean coasts.

Minoan Crete at its height and the first Mycenaean shaft graves. The eruption of Thera is dated about 1600 BCE by radiocarbon and about 1500 BCE by the older archaeological chronology, a standing debate; it devastates Aegean coasts but leaves no mark on a share this coarse.
Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece.
Interpolated: Rome expels its kings (509 BCE) and Cleisthenes' reforms follow at Athens (508 BCE); Greek cities and colonies keep growing.
Greek cities and colonies, Etruscan and Latin Italy, Phoenician and Iberian Spain.
Interpolated: after the Peloponnesian War and Alexander's conquests, which draw Greek settlers east, Rome unites Italy by 264 BCE; the Punic Wars follow.
Augustan Italy, Iberia and Greece: perhaps 15 million, almost half of Europe's people, the Roman Empire's heart.
After the Antonine plague (ev.antonine-plague), which struck the Mediterranean hardest.

Interpolated: the third-century crisis and the plague of Cyprian (249 to about 262) have lowered the Mediterranean's numbers; Constantine founds Constantinople (330), and the western empire's fall is still to come.
The western empire's fall: Italy's and Spain's cities shrink, and the Mediterranean loses its lead in Europe.
The Justinianic plague and the Gothic wars in Italy (535 to 554).
The Black Death kills perhaps half of Italy's and Spain's people in towns like Florence and Siena.
Plague in northern Italy (1629 to 1631) and Spain's seventeenth-century crisis.
Mass emigration from Italy, Spain and Portugal to the Americas holds the share nearly flat.
Italy and Spain now have the lowest births in the world, about 1.2 children per woman, and the Yugoslav wars (1991 to 1999) scatter the Balkans' people.
Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley may hold a brief Homo sapiens presence about 54,000 years ago, among Neanderthals; debated, and with no lasting population.
The Aurignacians of the Danube and the Swabian Jura, with the first figurines and flutes, and Chauvet's paintings about 36,000 years ago.
South-west France, the Franco-Cantabrian refuge, holds Western Europe's people at the glacial maximum; the north and the Alps are empty.
The Linear Pottery farmers spread from the Danube across the loess of Germany and northern France, about 5500 to 5000 BCE.
Celtic Gaul before Caesar's conquest, perhaps six to eight million.
Late Roman Gaul and the Rhineland, after the third-century crisis and before the Rhine frontier breaks at the end of 406.
The high-medieval clearing of forests in France and Germany: Western Europe becomes Europe's largest part.
France perhaps 17 to 20 million, the most populous kingdom in Christendom, before the great famine of 1315 and the plague.
The Black Death (ev.black-death).
Interpolated: France's wars of religion (from 1562) and the Dutch revolt (from 1568) kill hundreds of thousands, yet Western Europe's numbers keep pace with the world's.

Interpolated: the Thirty Years' War begins (1618). Most of Germany's losses to war, plague and hunger, perhaps a third of its people, fall in the 1630s; the value is kept on the line between its neighbours so Europe's parts still sum to Europe, and the band holds a later fall.
The Thirty Years War (1618 to 1648) costs Germany perhaps a third of its people, in some regions more than half, to war, plague and hunger.
The French Revolution begins. France's births have begun to fall, and its wars from 1792 to 1815 kill about a million and a half French soldiers on most estimates, so Western Europe's share eases.
France's births begin to fall a century before the rest of Europe's, and Western Europe's share eases from here.

Interpolated: industry spreads from Britain to Belgium, northern France and the Rhineland, and the first factory laws pass; Western Europe's share holds while France's births stay low and Germany's rise.
The Western Front: France and Germany each lose more than a million and a half soldiers.
Some twelve million Germans expelled from the east arrive in the occupied zones, 1945 to 1950.
Immigration, the refugees of 2015 and of Ukraine since 2022 among them, keeps Germany's and France's numbers rising while their births stay low.
Neanderthals hold Europe; archaic humans are not counted, and Apidima's skull, if it is an early sapiens, left no lasting population.
Apidima in Greece (about 210,000 years ago) may be an early sapiens venture with no descendants; counted as zero.
Glacial maximum: retreat to southern refugia.
The Roman peak.
After the Antonine plague.
After the first wave of the Justinianic plague.
High-medieval growth: about 70 million.
The Black Death: from about 74 to 50 million.
Europe's peak share, a quarter of humanity.
The war's deadliest years in Europe, the Holocaust and the war in the east (ev.eu.holocaust, ev.eu.eastern-front): Europe's share falls by about a tenth of a point a year.
Europe's war dead and the expulsions after it lower its share.
The postwar boom begins. Europe's births rise in the baby boom, but deaths fall faster in Asia, Africa and Latin America, so Europe's share falls by about a quarter of a point a year.
Interpolated: Europe's share falls by about 0.16 points a year through the 1950s.

changes.value: Fill: the report names 1870 to 1890 as the coarsest stretch of Oceania's subregions and the shares of the faiths. 1880 is filled for each. Oceania's parts add to its 0.3344 at 1880 on its own line between 1879.37 and 1885.8 (Australia and New Zealand + Melanesia + Micronesia + Polynesia; Polynesia = east + west), Australia and New Zealand from the censuses of 1881; the eight faiths add to 100. Recalled or interpolated (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

points.note: Zero: no people in Australia yet.
Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Begins: people cross the sea from Sunda to Sahul.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago.
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply, so the share falls.

The First Fleet lands at Sydney Cove. Aboriginal Australians perhaps 750,000, from 300,000 to over a million on the estimates; as a share of the parent this holds about 500,000, the gap being the parent's.
Falls: the smallpox of 1789 kills perhaps half the Eora around Sydney; whether it came from the First Fleet's stores or from Makassan trepangers in the north is debated.
Settlers pass 70,000 as the squatters' wool frontier opens, while smallpox (1789 and 1829 to 1831) and the frontier wars cut Aboriginal numbers.
About 405,000 settlers and convicts, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession.
Rises most: Victoria's gold rush more than doubles the settlers within a decade.
The colonies' censuses of 1881 count about 2.25 million settlers; Aboriginal people, mostly uncounted, perhaps 100,000 to 200,000 more.
About 3.8 million at Federation (1901); the Immigration Restriction Act begins the White Australia policy.
About 8.2 million: postwar immigration and the baby boom begin to lift Australia's share.
The postwar migration programme brings Britons and the displaced of Europe ('populate or perish'); with the baby boom Australia grows faster than the world.
Australia's peak share since 1950, about 11.4 million: from here the world's growth, at its fastest ever, outpaces Australia's as births fall after the boom.
The White Australia policy ends (1973); migration from Asia grows, but slower intakes and falling births let the share ease.
The low point of Australia's share: from the mid-2000s the mining boom draws record immigration, and Australia again grows faster than the world.
About 27 million; about three in ten born overseas, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples 3.2% at the 2021 census.

upsert.reason: The whole of the parent before about 1280; after that the parent less New Zealand's part.

points.note: Zero: no people reach Aotearoa New Zealand before Polynesian voyagers about 1280.
Still empty. Radiocarbon dates on rat-gnawed seeds and the earliest sites put first settlement about 1250 to 1300; an older claim of about 800, from dates on rat bones, is now rejected.
Begins: Polynesian voyagers from the Society and Cook Islands settle Aotearoa about 1280, a founding population of perhaps a few hundred.
Grows fast on moa and seals, and on kumara where it will grow; the moa are gone by about 1450.
About 100,000 Maori at Cook's visits (1769) on the usual estimate, between perhaps 85,000 and 150,000; here the parent's share times that against Australia's numbers.
A larger share of the subregion as Aboriginal numbers fall; the Musket Wars among iwi armed with traded guns (about 1807 to 1845) kill perhaps 20,000.
The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and organized settlement begin; Maori perhaps 80,000 after the Musket Wars and new diseases.
Falls: Maori about 60,000, settlers about 25,000.
Rises most: Otago's gold rush from 1861 and assisted migration; settlers outnumber Maori from about 1858, and the New Zealand Wars (1845 to 1872) take Maori land.
The census of 1881 counts about 490,000 settlers after Vogel's assisted immigration, and about 44,000 Maori.
Vogel's assisted immigration of the 1870s; Maori at their lowest, about 42,000 in 1896.
The influenza of 1918 kills about 9,000, Maori at about seven times the settlers' rate.
New Zealand's peak share since 1950, about 2.6 million at the height of its baby boom and assisted migration; it falls from here as births drop and New Zealanders leave for Australia.
Falls: emigration to Australia after 1976, net losses in most years to 1990, and slowing births.
The low point: from 2014 net migration turns strongly positive, New Zealanders returning from Australia and arrivals from Asia, and the share rises.
About 5.3 million, a sixth of the subregion's people; Maori about a sixth of New Zealand's, Pasifika peoples about a twelfth.

upsert.reason: Zero before about 1280; then the parent times New Zealand's share of the subregion's people, wider before the censuses of the 1850s.

points.note: Zero on the later arrival; Madjedbebe's luminescence dates of about 65,000 years would put people in northern Australia already, a debated reading.
Australia filled within a few thousand years of arrival; Lake Mungo's burials about 42,000 years ago (ev.oc.lake-mungo).
The glacial maximum dries the interior; people withdraw to refuges on the coasts and ranges.
The rising sea cuts Tasmania off (ev.anz.tasmanian-isolation) and drowns the Sahul shelf; foragers' numbers hold while farmers elsewhere multiply.

Interpolated. From about 4000 BCE backed blades, seed-grinding and new sites spread across mainland Australia and Pama-Nyungan languages spread from the Gulf country. Many read these as signs of more people, but the share still falls because farmers elsewhere multiply faster.
Polynesian voyagers settle Aotearoa about 1280, the last large land reached by people.

The First Fleet (ev.oc.first-fleet). As a share of the parent's 0.2% this holds about 570,000 people, against the usual estimates of about 750,000 Aboriginal Australians (from 300,000 to over a million) and about 100,000 Maori; the gap is the parent's (h.region-oceania), whose early-modern level is debated, and the band now reaches the usual estimates.
About 470,000 settlers, while Aboriginal numbers have fallen to perhaps 300,000 and Maori to 60,000, from smallpox, frontier killing and dispossession (ev.oc.depopulation).
The gold rushes (ev.oc.gold-rushes) more than double Australia's settlers in a decade.
The sum of Australia (about 8.2 million) and New Zealand (about 1.9 million).
Assisted passages from Britain and the displaced of Europe: migration and the baby boom carry Australia's and New Zealand's share up while the world grows faster than ever.
The subregion's peak share since 1950: both lands' booms end, and from here the world outgrows them.
The low point: the mining boom's immigration into Australia and, from 2014, New Zealand's returning migrants lift the share again.
About 32.5 million; immigration, from Asia above all since the 1970s, carries most of the growth.

upsert.reason: Declared the sum of Australia and New Zealand, which share its unit and hold every person in the subregion once.

points.note: Voyagers from the Philippines cross some 2,000 kilometres of open sea to the Marianas, about 1500 BCE, the longest sea crossing yet made (ev.mic.marianas).
Nan Madol on Pohnpei, the Saudeleur capital of basalt islets, at its height.
The Spanish-Chamorro wars and epidemics (1668 to 1695) cut the Marianas' people from perhaps 40,000 or more to under 5,000, too few to move the subregion's share by a thousandth.
Smallpox on Pohnpei (1854) kills perhaps half its people.
Japanese settlers in the South Seas Mandate outnumber the islanders by 1940; they are deported after 1945.
About 155,000: Guam with its American base, Kiribati, the Carolines, the Marshalls, the Marianas, Palau and Nauru.

Micronesia's peak share: high births on Kiribati and in the Federated States, and workers drawn to Guam and the Northern Marianas' garment factories; from the 1990s the compacts of free association let islanders move to the United States.
About 540,000 people; emigration to Guam, Hawai'i and the United States under the compacts of free association holds the numbers nearly flat as the world grows.
No one lives in East Polynesia before the voyages after the long pause, about 1025 by the short chronology.
Empty by the short chronology; the older 'long chronology', with East Polynesia settled from about 300 to 800, is now held by few, and the band leaves room for it (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Still empty by the short chronology, whose radiocarbon dates on short-lived plant remains put the first landfall in the Society Islands about 1025 to 1120 (ev.pol.society-islands).

Voyagers from Samoa settle the Society Islands about 1025 to 1120 and within a century the Cooks, the Marquesas, the Australs and the Tuamotus (ev.oc.polynesia-settlement): founding groups of a few hundred growing at 2 to 3% a year.
The east's islands fill: the Marquesan valleys and the Society Islands' chiefdoms build marae and terraces (ev.pol.era.chiefdoms), and their numbers draw level with the west's.

On the eve of contact, about 120,000 people, more than half of Polynesia's: the Marquesas perhaps 35,000 to 100,000, the Society Islands 35,000 to 70,000 (Cook's 204,000 for Tahiti is rejected), the Cooks about 17,000, the Tuamotus, Australs and Mangareva some 20,000 (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Wallis (1767), Bougainville and Cook (1769) at Tahiti bring venereal disease, tuberculosis and dysentery (ev.oc.cook-voyages): the east's numbers begin to fall (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).
Tahiti holds about 16,000 at the missionaries' count of 1797; whalers and traders reach the Marquesas, whose fall begins (ev.pol.marquesas).
Peruvian slavers take most of Tongareva's people in the northern Cooks (ev.pol.slave-raids), and smallpox reaches the Marquesas (1863).

The low point: about 37,000 in French Polynesia and the Cooks, perhaps a third of the east's numbers at contact; the Marquesas fall on to about 2,000 by the 1920s, while Tahiti, with Chinese and European settlers, begins to grow.
About 77,000: French Polynesia about 62,000 and the Cooks about 15,000.

France's nuclear testing centre at Moruroa and Fangataufa (1963 to 1996) brings work, money and migrants to Tahiti: French Polynesia grows faster than any other part of Polynesia, while Cook Islanders leave for New Zealand.
About 297,000: French Polynesia about 280,000, whose growth has slowed since the testing centre closed, and the Cook Islands about 15,000, most of whose people now live in New Zealand.

upsert.reason: The parent's value at each date times East Polynesia's part of it, from recalled counts of each island group (the Society Islands, the Marquesas, the Tuamotus and Australs, the Cooks); bands are the parent's band times the same part, widened before 1150 for the debated chronology.

points.note: No one lives in Polynesia before the first landfall in Tonga, about 880 BCE.
Lapita potters from Fiji land at Nukuleka in Tonga about 880 BCE and reach Samoa soon after (ev.pol.tonga-samoa-lapita): a few hundred settlers, the first people of Polynesia.
Tonga and Samoa fill with the descendants of the first few hundred settlers: growing at about 1% a year, they number perhaps ten thousand by 500 BCE (ev.pol.era.ancestral).
The long pause: Tonga, Samoa, 'Uvea and Futuna hold all of Polynesia's people for nearly two thousand years (ev.pol.era.ancestral).
Voyagers from Samoa settle the Society Islands about 1025 to 1120 (ev.pol.society-islands); the west's share eases as the east fills and the world grows.
On the eve of contact: about 95,000 to 100,000 people, Samoa perhaps 40,000 to 60,000 and Tonga 25,000 to 40,000; the west now holds a little under half of Polynesia's people.
Tonga's civil wars begin (1799) and last half a century, but Samoa sees few outsiders before the missions of 1830, so the west's numbers hold near 100,000 while the east's fall.
Peruvian slavers take people from Tuvalu, Tokelau and Niue (ev.pol.slave-raids); Tokelau loses nearly half its people.
About 70,000: the west's low point, some two thirds of its numbers at contact.
The influenza of November 1918 kills about 8,500 in Western Samoa, a fifth of its people, while American Samoa's quarantine keeps it out (ev.pol.samoa-influenza); numbers recover within a few years.
About 169,000: Samoa 82,000, Tonga 50,000, American Samoa 19,000 and the smaller islands 18,000; falling deaths make the west grow at about 3% a year.
The west's peak share: from the 1960s Samoans and Tongans leave in large numbers for New Zealand, the United States and Australia (ev.pol.diaspora).
About 395,000 at home (Samoa about 220,000, Tonga about 104,000, American Samoa about 45,000); more Samoans and Tongans now live abroad than in their islands.

upsert.reason: A note for the rise the report found unexplained.

points.note: Corrected from 0.003: no one lives in Polynesia before the first landfall in Tonga, about 880 BCE (ev.pol.tonga-samoa-lapita).
Corrected from 0.006, for the same reason; the Lapita people of these centuries live in Fiji, Vanuatu and New Caledonia, in Melanesia, where the share is now counted.

Lapita voyagers from Fiji reach Tonga about 880 BCE and Samoa soon after (ev.pol.tonga-samoa-lapita): a few hundred settlers, then the long pause of nearly two thousand years. Corrected from 0.008, which counted thousands here within a century of the first landfall.
Tonga and Samoa fill with the descendants of the first few hundred settlers: growing at about 1% a year, they number perhaps ten thousand by 500 BCE (ev.pol.era.ancestral).
The voyages east begin: the Society Islands and the Marquesas are settled about 1000 to 1100 (ev.oc.polynesia-settlement).

Raised from 0.022, with the values to 1791, so that the numbers on the eve of contact (about 215,000 in 1767) stand above, not below, those of 1800: the series had Polynesia growing while contact began to cut Tahiti's people. The usual pre-contact estimates run from about 180,000 to over 300,000 (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).
Wallis reaches Tahiti (June 1767): about 215,000 people in Polynesia as M49 draws it, more than half of them in the east.
Wallis (1767) and Cook (1769) at Tahiti: contact brings venereal disease, tuberculosis and dysentery, and the share falls while the world grows.
The Marquesas lose perhaps nine in ten of their people in the nineteenth century, and Tahiti's fall to about a fifth of Cook's estimate (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd).

The Peruvian slave raids of 1862 to 1863 carry off about 3,500 Polynesians and Micronesians, perhaps 1,500 of them from Tuvalu, Tokelau, Niue and the northern Cooks (ev.pol.slave-raids); Rapa Nui's losses count in South America. Raised from 0.010, a dip larger than the raids explain.
Corrected from 0.011, a rise of a tenth in five years that nothing explains: the subregion's numbers fall slowly through the 1860s and 1870s.

The low point: about 110,000 people, about half the numbers on the eve of contact as this series holds them (about 215,000 in 1767), and a third if the higher estimates of the Marquesas and Samoa hold (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

Raised from 0.006, with the values to 1945, from the colonial censuses as recalled (Western Samoa about 34,000, Tonga 23,000, French Polynesia 31,000, the Cooks 8,500): the series had held 0.006 to 1945 and then jumped by three fifths to 1950, where an earlier pass set the values from the UN's counts.
The influenza of 1918 kills about a fifth of Western Samoa's people (ev.pol.samoa-influenza) (Twinflow#9474).
About 210,000: Samoa, Tonga and French Polynesia grow at 2 to 3% a year as deaths fall, so the share rises toward the UN's count of 1950.

About 240,000 in Samoa, Tonga, French Polynesia, American Samoa, the Cook Islands, Tuvalu, Wallis and Futuna and Niue: numbers have recovered from the low of about 1900 and grow fast with falling deaths.

Polynesia's peak share since contact: from the 1960s Samoans, Tongans and Cook Islanders leave in large numbers for New Zealand, the United States and Australia, so the islands grow slower than the world.
About 700,000 at home; more Samoans and Tongans now live in New Zealand, Australia and the United States than in their islands (ev.pol.diaspora).

upsert.reason: A note for the rise the report found unexplained.

points.note: Corrected from 96.7: an interpolation artefact between the anchors at -300000 and -1000. Every tradition before the Vedic and Zhou ones is local and folk.
Corrected from an interpolation artefact.
Corrected from an interpolation artefact.
Corrected from an interpolation artefact.
Corrected from an interpolation artefact.
Corrected from an interpolation artefact. Egyptian, Sumerian and Indus religion count as local traditions here.
Kept so the eight shares sum to one hundred with Buddhism still small at Ashoka's accession (h.religion-2).
The Roman world's own cults, counted here, still hold almost all of its people.
The empire's temples lose most of their people between Constantine (312) and Theodosius's ban on sacrifice (391).
The Greco-Roman cults have given way to Christianity (h.religion-4); local traditions are now those of sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas, northern Europe, the steppe, Arabia and the islands.
Rises a little to 1400 as the Black Death and the Mongol wars shrink Eurasia's people while the Americas and Africa, where local traditions hold, are spared.
Local traditions lose most in the Americas, where their people die and the survivors are baptized.
The first Protestant missions land on Tahiti (1797); the conversions of the Pacific that follow move well under a tenth of a point of humanity, so the share keeps its slow drift.

Brahmanical religion spreads through the Ganges plain and south India after the Mauryas, as South Asia's share of humanity grows.
Holds: Theravada displaces the Hindu court cults of the mainland, from Pagan to Angkor, but those courts' followers are a fraction of a point of humanity beside India's own people.
The Buddha's teaching begins in the Ganges plain (ev.as.sramana).
The Buddha's own lifetime.
Ashoka's accession (ev.as.ashoka): Buddhism is still a minority movement of the Ganges plain; his patronage carries it across India and beyond.
After Ashoka; spreading to Central Asia.
Buddhism reaches China, by tradition under Emperor Ming (ev.as.buddhism-east).
Falls slowly: Buddhism's decline in India outweighs Theravada's spread across the mainland's villages from Pagan.

Falls as Europe's and the Americas' people multiply, with the north China famine of 1876 to 1879.
No Christians yet: Jesus's movement begins about 30 (ev.christianity-rise).
About 200,000 Christians in the Roman Empire by Hopkins's and Stark's reconstructions, near 0.1% of humanity; the upper band keeps the higher line of the World Christian Database.

After Constantine's conversion (312) the churches grow fastest: Stark's model has about 34 million Christians in 350, more than half the empire, from about 6 million in 300. Faster growth after 312 than before (MacMullen) and Stark's steady 40% a decade give similar values here.

Most of the Roman world has become Christian since Constantine (312) and Theodosius (380), with Armenia, Georgia, Aksum and the Church of the East in Persia: about a fifth of humanity. Stark's model has 34 million Christians already by 350; the World Christian Database about 22% at 500.
Nubia converts (540s to 570s), but the Justinianic plague (from 541) falls hardest on the Christian Mediterranean: the share holds.

The Arab conquests put Syria, Egypt, North Africa and Spain under Muslim rule, but their Christians convert to Islam only slowly over the next three centuries (Bulliet), so the share falls little yet.
Conversion to Islam in Egypt, Syria, Iraq and al-Andalus, fastest in the ninth and tenth centuries, takes the share to its low.
Latin Europe's people grow faster than the world's, and the north is now baptized.
The Church of the East in Asia shrinks after the Mongol conversions to Islam; the Black Death (1347 to 1351) falls hardest on Europe, so the share falls to 17% by 1400.
The Reformation (1517) divides Western Christianity without changing its share.
Revolutionary France's dechristianization (1793 to 1794) is reversed within a decade and the Pacific missions begin (1797); the Christian share holds near 22%.
Christians grow fastest of the faiths: Europe's and the Americas' populations outgrow Asia's, and the Second Great Awakening and the missionary societies spread churches on the frontiers.
Muhammad's first revelation, by tradition in 610 (ev.islam-rise): the Muslim community is a few followers in Mecca.
The caliphate's subjects were mostly not yet Muslim; conversion ran over the next three centuries.
Israelite religion and Zoroastrianism (ev.as.israel-bible, ev.as.zoroastrianism) separate from the local traditions they grew out of.
Zoroastrianism becomes the Achaemenid court's religion and Judaism takes its lasting shape in the Babylonian exile and return (ev.as.zoroastrianism, ev.as.israel-bible).
Jews of Judah and the diaspora, and Zoroastrians under the Achaemenids. The anchor of 0 at -1000 leaves Israelite religion among local traditions, a choice that could be revisited.
The Jewish diaspora spreads across the Hellenistic and Roman world, and Zoroastrianism holds Parthian Iran (ev.as.parthia).
Christianity absorbs much of the Roman world's Jewish and pagan population (ev.christianity-rise), and Buddhism and Christianity grow faster than Judaism and Zoroastrianism.
Jews expelled from Spain (1492) and Portugal (1496) move within the world, not out of their faith; Guru Nanak's teaching begins about 1499. The share holds.
Before most of the Holocaust's killing (ev.eu.holocaust).

By early 1943 most of the Holocaust's victims are dead: the death camps of Operation Reinhard and the shootings in the east killed most of them in 1942 (ev.eu.holocaust), so the Jewish share is already near its 1944 low.
By 1944 about five of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust are dead (ev.eu.holocaust): the Jewish share of humanity falls from about 0.7% to under 0.5%.

points.note: Zero: no states.
Tolls on goods moving through the first states: a twentieth of their revenue.
Han China's salt and iron monopolies, from 117 BCE, and Rome's harbour and frontier duties.
After the An Lushan rebellion the Tang raise about half their cash revenue from the salt monopoly.
Song China's commercial taxes and monopolies of salt, tea and wine pass its land tax: the first state to live mostly on goods.
Below the Song's height after the Mongol conquest of China.

England's excise state after 1688: by 1750 customs and excise are about three quarters of British revenue (Brewer's fiscal-military state). War between the European powers rewarded the states that could raise more (Warsift#b01b).
Customs and excise carry the nineteenth-century states (the United States lived on its tariff until 1913); the Qing add the lijin transit tax from 1853.
Tariffs come back after the free-trade decades: Germany's of 1879, France's of 1881 and 1892, and the United States' high wartime tariffs kept.
The Soviet turnover tax, levied on goods, pays most of a state that takes about a third of its economy's output.
Value-added tax spreads across Europe after 1967 from France's of 1954, and later to most of the world.
About three tenths of revenue, more in poorer countries, which lean on VAT and customs.
Zero until Britain's income tax of 1799: earlier levies on movables and tithes on produce are counted with land and goods.
Pitt's income tax, 1799, to pay for the war with revolutionary France.
Britain repeals its income tax in 1816: back to about zero.
Peel brings Britain's income tax back in 1842.
The Union's income tax of 1862, for the Civil War.
The American wartime income tax lapses (1872).
Prussia's income tax of 1891 and Bismarck's social insurance from 1883; Japan's income tax of 1887.
The United States' federal income tax, 1913.
Wartime income and excess-profits taxes in every belligerent: revenue from incomes rises more than fourfold in four years (Warsift#b01b: the war rewards the states that can raise more).
Falls back with peace but stays three times its 1913 level.
Income tax withheld from wages (the United States from 1943) turns it into a mass tax.
Incomes pay about half of all revenue at the war's height.

Peacetime: payroll contributions to the welfare states keep it rising for half a century, a rise that war competition does not explain (Warsift#b01b fits the wars, not this; its failure mode 'one path for all').
Income, profit and payroll taxes and social contributions: more than half of world revenue, about three fifths in rich states.
Zero: no states.
The first states (Uruk) take grain, cloth and labour from cultivators: about seven tenths of their revenue; the temple and royal estates' own produce is counted with what the state owns.
Land and poll taxes pay about seven tenths of Rome's and Han China's revenue.
Song China raises more from salt, wine, tea and commerce than from land; elsewhere the land tax still pays most.
The Mughal land revenue, the Ming single-whip land tax and the Ottoman tithe: most of the world's revenue is still levied on the harvest.
Fixed land taxes shrink in value with wartime inflation while income taxes rise.
Land and property taxes are about an eighth of revenue, and a twentieth by 1980.
Zero: no states.
Temple and royal estates are about a quarter of the first states' revenue.

Mongol tribute from subject peoples.
The Spanish crown's fifth of American silver, and the Aztec and Inca tribute systems taken over by Spain.
Crown lands are sold off and American silver fades with Spain's empire.

Turns up against the long fall: the Dutch Cultivation System's crop sales (from 1830) and Peru's state guano (from the 1840s) bring states revenue from what they own, while crown lands elsewhere are sold.
State railways (Prussia) and colonial monopolies (the Dutch Indies' cultivation system) count here.

No schools before writing: learning passed by imitation, stories, initiation and work.
Writing begins in Sumer and Egypt; the first scribal schools are too few to read above zero at this resolution.
The scribal schools of Sumer and Egypt: their first years of sign lists and copying are counted here, the advanced years as secondary; the boundary is this account's reading.
Protestant and Catholic reformers both push reading schools: Luther's call for schools, the Jesuit and parish schools, with Ming and Edo village schools.
The growth is almost all elementary: Prussia's and Scotland's parish schools, New England's common schools, Japan's temple schools (terakoya).
Compulsory elementary schooling spreads: Britain's Education Act (1870), France's Ferry laws (1881 to 1882), Meiji Japan's school law (1872).
France's Ferry laws (1881 to 1882) make primary school free and compulsory; Japan's schools reach about half its children.
Primary's share of all years is at its highest, nine in ten.
From here Barro and Lee's attainment by level (as recalled): primary is still about four in five years of school.
Slowing toward six years, where everyone completes primary; most of the growth is now above it.
The advanced years of scribal training (literary texts, mathematics, law) counted as a middle stage: about a tenth of all years.
Greek grammar and rhetoric schools spread with the Hellenistic cities.
Madrasas spread from the eleventh century and Song China's state schools prepare candidates for the examinations.
Humanist grammar schools and Jesuit colleges in Europe; Ming county and prefectural schools.
Its share of all years falls while mass primary schooling grows faster: lycées and gymnasia stay for the few.

Turns up: the American high-school movement (Goldin and Katz), from about one in ten American teenagers in high school in 1910 to most by 1940; Europe's secondary schools stay narrow until after 1945.
After 1945 secondary schooling spreads in Europe, Japan and the Soviet Union, then in the new states: the secondary turn carries most of the world's growth in years from here.
Secondary years pass a third of all years of school.
Still growing fastest in South Asia and Africa, where lower secondary is becoming universal.

Begins: Plato's Academy (about 387 BCE), Aristotle's Lyceum, the Museum of Alexandria, Taxila's teachers; the Han Imperial Academy (Taixue) follows in 124 BCE. Which ancient schools count as higher learning is a matter of definition.
The Later Han's Imperial Academy is said to have held some 30,000 students in the mid second century.
Nalanda in India (from the fifth century) and the Sui and Tang state academies.
The universities of Bologna, Paris and Oxford, the Nizamiyya madrasas of higher law and the Song academies.
The American GI Bill (1944) sends returning soldiers to college: the first step from elite to mass higher education.
Higher education turns from elite to mass (Trow's terms) in North America, Europe, Japan and the Soviet bloc from about 1960.
China expands its universities from 1999, from under a tenth of young people enrolled to over half by 2020; India and Latin America grow fast too.
About a tenth of all years of school; women now outnumber men in higher education in most countries.
Scribal schools of Sumer and Egypt.
Prussia's compulsory primary schools, Guizot's law for a primary school in every French commune (1833) and the common-school movement in Massachusetts (Horace Mann, from 1837).
Britain's Education Act of 1870 and the spread of compulsory schooling begin (ev.mass-schooling).

points.note: Starting value in a glacial stage (MIS 8) about 60 m below today; Antarctica's share is set at about a tenth of each glacial fall, as reconstructions of the last cycle give it.
Grows with the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: shrinks toward its interglacial size.
Grows again in the penultimate glacial (MIS 6).
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: by the start of the Last Interglacial Antarctica already holds less ice than today.

The Last Interglacial: about 3 m from Antarctica, above all a retreat of West Antarctica, the largest share of the highstand; how much, and whether East Antarctica's marine basins retreated too, is debated.
Glacial inception (MIS 5d): regrows as the world cools after about 116,000 years ago.
MIS 4: grows quickly with the northern sheets.
About 12.5 m at the glacial maximum, the most debated of the parts: reconstructions run from about 5 to 20 m.
Antarctica lags: still near its glacial size while the northern sheets have begun to melt.
A few metres to meltwater pulse 1A; some reconstructions give it much more (debated).
After the northern sheets are gone, Antarctica's slow retreat supplies most of the last 3.5 m of the Holocene rise, ending about 4,000 years ago.
Losing ice since the 1990s, faster since about 2010 as West Antarctica's glaciers speed up: about 1 cm of sea level since 2000.
Starting value, set at about a fiftieth of the glacial fall: mountain glaciers and ice caps, the Patagonian ice among them.
Advance in the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: retreat.
Advance again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: retreat to interglacial size.
Smaller than today in the Last Interglacial's warmth.
Advance at the glacial inception.
MIS 4: advance.
The mountain glaciers and ice caps of the glacial maximum, the Patagonian ice sheet among them: about 2.5 m (debated).
Retreat from the glacial maximum; the Patagonian ice thins.
Mid-Holocene glaciers about as small as in 2000, many smaller.
The neoglacial: glaciers grow back after about 4,000 years ago.
The cold of the sixth and seventh centuries (the Late Antique Little Ice Age).
Medieval warmth: glaciers smaller than in the Little Ice Age.
The Little Ice Age: glaciers advance in the Alps, Scandinavia and elsewhere from about 1550.
The Little Ice Age's last advances, about 1820 to 1850: glaciers hold about 8.5 cm of sea level more than in 2000.
The glaciers' last Little Ice Age advance (the Alpine glaciers reach their modern maximum about 1850 to 1855): they hold slightly more water than in 1820.
Retreat begins about 1850, the start of the modern rise.
The Little Ice Age ends: the Alpine glaciers retreat from their maxima of the 1850s.
About 2 cm since 2000; glaciers were the largest part of the rise from 1900 to 1990.
Starting value, set at about a fortieth of the glacial fall: in glacials Greenland's ice reaches out over its continental shelf.
Grows with the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: shrinks toward its present size.
Grows again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: northern summers peak and Greenland melts past its present size.
About 2 m smaller than today in the Last Interglacial (estimates from about 1 to 3.5).
Regrows after about 116,000 years ago as northern summers cool.
MIS 4: grows with the cold stage.
Larger at the glacial maximum, out to the edge of the continental shelf: about 3 m.
Begins to retreat from the shelf with the deglaciation.
Slightly smaller than in 2000 in the mid-Holocene warmth (debated), then regrowing in the neoglacial cooling to the Little Ice Age.
The neoglacial: Greenland's ice regrows past its 2000 size.
The Arctic warming of the 1920s to 1940s melts Greenland faster than any time until the 1990s.
Near balance from about 1970 to 1995.
About 2 cm of sea level since 2000, a fifth of the rise.
Pluvial lakes fill in the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: the pluvial lakes shrink.
They fill again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial's pluvial lakes.
Termination II: the pluvial lakes empty.
The Last Interglacial's green Sahara held lakes too; no estimate is recalled.
MIS 4's pluvial lakes.
The pluvial lakes of the glacial maximum, Lake Bonneville and Lake Lahontan in the American Great Basin among them, hold a few tenths of a metre.
Lake Agassiz forms at the Laurentide's southern edge as the pluvial lakes of the west shrink.
Lake Agassiz near its largest and the lakes of the green Sahara (mega-Chad among them) full: about half a metre of sea level held on land.
Lake Agassiz drains into Hudson Bay about 8,200 years ago; the Sahara's lakes are still full.
The Sahara dries and its lakes give their water back.
Before the great dams: land holds about a centimetre of sea level less than in 2000, because reservoirs have since held back more than pumped groundwater has released.
The great dam-building decades begin: reservoirs hold back about 3 cm of sea level by 2000 while groundwater pumping returns part of it.
Groundwater pumped from the aquifers of India, China, the Middle East and the American plains has outrun the dams since about 2000.
The northern sheets carry about five sixths of every glacial fall of the sea; the shares of the other parts are set from the last glacial cycle's reconstructions and scaled to each stage.
MIS 8: the northern sheets grow to a full glacial, about 75 m of sea level.
MIS 7c: most of the northern ice melts.
MIS 6, the penultimate glacial, builds the northern sheets again after MIS 7's warm substages.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6): the Eurasian ice sheet larger than at the last maximum and the North American smaller (debated); together about 92 m.
Termination II: nearly all of it gone by the start of the Last Interglacial.
Gone: the Last Interglacial, like today, has no northern ice outside Greenland.
Ice returns in MIS 5d.
MIS 4: the northern sheets grow quickly.
Toward the last glacial maximum: the Laurentide and Fennoscandian sheets reach their greatest extent between about 26,000 and 19,000 years ago.

The last glacial maximum: the Laurentide, Cordilleran, Fennoscandian, British-Irish and Barents-Kara sheets hold about 104 m of sea level (most reconstructions 90 to 115), most of the 125 m fall that exposed Beringia and Doggerland.
Retreat begins after about 19,000 years ago, slowly at first.

Meltwater pulse 1A, about 14,600 years ago (between -13000 and -12000 here): about 15 to 20 m of sea level in four centuries. Most reconstructions credit the collapse of the ice saddle between the Laurentide and Cordilleran sheets; others give Antarctica a large share (debated). Here the northern sheets give about 16 m and Antarctica about 2.5.
The Laurentide's last domes collapse over Hudson Bay; Lake Agassiz drains about 8,200 years ago.
Gone: the last Laurentide ice in Labrador and Nunavut melted about 6,700 years ago; zero from here on.
Starting value: a glacial ocean colder than today's, set at about a fiftieth of the glacial fall.
Cools in the MIS 8 glacial.
MIS 7c: warms.
Cools again in the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial maximum.
Termination II: warms to interglacial temperatures and past today's.
A warmer ocean in the Last Interglacial: about half a metre of the highstand.
Cools at the glacial inception.
MIS 4: cools.
A colder ocean takes less room: about 2.5 m at the glacial maximum.
Warms through the deglaciation.
The neoglacial cooling: the ocean colder than in 2000.
The ocean's warming takes up again after mid-century and speeds up from about 1970.
About 3.7 cm since 2000, the largest single part of the recent rise.
The MIS 8 glacial: the sea falls to about 90 m below today before MIS 7's warm stages.
MIS 7c, a warm substage: ice sheets shrink and the sea rises to within a few tens of metres of today's before falling into the penultimate glacial.
The penultimate glacial (MIS 6) builds its ice sheets: the sea falls about 70 m.
Rising to the Last Interglacial highstand, several metres above today.

The Last Interglacial highstand: about 6 to 9 m above today between about 126,000 and 117,000 years ago (Dutton and colleagues, as recalled; its size debated), with Greenland about 2 m and Antarctica, above all West Antarctica, about 3 m of it (h.sea.greenland, h.sea.antarctic).
The Last Interglacial ends about 116,000 years ago (ev.eu.eemian); ice builds again in MIS 5d and the sea falls.
The MIS 4 cold stage: ice sheets grow and the sea falls to about 80 m below today.
Just before meltwater pulse 1A.
Just after meltwater pulse 1A.

points.note: Foragers' material wealth (tools, ornaments) and relational wealth (ties to others) are shared fairly evenly: wealth Ginis about 0.25 to 0.35 in Borgerhoff Mulder and others' comparison, a top-tenth share of about a quarter.
Rich burials such as Sungir's (about 32,000 years ago) show that some foragers could concentrate prestige goods, rarely and briefly.
Rises with farming: stored grain, fields and herds can be held and handed down, and house sizes begin to diverge.
Draft animals, the plough and states: Kohler and others find Old World house-size Ginis near 0.6 by the Bronze Age, above the New World's, where there were no large draft animals.
The Roman senatorial and Han landlord elites: Scheidel's agrarian empires, where the richest tenth hold most land and slaves.
Falls: the collapse of Roman rule in the West destroys the great senatorial fortunes (Scheidel's leveller of state failure).
Falls: the Black Death kills a third or more in Europe and the Near East, land becomes cheap and labour dear, and wealth inequality falls for a century (Alfani's and Scheidel's plague leveller).
Plantations, colonial fortunes and the first industrial capital; from here the gap between countries adds to the gap within them.

Spanish America's new republics free the children of slaves (from 1821) and end slavery only slowly, to 1854; Indian Removal is about to begin. Nothing yet turns the slow rise in the richest tenth's share.

Britain abolishes slavery (1833 to 1838) and pays the slave-owners 20 million pounds, about two fifths of a year's government spending: their wealth in people becomes wealth in government bonds rather than vanishing, and the freed get nothing. The richest tenth's share is not cut by it.

Indian Removal (1830 to 1850) turns some 25 million acres of Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole land into land sold to settlers and planters: the expansion of cotton slavery that follows concentrates wealth in the American South.

The Great Mahele (1848) divides Hawaiian land among the crown, the government and the chiefs and, after 1850, lets foreigners buy it; within two generations most of it is held by a few planters. On the world's scale this is small; the rise goes on with industrial and colonial capital.
The peak: on the eve of 1914 the richest tenth hold about nine tenths of wealth in Britain and France (Piketty's series), while most of the world's people own almost nothing.

The plateau before the war: South Africa's Natives Land Act (1913) leaves the African majority about 7% of the land, and Haber and Bosch's ammonia (1913) begins in a few firms' hands; neither moves the world's share at this scale.
On the eve of the war wealth concentration is at its peak; the fall to 1918 is the war's, from destroyed capital, taxes and inflation.
Falls: the war destroys capital and raises taxes and inflation.
The crash wipes out paper fortunes in the United States, where the top tenth's share falls after 1929, and Mexico's land reform resumes; at world scale the share barely moves.

Turns down: the industrial cities pack workers into cellars, courts and back-to-backs at a few square metres each.
Turns down: bombing and fighting destroy a fifth of Germany's dwellings, much of Japan's cities and of the western Soviet Union; tens of millions are homeless.

Turns up for good: mass housing in Europe, the Soviet Union and Japan, suburbs in North America.

Day labourers in Rome's and Han China's cities, hired hands at harvest.

The industrial revolution's wage workers in Britain, Europe's rural day labourers and India's and China's hired hands: about an eighth of all hours.

Employees about a third of the world's working hours.

Wartime hours.
Wartime hours in the belligerents' factories and fields.
Wartime hours.

Fatimid Cairo's House of Knowledge (1005) and Ibn al-Haytham's optics.

points.note: The first Olmec and Zapotec glyphs and the 260-day calendar imply a handful of calendar specialists.

Classic Maya astronomers and scribes at Tikal, Palenque and Copan, with their eclipse and Venus tables.

The war sends the United States' chemists and physicists into war research and leaves it a National Research Council; American industry's laboratories (General Electric, Bell, DuPont) grow fastest of any.
