upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

First births (first): part.
- What it covers: Births of a woman's first child, per woman at the period's rates.
- Necessity pass: Whether women have children at all; childlessness, from celibacy in early modern Europe to the low-fertility societies of today, has no home without it.
- Independence pass: First births held near one per woman through the whole transition while third and later births collapsed; they fall only since about 2000.
- Universality pass: Every population has first births.

Second births (second): part.
- What it covers: Births of a woman's second child, per woman at the period's rates.
- Necessity pass: The two-child family, the norm the transition converged on, and the one-child families of China and East Asia have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Second births fell only after third births had, from about 1975, and fastest under China's one-child policy.
- Universality pass: Every population has second births.

Third and later births (later): part.
- What it covers: Births of a woman's third and later children, per woman at the period's rates.
- Necessity pass: Large families were most births for three hundred thousand years, and stopping after two or three is the fertility transition; without it family limitation has no home.
- Independence pass: Third and later births fell from about three to under one per woman between 1965 and 2025 while first births barely moved.
- Universality pass: Every population has third and later births, at least where women live long enough.

Births by the mother's age (under 20, 20 to 34, 35 and over) (age): dropped.
- What it covers: The same births divided by the mother's age.
- Necessity pass: Teen births, child marriage and the postponement of births in rich countries have their home here.
- Independence fail: A second, cross-cutting division of the same births: by age rather than by order. Both are additive; this carve follows order because stopping, which is what the transition was, shows in order, and keeps age as a rival carve for a later pass.
- Universality pass: Every mother has an age.

The proximate determinants: marriage, contraception, breastfeeding's infecundability, abortion (determinants): routed to Not parts: the determinants multiply rather than add (Bongaarts's indices), so they are a model of fertility, not a division of it; marriage is followed under belonging (h.marriage)..
- What it covers: What sets fertility below its biological maximum (Bongaarts).
- Necessity pass: Late marriage in early modern Europe, the pill and abortion, and long breastfeeding among foragers set fertility.
- Independence pass: Each moves on its own.
- Universality pass: Every population has them.

Completeness pass: Every birth is a first, a second or a third or later birth; the three sum to the total fertility rate. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Online by fixed line against by mobile phone only (access): a kind of concept.humanity.means.connection.news.online.
- What it covers: How people reach the internet.
- Necessity pass: Most of the world's newer users are online only by phone.

- What it covers: The systems under which birth fixes rank.
- Necessity pass: India's castes, Europe's estates and the chiefly ranks of Polynesia have histories of their own.
- Independence pass: Europe's estates fell after 1789 while caste endured in law until 1950 and in practice beyond.
- Universality fail: Each system belongs to some societies: kinds of hereditary rank, a classification, not parts of the share.

Rank fixed in law against rank kept by custom (in-law-or-custom): frontier.
- What it covers: Whether the state enforces hereditary rank or custom alone keeps it.

- Independence pass: Rank in law fell faster than rank in custom.
- Universality uncertain: Before states there is no law to fix it in; and how strong custom is cannot be read at world scale.

- What it covers: The share in each M49 area.
- Necessity pass: South Asia's caste society holds much of it.

Killings by the sex of the killed (sex): dropped.

- Independence fail: A cross-classification by means.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Belonging is carved into 2 parts: Marriage, Kin groups beyond the household.

How the parts make the whole work: Belonging, as this account follows it, is the household people live in (the parent's measure, people per household), how households are formed (marriage, followed as women's age at first marriage) and how far people belong to kin groups beyond the household (the share living under corporate descent groups). Foragers lived in households of about five, married young and belonged mostly to bilateral bands, with clans in some (Aboriginal Australia); farming and states spread clans and lineages over most of humanity, about three fifths from the Bronze Age to 1500. Western Europe's kin groups dissolved under the Church's marriage rules while its marriage age rose (the European marriage pattern), a combination found nowhere else; China's lineages, strengthened under the Song and Ming, were broken in the 1950s; elsewhere kin groups thin with cities and schooling, and households shrink since 1960. The three move apart, which is why the debate over Europe's divergence (kinship intensity against institutions) needs all three.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Voluntary associations (universality).

Merged: Living alone into household.
Routed elsewhere: The household to The parent's own measure, people per household (h.belonging)., The local community to Habitat: the share in towns and cities (h.habitat) and settling down (h.habitat.mobile)..

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The household (household): routed to The parent's own measure, people per household (h.belonging)..
- What it covers: The group people live and eat with.
- Necessity pass: Every person lives in some household; its size and form are the first fact of belonging.
- Independence pass: Household size fell after 1950 apart from marriage age and kin groups.
- Universality pass: Every population lives in households.

Marriage (marriage): part.
- What it covers: How households are formed: who marries, and when; followed as women's mean age at first marriage.
- Necessity pass: The European marriage pattern (late marriage, many never marrying, west of Hajnal's line), child marriage in South Asia and its decline, and the later marriages of the twentieth century have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Marriage age rose in north-western Europe from about 1500 while household size held, and rose worldwide after 1970 while kin groups were already dissolving.
- Universality pass: Every population forms unions that found households.

Kin groups beyond the household (descent): part.
- What it covers: How far people belong to corporate descent groups (clans, lineages, tribes reckoned by descent) that hold land in common, arrange marriages or settle disputes and feuds.
- Necessity pass: Clan and lineage politics (China's lineage halls, the tribes of the Middle East and Central Asia, African lineages), their dissolution in western Europe under the Church's rules on cousin marriage (the debated root of Europe's individualism: Henrich, Schulz and colleagues) and in China under collectivization have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Kin groups dissolved in western Europe between about 600 and 1500 while household size and marriage age changed little; China's lineages were broken in the 1950s apart from marriage age; they persist in much of Africa and the Middle East while households shrink.
- Universality pass: Every population reckons descent; the share living under corporate descent groups is an axis on which every population has a value, from foragers' bilateral bands to clan societies.

Voluntary associations (associations): frontier.
- What it covers: Groups people choose to join: guilds, confraternities, churches by choice, clubs, unions, parties.
- Necessity pass: Civil society, from medieval guilds to the mass organizations of the twentieth century.
- Independence pass: They grow as kin groups dissolve.
- Universality uncertain: Foragers' sodalities and age sets count, but no world measure of membership can be read back; kept as a frontier part.

The local community (community): routed to Habitat: the share in towns and cities (h.habitat) and settling down (h.habitat.mobile)..
- What it covers: The face-to-face community: band, village, neighbourhood.
- Necessity pass: The scale at which most people lived.
- Independence fail: Its size is the settlement's, which habitat follows (h.habitat and settling down).
- Universality pass: Every population.

Living alone (alone): merged into household.
- What it covers: The share of people in one-person households.
- Necessity pass: Rising fast in rich countries since 1960.
- Independence fail: A tail of the household's size, which the parent's measure follows.
- Universality fail: Near zero before modern times outside monasteries and the widowed.

Completeness uncertain: Marriage, household and descent, the structure construction's three, each have a home: marriage and kin groups as parts, the household as the parent's measure. The Outline's sodalities and voluntary associations have none measured and are kept as a frontier part. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Understanding is carved into 2 parts: Schooling, Command of number.

How the parts make the whole work: Understanding, as this account follows it, is reading and writing (the parent's measure, the share of adults literate), the years spent being taught (schooling) and the command of number (numeracy); they can all rise together and are followed as separate processes. Numeracy rose first and furthest before modern schooling, with calendars, taxes and trade: about a third of adults in the Roman world, half by 1500, with East Asia ahead; literacy spread later and unevenly, a few per cent of humanity until printing and Protestant teaching lifted Europe's; schooling in years was a sliver until the nineteenth century's compulsory schools and then carried the twentieth century's whole rise, from one year to nine. Knowledge held in store and discovery have no world series and are kept as frontier parts.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Knowledge held in store (universality), Discovery (universality).

Routed elsewhere: Reading and writing to The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding)..

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Reading and writing (literacy): routed to The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding)..
- What it covers: The share of adults who can read and write.
- Necessity pass: Writing holds knowledge outside heads; its spread is the first fact of understanding's history.
- Independence pass: Literacy rose in Protestant Europe before mass schooling, and apart from numeracy.
- Universality pass: An axis: zero before writing.

Schooling (schooling): part.
- What it covers: The years adults spent being formally taught.
- Necessity pass: Mass schooling, compulsory from the nineteenth century and universal in the twentieth, and the secondary and university expansion since 1950 have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Years of school went on rising after literacy neared its ceiling in the rich world; literacy rose before schooling in early modern Europe through church and home teaching.
- Universality pass: An axis: every population teaches its young, and formal schooling is zero where it is absent.

Command of number (numeracy): part.
- What it covers: The share of adults who can count, reckon and know their age in years: basic numeracy, read from the age heaping of censuses and records (the ABCC index of A'Hearn, Baten and Crayen).
- Necessity pass: Reckoning is the skill of trade, taxes and calendars; East Asia's high numeracy before mass literacy and the early modern 'numeracy revolution' in north-western Europe (Baten) have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Numeracy ran ahead of literacy in Qing China and Japan, and literacy ahead of numeracy in parts of Protestant Europe; they move apart.
- Universality pass: An axis: every population counts something; knowing one's age in years needs a calendar, which foragers lack, so their value is near zero.

Knowledge held in store (stored): frontier.
- What it covers: Books, archives and libraries: knowledge kept outside heads.
- Necessity pass: Printing's flood of books (Buringh and van Zanden) and the libraries of Alexandria, Baghdad and Song China.
- Independence pass: Book production rose apart from literacy rates.
- Universality uncertain: An axis from zero before writing; but no world series of books or titles per person can be read before about 1500 outside Europe and China, so it stays a frontier part.

Discovery (discovery): frontier.
- What it covers: New knowledge made: science and invention.
- Necessity pass: The Scientific Revolution and the rise of research.
- Independence pass: It concentrates in a few places apart from mass literacy.
- Universality uncertain: Every population discovers, but no world measure can be read back across the range; kept as a frontier part.

Completeness uncertain: Learning's duration (schooling) and storage's capacity (literacy, the parent's measure) have homes; reckoning (numeracy) is added; storage's durability and access (knowledge held in store) and discovery are frontier parts without a world series; language is outside understanding as this account follows it. Checked against The structure construction's carve of knowledge (learning: transmitters and duration; storage: capacity, durability and access; discovery: generation and selection; language) in structure/history-tree.mjs, and the education indicators of Barro and Lee and of UNESCO, as recalled.. Still without a home: Knowledge held in store (frontier); Discovery (frontier); Language.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.understanding","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding","candidates":[{"key":"literacy","label":"Reading and writing","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding)."},{"key":"schooling","label":"Schooling","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"numeracy","label":"Command of number","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"stored","label":"Knowledge held in store","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"discovery","label":"Discovery","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The structure construction's carve of knowledge (learning: transmitters and duration; storage: capacity, durability and access; discovery: generation and selection; language) in structure/history-tree.mjs, and the education indicators of Barro and Lee and of UNESCO, as recalled.","missing":["Knowledge held in store (frontier)","Discovery (frontier)","Language"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Leisure time (leisure): routed to The parent's own measure, hours of leisure a day (h.play)..
- What it covers: The hours a day free of work and the body's needs.
- Necessity pass: Play needs time.
- Independence pass: It moves against toil.
- Universality pass: Every population has free hours.

Mass media (media): part.
- What it covers: The share of people reached regularly by print, radio, television or the internet: stories, music and images made for many.
- Necessity pass: How people's stories, music and images reach them changed more in a century than in all history before.
- Independence pass: Media reach rose from 6% to 94% while leisure hours rose only from about 3.5 to 5.7.
- Universality pass: An axis: zero before printing.

The arts and those who make them (arts): frontier.
- What it covers: Music, dance, image-making, storytelling and their makers.
- Necessity pass: Cave painting, epic, temple sculpture, the novel, film.
- Independence pass: Artistic production follows patronage and markets apart from leisure.
- Universality uncertain: Every population makes art (debated before about 100,000 years ago), but no world measure, such as artists per thousand people or works made, can be read across the range.

What people spend on play: feasts, festivals, entertainment (spending): frontier.
- What it covers: The share of what households spend on feasts, ceremonies, recreation and culture.
- Necessity pass: Feasting and festival spending ordered the agrarian year; recreation is a large modern budget item.
- Independence pass: It moves with income apart from hours.
- Universality uncertain: Household budgets read it only from about 1900; before, it is guesswork; kept as a frontier part.

Festival and rest days a year (festivals): merged into leisure.
- What it covers: Days given to feasts, holy days and rest.
- Necessity pass: The medieval calendar's holy days, the Protestant cut in them, the weekend and paid holidays.
- Independence fail: They are leisure time counted in days rather than hours, the parent's own measure.
- Universality pass: Every population keeps feast days.

Completeness uncertain: Audiences have a home in mass media; forms and production (the arts and their makers, and what is spent on them) have no world measure and stay frontier parts. Checked against The structure construction's carve of arts and play (forms, production, audiences) in structure/history-tree.mjs, and the Outline of Cultural Materials' sections on recreation and fine arts, as recalled.. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Schooling (concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling):
- What it is: Schooling: the years adults have spent being formally taught, the world's mean years of school among adults.
- What the carve is for: To follow how the world's schooling grew and in what stages: from scribal and elementary schools to mass primary schooling, then the turn to secondary and higher learning that drives most of the growth since 1950.
- The range it claims: Every human society from 300,000 years ago to 2025; where there are no schools every part is zero.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Schooling is a kind of Instruction: learning arranged by someone whose task is to teach: Schooling is instruction given in a school: set apart from work and the household, to groups of learners, by teachers, in a sequence of stages that a learner passes through in order. Other kinds within it: Apprenticeship in a workshop or on the land, Tutoring in the household, Initiation into a cult's or guild's knowledge, Military drill.
2. Instruction: learning arranged by someone whose task is to teach is a kind of A way knowledge passes between people: Instruction is arranged and intended by a teacher, where the other ways pass knowledge as a by-product of living, working and talking together. Other kinds within it: Imitation and observation while working, Stories, songs and rites, Reading and media, Conversation among peers.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Schooling is carved into 3 parts: Primary schooling, Secondary schooling, Higher learning.

How the parts make the whole work: The three stages sum to the parent's years at every date: a learner passes through them in order, so the world's schooling grows first by the first stage and then by the upper ones as the first saturates near six years. Before 1800 nearly nine in ten years were elementary; mass primary schooling from 1800 to 1950 kept that share; from 1950 the secondary turn and from 1960 the turn to mass higher education carry most of the growth, so that by 2025 about half the years are above primary. The split before 1950 is a sketch read from enrolment histories (Lee and Lee's long series, Barro–Lee, the Wittgenstein Centre reconstructions, as recalled); the alternative carves, by sex and by who keeps the school, cut the same years another way.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Pre-primary schooling (necessity), Women's and men's years of school (independence), Who keeps the school: state, religious body, private (independence).

Routed elsewhere: Apprenticeship to Provisioning and toil (h.provisioning, h.toil): learning while working is not schooling; vocational schools are counted as secondary., What the years teach to Understanding's own measures: literacy (h.understanding) and numeracy (h.understanding.numeracy)..

Routing sample: 12 case(s); 2 with no home among the parts (A Kenyan child in a pre-primary class, 2020; An apprentice tailor learning in a Bamako workshop); 0 with two or more parts as homes.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling","form":"processes","cutRecorded":true,"parts":[{"key":"primary","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling.primary","processId":"h.schooling.primary"},{"key":"secondary","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling.secondary","processId":"h.schooling.secondary"},{"key":"tertiary","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling.tertiary","processId":"h.schooling.tertiary"}],"process":"h.schooling","routingCases":12}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Primary schooling (primary): part.
- What it covers: The first stage of school: reading, writing, reckoning and the catechism or classics' first texts, from the scribal schools' sign lists and the village and temple schools to compulsory elementary schools (ISCED 1).
- Necessity pass: Without the first stage nobody reaches the others and most of the world's years of school before 1950 have no home.
- Independence pass: It grows and saturates on its own course: near six years where all complete it, while the upper stages keep growing; the coupling is that the upper stages need it first, a sequence, not a shared cause.
- Universality pass: Every society with schools has a first stage; where there are none it reads zero on the same axis, as the tree pass read the human addition to carbon dioxide.

Secondary schooling (secondary): part.
- What it covers: The middle stage: the advanced years of the scribal schools, grammar and Latin schools, gymnasia, madrasas' upper teaching, Chinese county and prefectural schools, and modern lower and upper secondary and vocational schools (ISCED 2 to 4).
- Necessity pass: Without it the turn that adds most of the world's years since 1950 has no home, and the professions, clergy and officials of agrarian states had no stage between reading and the universities.
- Independence pass: It moves apart from primary: the American high-school movement from 1910 and Europe's and Asia's secondary expansion after 1945 grew it while primary changed little in those places; its growth is set by states' choices to extend compulsion and by the returns to it.
- Universality pass: On the axis reading: wherever schooling has more than a first stage it has a middle one, and it reads zero where it does not. Read strictly, it fails before the scribal schools' advanced years, and with it every part but primary; the axis reading is the one this account uses, the strict one the alternative.

Higher learning (tertiary): part.
- What it covers: The highest stage: the academies of Athens and Alexandria, the Han Imperial Academy, Nalanda, the madrasas of higher law, the medieval universities, and modern colleges and universities (ISCED 5 to 8).
- Necessity pass: Without it the move from elite to mass higher education since 1960, now about a tenth of all years of school, has no home, nor the institutions where learning was made as well as passed on.
- Independence pass: It expands on its own course: China's universities grew tenfold after 1999 while its secondary schooling grew slowly; it follows states' and families' choices and the returns to degrees.
- Universality pass: On the axis reading, as for secondary: zero before the first academies of higher learning about 400 BCE, a part wherever they exist.

Pre-primary schooling (preprimary): frontier.
- What it covers: Kindergarten and nursery classes before the first stage (ISCED 0).
- Necessity uncertain: The parent's measure, like the Barro–Lee and Wittgenstein Centre series, counts years from primary on; pre-primary years are not in it.
- Independence pass: It grows on its own course since the 1960s.
- Universality pass: Zero where it does not exist.

Women's and men's years of school (by-sex): frontier.
- What it covers: The same years divided by the learner's sex: the closing of the gender gap, from almost no girls schooled to more women than men in higher education in most countries.
- Necessity pass: The gap's closing is one of schooling's great changes.
- Independence fail: Not a part beside the stages: every year of school is both a stage and a learner's sex, so it is another cut of the same total, and its halves are means that average to the parent rather than sum to it. Kept as the alternative carve.
- Universality pass: Every learner has a sex.

Who keeps the school: state, religious body, private (provider): frontier.
- What it covers: The same years divided by who keeps the school: temples, churches and mosques, private teachers and fee-paying schools, and states.
- Necessity pass: The shift from religious to state schooling in the nineteenth century is a large change.
- Independence fail: Another cut of the same years, not a part beside the stages; kept as an alternative carve.
- Universality pass: Every school is kept by someone.

Apprenticeship (apprenticeship): routed to Provisioning and toil (h.provisioning, h.toil): learning while working is not schooling; vocational schools are counted as secondary..
- What it covers: Learning a craft or trade by working under a master.
- Necessity fail: Schooling works without it: it is a sibling kind of instruction in the climb, not a stage of school.
- Independence pass: It moves apart from schooling.
- Universality fail: Found only where crafts are passed on by masters.

What the years teach (learning): routed to Understanding's own measures: literacy (h.understanding) and numeracy (h.understanding.numeracy)..
- What it covers: How much is learned in a year of school: test scores, harmonized learning outcomes, learning-adjusted years.
- Necessity pass: A year of school in one place teaches far more than in another.
- Independence fail: Not a part of years: it is the quality of the same years, read as what people can do, which understanding's other measures already follow.
- Universality pass: Every school teaches something.

Completeness pass: Every year the parent counts falls in one of the three stages; the only ISCED level left out, pre-primary (0), is outside the parent's measure and kept as a frontier part. Older systems are mapped onto the stages by what they taught, which is this account's reading. Checked against UNESCO's International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED 2011): levels 0 to 8, grouped as primary (1), secondary with post-secondary non-tertiary (2 to 4), and tertiary (5 to 8).. Still without a home: Pre-primary years, outside the parent's measure; Religious instruction outside schools (catechism classes, Quran schools held in homes), counted only where they are schools.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding.schooling","candidates":[{"key":"primary","label":"Primary schooling","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"secondary","label":"Secondary schooling","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"tertiary","label":"Higher learning","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"preprimary","label":"Pre-primary schooling","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"by-sex","label":"Women's and men's years of school","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"provider","label":"Who keeps the school: state, religious body, private","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"apprenticeship","label":"Apprenticeship","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","routedTo":"Provisioning and toil (h.provisioning, h.toil): learning while working is not schooling; vocational schools are counted as secondary."},{"key":"learning","label":"What the years teach","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Understanding's own measures: literacy (h.understanding) and numeracy (h.understanding.numeracy)."}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"UNESCO's International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED 2011): levels 0 to 8, grouped as primary (1), secondary with post-secondary non-tertiary (2 to 4), and tertiary (5 to 8).","missing":["Pre-primary years, outside the parent's measure","Religious instruction outside schools (catechism classes, Quran schools held in homes), counted only where they are schools"]}}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Settling down (concept.humanity.means.habitat.mobile):
- What it is: Living without a fixed dwelling: the share of all living people who move their homes with the seasons, the herds or their trade.
- What the carve is for: To follow who the mobile were and how each way of moving rose and fell: foragers shrinking with farming's spread, herders rising with domesticated animals and the horse, carriers and service nomads living off settled markets, and states settling all three.
- The range it claims: Every human population from 300,000 years ago to 2025, as a world share.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Settling down is a kind of A dimension of how a population settles: Settling down is whether people keep a fixed dwelling at all; the other dimensions are how densely they live (towns and cities), how great their largest places grow and how much land they take and use. Other kinds within it: A use of land (farmland taken), Living in towns and cities, The greatest settlement.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Settling down is carved into 3 parts: Mobile foragers, Mobile herders, Peripatetic trades.

How the parts make the whole work: The three ways of moving sum to the parent at every date (MECE#ae19): Salzman's foraging, pastoral and peripatetic nomads. Foragers are all of the mobile until farming; their share falls as farmers outnumber them, slowly at first (about nine in ten of the remaining foragers still move) and then with the settler colonies after 1500. Herders appear with domesticated goats, sheep and cattle, grow with wagons and then horses and camels, and are the larger part of the mobile from about 1600; states settle them from the eighteenth century (the Qing and Russia), by force in the twentieth (Soviet collectivization) and by drought and markets since. Peripatetic carriers, smiths and entertainers live off settled markets and armies, are most numerous in South Asia, and decline with the railways and the laws that forced them to settle. The cases routed elsewhere are settled or unhoused by the parent's definition and test its boundary. The split is a sketch: the parent's band, the share of foragers who are mobile (taken as about nine in ten after farming, lower after 1500) and the size of India's nomadic castes carry most of the uncertainty (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b).

Merged: Sea nomads into foragers.
Routed elsewhere: Sedentary foragers to Settled, by the parent's own definition; their living is followed under foraging (h.foraging)., Shifting cultivators to Settled, by the parent's own definition; their fields are followed as shifting cultivation, a kind under cropland (h.farmland.cropland)., People without shelter to Shelter (h.sustenance.shelter): lacking a home is a want of shelter, not a mobile way of living; refugees are followed through the Events that displace them..

Routing sample: 12 case(s); 4 with no home among the parts (A Natufian village of round stone houses, 12,000 BCE; A Kwakwaka'wakw winter village on North America's north-west coast; A Lua' shifting-cultivator village in northern Thailand that moves every decade; A man sleeping rough in Mumbai, 2020); 0 with two or more parts as homes.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.habitat.mobile","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.mobile","form":"processes","cutRecorded":true,"parts":[{"key":"foragers","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.mobile.foragers","processId":"h.habitat.mobile.foragers"},{"key":"herders","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.mobile.herders","processId":"h.habitat.mobile.herders"},{"key":"peripatetic","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.mobile.peripatetic","processId":"h.habitat.mobile.peripatetic"}],"process":"h.habitat.mobile","routingCases":12}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Mobile foragers (foragers): part.
- What it covers: Bands that move camp to follow game, plant foods and water, and sea nomads who forage the sea from their boats (the Moken, the Bajau Laut, the Orang Laut).
- Necessity pass: For 290,000 of the 300,000 years it is all of the mobile, and all of humanity.
- Independence pass: It falls as farmers take land and outnumber foragers, a course set by farming's spread and later by settler colonies; herders and service nomads rise and fall on other causes.
- Universality pass: Mobile foragers exist in every era from the first people to now.

Mobile herders (herders): part.
- What it covers: Pastoral nomads and transhumant households who move with their herds of sheep, goats, cattle, camels, horses, yaks or reindeer: from the Saharan cattle herders and the steppe's wagon and mounted nomads to the Bedouin, Fulani, Maasai, Somali, Kazakhs, Mongols, Tibetans and Sami.
- Necessity pass: Without it most of the mobile since about 1600, and the steppe peoples whose conquests made the largest land empire, have no home in this measure.
- Independence pass: It rises with domestic animals, the horse and the camel, and falls when states fence, tax and settle herders (the Qing and Russia from 1750, Soviet collectivization, the Sahel's droughts), apart from foragers' decline.
- Universality pass: On the axis reading: zero before herding, about 10,000 years ago, a part wherever herds are kept by moving households. Read strictly it fails for most of the range, which this account records as the alternative reading.

Peripatetic trades (peripatetic): part.
- What it covers: Groups who move to sell goods and services to settled people rather than live off land or herds: carriers, smiths, tinkers, traders and entertainers, such as India's Banjara caravans and nomadic castes, the Roma and Dom, Europe's Travellers.
- Necessity pass: The parent's own meaning counts them, and in South Asia they were millions until the railways: without this part they would be uncounted or misfiled as herders.
- Independence pass: Their numbers follow markets, armies' supply and laws on vagrancy and settlement (India's Criminal Tribes Act of 1871, European laws against Gypsies), not the land open to foragers or herders.
- Universality pass: On the axis reading: zero before settled markets, a part wherever they exist.

Sedentary foragers (sedentary-foragers): routed to Settled, by the parent's own definition; their living is followed under foraging (h.foraging)..
- What it covers: Foragers who live in permanent villages: the Natufians, the Jomon, the peoples of North America's north-west coast and California.
- Necessity fail: They have fixed dwellings, so they are not in this measure.
- Independence pass: They move apart from the mobile.
- Universality fail: Found only in rich environments from about 13,000 years ago.

Shifting cultivators (shifting): routed to Settled, by the parent's own definition; their fields are followed as shifting cultivation, a kind under cropland (h.farmland.cropland)..
- What it covers: Farmers who clear fields, crop them for a few years and move the village every decade or so.
- Necessity fail: Their villages stand for years at a time; the parent counts them as settled.
- Independence pass: Apart from the mobile.
- Universality fail: Only where forest farming is practised.

Sea nomads (sea-nomads): merged into foragers.
- What it covers: Boat-dwelling peoples of South-east Asia who fish and gather from the sea.
- Necessity uncertain: Too few to follow on their own at a world scale.
- Independence uncertain: They live by foraging, at sea.
- Universality fail: Only in island South-east Asia and the Mergui archipelago.

People without shelter (unhoused): routed to Shelter (h.sustenance.shelter): lacking a home is a want of shelter, not a mobile way of living; refugees are followed through the Events that displace them..
- What it covers: The homeless and those displaced into camps, who lack a dwelling but do not move with seasons, herds or trade.
- Necessity fail: The concept is a way of living that moves the home, not the lack of one.
- Independence pass: It follows poverty, war and housing, not mobility.
- Universality fail: Found mostly in cities and wars.

Completeness pass: Salzman's three kinds of nomads map onto the three parts; the other ways of living without a long-fixed home in the outline (sedentary foragers, shifting cultivators) are settled by the parent's definition and routed; the unhoused are routed to shelter. Checked against The Outline of Cultural Materials' settlement and subsistence headings (settlement patterns, the annual cycle, pastoral activities, peddling and itinerant trade) and Salzman's typology of nomadism (hunter-gatherer, pastoral and peripatetic nomads).. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The wild animals (concept.dim.earth.wild-animals):
- What it is: The wild animals: the living world's animal populations that people neither breed nor keep, on land, in the sea and in the air; followed at the parent by the biomass of wild land mammals.
- What the carve is for: To follow where and when people took the wild animals down: the large land mammals at the end of the Pleistocene and with farming, the whales and seals from the seventeenth century, and the fish of the open sea from the industrial fisheries on. These losses came in different millennia, places and ways, and the parent's land measure shows only the first.
- The range it claims: The Earth's wild animals from 300,000 years ago to 2025, as world biomass in carbon.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The wild animals is a kind of A population of living things: The wild animals are the animal populations that live and breed without people's keeping, set apart from livestock and pets, from people themselves, and from the plants and microbes of the living world. Other kinds within it: Humanity, Livestock, The plant cover, Microbes.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The wild animals is carved into 2 parts: Wild sea mammals, Wild fish of fishable size.

How the parts make the whole work: The wild animals are followed in three vertebrate groups, each by its own biomass in carbon: land mammals at the parent, sea mammals and fishable fish as parts. They are not summed: the parent's measure is land mammals only, and widening it to all wild animals would change an existing measure, which this pass does not do; the three stand side by side under the concept. Their losses are three episodes, not one: the land's large mammals fell at the end of the Pleistocene and again with farming and the nineteenth century; the sea mammals fell from the 1600s to the 1980s and have begun to recover; fish of fishable size fell mostly after 1880 and fastest from 1950 to 1990. Birds and invertebrates stay frontier parts until a world series exists. All values are sketches from the census literature as recalled (Bar-On and colleagues 2018, Greenspoon and colleagues 2023, Christensen and colleagues 2014, Bianchi and colleagues 2021), to be checked.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Wild birds (universality), Wild insects and other arthropods (necessity, universality), Large and small land mammals (independence).

Routed elsewhere: Wild land mammals to The parent's own measure (h.earth.wild-animals, the biomass of wild land mammals)., Livestock to Not wild: followed through farmland (h.farmland.pasture) and food (h.food.animal)..

Routing sample: 12 case(s); 6 with no home among the parts (Mammoths on the Siberian steppe, 20,000 years ago; Bison on the Great Plains, 1800; Passenger pigeons in the forests of eastern North America, 1850; Antarctic krill; Cattle on an Argentine estancia, 1900); 0 with two or more parts as homes.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.dim.earth.wild-animals","conceptId":"concept.dim.earth.wild-animals","form":"processes","cutRecorded":true,"parts":[{"key":"sea-mammals","conceptId":"concept.dim.earth.wild-animals.sea-mammals","processId":"h.earth.wild-animals.sea-mammals"},{"key":"fish","conceptId":"concept.dim.earth.wild-animals.fish","processId":"h.earth.wild-animals.fish"}],"process":"h.earth.wild-animals","routingCases":12}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Wild land mammals (land): routed to The parent's own measure (h.earth.wild-animals, the biomass of wild land mammals)..
- What it covers: Wild mammals on land, from mammoths and ground sloths to deer, wild boar, elephants and rodents: the parent's own measure.
- Necessity pass: The end-Pleistocene extinctions and the loss of wild herds to fields and pasture have their home here.
- Independence pass: It fell most at the end of the Pleistocene and again since 1850, on land, by hunting and the taking of habitat.
- Universality pass: In every era.

Wild sea mammals (sea-mammals): part.
- What it covers: Whales, dolphins and porpoises, seals, sea lions and walruses, and sea cows.
- Necessity pass: Without it whaling and sealing, among the largest takings of wild animal mass in history, have no home.
- Independence pass: It fell from the 1600s to the 1980s by commercial whaling and sealing, at sea, while land mammals fell by other causes and at other times; since the 1986 moratorium it has recovered while land mammals kept falling.
- Universality pass: Sea mammals live in every era of the range.

Wild fish of fishable size (fish): part.
- What it covers: Wild fish of 10 grams to 100 kilograms in the seas and fresh waters, the sizes fisheries take; the far larger mass of small fish of the ocean's twilight zone is left out.
- Necessity pass: Fishing takes more wild animal mass each year than any other human taking; without this part the industrial fisheries' effect on the living world has no home.
- Independence pass: It fell mostly after 1880 and fastest from 1950 to 1990, by steam trawlers, then sonar, synthetic nets and factory freezers, on its own course.
- Universality pass: Fish in every era.

Wild birds (birds): frontier.
- What it covers: Wild birds on land and at sea: from the passenger pigeon's billions to the seabird colonies.
- Necessity pass: Extinctions on islands after human arrival (the moa, the dodo) and the recent fall of farmland birds belong here.
- Independence pass: They fall by island colonization and farmland change, apart from mammals and fish.
- Universality uncertain: Present in every era, but no world series of their mass exists before about 1970 (North American and European counts), so the number test is not met yet.

Wild insects and other arthropods (arthropods): frontier.
- What it covers: Insects, spiders, crustaceans such as krill: the largest wild animal mass.
- Necessity uncertain: Their mass dwarfs all the vertebrates, but how people changed it before the 1980s is unknown.
- Independence pass: Their declines (or not) follow pesticides, land use and climate.
- Universality uncertain: Present always; the insect decline debate (Hallmann and colleagues against van Klink and colleagues) shows the data are local and recent.

Large and small land mammals (by-size): frontier.
- What it covers: The parent's land mammals divided by body size: megafauna over about 44 kg against smaller mammals.
- Necessity pass: The end-Pleistocene extinctions took mostly the large.
- Independence fail: Another cut of the parent's own measure, not a part beside the sea and its fish; kept as the alternative carve of land mammals.
- Universality pass: Every era has large and small mammals.

Livestock (livestock): routed to Not wild: followed through farmland (h.farmland.pasture) and food (h.food.animal)..
- What it covers: Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and other kept animals.
- Necessity fail: Not part of the wild animals.
- Independence pass: It grows as wild mass falls.
- Universality fail: Only after domestication.

Completeness uncertain: The three vertebrate groups people have taken down most, by mass, have homes (land mammals at the parent, sea mammals and fish as parts); birds, arthropods and the other invertebrates have none yet because no honest world series of them exists before recent decades. Checked against Bar-On, Phillips and Milo's census of the biomass distribution on Earth (2018): wild land mammals, wild marine mammals, wild birds, fish, arthropods, annelids, molluscs and cnidarians.. Still without a home: Wild birds; Arthropods, molluscs and other invertebrates; Fish under 10 g of the ocean's twilight zone.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.dim.earth.wild-animals","conceptId":"concept.dim.earth.wild-animals","candidates":[{"key":"land","label":"Wild land mammals","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The parent's own measure (h.earth.wild-animals, the biomass of wild land mammals)."},{"key":"sea-mammals","label":"Wild sea mammals","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"fish","label":"Wild fish of fishable size","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"birds","label":"Wild birds","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"arthropods","label":"Wild insects and other arthropods","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"by-size","label":"Large and small land mammals","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"livestock","label":"Livestock","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","routedTo":"Not wild: followed through farmland (h.farmland.pasture) and food (h.food.animal)."}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"Bar-On, Phillips and Milo's census of the biomass distribution on Earth (2018): wild land mammals, wild marine mammals, wild birds, fish, arthropods, annelids, molluscs and cnidarians.","missing":["Wild birds","Arthropods, molluscs and other invertebrates","Fish under 10 g of the ocean's twilight zone"]}}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Marriage (concept.humanity.wants.belonging.marriage):
- What it is: Marriage: a union between partners that the others of a society recognize, setting rights and duties over sex, children, work and property between the partners and their kin; followed at the parent by women's mean age at first marriage.
- What the carve is for: To follow marriage through its life: when and how it is formed, how many partners it joins, and how it ends; so that the European marriage pattern, the decline of polygyny and the divorce revolution each have a home.
- The range it claims: Every human society from 300,000 years ago to 2025, as world measures; every known society recognizes some form of marriage, and it is assumed for the earliest people.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Marriage is a kind of A recognized union between persons: Marriage is the recognized union that sets rights over sex and children and joins the partners' kin; the other unions make kin or partners for other ends. Other kinds within it: Adoption, Sworn and blood brotherhood, Godparenthood, A business partnership.
2. A recognized union between persons is a kind of A tie between persons: A recognized union is made by an act the society witnesses and enforces, where other ties come by birth, by liking or by dependence. Other kinds within it: Descent: kinship by birth, Friendship, Patronage and clientship, Membership of an association.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Real cases sent through the carve, with the candidates each belongs to:
1. A Hadza couple separate after a few years and each remarries: ending
2. A Yoruba trader takes a second wife, 1900: plural
3. A Song dynasty official keeps concubines beside his principal wife: plural
4. An English yeoman's daughter marries at 26, 1650: formation
5. A Javanese village woman divorces and remarries in the 1950s, when about half of marriages there ended in divorce: ending
6. A Rajput family arranges their daughter's marriage at fourteen, 1900: formation, choice
7. An American couple divorce in 1980 under a no-fault law: ending
8. A Mormon plural household in Utah, 1870: plural
9. A Swedish couple raising children together without marrying, 2010: cohabitation
10. A Tokugawa village woman divorces and remarries, 1800: ending

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Marriage is carved into 2 parts: Plural unions, How marriages end.

How the parts make the whole work: A marriage is formed, joins one or more partners, and ends: the parent follows its formation by women's age at first marriage, and the two parts follow its form and its end. Plural unions were common among foragers and early farmers, fell as states and churches made monogamy the norm for most of the world's people, and have stayed near three in a hundred married women since 1900 because Africa's growing share of humanity balances the fall of polygyny within Africa. Divorce was frequent among foragers, rare in the great agrarian civilizations of China, India and Christian Europe though common in Java, the Malay world, Tokugawa Japan and many African and Muslim societies, and has risen since 1960 with no-fault laws, women's earnings and China's reforms. Choice of spouse, the never-married and unions without marriage stay frontier parts. All values are sketches, weighted by population from ethnographic and demographic sources as recalled (Murdock's atlas, Marlowe's forager sample, Pew's household survey, national divorce statistics), to be checked.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Same-sex marriage (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.belonging.marriage).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Who chooses the spouse (independence), Who never marries (independence), Unions without marriage (necessity).

Routed elsewhere: Forming a marriage: when to The parent's own measure (h.marriage, women's mean age at first marriage)., Marrying kin to Kin groups beyond the household (h.belonging.descent): marrying kin is part of kinship intensity..

Routing sample: 12 case(s); 5 with no home among the parts (An English yeoman's daughter marries at 26, 1650; A Rajput family arranges their daughter's marriage at fourteen, 1900; A Swedish couple raising children together without marrying, 2010; A Pakistani family marries a daughter to her first cousin; Two women marry in the Netherlands, 2001); 0 with two or more parts as homes.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.belonging.marriage","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.belonging.marriage","form":"processes","cutRecorded":true,"parts":[{"key":"plural","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.belonging.marriage.plural","processId":"h.marriage.plural"},{"key":"ending","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.belonging.marriage.ending","processId":"h.marriage.ending"}],"process":"h.marriage","routingCases":12}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Forming a marriage: when (formation): routed to The parent's own measure (h.marriage, women's mean age at first marriage)..
- What it covers: When people first marry: the parent's own measure, women's mean age at first marriage.
- Necessity pass: Every marriage is formed; its timing sets fertility and household formation.
- Independence pass: It rose in north-western Europe from the 1400s and everywhere since 1950 on its own course.
- Universality pass: In every society.

Plural unions (plural): part.
- What it covers: Marriages joining one husband to more than one wife (polygyny), with recognized concubines counted, and the rare unions of one wife with several husbands (polyandry).
- Necessity pass: Most societies in the ethnographic record allow polygyny; without this part the turn to monogamy as a norm (Greece and Rome, the Church, modern states) and polygyny's persistence in Africa have no home.
- Independence pass: Coupled with young brides (polygyny draws on younger women), but it moves apart: Africa's polygyny fell from the 1950s while its age at marriage rose slowly, and Europe's age rose for centuries with polygyny unchanged at zero.
- Universality pass: Every society has a rule on the number of spouses; the share is defined everywhere, zero where monogamy is enforced.

How marriages end (ending): part.
- What it covers: Whether marriages end by divorce or separation, rather than by a partner's death.
- Necessity pass: Without it foragers' serial marriages, the near-indissoluble marriages of Christian Europe and Confucian China, the high divorce of Java and Tokugawa Japan, and the divorce revolution after 1960 have no home.
- Independence pass: It follows law and religion (the Church's indissolubility, no-fault divorce from 1969), women's earnings and kin's power, apart from age at marriage and polygyny.
- Universality pass: Every marriage ends, by death or divorce; the share is defined everywhere.

Who chooses the spouse (choice): frontier.
- What it covers: Whether kin arrange the marriage or the partners choose: from arranged child marriage to the love match.
- Necessity pass: The turn from arranged to chosen marriage is one of the great changes.
- Independence uncertain: Closely tied to kin groups' power (h.belonging.descent, whose measure counts groups that arrange marriages) and to age at marriage; no world series exists.
- Universality pass: Every marriage is chosen by someone.

Who never marries (never-married): frontier.
- What it covers: The share of women never married by fifty: high in the European marriage pattern (a tenth to a fifth) and today in East Asia and the West.
- Necessity pass: The other half of Hajnal's European pattern.
- Independence uncertain: Moves with age at marriage in Hajnal's pattern; no world series before censuses.
- Universality pass: Defined in every society.

Unions without marriage (cohabitation): frontier.
- What it covers: Couples living together and raising children without marrying: Scandinavia and Latin America's consensual unions.
- Necessity uncertain: Whether they belong under marriage or beside it is the question.
- Independence pass: They grow as marriage is delayed.
- Universality pass: Informal unions exist everywhere.

Marrying kin (cousin): routed to Kin groups beyond the household (h.belonging.descent): marrying kin is part of kinship intensity..
- What it covers: Marriage between cousins and within the lineage.
- Necessity uncertain: It shapes who is married to whom, not marriage's timing, number or end.
- Independence fail: Moves with the strength of kin groups.
- Universality pass: Defined everywhere.

Same-sex marriage (same-sex): a kind of concept.humanity.wants.belonging.marriage.
- What it covers: Marriage between partners of the same sex, recognized in law since 2001.
- Necessity fail: Marriage works without it in most of the range.
- Independence pass: Its spread follows law.
- Universality fail: Recognized only in some societies and eras: a kind of marriage, not a part.

Completeness pass: The outline's headings fall into formation (basis, mode, arranging, nuptials: the parent's timing, with choice as a frontier part), form (plural marriage, secondary marriages: plural unions) and termination (how marriages end); regulation of whom one may marry is routed to kin groups and irregular unions stay a frontier part. Checked against The Outline of Cultural Materials' marriage headings (580s: basis of marriage, regulation of marriage, mode of marriage, arranging a marriage, nuptials, termination of marriage, secondary marriages, plural marriage, irregular unions) and Murdock's Ethnographic Atlas codes for marriage.. Still without a home: Who chooses the spouse, without a world series; The share never married; Unions without {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Mass media (concept.humanity.wants.play.media):
- What it is: Mass media: stories, music, images and news made once and copied or broadcast to many, followed by the share of people they reach regularly.
- What the carve is for: To decide whether the reach of mass media is made of parts worth following apart, or stays one number.
- The range it claims: Every human population from 300,000 years ago to 2025; zero before printing.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Mass media is a kind of Communication from one to many: Mass media reach many people at once with the same made content by copying or broadcast, where other ways of speaking to many reach only those present. Other kinds within it: Preaching and recitation, Theatre and spectacle, Proclamations and the town crier.
2. Communication from one to many is a kind of A way knowledge passes between people: Communication from one to many passes the same content to many at once, where instruction is arranged for learners and imitation passes knowledge as a by-product. Other kinds within it: Instruction, Imitation and observation while working, Conversation among peers.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Mass media is kept whole, as a kind of Communication from one to many: No carve of mass media pays now: the media are kinds that overlap and replace one another, so their reaches do not sum to the share reached; the content cut and the output of copies have no world series before the twentieth century; being online and the speed of news are already followed under connection. Reopen when a world series of copies made per person (books, newspapers, broadcast hours) or of hours spent with media can be built, or when the Events that move media or its unexplained moves grow by half.

How the parts make the whole work: Mass media stay one number, the share reached regularly. The candidates were kinds that succeed and overlap one another within that reach (print, radio, television, internet), another cut of it (content), a sibling measure of output (copies made), or measures already followed under connection (being online, the speed of news).

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Print, radio, television, internet (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.play.media).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Copies made (independence, universality), What media carry: news, entertainment, teaching, advertising (independence).

Routed elsewhere: Being online to Internet (h.internet), followed under connection., How fast news travels to Moving words (h.connection.news)..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.play.media","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.play.media","form":"processes","cutRecorded":false,"parts":[],"process":"h.media"}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Print, radio, television, internet (by-medium): a kind of concept.humanity.wants.play.media.
- What it covers: The reach of each medium in turn.
- Necessity fail: Media reach people without any one of them: each medium is a way of reaching, and they replace one another within one need.
- Independence fail: They overlap: one person read, listened and watched, so their reaches do not sum to the parent, and each rises partly by taking the others' audience.
- Universality fail: Each exists only from its invention: print from about 1450, radio from the 1920s, television from the 1950s, the internet from the 1990s. Kinds, not parts.

Copies made (copies): frontier.
- What it covers: How much is produced: manuscripts and books per person (Buringh and van Zanden), newspapers printed, broadcast hours.
- Necessity pass: The output of copies is the other side of reach.
- Independence uncertain: Output and reach rise together; it is a sibling measure of the same process rather than a part of reach.
- Universality uncertain: A series exists for western Europe from 500 to 1800 and for the world only patchily.

What media carry: news, entertainment, teaching, advertising (content): frontier.
- What it covers: The same reach cut by content.
- Necessity pass: The balance of news and entertainment matters.
- Independence fail: Another cut of the same reach, not a part beside it; no world series.
- Universality pass: Every medium carries some content.

Being online (internet): routed to Internet (h.internet), followed under connection..
- What it covers: The share of people online.
- Necessity fail: Already followed elsewhere.
- Independence fail: A kind of medium, as above.
- Universality fail: Only from the 1990s.

How fast news travels (speed): routed to Moving words (h.connection.news)..
- What it covers: The speed of the fastest regular message.
- Necessity fail: Speed is a property of carrying, not of reach.
- Independence pass: It moves apart from reach.
- Universality pass: Defined in every era.

Completeness uncertain: Every heading is either a kind of medium (kinds), a measure already followed (internet, news speed), or another cut of the same reach (content, copies); none is a part that sums to reach. Checked against The Outline of Cultural Materials' communication headings (gestures and signs, transmission of messages, dissemination of news and information, mass media, public opinion)..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.play.media","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.play.media","candidates":[{"key":"by-medium","label":"Print, radio, television, internet","outcome":"kind","necessity":"fail","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","kindOf":"concept.humanity.wants.play.media"},{"key":"copies","label":"Copies made","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"content","label":"What media carry: news, entertainment, teaching, advertising","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"internet","label":"Being online","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","routedTo":"Internet (h.internet), followed under connection."},{"key":"speed","label":"How fast news travels","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Moving words (h.connection.news)."}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The Outline of Cultural Materials' communication headings (gestures and signs, transmission of messages, dissemination of news and information, mass media, public opinion)."}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Belief (concept.humanity.wants.meaning.belief):
- What it is: Belief: what people hold the world's powers and order to be, followed by the share who hold that a god, gods or an impersonal law (karma, Heaven's mandate) watch and repay moral conduct.
- What the carve is for: To answer the model's question of what this share is made of: whether its believers divide into categories worth following apart (what the trust rests on, what is judged, when it is repaid), or whether it stays one number.
- The range it claims: Every human population from 300,000 years ago to 2025, read for persons.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Belief is a kind of A belief about the powers and order of the world: Moral belief holds that the world's powers watch and repay conduct between people; other beliefs about them concern their number, their nature, their demands for rites, or whether they exist at all. Other kinds within it: Belief in spirits and ancestors who demand rites, Belief in a creator, Naturalism: no powers beyond nature.
2. A belief about the powers and order of the world is a kind of Something people hold true: Beliefs about the world's order concern what governs it and what it asks of people, where other held beliefs concern matters of fact, history or the self. Other kinds within it: Knowledge of nature, Beliefs about the past and descent, Beliefs about persons and the self.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Belief is kept whole, as a kind of A belief about the powers and order of the world: No carve of belief pays now: its believers divide by ground (a judging god or an impersonal law) and by when conduct is repaid, but both follow tradition membership, already followed by the eight tradition shares, and Hindu, Buddhist and Chinese believers often hold gods and an impersonal law at once, so the categories are neither exclusive for persons nor independent of the traditions. Intensity of belief has no series before the surveys of the 1980s. Reopen if the tradition shares are re-filed (an open question since the tree pass), if a world series of belief by ground can be built from surveys and the codings of moralizing gods, or when the Events that move belief or its unexplained moves grow by half.

How the parts make the whole work: Belief stays one number, the share holding that a power watches and repays conduct. Its believers do divide by what the trust rests on (a judging god or an impersonal law) and by when conduct is repaid, but both divisions follow tradition membership, which the eight tradition shares already follow, and many people hold more than one ground at once; dividing them would re-read those shares rather than follow a process that moves apart. This answers the model's question of what the share is made of for now.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): When conduct is repaid: in this life, after death, in the next birth (a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.belief).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: What the trust rests on: a judging god or an impersonal law (independence), How firmly it is held (independence, universality).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

What the trust rests on: a judging god or an impersonal law (ground): frontier.
- What it covers: Believers divided by the ground of judgment: a personal god or gods (the Abrahamic traditions, Zoroaster's) against an impersonal law (karma, Heaven's mandate).
- Necessity pass: The contrast between a judging God and the law of karma is one of the great divides in the history of belief.
- Independence fail: It follows tradition membership, which the eight tradition shares already follow, so dividing believers by ground would mostly re-read those shares; and within the Hindu, Buddhist and Chinese traditions many hold both gods who judge and a law that repays, so persons do not fall into one category.
- Universality pass: Every believer trusts some ground.

What is judged: ritual or conduct (what-judged): routed to The parent's own boundary: the measure counts only powers that judge conduct between people; spirits that punish ritual lapses are outside it by definition..
- What it covers: Whether the powers punish neglected rites and slights to themselves or harm done to other people.
- Necessity fail: Already the measure's definition.
- Independence fail: Not a part beside the measure but its edge.
- Universality pass: Every society's powers judge something.

When conduct is repaid: in this life, after death, in the next birth (when-repaid): a kind of concept.humanity.wants.meaning.belief.
- What it covers: The timing of reward and punishment: misfortune now, heaven and hell, rebirth.
- Necessity fail: Moral belief works whatever the timing; the timings are kinds of it.
- Independence fail: Follows tradition, as the ground does.
- Universality fail: Each timing belongs to some traditions only.

How firmly it is held (intensity): frontier.
- What it covers: Certainty and importance of belief: from conviction to nominal assent.
- Necessity pass: Secularization is partly a loss of intensity before a loss of belief.
- Independence uncertain: Another reading of the same persons, not a part of them.
- Universality uncertain: Measured only by surveys since the 1980s (World Values Survey, Pew, Gallup).

Unbelief chosen or imposed (unbelief): routed to No religion (h.religion-7), whose kinds already divide chosen secularity from unbelief imposed by state atheism..
- What it covers: Those who hold no judging power, by their own choice in free societies or under state atheism.
- Necessity fail: Outside the believers this share counts.
- Independence pass: It moves on its own course.
- Universality fail: Large only since 1917.

Completeness uncertain: The outline's headings sort into kinds of belief (spirits and gods, cosmology) or into what the tradition shares already follow; none gives a part of the believing share that moves apart from tradition membership. Checked against The moralizing-gods codings of Swanson's and Peoples and Marlowe's cross-cultural samples and the Outline of Cultural Materials' religious beliefs headings (general character of religion, cosmology, spirits and gods, sacred objects and places, theology)..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.meaning.belief","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.meaning.belief","candidates":[{"key":"ground","label":"What the trust rests on: a judging god or an impersonal law","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"what-judged","label":"What is judged: ritual or conduct","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The parent's own boundary: the measure counts only powers that judge conduct between people; spirits that punish ritual lapses are outside it by definition."},{"key":"when-repaid","label":"When conduct is repaid: in this life, after death, in the next birth","outcome":"kind","necessity":"fail","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","kindOf":"concept.humanity.wants.meaning.belief"},{"key":"intensity","label":"How firmly it is held","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"unbelief","label":"Unbelief chosen or imposed","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","routedTo":"No religion (h.religion-7), whose kinds already divide chosen secularity from unbelief imposed by state atheism."}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The moralizing-gods codings of Swanson's and Peoples and Marlowe's cross-cultural samples and the Outline of Cultural Materials' religious beliefs headings (general character of religion, cosmology, spirits and gods, sacred objects and places, theology)."}}}

The carve of Water held on land: its parts and how they make it work

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Water impounded behind dams (reservoirs): frontier.
- What it covers: Water stored in artificial reservoirs, mostly since 1950.
- Necessity pass: The great dams of 1950 to 1990 hold back about three centimetres of sea level (Chao and colleagues, as recalled).
- Independence pass: Set by dam building, apart from groundwater and climate.
- Universality pass: On the axis reading, zero before dams.

Groundwater pumped and not returned (groundwater): frontier.
- What it covers: Water taken from aquifers faster than it recharges, which reaches the sea.
- Necessity pass: Pumping since 1950 adds one to two centimetres of sea level, roughly offsetting the dams.
- Independence pass: Set by irrigation and pumps.
- Universality pass: On the axis reading, zero before deep pumping.

- Necessity pass: Most of the ice.

- Universality pass: Throughout.

- What it covers: The ice of the Peninsula and its ice shelves.
- Necessity uncertain: Small in sea-level terms.
- Independence pass: Its shelves (Larsen B, 2002) break up on their own course.
- Universality pass: Throughout.
