upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Findings from the carves after the first six (claude.finding.deeper-tree-1 covers energy, sea level, farmland, revenue, toil and exchange). All values are recalled and tagged sketch or inferred; none is checked (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. Composition hides opposite moves. Plural unions (h.marriage.plural) have stayed near three in a hundred married women since 1900 although polygyny fell within Africa, because Africa's share of humanity rose: a world share flat for a century made of two strong opposite movements. Prediction, to test against the Demographic and Health Surveys: if the within-Africa fall continues at its pace since 1990, the world share falls below 2.5 by 2050 despite Africa's growth.

2. Divorce has a U shape. How marriages end (h.marriage.ending) runs from about a third of first marriages among foragers to about one in fifteen in 1800, when China, India and Christian Europe, most of humanity, hardly divorced, and back to about one in five by 2025. The low point is an agrarian and religious achievement, not a human constant; Java, the Malay world and Tokugawa Japan were the exceptions inside it.

3. Herders' share turns twice. Mobile herders (h.habitat.mobile.herders) peak at 3000 BCE with the Yamnaya wagon nomads, dip by 2200 BCE, then rise again with mounted nomadism to about 500 BCE. The dip is defensible but was not noted in the values: the Bronze Age steppe peoples after the Yamnaya (Sintashta, Srubnaya, Andronovo) lived in villages, the drying Sahara ended its cattle nomadism, and farming populations grew faster. Herders pass foragers as the larger part of the mobile between 1600 and 1650. The parent's note at 1206 says herders were a third of the mobile; this split makes them two in five, because it counts some foragers as settled.

4. Three episodes, not one, of taking the wild animals. Land mammals (the parent) fell at the end of the Pleistocene and again since 1850; sea mammals (h.earth.wild-animals.sea-mammals) fell from the 1600s to the 1980s and are the only wild-animal measure in the account that now rises, since the 1986 moratorium; fish of fishable size (h.earth.wild-animals.fish) fell mostly after 1880 and fastest from 1950 to 1996. The fish level is debated (stock assessments against catch reconstructions and whole-ocean models), and the band holds both.

5. Schooling grew by stages. The secondary turn after 1950 carries most of the growth in years; secondary passes a third of all years about 2000 and higher learning reaches a tenth by 2025 (h.schooling.primary, .secondary, .tertiary). The stage boundary in older systems is this account's reading.

6. Numeracy ran ahead of literacy until about 1900 (h.understanding.numeracy against h.understanding): in 1800 about three in five adults knew their age exactly, while about one in eight could read.

7. Kin groups: the largest single fall in kin groups beyond the household (h.belonging.descent) is China's land reform and collectivization, 1950 to 1954, not Europe's slow dissolution under the Church's marriage rules, which had too few people to move the world share much.

Kept whole this session, each with its reason and what would reopen it: mass media (its media are overlapping kinds), belief (its grounds follow the tradition shares), water held on land (its human parts are centimetres that nearly cancel; their home is a fresh-water process), Antarctica's and Greenland's ice (their parts matter for the Last Interglacial and after 2025)."}
upsertNodes.title: What the later carves of the deeper-tree pass show

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"What this pass did. It read the construction back, then went deeper into the tree of processes with the conceptual decomposition (ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, MandatoryAbstraction#ac44, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f), every carve recorded with life_carve_record and the graph rebound after every revision. Fourteen carves cut a process into parts: energy for warmth, light and work; sea level; farmland; state revenue; toil; exchange; child mortality; continuation; belonging; understanding; schooling; settling down; the wild animals; marriage. Their parts were opened with values at every date of the parent, tagged and banded, with notes where values turn: the tree went from 113 processes to 152. Nineteen processes were kept whole with their reasons (the eight tradition shares, internet, foraging, health, hereditary rank, homicide, food-getting work, mass media, belief, water held on land, Antarctica's and Greenland's ice), and one attempt (beauty and play) found only one part passing and recorded no cut. The climb of hereditary rank, which had filed a part as a kind, was relabelled (SpecializationEdge#4d20). The six M49 areas and every existing measure were kept; no measure was re-hung. Findings: claude.finding.deeper-tree-1 and claude.finding.deeper-tree-2.

What it leaves open, for the next pass.
1. Untested parts: internet under connection, food-getting work and foraging under provisioning, the development index under what matters to people, and the eight tradition shares under regular worship sit under carved parents without being tested in their carves. Re-carving those parents with them among the candidates is the re-filing choice this pass was asked not to make.
2. Fresh water: the Earth's own carve holds fresh water as a frontier part with independence uncertain. One argument to promote it: the green Sahara came and went with the orbit's insolation, not with global mean temperature, so the drylands move apart from the parent. A candidate measure is the desert share of ice-free land; people's use of fresh water (impounded, withdrawn) is where dams and groundwater pumping belong, as the keep-whole of water held on land says. Promoting it means re-recording the Earth's carve under its cut id with all its candidates.
3. Values to check or correct: the Christian share in late antiquity (6% at 500, 12% at 1000) looks low against Stark's model and must move with its sibling shares; fodder for working animals sits outside the energy accounting; the parent's energy values run low from 1960 to 2014 against the sum of the parts' sources; the herders' dip after 3000 BCE has no note in its values (see claude.finding.deeper-tree-2).
4. Frontier parts recorded but not opened: associations; stored knowledge and discovery; the arts and spending on play; body mass; homicide by relation; women's height; public debt; housework; the division of labour by sector; pre-primary schooling and schooling by sex and by provider; wild birds, arthropods and land mammals by size; who chooses the spouse, the never-married, unions without marriage; media's copies and content; belief's ground and intensity; the budget parts of land water and of the two ice sheets.
5. Alternative carves recorded beside the chosen ones: fertility by mother's age, energy by converter, exchange by reach.
6. The newly opened parts are all sketched and stand first in the deepen check (fish, sea mammals, kin groups, mobile foragers and herders); the next pass should check them against sources before carving them further.
7. The process-unobserved question: almost all of the new parts hold values but no Event observes them. Events worth linking: the 1986 whaling moratorium, the Criminal Tribes Act of 1871, Soviet collectivization of the herders, China's 1950 Marriage Law and land reform, no-fault divorce from 1969, the GI Bill, the 1992 cod collapse.
8. Four Events with linked but unweighed causes (the Roman Empire, the Antarctic Treaty, the rise of Christianity and one more), and the model's standing questions on laws and spatial positions.
9. Record-keeping: one keep-whole of Antarctica's ice was first recorded by mistake on a side branch (model 9108bc6d), from the same parent as the keep-whole of water held on land; it was recorded again on the main line and the branch is unused. The schooling carve's routing flags two cases without a home among its parts (a pre-primary class, an apprentice), and the carves of wild animals and marriage flag the cases routed to their parents' own measures; these are deliberate tests of each carve's boundary, not missing parts.
10. The construction file in the repository has not been re-exported for this pass."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"plan","text":"Continuing on 2026-10-18 at graph r256 (74c743ac), bound to model r229 (159e05b4), the only head the saved-work listing shows, on the Meaning Model 0.14.0 engine with the project's Sema vocabulary (store/sema/world-history.db, 617 patterns). Read back through life_construction_replay (all 257 graph revisions at outline level, the last seventeen at reasoning level) and the closing notes whole (claude.pass.deeper-tree.closing, claude.finding.deeper-tree-1, claude.plan.deeper-tree-pass, note.review-pass.closing, claude.plan.next-pass-9), then life_model_outline and life_model_questions.

What the reading showed.
1. The time schedule is filled at all four levels for all 152 processes; the coverage report says the last pass is done. So filling in this pass means values where new links and new processes need them.
2. The tree has 151 decomposition edges, and no process declares that it is the sum of its parts, although 21 wholes are built that way: child mortality by age, births by order, carbon dioxide (the carbon cycle's level and the human addition), exchange, farmland, food, forest, the mobile, output per person by sector, state revenue, schooling, sea level, toil, war, and the region shares of Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas, Latin America, Asia, Europe and Oceania. Safety is described as homicide plus war. Energy for warmth is not the sum of its children, because it includes the food people eat, which no child holds.
3. The breadth check names Events that move no process: 235 judged for the history of the Americas, 226 for Asia's, 279 for politics', and more groups behind them. 98 processes hold values but no Event names them (process-unobserved).
4. The deepen check names wild fish first, then wild sea mammals and kin groups beyond the household, all sketched by the last pass.
5. The live viewer cannot open the graph: its construction history now exceeds the 480 MiB portable-file limit. It opens on the model. The same limit may stop life_construction_export, which the last pass left undone.

The plan, in this order, each step recorded with its reasons and the graph rebound after every model revision:
(1) Check the parts against the whole: declare aggregate sum on the wholes whose parts share their unit and add up to them (MECE#ae19: the parts of each are exclusive and exhaustive along one criterion), then resolve every contradiction the report names, with the reason on the value.
(2) Widen: answer the breadth check group by group. Where an Event changes a process the model has, name it in the Event's process_ids and give the process a value at it. Where a group shows a change no process follows, open it as a new process with a measure that passes the number test and values at every level of the schedule. Where neither pays, record why with life_breadth_record.
(3) Deepen: answer the deepen check with life_carve_record (ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f, MarginalValueRule#6611), opening the parts that pass with measures and values.
(4) Fill: every new process and every newly linked Event valued, banded and tagged, until the coverage report says done again.
Kept as they are: the six M49 areas, the existing measures and their parents; nothing is re-hung. Every value is recalled, tagged sketch or inferred, and shares one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca); debated points are given with their alternatives (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b)."}

How the parts make the whole work: World output is the sum of the output made in the five inhabited M49 areas; Antarctica makes none of its own. At every date the five parts sum to h.means, which declares itself their sum. Divided by each area's people (its share of humanity, h.region-*, times h.humanity) they give output per person by area, and their ratios carry the Great Divergence: near parity under the Malthusian ceiling until 1500 (MalthusianTrap#0f6b), Europe and its settler offshoots pulling ahead from 1800 as fossil energy lifted the land's bound (Sunbound#c94c), Asia's share of world output falling from about three fifths in 1820 to about a quarter by 1913 and a fifth around 1950, and rising again to about half by 2025. The values are recalled from the Maddison Project's regional estimates as converted to the M49 areas, with Asia taken as the residual so that the parts sum exactly to the account's own world output; none is checked (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

Routed elsewhere: Output by M49 subregion to The next level of each area's own carve, as humanity's people are carved by subregion; left for a later pass., Output by sector to The carve of provisioning by sector (carve.concept.humanity.means.provisioning), per person..

How the parts make the whole work: World output is the sum of the output made in the five inhabited M49 areas; Antarctica makes none of its own. At every date the five parts sum to h.means, which declares itself their sum. Divided by each area's people (its share of humanity, h.region-*, times h.humanity) they give output per person by area, and their ratios carry the Great Divergence: near parity under the Malthusian ceiling until 1500 (MalthusianTrap#0f6b), Europe and its settler offshoots pulling ahead from 1800 as fossil energy lifted the land's bound (Sunbound#c94c), Asia's share of world output falling from about three fifths in 1820 to about a quarter by 1913 and a fifth around 1950, and rising again to about half by 2025. The values are recalled from the Maddison Project's regional estimates as converted to the M49 areas, with Asia taken as the residual so that the parts sum exactly to the account's own world output; none is checked (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The breadth check names hundreds of Events in the regional histories (235 for the Americas, 226 for Asia, 121 for Africa, 134 for Oceania) and 279 in politics' that move no process. Reading the Americas' list shows what they change: states and empires rising and falling, conquest and colonies, independence and revolutions, booms, depressions and industry, epidemics and migrations, slavery and its end, wars, democracy and religion. Demographic, war, voice, bondage and religious Events can name processes the model already follows; two kinds of change had no home at all, so two were opened before the Events are linked.

1. Output made in each M49 area (h.means.africa, .americas, .asia, .europe, .oceania), as a second carve of how people get it, by place (carve.concept.humanity.means.places, recorded at r236 and re-recorded at r237 to restore its earlier climb). Measured in trillion 2011 dollars so the five sum to world output, which declares itself their sum; total output, not output per person, because a per-person measure is undefined in the Americas and Oceania before people arrive. Asia is the residual. The shares of world output this gives follow Maddison's within a few points (Asia 62% in 1500, 57% in 1820, 27% in 1913, half in 2025); Europe passes Asia between 1870 and 1890, the Americas pass Europe only in 1944, Europe passes the Americas again by 1960 (with all of Russia in Europe), and Asia passes both in the 1990s (MalthusianTrap#0f6b before 1800, Sunbound#c94c after).

2. Colonial rule (h.colonial): the share of humanity in dependencies ruled from a metropole overseas, opened as the series the politics carve called for (its empire candidate: a kind of scale of rule), filed under the largest polity's process as a kind (semantic_subtype). Zero before Ceuta (1415) by definition; about 2% after the conquests of Mexico and Peru, falling to 1.5% by 1600 as the colonized die; doubling with Bengal (1757 to 1765); a fifth of humanity by 1820 with India; three in ten by 1900; its peak, a third, about 1940; 11% after Asia's independence (1947 to 1949); 2.5% by 1962; a twentieth of a percent now. Every boundary of the definition is debated and stated as an alternative in the notes (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): Rome's overseas provinces, Russia's land empire, Manchukuo, occupied China, Puerto Rico.

Both rest on recalled figures sharing one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca). Next: link the regional and political Events to these and to the existing processes they move, with values where the coverage report then asks for them."}
upsertNodes.title: Widening: output by M49 area and colonial rule, opened for the regional and political Events

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Done at model r230 to r242.

1. Declared. 23 wholes now declare that they are the sum of their parts (scale.aggregate = sum): child mortality by age; births per woman by order; carbon dioxide (the carbon cycle's level and the human addition); trade by kind; farmland; food by source; forest by climate domain; the mobile by how they move; output per person by sector; state revenue by base; schooling by stage; sea level by where the water is held; toil by who directs the hours; war by kind; safety as homicide plus war; the shares of Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, the Americas, Latin America, Asia, Europe and Oceania by subregion; and world output by M49 area (h.means, from r242). Energy for warmth is not declared: it counts the food people eat, which none of its parts holds.

2. How. life_values_record sets aggregate only when it opens a process; passing it for an existing process re-records the value given and leaves the declaration out (r230, r231). The declaration was made by life_model_revise, restating each process with scale.aggregate (r232). The same holds for bounds (r239, r240).

3. Units. The check compares a whole only with parts whose unit string is identical. 19 parts opened by the deeper-tree pass had the same unit worded differently and were aligned with their parents' wording (r234): trade by kind, revenue by base, the mobile, sea level's six parts and toil's three. Left uncompared on purpose, because aligning them would misdescribe a part or change a measure this pass keeps as it is: child mortality's age bands ('% of live births' against '% dying before age 5'), cropland and pasture ('% of ice-free land' against '% of ice-free land as crops or pasture'), and homicide and war under safety. Their sums were checked by reading the values: they hold at the dates read.

4. Result. Contradictions 0 and residuals 0 throughout: no part exceeds its whole and no whole is left unexplained. The parts were built as their parent times a share at every parent date, so the check confirms the bookkeeping, not the shares; a share can be wrong and still sum (MECE#ae19: exclusive and exhaustive does not make each part right)."}

revision.reason: Rebind to r247, after the four revisions that link the Americas' Events to the processes they change.

Breadth check answered: Most of the group is now linked, and the rest is not worth a new process. Of the 271 Events placed in the Americas, 154 now name the processes they change (r244 to r247), and the processes were given values where the links found them silent (r248 to r254), until the coverage report found none passing over its Events. What they change was already followed: the subregions' shares of humanity, the Americas' output, colonial rule, bondage and compelled work, war by kind, homicide, voice, foraging, freight, cropland, pasture, tropical forest, wild fish (the Grand Banks) and hereditary rank (the castas). The 131 judged for the Americas that stay unlinked fall into three kinds. (1) Below the resolution of world and M49 measures: a single city, chiefdom, massacre, treaty or doctrine (Cahokia, Chaco, Crow Creek, Mayapán, the Tarascan state, the Falklands, Tordesillas, the Monroe Doctrine, the Louisiana Purchase). (2) Carried by a linked Event: the Mississippian period carries the entradas, the Haitian Revolution Leclerc's expedition, the Second World War Pearl Harbor, the dictatorships Chile's coup and the Dirty War. (3) What they change has no process, and opening one does not pay now: change within Christianity (Pentecostal growth, liberation theology, the Great Awakening) moves people between traditions, not into or out of the faith, and would need a carve of the kept-whole h.religion-4; the missile crisis, a near miss, moves no measure. By the routing test (RoutingSanityCheck#71bd) every Event with a world-scale change found a home among existing processes, so no new process earns its keep for this region (MarginalValueRule#6611). Reopen if a regional history of the Americas is opened, where these Events would move the region's own measures.

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: Most of the group is now linked, and the rest is not worth a new process. Every kind of change the group showed already had a process: war deaths by kind (the Opium, Korean, Iran–Iraq, Indochina and Syrian wars, the Armenian genocide, the Cultural Revolution, Partition), hunger deaths (Bengal, the El Niño famines, northern Vietnam, the Soviet famine), colonial rule (the Company, the Raj, the VOC, French Indochina, Japan's Korea, the independences of 1946 to 1957), the largest polity and the share under a state (Akkad, Assyria, Maurya, Sui, Ming, Yuan), foraging (the Fertile Crescent, millet, rice, Mehrgarh, the Austronesian and mainland farmers), Asia's output (Japan's miracle, the tigers, the Asian crisis), extreme poverty (Doi Moi, the New Order, the region's escape from poverty), compelled work (the Cultivation System, the romusha, the Burma railway), bondage and rank (Joseon's slaves and yangban, the Vedic varnas, Siam's abolition), sea level (Sundaland), tropical forest (oil palm) and South-eastern Asia's share of humanity. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Politics (concept.humanity.means.politics):
- What it is: Politics as a means: making and enforcing decisions binding on a population, and taking from it what rule needs, from a band's consensus to empires and modern states. Measured by the share living under a state, with state revenue and the largest polity beneath it.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of rule that change apart, which the state share hides: how much rulers take and can do (capacity), how far one rule reaches over humanity (scale), and into how many autonomous units humanity is divided (fragmentation); and, routed elsewhere, who has a say (voice) and how rule is fought over (war); so that the rise of states, empires, unifications and breakups, fiscal-military and welfare states, colonial rule and decolonization each have a home.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, bands and chiefdoms as much as states and empires; measured for all living people, all output or all polities.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Politics is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Politics is the means of ruling: decisions binding on a population and the taking that pays for them. Other kinds within it: Provisioning, Habitat, Connection, Exchange, Force.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Politics is carved into 3 parts: Capacity, Scale of rule, Fragmentation: how many autonomous polities share humanity.

How the parts make the whole work: Politics as this account follows it is the reach of the state (the parent's own measure), its capacity (what rulers take, read by revenue as a share of output), its scale (how much of humanity the largest rule holds) and its fragmentation (how many autonomous polities humanity is divided into). The four change apart: states spread over humanity for five thousand years; the largest rule reached a fifth to a quarter of humanity under the Achaemenids, Han and Rome and again under the Ming and Qing and never more; capacity stayed near 5% of output until the fiscal-military and welfare states tripled it in the twentieth century; and the number of autonomous units rose with people to most of a million in the Bronze Age, fell as states absorbed bands, villages and chiefdoms and as the colonial partition claimed the last stateless lands, and rose again among states after 1945. Warsift#b01b predicts the long fall where war sifts polities, and fails where they multiply by agreement (decolonization) or breakup (1991). Independent states are a kind of autonomous polity, followed as their own count from the first city-states; empire over other peoples is a kind of scale, followed as colonial rule. Voice is routed to Freedom and power, fighting over rule to war and force; law and the form of rule stay frontier.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Rule over other peoples (a kind of concept.humanity.means.politics.scale), Independent states (a kind of concept.humanity.means.politics.fragmentation).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Law and justice (independence), Form of rule (necessity).

Routed elsewhere: Reach of the state to h.politics's own measure, the share living under a state, which reads it already, Voice to Freedom and power (h.voice), the share living in democracies with broad suffrage, where the first pass filed it, Fighting over rule to War (h.war) under safety for its dead and Force (h.means.force) for the people under arms.

Routing sample: 15 case(s); 7 with no home among the parts (The Inca state extends rule over the Andes in the fifteenth century; The British Raj: India ruled from London, 1858 to 1947; Decolonization in Africa, 1957 to 1975; Women's suffrage after 1918; The Code Napoleon, 1804); 1 with two or more parts as homes (The First Emperor unifies China, 221 BCE: scale, fragmentation).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.politics","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.politics","form":"processes","cutRecorded":true,"parts":[{"key":"capacity","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.politics.capacity","processId":"h.revenue"},{"key":"scale","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.politics.scale","processId":"h.largest-polity"},{"key":"fragmentation","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.politics.fragmentation","processId":"h.polities"}],"process":"h.politics","routingCases":15}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Reach of the state (reach): routed to h.politics's own measure, the share living under a state, which reads it already.
- What it covers: Whether people live under a state at all: rule by a permanent centre with officials, tribute or taxes, as against bands, tribes and chiefdoms.
- Necessity pass: The spread of the state from nothing in 3500 BCE to nearly everyone is politics' longest change.
- Independence pass: It reached 99% by 1945 while capacity kept rising and scale fell.
- Universality pass: Every population lives under a state or does not; zero for foragers.

Capacity (capacity): part.
- What it covers: How much rulers take from what a population makes, and so what they can do: armies, officials, works and, later, schools, pensions and health care.
- Necessity pass: The fiscal-military states of early modern Europe, Song China's commercial taxes and the twentieth century's rise from about 10% to 30% of output, the welfare state, have no home without it (Tilly's coercion and capital; Brewer's sinews of power).
- Independence pass: Revenue tripled between 1910 and 1950 while the state share barely moved and the largest polity's share fell.
- Universality pass: Every population sustains its rule somehow; for bands and most chiefdoms the measure is near zero.

Scale of rule (scale): part.
- What it covers: How far one rule reaches over humanity: the size of the largest polity, from Akkad to the Achaemenids, Han and Rome, the Mongols, Ming and Qing China and the British Empire.
- Necessity pass: The rise and fall of the great empires is what a political history of the world most often narrates; without scale it has no home.
- Independence pass: The largest polity fell from about a quarter to a seventh of humanity after 400 while the state share held; it shrank after 1820 while capacity rose.
- Universality pass: Every population has a largest unit of rule, if only a band of a few dozen.

Fragmentation: how many autonomous polities share humanity (fragmentation): part.
- What it covers: The number of political units that answer to no higher authority, making their own war and peace and paying no tribute or tax to an outside ruler: forager bands, autonomous villages, chiefdoms, city-states, kingdoms, empires and sovereign states. From about ten thousand bands 300,000 years ago to most of a million units in the Bronze Age and about three hundred now.
- Necessity pass: Unifications and breakups (Qin in 221 BCE, Germany and Italy in 1859 to 1871, the Soviet Union's fifteen states in 1991), the Scramble for Africa's absorption of hundreds of kingdoms and stateless peoples, decolonization's eighty new states and Warsift#b01b's prediction that war between polities lowers their number have no home without it: the routing sample of the first carve sent the Soviet breakup to this candidate, where it found no part.
- Independence pass: Judged again: the first carve (r133) failed it as the other side of the size distribution the largest polity reads. The links of this pass show the two varying apart. Decolonization raised the number of sovereign states from about 70 to about 150 between 1945 and 1975, and the Soviet breakup added 15 in 1991, while the largest polity's share (China's) did not move; the consolidation of bands and villages into states cut autonomous units from about three quarters of a million to a few thousand while the largest polity's share stayed between a seventh and a third from 500 BCE on. One rule can hold a quarter of humanity while the rest fragments or unifies; the largest share and the count of units are separate readings, as a country's largest city and its number of towns are.
- Universality pass: Every population lives in some number of autonomous units, from forager bands to sovereign states.

Rule over other peoples (empire): a kind of scale.
- What it covers: Empire: rule by one people's centre over conquered or colonized peoples who have no part in it; above all the overseas colonial empires of 1500 to 1975, followed as colonial rule (h.colonial).
- Necessity pass: Colonial rule and decolonization (1945 to 1975) are among the largest political changes of the modern world.
- Independence pass: Decolonization ended colonial rule for about a third of humanity without changing the state share and while revenue rose.
- Universality fail: Only where a state rules other peoples, so a kind of scale, followed as colonial rule from 1415.

Independent states (states): a kind of fragmentation.
- What it covers: The autonomous polities that are states: city-states, kingdoms, empires and sovereign states, from the first Sumerian city-states to about two hundred now.
- Necessity pass: The sovereign states' system after 1648, Europe's five hundred polities becoming about thirty by 1900, and the near-tripling of states since 1945 are read by it.
- Independence pass: The number of states rose after 1945 while the number of all autonomous units fell, as the last unadministered peoples came under states.
- Universality fail: None before the first states about 3500 BCE: a kind of autonomous polity, not a part.

Voice (voice): routed to Freedom and power (h.voice), the share living in democracies with broad suffrage, where the first pass filed it.
- What it covers: Who has a say in rule: councils, assemblies, elections, suffrage.
- Necessity pass: Democratization is a central political change.
- Independence pass: Voice spread after 1945 apart from capacity and scale.
- Universality pass: Every population decides somehow.

Law and justice (law): frontier.
- What it covers: The rules rule follows and how disputes and crimes are judged: codes, courts, the rule of law and its absence.
- Necessity pass: Fukuyama counts the rule of law among the three components of political order; law codes from Ur-Nammu to the Tang Code and the Code Napoleon have no other home.
- Independence uncertain: A world measure exists only from 1789 (V-Dem's rule of law index); before that, a share living under written law would mostly restate the state share.
- Universality pass: Every population has norms and ways of judging.

Form of rule (form): frontier.
- What it covers: Who rules and how they are chosen and constrained: chiefs, kings, emperors, oligarchies, republics, party states.
- Necessity uncertain: Monarchy's decline after 1789 and the party states of the twentieth century are large changes, but they are categories competing for one pool, better followed as a Cut of regime types than as a number.
- Independence pass: Monarchies fell after 1917 apart from capacity.
- Universality pass: Every population has some form of rule.

Fighting over rule (fighting): routed to War (h.war) under safety for its dead and Force (h.means.force) for the people under arms.
- What it covers: Wars, rebellions and coups fought over who rules.
- Necessity pass: Much rule is won by force.
- Independence fail: Its history is the history of war and force, which have homes.
- Universality pass: Every population fights.

Completeness uncertain: The state is read by reach, capacity, scale and fragmentation; accountable government by voice, routed to Freedom and power; polities by scale and fragmentation, government by capacity, membership and participation by voice. The rule of law and the form of rule still have no measured home, so completeness stays uncertain. Checked against Fukuyama's three components of political order (the state, the rule of law, accountable government), Mann's political power within the IEMP model, and the structure construction's own politics node (polities: scale and order among polities; rule; government; law and justice; membership and participation) in structure/history-tree.mjs.. revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The group's Events, read whole, change four things. (1) Into how many units humanity is divided: unifications, partitions, breakups, independences, conquests of stateless peoples and the treaties of the states' system. No process followed this; the politics carve had merged it into scale. It is now followed by the count of autonomous polities (h.polities, opened r292 under h.politics after the carve was re-recorded at r291) and its kind, independent states (h.polities.states), and 25 Events name them (r293): the Zhou enfeoffments, the poleis, Qin, the Mongols, Constantinople, Westphalia, the fiscal-military state, the partitions of Poland, the American and Latin American independences, Vienna, Liberia, the unifications of Italy and Germany, the Berlin conference and the Scramble, Versailles, Israel, decolonization, the year of Africa, the Caribbean's and the Pacific's independences, the Soviet and Yugoslav breakups and Timor-Leste. (2) Who rules and how far: already followed by colonial rule, the largest polity, the share under a state and voice, which earlier passes and this one linked (the Atlantic revolutions, the Roman Republic, Athens, fascism, the Iron Curtain, India's democracy). (3) Fighting over rule: war by kind. (4) What remains unlinked, about 169 Events, is mostly the form of rule and its constraints: revolutions that replace one kind of ruler with another (Iran 1979), coups (Chile 1973), constitutions and charters (Magna Carta, the Glorious Revolution, the secret ballot), dynasties and courts, and treaties that order relations among states without changing their number (the Antarctic Treaty, the Monroe Doctrine). The politics carve keeps the form of rule (a Cut of regime types) and law and justice as frontier alternatives; following them needs that Cut, which this pass does not open (MarginalValueRule#6611). {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Force (concept.humanity.means.force):
- What it is: Force as a means: the means of organized violence a population keeps, which the carve of how people get it defined as who is kept under arms, with what weapons and at what cost, and followed only by how many people are kept under arms (per 1,000 people).
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of force that change apart, which the count of people under arms hides: the destructive power of weapons, from spears to siege engines, gunpowder and the hydrogen bomb, and what a population gives up for its armed force, from a band's raids to the fiscal-military states, the world wars and the Cold War; so that the security Events that change neither war's dead nor the people under arms (gunpowder, the atomic bomb and the tests, the peace dividend) have a home.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, bands as much as states; measured for all of humanity.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Force is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Force is the means of organized violence a population keeps against others and its own: fighters, weapons and what they cost. Other kinds within it: Provisioning, Exchange, Habitat, Connection, Politics.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Force is carved into 2 parts: Arms: the destructive power of weapons, Spending on force: what a population gives up for it.

How the parts make the whole work: Force as this account follows it is the people a population keeps under arms (the parent's own measure), the destructive power of the weapons they wield (arms, read by the most destructive single weapon in service) and the share of output the population gives up for them (spending). The three change apart: the most destructive blow grew from a spear's few hundred joules to a siege engine's tens of thousands, gunpowder's millions and billions and the hydrogen bomb's hundred quadrillion, mostly in steps that armies' size does not show; people under arms rose and fell with mass mobilization; and spending, a few percent of output in agrarian states, rose to a third in the world wars and settled near six in the Cold War and two and a half after it. Nuclear warheads are a kind of arms, followed as their own count from 1945; how fighters are raised and the works that protect against attack stay frontier. SecurityDilemma#a61b predicts the arms race the warheads and spending show between 1950 and 1986, and Warsift#b01b the link between spending and the sifting of polities.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Nuclear warheads (a kind of concept.humanity.means.force.arms).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: How fighters are raised and held (independence), Protection: walls, forts and armour (universality).

Routed elsewhere: People under arms to h.means.force's own measure, people under arms per 1,000 people, which reads it already, War's toll to War (h.war) and its parts under violence, causes of death.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

People under arms (fighters): routed to h.means.force's own measure, people under arms per 1,000 people, which reads it already.
- What it covers: Who is kept under arms: warriors, levies, standing soldiers, conscripts.
- Necessity pass: Mass armies, the levée en masse and demobilization are the core of military history.
- Independence pass: The share under arms quadrupled in each world war under unchanged weapons' power and fell after 1990 while the arsenals' yield barely moved.
- Universality pass: Every population keeps some people for fighting, or none, which is a value of the measure.

Arms: the destructive power of weapons (arms): part.
- What it covers: How much destruction the most powerful weapon in service can deliver at once: the thrust of a spear, a battering ram, a siege engine's stone, a gunpowder mine, a bomb.
- Necessity pass: Gunpowder, the bastion fort's answer to cannon, the dreadnought and the atomic and hydrogen bombs have no home without it; the Long Peace between great powers is usually explained by nuclear deterrence, which the account cannot read without the weapons' power.
- Independence pass: The bomb multiplied the most destructive weapon's yield about five hundredfold in 1945 while the share under arms fell from 30 to 10 per 1,000 within a year; armies grew tenfold in the military revolution while the largest blow stayed that of a gunpowder mine of a ton or so.
- Universality pass: Every population has a most destructive weapon, a thrusting spear at least.

Spending on force: what a population gives up for it (spending): part.
- What it covers: The share of a population's output given to its armed force: fighters' keep and pay, weapons, fortifications and war.
- Necessity pass: The fiscal-military state (Brewer, Tilly), the world wars' economies that gave a third or more of output to war, the Cold War's burden and the peace dividend after 1990 have no home without it; revenue holds what states take, not what goes to force, and wartime spending ran far beyond revenue on borrowing.
- Independence pass: Spending and people under arms move apart as arms become capital-intensive: the Cold War took about 6% of world output with 7 to 9 per 1,000 under arms, while the Napoleonic wars put 8.7 per 1,000 under arms for perhaps 5% of output; spending on missiles and aircraft rose while armies shrank.
- Universality pass: Every population gives some of its effort to fighting and its means, if only a band's raids and weapons.

How fighters are raised and held (organization): frontier.
- What it covers: Warrior bands, levies, militias, mercenaries, standing professional armies, conscripts.
- Necessity pass: The standing army, conscription and the professional volunteer force mark the eras of force.
- Independence uncertain: These are categories competing for one pool, the people under arms, better followed as a Cut of fighters by how they are raised than as a number beside them.
- Universality pass: Every population raises its fighters somehow.

Protection: walls, forts and armour (protection): frontier.
- What it covers: The works and gear that shield against attack: palisades, city walls, the Great Wall, bastion forts, armour, shelters.
- Necessity pass: The walls of Uruk and Jericho, the Great Wall and the trace italienne are among the largest works people ever built.
- Independence pass: Fortification answered arms but on its own clock: the bastion fort followed cannon by half a century, and walls lost their use while armies grew.
- Universality uncertain: Many bands built no defences at all; protection may be a kind of force, found where people are settled, rather than a part of every case.

Nuclear warheads (nuclear): a kind of arms.
- What it covers: The nuclear weapons held by states, counted as warheads.
- Necessity pass: The arms race, the test-ban and arms-control treaties and the nine nuclear states are read by it.
- Independence pass: The count rose fifteenfold from 1960 to 1986 while the largest weapon's yield fell; it fell by four fifths after 1986 with little change in the largest weapon.
- Universality fail: None before 1945: a kind of arms, not a part.

War's toll (toll): routed to War (h.war) and its parts under violence, causes of death.
- What it covers: The dead of organized violence.
- Necessity pass: What force costs in lives is a central measure of security.
- Independence fail: It is what force does, not what is kept: already followed under staying alive.
- Universality pass: Every population loses people to organized violence or does not.

Completeness uncertain: Fighters (the parent's measure), arms and spending give a working account of the means kept for organized violence: who fights, how destructive their weapons are and what the population gives up for them. How fighters are raised and the works that protect against attack stay frontier: the first is a Cut over fighters, the second may be a kind found only where people are settled. Checked against The usual components of military power in strategic studies (manpower, materiel, budget, organization and doctrine, fortification), and the structure construction's own security node (war between groups: toll, organization, means) in structure/history-tree.mjs.. Still without a home: How fighters are raised (a Cut of levies, standing forces, conscripts, volunteers); Protection: walls, forts and armour.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.force","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.force","candidates":[{"key":"fighters","label":"People under arms","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"h.means.force's own measure, people under arms per 1,000 people, which reads it already"},{"key":"arms","label":"Arms: the destructive power of weapons","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"spending","label":"Spending on force: what a population gives up for it","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"organization","label":"How fighters are raised and held","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass"},{"key":"protection","label":"Protection: walls, forts and armour","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"nuclear","label":"Nuclear warheads","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"arms"},{"key":"toll","label":"War's toll","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","routedTo":"War (h.war) and its parts under violence, causes of death"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The usual components of military power in strategic studies (manpower, materiel, budget, organization and doctrine, fortification), and the structure construction's own security node (war between groups: toll, organization, means) in structure/history-tree.mjs.","missing":["How fighters are raised (a Cut of levies, standing forces, conscripts, volunteers)","Protection: walls, forts and armour"]}}}

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: Read whole, the group's Events that named nothing were mostly about the means of war, which the account held only as people under arms: gunpowder, the atomic bombs, the hydrogen-bomb tests, the arms race, the world wars' economies and the peace dividend. Force had never been carved; it now is (carve.concept.humanity.means.force, r300), with two parts opened at r301 and valued over the whole span: arms, the energy of the most destructive weapon in service (h.means.force.arms), and spending on force as a share of world output (h.means.force.spending), with nuclear warheads as a kind of arms (h.means.force.arms.nuclear). Eleven Events now name them or war (r303): gunpowder, nuclear weapons, Hiroshima, Castle Bravo, the Pacific tests, both world wars, the fiscal-military state, the end of the Cold War, the Long Peace and the Crusades. What stays unlinked, about 75 Events, is of three kinds. (1) Single battles, sieges and raids carried by the wars that hold them (Pearl Harbor by the Pacific war, Gallipoli by the First World War, Tet and Dien Bien Phu by the Indochina wars, Adwa, Tondibi, Mbwila, Bach Dang). (2) Coups and seizures of power (Chile 1973, Guatemala 1954), which change the form of rule, a frontier of the politics carve, more than any measure of force. (3) Near misses and doctrines that change no measure (the Cuban missile crisis, the Monroe Doctrine). None earns a process at this resolution (MarginalValueRule#6611); reopen with a Cut of regime types, or if a regional history is opened.

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: Most of the group is now linked, and the rest is not worth a new process. Of the 87 Events placed in Europe that named no process, 50 now name the processes they change (r285, r286) and seven more name the counts of states and polities (r293); with the world Events linked at r284 and values added where the links found processes silent (r287 to r290), the coverage report again finds none passing over its Events. What they change was already followed, or is now: war by kind, contestation, the vote and rank, compelled work, revenue and its bases, spending on force, trade and Europe's output, making and the urban share, passenger speed and freight, infection, hunger, higher learning, sea level and the ice, Europe's share and, for the first time, its four subregions' shares (the emigration, the expulsions, the Irish famine, the Mongols in Rus', the poleis, the Vikings, the Thirty Years' War). The 24 still unlinked are Europe's eras (carried by the Events inside them), courts and dynasties (Byzantium, the Franks, al-Andalus, the Ottoman Balkans), ideas without a process of discovery (the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, Greek philosophy, the scientific revolution), art and monuments (Aurignacian art, the megaliths, the Minoan and Mycenaean palaces), Neanderthals (not counted by humanity's measures), single eruptions, charters (Magna Carta, the Glorious Revolution), the witch hunts (about 100,000 dead over more than a century, under a hundredth of a death per 100,000 a year at world scale) and the Great Schism (a change between branches of one faith). The making of new knowledge is the one kind with no home: the carve of how people get it keeps it as a frontier, and the knowledge group of the breadth check will ask for it on its own; it is not opened for Europe's sake (MarginalValueRule#6611). {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Done at model r284 to r305. Every value is recalled, sketched or inferred, and shares one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. Links. 135 Events that named no process now name the processes they change: 49 world Events (r284), 50 of Europe's (r285, r286), 25 political (r293) and 11 of security (r303). Processes that no Event named fell from 61 to 33: the causes of death, child mortality by age, adult survival, the carbon cycle's parts, the forest domains, the sea-level parts, Europe's four subregions, primary and higher schooling, revenue by base, the stores burned, births by order and others now have Events that move them. Values were added where the links found 23 processes silent (r287 to r290), most on the line between neighbours; where an Event moved a measure the value says so (the first passenger railway in 1830, Britain's emancipation in 1834, manhood suffrage in France in 1848, the Irish famine). War, a rate averaged to the next date, was re-split so each block's total is kept (490 to 200 BCE at Alexander, 1789 to 1800 at April 1792).

2. The count of polities (h.polities, h.polities.states, r292). Autonomous units rise with people while everyone lives in bands (about 9,000 three hundred thousand years ago, 130,000 at the Holocene's start), pass half a million with farming villages, peak near three quarters of a million in the late Bronze Age (Carneiro's order of magnitude for 1000 BCE) and fall as states absorb bands, villages and chiefdoms: by a quarter after the Black Death and the Mongol wars, again as the Americas' peoples die, and fastest with the colonial partition of 1870 to 1914. After 1950 the count is about three hundred, two thirds of them states. Independent states run from the first Sumerian cities to some 900 when the Greek poleis were most numerous, fall by two thirds with Qin, the Hellenistic kingdoms and Rome, recover to about 650 by 1500, fall to about 70 by 1900 (the Holy Roman Empire's end, the unifications, the Scramble) and rise to about 197 since 1945.
- Warsift#b01b, read against it: the three great falls in states (490 to 200 BCE, Europe's 1500 to 1900, 1300's Mongol absorption) come with high war between polities (32 to 45 per 100,000 a year in the first), as the card predicts; the rise since 1945 comes with war between polities at its lowest, by agreement and breakup, which the card's own clause excludes (no elimination); the rise between 500 and 1206 is fragmentation after empires, which the card does not cover. A test still to make: a European series should show war rates in Europe above the world's from 1500 to 1815 while Europe's states fell from about 500 to about 40.
- A tension found, not resolved: the share under a state (h.politics) leaves 2% of people outside states in 1920 and 0.05% in 2025 (about four million people), which at the units' sizes would make tens of thousands of autonomous units today; the count of polities is set directly after 1920 from the record of unadministered and uncontacted peoples (about a hundred groups now). One of the two readings is wrong for the twentieth century; a count of people beyond effective administration in 1920, 1950 and 2025 would settle it.

3. The means of war (carve of force, r300; h.means.force.arms, .spending, .arms.nuclear, r301). The most destructive weapon in service moves in steps that neither war's dead nor the people under arms show: the siege engines of antiquity, gunpowder's bombs (1232) and mines (about 1500), Messines (1917), the atomic bombs (1945) and the hydrogen bomb in service (1954); it falls after 1976 as accuracy replaces yield. Spending on force sits near 2 to 4% of world output for three thousand years, about half or more of what states take, jumps to about a fifth in 1918 and a third in 1944 (beyond revenue, on borrowing), settles near 6% in the Cold War and falls to about 2.5% after 1990. Nuclear warheads: 2 in 1945, about 70,000 in 1986, about 12,200 now.
- SecurityDilemma#a61b, read against it: the superpowers had no common authority and each answered the other's build-up; the card predicts the spiral eases when capacity can be verified, and the warheads turn down after the INF treaty (1987), the first with on-site inspection, and START (1991). The fit is after the fact: the history was known before the series was drawn, so it is a consistency check, not a test.

4. A record-keeping slip and its repair: claude.revision.r285-placeholder."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Fighting within a polity (concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.within):
- What it is: Fighting within a polity: deaths in organized fighting inside one polity, over who rules it or whether it holds together, and between armed groups inside it; the part of war and massacre that the war carve set apart from fighting between polities and one-sided killing.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Fighting within a polity is a kind of War and massacre: Fighting within a polity is organized killing among people of one polity, as against fighting between polities and the one-sided killing of the unarmed. Other kinds within it: Fighting between polities, One-sided killing.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Fighting within a polity is carved into 3 parts: Over who rules, Over whether it holds together, Between armed groups, none of them the state.

How the parts make the whole work: Fighting within a polity is fighting over its government, over whether it holds together, or between armed groups none of which governs it; the three sum to it at every date, in its unit. Wars for the centre carry most of its dead in most centuries and all its great peaks: the Han's end, the Tang's, the Yuan's and the Ming's, the Taiping and the Russian and Chinese civil wars, the dynastic cycle's crises that StructuralDemographicCycle#8433 describes. Wars over territory rise when empires break (Spanish America from 1808, the American and Dungan wars of the 1860s, the postcolonial secessions from 1960) and carry a third to a half of the toll after 1950. Fighting between non-state groups is a steady minor part, largest where states fail or have not reached (Somalia, Congo) and where criminal armies fight (Mexico).

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Coups and seizures of power (a kind of concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.within.government).

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Over who rules (government): part.
- What it covers: Fighting over control of the polity's government: civil wars for the throne or the state, rebellions that aim to replace the ruler or the regime, revolutions, warlord wars for the centre.
- Necessity pass: The deadliest internal wars in history were fought for the centre: the Yellow Turbans and the Han's warlords, An Lushan, the Ming's fall, the Taiping, the Russian and Chinese civil wars.
- Independence pass: It peaks in 184, 1618 to 1650, 1850 to 1864 and 1918 to 1949 while wars over territory stay low; after 1945 wars of secession carry a larger share while wars for the centre fall.
- Universality pass: Every polity with a ruler can be fought over; zero among bands.

Over whether it holds together (territory): part.
- What it covers: Fighting over a region's secession, independence or autonomy within the polity: wars of secession and separation, provincial and ethnic revolts for self-rule.
- Necessity pass: The American Civil War, the Dungan revolt, the wars of Spanish America's separation, Biafra, Bangladesh's war of 1971, Eritrea, the Tamil and Kurdish wars and the breakups of Yugoslavia have no other home inside fighting within a polity.
- Independence pass: It rises in 1808 to 1826, 1861 to 1877 and 1967 to 1971 when wars for the centre are low, and it can be ended by partition while the government stands.
- Universality pass: Every polity that holds more than one region or people can be fought over whether it holds together; zero among bands.

Between armed groups, none of them the state (nonstate): part.
- What it covers: Organized fighting inside a polity between groups none of which is its government: lords' private wars and clan feuds, communal fighting, militias and warlords after a state's collapse, criminal cartels' wars.
- Necessity pass: Medieval private war, the feuds of clans and lineages, Somalia's clan wars after 1991, Congo's militias and Mexico's cartel wars since 2006 are fought over neither the government nor a territory's separation.
- Independence pass: Mexico's cartel wars raised it after 2006 with no change in fighting over government or territory; Somalia's state collapse moved deaths from it to it while the others fell.
- Universality pass: Every polity can hold armed groups that fight each other without the ruler as a party; zero among bands.

Coups and seizures of power (coups): a kind of government.
- What it covers: The armed seizure of government by a faction of the ruling group.
- Necessity pass: Most changes of rule in many eras.
- Independence pass: Coups can be frequent with few deaths.
- Universality fail: A form of fighting over who rules, found where a ruling group holds arms: a kind of government.

Terrorism (terror): routed to the part whose stake the group pursues (government, territory or none); recorded earlier as a kind of fighting within a polity.
- What it covers: Killing by small organized groups to frighten a wider public.
- Necessity pass: Political violence of the last century and a half.
- Independence fail: A tactic, not a stake: each group's terror serves a fight over government, territory or neither.
- Universality fail: A modern form.

Wars of colonies for independence (colonial-independence): routed to fighting between polities, by the war carve (extrasystemic wars are fighting between polities); earlier passes counted Spanish America's wars and Algeria's under fighting within a polity, and this carve keeps them under territory where the parent holds them.
- What it covers: Wars fought by colonized peoples against the metropole for independence: Algeria, Indochina, Kenya, Angola.
- Necessity pass: Decolonization's wars are large.
- Independence uncertain: Whether a colony is part of the metropole's polity decides whether its war is within or between; the parent's values have taken both answers.
- Universality fail: Only where colonies exist.

Deaths from internal war's famine and disease (war-famine): routed to Hunger (h.alive.hunger) and infection (h.alive.infection), as in the war carve; the parent's Taiping values appear to include them, a question the war carve already records.
- What it covers: People who die of the famine and disease a civil war brings.
- Necessity pass: In the Taiping war most of the dead died this way.
- Independence fail: Their deaths are famine and infection deaths.
- Universality pass: Every long civil war brings them.

Completeness pass: Every death in fighting within a polity has one home: the fighting is over the government, over a territory's separation, or between groups none of which is the government. Coups are a kind of the first; terrorism is a tactic routed to the part whose stake it serves. One seam stays open: whether a colony's war of independence is within the metropole's polity or between polities, which the parent's values have answered both ways; this carve keeps those deaths under territory where the parent holds them. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Colonial rule (concept.humanity.means.politics.scale.empire.colonial):
- What it is: Colonial rule: the share of all living people who live in dependencies ruled from a metropole overseas, with no part in the government that rules them, as h.colonial measures it from Ceuta (1415) to Puerto Rico now.
- What the carve is for: To follow where the colonized lived, which one share hides: the Atlantic islands and Spanish and Portuguese America that held almost all of it until the 1750s, India and South-east Asia that held most of it from Bengal (1757) to 1947, Africa that held most of what remained after 1948, and the Caribbean and Pacific islands of today; so that the regional Events of conquest and independence each move the part they belong to.
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, measured for all of humanity; zero before 1415 by the parent's definition.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Colonial rule is a kind of Rule over other peoples: Colonial rule is rule over other peoples from a metropole overseas, as against land empires and conquest states. Other kinds within it: Land empires over conquered peoples (the Mongols, the Ottomans, Russia's Siberia), Conquest dynasties ruling their own empire (the Qing, the Mughals), Military occupation.
2. Rule over other peoples is a kind of Scale of rule: Rule over other peoples is scale reached by ruling people who have no part in the rule. Other kinds within it: The largest polity's own people.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Colonial rule is carved into 5 parts: Colonial rule in Africa, Colonial rule in the Americas, Colonial rule in Asia, Colonial rule in Europe, Colonial rule in Oceania.

How the parts make the whole work: Colonial rule is the sum of the people ruled from overseas in each M49 area; the five parts add to it at every date in its unit. The carve shows three successive colonial worlds that the one share runs together: an Atlantic one (the Atlantic islands, then Spanish and Portuguese America, almost all of colonial rule from 1415 to about 1757), an Asian one (Bengal from 1757, then most of India, Java, Indochina, Korea and Taiwan: three quarters or more of it from 1800 to 1946), and an African one (from the Scramble of 1881 to Portugal's exit in 1975, most of what was left after 1948), followed by a small Caribbean and Pacific remainder. VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd explains the Americas' fall of 1550 to 1600 without any colony being lost.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: By form of rule (necessity, independence, universality).

Dropped: By the ruling state.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Colonial rule in Africa (africa): part.
- What it covers: People living in Africa (M49 002, by 2026 borders) under rule from overseas.
- Necessity pass: The Scramble, the colonial economy and the independences of 1956 to 1990 have no other home.
- Independence pass: It rose from 1 to 7% of humanity between 1881 and 1912 while Asia's part barely moved, and kept rising after 1947 while Asia's collapsed.
- Universality pass: Every date has people living in Africa who are or are not ruled from overseas; zero is a value, as before the first forts.

Colonial rule in the Americas (americas): part.
- What it covers: People living in the Americas (M49 019) under rule from overseas.
- Necessity pass: The conquest of Mexico and Peru, the colonial Americas and the independences of 1776 to 1826 and 1962 to 1983 have no other home.
- Independence pass: It fell by half from 1550 to 1600 as the colonized died while no other part moved, and fell to almost nothing in 1810 to 1826 while India's part rose.
- Universality pass: Every date has people living in the Americas, or none before the peopling; zero is a value.

Colonial rule in Asia (asia): part.
- What it covers: People living in Asia (M49 142) under rule from overseas.
- Necessity pass: Company and Crown rule in India, the Dutch Indies, French Indochina, Japan's Korea and Taiwan and their independences of 1945 to 1957 carry most of colonial rule's history.
- Independence pass: It jumped with Bengal (1757 to 1765) and fell by six sevenths in 1945 to 1949 while Africa's part rose.
- Universality pass: Every date has people living in Asia who are or are not ruled from overseas.

Colonial rule in Europe (europe): part.
- What it covers: People living in Europe (M49 150, by 2026 borders) under rule from overseas: the Atlantic islands of 1415 to 1500 (by today's borders part of Spain and Portugal), Malta, the Ionian Islands, Cyprus and Gibraltar.
- Necessity pass: The first colonies, Ceuta, Madeira, the Azores and the Canaries, lie in today's Europe, and without a home for them the parent's first century has none.
- Independence pass: It holds all of the parent before 1492 and a few hundredths of a percent after, moving with Malta's and Cyprus's rule and independence, apart from the other parts.
- Universality pass: Every date has people living in Europe; zero is a value.

Colonial rule in Oceania (oceania): part.
- What it covers: People living in Oceania (M49 009) under rule from overseas: the Australian colonies before self-government, New Zealand, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, the Pacific island colonies and today's American and other territories.
- Necessity pass: The Pacific's partition and its independences of 1962 to 1980 have no other home.
- Independence pass: It moves with the Pacific's partition and independence, apart from the others.
- Universality pass: Every date has people living in Oceania, or none before Sahul's peopling; zero is a value.

By the ruling state (metropole): dropped.
- What it covers: Colonial rule divided by metropole: Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Britain, France, Japan, the United States, Belgium, Germany, Italy.
- Necessity pass: Who ruled matters to every colonial history.
- Independence pass: Empires rose and fell apart.
- Universality fail: Each empire exists only in some centuries: a partition by kinds whose members come and go; kept as an alternative reading for a later pass, not a carve.

By form of rule (form): frontier.
- What it covers: Settler colonies, colonies of exploitation, protectorates, company rule, mandates.
- Necessity uncertain: The forms overlap and change one into another (Bengal from company to Crown).
- Independence uncertain: Categories competing for one pool, better a Cut than parts.
- Universality fail: Each form exists only in some empires and times.

Completeness pass: Every person under colonial rule lives in exactly one M49 area by 2026 borders; Antarctica has no permanent people. Parts by area are exclusive and exhaustive along one criterion (MECE#ae19), the same partition the account uses for humanity and output. Checked against The UN M49 standard's areas, the partition the account already uses for where humanity lives and where output is made..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.politics.scale.empire.colonial","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.politics.scale.empire.colonial","candidates":[{"key":"africa","label":"Colonial rule in Africa","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"americas","label":"Colonial rule in the Americas","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"asia","label":"Colonial rule in Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"europe","label":"Colonial rule in Europe","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"oceania","label":"Colonial rule in Oceania","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"metropole","label":"By the ruling state","outcome":"dropped","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail"},{"key":"form","label":"By form of rule","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"uncertain","universality":"fail"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"The UN M49 standard's areas, the partition the account already uses for where humanity lives and where output is made."}}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Colonial rule (h.colonial) is now the declared sum of five parts by the M49 area where the colonized live (revisions 314 to 318), each set from which colonies held how many people and summing to the parent at every date. What the parts show:

1. Three regimes, one after another. Before 1760 colonial rule is American: Spanish and Portuguese America are nine tenths of it, and its 1550 to 1600 fall is the conquered dying of epidemics, war and forced labour, with no colony lost (VirginSoilEpidemic#d1fd). From Plassey (1757) to 1947 it is Asian: British India alone is most of it, so the parent's long climb to a third of humanity in 1940 is mostly India's population growth under one ruler. From 1948 to the 1970s it is African, and its end is two falls, 1960 to 1962 and 1974 to 1976. After 1997 what remains is Caribbean and Pacific, most of it Puerto Rico.
2. The largest fall of rule from overseas ever (1946.5 to 1948, Asia from 20.7% to 3.1% of humanity) is one decision about one colony, not decolonization as a wave. The wave (ev.decolonization) is real in the count of states (h.polities.states) and in Africa; in people it is India.
3. Definitions move the parts as much as events do. The Atlantic islands leave Europe's part in 1822 because they send deputies to the Cortes, Australia and New Zealand leave Oceania's in 1855 to 1857 by responsible government, and the French Caribbean leaves the Americas' in 1946 as départements. Each is the parent's own rule (no part in the government that rules them) applied, and each is debated: Aboriginal Australians and most Māori had no vote after self-government either. The bands carry some of this, not all.

Where the parts strain against the whole (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b):
- At 1800 the Asian part is the parent's remainder and implies about 70 million colonized in Asia, against a count of about 55 million: the parent's sketch at 1800 may be a point or two high.
- From 1954 to 1957 the Asian remainder (about 1.2%) is double a count of Asia's remaining colonies (about 0.6%): either the parent or Africa's part is about half a point high there. A recount of Africa's colonies in the 1950s (about 160 million people, 5.7%) suggests it is Africa's part, set at 6.9% in 1956, and so the parent with it.
- Asia's part reads 0.08% in 1970 against a count of about 0.14% (Hong Kong, Macau, Timor and the Gulf protectorates); within its band.
These are left as they are rather than adjusted to fit, so the next pass can test them against counts by territory.

Europe's part has no Event of its own and stays unobserved; it is small (at most 0.08% of humanity) and its turns are explained in its notes."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Fighting between polities (concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.between):
- What it is: Fighting between polities: soldiers and civilians killed in fighting between two or more polities, from raids between bands and villages to wars between states, as deaths per 100,000 people a year.
- What the carve is for: To follow how deadly war between polities has been for humanity across its whole span, and to say which kinds of it carry its peaks and its long fall, if any division of it pays for its cost.
- The range it claims: Every human society from 300,000 years ago to 2025, wherever polities fight one another.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Fighting between polities is a kind of War and massacre: Fighting between polities sets polity against polity; fighting within a polity is over who rules it or whether it holds together; one-sided killing has an organized killer and victims who do not fight back. Other kinds within it: Fighting within a polity, One-sided killing.
2. War and massacre is a kind of Violence: War and massacre is organized and collective; homicide is killing between persons outside it. Other kinds within it: Homicide.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Fighting between polities is kept whole, as a kind of War and massacre: Every candidate failed universality, stayed uncertain on independence, or passed at a cost the evidence does not repay: the regional division is complete but would be five sketched series drawn from the same few numbers that set the whole. Reopen it when a regional series of battle deaths over centuries is checked, when the seam between civilians killed in fighting and one-sided killing is redrawn, or when the Events that move fighting between polities grow by half (from 53).

How the parts make the whole work: No division of fighting between polities pays for itself now. The kinds of polity that fight and the scale of wars are kinds of particular eras, not parts of every case; combatants and civilians is the most telling division, but it needs the seam with one-sided killing and the war carve's exclusion of famine deaths redrawn first; and the regional division, though complete, would multiply sketched series without new evidence (MarginalValueRule#6611). The whole is kept, its 53 Events placed by region already, so a later pass can open the regional parts from those Events when a regional count of battle deaths over the long run (such as Brecke's Conflict Catalog) is checked.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): By the kind of polity that fights, Great-power wars and lesser wars.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Combatants and civilians killed (independence, universality), By the M49 area where the deaths happen (declared).

Routed elsewhere: By weapon to h.means.force.arms, the means of force.
