upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

By the kind of polity that fights (polity-type): kind.
- What it covers: Wars between states, between states and non-state polities (bands, tribes, chiefdoms), and between non-state polities.
- Necessity pass: Each pairing carries a share of the deaths, and raids between non-state polities are most of them before 3000 BCE.
- Independence pass: Wars between states can rise while raiding between villages falls; the two are set by different things.
- Universality fail: States exist only from about 3500 BCE; before that every war is between non-state polities, so the state pairings are kinds of a historical period, not parts of every case.

Combatants and civilians killed (combatant-status): frontier.
- What it covers: Soldiers and warriors killed in fighting, and non-combatants killed in it.
- Necessity pass: Both carry deaths in every era, and the civilian share is what separates the world wars from earlier great-power wars.
- Independence uncertain: Civilians killed in fighting shade into one-sided killing (sieges, reprisals, bombing of cities) and into deaths from war's famine and disease, which the war carve's frame leaves out; the seam with h.war.one-sided would have to be redrawn first.
- Universality uncertain: In raids between bands the line between warrior and non-combatant is often absent: every adult man may be both.

By the M49 area where the deaths happen (region): frontier.
- What it covers: Deaths in fighting between polities in Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania.
- Necessity pass: Each area has carried the world's worst wars at some time: Asia's Mongol and Qing conquests, Europe's world wars, the Americas' conquest.
- Independence pass: Each area's wars rise and fall on their own; a war across two areas splits by where its deaths fall.
- Universality pass: Every death happens somewhere, in every era.

Great-power wars and lesser wars (scale): kind.
- What it covers: Wars with a great power on each side, and the rest.
- Necessity pass: Great-power wars carry most deaths in the modern record (Levy's count).
- Independence pass: Lesser wars continue through great-power peace, as after 1945.
- Universality fail: A system of great powers is a feature of the state system of the last five centuries, perhaps of earlier multi-state systems; it is absent in most of the range.

By weapon (means): routed to h.means.force.arms, the means of force.
- What it covers: Deaths by edged weapons, firearms, artillery, bombing and so on.
- Necessity fail: The weapons are the means of war, followed already as h.means.force.arms; a division of deaths by weapon would duplicate them without telling more about how deadly war is.
- Independence uncertain: One battle kills by several weapons at once.
- Universality pass: Every war uses some weapon.

Completeness uncertain: Only the regional division would make a complete and exclusive set (MECE#ae19) over the whole range; the division by kind of polity and by scale are kinds of particular eras, and combatants and civilians needs the seam with one-sided killing redrawn first. The regional division passes the tests but would be five series of about 155 dates each, almost all sketched before 1500, from the same few recalled numbers that set the whole (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): it would add rows, not knowledge. Checked against The categories of the Correlates of War project (inter-state, extra-state, intra-state and non-state wars) and the UCDP's state-based conflicts, both made for counting wars rather than for this carve.. Still without a home: Deaths from war's famine and disease, outside the war carve's frame.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.between","conceptId":"concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.between","candidates":[{"key":"polity-type","label":"By the kind of polity that fights","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail"},{"key":"combatant-status","label":"Combatants and civilians killed","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"region","label":"By the M49 area where the deaths happen","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"scale","label":"Great-power wars and lesser wars","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail"},{"key":"means","label":"By weapon","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass","routedTo":"h.means.force.arms, the means of force"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The categories of the Correlates of War project (inter-state, extra-state, intra-state and non-state wars) and the UCDP's state-based conflicts, both made for counting wars rather than for this carve.","missing":["Deaths from war's famine and disease, outside the war carve's frame"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"This pass filled the world with values, widened it where Events showed change no process followed, deepened it where a carve paid, and checked parts against wholes, through the Meaning Model's tools.

WHAT IT DID
- Linked Events to the processes they move: 49 Events of the world as a whole, 50 of Europe, 25 of politics, 11 of security, 14 of internal war, and 7 colonial Events to the regional parts of colonial rule. Every gap these links opened was filled with values, so by the coverage report no process passes over its Events; processes no Event observes went from 61 to 34.
- Opened 13 processes with measures and values across the whole span: the number of autonomous polities (h.polities) and of independent states (h.polities.states), from the politics carve re-recorded at revision 291; the destructive power of the strongest weapon (h.means.force.arms), the share of world output spent on armed force (h.means.force.spending) and nuclear warheads (h.means.force.arms.nuclear), from the force carve (300); fighting within a polity over who rules, over territory and between non-state groups (h.war.within.government, .territory, .nonstate), from its carve (306); and colonial rule in Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania (h.colonial.africa and the rest), from the colonial carve (313), opened at revisions 314 and 315.
- Declared two sums that add up at every date: fighting within a polity (h.war.within, 312) and colonial rule (h.colonial, 317). Both changed the process scale, so a world on an earlier revision cannot adopt them in place.
- Answered the breadth check three times: politics' Events modeled by h.polities (299), security's by h.means.force.arms (304), Europe's not modeled (305), since its Events change measures the model already follows by area.
- Answered the deepen check for fighting between polities by keeping it whole (319): every division failed universality, stayed uncertain on independence, or would multiply sketched series without new evidence (MarginalValueRule#6611); a regional division is complete and is the one to open when a regional series of battle deaths over centuries is checked.
- Weighed the causes of eight outcomes with stated contrasts (ContrastClass#7398): the Roman Empire, the Antarctic Treaty, the rise of Christianity, the French Revolution, Cook's voyages, the First Fleet, the Pacific islands' independence and the scientific revolution (320, 321).
- Corrected the Christian share from 1 to 1300 (322, 323): it was about a fifth of humanity by 500, not 6%, and near 0.1% at 200, not 1.5%; the difference came out of local and folk traditions, and a value at 350 shows the rise after Constantine. Explained the herders' dip at 2200 BCE and Oceania's colonial turns.
- Findings are in claude.finding.fill-widen-2 (the earlier part of the pass) and claude.finding.colonial-parts (colonial rule as three regimes, American, Asian and African, and where the parts strain against the whole).

SLIPS AND REPAIRS
- Twice (revisions 285 and 308) an Event was upserted with a placeholder description and only part of a batch was linked; both were restored word for word from the model at the next revision (286, 309), with notes claude.revision.r285-placeholder and claude.revision.r308-placeholder. An Event upsert replaces the whole record: read every field back from the current model first.
- The graph was not rebound after revisions 315 and 316 one by one; it was rebound at 317, which carries both.
- The keep-whole record for fighting between polities misstates the war carve's frame on famine deaths; corrected in claude.revision.r319-famine-frame.

WHAT IT LEAVES OPEN
- Politics: the residual of h.politics (people outside any state: 2% in 1920, 0.05% in 2025) and h.polities' direct modern values pull against each other; the regime-type Cut and the law frontier of the politics carve are unopened.
- Colonial rule: the parent's sketch at 1800 and its values from 1954 to 1957 look high against counts by territory (see claude.finding.colonial-parts); Europe's part has no Event; the seam between wars of independence (fighting within a polity) and colonial wars (between polities) is undrawn.
- War: the frame-versus-parts inconsistency on famine deaths; the deepen list now starts with one-sided killing, independent states, the people of Australia and New Zealand, fighting over who rules and work under compulsion.
- Breadth: groups of Events still naming no process, judged for population (45), beliefs and norms (32), knowledge (21), habitat (21) and the Earth (16), among 34 candidates; the knowledge and discovery frontier is unmodeled.
- 12 parts sit under carved processes without being tested in their carves: the internet under connection, food-getting and foraging under provisioning, the development index under what matters to people, and the eight religious shares under regular worship, which are shares of people rather than parts of worship and should move or be carved again.
- 34 processes no Event observes, among them the boreal and subtropical forests, Central, Southern and Western Asia's people and Oceania's output; belief (h.meaning.belief) is still one undivided number; the coarsest stretch left is 1820 to 1850 in survival and household measures; the causes queue goes on (women's suffrage, the Bantu expansion, the Scramble for Africa, the Aztec Triple Alliance first); the spatial-resolution question is unanswered.
- The repository's construction/history-numbers.construction.json, construction/MANIFEST.json and README.md still describe the head before this pass: export the construction and update them when the work is to be published."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Connection (concept.humanity.means.connection):
- What it is: Connection as a means: moving people, goods and words between places. The parent's own measure is the fastest regular passenger speed; moving goods (freight per person) and moving words (message speed) are its parts, and being online is a kind of moving words.
- What the carve is for: To follow the things connection carries, which change apart and which passenger speed alone hides: how fast people travel (the parent), how much freight moves (goods), how fast words travel (news), and, re-recorded now, how many people have moved home to live away from where they were born (migration), the frontier part the first record of this carve left without a measure. - The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, from foragers carrying their goods and news on foot to container ships, fibre networks and today's 300 million migrants; measured for the world.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Connection is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Connection is the means of moving people, goods and words between places; the other means are getting and making things, place, trading, ruling and fighting. Other kinds within it: Provisioning, Habitat, Exchange, Politics, Force.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Connection is carved into 3 parts: Moving goods, Moving words, Moving home: people living outside the country of their birth.

How the parts make the whole work: Connection as this account follows it is moving people (the parent's own measure, passenger speed), moving goods (freight per person), moving words (message speed) and, now opened, moving home (the share of people living outside the country of their birth). They change apart and on different clocks. For millennia all moved at the pace of feet, animals and sails; the telegraph freed words from travel between 1794 and 1866; railways and steamships multiplied freight from the 1830s. Migration follows its own clock: among foragers about one person in fifty lived across one of today's lines from their birthplace; farming's sedentism lowered that to under one in a hundred for five thousand years; the slave trade and then the mass migrations of 1846 to 1914 raised it to about 2.5%; quotas, war and depression held it there; expulsions, Partition and the postwar displaced lifted it near 3% by 1950; and the Gulf's workers, the end of the Soviet Union's internal borders and the global labour market carry it to 3.7% now. A steamship voyage is both a passenger's speed and an emigrant's move: the indentured workers' case has two homes, the means and the moving, which is why the carve keeps speed at the parent and volume as a part (RoutingSanityCheck#71bd records it as a warning, not a defect). Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Being online (a kind of concept.humanity.means.connection.news).

Routed elsewhere: Moving people to h.connection's own measure, the fastest regular passenger speed, which reads it already, Mass media to Beauty and play (h.media), where the first pass filed the share reached by print, radio, television or internet.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Moving people (people): routed to h.connection's own measure, the fastest regular passenger speed, which reads it already.
- What it covers: How fast and far people travel: the parent's own measure, the fastest regular passenger speed.
- Necessity pass: Horses, sailing ships, railways and airliners have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Passenger speed barely moved from the horse to 1830, while news speed jumped with the semaphore and telegraph.
- Universality pass: Every population travels.

Moving goods (goods): part.
- What it covers: How much freight a population moves and how far: by porters, pack animals, carts, boats, ships, railways, trucks and pipelines.
- Necessity pass: Bulk shipping made distant grain, coal and ore cheap; the steamship, the railway and the container ship have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Freight per person doubled between 1970 and 2025 while the fastest passenger speed fell back from Concorde's to a jet's; it grew a hundredfold from 1820 to 1970 while news speed had already reached its limit.
- Universality pass: Every population carries goods, foragers on their backs.

Moving words (news): part.
- What it covers: How fast messages travel between distant places: runners, mounted relays, signal fires and semaphores, telegraph, radio, cable and fibre.
- Necessity pass: The telegraph decoupled news from travel in the 1840s; the Persian and Mongol relay posts have no other home.
- Independence pass: Message speed rose a thousandfold with the semaphore and telegraph (1794 to 1866) while passenger speed rose fivefold.
- Universality pass: Every population passes news.

Moving home: people living outside the country of their birth (migration): part.
- What it covers: People who have moved to live away from where they were born, read as the share of all living people who live outside the country of their birth, with countries taken by their 2026 borders as a fixed grid of places (as the account takes the M49 areas), whatever the borders were when they moved: the international migrant stock of the UN's statistics, read back over the whole range. Forced and free, settlers, the enslaved, refugees, workers and their families all count; moves within a country of 2026 do not.
- Necessity pass: The Atlantic slave trade, the European and Asian mass migrations of 1846 to 1940, the population exchanges and expulsions of 1919 to 1950, Partition, the Gulf's migrant workers and today's 300 million migrants have no home without it; the breadth check names some forty Events of the account that move no process because this part was missing.
- Independence pass: Migration follows wages, land, wars and laws, not speed: the share living abroad fell from about 1914 to 1945 while passenger speed rose from 95 to 420 km/h, and it rose from about 2.8% to 3.7% between 2000 and 2025 while the fastest regular speed fell back with Concorde's end; it moves apart from freight, which grew through the interwar years when migration was cut by quotas.
- Universality pass: Revised from uncertain in the first record of this carve: with countries taken by their 2026 borders as a fixed grid, the measure has a meaning at every date, as the M49 areas have; before states it counts moves across lines that were not borders then, which the band and the notes carry. Every population has people living away from where they were born.

Being online (online): a kind of news.
- What it covers: Using the internet.
- Necessity pass: Two thirds of humanity now.
- Independence pass: Spread after 1995 apart from freight and travel.
- Universality fail: Exists only since the 1970s and for the public since 1991: a kind of moving words, which reads who can send and receive rather than how fast.

Mass media (broadcast): routed to Beauty and play (h.media), where the first pass filed the share reached by print, radio, television or internet.
- What it covers: Words sent to many at once.
- Necessity pass: Print and broadcasting.
- Independence uncertain: Reach, not speed.
- Universality fail: Only since print.

Completeness pass: Passengers are the parent's measure, freight is goods, messages are news, and people who moved home are migration: travel and transportation, communication and migration all have homes. The Outline of Cultural Materials files migration under demography (sections 166 and 167, internal migration and immigration and emigration); this account's tree has no separate population node beside humanity's own count and its places, and the frame of connection names moving people, so migration is followed here as the volume of people moved, beside their speed. Moves within a country of 2026 (the Great Migration in the United States, China's internal migrants) are not counted by this measure; the share living in towns (h.habitat) carries most of their effect. Checked against The three things transport and communication histories follow (passengers, freight and messages); the Outline of Cultural Materials sections 48 (travel and transportation), 20 (communication) and 16 (demography: 166 internal migration, 167 immigration and emigration); the UN's international migrant stock.. Still without a home: Internal migration within today's countries (no world series before about 1990); Forced displacement as its own stock (refugees and the internally displaced, about 120 million in 2024 by UNHCR's count).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.connection","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.connection","candidates":[{"key":"people","label":"Moving people","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"h.connection's own measure, the fastest regular passenger speed, which reads it already"},{"key":"goods","label":"Moving goods","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"news","label":"Moving words","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"migration","label":"Moving home: people living outside the country of their birth","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"online","label":"Being online","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"news"},{"key":"broadcast","label":"Mass media","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"fail","routedTo":"Beauty and play (h.media), where the first pass filed the share reached by print, radio, television or internet"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"The three things transport and communication histories follow (passengers, freight and messages); the Outline of Cultural Materials sections 48 (travel and transportation), 20 (communication) and 16 (demography: 166 internal migration, 167 immigration and emigration); the UN's international migrant stock.","missing":["Internal migration within today's countries (no world series before about 1990)","Forced displacement as its own stock (refugees and the internally displaced, about 120 million in 2024 by UNHCR's count)"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Habitat (concept.humanity.means.habitat):
- What it is: Habitat as a means: the places a population makes to live in and the land it turns to its use, from camps to megacities and from hunting grounds to fields and pastures. The parent's own measure is the share living in towns and cities; settling down, the greatest settlement and farmland are its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of how people occupy the Earth that change apart, which the urban share hides: how much of the Earth people live on at all (range, opened now), whether they have fixed homes (settling down), whether they live in towns, how large the greatest cities grow, and how much land they turn into fields and pasture. Re-recorded because the breadth check names some twenty-five Events of first peopling and abandonment (Sahul, Europe, the Americas, Tasmania, the Greater Antilles, the Arctic, Madagascar, Remote Oceania, the glacial maximum's refuges) that move no process: where on Earth people live had no measure of its extent.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, mobile foragers and herders as much as villagers and city dwellers; measured for all living people or all of today's ice-free land.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Habitat is a kind of A means of living: a way a population gets what it wants: Habitat is the means made of place: the land people live on, the settlements they build and the land they turn to their use. The other means are getting and making things, moving people, goods and words, trading, ruling, and fighting. Other kinds within it: Provisioning, Connection, Exchange, Politics, Force.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Habitat is carved into 4 parts: Range: the land people live on and use, Settling down, The greatest settlement, Farmland.

How the parts make the whole work: Habitat as this account follows it is how a population occupies the Earth: how much of the land it lives on (range), whether it has fixed homes (settling down), whether those homes are in towns (the parent's own measure), how large its greatest settlement grows, and how much land it turns into fields and pasture. The five change apart and in order. Range came first and did most of its growing before any of the others existed: Homo sapiens held perhaps a tenth of today's ice-free land in Africa 300,000 years ago, a fifth when the Last Interglacial greened the Sahara and opened the Levant, about two fifths by 37,000 years ago after the dispersal into Asia, Sahul and Europe, a third again at the glacial maximum as the north and the Australian interior were abandoned, and four fifths by 10,000 years ago once the Americas were peopled (WaveOfAdvance#4cec across the continents, with sea crossings as long-distance jumps the card leaves out). After that range barely moved, a point or two with the drying Sahara and the Arctic peoples, and fractions with the islands from Madagascar to Aotearoa, while people settled (from 12,500 BCE), built towns (from about 4000 BCE), grew cities and cleared farmland. Farmland lies inside range, so range bounds it from above. Sema: ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, MandatoryAbstraction#ac44, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f, MECE#ae19, WaveOfAdvance#4cec.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Built land and works (necessity, universality).

Routed elsewhere: Living in towns to h.habitat's own measure, the share living in towns and cities, which reads it already, Roads, canals and ports to Connection (h.connection), which follows how fast and far people and goods move, Housing to Shelter under Sustenance and comfort (h.sustenance.shelter), the room each person has.

Routing sample: 11 case(s); 3 with no home among the parts (China's urban share rising from under a fifth in 1978 to about two thirds by 2023; Haussmann's rebuilding of Paris with boulevards, sewers and water mains, 1853 to 1870; The Roman road network and the Grand Canal of China); 0 with two or more parts as homes.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.habitat","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat","form":"processes","cutRecorded":true,"parts":[{"key":"range","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.range","processId":"h.habitat.range"},{"key":"mobile","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.mobile","processId":"h.habitat.mobile"},{"key":"largest-city","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.largest-city","processId":"h.largest-city"},{"key":"farmland","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.farmland","processId":"h.farmland"}],"process":"h.habitat","routingCases":11}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Range: the land people live on and use (range): part.
- What it covers: How much of the Earth lies within humanity's range: the share of today's ice-free land that resident Homo sapiens live on or use at least seasonally.
- Necessity pass: The first peopling of Asia, Sahul, Europe and the Americas, the retreat to refuges at the glacial maximum, the green and the empty Sahara, the Arctic peoples' crossing to Greenland, Madagascar, Iceland and the islands of Remote Oceania to Aotearoa in about 1280 have no home without it; the regional shares say where the people were, not how much of the Earth they held.
- Independence pass: Range grew from about a tenth to four fifths of the land between 130,000 and 10,000 years ago while there were no towns, no fixed homes and no fields; it has hardly moved since farming while the urban share went from zero to 58% and farmland from nothing to over a third of the land. It shrinks and grows with the ice and the Sahara, which the other parts do not follow.
- Universality pass: Every population has a range, however small; the measure is defined at every date of the range.

Settling down (mobile): part.
- What it covers: Whether people have a fixed home: mobile foragers and pastoral nomads move with the seasons; farmers, townspeople and sedentary foragers stay.
- Necessity pass: Settling down is the first and largest change in how people live on the land, beginning with the Natufians about 12,500 BCE, five thousand years before towns; the mounted nomads of the steppe, Arabia and the Sahara have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It changes apart from the urban share (sedentism without towns for five millennia), from farmland (pastoral nomads use vast pastures while staying mobile) and from range (mobile foragers filled the continents; sedentism added no land).
- Universality pass: Every population either moves its homes or does not; the measure is 100% for the deep past and under 1% now.

Living in towns (towns): routed to h.habitat's own measure, the share living in towns and cities, which reads it already.
- What it covers: Whether people live in towns and cities or in the countryside.
- Necessity pass: Urbanization is habitat's main modern change.
- Independence pass: The urban share rose from 7% to 58% after 1800 while the largest city, farmland and range changed by other amounts.
- Universality pass: Every population lives somewhere on the scale from camp to city; zero for foragers.

The greatest settlement (largest-city): part.
- What it covers: How large the greatest settlement on Earth grows: the reach of what a place can gather and feed.
- Necessity pass: The scale of the greatest city is the classic reading of organization, from Uruk to Rome, Chang'an, Baghdad, Hangzhou, London and Tokyo.
- Independence pass: Rome reached a million when the urban share was about 5%; the largest city fell by more than half after 200 while the urban share barely moved; it flattened after 1990 while the urban share kept rising.
- Universality pass: Every population has a largest settlement, if only a camp of a few dozen.

Farmland (farmland): part.
- What it covers: The land a population turns into fields and pasture.
- Necessity pass: Clearing land for fields and pasture is the largest human transformation of the Earth's surface, from nothing to over a third of ice-free land.
- Independence pass: Farmland stopped growing after about 2000 while the urban share and the largest city kept rising; it grew fastest 1850 to 1950 on frontiers with few towns, and always inside a range that barely moved. Farmland lies within range; range can be wide with no farmland at all.
- Universality pass: Every population uses land; the measure is zero for foragers.

Built land and works (built): frontier.
- What it covers: Land covered by buildings, streets and works: built-up area, and the water, sewer and power networks of settlements.
- Necessity uncertain: Sprawl and infrastructure are a large modern change, but before satellite mapping (from 1975) the world's built-up area is reconstructed from urban population times assumed densities, so a series would only restate the urban share; open it when an independent reading exists.
- Independence pass: Urban densities have fallen for two centuries (Angel's Planet of Cities), so built land grows apart from the urban share.
- Universality uncertain: Mobile foragers build almost nothing that lasts.

Roads, canals and ports (roads): routed to Connection (h.connection), which follows how fast and far people and goods move.
- What it covers: The networks that tie settlements together.
- Necessity pass: They tie the habitat together.
- Independence fail: Their history is the history of moving people and goods.
- Universality uncertain: Foragers' paths are networks too.

Housing (housing): routed to Shelter under Sustenance and comfort (h.sustenance.shelter), the room each person has.
- What it covers: The dwellings in settlements.
- Necessity pass: Settlements are made of dwellings.
- Independence uncertain: Read as comfort, not as a means.
- Universality pass: Every population shelters.

Completeness uncertain: Where people live is now read by its extent (range) beside its pattern (settling down and the urban share), its peak (the greatest settlement) and the land turned to use (farmland); housing is routed to shelter, streets and traffic to connection. Built-up area and utilities still have no independent world reading before 1975, so completeness stays uncertain. Range also answers the HABITAT node of the structure construction's tree (range: where on Earth people live), whose regional shares give the distribution but not the extent. Checked against The Outline of Cultural Materials, sections 31 (land use) and 36 (settlements: settlement patterns, housing, streets and traffic, sanitation, public utilities, commercial and public facilities, urban and rural life); the land-use classes of the HYDE reconstructions (cropland, pasture, built-up area); the structure construction's habitat node (range, settlement, land and environment) in structure/history-tree.mjs.. Still without a home: Built-up land and public works (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.habitat","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat","candidates":[{"key":"range","label":"Range: the land people live on and use","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"mobile","label":"Settling down","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"towns","label":"Living in towns","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"h.habitat's own measure, the share living in towns and cities, which reads it already"},{"key":"largest-city","label":"The greatest settlement","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"farmland","label":"Farmland","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"built","label":"Built land and works","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"roads","label":"Roads, canals and ports","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"uncertain","routedTo":"Connection (h.connection), which follows how fast and far people and goods move"},{"key":"housing","label":"Housing","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Shelter under Sustenance and comfort (h.sustenance.shelter), the room each person has"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The Outline of Cultural Materials, sections 31 (land use) and 36 (settlements: settlement patterns, housing, streets and traffic, sanitation, public utilities, commercial and public facilities, urban and rural life); the land-use classes of the HYDE reconstructions (cropland, pasture, built-up area); the structure construction's habitat node (range, settlement, land and environment) in structure/history-tree.mjs.","missing":["Built-up land and public works (frontier)"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Understanding (concept.humanity.wants.understanding):
- What it is: Understanding: what people know of the world and how they come to know it, followed as the share of adults who can read and write (h.understanding), with schooling and the command of number as its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of understanding that move apart: the time spent being taught (schooling), the command of number (numeracy) and, re-recorded now, the making of new knowledge (discovery), which the first record of this carve kept as a frontier part for want of a world measure. The breadth check names the knowledge group's Events (the Museum of Alexandria, the House of Wisdom, the universities, the scientific revolution, the Enlightenment, the Geophysical Year, Apollo, microelectronics) that move no process because discovery had none.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, followed as world measures of adults or of all living people.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Understanding is a kind of A condition of a life that people seek: Understanding: knowing about the world and being able to learn more. Other kinds within it: Belonging, Standing among others, Meaning.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Understanding is carved into 3 parts: Schooling, Command of number, Discovery: the people who make new knowledge.

How the parts make the whole work: Understanding, as this account follows it, is reading and writing (the parent's measure), the years spent being taught (schooling), the command of number (numeracy) and the making of new knowledge (discovery); they can all rise together and are followed as separate processes. Numeracy rose first and furthest before modern schooling, literacy spread later and unevenly, schooling carried the twentieth century's rise; discovery stays near zero for most of the range and then grows fastest of all. No forager or early farmer made inquiry their main work; from Babylon's and Egypt's temple astronomers to Alexandria's Museum and the House of Wisdom, people kept for inquiry were about one or two in a million for four thousand years, rising and falling with patrons, not with literacy; from the scientific revolution the number roughly doubled every generation or so (Price's growth of science), to about 30 per million in 1900, 220 in 1950 and some 1,300 now, as states and firms came to pay for research. Sema: ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, MandatoryAbstraction#ac44, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f, CumulativeCulture#4f93 (knowledge accumulates when enough people learn from one another, and discovery is where it is added).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Knowledge held in store (universality).

Routed elsewhere: Reading and writing to The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding).

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Reading and writing (literacy): routed to The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding).
- What it covers: The share of adults who can read and write.
- Necessity pass: Writing holds knowledge outside heads; its spread is the first fact of understanding's history.
- Independence pass: Literacy rose in Protestant Europe before mass schooling, and apart from numeracy.
- Universality pass: An axis: zero before writing.

Schooling (schooling): part.
- What it covers: The years adults spent being formally taught.
- Necessity pass: Mass schooling, compulsory from the nineteenth century and universal in the twentieth, and the secondary and university expansion since 1950 have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Years of school went on rising after literacy neared its ceiling in the rich world; literacy rose before schooling in early modern Europe through church and home teaching.
- Universality pass: An axis: every population teaches its young, and formal schooling is zero where it is absent.

Command of number (numeracy): part.
- What it covers: The share of adults who can count, reckon and know their age in years, read from age heaping (the ABCC index).
- Necessity pass: Reckoning is the skill of trade, taxes and calendars; East Asia's high numeracy before mass literacy has no home without it.
- Independence pass: Numeracy ran ahead of literacy in Qing China and Japan, and literacy ahead of numeracy in parts of Protestant Europe.
- Universality pass: An axis: every population counts something; knowing one's age in years needs a calendar, which foragers lack, so their value is near zero.

Knowledge held in store (stored): frontier.
- What it covers: Books, archives and libraries: knowledge kept outside heads.
- Necessity pass: Printing's flood of books (Buringh and van Zanden) and the libraries of Alexandria, Baghdad and Song China.
- Independence pass: Book production rose apart from literacy rates.
- Universality uncertain: An axis from zero before writing; but no world series of books or titles per person can be read before about 1500 outside Europe and China, and after 2000 books are a falling share of what is stored, so it stays a frontier part.

Discovery: the people who make new knowledge (discovery): part.
- What it covers: New knowledge made: inquiry in the sciences, scholarship and invention, read by the people whose main work it is.
- Necessity pass: The scientific revolution, the research university and the industrial laboratory, the twentieth century's research workforce and the knowledge group's Events (the Museum, the House of Wisdom, the Enlightenment, the Geophysical Year, Apollo) have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It concentrates in a few places apart from mass literacy: Alexandria and Baghdad held their scholars when literacy was a few per cent; the number of researchers grew about fourfold from 1950 to 1970 while literacy rose by a third; it rose again after 2000 with China's research, when schooling's growth had slowed.
- Universality pass: Revised from uncertain in the first record of this carve: the measure is defined at every date, zero where no one makes new knowledge their main work (all foragers and early farmers, so all of humanity before about 3000 BCE), and its deep values are guesses with wide bands, as other measures here are; every population discovers, but only some keep people for it.

Completeness uncertain: Learning's duration (schooling), storage's capacity (literacy, the parent's measure), reckoning (numeracy) and now the generation of new knowledge (discovery) have homes; storage's durability and access (knowledge held in store) remains a frontier part without a world series, and language is outside understanding as this account follows it. Checked against The structure construction's carve of knowledge (learning: transmitters and duration; storage: capacity, durability and access; discovery: generation and selection; language) in structure/history-tree.mjs; UNESCO's science and education statistics; Derek de Solla Price's Little Science, Big Science (1963) on the growth of the scientific workforce.. Still without a home: Knowledge held in store (frontier); Language.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.understanding","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding","candidates":[{"key":"literacy","label":"Reading and writing","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding)"},{"key":"schooling","label":"Schooling","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"numeracy","label":"Command of number","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"stored","label":"Knowledge held in store","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"discovery","label":"Discovery: the people who make new knowledge","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The structure construction's carve of knowledge (learning: transmitters and duration; storage: capacity, durability and access; discovery: generation and selection; language) in structure/history-tree.mjs; UNESCO's science and education statistics; Derek de Solla Price's Little Science, Big Science (1963) on the growth of the scientific workforce.","missing":["Knowledge held in store (frontier)","Language"]}}}

revision.reason: Carve of The wild animals: The breadth check's population group holds the Events of the other kinds of human (the Denisovans, the Neanderthals' disappearance, Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis, the last Homo erectus at Ngandong) that move no process. In this account humanity is Homo sapiens, and the wild animals carve sets the living world's unkept animal populations apart from it, so the other lineages are a kind of the wild animals: they fail universality because none lives after about 30,000 years ago. This re-records the carve under the same cut with that kind added, every other candidate kept with its earlier verdicts, and states the alternative (archaic humans as subspecies of Homo sapiens, in humanity).

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The wild animals (concept.dim.earth.wild-animals):
- What it is: The wild animals: the living world's animal populations that people neither breed nor keep, on land, in the sea and in the air; followed at the parent by the biomass of wild land mammals, with sea mammals and fish of fishable size as parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow where and when people took the wild animals down (the large land mammals at the end of the Pleistocene and with farming, the whales and seals from the seventeenth century, the fish of the open sea from the industrial fisheries on), and, re-recorded now, to give a home to the other kinds of human who shared the Earth with Homo sapiens until about 40,000 years ago: the breadth check names Events of the Neanderthals, the Denisovans, Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis and the last Homo erectus that move no process.
- The range it claims: The Earth's wild animals from 300,000 years ago to 2025, as world biomass in carbon and, for the kinds whose number matters more than their mass, as counts.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The wild animals is a kind of A population of living things: The wild animals are the animal populations that live and breed without people's keeping, set apart from livestock and pets, from people themselves (Homo sapiens, humanity in this account), and from the plants and microbes of the living world. Other kinds within it: Humanity, Livestock, The plant cover, Microbes.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The wild animals is carved into 2 parts: Wild sea mammals, Wild fish of fishable size.

How the parts make the whole work: The wild animals are followed in three vertebrate groups by their biomass in carbon (land mammals at the parent, sea mammals and fishable fish as parts), not summed, and in one kind by count: the other kinds of human. Their losses are four episodes, not one. The other humans went first: Homo erectus in Java before Homo sapiens came, then within about twenty thousand years of the dispersal every other lineage, so that from roughly 40,000 to 30,000 years ago Homo sapiens is the only human on Earth, carrying a few per cent of Neanderthal and Denisovan ancestry. Whether competition, climate, small numbers or absorption by interbreeding ended them is debated, and the evidence in hand fits more than one (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b); WaveOfAdvance#4cec's own failure mode, land taken as empty, is the warning: the fronts of the dispersal met people already there. Then the land's large mammals fell at the end of the Pleistocene and again with farming and the nineteenth century; the sea mammals fell from the 1600s to the 1980s and have begun to recover; fish of fishable size fell mostly after 1880. Birds and invertebrates stay frontier parts. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Wild land mammals (land): routed to The parent's own measure (h.earth.wild-animals, the biomass of wild land mammals)..
- What it covers: Wild mammals on land, from mammoths and ground sloths to deer, wild boar, elephants and rodents: the parent's own measure.
- Necessity pass: The end-Pleistocene extinctions and the loss of wild herds to fields and pasture have their home here.
- Independence pass: It fell most at the end of the Pleistocene and again since 1850, on land, by hunting and the taking of habitat.
- Universality pass: In every era.

Wild sea mammals (sea-mammals): part.
- What it covers: Whales, dolphins and porpoises, seals, sea lions and walruses, and sea cows.
- Necessity pass: Without it whaling and sealing, among the largest takings of wild animal mass in history, have no home.
- Independence pass: It fell from the 1600s to the 1980s by commercial whaling and sealing, at sea, while land mammals fell by other causes and at other times; since the 1986 moratorium it has recovered while land mammals kept falling.
- Universality pass: Sea mammals live in every era of the range.

Wild fish of fishable size (fish): part.
- What it covers: Wild fish of 10 grams to 100 kilograms in the seas and fresh waters, the sizes fisheries take.
- Necessity pass: Fishing takes more wild animal mass each year than any other human taking; without this part the industrial fisheries' effect on the living world has no home.
- Independence pass: It fell mostly after 1880 and fastest from 1950 to 1990, by steam trawlers, then sonar, synthetic nets and factory freezers, on its own course.
- Universality pass: Fish in every era.

Other kinds of human (hominins): a kind of concept.dim.earth.wild-animals.
- What it covers: The hominin lineages other than Homo sapiens alive at the date: Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo erectus in Java, Homo floresiensis, Homo luzonensis, Homo naledi and the archaic Africans of Kabwe, wild in the sense of this carve (not Homo sapiens, not kept), whatever their minds, which the account's Events record (the signs of Neanderthal minds, ev.eu.neanderthal-minds). Counted as lineages because their numbers are unknown within a factor of ten.
- Necessity pass: Without it the disappearance of every other kind of human, which leaves Homo sapiens alone on the Earth from about 40,000 to 30,000 years ago, and the interbreeding that left about 2% Neanderthal ancestry in every population outside Africa and Denisovan ancestry in Melanesia and Asia, have no home.
- Independence pass: The lineages end at their own dates, with Homo sapiens' arrival and the climate: Homo erectus in Java about 108,000 years ago, before sapiens came; floresiensis and luzonensis about 50,000, the Neanderthals about 40,000; the mass of wild land mammals fell later, with the megafauna.
- Universality fail: There are none after about 30,000 years ago, so it is a kind of the wild animals for the range's first nine tenths, not a part of every case.

Wild birds (birds): frontier.
- What it covers: Wild birds on land and at sea.
- Necessity pass: Extinctions on islands after human arrival (the moa, the dodo) and the recent fall of farmland birds belong here.
- Independence pass: They fall by island colonization and farmland change, apart from mammals and fish.
- Universality uncertain: Present in every era, but no world series of their mass exists before about 1970, so the number test is not met yet.

Wild insects and other arthropods (arthropods): frontier.
- What it covers: Insects, spiders, crustaceans such as krill: the largest wild animal mass.
- Necessity uncertain: Their mass dwarfs all the vertebrates, but how people changed it before the 1980s is unknown.
- Independence pass: Their declines (or not) follow pesticides, land use and climate.
- Universality uncertain: Present always; the insect decline debate (Hallmann and colleagues against van Klink and colleagues) shows the data are local and recent.

Large and small land mammals (by-size): frontier.
- What it covers: The parent's land mammals divided by body size: megafauna over about 44 kg against smaller mammals.
- Necessity pass: The end-Pleistocene extinctions took mostly the large.
- Independence fail: Another cut of the parent's own measure, not a part beside the sea and its fish; kept as the alternative carve of land mammals.
- Universality pass: Every era has large and small mammals.

Livestock (livestock): routed to Not wild: followed through farmland (h.farmland.pasture) and food (h.food.animal)..
- What it covers: Cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and other kept animals.
- Necessity fail: Not part of the wild animals.
- Independence pass: It grows as wild mass falls.
- Universality fail: Only after domestication.

Completeness uncertain: The three vertebrate groups people have taken down most, by mass, have homes (land mammals at the parent, sea mammals and fish as parts), and the other kinds of human now have one as a kind; birds, arthropods and the other invertebrates have none yet because no honest world series of them exists before recent decades. Checked against Bar-On, Phillips and Milo's census of the biomass distribution on Earth (2018): wild land mammals, wild marine mammals, wild birds, fish, arthropods, annelids, molluscs and cnidarians; the hominin record as the palaeoanthropological literature reports it (Homo neanderthalensis, the Denisovans, H. erectus at Ngandong, H. floresiensis, H. luzonensis, H. naledi, Kabwe).. Still without a home: Wild birds; Arthropods, molluscs and other invertebrates; Fish under 10 g of the ocean's twilight zone.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.dim.earth.wild-animals","conceptId":"concept.dim.earth.wild-animals","candidates":[{"key":"land","label":"Wild land mammals","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The parent's own measure (h.earth.wild-animals, the biomass of wild land mammals)."},{"key":"sea-mammals","label":"Wild sea mammals","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"fish","label":"Wild fish of fishable size","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"hominins","label":"Other kinds of human","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"concept.dim.earth.wild-animals"},{"key":"birds","label":"Wild birds","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"arthropods","label":"Wild insects and other arthropods","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"by-size","label":"Large and small land mammals","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"livestock","label":"Livestock","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","routedTo":"Not wild: followed through farmland (h.farmland.pasture) and food (h.food.animal)."}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"Bar-On, Phillips and Milo's census of the biomass distribution on Earth (2018): wild land mammals, wild marine mammals, wild birds, fish, arthropods, annelids, molluscs and cnidarians; {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Range: the land people live on and use (concept.humanity.means.habitat.range):
- What it is: Range: how much of today's ice-free land (about 134 million km2) lies within the regular reach of a resident Homo sapiens population at the date, lived on or used at least seasonally, measured for the world in % of that land.
- What the carve is for: To say where on Earth range was gained and lost, so that each first peopling, each abandonment and each return has a home in the part of the land it changed, and so that the parts, bounded by how much land each area holds, test the world's sketched curve.
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all resident Homo sapiens, over the land of today's six areas (Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania by the UN M49 standard and 2026 borders, and Antarctica).

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Range: the land people live on and use is a kind of The range of a living population: the area its members live on or use: Range in this account is Homo sapiens' range alone, measured as a share of today's ice-free land; the other kinds of human, the wild animals, crops and livestock have ranges of their own. Other kinds within it: The ranges of the other kinds of human, The range of a wild animal, such as the mammoth's, The range of a crop or of livestock.
2. The range of a living population: the area its members live on or use is a kind of A spatial extent: how much of the Earth's surface something occupies: An extent held by a population that moves and spreads, rather than by a cover that grows in place. Other kinds within it: Forest cover, Ice cover, Farmland: the land turned to fields and pasture.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Range: the land people live on and use is carved into 6 parts: Range in Africa, Range in the Americas, Range in Asia, Range in Europe, Range in Oceania, Range in Antarctica.

How the parts make the whole work: Range is the sum of six parts, the land within reach in each area, and each part is capped by how much land its area holds (Africa about 22.7, the Americas 29.0, Asia 23.6, Europe 17.5 with all of Russia, Oceania 6.4, Antarctica 0.04 points of the world's ice-free land). Read by area, range is a sequence of areas entered, not one curve. For about 250,000 years it is Africa's alone, swinging with the Sahara's rains, with brief excursions into the Levant (Misliya, Skhul and Qafzeh) and perhaps Greece. Between about 60,000 and 40,000 years ago Asia, Oceania and Europe are entered within twenty thousand years of one another, by fronts on land (WaveOfAdvance#4cec) and sea crossings the card leaves out; the fronts met Neanderthals and Denisovans, so the land was not empty (the card's own failure mode). The glacial maximum takes back about a quarter of what was held, mostly in Europe and Siberia, Australia's interior and the Sahara. The Americas carry the whole rise from about 13,000 to 10,000 BCE. After that only the drylands (the Sahara and Arabia, green and then empty), the Arctic (the Paleo-Inuit) and the islands (Lapita, Madagascar, Iceland, Remote Polynesia to Aotearoa) move it, by fractions. The caps showed one error in the whole: its values from 14,600 to 11,000 BCE had the Americas filled about two thousand years before the account's own Events date their peopling (Monte Verde about 12,500 BCE), and are corrected with the parts. Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Range by kind of land: forest, grassland, desert, tundra, mountain (independence), Land lived on all year, and land used only in some seasons (necessity, independence).

Routed elsewhere: How densely the land in range is peopled to Humanity (h.humanity) over range, and the people living in each M49 area (h.region-*).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Range in Africa (africa): part.
- What it covers: The share of the world's ice-free land that lies in Africa (M49 002, about 22.7% of it) and within Homo sapiens' range at the date.
- Necessity pass: The first 250,000 years of range are almost all Africa's; the green and the empty Sahara (the Last Interglacial, the African Humid Period and its end) and Madagascar's settlement have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Africa's range swings with the Sahara's rains, which follow the orbit's insolation, while Asia's grew with the dispersal and Europe's fell at the glacial maximum: at the African Humid Period's end (4000 to 3000 BCE) Africa loses about 1.6 points while the Americas, Europe and Oceania hold.
- Universality pass: Africa's land exists at every date of the range; its part is never zero.

Range in the Americas (americas): part.
- What it covers: The share of the world's ice-free land that lies in the Americas (M49 019, with Greenland's ice-free coast and Hawai'i, about 29.0%) and within range.
- Necessity pass: The peopling of the Americas is the largest single gain in range after the dispersal, nearly a third of all land; White Sands, Monte Verde, Clovis, the Paleo-Inuit's Arctic and the empty floodplains after 1492 have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It rises from near zero to about 24 points between 16,000 and 10,000 BCE while Africa's and Asia's parts barely move, and it dips after 1492 by epidemic while every other part holds.
- Universality pass: The land of the Americas exists at every date; its part is zero before people arrive, as other measures here are zero before what they count exists.

Range in Asia (asia): part.
- What it covers: The share of the world's ice-free land that lies in Asia as M49 draws it (142: without Russia, which M49 places in Eastern Europe; about 23.6%) and within range.
- Necessity pass: Skhul and Qafzeh, Arabia's green phases, the coastal dispersal to Sunda, Tibet's high pastures and the Rub' al Khali's emptiness have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Asia's part grows in the dispersal (60,000 to 40,000 years ago) while Africa's holds, and dries with Arabia in the mid-Holocene apart from the Americas' and Oceania's.
- Universality pass: Asia's land exists at every date; its part is zero or near it only before the first excursions into the Levant.

Range in Europe (europe): part.
- What it covers: The share of the world's ice-free land that lies in Europe as M49 draws it (150: with all of Russia, so Siberia counts here; about 17.5%) and within range.
- Necessity pass: Homo sapiens' arrival in Europe and Siberia, the Yana River camp in the Arctic, the retreat to refuges at the glacial maximum, the resettlement of the north in the Bølling warmth and Iceland's settlement have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Europe's part falls by about half at the glacial maximum, by ice and polar desert, while Oceania's falls by a third and the Americas' begins; it alone carries the far north's swings.
- Universality pass: Europe's land exists at every date; its part is zero before about 45,000 years ago, apart from brief excursions (Apidima in Greece, about 210,000 years ago, is debated).

Range in Oceania (oceania): part.
- What it covers: The share of the world's ice-free land that lies in Oceania (M49 009: Australia, New Zealand, New Guinea and the Pacific islands except Hawai'i, about 6.4%) and within range.
- Necessity pass: Sahul's peopling, the withdrawal from Australia's interior at the glacial maximum, Lapita's voyages and the settlement of Aotearoa have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Oceania's part is set by sea crossings and Australia's aridity, apart from the land bridges and ice that set the others; it grows last of all, about 1280, when nothing else moves.
- Universality pass: Oceania's land exists at every date; its part is zero before Sahul is reached.

Range in Antarctica (antarctica): part.
- What it covers: The share of the world's ice-free land that lies in Antarctica (its ice-free coasts, nunataks and dry valleys, about 0.04%) and within range: sealers' camps from the 1820s, stations from 1904 and the treaty's science.
- Necessity pass: Without it the six areas would not cover the land the measure counts, and the sealers, the stations and the treaty's science would have no home in range; small as it is, the account's Antarctic Events need it.
- Independence pass: Antarctica's part moves with sealing, exploration and science, apart from every other area.
- Universality pass: Its ice-free land exists at every date; the part is zero for all but the last two centuries.

Range by kind of land: forest, grassland, desert, tundra, mountain (biome): frontier.
- What it covers: The same range divided by the land's cover rather than by where it lies.
- Necessity pass: After the Holocene began, range moves almost only in deserts and the Arctic: a division by kind of land would show that directly.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Moving home: people living outside the country of their birth (concept.humanity.means.connection.migration):
- What it is: Moving home: the share of all living people who live outside the country of their birth, with countries taken by their 2026 borders as a fixed grid, forced and free movers alike.
- What the carve is for: To say where the people living away from their birthplace live, so that each migration the account records (the slave trade, Rome's captives, the mass migrations, the wars' forced labour and expulsions, Partition, the Gulf's workers, today's refugees) has a home in the area that received it, and so that regional counts (censuses from about 1850, the UN's series from 1960) test the world curve.
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living Homo sapiens, over the five inhabited areas of the UN M49 standard by 2026 borders (Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe with all of Russia, Oceania).

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Moving home: people living outside the country of their birth is a kind of The people of a population who live away from where they were born: Counted by country of birth on the 2026 grid, so a move inside one of today's countries is not counted; settlers, the enslaved, refugees, workers and their families all count. Other kinds within it: Internal migrants within today's countries, The displaced: refugees and the internally displaced, Seasonal and circular movers.
2. The people of a population who live away from where they were born is a kind of A distribution of people over places: It divides people by whether their place of living differs from their place of birth, not by where they live alone. Other kinds within it: The share of people living in each M49 area, The share living in towns and cities.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Moving home: people living outside the country of their birth is carved into 5 parts: Migrants living in Africa, Migrants living in the Americas, Migrants living in Asia, Migrants living in Europe, Migrants living in Oceania.

How the parts make the whole work: The share of humanity living outside the country of its birth is the sum of the migrants living in each of five areas, and read by area it is a sequence of receiving regions rather than one curve. Among foragers it sits where people are, mostly Africa's many small cells of today's map; in the agrarian millennia Asia holds most of it (deportations, nomads, captives), with Europe's part swelling when Rome brings in its captives (about 40% of the world's migrants at the Republic's end). From about 1600 to 1920 the Americas take the lead, first with enslaved Africans and settlers, then with the mass migration of 1846 to 1914, when they hold about half. The wars move it to Europe (forced labour in 1944, the expulsions of 1944 to 1950) and Partition to Asia (1947 to 1948). Since 1990 Europe and Asia each hold nearly a third, Asia through the Gulf's workers and its refugees, and the Americas about a quarter. The UN's series by region of destination from 1990 sets the recent parts; before 1960 they are reasoned from censuses as recalled and from the flows the account's Events record (EvidenceDependence#23ca). {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Migrants living in Africa (africa): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Africa (M49 002, by 2026 borders) and were born in another country.
- Necessity pass: The forager era's movers, Arab and Berber settlement in North Africa, the colonial settlers of Algeria and South Africa, the labour migrations to the mines and cocoa farms and today's refugees in Uganda and Sudan's neighbours have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Africa's migrants leave with the pieds-noirs in 1962 while Europe's rise, and grow after 2010 with the Sahel's and Sudan's refugees while the Americas' share flattens.
- Universality pass: Africa holds people at every date, and some of them always live away from their country of birth by today's lines.

Migrants living in the Americas (americas): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in the Americas (M49 019, by 2026 borders) and were born in another country.
- Necessity pass: The Atlantic slave trade's survivors, the European settlers, the mass migration of 1846 to 1914, the indentured Asians and today's Venezuelans and Central Americans have no home without it; for 1850 to 1920 it is about half of the world's migrants.
- Independence pass: It falls from 1920 to 1970 with the quota acts and the Depression while Europe's and Asia's rise with war and Partition; it rises again after 1965 with new laws.
- Universality pass: Zero before the Americas were peopled, as the part is zero before what it counts exists; every later date has some.

Migrants living in Asia (asia): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Asia as M49 draws it (142: without Russia) and were born in another country.
- Necessity pass: Assyria's deportations, the Mongols' captives, the Nanyang Chinese and Indians of South-east Asia, Koreans in Japan, Partition's refugees, Afghanistan's refugees and the Gulf's workers have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It jumps with Partition (1947 to 1948) while every other area's share holds, and rises with the Gulf after 1973 while Africa's falls.
- Universality pass: Asia holds people from the first excursions into the Levant on, and some always live away from their birthplace by today's lines.

Migrants living in Europe (europe): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Europe as M49 draws it (150: with all of Russia, so Siberia's and the Soviet republics' movers are here when they live in Russia) and were born in another country.
- Necessity pass: Rome's foreign-born slaves, the migration period, the moves across today's lines inside the Habsburg and Russian empires, the wars' forced labourers, the expellees of 1944 to 1950, the Windrush generation and the guest workers have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It peaks in 1944 with forced labour and in 1946 to 1950 with the expulsions, apart from the Americas' fall; it rises after 1990 with the European Union's open borders and Ukraine's refugees apart from Asia's Gulf.
- Universality pass: Zero before Homo sapiens reaches Europe, about 45,000 years ago; every later date has some.

Migrants living in Oceania (oceania): part.
- What it covers: The share of all living people who live in Oceania (M49 009, by 2026 borders) and were born in another country.
- Necessity pass: The First Fleet's convicts, the gold rushes, the indentured Indians of Fiji, the labour trade to Queensland and the postwar migration that remakes Australia and New Zealand have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It rises with the Australian gold rush of the 1850s and the postwar schemes of 1947 to 1970 on its own clock.
- Universality pass: Zero before Sahul is reached; every later date has some.

By the area where the migrants were born (origin): frontier.
- What it covers: The same share divided by area of birth instead of area of living.
- Necessity pass: Africa's enslaved and Europe's emigrants of 1846 to 1914 are the two great sources; a division by origin would show them.
- Independence fail: Another cut of the same measure along another criterion, not a part beside the areas of living: mixing the two would count each migrant twice (MECE#ae19). Kept as the alternative carve.
- Universality pass: Every migrant was born somewhere.

Moved by force, and moved free (forced): frontier.
- What it covers: The same share divided by how the move was made: the enslaved, deported, expelled and those who fled war, against settlers, workers and families who chose to go.
- Necessity pass: Before 1820 most people living across today's lines from their birthplace in the Americas were enslaved Africans, and the twentieth century's peaks are expulsions and flight; the distinction is the first one migration histories draw.
- Independence fail: Another criterion for the same measure, so not a part beside the areas; and the seam is debated (indentured labour, famine emigrants, workers recruited under compulsion), so it would need its own rule before it could be read.
- Universality pass: Every era has both forced and free movers.

Station residents in Antarctica (antarctica): dropped.
- What it covers: The one to four thousand people who live in Antarctica's stations, all born elsewhere.
- Necessity fail: At most about 0.00005% of humanity: no value it takes changes the whole, and the stations' history already has a home in Antarctica's range (h.habitat.range.antarctica).
- Independence pass: It moves with the stations, apart from every other area.
- Universality fail: Zero before 1898, when the Belgica first wintered.

Completeness pass: Every person living outside the country of their birth lives in one of the five inhabited areas (or in Antarctica's stations, a few thousand people, left out as below any value the whole can show), so the five parts sum to the whole at every date. The grid's choices are kept in the meanings: M49 places all of Russia in Europe, so Soviet and Russian movers living in Russia are Europe's, and those living in Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan are Asia's. Checked against The UN DESA International Migrant Stock, which divides the world's migrants by region of destination (Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, Northern America, Oceania), as recalled, to be checked.. Still without a home: Station residents in Antarctica (dropped as negligible).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.connection.migration","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.connection.migration","candidates":[{"key":"africa","label":"Migrants living in Africa","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"americas","label":"Migrants living in the Americas","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"asia","label":"Migrants living in Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"europe","label":"Migrants living in Europe","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"oceania","label":"Migrants living in Oceania","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"origin","label":"By the area where the migrants were born","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"forced","label":"Moved by force, and moved free","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"antarctica","label":"Station residents in Antarctica","outcome":"dropped","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"The UN DESA International Migrant Stock, which divides the world's migrants by region of destination (Africa, Asia, Europe, Latin America and the Caribbean, Northern America, Oceania), as recalled, to be checked.","missing":["Station residents in Antarctica (dropped as negligible)"]}}}
