{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Done at model r331 to r345. Every value is recalled or reasoned, tagged sketch or inferred, and shares one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. Range by area (carve.concept.humanity.means.habitat.range, r334; parts opened r335 to r337, declared the sum at r338). The six parts, each capped by its area's share of today's ice-free land (Africa 22.7, the Americas 29.0, Asia 23.6, Europe 17.5 with all of Russia, Oceania 6.4, Antarctica 0.04 points), turn one sketched curve into a sequence of areas entered: Africa alone for about 250,000 years, swinging with the Sahara; Asia, Oceania and Europe within twenty thousand years of the dispersal; the Americas carrying the whole rise of 13,000 to 10,000 BCE; then only drylands, the Arctic and islands. WaveOfAdvance#4cec holds for the land fronts; its own failure mode (empty land assumed) is the reminder that Europe's and Asia's fronts met Neanderthals and Denisovans.
- A correction the caps forced. Range from 14,600 to 10,000 BCE had the Americas filled about two thousand years before the account's own Events date their peopling (ev.am.peopling from 14,000 BCE, Monte Verde about 12,500 BCE): a note at -14600 read '14,500 years ago' as 14,500 BCE. Seven values were lowered (50 to 38 at -14600, 82 to 78 at -10000), each with its reason. Where else the account mixes 'years ago' with BCE in its notes is worth a scan: the -10000 note also called the Holocene's start, which is 9700 BCE.
- A choice of the grid, kept in the parts' meanings: M49 puts all of Russia in Europe, so Siberia's peopling (the Yana River, 32,000 years ago) is Europe's, and Hawai'i belongs to the United States by 2026 borders, so its Polynesian settlement is the Americas'.
- The rise of range after 1760 (87.6 to 90.5) is the least supported stretch of the whole: by area it has to come from the Sahara's and Arabia's cores entering regular use by motor, the Russian and Canadian Arctic islands and Antarctica's stations. Whether desert crossing by roads and oil camps counts as 'regular reach' is a definitional choice the measure does not settle (MetricReading#56a9); a stricter reading would hold range near 88 since 1800.

2. Migration by the area where migrants live (carve.concept.humanity.means.connection.migration, r341; parts opened r342 and r343, declared the sum). From 1990 the parts follow the UN's counts by region as recalled; before, they are reasoned. Read by area, the share living abroad is a sequence of receiving regions: Africa's many small cells among foragers; Asia in the agrarian millennia; Europe at about two fifths under Rome; the Americas from about 1600 to 1920 (about half of all migrants in 1910); Europe again in the wars (forced labour in 1944, the expulsions of 1946); Asia with Partition (its part rises by two fifths in 1947 and 1948); since 1990 Europe and Asia about a third each and the Americas a quarter.
- What the 2026 grid does to the past: about half of Europe's migrants in 1910 are moves inside empires that today's borders divide (Czechs in Vienna, Poles of Posen in the Ruhr, Ukrainians and Balts in Russia's cities); the account counts them as migrants because it counts by today's countries, which no census of the time did. A count by contemporary borders would put Europe's 1910 part at perhaps a third of this.
- Two frontier carves are kept: by area of birth and by whether the move was forced. The second is the more telling for the era before 1850, when most of the Americas' foreign-born were enslaved Africans, but its seam (indenture, famine flight, recruited labour) needs a rule first.
- The routing sample's case with no home, researchers wintering at McMurdo, is deliberate: Antarctica's station residents were dropped as negligible.

3. Links. 22 peopling Events name the range part of their area; 30 migration Events the part of the receiving area; 9 of Antarctica's 14 Events name Antarctica's range, its ice (h.sea.antarctic) or the sea mammals (breadth answer note.breadth.events.importance.region.antarctica.r340). Every Event was upserted whole after its fields were read back from the model in pieces.

4. A pitfall for the next pass. The four processes opened at r328 do carry their parents' subject, but parts opened without process.subject (the first record of range in Africa at r335) are held by the coverage report to every Event in the model; give every new part its parent's subject when it is opened."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Discovery: the people who make new knowledge (concept.humanity.wants.understanding.discovery):
- What it is: Discovery: the people whose main work is making new knowledge (inquiry in the sciences, scholarship and invention), counted per million of all living people.
- What the carve is for: To say where the people kept for inquiry work, so that the moves of its centre (Babylon and Egypt's temples, Alexandria's Museum, India's and China's astronomers, Baghdad's House of Wisdom, Cairo and Córdoba, Europe's universities and academies, the American laboratories, China's research) have a home, and so that regional counts (UNESCO's from the 1990s) test the world curve.
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, over the five inhabited areas of the UN M49 standard by 2026 borders (Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe with all of Russia, Oceania); zero everywhere before anyone made inquiry their main work.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Discovery: the people who make new knowledge is a kind of A population's specialists: people kept for one kind of work: Kept for making new knowledge, rather than for fighting, worship, rule or keeping records; their number depends on who pays for them. Other kinds within it: People under arms, Priests and religious specialists, Scribes and officials.
2. A population's specialists: people kept for one kind of work is a kind of The division of a population's labour: Counts the people a society can spare from getting food and goods for a given work, not the work's output. Other kinds within it: Work under compulsion, Food-getting work.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Discovery in Africa (africa): part.
- What it covers: People whose main work is making new knowledge and who work in Africa (M49 002, by 2026 borders), per million of all living people.
- Necessity pass: Egypt's temple astronomers and physicians, the Museum of Alexandria (Euclid, Eratosthenes, Ptolemy), Fatimid Cairo (Ibn al-Haytham) and Fez and Timbuktu's scholars have no home without it: from about 280 BCE to 200 CE Alexandria holds a quarter or more of the world's inquiry.
- Independence pass: Africa's part falls after 400 with Alexandria's decline while Asia's holds, and rises about 1000 with Cairo apart from Europe's.
- Universality pass: Africa's people exist at every date; its part is zero where the world's is, before temple inquiry begins.

Discovery in the Americas (americas): part.
- What it covers: People whose main work is making new knowledge and who work in the Americas (M49 019, by 2026 borders), per million of all living people.
- Necessity pass: The Maya astronomers and calendar priests, then the American Philosophical Society, the land-grant universities, Edison's and Bell's laboratories and the twentieth century's American science have no home without it: from about 1945 to 1990 it holds a third to two fifths of the world's researchers.
- Independence pass: It rises fastest from 1918 to 1950 while Europe's share falls in the wars, and falls as a share after 1990 while Asia's rises.
- Universality pass: Zero before the Americas' first calendar specialists, as the whole is zero before inquiry; every later date has some.

Discovery in Asia (asia): part.
- What it covers: People whose main work is making new knowledge and who work in Asia as M49 draws it (142, by 2026 borders: without Russia, and with all of Türkiye, so Constantinople's scholars are here), per million of all living people.
- Necessity pass: Babylon's astronomers, the Hundred Schools, Indian mathematics, Han and Song China's bureaus, the House of Wisdom, Maragha and Samarkand's observatories, Meiji Japan and today's Chinese and Korean research have no home without it; it holds most of the world's inquiry from about 500 to 1500 and again after 2010.
- Independence pass: Its share falls from about 1450 to 1900 while Europe's rises, and rises from 1970 on while Europe's falls.
- Universality pass: Zero where the world's is; every later date has some.

Discovery in Europe (europe): part.
- What it covers: People whose main work is making new knowledge and who work in Europe as M49 draws it (150, by 2026 borders: with all of Russia), per million of all living people.
- Necessity pass: Athens's schools, Rome's scholars, Córdoba and Toledo, the universities, the scientific revolution, the academies, the research university and the Soviet science system have no home without it; it holds most of the world's inquiry from about 1550 to 1940.
- Independence pass: It rises while Asia's falls (1450 to 1900), falls in the world wars while the Americas' rises, and drops with the Soviet collapse after 1990 while Asia's grows.
- Universality pass: Zero before Greece's first natural philosophers; every later date has some.

Discovery in Oceania (oceania): part.
- What it covers: People whose main work is making new knowledge and who work in Oceania (M49 009, by 2026 borders), per million of all living people.
- Necessity pass: Australia's and New Zealand's observatories, universities and CSIRO have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It grows on its own clock from the colonial observatories of the 1820s.
- Universality pass: Zero before 1820; every later date has some.

Who keeps them: rulers and states, religious houses and schools, firms and private means (patron): frontier.
- What it covers: The same count divided by who pays for inquiry.
- Necessity pass: Inquiry rises and falls with its patrons: courts and temples for four thousand years, then churches and endowed colleges, then states and, from the 1870s, firms; this is the account's main explanation of the curve.
- Independence fail: Another criterion for the same count, not a part beside the areas; and its seams are debated (a medieval university is church and town at once, a Soviet institute state and party), so it needs its own rule first.
- Universality pass: Every researcher has some patron or private means.

By field: natural sciences and engineering, medicine, social sciences and humanities (field): a kind of concept.humanity.wants.understanding.discovery.
- What it covers: The same count divided by subject.
- Necessity uncertain: Fields matter for what is discovered, less for how many make it their work.
- Independence fail: Another criterion for the same count.
- Universality fail: The fields are distinct only from the nineteenth century; Aristotle, Ibn Sina and Shen Kuo worked across all of them.

Researchers in Antarctica (antarctica): dropped.
- What it covers: The scientists of Antarctica's stations, about a thousand to four thousand people.
- Necessity fail: About 0.1 to 0.5 per million of humanity, a hundredth of a percent of the whole; their science already has a home in Antarctica's range (h.habitat.range.antarctica).
- Independence pass: It moves with the stations.
- Universality fail: Zero before 1898.

Completeness pass: Every researcher works in one of the five inhabited areas (or in Antarctica's stations, dropped as negligible), so the five parts sum to the whole at every date. The grid's choices are kept in the meanings: Constantinople is in Türkiye and so Asia's, Córdoba in Spain and so Europe's, Alexandria and Cairo in Egypt and so Africa's, and Soviet science in Russia Europe's. Checked against UNESCO's Science Report regional tables of researchers (Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania), as recalled, to be checked; Derek de Solla Price's Little Science, Big Science (1963) for the growth since 1650.. Still without a home: Researchers in Antarctica (dropped as negligible).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.understanding.discovery","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding.discovery","candidates":[{"key":"africa","label":"Discovery in Africa","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"americas","label":"Discovery in the Americas","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"asia","label":"Discovery in Asia","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"europe","label":"Discovery in Europe","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"oceania","label":"Discovery in Oceania","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"patron","label":"Who keeps them: rulers and states, religious houses and schools, firms and private means","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass"},{"key":"field","label":"By field: natural sciences and engineering, medicine, social sciences and humanities","outcome":"kind","necessity":"uncertain","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","kindOf":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding.discovery"},{"key":"antarctica","label":"Researchers in Antarctica","outcome":"dropped","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"fail"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"UNESCO's Science Report regional tables of researchers (Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe, Oceania), as recalled, to be checked; Derek de Solla Price's Little Science, Big Science (1963) for the growth since 1650.","missing":["Researchers in Antarctica (dropped as negligible)"]}}}

Rebind to r351 (through r350): the Tepanec war added as an Event, and the causes of women's suffrage, the Bantu expansion, the Scramble for Africa and the Aztec Triple Alliance weighed against stated contrasts.

Breadth check answered: Partly linked, and the rest not followed now, with one candidate named for the next pass. Seven of the group's Events now name what they change (model r352). The conversions move the tradition shares: Aksum's turn to Christianity (h.religion-4 from h.religion-0), Indic kingship in South-east Asia (h.religion-1 and -2 from -0), Dvaravati and the Theravada mainland (h.religion-2, from Hindu courts), and the Jesuit missions among the Guaraní (h.religion-4 from -0). Two revivals that change worship within a tradition move regular worship (h.meaning): the Great Awakening and the Pentecostal rise in Latin America, which leaves the Christian share as it was. The other Events change things no measure here follows, and none of them forms a group a new world measure would carry well. Monuments and ritual centres (Göbekli Tepe, Sechin Alto, Lalibela) say that people built for the sacred, not how many worshipped or what they believed. Persecutions (the witch-hunts, about 40,000 to 60,000 executed over a century) are too few in deaths to move a world rate, and their judicial killing sits between homicide and one-sided killing as this account defines them. Movements inside one tradition (liberation theology, Melanesia's cargo cults and churches) change neither the shares nor worship measurably. Short-lived reforms (Akhenaten's Aten) left no lasting share. The candidate worth opening next is the people kept for worship: monks, nuns, priests and temple staff per thousand people, a sibling of discovery's people kept for inquiry, which would give desert monasticism, the sangha's monasteries, the Reformation's dissolutions and secularization a measure; it is left for the next pass because it belongs under regular worship (h.meaning), whose carve still holds the eight tradition shares as untested parts that the closing note of fill-widen-2 says should move or be carved again, and this pass keeps the existing measures where they hang.

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: Partly linked, and the rest not followed now. At model r339 and r354 seven of the group's Events came to name what they change: Antarctica's ice loss and glacial cycles (h.sea.antarctic), sealing and whaling (h.earth.wild-animals.sea-mammals), the Americas' megafauna extinction (h.earth.wild-animals), the ice-free corridor (range in the Americas), the Black Summer fires (h.forest.temperate) and Tōhoku (h.alive.injury). What is left are mostly single eruptions (the Campanian Ignimbrite, Thera, Hunga Tonga), whose effects on the world's measures are either brief and within the bands of global temperature as this account samples it, or argued (the Campanian eruption's effect on Europe's people); the spread of wild cereals before farming, which the plant cover's measures by climate zone do not separate; Aboriginal fire on the land, whose effect on Australia's vegetation is debated; and the ozone hole. The one candidate worth a process is stratospheric ozone over Antarctica in spring, in Dobson units: flat near 300 for all of human history, falling to about 100 in the 1990s and recovering slowly after the Montreal Protocol; it would be one curve with two Events on it and a long flat line, so it waits until the account follows the atmosphere's composition beyond carbon dioxide.

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: Partly linked, and the rest not followed now, with the candidate that would take them named. With discovery opened by area this pass (r347, r348), the group's Events of inquiry now name the part for their area: the Museum's Alexandria, the House of Wisdom, Greek philosophy, the universities, the scientific revolution, the Enlightenment, Apollo and American computing (r349), and Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah and Mesoamerica's first writing and calendars (r356). What remains is mostly about how knowledge is stored and copied: paper in Han China, woodblock printing, Hangul, the alphabet. Literacy (h.understanding) already takes the ones that changed who could read; the others change the cost and durability of keeping knowledge, which is the frontier part 'knowledge held in store' of the understanding carve (r326), kept frontier because no world series of books or texts per person can be read before about 1500 outside Europe and China. Tasmania's isolation, the loss of skills in a small cut-off population (CumulativeCulture#4f93), has no world measure: it is a regional case of the mechanism, best followed if a local history of Tasmania is opened. revision.reason: Breadth check answered: Mostly linked, and the rest not followed. The population group's migrations and peoplings were linked in the stopped pass and in this one (to migration and range and their area parts, r330, r339, r345). At r358 four more name what they change: the Ebola epidemic and Leclerc's yellow fever (deaths from infection), the opioid epidemic (deaths from injury, counted as poisonings) and de Soto's and Coronado's expeditions (the people of Northern America). What is left is about descent rather than number: the deep splits of human lineages that genomes record (the Khoe-San branching off about 300,000 to 200,000 years ago, and others like it). They change how humanity's ancestry is structured, which no measure here follows; a process for it (for example the share of living people's ancestry from each deep lineage) would need a genomic reconstruction this account cannot sketch honestly at world scale. Reopen if the account follows ancestry or admixture as its own measure.

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: Not followed now, with the candidate that would take most of them named. As the check's examples show (Çatalhöyük, Great Zimbabwe, Cahokia), the group's unlinked Events are single towns and their monuments, mostly of 5,000 to 30,000 people. Habitat as this account follows it is world measures: the share living in towns (h.habitat), the greatest settlement (h.largest-city), settling down (h.habitat.mobile), farmland and range with its area parts; a town of 15,000 moves none of them by a visible amount, and the first peoplings and abandonments that do move range were linked this pass (r339, r354). The process that would give such Events a home is the number of cities and towns above a threshold (for example cities of 100,000 or more, from Chandler's, Modelski's and Reba and colleagues' reconstructions), which follows urban networks that the urban share and the largest city hide; at 100,000 it would still miss these towns, and at 10,000 its early counts would be guesses of a few dozen. It is left for a pass that checks one of those reconstructions. Reopen when it is opened or when a regional history (Mesoamerica, the Mississippi, the Zimbabwe plateau) is opened by encapsulation.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"This pass went on from the stopped pass of r309 to r317 (which had re-recorded four carves and opened migration, range, discovery and the other kinds of human at model r328 to r330 without a plan or closing note), from model r330 to r362, through the Meaning Model's and Sema's tools. Plan: claude.plan.fill-widen-pass-3. By the coverage report the pass is done: every level of the time schedule filled, no process empty, none passing over its Events and no reading flat (r348, and again at r362 after this pass's own links).

WHAT IT DID
- Fill: the 16 level-4 values the four new processes lacked, and values at every stretch where a process passed over its Events, each guessed within its neighbours with a band and a reason where an Event moves it.
- Deepen, by area of the land (MECE#ae19), three carves with life_carve_record: range into six areas (r334; parts r335 to r337), migration into the five areas that receive the movers (r341; r342, r343), discovery into the five areas where researchers work (r346; r347, r348). Every part has a value at every date of its whole, is filed under humanity as its whole is, and each whole is declared the sum of its parts; the report finds no contradiction. Frontier carves kept: range by kind of land and by season of use; migration by area of birth and by forced or free movement; discovery by patron.
- A correction the parts forced: range from 14,600 to 10,000 BCE was lowered (50 to 38 at -14600, 82 to 78 at -10000), since it had the Americas peopled about two thousand years before the account's own Events date it.
- Widen: 22 peopling Events now name the range part of their area, 30 migration Events the receiving area's part, 10 Events of inquiry the discovery part of theirs; 9 of Antarctica's Events name Antarctica's range, its ice or the sea mammals; 7 Events of beliefs the tradition shares or worship; 4 of the Earth's Events the wild animals, range, forest or injury; 4 of population's infection, injury or Northern America's people. Breadth answers recorded with their reasons and the candidate process each group would need: Antarctica, beliefs (people kept for worship), the Earth (stratospheric ozone), knowledge (knowledge held in store), population (ancestry), habitat (cities above a threshold). Every Event was upserted whole after its fields were read back from the model in pieces.
- Causes weighed against stated contrasts (ContrastClass#7398) for women's suffrage, the Bantu expansion, the Scramble for Africa and the Aztec Triple Alliance, with the Tepanec war added as an Event (r350).
- Findings: claude.finding.range-migration-parts and claude.finding.discovery-causes. Sufficiency notes: claude.sufficient.spatial.r362, claude.sufficient.belief.r362.
- Sema used and resolved: ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, MandatoryAbstraction#ac44, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f, MECE#ae19, MarginalValueRule#6611, WaveOfAdvance#4cec, CumulativeCulture#4f93, ContrastClass#7398, EvidenceDependence#23ca, EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b, MetricReading#56a9.

SLIPS
- The graph was not rebound after r331 and r332 one by one; it was rebound at r333 and after every later revision (carve and breadth records rebind it themselves).
- Range in Africa was first opened without process.subject (r335), so the report held it to every Event in the model; it was filed under humanity at r336. Give every new part its parent's subject when opening it.
- The population breadth answer describes its remainder from the check's examples (genomic lineage splits); its 14 remaining Events were not all read, so the answer may be too narrow.

WHAT IT LEAVES OPEN, each able to wait because the coverage measure holds without it
- Breadth: arts and play (25 Events), exchange (28), provisioning (23), connection (11) and wealth (10) still name no process; the exchange and provisioning groups look the most linkable to measures the model has.
- Deepen: migrants living in the Americas leads the check, then one-sided killing, range in Antarctica and in Oceania, the people of Australia and New Zealand, independent states and fighting over who rules; the tradition shares lost their kept-whole status as their Events grew.
- The model's questions: unweighed causes of the Classic Maya, the Inca empire, the decimal zero and the Fertile Crescent's farming; 34 processes no Event observes, among them discovery in Oceania.
- Checks: the area parts rest on recalled land areas, censuses, the UN DESA migrant stock by region and UNESCO's researchers by region, all to be checked; range's rise after 1760 depends on whether motor roads and oil camps count as regular reach (MetricReading#56a9); migration by 2026 borders counts moves inside past empires, so Europe's 1910 part is several times what a contemporary census would show; some older notes may read 'years ago' as BCE, as the range note at -14600 did, and are worth a scan.
- Standing items from claude.closing.fill-widen-2: politics' residual against the count of polities, colonial rule's high values at 1800 and 1954 to 1957, the war frame on famine deaths, 12 parts filed under carved processes without being tested in their carves, and the re-hanging of measures, which this pass, by instruction, left alone.
- The repository's construction/history-numbers.construction.json, construction/MANIFEST.json and README.md still describe a head before the last three passes; export the construction and update them when the work is to be published."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Done at model r346 to r362. Values are recalled or reasoned and share one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. Discovery by area (carve.concept.humanity.wants.understanding.discovery, r346; parts r347 and r348, declared the sum). The people kept for inquiry follow patrons, and their centre moves: Asia holds about two thirds about 500 BCE (Babylon, Ionia, which lies in Türkiye, the Hundred Schools, India); Alexandria about a quarter at 200 BCE; Asia three quarters from about 500 to 1000 (India, China, Constantinople, Baghdad), with Cairo and Córdoba beside it; Europe passes Asia about 1550 and holds two thirds to three quarters from 1650 to 1900; the Americas rise from about 1890 and hold two fifths just after 1945; Europe, with Soviet science, stays near half until 1990, then its share falls by about a seventh in six years as Russia's and Ukraine's research staff halve; Asia passes Europe about 2006. CumulativeCulture#4f93 frames why the stock grows with connected, numerous learners; the moves themselves follow who pays, which is why the patron frontier of this carve is the next carve to try.
- Prediction to test against UNESCO's regional tables (to be checked, not yet looked at): Asia's researchers outnumber Europe's (with Russia) from the mid-2000s, and the Americas' share falls below a quarter by about 2015.
- Discovery in Oceania has no Event of its own; the account records no Oceanian institution of science.

2. Four cause readings (ContrastClass#7398), each sketched with wide bands. Women's suffrage, against most of the world's women still voteless in 1971: decolonization and mass schooling rank first (each 0.35), the two world wars next (0.15 each), the labour movement (0.10) and Seneca Falls last (0.05). The Bantu expansion, against farmers staying in the Nigeria and Cameroon borderlands: Africa's own crops first (0.80), the drying (0.25) and iron (0.20) after. The Scramble for Africa, against Europe staying at the coasts: industrialization far first (0.75), the German and Italian unifications next (0.20), the occupation of Egypt (0.10), and the Suez Canal, the Berlin conference, the mineral revolution and rinderpest small. The Aztec Triple Alliance, against the Basin staying under the Tepanecs: the Tepanec war (added as an Event at r350) first (0.65), Toltec legitimacy (0.10), Teotihuacan's precedent small. Differences do not sum.
- A gap in the Bantu reading: its 'drying' cause is linked to the end of the African Humid Period (4000 to 3000 BCE), while its reason also cites the rainforest's contraction about 2500 years ago, which has no Event."}

The live viewer opens on the model only: the graph's construction history is now larger than the viewer's portable limit (480 MiB).

What the report says at r362. Fill: every level of the time schedule is filled, no process is empty, none passes over its Events. Breadth: Events naming no process, judged for arts and play (25 of 27), exchange (28 of 64), provisioning (23 of 75), connection (11 of 37) and wealth (10 of 45). Deepen: migrants living in the Americas first, then one-sided killing and range in Antarctica. Questions: unweighed causes of the Classic Maya, the Inca empire, the decimal zero and the Fertile Crescent's farming; 34 processes no Event observes; belief stays whole by claude.sufficient.belief.r362.

Reading the groups' Events whole shows what they change.
- Arts and play: the first ornaments and images (Bizmoune, Blombos, the Aurignacian, Sulawesi, the rock art of Africa and Australia) and the arts made by specialists for courts and temples (Olmec, Nok, Igbo-Ukwu, Ife, Lalibela, Borobudur, the Gupta, Heian, the Renaissance). The carve of beauty and play (r215) kept the arts as a frontier part for want of a world measure; discovery has since been opened on the same kind of measure, people kept for one kind of work per million, so the arts can be too.
- Provisioning, wealth and exchange: metalworking and mines (Old Copper, the Andes, mainland bronze, West African iron, Panguna, Nauru's phosphate, guano and nitrates) change what is dug from the Earth, which h.earth.resources follows as one tonnage that hides its three classes; forager ways of life, pottery and early exchange networks change no world measure the model keeps; most of the rest move measures the model has.
- Connection: voyages and contacts; a few move populations or rule (Cook in Hawai'i, Spain in the Marianas, the New Guinea highland patrols).

The plan, in this order, the graph rebound after every model revision:
(1) Re-carve beauty and play with life_carve_record (ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, MandatoryAbstraction#ac44, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f); open the parts that pass with values at every date of the schedule; link the arts Events.
(2) Carve the Earth's stores into building and industrial minerals, metal ores and fossil fuels, each at every date of the whole, declared their sum (MECE#ae19); link the metal and mining Events.
(3) Link the exchange, provisioning, wealth and connection Events that move processes the model has, give values where the links open gaps, and answer each breadth group with life_breadth_record.
(4) Link Events to the unobserved processes they plainly move.
(5) Answer the deepen check for migrants in the Americas, one-sided killing and range in Antarctica.
(6) Weigh the four outcomes' causes against stated contrasts (ContrastClass#7398).
(7) Record one closing note.
Kept as they are: the six M49 areas, the existing measures and their parents; nothing is re-hung. Every value is recalled, sketched or inferred and shares one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca); debated points are stated with their alternatives (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b); silence in the record counts only as far as the search could have found it (AbsenceEvidence#10a3). An Event upsert replaces the whole record, so every field is read back from the current model first."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Beauty and play (concept.humanity.wants.play):
- What it is: Beauty and play: the arts, games, festivals and leisure people make and enjoy for their own sake, followed as hours of leisure a day (h.play), with the share reached by mass media (h.media) as its one tested part.
- What the carve is for: To give the arts themselves a home in the account, which the first record of this carve (r215) kept as a frontier for want of a world measure: the first ornaments and images (Bizmoune, Blombos, the Aurignacian, Sulawesi, the rock art of Africa and Australia) and the arts made by people kept for them by courts, temples and markets (the Olmec, Nok, Igbo-Ukwu, Ife, Lalibela, Borobudur, the Gupta, Heian, the Renaissance, the cinema), so that the Events of the arts move measures the model follows, beside leisure time and mass media.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, followed as world measures; a part may stand at zero before the practice it counts exists, as discovery and people under arms do.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Beauty and play is a kind of A condition of a life that people seek: Beauty and play: what people do and make for its own sake, rather than to stay alive, to be fed, to belong, to know or to rank. Other kinds within it: Understanding, Meaning, Belonging, Standing among others, Sustenance and comfort.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Beauty and play is carved into 3 parts: Mass media, The arts' makers: people kept for the arts, Image and ornament: populations that make lasting art.

How the parts make the whole work: Beauty and play as this account follows it is leisure time (the parent's hours of leisure a day), image and ornament (the share of people whose populations make lasting art, a lower bound on the arts' presence), the arts' makers (people kept to make the arts for others, per million) and mass media (the share reached by copies made for many). Leisure gives the time; image and ornament show that a population makes lasting art at all; makers say how much of its labour a society spends on art for patrons and markets, within what its surplus can keep (SurplusBound#7fe3); media say how many receive art made by others. They move on different clocks: image and ornament in deep prehistory, with population density and connection (CumulativeCulture#4f93); makers with chiefdoms, states, cities and their courts and temples; media with printing and broadcasting; leisure against toil. Together they say when people had time for the arts, whether they made lasting art, how many were kept to make it, and how far it reached. Forms that leave no trace before writing, spending on play, and games and sport stay frontier parts.

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: What people spend on play: feasts, festivals, entertainment (universality), Games and sport (universality).

Merged: Festival and rest days a year into leisure.
Routed elsewhere: Leisure time to The parent's own measure, hours of leisure a day (h.play)..

Routing sample: 10 case(s); 4 with no home among the parts (The weekend and paid holidays, twentieth century; Village feasts at harvest; The first ball court at Paso de la Amada, about 1650 BCE; A San storyteller's tale by the fire, 1950s); 0 with two or more parts as homes.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"synthesis","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.play","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.play","form":"processes","cutRecorded":true,"parts":[{"key":"media","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.play.media","processId":"h.media"},{"key":"makers","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.play.makers","processId":"h.play.makers"},{"key":"images","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.play.images","processId":"h.play.images"}],"process":"h.play","routingCases":10}}

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Leisure time (leisure): routed to The parent's own measure, hours of leisure a day (h.play)..
- What it covers: The hours a day free of work and the body's needs.
- Necessity pass: Play and the arts need time free of work.
- Independence pass: It moves against toil: down with farming, down again with early industry, up after 1870.
- Universality pass: Every population has free hours.

Mass media (media): part.
- What it covers: The share of people reached regularly by print, radio, television or the internet: stories, music and images made once and copied for many.
- Necessity pass: How people receive stories, music and images made by others changed more in a century than in all history before; the audiences of the arts have their home here.
- Independence pass: Reach rose from 6% to 94% after 1900 while leisure rose from 3.5 to 5.7 hours and the arts' makers per million roughly doubled: it follows copying and broadcasting, not free time or patronage.
- Universality pass: An axis every population has a reading on: zero before printing.

The arts' makers: people kept for the arts (makers): part.
- What it covers: People whose main work is making the arts for others who keep or pay them: images, sculpture, ornament, music, dance, drama, poetry, story and film, and games and sport played before an audience.
- Necessity pass: Without it the arts made by specialists have no home: the Olmec heads, Nok's terracottas, the bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu and Ife, Lalibela's churches, Borobudur's reliefs, Kalidasa's drama, the Tale of Genji's court, the Renaissance workshops, Hollywood. They change how much of a population's labour goes to the arts, which neither leisure nor media reach measures.
- Independence pass: Makers rise with chiefdoms, states and cities, bounded by the surplus that keeps them (SurplusBound#7fe3), while leisure hours fall with farming; they exist three thousand years before printing gives media any reach, and their number roughly doubles after 1900 while media reach rises fifteenfold.
- Universality pass: Every population divides its labour, and the share it keeps for the arts has a reading everywhere: zero among egalitarian foragers, a few hundred per million in agrarian states, a few thousand now. The measure is zero for most of the range, as discovery's and the people under arms' are; the dimension is not a kind.

Image and ornament: populations that make lasting art (images): part.
- What it covers: Whether a population makes lasting ornaments and images (beads and pendants, engraved, painted or carved marks and figures), read as the share of all living people in such populations.
- Necessity pass: Without it the oldest record of the arts has no home: the shell beads of Bizmoune and Taforalt, Blombos's ochre kit and engravings, the Aurignacian ivories and Chauvet, the paintings of Sulawesi, the rock art of the Sahara and of Australia. Makers count none of them, since none of their makers was kept for the work.
- Independence pass: It rises between about 150,000 and 30,000 years ago and is near its ceiling before any population keeps a single maker; it moves with population density and connection, which decide whether such a practice is kept and passed on (CumulativeCulture#4f93), not with surplus, leisure or copying.
- Universality pass: Every population has a reading: it makes lasting ornaments or images or it does not. Positive inference, of moderate strength: every living human population makes them, and the share is near its ceiling by about 30,000 years ago; how many populations made them before about 100,000 years ago is debated.

What people spend on play: feasts, festivals, entertainment (spending): frontier.
- What it covers: The share of what households and rulers spend on feasts, ceremonies, recreation and culture.
- Necessity pass: Feasting and festival spending ordered the agrarian year; recreation and culture are a large modern budget item.
- Independence pass: It moves with income apart from hours and makers.
- Universality uncertain: Household budgets read it only from about 1900; before that it is guesswork across the range. Kept as a frontier part, as in r215.

Festival and rest days a year (festivals): merged into leisure.
- What it covers: Days given to feasts, holy days and rest.
- Necessity pass: The medieval calendar's holy days, the Protestant cut in them, the weekend and paid holidays.
- Independence fail: They are leisure time counted in days rather than hours, the parent's own measure.
- Universality pass: Every population keeps feast days.

Games and sport (games): frontier.
- What it covers: Contests played by rules for their own sake and watched by others: the Mesoamerican ballgame, the Olympic games, chariot racing, football and rugby.
- Necessity pass: Organized games ordered festivals for three thousand years (the ballgame, Olympia) and fill much of modern leisure and media.
- Independence pass: Their organization changes apart from leisure hours: the codification of football and rugby (1863, 1871) and the modern Olympics (1896) came with railways and schools, not with more free time.
- Universality uncertain: Every population plays games, but organized contests with fixed rules and audiences are a kind that many populations lack, and no world measure reads the forms or followings of games across the range. Their paid players are counted among the arts' makers; the hours played are leisure.

Completeness uncertain: Against the structure construction's carve of arts and play (forms, production, audiences): production has its home in the arts' makers, audiences in mass media, time in the parent's leisure, and forms only by their lasting traces, in image and ornament. Forms that leave no trace before writing (music, dance, story), what is spent on play, and games and sport stay without a measured home. Checked against The structure construction's carve of arts and play into forms, production and audiences (structure/history-tree.mjs), and the Outline of Cultural Materials' sections on recreation and the fine arts, as recalled.. Still without a home: Forms that leave no lasting trace before writing (music, dance, story): no world measure; What people spend on play (frontier); Games and sport (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.play","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.play","candidates":[{"key":"leisure","label":"Leisure time","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The parent's own measure, hours of leisure a day (h.play)."},{"key":"media","label":"Mass media","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"makers","label":"The arts' makers: people kept for the arts","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"images","label":"Image and ornament: populations that make lasting art","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"spending","label":"What people spend on play: feasts, festivals, entertainment","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"festivals","label":"Festival and rest days a year","outcome":"merged","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"pass","mergedInto":"leisure"},{"key":"games","label":"Games and sport","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The structure construction's carve of arts and play into forms, production and audiences (structure/history-tree.mjs), and the Outline of Cultural Materials' sections on recreation and the fine arts, as recalled.","missing":["Forms that leave no lasting trace before writing (music, dance, story): no world measure","What people spend on play (frontier)","Games and sport (frontier)"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The Earth's stores (concept.dim.earth.resources):
- What it is: The Earth's stores as this account follows them: the minerals and fossil fuels taken from the Earth in a year, per living person (h.earth.resources), as material flow accounts count them, without harvested biomass.
- What the carve is for: To follow the three classes of what is dug from the Earth, which change apart and which one tonnage hides: the stone, sand, gravel and clay that build houses, monuments, cities and roads; the metal ores smelted for tools, weapons, coins and machines; and the coal, oil and gas burned since about 1000 and above all since 1800. So that metalworking (Old Copper, the Balkans' smelters, the Andes, West African iron, mainland bronze), mining booms (Potosí, Zacatecas, Minas Gerais, the gold rushes, the Rand, Panguna, Nauru) and the great acceleration each have a home, and so that the tonnage can be checked against the material flow accounts class by class.
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living people; a class may stand at or near zero before it is used, as metal ores do before about 5000 BCE and fossil fuels before about 1000.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The Earth's stores is a kind of A population's material throughput: the matter it draws from its surroundings in a year: The Earth's stores are drawn from the crust's non-living deposits (rock, ore and fossil carbon), rather than from the living harvest of crops, fodder, wood and fish. Other kinds within it: Harvested biomass, Water withdrawn.
2. A population's material throughput: the matter it draws from its surroundings in a year is a kind of Social metabolism: the flows a society draws from its surroundings and returns to them: Material throughput counts the matter a society draws, by mass, rather than the energy it draws or the wastes and emissions it returns. Other kinds within it: A population's energy throughput, Wastes and emissions returned.
3. Social metabolism: the flows a society draws from its surroundings and returns to them is a kind of A flow of energy or matter through an open system: The system is a society, whose flows pass through its techniques and institutions rather than through one body. Other kinds within it: A body's metabolism, An ecosystem's flow of energy and nutrients.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"The Earth's stores is carved into 3 parts: Building and industrial minerals, Metal ores, Fossil fuels.

How the parts make the whole work: The Earth's stores as this account follows them are the three classes the material flow accounts count outside the living harvest, and at every date the three sum to the whole. Building and industrial minerals, the bulk at nearly every date, follow houses, monuments, then cities and roads. Metal ores, a few kilograms per person until the iron age and about an eighth of the tonnage now, follow tools, weapons, coins and machines. Fossil fuels, negligible until coal in Song China and Britain, follow the turn from the land-bound economy to the stock-fed one (Sunbound#c94c) and were nearly half the tonnage from 1900 to 1950. Their sum is the tonnage per person; their shares show which kind of growth is under way: metal (the iron age, the silver century, the steel century), burning (the century after 1850) or building (after 1950, and China after 2000). One seam crosses the tree: fossil tonnage and the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores) measure nearly the same flow in different units and must turn together.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Uranium ores (a kind of concept.dim.earth.resources.metals).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Into stocks or burned: what becomes of what is dug (independence).

Routed elsewhere: Harvested biomass to Not part of the Earth's stores by the parent's definition: the living harvest is followed as food (h.food), fuel from the living harvest (h.warmth.harvest), farmland (h.farmland) and the wild animals (h.earth.wild-animals)., Water withdrawn to The Earth carve's frontier part fresh water, and water held on land (h.sea.land-water), whose kept-whole record places people's impounding and pumping there..

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Building and industrial minerals (minerals): part.
- What it covers: Stone, sand, gravel, clay and earth for building, limestone for lime and cement, and the minerals of industry and farming (salt, gypsum, phosphate rock, guano and nitrates).
- Necessity pass: Without it the bulk of what people dig has no home: flint and ochre for the first tools, mud brick and lime plaster for the first villages, the stone of monuments, Roman concrete, and the sand, gravel and cement of the cities and roads that are half of all extraction now.
- Independence pass: It follows building: nearly flat at about half a tonne per person through the century of coal and iron (1850 to 1910), when fuels and ores grew tenfold, then up fourfold after 1950 and again with China's building after 2000, when fossil fuels per person rose by about a third.
- Universality pass: Every population takes stone: the first draw on the Earth's stores is flint for tools and ochre for colour, 300,000 years ago.

Metal ores (metals): part.
- What it covers: The ores of iron, copper, tin, lead, zinc, gold, silver, aluminium and the other metals, as mined.
- Necessity pass: Without it copper, bronze and iron, the silver of Potosí and Zacatecas, the gold of Minas Gerais, California, Victoria and the Rand, and the copper of Panguna and the steel of the twentieth century have no home: they change what tools, weapons, coins and machines are made of.
- Independence pass: Its turns are its own: the Bronze and Iron Ages, Rome's mines and their collapse (the lead in Greenland's ice), the silver century, the steel century after 1870 and the ore boom of 2003 to 2014; ores per person tripled from 1950 to 1970 and doubled again after 2000, apart from building's and burning's clocks.
- Universality pass: The class has a reading at every date: zero before smelting, as the measure is zero for most of the range; it is a class of what is dug, not a kind of society.

Fossil fuels (fossil): part.
- What it covers: Coal, lignite and peat, crude oil and natural gas, by mass, and the bitumen of the Bronze Age.
- Necessity pass: Without it the turn from the land-bound economy to the stock-fed one (Sunbound#c94c) has no home in what is dug: coal in Song China and Britain, oil from 1859, gas after 1950, about a fifth of the tonnage now.
- Independence pass: It rose fastest from 1850 to 1910 and from 1950 to 1973, flattened after the oil shocks while building minerals kept rising, and rose again with China's coal after 2000. Its tonnage is coupled to the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores, in GJ per person) under sustenance: a seam across the tree, recorded in the synthesis, not a coupling between this carve's siblings.
- Universality pass: The class has a reading at every date, near zero before about 1000; a class of what is dug, not a kind of society.

Harvested biomass (biomass): routed to Not part of the Earth's stores by the parent's definition: the living harvest is followed as food (h.food), fuel from the living harvest (h.warmth.harvest), farmland (h.farmland) and the wild animals (h.earth.wild-animals)..
- What it covers: Crops, fodder, wood and fish taken from the living world.
- Necessity fail: The parent's measure excludes it by definition; nothing of the Earth's stores is lost without it.
- Independence pass: It moves with farming and population, apart from mining.
- Universality pass: Every population harvests the living world.

Water withdrawn (water): routed to The Earth carve's frontier part fresh water, and water held on land (h.sea.land-water), whose kept-whole record places people's impounding and pumping there..
- What it covers: Fresh water taken from rivers, lakes and aquifers for fields, towns and industry.
- Necessity fail: Material flow accounts keep water outside extraction, as the parent's measure does; its mass would swamp every other class.
- Independence pass: Irrigation and dams move it apart from mining.
- Universality pass: Every population draws water.

Uranium ores (uranium): a kind of metals.
- What it covers: Ores mined for nuclear fuel and weapons from the 1940s.
- Necessity pass: The fuel of reactors and bombs.
- Independence pass: Its booms (1950s, 1970s) are its own.
- Universality fail: Mined only from the 1940s: a kind of metal ore, counted in that class.

Into stocks or burned: what becomes of what is dug (fate): frontier.
- What it covers: An alternative carve of the same tonnage by fate: built into lasting stocks (buildings, roads, machines) or burned and dissipated.
- Necessity pass: The growth of stocks in place (Krausmann and colleagues' material stocks) is what the great acceleration left behind.
- Independence uncertain: It follows the classes closely: minerals and metals mostly go into stocks, fossil fuels are mostly burned; as a second carve it would double the classes rather than add a dimension.
- Universality pass: Everything dug either lasts or is used up.

Completeness pass: The economy-wide material flow accounts divide extraction into four classes: biomass, metal ores, non-metallic minerals and fossil energy materials. The parent excludes biomass by definition, so the other three exhaust it (MECE#ae19): every tonne the parent counts belongs to exactly one of them, and at every date the three sum to the whole. Checked against The classification of economy-wide material flow accounting (Eurostat's methodological guide; the UNEP International Resource Panel's global material flows database), as recalled..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.dim.earth.resources","conceptId":"concept.dim.earth.resources","candidates":[{"key":"minerals","label":"Building and industrial minerals","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"metals","label":"Metal ores","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"fossil","label":"Fossil fuels","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"biomass","label":"Harvested biomass","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Not part of the Earth's stores by the parent's definition: the living harvest is followed as food (h.food), fuel from the living harvest (h.warmth.harvest), farmland (h.farmland) and the wild animals (h.earth.wild-animals)."},{"key":"water","label":"Water withdrawn","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The Earth carve's frontier part fresh water, and water held on land (h.sea.land-water), whose kept-whole record places people's impounding and pumping there."},{"key":"uranium","label":"Uranium ores","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"fail","kindOf":"metals"},{"key":"fate","label":"Into stocks or burned: what becomes of what is dug","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"The classification of economy-wide material flow accounting (Eurostat's methodological guide; the UNEP International Resource Panel's global material flows database), as recalled."}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Done at model r363 to r376. Every value is recalled or reasoned, tagged sketch or inferred, and shares one foundation (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. The arts' makers beside discovery's researchers (h.play.makers, h.understanding.discovery, both people kept per million). Courts and temples kept makers of art three thousand years before anyone kept researchers: about 130 per million at 3000 BCE against about 0.1, about 550 against about 1 at 1 CE (some five hundred to one), about 850 against 4.5 in 1800 (about two hundred to one), 1,300 against 30 in 1900, and 2,500 against 1,450 now, under two to one. Patrons paid for beauty, rank and worship long before they paid for new knowledge; the steep rise of research after 1900 is an institutional change (the research university, the industrial laboratory, war research), not a rise in what surplus allows. SurplusBound#7fe3 bounds all non-food specialists together at about a tenth to a fifth of agrarian populations; the makers of art are a few in ten thousand of them, so the bound never binds them: their number follows patrons' choices and markets, not the size of the surplus.
- Prediction to test against censuses (not yet looked at): where occupational censuses exist before 1900 (England and Wales 1841 to 1901, France, the United States), artists, musicians, actors and writers together should be a few per thousand of all people, several times the world figure, with Asia's and Africa's courts well below them.

2. Image and ornament (h.play.images). The share of people in populations that make lasting art rises from about 15% at 100,000 years ago to about three quarters at 40,000, crossing half as the dispersal from Africa carries the practice; the bands hold three readings (gradual emergence, a late revolution, a demographic flicker: EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b). A distinguishing test recorded in the series reason (DistinguishingTest#0439): if density decides (CumulativeCulture#4f93), the oldest ornaments should cluster where and when genomes and site counts show the densest Middle Stone Age populations.

3. The Earth's three stores (carve r368, parts r369, declared their sum at r370). The tonnage per person was nearly all building and industrial minerals until 1800 (fossil fuels and ores together under a twentieth). Fossil fuels then grew from 0.02 to about 0.7 tonnes a head between 1800 and 1913, while building minerals stayed near half a tonne for sixty years (1850 to 1910): from about 1890 to the 1940s fossil fuels outweighed building minerals, a carbon age of extraction. After 1950 building took over again (cement, sand and gravel), and since 2000 China's building drove two thirds of the rise: minerals about 67% of the tonnage now, fossil fuels 20%, metal ores 13%. Metal ores per person grew a hundredfold from 1850 to 2025, faster than either other class.
- The seam with energy, used as a check: fossil tonnage and the energy drawn from stores (h.warmth.stores) must keep a ratio near the fuels' energy per tonne. It held within about a tenth at every date but three; 1918, 1945 and 1965 were corrected at r376 (claude.revision.fossil-seam-r376 is this note's third point; the corrections carry their reasons on the values).
- Raised the whole at 1890, 1900 and 1910 (r369) to the figure its own 1900 note gives (Krausmann and colleagues, about 1.06 tonnes a head in 1900), so that building minerals do not fall per person while railways and cities grow.

4. Links. 22 Events of the arts, 32 of metalworking, mining, building and burning, and the Events of Oceania's output, state property revenue and contract work now name what they change; processes no Event observes fell from 34 to 31 (counting the new parts once linked). Every gap the links opened was filled on the line between neighbours, with sums kept (r372 to r375)."}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Understanding (concept.humanity.wants.understanding):
- What it is: Understanding: what people know of the world and how they come to know it, followed as the share of adults who can read and write (h.understanding), with schooling, the command of number, the making of new knowledge and the languages that knowledge is held and passed on in as its parts.
- What the carve is for: To follow the parts of understanding that move apart: the time spent being taught (schooling), the command of number (numeracy), the making of new knowledge (discovery) and, added now, language, which the last record of this carve named as still without a home. The breadth check names the society group's Events of residential schools and the stolen generations, which took children from their languages, and the model holds the spread of whole language families with farmers and herders (Bantu, Austronesian, Pama-Nyungan, the steppe migrations) linked to nothing that follows language.
- The range it claims: Every human population at every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, followed as world measures of adults, of all living people or of the world's languages.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Understanding is a kind of A condition of a life that people seek: Understanding: knowing about the world and being able to learn more, set apart from belonging to others, standing among them and finding meaning. Other kinds within it: Belonging, Standing among others, Meaning.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Understanding is carved into 4 parts: Schooling, Command of number, Discovery: the people who make new knowledge, Language: the living languages.

How the parts make the whole work: Understanding, as this account follows it, is reading and writing (the parent's measure), the years spent being taught (schooling), the command of number (numeracy), the making of new knowledge (discovery) and the languages all of it is held in (language). They can all rise together and are followed as separate processes. Numeracy rose first and furthest before modern schooling, literacy spread later and unevenly, schooling carried the twentieth century's rise, and discovery stays near zero for most of the range and then grows fastest of all. Language runs the other way for most of history: the number of languages grew with the people who spread over the world and with the farmers of the tropics, each small community drifting into a tongue of its own, and has fallen since farmers', herders' and empires' languages spread and above all since 1500, as conquest, epidemics, nation-states and schooling in national languages ended thousands. One part of understanding therefore narrows as the others widen: more people read, count and are taught, in fewer languages. Sema: ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, MandatoryAbstraction#ac44, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f, CumulativeCulture#4f93 (knowledge accumulates when enough people learn from one another, and a language is the community that can).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Knowledge held in store (universality).

Routed elsewhere: Reading and writing to The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Reading and writing (literacy): routed to The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding).
- What it covers: The share of adults who can read and write.
- Necessity pass: Writing holds knowledge outside heads; its spread is the first fact of understanding's history.
- Independence pass: Literacy rose in Protestant Europe before mass schooling, and apart from numeracy.
- Universality pass: An axis: zero before writing.

Schooling (schooling): part.
- What it covers: The years adults spent being formally taught.
- Necessity pass: Mass schooling, compulsory from the nineteenth century and universal in the twentieth, and the secondary and university expansion since 1950 have no home without it.
- Independence pass: Years of school went on rising after literacy neared its ceiling in the rich world; literacy rose before schooling in early modern Europe through church and home teaching.
- Universality pass: An axis: every population teaches its young, and formal schooling is zero where it is absent.

Command of number (numeracy): part.
- What it covers: The share of adults who can count, reckon and know their age in years, read from age heaping (the ABCC index).
- Necessity pass: Reckoning is the skill of trade, taxes and calendars; East Asia's high numeracy before mass literacy has no home without it.
- Independence pass: Numeracy ran ahead of literacy in Qing China and Japan, and literacy ahead of numeracy in parts of Protestant Europe.
- Universality pass: An axis: every population counts something; knowing one's age in years needs a calendar, which foragers lack, so their value is near zero.

Knowledge held in store (stored): frontier.
- What it covers: Books, archives and libraries: knowledge kept outside heads.
- Necessity pass: Printing's flood of books (Buringh and van Zanden) and the libraries of Alexandria, Baghdad and Song China.
- Independence pass: Book production rose apart from literacy rates.
- Universality uncertain: An axis from zero before writing; but no world series of books or titles per person can be read before about 1500 outside Europe and China, and after 2000 books are a falling share of what is stored, so it stays a frontier part.

Discovery: the people who make new knowledge (discovery): part.
- What it covers: New knowledge made: inquiry in the sciences, scholarship and invention, read by the people whose main work it is.
- Necessity pass: The scientific revolution, the research university and the industrial laboratory, the twentieth century's research workforce and the knowledge group's Events (the Museum, the House of Wisdom, the Enlightenment, the Geophysical Year, Apollo) have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It concentrates in a few places apart from mass literacy: Alexandria and Baghdad held their scholars when literacy was a few per cent; the number of researchers grew about fourfold from 1950 to 1970 while literacy rose by a third; it rose again after 2000 with China's research, when schooling's growth had slowed.
- Universality pass: The measure is defined at every date, zero where no one makes new knowledge their main work (all foragers and early farmers, so all of humanity before about 3000 BCE), and its deep values are guesses with wide bands, as other measures here are.

Language: the living languages (language): part.
- What it covers: The languages in which people think, teach and pass on what they know, followed as the number of distinct languages spoken as a first language by some community, counting mutually unintelligible varieties as Glottolog and Ethnologue do.
- Necessity pass: Without it, the spread of whole language families with farmers and herders (Bantu, Austronesian, Indo-European, Pama-Nyungan), the spread of empires' languages (Akkadian, Latin, Arabic, Quechua, Spanish, English), the loss of languages since 1500, and the residential schools and stolen generations that took children from their languages have no home; and every other part of understanding is held and handed on in some language.
- Independence pass: The count rose as foragers spread over the world without writing, schooling or numbers; it fell in the Americas after 1500 while literacy rose in Europe; and mass schooling in national languages speeds the loss without forcing it: Papua New Guinea keeps more than 800 languages as schooling spreads, and Hawaiian and Maori revivals run through schools.
- Universality pass: Every human population speaks, and the count is defined at every date. When language as we know it began is debated (with Homo sapiens or before it, against a late origin some 100,000 to 50,000 years ago); that widens the bands of the deep values, not the definition.

Completeness uncertain: Learning's duration (schooling), storage's capacity (literacy, the parent's measure), reckoning (numeracy), the generation of new knowledge (discovery) and now language have homes. Storage's durability and access (knowledge held in store) remains a frontier part without a world series. Checked against The structure construction's carve of knowledge (learning: transmitters and duration; storage: capacity, durability and access; discovery: generation and selection; language) in structure/history-tree.mjs; UNESCO's science and education statistics; Glottolog and Ethnologue's catalogues of the world's languages.. Still without a home: Knowledge held in store (frontier).","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.wants.understanding","conceptId":"concept.humanity.wants.understanding","candidates":[{"key":"literacy","label":"Reading and writing","outcome":"routed","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"The parent's own measure, the share of adults literate (h.understanding)"},{"key":"schooling","label":"Schooling","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"numeracy","label":"Command of number","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"stored","label":"Knowledge held in store","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"uncertain"},{"key":"discovery","label":"Discovery: the people who make new knowledge","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"language","label":"Language: the living languages","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","checkedAgainst":"The structure construction's carve of knowledge (learning: transmitters and duration; storage: capacity, durability and access; discovery: generation and selection; language) in structure/history-tree.mjs; UNESCO's science and education statistics; Glottolog and Ethnologue's catalogues of the world's languages.","missing":["Knowledge held in store (frontier)"]}}}

Breadth check answered: Ten of the society group's Events named no process. Eight now name what they change (r386): the New Laws and Palmares change the share held in bondage; the Cape Colony changes colonial rule in Africa and bondage; blackbirding changes compelled work and migration into Oceania; the 'social laboratory' changes the terms of work for an employer; Maori Aotearoa extends Oceania's range and people. Residential schools and the stolen generations took children from their languages, which no process followed; the count of living languages (h.understanding.languages) now follows it, opened as the language part of the carve of Understanding (r384, r385), which had named language as missing, and the language-family Events (Bantu, Austronesian, Pama-Nyungan, the steppe migrations, the Taino) are linked to it too. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"Migrants living in the Americas is carved into 2 parts: Migrants living in Northern America, Migrants living in Latin America and the Caribbean.

How the parts make the whole work: The Americas' migrants are those of Northern America and those of Latin America and the Caribbean; the two sum to the whole, and the sum is declared. Before 1492 the hemisphere's movers follow its people, most of them in Mesoamerica and the Andes, so Latin America holds four fifths or more after the first peopling. For three centuries after 1492 most of them are in Latin America and the Caribbean: the Africans of the slave trade, nine tenths of whom were landed there and died so fast that the African-born stayed most of the enslaved, and the Iberian settlers. Northern America's part rises from a few per cent in 1600 to about a third by 1820, and with the mass migration from 1845 to four fifths by 1870. Argentina's and Brazil's Europeans keep Latin America's count rising to about 1950 while the United States' quotas shrink the north's from 1920 to 1965; after 1965 the north climbs again to about 86% around 2000 to 2010, and Venezuela's exodus lifts Latin America's part to about a fifth by 2025. Frontier axes, origin and force, cut across both parts and stay recorded. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Migrants living in Northern America (northern): part.
- What it covers: People living in the United States, Canada, Greenland, Bermuda or Saint Pierre and Miquelon outside the country of their birth, as a share of all living people.
- Necessity pass: The mass migration to the United States and Canada from 1845 to 1914, the quota acts of 1921 and 1924, the Hart-Celler Act of 1965 and today's 61 million, a fifth of the world's migrants, have their own trajectory, which the Americas' one share mixes with the south's.
- Independence pass: The north's count fell from 1920 to 1965 under the quotas while Latin America's rose to about 1950 with Europeans going to Argentina and Brazil; after 1965 the north climbed while the south's share fell to the 1990s, and the south then rose with Venezuela's exodus while the north's growth slowed.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date by 2026 borders: zero before the peopling of the Americas, and the first migrants of the hemisphere lived in what is now Northern America (White Sands, about 21,000 years ago, if its dates hold).

Migrants living in Latin America and the Caribbean (latin): part.
- What it covers: People living in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean or South America outside the country of their birth, as a share of all living people.
- Necessity pass: Nine tenths of the Africans carried by the Atlantic slave trade were landed in Brazil and the Caribbean, with the Iberian settlers; Argentina's and Brazil's mass migrations, the indentured Indians and Chinese of the Caribbean and Peru, and Venezuela's exodus have no home without it.
- Independence pass: From 1500 to about 1820 it held most of the hemisphere's migrants while the north's colonies were small; it kept rising until about 1950 when the north's fell, and its recent rise comes from migration within Latin America, not from the north's policies.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date by 2026 borders: zero before people reached it, and after about 14,500 years ago (Monte Verde) it holds most of the hemisphere's people and so most of its movers.

Migrants living in the Caribbean (caribbean): merged into latin.
- What it covers: The Caribbean subregion's migrants, apart from Central and South America's.
- Necessity uncertain: The islands held most of the hemisphere's African-born in the 1700s, which would show; after 1850 they are a small and falling part.
- Independence pass: The islands' count fell after the British and French abolitions while Brazil's and Argentina's rose.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date.

Migrants by where they were born (origin): frontier.
- What it covers: The same migrants divided by their continent of birth (Europe, Africa, Asia, elsewhere in the Americas).
- Necessity pass: The turn from European and African to Latin American and Asian origins after 1965 is a large part of the story.
- Independence fail: An axis across the parts, not a part: every migrant has both a place of birth and a place of residence, so its categories cut through northern and latin rather than beside them.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date.

Migrants brought by force (forced): frontier.
- What it covers: The enslaved and the indentured among the Americas' migrants.
- Necessity pass: Before 1820 most of the hemisphere's migrants were enslaved Africans.
- Independence fail: Another axis across the parts: the enslaved were landed in both, so forced and free cut through northern and latin; their bondage is followed by h.freedom and h.toil.compelled.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date.

Completeness pass: The two parts are the M49 division of the Americas and sum to it; every place in the hemisphere falls in one of them. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving The arts' makers: people kept for the arts (concept.humanity.wants.play.makers):
- What it is: The arts' makers: people whose main work is making images, sculpture, ornament, music, dance, drama, poetry, story or film, or playing games and sport before an audience, for others who keep or pay them, per million of all living people (h.play.makers).
- What the carve is for: To follow who keeps the makers of art, which one number hides: for five thousand years nearly all were kept by rulers, nobles and temples; markets of buyers and paying audiences grew from the Song cities, the Renaissance workshops, Edo's theatres and the printed book until they kept most makers by about 1820; and after 1917 and 1945 public bodies (the Soviet and Chinese state troupes, Europe's subsidized theatres and orchestras, the state broadcasters) kept a quarter or more, until the Soviet system's end. The deepen check names this process first (16 Events, every value sketched).
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living Homo sapiens: zero before anyone was kept for the arts, and the kept makers of chiefdoms, temple states, empires, markets and modern states after.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The arts' makers: people kept for the arts is a kind of A population's specialists: people kept for one kind of work: The arts' makers are the specialists whose work is beauty, story and performance for others, set apart from those kept to make new knowledge, to serve the gods, to fight, to govern and keep records, or to make ordinary goods. Other kinds within it: Discovery: the people who make new knowledge, People kept for worship, People under arms, Officials and scribes, Craftsmen of ordinary goods.
2. A population's specialists: people kept for one kind of work is a kind of A division of a population's labour: Specialists are the part of a population's labour that does not get its own food, fed from the food producers' surplus (SurplusBound#7fe3). Other kinds within it: Food-getting work, Work for one's own household, Work under compulsion.
