How the parts make the whole work: The arts' makers are those kept by patrons, those living from markets and those kept by public bodies, each placed by the source of most of their income; the three sum to the whole at every date, and the sum is declared. Read together they show what one number hid. Patrons kept nearly every maker for five thousand years and kept roughly the same number per person from the first century to the eighteenth (about 400 to 475 per million): the growth of the arts' workforce before 1800 is almost all markets, which went from a few per cent in antiquity to a sixth in the Song cities and a third by 1650, and kept most makers by about 1820. Patrons' makers depend on elite surplus and taste; markets' on many buyers' incomes and on copying (printing, recording, broadcasting); public bodies' on budgets and ideology. Kept by patrons: rulers, nobles, temples and churches (patrons): part.
- What it covers: Makers whose main income comes from a ruler's or noble's household, or from a temple, monastery or church, as members of its workshops and ensembles or by its commissions: court painters, temple sculptors, palace musicians, griots of a lineage, cathedral organists.
- Necessity pass: For five thousand years nearly every kept maker lived in a court or temple: Sumer's and Egypt's workshops, the Olmec sculptors, the Gupta and Heian courts, Ife, Benin, Lalibela, Borobudur and the Renaissance commissions have no home without it, and its fall with the courts after 1789 is half the story of the arts' modern economy.
- Independence pass: It held near 400 to 475 per million from the first century to the eighteenth while markets grew tenfold; it fell after 1789 as markets rose, and kept falling after 1917 while public bodies rose: it moves apart from both.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date: zero before anyone was kept, then present wherever chiefs, kings or temples kept makers, and still present now in churches, royal households and private patrons.

Living from markets: buyers and paying audiences (markets): part.
- What it covers: Makers whose main income comes from selling works, copies or tickets to many buyers, or from wages paid by firms that do: painters for the open market, actors and musicians of commercial theatres and halls, authors paid by publishers, studio and record-company performers, professional players of sport, and makers paid through advertising.
- Necessity pass: The Song cities' entertainment quarters, the Dutch picture market, Elizabethan and Edo theatres, the printed book's authors, the music hall, Hollywood, recorded music, professional sport and streaming have no home without it; it keeps most makers from about 1820.
- Independence pass: It grew from a few per cent of makers in antiquity to over half by 1820 while patrons stayed flat, and kept growing in the West while public bodies took most makers in the Soviet bloc and China; the pandemic of 2020 cut it while salaried public makers kept their posts.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date: zero before markets for art existed, a small share in the cities of antiquity, most makers now.

Kept by public bodies (public): part.
- What it covers: Makers paid from public revenue by bodies that act as public services rather than as a ruler's household: city festivals, state and municipal theatres, opera houses and orchestras, academies, state troupes, public broadcasters, and artists' unions that pay salaries.
- Necessity pass: Athens's civic festivals, the Soviet theatres and composers' union after 1917, China's state troupes after 1949, Europe's subsidized stages and orchestras and the public broadcasters have no home without it; it kept a quarter to a third of all makers from about 1950 to 1990.
- Independence pass: It rose after 1917 and 1949 while patrons fell and markets held, and fell after 1991 while markets rose; it is set by state budgets and ideology, not by courts or buyers.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date: zero before civic or state bodies paid makers as a public service, small from the Greek festivals to 1900, large after 1917.

Makers by art form: images, music, performance, words, sport (by-form): frontier.
- What it covers: The same makers divided by what they make: images and objects, music, drama and dance, words, sport.
- Necessity pass: The rise of the performer with cinema, radio and sport, and the decline of makers of art wares with industry, are real turns.
- Independence uncertain: The forms rise and fall together with the keepers who pay for them more than apart, and no world series by form can be read before about 1900.
- Universality pass: Every form can be made in every society; each is defined at every date.

Makers by the M49 area where they work (by-area): frontier.
- What it covers: The same makers divided by the area of the world where they work, as discovery is.
- Necessity pass: Asia's courts held most makers until 1800, Europe's and the Americas' markets most after.
- Independence pass: Areas move apart with their courts and markets.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date by 2026 borders.

Art made by people whose main work is something else (amateurs): routed to Image and ornament (h.play.images) and leisure (h.play), which follow art made by everyone.
- What it covers: The beads, carvings, songs and dances of people who are not kept for them.
- Necessity fail: Outside the measure by its definition: people kept for the arts, not people who make art.
- Independence pass: Amateur making goes on whatever the keepers do.
- Universality pass: Every society makes art.

Completeness pass: Every kept maker has one main source of income, and the three keepers cover them: personal and religious patrons, buyers and audiences, public bodies. A maker with several sources (Shakespeare's company, Bach paid by Leipzig's council for church music) is placed by the source of most of their income, as a household's livelihood is placed by the source of most of its food. Checked against the three sources of income in the economics of the arts, earned income, private contributions and government support (Baumol and Bowen, Performing Arts: The Economic Dilemma, 1966), as recalled, to be checked. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving Range in Antarctica (concept.humanity.means.habitat.range.antarctica):
- What it is: Range in Antarctica: the share of the world's ice-free land that lies in Antarctica (its ice-free coasts, nunataks and dry valleys, about 0.04% of the land) and is used or visited regularly by people at the date (h.habitat.range.antarctica).
- What the carve is for: To see whether Antarctica's range is made of parts that move apart, which one share would hide: the sealers' beaches of the 1820s, the whalers' shore stations from 1904, the permanent bases from 1944, and the research stations, field camps and tourist landings since the Geophysical Year. The deepen check names it (8 Events, 2 at the top of an importance scale, every value sketched).
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025: zero until sealers land on the South Shetlands about 1820, then seasonal camps, shore stations and stations.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. Range in Antarctica is a kind of Range: the land people live on and use: Antarctica's range is the one part of humanity's range never peopled by a native population: it is reached only from the 1820s, by seasonal workers and then by state-funded stations under the Antarctic Treaty, and nobody is born, lives and dies there as a member of a resident population. Other kinds within it: Range in Africa, Range in the Americas, Range in Asia, Range in Europe, Range in Oceania.

A division by kind of use fails independence and universality: sealing, whaling, stations and tourism follow one another on the same beaches and points, so they are kinds of presence, not parts. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

By kind of use: sealing and whaling camps, research stations, tourism (by-use): a kind of concept.humanity.means.habitat.range.antarctica.
- What it covers: The ice-free land in use divided by what brings people there: seasonal hunting of seals and whales, stations and field science, visits by tourists.
- Necessity pass: The shift from hunters' beaches to state stations after 1944 is the main turn in Antarctica's human history.
- Independence fail: The same few beaches and points serve every use in turn: Deception Island was a whaling station, then a base, now a tourist landing; the uses replace one another on the same ground rather than adding land of their own, so their shares cannot move apart without double counting.
- Universality fail: Each use exists only in an era: sealing from 1820 to the 1890s, shore whaling from 1904 to the 1960s, stations from 1944, tourism from 1966. They are kinds of presence, not parts every date has.

Range on the Antarctic Peninsula and its islands (peninsula): frontier.
- What it covers: The ice-free ground of the Peninsula, the South Shetlands and the South Orkneys within regular reach.
- Necessity pass: Most landings, most bases and nearly all tourism are here.
- Independence pass: It was reached a century and more before East Antarctica's coast and dry valleys.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date, zero before 1820.

Range in East Antarctica and the Ross Sea coast (east): frontier.
- What it covers: The ice-free ground of the rest of the continent: the Ross Sea coast, the dry valleys, the coastal oases of East Antarctica.
- Necessity pass: The Ross Sea huts of the heroic age and the stations of the Geophysical Year are here.
- Independence pass: Reached from 1899 and mainly after 1956.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date, zero before 1899.

Completeness uncertain: The two sectors would cover the continent's ice-free land, but their values would be thousandths of a percent of the world's land, read from station lists and landing sites that have not been checked; the kinds of use do not divide the land without double counting. Still without a home: A checked list of stations and landing sites with the ice-free area each puts within regular reach.","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.humanity.means.habitat.range.antarctica","conceptId":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.range.antarctica","candidates":[{"key":"by-use","label":"By kind of use: sealing and whaling camps, research stations, tourism","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","kindOf":"concept.humanity.means.habitat.range.antarctica"},{"key":"peninsula","label":"Range on the Antarctic Peninsula and its islands","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"east","label":"Range in East Antarctica and the Ross Sea coast","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"uncertain","missing":["A checked list of stations and landing sites with the ice-free area each puts within regular reach"]}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

By M49 subregion: Australia and New Zealand, Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia (subregions): frontier.
- What it covers: The land within range divided by the four M49 subregions of Oceania.
- Necessity pass: Each subregion was peopled at a different time, and Australia and New Zealand together mix the earliest and the last peopling of any large land.
- Independence pass: Melanesia's islands and Micronesia and Polynesia filled thousands of years after Australia, and New Zealand three thousand years after Fiji.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date by 2026 borders, zero before each was reached.

Near and Remote Oceania (near-remote): frontier.
- What it covers: The land within range divided between Near Oceania (Sahul, the Bismarcks and the main Solomons, reachable within sight of land) and Remote Oceania (everything east and north of them, reachable only by voyaging out of sight of land).
- Necessity pass: The boundary marks the two great movements of Oceania's peopling and the 25,000 years between them (Green 1991).
- Independence pass: Near Oceania was full by about 30,000 years ago; Remote Oceania stayed empty until about 1500 BCE.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date.

Completeness pass: Either division covers Oceania's land without overlap: the four M49 subregions by 2026 borders, or Near and Remote Oceania by Green's boundary east of the Solomons. Checked against the UN M49 standard and Green, 'Near and Remote Oceania', in Pawley (ed.), Man and a Half (1991), as recalled. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving One-sided killing (concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.one-sided):
- What it is: One-sided killing: people killed by organized groups while not fighting back (massacres of camps, villages and cities, genocide, politicide and campaigns of mass execution), whoever does it and whether or not a war is being fought, per 100,000 living people a year, averaged to the next date (h.war.one-sided).
- What the carve is for: To follow who does the killing, which one rate hides: before states every massacre was the work of raiding parties of bands and villages; states took most of it over, by conquest massacres and terror, and the twentieth century's peaks are nearly all states' work; groups that are not states take a larger part again where states fail or break up (Partition, the Lord's Resistance Army, the Islamic State, Boko Haram). The deepen check names this process (17 Events, values mostly sketched).
- The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, for all living Homo sapiens: the massacres of foragers' camps and farmers' villages, the sacks and deportations of the first states and empires, and the genocides, politicides and militia killings of the modern world.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. One-sided killing is a kind of War and massacre: One-sided killing is the organized killing whose victims do not fight back, set apart from fighting between polities and fighting within a polity, where both sides are armed. Other kinds within it: Fighting between polities, Fighting within a polity.
2. War and massacre is a kind of Violence: War and massacre is violence by organized groups, set apart from homicide, killing by individuals or small groups outside organized fighting. Other kinds within it: Homicide.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"One-sided killing is carved into 2 parts: Killing by states, Killing by groups that are not states.

How the parts make the whole work: One-sided killing is killing by states plus killing by groups that are not states, each massacre counted once, by the organization that carried it out; the two sum to the whole at every date, and the sum is declared. Read together they show a hand-over that one rate hid. Before the first states every massacre was a raid by one band or village on another, at rates this account sketches at 8 to 9 per 100,000 a year with wide bands (debated: they rest on a few dozen sites). From about 3000 BCE states took most of it over, by conquest and terror, while their spread suppressed raiding: by 1 CE states did about seven tenths of it, and nearly all of the great peaks after (the Mongols, the Dzungars, Armenia, the Holocaust, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Rwanda). Groups that are not states took the larger part only where states had failed or were breaking: the Yellow Turban years, the Taiping and Dungan wars, Ukraine in 1919, Partition, and since 2014 the Islamic State and the Sahel's jihadists. The two parts carry the old debate without settling it (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): on one reading states pacify, since the non-state part falls as they spread (Hobbes, Pinker, Elias); on the other states are the greatest killers, since the state part holds the worst years (Rummel, Scott). Both readings are true of different parts. Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Killing of a polity's own subjects against killing of others (independence).

Routed elsewhere: Deaths by starvation imposed by policy to Hunger (h.alive.hunger), with the claim of intent recorded on each famine's Event.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Killing by states (states): part.
- What it covers: One-sided killing by a polity's government and those acting for it: its armies, police, camp guards and secret services, and militias it arms and directs. A rebel movement that rules territory as a recognized or de facto state counts here only once it governs.
- Necessity pass: The Assyrian and Mongol massacres, the Dzungar genocide, the Herero and Armenian genocides, the Holocaust, Bangladesh, Cambodia and Rwanda, the twentieth century's peaks, have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It rises with conquest and with regimes that kill their own subjects, and falls with their end, apart from what raiders and militias do: it was near zero at Partition, when communal militias killed most, and has been below the non-state part since 2014.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date: zero before the first states about 3500 BCE, present wherever states have ruled since.

Killing by groups that are not states (nonstate): part.
- What it covers: One-sided killing by organized groups that do not govern a state: raiding parties of bands, villages and tribes, pirates and bandit armies, rebel armies before they rule, communal militias and mobs organized for killing, and terrorist groups.
- Necessity pass: Every massacre before states (Nataruk, Talheim, Crow Creek), the raids of Vikings and steppe bands, the pogroms, Partition's communal killings, the Lord's Resistance Army, the Islamic State and Boko Haram have no home without it.
- Independence pass: It fell as states spread and suppressed raiding, while the state part rose; it rises where states fail (the Taiping and Dungan years, Ukraine in 1919, Partition, the Sahel and Iraq since 2014), not when strong states kill.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date: all one-sided killing before states, a smaller part since.

Killing of a polity's own subjects against killing of others (by-target): frontier.
- What it covers: The same killings divided by whether the victims were subjects of the killers' polity or of another.
- Necessity pass: Rummel's democide turns on governments killing their own people.
- Independence uncertain: The same campaign often kills both: the Holocaust killed German Jews and the Jews of conquered Europe, the Mongol sacks killed the subjects of rival states that became the Mongols' own; the boundary moves with conquest during the killing.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date.

Genocide, politicide, reprisal and sack (by-intent): a kind of concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.one-sided.
- What it covers: The same killings divided by what they aimed at: destroying a people, destroying a political group, punishing resistance, or plunder.
- Necessity pass: The legal and moral debates turn on intent.
- Independence fail: Intent is mixed within most campaigns and is read after the fact from words and patterns that historians dispute; the categories overlap rather than divide.
- Universality fail: Genocide and politicide as categories are modern; a sack and a genocide can be the same act read two ways.

Deaths by starvation imposed by policy (famine-by-policy): routed to Hunger (h.alive.hunger), with the claim of intent recorded on each famine's Event.
- What it covers: People starved by requisitions, sieges and blockades meant to kill or careless of killing: the Holodomor, the Great Leap's famine, the hunger plan in the occupied east.
- Necessity fail: Outside the measure: they are counted under hunger (h.alive.hunger), and counting them here too would count them twice; the debate over whether some were genocide is recorded on their Events.
- Independence pass: They follow food policy, not massacres.
- Universality pass: Sieges have starved people since the first walled towns.

Completeness pass: Every organized group that kills people who are not fighting back either governs a state or does not, so the two parts cover every case; a militia armed and directed by a government is counted with the state (Rwanda's Interahamwe, Indonesia's militias of 1965, the Janjaweed), a rebel army that rules territory as a state only once it governs. Checked against the Uppsala Conflict Data Program's one-sided violence data set, which records one-sided violence by governments and by formally organized groups that are not governments, as recalled, to be checked; and against Rummel's democide, which counts governments alone. Checked against UCDP One-sided Violence Dataset (government and non-state perpetrators); Rummel, Death by Government (1994)..","data":{"schema":"meaning-model-carve/v1","part":"tests","cutId":"carve.concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.one-sided","conceptId":"concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.one-sided","candidates":[{"key":"states","label":"Killing by states","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"nonstate","label":"Killing by groups that are not states","outcome":"part","necessity":"pass","independence":"pass","universality":"pass"},{"key":"by-target","label":"Killing of a polity's own subjects against killing of others","outcome":"frontier","necessity":"pass","independence":"uncertain","universality":"pass"},{"key":"by-intent","label":"Genocide, politicide, reprisal and sack","outcome":"kind","necessity":"pass","independence":"fail","universality":"fail","kindOf":"concept.causes-of-death.violence.war.one-sided"},{"key":"famine-by-policy","label":"Deaths by starvation imposed by policy","outcome":"routed","necessity":"fail","independence":"pass","universality":"pass","routedTo":"Hunger (h.alive.hunger), with the claim of intent recorded on each famine's Event"}],"completeness":{"verdict":"pass","checkedAgainst":"UCDP One-sided Violence Dataset (government and non-state perpetrators); Rummel, Death by Government (1994)."}}}

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"analysis","text":"Done at model r395 to r409. Every value is recalled or reasoned, tagged sketch, and shares one foundation with its parent (EvidenceDependence#23ca).

1. Migrants in the Americas (r395, r396). Declared the sum of Northern America and Latin America and the Caribbean; the 14 migration Events name the half that received the movers. Nothing new in the values, which the stopped pass had set; the parts are now observed at their Events.

2. Who keeps the makers of art (carve r397, parts r398, sum r399, links r401). Patrons kept nearly every maker for five thousand years, and kept about the same number per person from the first century to the eighteenth: about 470 per million at 1 CE and 476 at its peak in 1600. So the whole rise of the arts' workforce before 1800, from 550 to 850 per million, is the rise of markets, from about 55 per million (a tenth) in the Roman and Han cities to about 90 (a sixth) in the Song cities' entertainment quarters, 210 (three in ten) by 1600 and 460, more than patrons, by 1820. Patrons fall after 1789 and again after 1917 and 1947; public bodies rise from a fiftieth of all makers to about three tenths between 1950 and 1965 (the Soviet bloc's and China's state troupes, studios and unions, Europe's subsidized stages and broadcasters) and fall back to a sixth after 1991. The pandemic year shows the parts' different exposure: markets fell from 1,872 to 1,710 per million while public bodies held. A prediction to test, not yet looked at: where occupational censuses exist (England and Wales from 1841, France, the United States), the self-employed and firm-employed share of artists, musicians and actors should be above half by 1850 and above three quarters by 1900; Soviet employment statistics should show 0.5 to 1 million arts workers on state payrolls by 1970. SurplusBound#7fe3 bounds all of them together and binds none of them: patrons' makers follow elite taste and revenue, markets' makers follow mass incomes and the copying technologies (printing, recording, broadcasting), public makers follow budgets and ideology.

3. Who kills the unarmed (carve r404, parts r405, sum r408, links r409). Before states every massacre in the account is a raid by bands or villages, at the parent's sketched 8 to 9 per 100,000 a year (debated; a few dozen sites). From about 3000 BCE states take over most of it while suppressing raiding: about seven tenths by 1 CE, and nearly all of the great peaks after (the Mongols at 24 of the 1206 stretch's 25, the Armenian genocide at 14 of 15, the Holocaust years at 148 of 150, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Rwanda at 39 of 42.5). Groups that are not states hold the larger part only where states had failed or were breaking: the Han's end in 184 (6 of 10), the late Ming's rebel armies in 1618 (6.75 of 15), the Taiping and Dungan years (half), Partition (7.5 of 10) and, since 2014, the Islamic State, Boko Haram and the Sahel's jihadists. The carve carries the debate over the state without settling it (EvidenceUnderdetermination#999b): the non-state part's fall with state formation is the pacification Hobbes, Elias and Pinker describe; the state part's hold on the worst years is Rummel's and Scott's case; both are true of different parts. Militias a government arms and directs are counted with the state (Rwanda's Interahamwe, Indonesia 1965, the Janjaweed), as UCDP and Rummel would; a reader who counts them apart would raise the non-state part in those years. Deaths by starvation imposed by policy outside war (the Holodomor, the Great Leap) stay under hunger; famine deaths a war causes stay with that war, as the war carve's frame says (see claude.revision.r319-famine-frame).

4. Kept whole, with reasons: range in Antarctica (r402: kinds of use replace one another on the same beaches; sectors would pass but split at most 0.03% of the world's land into sketched thousandths) and range in Oceania (r403: both the M49 subregions and Near and Remote Oceania pass, but Remote Oceania's whole peopling is a quarter of a point of the world's land, and the subregions' people series already follow it).

Slip: the deepen check named the arts' makers' parts again at once (patrons first), as every value of a newly opened part is sketched; that is the report working as designed, not a defect of the carve, and the parts are not carved again now (MarginalValueRule#6611)."}

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of violence (r136) left two things without a home. (1) Killing by a group's own rule: judicial and customary executions (and among foragers the collective killing of a dangerous member), the sacrifice of retainers and captives (Ur's royal tombs, Kerma, the Shang, the Aztec temples), and killings by police. It passes the tests once the frame is deliberate killing: necessary (the witch-hunts' 40,000 to 60,000 executions, Tudor and Qing justice, the Aztec sacrifices, the abolition of the death penalty in most countries since 1960 have no home), independent (it fell in Europe after 1750 on its own timetable) and universal (every society puts some of its members to death). It is not followed now for one reason only: the carve divides violent death as the parent measures it, homicide plus war (h.safety), and that measure leaves these deaths out, so a part opened under it would not be part of what its parent counts; widening h.safety is a change to an existing measure, which this pass leaves as it is. Political mass executions (the Great Terror, the Khmer Rouge's) are already counted under one-sided killing (h.war.one-sided.states), and policy famines under hunger. The measure that would follow the rest is named for the pass that widens h.safety: killing by a group's own rule, per 100,000 living people a year, sketched at perhaps 1 to 5 among foragers (Boehm and Wrangham on collective execution), higher in the first states with retainer and captive sacrifice, about 4 per 100,000 of the world's people from the Aztec sacrifices alone in the fifteenth century, a European peak about 1550 to 1650, and under 0.5 since 1950 (a few thousand executions a year, most in China and Iran, and some tens of thousands of police killings). The Events it would take are already in the model (the witch-hunts, the Sumerian city-states' and Kerma's sacrificed retainers, the French Revolution's executions). (2) Violence that does not kill (assault, rape, torture, the beating of wives and children) lies outside the carve's frame, which is violence as a cause of death, and no world measure reads it before victimization surveys of the late twentieth century; it is the frame's boundary, not a missing part (AbsenceEvidence#10a3: silence in older records is not its absence). MarginalValueRule#6611.

- What the carve is for: To follow the conditions every society lives within and draws on, so that climate swings, drowned coasts, vanished animals, the stores people dig up and the nutrients that feed their crops each have a home, and so that what people do to the Earth since farming and above all since 1850 can be read against what the Earth does on its own. How the parts make the whole work: The Earth as setting is carved into six parts: the air and the climate it holds, land and sea, the plant cover, the wild animals, the Earth's stores and, added now, the nitrogen cycle. The Earth's setting at any date is the joint state of its air, its seas and ice, its plants, its animals, its stores and the nutrient flows that let plants grow. The air and the orbit set the temperature (the parent's own measure), which moves the seas and the plant cover on slower clocks; plants and wild animals are what foragers live on and among; the stores are what toolmakers and then industry dig up; and the nitrogen people fix decides how much food the land can grow. For most of the span the setting changes on its own and humanity adapts; since farming, people clear the plants, kill the animals and, with legumes and paddy rice, add a little nitrogen; since 1850 they draw on the stores so fast that the air and the temperature follow, and since 1913 they fix more nitrogen than all the land's own microbes. Fresh water, aerosols and novel entities are not parts beside these but things already held in them. Each coupling is a seam between this part of History and humanity, recorded on the verdicts. {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

The air and the climate it holds (climate): part.
- What it covers: The composition of the atmosphere and the temperature and rainfall it sets; followed by carbon dioxide beside the parent's own measure, global temperature.
- Necessity pass: The glacial cycles (carbon dioxide from 180 to 280 parts per million), the Holocene's stable warmth and the rise to 425 since 1850 need a home; they set what grows and where people can live.
- Independence pass: Carbon dioxide and temperature move together in the glacial cycles, but each also moves apart: orbital forcing warms first at the terminations, eruptions such as Toba and Tambora cool for years without changing carbon dioxide, and the industrial rise in carbon dioxide ran decades ahead of the warming.
- Universality pass: Every date has an atmosphere and a climate.

Land and sea (land-and-sea): part.
- What it covers: The extent of land, ice and sea, the coastlines between them, and the water held on land; followed by global mean sea level and its six contributions.
- Necessity pass: Beringia, Sundaland, Sahul and Doggerland exposed and drowned, the coasts every early crossing followed, need a home.
- Independence pass: Sea level rose 120 metres after the glacial maximum over ten thousand years while temperature had settled; it changes on its own slow clock.
- Universality pass: Every date.

The plant cover (vegetation): part.
- What it covers: The living world's plants, followed by the share of land under forest in four climatic domains.
- Necessity pass: The spread of forest after the glacial, the green Sahara and its drying, and the clearing of forests by farmers need a home.
- Independence pass: Forest is cleared by people under an unchanged climate and returns where fields are abandoned, apart from carbon dioxide and sea level.
- Universality pass: Every date.

The wild animals (wild-animals): part.
- What it covers: The living world's wild animals, followed by the biomass of wild land mammals, with sea mammals and fish as parts.
- Necessity pass: The extinction of the megafauna, the slaughter of the bison and of Africa's herds, whaling and the industrial fisheries have no other home.
- Independence pass: The megafauna vanished from the Americas while forests spread; the bison were killed in fifteen years while the prairie stood.
- Universality pass: Every date has wild animals.

The Earth's stores (resources): part.
- What it covers: Stone, sand, clay, ores and fossil fuels laid down in the crust that people dig up; followed by how much of them people take each year.
- Necessity pass: Flint and ochre, copper and tin, iron, coal and concrete have no home without the stores they come from.
- Independence pass: The draw on the stores changes apart from climate and the living world; it is coupled to carbon dioxide through fossil fuels, a seam recorded here.
- Universality pass: Every society takes stone for tools and ochre for colour; the draw is tiny for foragers, a value of the measure.

The nitrogen cycle: nitrogen fixed by people (nutrient-cycles): part.
- What it covers: The flows of the nutrients that limit plant growth, followed by the reactive nitrogen people add to the land each year: fixed by sown legumes and paddy rice, by industrial ammonia synthesis from 1913 and by burning fuel, read against the land's own biological fixation of about 60 to 120 Tg a year. Phosphorus, mined from rock, is counted among the Earth's stores.
- Necessity pass: Industrial nitrogen fixation since 1913 feeds perhaps two fifths to a half of humanity (Smil) and has no home without it; nor do the legume rotations of Europe's agricultural revolution, the dead zones of coastal seas, or the planetary boundary for nitrogen, crossed in the 1960s.
- Independence pass: Nitrogen fixed by people rose tenfold between 1913 and 2010 while forest, wild animals and sea level moved little; it follows fertilizer and crops, not carbon or ice.
- Universality pass: Every date has a nitrogen cycle; people's addition is zero before farming and a value of the measure after.

- What it covers: Rivers, lakes, groundwater and rain.
- Necessity pass: The drying of the Sahara, the irrigation of Mesopotamia and the Aral Sea's loss need a home.
- Independence fail: It divides between parts already held: rain and its swings are climate; lakes, aquifers, soil water and reservoirs are the water held on land, a part of land and sea (h.sea.land-water); what people withdraw is a use, followed with provisioning and farmland.

- What it covers: Dust, soot, sulphate and the ozone layer.

- What it is: The Earth as humanity's setting: what the Earth supplies to and imposes on every human society.
- What the carve is for: To follow the conditions every society lives within and draws on, so that climate swings, drowned coasts, vanished animals, the stores people dig up and the nutrients that feed their crops each have a home, and so that what people do to the Earth since farming and above all since 1850 can be read against what the Earth does on its own. - The range it claims: Every date from 300,000 years ago to 2025, followed as global measures; the parent's own measure is global mean temperature against 1850 to 1900.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. The Earth as setting is a kind of The setting of a lifecycle: The Earth as setting is the setting of humanity's lifecycle: the air, seas, ice, plants, animals, stores and nutrient flows of one planet, set apart from the setting of a person's or a city's life, which is a place within it. Other kinds within it: The place of a person's life, The site of a city.

How the parts make the whole work: The Earth as setting is carved into six parts: the air and the climate it holds, land and sea, the plant cover, the wild animals, the Earth's stores and, added now, the nitrogen cycle. The Earth's setting at any date is the joint state of its air, its seas and ice, its plants, its animals, its stores and the nutrient flows that let plants grow. The air and the orbit set the temperature (the parent's own measure), which moves the seas and the plant cover on slower clocks; plants and wild animals are what foragers live on and among; the stores are what toolmakers and then industry dig up; and the nitrogen people fix decides how much food the land can grow. For most of the span the setting changes on its own and humanity adapts; since farming, people clear the plants, kill the animals and, with legumes and paddy rice, add a little nitrogen; since 1850 they draw on the stores so fast that the air and the temperature follow, and since 1913 they fix more nitrogen than all the land's own microbes. Fresh water, aerosols and novel entities are not parts beside these but things already held in them. Each coupling is a seam between this part of History and humanity, recorded on the verdicts. Breadth check answered: The carve of the wild animals (r327) left wild birds, arthropods and the other invertebrates, and the small fish of the ocean's twilight zone without a home. All three pass necessity and independence (island bird extinctions after human arrival, the moa and the dodo; the recent fall of farmland birds and the insect-decline debate; the mesopelagic fish untouched until lately), but none can yet carry a world measure across the span: wild bird biomass has world estimates only from about 1970 (Bar-On, Phillips and Milo give about 2 Mt C now; North America lost about 29% of its birds from 1970 to 2017 by Rosenberg and colleagues), insect biomass trends are local and disputed (Hallmann and colleagues against van Klink and colleagues), and twilight-zone fish are uncertain within a factor of ten now. A series from 300,000 years ago would be guesses about guesses, adding no turn the land mammals, sea mammals and fish already show: losses by island colonization and hunting, then by land use and industrial fishing. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611, AbsenceEvidence#10a3); reopen when a world bird series before 1970 or a checked insect trend is read, or when island extinctions are followed as a count of species lost.

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of humanity into ends and means (r103) left two things without a home, and both have one now, so the carve's completeness is answered by later carves rather than by carving it again. (1) The means of organized violence as a means rather than a toll: followed since r109 by force (h.means.force, people under arms per 1,000), a part of how people get it, and since r300 by its parts, the destructive power of weapons (h.means.force.arms, with nuclear warheads as a kind) and spending on force (h.means.force.spending). (2) The making of new knowledge: followed since r328 by discovery (h.understanding.discovery, people kept to make new knowledge per million), with its five parts by area since r347; it is filed under understanding, an end, because knowledge is sought for itself as well as for what it makes possible, and its use as a means (the research laboratory's inventions, war research) is a seam with provisioning and force, recorded on discovery's carve (r346). The carve of humanity itself stays as recorded (two parts, the ends and the means); no part is missing from it, and the twelve dimensions of the structure construction remain a rival carve of the same whole, the open choice this pass does not make.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"foundation","text":"The claim frame for carving How people get it (concept.humanity.means):
- What it is: How people get what matters to them: what a population does to secure the conditions of its members' lives.
- What the carve is for: To follow the means a population commands, so that farming, trade, cities, roads and ships, states, armies, the wealth people hold and the organizations of their faiths each have one home, and so that the means can be read against the ends they serve; the parent's own measure is world output. Carved again because the breadth check names this carve's open completeness: the first record (r108) left ideological organization as a means, the size of wealth held and the making of new knowledge without a home.
- The range it claims: Every human society from 300,000 years ago to 2025, followed as world measures.

The climb before the carve, nearest broader kind first:
1. How people get it is a kind of The means a population commands: Human means are learned and accumulated, held in techniques, institutions and things that outlast those who made them. Other kinds within it: The means an animal population commands: its range and its bodies, The means of an institution: its funds, staff and powers.

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"decision","text":"How people get it is carved into 8 parts: Provisioning, Exchange, Habitat, Connection, Politics, Force, Wealth held: years of output, Organized belief: people kept to serve a faith.

How the parts make the whole work: A population's means are the joint state of what it produces, how its goods pass, where it settles, how far and fast it reaches, how it decides and rules, what force it keeps, what wealth it holds and how its faiths are organized. World output, the parent's own measure, is what production yields once the other means have done their work: trade lets each place make what it makes best, cities and roads let work be divided further, states keep the peace and take a share, force defends or takes what the rest produce, the wealth held is the stock of land and capital production works with, and the organizations of faith bind people to act together beyond kin and state. The two parts added now move on clocks of their own: wealth held rose from a fraction of a year's output among foragers to five or six years in the agrarian empires, held near there into 1910, fell by half in the world wars and has climbed back since 1980; the people kept to serve a faith rose with the temple states to perhaps eight in every thousand in the medieval centuries, when monasteries and churches were among the largest owners of land, and have fallen for five centuries to under one and a half. Seams are recorded on the verdicts (wealth and its distribution under standing; organized belief and worship under meaning; discovery under understanding). Sema: ConceptualDecomposition#f1f4, MandatoryAbstraction#ac44, DecompositionGate#1b2d, RoutingSanityCheck#71bd, Synthesis#4f1f, ArchiveServingFrontier#2765.

Kinds, not parts (found only in some cases): Parties and movements of a secular creed (a kind of concept.humanity.means.devotion).

Frontier alternatives, kept with their verdicts for later evidence: Know-how (independence).

Routed elsewhere: The making of new knowledge to Discovery (h.understanding.discovery), under understanding, Work to Provisioning (h.food-work) and sustenance (h.toil).

upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Provisioning (provisioning): part.
- What it covers: Producing food, energy and things; followed by output per person.
- Necessity pass: Foraging, farming and industry, and output per person's long flat stretch and modern rise, need a home.
- Independence pass: Output per person rose in the industrial revolution without a matching change in trade's share or in states' reach, and states spread for millennia at flat output.
- Universality pass: Every society produces.

Exchange (exchange): part.
- What it covers: Passing goods between people beyond the household; followed by trade as a share of world output.
- Necessity pass: Long-distance trade, the first and second globalizations and their collapse in 1914 to 1945 need a home.
- Independence pass: Trade's share fell from 1914 to 1945 while output and cities kept growing.
- Universality pass: Every society exchanges, if only by sharing and gift.

Habitat (habitat): part.
- What it covers: Where and how densely people settle and what land they take; followed by the share living in towns and cities.
- Necessity pass: Sedentism, cities and urbanization need a home.
- Independence pass: The urban share stood near 10% for two thousand years while output and states grew.
- Universality pass: Every society settles somewhere, in camps at least.

Connection (connection): part.
- What it covers: Carrying people, goods and word across space; followed by the fastest regular passenger speed.
- Necessity pass: Horses, ships, railways, aircraft, the telegraph and the internet need a home.
- Independence pass: The telegraph and the jet changed connection apart from what was traded and how people were governed.
- Universality pass: Every society moves people, goods and word, on foot and by voice at least.

Politics (politics): part.
- What it covers: Deciding and acting together, and ruling; followed by the share of people living under a state.
- Necessity pass: States, empires and their reach need a home.
- Independence pass: States spread across Africa and the Americas apart from output per person and trade.
- Universality pass: Every society decides together, bands included; living under no state is a value of the measure.

Force (force): part.
- What it covers: The means of organized violence a population keeps; followed by people under arms per 1,000, with arms and spending as parts.
- Necessity pass: Military history has no home without it: mass armies, the military revolution, the levee en masse, the world wars' mobilizations and the demobilization after the Cold War.
- Independence pass: Armies grow and shrink apart from who rules and how much is produced: mobilization quadrupled the share under arms in each world war under unchanged regimes.
- Universality pass: Every society meets the possibility of violence from outsiders; where no one is kept under arms, zero is a value of the measure.

Wealth held: years of output (wealth): part.
- What it covers: The stock of land, livestock, buildings, tools, machines and the financial claims on them that a population owns, net of its debts to itself, measured against what it produces in a year: the wealth-to-output ratio. Who holds it is followed under standing (h.standing.wealth).
- Necessity pass: Property in land and herds, the accumulation of capital, its destruction in the world wars and its return since 1980 (Piketty's U-curve) have no home without it: output is a flow, and nothing else follows the stock behind it.
- Independence pass: The ratio fell by half between 1910 and 1950 while output per person kept rising, and rose again after 1980 while growth slowed; agrarian societies held five years and more of output in land while their output per person stood still. Its distribution moves apart again: the richest tenth's share fell after 1914 with the ratio but rose after 1980 faster than it.
- Universality pass: Every society holds things, a forager band its tools, ornaments, shelters and canoes; the measure is small for foragers, a value of it, not its absence.

Organized belief: people kept to serve a faith (devotion): part.
- What it covers: The organizations through which a shared faith makes people act together (temples, churches, monastic orders, the ulama, the sangha), followed by the people they keep: priests, monks, nuns, temple and church staff, imams and teachers of a faith whose main work it is, per 1,000 living people. The share taking part in worship is followed as an end, under meaning (h.meaning).
- Necessity pass: Mann's ideological power, the capacity of a faith's organizations to make people act together, had a home only as an end (worship): the temple households of Sumer and Egypt, the Buddhist sangha and the Christian monasteries, the medieval Church that held a quarter of Europe's land, the Reformation's dissolutions, the Jesuits' missions and the communist states' closing of temples have no home as a means without it.
- Independence pass: It moves apart from politics and force: the monasteries grew in China and Europe as states fragmented (400 to 800); the Reformation cut Protestant Europe's clergy while its states grew; the share of people kept for faiths fell for two centuries while the share taking part in worship fell far less, and the communist states cut it to near nothing in the 1960s while their armies grew.
- Universality pass: Every society has a sacred and someone who tends it; where no one is kept for it, as among foragers whose shamans also hunt and gather, zero is a value of the measure.

Parties and movements of a secular creed (parties): a kind of devotion.
- What it covers: Mass parties, revolutionary movements and their full-time cadres.
- Necessity pass: The communist and fascist parties of the twentieth century organized belief on the scale of churches.
- Independence pass: They grew as churches were closed.
- Universality fail: Modern: none before the nineteenth century. A kind of organized belief, not counted in its measure, which follows faiths.

Know-how (know-how): frontier.
- What it covers: The techniques a population commands.
- Necessity pass: Invention drives most of the means.
- Independence fail: A technique is the means by which another part is realized (ploughs in provisioning, ships in connection, guns in force), as the structure construction found when it rejected technology as a dimension.
- Universality pass: Every society.

The making of new knowledge (discovery): routed to Discovery (h.understanding.discovery), under understanding.
- What it covers: Research, scholarship and invention as a means.
- Necessity pass: The research university and the industrial laboratory make new means.
- Independence fail: Already followed as discovery (h.understanding.discovery), filed under understanding because knowledge is sought for itself; its use as a means is a seam, not a second home.
- Universality pass: Defined at every date.

Work (work): routed to Provisioning (h.food-work) and sustenance (h.toil).
- What it covers: How labour is divided, directed and how much of life it takes.
- Necessity pass: Labour history needs a home.
- Independence fail: Who works at getting food is followed under provisioning (h.food-work) and how long and under whom people work under sustenance (h.toil and its parts); a part here would hold both twice.
- Universality pass: Every society.

Completeness pass: Against Michael Mann's four sources of social power, a list made for another purpose, every source now has a home among the means: ideological power in organized belief, economic power in provisioning, exchange and wealth held, military power in force, political power in politics. Against the structure construction's twelve dimensions, the means' dimensions (provisioning, exchange, wealth, habitat, connection, politics, security) have homes, and knowledge's making is routed to discovery. Checked against Mann, The Sources of Social Power (1986), as recalled, and structure/history-tree.mjs. Checked against Michael Mann's IEMP model of the sources of social power (The Sources of Social Power, 1986), as recalled; the structure construction's twelve dimensions upsertNodes.title: The four tests for the carve of How people get it

revision.reason: Rebind to r423 (through r419 to r422): wealth held and organized belief opened under how people get it with values from 300,000 years ago to 2025 (r419 to r422), and 15 Events linked to them (r423).

Breadth check answered: The carve of force (r300) left two things without a home. (1) How fighters are raised and held (warrior bands and kin, levies and militias, mercenaries and standing professionals, conscripts, volunteers) is not a part beside people under arms, arms and spending but a division of the people under arms themselves: categories competing for one pool, which belong in a Cut series on the fighters, read at every block of the time schedule, not in a number. It is named for a pass that records series: 'How do the world's people under arms divide by how they were raised?', answers kin and warrior bands, levies and militias, paid professionals and mercenaries, conscripts, volunteers; expected to be nearly all warrior bands before states, levies and militias in the agrarian empires with professional cores (Rome's legions, the Ottoman janissaries), conscripts from the levee en masse of 1793 to the 1970s, and volunteers again in most rich states since. (2) Protection (walls, forts, armour) fails universality as a part: many bands built no defences, so it is a kind of force found where people are settled; and no world series of fortification can be stated. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611).
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: How fighters are raised, and the works that protect against attack is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of habitat (r325) left built-up land and public works (the area under buildings, streets and works, and the water, sewer and power networks of settlements) without a home. Its independence passes (urban densities have fallen for two centuries, so built land grows apart from the urban share, as Angel's Planet of Cities shows), but before satellite mapping from 1975 the world's built-up area is reconstructed from urban population times assumed densities (HYDE's built-up layer is made that way), so a series before 1975 would restate the urban share and the largest city rather than add a reading of its own; and mobile foragers build almost nothing that lasts, which leaves its universality uncertain. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611, MetricReading#56a9: a measure derived from another is not a second reading of the world). Reopen when an independent reconstruction of built area before 1975 is checked (archaeological site areas for the ancient cities, cadastral maps for the early modern), or when sanitation and water supply are followed as shares of people served, which do have readings from about 1850.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Built-up land and public works is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of politics (r291) left law and justice and the form of rule without a home. (1) The form of rule (who rules and how they are chosen: no state, chiefly or royal rule, oligarchic and aristocratic republics, party states, democracies, rule from overseas) passes necessity and independence, but its categories compete for one pool, the world's people, so it belongs in a Cut series, not a number; it is the most rewarding opening the breadth check has left, and is named for the next pass: 'How do the world's living people divide by the kind of highest authority they live under?', answers no state, monarchy or chiefly rule over a state, non-elected republic or oligarchy, party or military state, electoral democracy, colonial rule from overseas, read at every block of the time schedule with readings nested coarse to fine. Its long course is already constrained by measures the account holds: the share under no state is the complement of h.politics, colonial rule is h.colonial, and democracies are h.voice, so the series must agree with them. It is not recorded now because a nested series over all four levels of the schedule, consistent with three existing measures, is a pass's work in itself. (2) Law and justice (codes, courts, the rule of law) has a world reading only from 1789 (V-Dem's rule of law index); before that a share living under written law would restate the share living under a state. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611).
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Law and justice, and the form of rule is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of what matters to people (r107) left two of Nussbaum's capabilities without a home of their own. (1) Holding property on an equal basis with others: the account now follows the wealth people hold as a means (h.means.wealth, opened at r419) and who holds it under standing (h.standing.wealth, the richest tenth's share), so what the capability asks, how equally assets are held, is read by the second; a separate end would count it twice. (2) Concern for other species and the natural world: a real end in many traditions, but no world measure of it can be stated that is not a measure of the living world itself (forest, the wild animals, sea mammals, fish) or of a modern practice (protected areas, about 17% of land by 2020, with readings only from about 1960). Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611); reopen if the share of land under protection is opened as a measure of the living world's care, with the sacred groves and hunting reserves of earlier centuries as its older kinds. (Recorded again on the main line: an identical answer was first registered in parallel from the same parent as the politics answer, on a side branch, model 41ffd0d2, which no graph follows.)
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Holding property, and living with other species is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of staying alive and well (r121) left the years lived in ill health and disability, and mental health, without a home. Both pass necessity and independence, but neither has a world reading before the Global Burden of Disease study's series from 1990 (healthy life expectancy, disability-adjusted life years, the burden of depression and anxiety); before that, a value would be life expectancy times a guessed fraction, a restatement of survival rather than a reading of ill health. The body's condition in earlier centuries is read through stature (h.health) and the causes of death, which carry what can be said. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611, AbsenceEvidence#10a3: that the past left few records of suffering is no evidence of its absence). Reopen if healthy life expectancy is opened from 1990 with a sketched course before it bounded by stature and morbidity studies of past populations (skeletal lesions, enamel defects), which bioarchaeology can supply.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Years lived in ill health, and mental health is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of belonging (r213) left voluntary associations (guilds, confraternities, clubs, unions, parties, foragers' sodalities and age sets) without a home. They pass necessity and independence (they grow as kin groups dissolve), but no world measure of membership can be read back before the twentieth century; the one candidate with readings, union membership as a share of workers (from about 1880 in the industrial countries, the ILO's from about 1950), was named by the society group's breadth answer (r390) and would sit under work for an employer, not belonging. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611); reopen with that union series, or when guild and confraternity membership in early modern European and Chinese cities is read as a share of townspeople.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Voluntary associations is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of meaning (r127) left two of Smart's dimensions of religion without a measured home. (1) The institutional dimension (full-time religious specialists and the bodies that keep them: temples, churches, the sangha, the ulama) was kept as a frontier part 'worth opening if a series of full-time religious specialists per 1,000 people can be read'. It is now followed by organized belief (h.means.devotion), opened at r419 as a part of how people get it, the counterpart of force's people under arms (Mann's ideological power), with values from 300,000 years ago to 2025 and linked to the first monastic orders, Christian monasticism, Buddhism's spread east, the Tang's suppression, Pagan and the Theravada monasteries, the Reformation, the French and Russian revolutions and the communist suppressions; meaning keeps the end, the share taking part in worship, and the seam between them is recorded on both carves. (2) The experience of the sacred (trance, visions, mystical states, prayer felt as answered) still has no world measure across the span, since surveys of religious experience begin in the twentieth century; it stays a frontier alternative of meaning's carve.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Religious specialists and institutions, and the experience of the sacred is followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of beauty and play (r363) left three things without a measured home. (1) The forms that leave no lasting trace before writing (music, dance, story) are in every population but no world measure can read them across the span; their makers, once kept, are counted among the arts' makers (now divided by who keeps them, r397), and their audiences, once copied, in mass media. (2) What people spend on feasts, festivals and entertainment has household-budget readings only from about 1900. (3) Games and sport: their paid players are counted among the arts' makers (markets, since the codification of football and rugby), the hours played are leisure, and organized contests with fixed rules and audiences are a kind many populations lack. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611, AbsenceEvidence#10a3); reopen if festival and holy days a year are opened as a count beside leisure hours, which has readings for the medieval calendars and the Protestant cuts in them.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Forms without a lasting trace, spending on play, games and sport is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of standing (r150) left women's standing against men and esteem (how people feel they stand) without a measured home. Women's standing passes necessity and independence, but no world measure of it reaches back before the 1990s (the gender development and inequality indices) or, for law, before V-Dem's women's civil liberties index from 1789; parts of it are already read elsewhere (women's vote under voice, women's age at marriage, plural unions). Esteem is a reading of persons with no world series at all. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611). The candidate most worth opening is women's legal standing, the share of the world's women living where married women can own property and sue in their own name, which has a clear course (coverture's laws repealed from 1839 to the 1970s, Islamic and customary law's own rules) and Events in the account (the women's vote, Seneca Falls); it would sit under freedom beside voice.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Women's standing, and esteem is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of sustenance and comfort (r129) left clothing and household goods without a measured home. Clothing: a world series of textile fibre per person exists from about 1900; before that, cotton's spread and the industrial revolution's cheap cloth are well told but would be sketched as one number per person with bands wider than the change, and its comfort is mostly warmth, which energy already carries. Household goods: the consumer and industrious revolutions are read in probate inventories and household surveys for some places and times only. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611); reopen if fibre per person is opened from 1900 with its earlier course bounded by Europe's and China's textile output (Riello, Broadberry), which would also give the cotton revolution's Events (Lancashire, the cotton gin, India's handloom collapse) a measure to move.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Clothing and household goods is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The carve of understanding (r384) left knowledge held in store (books, archives, libraries: knowledge kept outside heads) as a frontier part, for universality uncertain. It passes necessity and independence (book production rose apart from literacy), but a world series of books or titles per person can be read only from about 1450 in Europe (Buringh and van Zanden) and for Song and later China in pieces; before printing, manuscripts and tablets are counted only for a few libraries; and after 2000 books are a falling share of what is stored, so one measure would change its meaning midway (MetricReading#56a9: one definition must hold over the series). Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611). The candidate, if opened, is new titles printed per million people a year from 1450, with Europe's and China's series summed and the rest of the world sketched; Printing in East Asia and printing with movable type in Europe, already Events of the account, would name it.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: Knowledge held in store is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The stopped pass linked the exchange group's other Events (r377). One remains: mobile money in Africa, from M-Pesa in 2007. It changes how payments move and who can make them (Kenya's households reached by a phone-based account, and the remittances sent home that way), which no measure of the account follows: trade between peoples (h.exchange) does not see it, the share online (h.internet) does not count the feature phones it runs on, and its effect on extreme poverty, about 2% of Kenyan households by Suri and Jack's study, does not show at world scale. Not followed now (MarginalValueRule#6611). The measure that would follow it is the share of the world's adults with an account at a bank or a mobile-money provider (the World Bank's Findex, from 2011: about half then, three quarters by 2021), which would also take the savings banks and credit societies of earlier centuries as its older kinds.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: What the last Event of exchange changes: mobile money is not followed

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The one Event within Africa's Middle Stone Age that named no process, Still Bay and Howiesons Poort (about 77,000 to 59,000 years ago), now observes image and ornament (h.play.images, r436): its engraved ochre and ostrich eggshell and shell beads show southern African populations making lasting art, and its toolkits' fading and return is the flicker that measure's bands hold (CumulativeCulture#4f93). Its hafted microliths and heat treatment change technique, which the account follows only through what techniques do (the structure construction's rejection of technology as a dimension), so no further link is made.
Record 1 understanding note held by claude.

upsertNodes.title: Breadth check: What Still Bay and Howiesons Poort change is linked

revision.reason: Breadth check answered: The one Event within the agrarian age that named no process, the era of the first farmers (9700 to 3500 BCE), now names farmland (h.farmland), the share living by foraging (h.foraging), the share without a fixed dwelling (h.habitat.mobile) and nitrogen fixed by people (h.earth.nitrogen) (r438): the world-scale changes its description names, as farming peoples spread and absorb foragers. Its finer Events (each centre of domestication, Catalhoyuk, the first copper) already carry their own links.

A conditioned division would need the parent recorded as a series, which it is not (it was registered as a single Cut on ev.columbian-exchange), and its shares would be guesses inside a guess; not recorded now (MarginalValueRule#6611). Reopen when the parent is recorded as a series, or when the epidemics are read decade by decade for central Mexico and the Andes, where the counts of tributaries allow it.

{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Renouncers in communities: monks, nuns and ascetic orders (renouncers): a kind of concept.humanity.means.devotion.
- What it covers: People kept to live a life given to a faith, apart from family and work: the Buddhist and Jain sangha, Christian monks, nuns and friars, Daoist monastics.
- Necessity pass: Most of devotion's falls are theirs: the Huichang suppression of 845, the Reformation's dissolutions, the secularizations from 1789, China after 1950 and Tibet after 1959, the Cultural Revolution. Without them the whole could not hold its largest moves.
- Independence pass: They can be dissolved without the clergy who serve lay people changing: England dissolved its monasteries in 1536 to 1540 and kept its parish clergy.
- Universality fail: None before the sramana orders about 500 BCE; none by design in Islam, Judaism, Zoroastrianism or the Protestant churches; none in the temple states of Sumer and Egypt. Found in some cases only, so a kind of devotion, not a part.

Officiants serving lay people (officiants): frontier.
- What it covers: People kept to perform rites, teach and judge for lay believers: priests, pastors, imams and ulama, rabbis, Brahmin temple and household priests.
- Necessity pass: Every faith that keeps anyone keeps officiants; without them the whole would lose most of its people in most eras.
- Independence pass: Their numbers follow congregations and endowments, not the fate of monasteries.
- Universality pass: Every society that keeps people for a faith keeps officiants, from Eridu's temple to today's pastors.

By tradition: Buddhist, Christian, Muslim, Hindu and other specialists (traditions): frontier.
- What it covers: The same people divided by the faith they serve.
- Necessity pass: The traditions keep very different numbers per believer: a Theravada village keeps several monks, a Sunni congregation one imam.
- Independence pass: One tradition's clergy can be suppressed while another's grow.
- Universality fail: Each tradition exists only from its founding and only where it spread; the account already follows the believers of each in the tradition shares (h.meaning.tradition).

By what keeps them: endowments, offerings and tithes, the state's pay (keep): dropped.
- What it covers: The same people divided by what feeds them: temple and monastic estates and waqf, gifts and tithes, salaries from rulers.
- Necessity uncertain: The source of keep explains why dissolutions were possible (endowed land can be seized), but this is a division of income, not of people.
- Independence fail: One priest is often kept by all three at once: a benefice's land, fees for rites and a royal stipend.
- Universality pass: Some keep of one of these kinds is found wherever people are kept for a faith.

Completeness uncertain: Renouncers and officiants together would hold every case routed, but renouncers fail universality, so the only part that passes is the officiants, which alone would be the whole less one kind, not a division. The division by tradition is a Cut over faiths, possible but resting on today's counts and a few earlier ones. upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Courts: rulers and their households (courts): frontier.
- What it covers: Makers kept in rulers' palaces and ateliers: the Song painting academy, the Mughal kitabkhana, the Ottoman nakkashane, Versailles.
- Necessity pass: The courts carry the part's peaks: the ateliers of the Mughals, Safavids, Ottomans and Ming about 1600, Europe's courts.
- Independence fail: Under sacral kingship court and temple are one keeper: Egypt's king is the gods' high priest and the temple and palace workshops one economy; so too the Inca, the Classic Maya and Angkor. The line between courts and temples cannot be drawn there.
- Universality fail: Absent where there are no rulers with households: the chiefdoms' and early temples' keepers, the Greek poleis' citizen patrons.

Temples, monasteries and churches (temples): frontier.
- What it covers: Makers kept by religious bodies: temple sculptors and dancers, monastic scribes and illuminators, cathedral choirs.
- Necessity pass: Much of the lasting art of the agrarian age was made for temples and churches.
- Independence fail: As for courts: under sacral kingship the temple's keep is the ruler's; and a monk who illuminates manuscripts is counted already among the people kept to serve a faith (h.means.devotion), so the two measures would overlap.
- Universality fail: Absent where faiths keep no makers: Islam's mosques keep few figurative artists, and the Song literati painted outside temples.

Nobles, merchants and private households (private): frontier.
- What it covers: Makers kept by rich households that are not rulers: Roman senators' households, the Medici and Venetian families, Japan's daimyo and merchants, today's private patrons and foundations.
- Necessity pass: Private patronage carries much of Renaissance and Edo art.
- Independence uncertain: The same maker often served court, church and family in turn (Michelangelo for popes and Medici), and a noble household is often part of a court.
- Universality fail: Absent in the first temple states, where all keep runs through palace and temple.

Completeness uncertain: Courts, temples and private households together would hold every routed case, but no candidate passes universality and courts and temples are not independent under sacral kingship, so no set of parts divides the whole. upsertNodes.text:
{"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"assessment","text":"Each candidate tested against the frame for necessity, independence and universality, then the parts together for completeness.

Of its own subjects (own): frontier.
- What it covers: People a state kills among those it rules as its own: the Great Terror, the Khmer Rouge's killings, Argentina's disappeared.
- Necessity pass: Much of the twentieth century's killing by states was of their own subjects.
- Independence fail: The line between subjects and others moves with conquest and annexation: the Holocaust killed German Jews and the Jews of occupied Poland in the same camps by the same orders; Leopold's Congo Free State killed people it ruled as conquered.
- Universality pass: Every state has killed some of its own subjects.

Of people under conquest, occupation or enemy rule (others): frontier.
- What it covers: People a state kills among those it conquers, occupies or fights: the sack of cities, the conquests of the Americas, Nanjing 1937.
- Necessity pass: Conquest's massacres carry the part's spikes before 1900.
- Independence fail: As above: the conquered become subjects, and a killing begun as reprisal against occupied people continues as the persecution of subjects.
- Universality pass: Every state that has conquered has killed some of the conquered.

By intent: genocide, politicide, reprisal and sack (intent): frontier.
- What it covers: The same deaths divided by what the killing was for: to destroy a group, to destroy political opponents, to punish or terrorize in war.
- Necessity pass: The intents differ in how they end: genocides end with the killers' defeat, reprisals with the war.
